So I actually have probably another 20-30 hours on this game. I had "downloaded" it previously, but I liked it so much I figured I should buy it to show my support.
This is one of my favorite games. If you like roguelikes, but still want a bit of progression, this game is for you. Sometimes, even if you die really quick, you were able to get enough gold to buy an upgrade to your manor, that made those 5 minutes worth it. This compared to traditional roguelikes where you can spend a half hour and die, and you pretty much just wasted that half hour.
Because of this system, it does take awhile to get going. Until you get the skills, and some basic upgrades, you will be dieing really easily. I'm now at the point where just about every playthough I'm able to buy one or two upgrades.
My only real complaint about this game is the difficulty scale. This game has four areas, each one harder than the previous. I find the jump in the scaling a bit extreme. Where I can stomp through the first area, the second I'm at par with, and the third I get slaughtered. So right now I'm just grinding away until I can get stronger.
All in all, I highly recommend this game. I also recommend using a controller, makes the game much simpler. The controls are fluid, the graphics get the job done, and there is a basic enough storyline to keep you interested as you rip through hundreds of enemies in your hundreds of lives.

My experience:
I loaded up the game and - after fiddling with the settings to make it run even semi-playably - decided to head out and find some game. Literally one minute after leaving the cottage I heard the warning call of a bear. I looked at the handy audio direction indicator and there the bear was, casually strolling at me. WTF?? I decided to take a shot at it. The bear reacted by taking a few running steps and then getting stuck on an invisible wall. I shot at it again, and again it took a few steps and stopped. This time it turned to face me head on and stare me with its big, quizzical eyes, as if it was hoping me to end its buggy virtual existence. I did.
Now, in the original theHunter, running around and shooting your gun tended to have the side effect of making you unable to see a single hair of an animal for the next ~30 minutes. Not the case with this game, it seems! Just as I had finished slaughtering the poor Pooh, I SAW A BLACKTAIL DEER LOOKING AT ME, COMPLETELY PLACID. AND HEARD ANOTHER BEAR. What is this? Russian oligarch hunting simulator with tame animals tied down for you to shoot at on your private ranch?
Thanks for turning the only somewhat respectable hunting simulator in the world into a dumbed-down shooting gallery for the Adderall generation. A bold move, I would say, as the niche appeal of the original game was the only thing keeping it afloat. Let's see how it pays off.
EDIT: It is entirely possible the game was bugged and/or the game makes sure you see an animal the first time you play the missions. Or I just got extremely lucky. However, I wanted to keep my playtime short to keep my eligibility for the refund program, after seeing the glitches and framerate issues. I'm open to trying this game again at a later date - but at this time I cannot recommend it.

Serenely relaxing and ridiculously enthralling - as unlikely as it seems, you have to try it to believe it. An incredibly surprising success.
Euro Truck Simulator 2 (aka ETS2) is
premier truck driving simulator game available on Steam. Very few games (actually, are there even any?) rival its amazing depth. Its Czech developer SCS Games is well-known for their truck simulator games, and securing the licenses of all the trucks you see in the game is no easy feat.
You play as a trucker, delivering various loads of cargo from city to city. Journeys can be very long or very short, depending on where you start from and where you end. In addition to the whole driving aspect, you're also in charge of running a truck delivery company (it starts out with the grand employee total of 1 - yourself, but then expands as you hire more workers and buy more trucks).
For the most part, the simulations in this game are very accurate. Trucks feel like a joy to drive (acceleration when the truck is transporting a heavy load is terrible, as it should be). Your employees also take jobs lasting several hours and you are credited the money (in-game) when you are done. If you have the money (real-life) to spare, for increased realism you can use a physical steering wheel controller and TrackIR so you can realistically drive the truck and look around.
Although there is an amazing degree of realism in the truck models and world textures, there does not seem to be
(I stress "as much" here because there is a certain amount...just not as much) care put into the menus. Compared to the rest of the game they feel comparatively close to a mere afterthought. Consider, however, that this is but a merely minor nitpick of mine, as you won't actually be spending most of the game looking at the menus, but rather driving.
A slightly more frustrating flaw detailed here is one that is very likely to spike blood pressures. As much as I want to be nice about it, because this is a game I really like, I'm going to go all out here and say: ♥♥♥♥ the AI drivers with a force of a thousand suns. They are among the most suicidal and idiotic computer AI I've had the misfortune of playing with. They refuse to give you the right of way, they refuse to stop while you're turning out (and cause some much unneeded fines/damage), they are literally douches in general. Come to think about it, isn't that a sadly accurate simulation of most drivers nowadays?
The good news is, you can disable the AI by playing on a multiplayer server. You have to download this
client. Do note that you
need to downgrade your game version in order to run this - thankfully, older ETS2 game versions are preserved as "betas" in Steam for that purpose. The only downside is that you aren't allowed to auto-park your truck on these servers, and I can tell you this first-hand, parking is HARD.
Time to end off with a few funny anecdotes: This is actually quite a fun game to stream gameplay of, both for the streamer and for the viewer. Especially when the streamer reads chat while driving, gets distracted and goes pinball trucking off the road rails and/or trees!
Another fun thing to do, if the streamer hasn't changed default controls, is to ask him to use camera mode 8. If you have this game, you'll know what it does. Then see how long he goes without crashing. HAHA!
Game has been bundled a few times. The most recent bundle, as far as I know, did not contain any DLC. Try to wait for the
to hit a sale.
As far as DLC recommendations go, I'd recommend as bare minimum the High Power Cargo Pack and the Going East expansions. The Scandinavia expansion seems great too (note that I don't actually have it at this point though).

I first heard of Undertale, much after the fact and much after the initial flood of lets plays concluded, I looked it up on Steam, bought the game and the soundtrack at the same time (I think it was on sale), and started as soon as I could, somehow avoiding the spoilers after being ignorant to this game's existence for somewhere between four and six months.
I played through it my way, trying to be nice but fighting when I felt I had to. Didn't look anything up. Didn't cheat. Didn't spoil. Without going into too much detail, it was probably the best experience I've had with a narrative-driven game in quite some time, and I feel lucky as hell that I got a chance to enjoy it on my own merit without "pacifism pressure". Honestly, at the time, it felt like a truly great game, and once I beat the Pacifist run, I started to look deeper, learned how to do Genocide, got impatient at Hotland and didn't return until my brother begged me to download the game for him to go through. Sadly, I couldn't enjoy the Genocide ending as much, partly because with the game's designed, I don't think I'm *supposed* to enjoy it, and partly because I had waited so long that I kinda had a clue as to what would happen.
Overall, at the time, I would've said the game was at least 9.5 out of 10, especially once I started to hear about the game's hidden depths, details often overlooked upon first glance, and excluded/extremely rare content
. However, as I started to look further into the fandom and as I heard about it, it started to wear on that people take this game way too seriously or way too... strangely. Mass hatred towards people who "play the game wrong", quoting things with no contextual parallels (determination, bad times and esp. dunked on, goatmom, hOI, the OST), and ... "Undertail"... sorry, but seeing "goatmom" in lingerie, and so soon after the Pacifist ending... no. On top of that, oversaturation of the game's content can make it tiring to experience the same content over and over. This is especially present in people in early 2017 claiming the game is "dead", that there is nothing else to find, or that the game wasn't as good as they initially thought. Yeah, after some time, your initial feelings towards a story-focused game are going to fade over time, but the fact that there are entire YouTube channels with 6 digit fanbases *really* ages the game quicker. And yeah, I'll admit, in retrospect, some elements of the game lose their effect after the first experience.
It's like an addict chasing their first and most intense high with every reload.
Yet, despite the extreme oversaturation and questionable fan content (and please don't get me wrong, there is some great content, but it's safe to say that the crap outnumbers the good stuff 2:1), I still believe this game is a 9.5, at least for me. Nothing's really tainted my initial enjoyment, and while the fandom can be frequently cringy, I do believe that, if you're lucky enough to get a chance to enjoy the game the way it's meant to be enjoyed (which, itself, is up for debate. I mean to say "enjoy it for yourself" and "untainted and unspoiled"), you're gonna have a very good time with some very real feels. Sorry for writing such a long review, I mostly just wanted to get my two cents out. PS: Why do people think this game is monumental? Morality-driven narratives is not a new concept, several games did it before, especially thinking of Catherine, Mass Effect, surely some others. The concept of being nice to "monsters" is also by far not new. While specifically bullethell might be new to the genre of RPGs, several RPGs use "unusual" turn-based combat systems before, never mind games beyond RPGs. Sorry, for real now, this isn't too organized but I just want to dump my thoughts out.

Prison Architect Review
Probably the best early-access game ever to hit Steam. Prison Architect is a creative sandbox game in which you build and manage a prison. The addictive concept, depth and easy to use interface makes this one of the most intriguing and enjoyable games I have played in a long time.
The top-down presentation is simple yet superb. The user-friendly interface makes navigation simple and easy to use. There is quite a lot of stuff to do in terms of construction and designing so having such a well-designed layout of functions is crucial to this games brilliance. The strategic depth here is also incredible and the way you design your prison and how you manage prisoners happiness can be huge factors to your overall success.
The bigger your prison becomes; the tougher it is to manage. Suddenly you have maximum security prisoners at your door and it's up to you to expand and enhance your prison to accommodate the influx whilst keeping people including staff and fellow inmates happy and safe. There is a considerable challenge here particularly when you grow your prison and the population. The level of depth in the design of your prison along with the management strategy aspect is simply staggering.
Overall, Prison Architect is an amazing game even at alpha stage. It's polished and incredibly well designed in all areas. The developers have done an amazing job so far and this game will only grow further in months to come.

It's between Borderlands 2 and Elite (C64) for my favorite game of all time.
The characters are well balanced compared to other games of the same age and all of the DLCs add real variety to the game.
It is quite easy to spend 100+ hours to play one character through from Normal, True and Ultimate modes playing all quests, add to that the Digistruct peak DLC and you have 80 levels and the ability to reset Ultimate Vault hunter mode on completion if you wish to.
All the DLCs are available for each playthrough and can range from about 20 hours to as little as 2 hrs for some of the Headhunter pack DLCs.
As you play a new character through each quest, the level of difficulty for each enemy type increases slowly, which is offset by list of challenges contributing to a Badass score feeding buffs.

The scaling is better than most games I've played once you get used to the combinations of weapons and elementals needed to do the most damage, and the location of critical hit points for the more powerful enemy types.
Loot is mostly from a random drop mechanism so the more side quests you do, the more enemy you kill, the more chance you have to get some of the more unusual and rare gear. Gear can be passed down to your next character if needed but only 4 pieces at a time which becomes tedious.
Multiplayer is great fun and the only way to defeat some of the DLC bosses at higher levels.
The only real annoyances are not having the ability to start a character in TVHM (True Vault Hunter Mode) or UVHM without having to play through Normal mode first, and a very small inventory compared to the variety of loot available or needed for specific quests as the difficulty increases.
Overall a great game, and if you are ever laid up for an extended period of time, a damn good time waster.

This game is like crack for folks that love to optimize and tweak things. There's 6 characters, and each has a different play-style, and even sub-play styles (you can have 2 of the same character, but they play differently depending on the skills they chose).
As you build your character(s) you can adjust points and try various things. You can collect loot and then find ways to synergize it with specific skills. Each character plays a bit differently, and you can get hooked finding ways to make each one work for your play style(s). Some take a while, but ultimately you find some level when the character "clicks" with you, and you go "a ha! now I'm having fun playing this one!"
Unfortunately, as entertaining as the campaign is, it gets boring running it 18 times (6 characters x 3 difficulty play-throughs). And to max your character you must play-through each difficulty, since they drastically cut down the amount of xp you earn once you top a certain level on difficulties (eg: after level 30 on first play-through & after 50 on second).
Third play-through forces you to use the "slag" mechanic to cover enemies in goop to increase damage from other elements (fire, shock, acid, etc). This will either intrigue you or drive you nuts. The amount of folks that drop-off after the second play-through is drastic via co-op.
I was a bit disappointed that the GOTY edition didn't include everything (had to buy the 2nd ultimate upgrade pack and headhunter packs separately). But, look at the time I've spent playing this thing. I think I've gotten my money's worth. Plus, I popped the extra cash for the headhunter packs and the 2nd upgrade pack. I enjoyed the game, and I felt it was worth it.
My main issue is that while early on the game is about skill min/max'ing, late / end-game is all about loot farming. You can only min/max your skills so much. Eventually in third play-through the enemies are so difficult you need really great gear to get you by. So, it becomes a farm-fest. And everyone's almost always goes for the same gear. Doesn't matter what character you have, almost all of them have an exclusive set of "leet gear" to farm for (sometimes the same gear amongst characters).
There's already less folks playing in third play-through due to slag mechanic being annoying. Then the aging game has a drop-off of players (obviously). But, late-game / end-game co-op (eg: level 65+) is pretty much just folks standing around duplicating their ultra-leet gear to each other (using a glitch) or farming raid bosses for gear. Essentially it just becomes a grind simluator. And it's BORING.
It's like playing a F2P game that starts skill-based then you realize at some point it's pay-to-win. This game starts skill-based (yours and your characters), but at the end it's all about what gear you can find / farm / dupe / cheat-make / whatever.
Likewise, when you finally get your character to ultra bad-a** level 72 with some good gear ... there's no challenges left. You're all decked out, and that's it. You can run the Digistruct Peak DLC multiple times to achieve "overpower" (OP) levels and more gear. But... that's pretty much it. So, it gets massively boring late-game. You've spent so much time gearing up, levelling up... and all for naught.
Also, playing the game feels like playing a huge spreadsheet. You realize that each level just levels up enemies and guns and everything else... but there's just the ever-so-slightest skew to make it a tiny, fraction more challenging and in the bad guys' favor. As you hit high levels you can't help but feel that levelling up is just an artificial way of making you feel like you're progressing some how when all it really does is just make the enemies harder and give you another skill point to allocate to something (hopefully) useful.
In the end, the enemies are bullet-sponges, ridiculously challenging, and your skills seem near-ineffectual sometimes... and that's when the loot farming / grinding kicks in. Notice that youtube videos showing how to defeat certain bosses "easily" always have the guy showing off all the legendary loot he has. That legendary loot took days if not weeks or months to get. Wander around and open chests all you want, you won't find anything as good as often as if you jsut farmed.
So, it boils down to farm-grind-loot simulator.
Starting a new character is exhilirating. Hitting mid-way is fun, as you become more proficient with them. Hitting end game feels hollow and meaningless.
Best parts in the game are when you finally "click" with the character you're playing and find a playstyle with them that makes them tear through things. Also, when you co-op with folks that know what they doing and you all work well as a team. You can plow through things, save each others bacon, ect, ect.
Sadly, a lot of co-op sessions are marred by some jerk that just hoovers up all the best loot without sharing, or some bozo that keeps going down b/c they don't know how to play their character, or the game host kicks you all out of the game right as the boss character is defeated and dropping the good loot, or some bone-head says "hey, let's dupe this stuff" and then you grind to a halt while folks spend hours jerking themselves off on loot exchange.
It's a really good game, but end-game is hollow and holds no further challenges.

Rouge Legacy makes the exploration and risk-vs-reward aspects of the Rougelike (aka Deathlab) genre, one I enjoy greatly, more accessible by giving the player a form of persistence after death. When the player dies in Rouge Legacy, the money their character had collected is passed onto their next character, and upgrades purchased with earlier gold will always be inherited by any future characers, meaning the player characters get stronger with each attempt on the castle's bosses. This fact combined with tight, simple controls and big, colorful sprites make Rouge Legacy by far more accessible than any other Deathlab I've played, without sacrificing any of the Real Decisions (TM) that I love the genre for.

If you are looking to play a great single player game, Mad Max is definitely the game for you. The graphics are great and it is very well optimized. There's so much customization and the world is huge, and it does a good job of representing what Earth would look like if it were scorched.

Mad Max follows a similar formula to most games.. but what sets it apart is the attention to detail that has gone into every facet of the game.
Literally everything about this game, from sound effects, combat, visuals, car driving fighting has been exquisitely done.
Although you will be doing things repetitively, the way that these things are done and the design that has gone into these activities makes it a joy to do it for a long while.
The only negative aspect is that there is no New game mode where you can do it all over again with all of your acquired abilities/ weapons.    But on the other hand, even the beginning when you are just starting out has its charm.  This is not one of those games that start out boring and dull and only get good later on.  From the get go you will be feeling every skull cracking blow, every piece of metal grinding on metal, every blast from the shotgun.
All developers should take a queue from this game if they want to keep selling games at a $50 price point.   Although due to most games being dumbed down to the point that I refuse to paying full price, I have to admit that I think that this game is one of the (very) few that is deserving of being sold as an actual AAA game.

I bought this hoping it would be The Hunter 2. It's more like The Hunter Lite. It's a shooting gallery with pretty graphics. The difficult hunts that made the original so appealing are replaced with animals everywhere with no sense of self preservation. They call constantly and let you walk right up to them before they run.. And they even call several times specifically to warn you that they are about to run. So you can just run around at a full sprint and wait for the warning calls then stop and shoot them. Often times a shot doesn't even spook near by animals so you can lay waste to entire herds in a short time. The leveling grind also promotes this style of gameplay, needing to both earn ridiculous amounts of cash to buy new equipment as well as needing a ton of XP to unlock the ability to even purchase it. On the plus side its pretty, the landscapes are massive, the draw distance has nearly doubled and the shooting feels a lot better than classic. The game has a lot of potential but this isn't early access, this is a full release and they have no obligation to change anything. This combined with the history of Primal leaves one with doubts about the future of this title. Hopeful doubts, but doubts nonetheless.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is simply the best simulator I have played in a very long time.  It's engaging simulation and eye-catching graphics is hard to ignore, and it boasts a large scaled map of the entirety of Europe.  It includes licensed trucks from over 8 brands, including Volvo and Iveco.  In the end, this is a game that should not be ignored.  If you have the money, get it.

I know absolutely nothing about trucks, cars, etc... but I never thought that this game would be so much fun. The realism in this game is ridiculous. Really good graphics, great feel (especially with a G27 racing wheel), and you can also listen to your own music while driving, or a radio station from the internet. When you have a bad day, this is a game to go to. Very relaxing.... that is.. if you know how to drive of course, then I guess it wouldn't be so relaxing. Overall 9/10 for me. If you love to drive, this is a must have, and this comes from a person who could care less about Mack Trucks.

Euro Truck simulator 2 is a 'special' game because of it tendencies to make the player drift off into a world where you only have to focus on one thing: Driving. The game is unique as it delivers an experience that no other game ive played offers such as: Graphics that are simply breathtaking when on the specific high setting, the amount of attention to detain put into this game and it's world shows enomous dedication and a good eye, although the cities arent the actual size that probably should be, the major cities are quite realistic and have that original feel to them.
The mechanics of the game are quite fair as if you speed you get a ticket, break rules: ticket and ect. The game is fairly good with its mechanics physics wise, I have yet to see a time where my truck has slingshoted out into the air. You can do everything that a truck can mostly do such as honk the horn, indicate, fill up with fuel (essential), cruise control, lights, manual gearboxes... the works essentially.
The most unique thing about this game is that since it is just about driving, it has the sense of meditation or zen to it, usually I feel after playing an hour of the game refreshed or it clears your mind, it's also great before sleep as with other games where you find you are always looking around for dangers or involving yourself too much in typing or whatever, in this game it's simple, stressfree and overall very enjoyable. This game is great for all ages and especially those who are truck enthusiasts, people who dont mind sitting down for an hour or two and just relax will love the game and everything in it. The combination of just driving through the beautiful landscape is fully worth the money to look at and there is a wide selection of trucks to choose as well.
Overall, I thoroughly enjoy this game and recommend it to all who look at the game and this review, and to all that buy the game:
HAPPY DRIVING!

Prison Architect Review
Probably the best early-access game ever to hit Steam. Prison Architect is a creative sandbox game in which you build and manage a prison. The addictive concept, depth and easy to use interface makes this one of the most intriguing and enjoyable games I have played in a long time.
The top-down presentation is simple yet superb. The user-friendly interface makes navigation simple and easy to use. There is quite a lot of stuff to do in terms of construction and designing so having such a well-designed layout of functions is crucial to this games brilliance. The strategic depth here is also incredible and the way you design your prison and how you manage prisoners happiness can be huge factors to your overall success.
The bigger your prison becomes; the tougher it is to manage. Suddenly you have maximum security prisoners at your door and it's up to you to expand and enhance your prison to accommodate the influx whilst keeping people including staff and fellow inmates happy and safe. There is a considerable challenge here particularly when you grow your prison and the population. The level of depth in the design of your prison along with the management strategy aspect is simply staggering.
Overall, Prison Architect is an amazing game even at alpha stage. It's polished and incredibly well designed in all areas. The developers have done an amazing job so far and this game will only grow further in months to come.

After 500+ hours on this account and over 1200 hours on my old account i can safely say rust is the BEST game you can buy that has this much of an active DEV team. They come out with updates every week and always keep you in on the loop of the game, they never let anything unbalanced slip through. Let's get to the meat and list what I DON'T like about the game...
1. It doesn't have any piggy-back hauls. You should at least be able to pull 2 short trailers at once and drop them off at different locations, as well as being able to choose your own piggy-back haul from 2 different suppliers. Killing 2 jobs in 1 long haul would be awesome.
2. Not enough truck accessories. I've seen truckers really deck-out their ride and practically pimp it with mutliple lights, neon ground FX, DVD / TV, game consoles, outrageous stereo systems, interior uphostery upgrades, even compact microwaves and fridges, but nope ... none of that here ... bummer.
3. No animated cut scenes. It really needs some, especially during transit on ferries and trains.
4. Resting process is lame and empty. It needs an actual restroom break and/or a trip inside a convenience store while refueling. Truckers got to have their coffee, jerky, and twinkies ... you know?
5. Headlight and Taillight systems of A.I. traffic is rather dull and dim both in the mirrors and on the highway. This might be hardware related, so maybe we just need a slider adjustment to brighten them and add oncoming traffic lense flare.
6. No functioning radios, No CB chatter whatsoever, not even a check-in for dispatch. The best you can do is to find a stream link to an online scanner or CB repeater and add it to the game's stream player list.
7. No physical viewable damage to anything. The game really needs this to be an ultimate hit.
Things that I like...
1. Love the engine and environment sound FX. Most realistic samples I've ever heard so far.
2. I really enjoy picking up a load from a quarry. It's almost as if I can feel the weight of the trailer tugging on the tractor. Plus the gearing sounds climbing the hill out of there is super awesome too. I'm impressed!
3. More sound FX ... DAMAGE EFFECTS. Those sounds make it fun to deliberately tear up your truck. Just needs some physical damage to go with it.
4. Really like all the city layouts. Some are very spacious.
5. Pedestrians are a nice touch.
6. So many roads to choose from.
7. Scenery is very pleasant outside of towns.
8. The ability to hitch and unhitch at will is very cool.
9. Extra lighting accessories are a big plus. Very helpful for night driving.
10. A.I. vehicles have quality intelligence worthy of being obstacles.
As you can see, I like it more than I hate it. I probably would recommend it.

I first heard of Undertale, much after the fact and much after the initial flood of lets plays concluded, I looked it up on Steam, bought the game and the soundtrack at the same time (I think it was on sale), and started as soon as I could, somehow avoiding the spoilers after being ignorant to this game's existence for somewhere between four and six months.
I played through it my way, trying to be nice but fighting when I felt I had to. Didn't look anything up. Didn't cheat. Didn't spoil. Without going into too much detail, it was probably the best experience I've had with a narrative-driven game in quite some time, and I feel lucky as hell that I got a chance to enjoy it on my own merit without "pacifism pressure". Honestly, at the time, it felt like a truly great game, and once I beat the Pacifist run, I started to look deeper, learned how to do Genocide, got impatient at Hotland and didn't return until my brother begged me to download the game for him to go through. Sadly, I couldn't enjoy the Genocide ending as much, partly because with the game's designed, I don't think I'm *supposed* to enjoy it, and partly because I had waited so long that I kinda had a clue as to what would happen.
Overall, at the time, I would've said the game was at least 9.5 out of 10, especially once I started to hear about the game's hidden depths, details often overlooked upon first glance, and excluded/extremely rare content
. However, as I started to look further into the fandom and as I heard about it, it started to wear on that people take this game way too seriously or way too... strangely. Mass hatred towards people who "play the game wrong", quoting things with no contextual parallels (determination, bad times and esp. dunked on, goatmom, hOI, the OST), and ... "Undertail"... sorry, but seeing "goatmom" in lingerie, and so soon after the Pacifist ending... no. On top of that, oversaturation of the game's content can make it tiring to experience the same content over and over. This is especially present in people in early 2017 claiming the game is "dead", that there is nothing else to find, or that the game wasn't as good as they initially thought. Yeah, after some time, your initial feelings towards a story-focused game are going to fade over time, but the fact that there are entire YouTube channels with 6 digit fanbases *really* ages the game quicker. And yeah, I'll admit, in retrospect, some elements of the game lose their effect after the first experience.
It's like an addict chasing their first and most intense high with every reload.
Yet, despite the extreme oversaturation and questionable fan content (and please don't get me wrong, there is some great content, but it's safe to say that the crap outnumbers the good stuff 2:1), I still believe this game is a 9.5, at least for me. Nothing's really tainted my initial enjoyment, and while the fandom can be frequently cringy, I do believe that, if you're lucky enough to get a chance to enjoy the game the way it's meant to be enjoyed (which, itself, is up for debate. I mean to say "enjoy it for yourself" and "untainted and unspoiled"), you're gonna have a very good time with some very real feels. Sorry for writing such a long review, I mostly just wanted to get my two cents out. PS: Why do people think this game is monumental? Morality-driven narratives is not a new concept, several games did it before, especially thinking of Catherine, Mass Effect, surely some others. The concept of being nice to "monsters" is also by far not new. While specifically bullethell might be new to the genre of RPGs, several RPGs use "unusual" turn-based combat systems before, never mind games beyond RPGs. Sorry, for real now, this isn't too organized but I just want to dump my thoughts out.

Reminiscent of From Software's Souls series, this game can be grueling, but rewarding. The core gameplay is a lot of fun with really frantic action and high mortality rates, and it is tempered with the ability to upgrade your keep (and subsequently yourself), armor and equip runes. Lower level upgrades are essential to all skill levels, and also present the player with new gameplay options by unlocking new classes, but at the higher levels these help to keep less skilled players alive longer and give even skilled players a fighting chance against the later sections. With randomized dungeons and rewards, the replay value is really high, unfortunately it also causes the game to slow down towards the middle if you don't have the skill to progress and haven't encountered enough upgrades in the dungeon to help outfit your character in a way that matches your play style.
I would recommend it at a sale price of $6-$8.

*Review only after playing the first episode*
You *have* to play Life is Strange before playing Life is Strange: Before the Storm in order to understand the characters and why they act the way they do.
Pros:
I'm so happy that they decided to tell the story of Chloe and Rachel before Max came back to Arcadia Bay. I like that you get to learn more about Chloe's personality through her graffiti art and hidden love of science as well as the choices her character gives you. The Mixtape feature is awesome and so is Collector's mode for all of you Achievement Hunters. The artwork seems much smoother and more polished in this game. Overall, I've laughed and cried with Chloe throughout this first episode and I can't wait to explore the other two episodes.
Cons:
- (Visual/Technical) The overall mobility and movement felt a bit different compared to LiS. I just finished playing LiS again (for the 100th time) before starting the first episode here and it felt like my movement and ability to look around was more limited/stiff? I could be totally off. It just felt like it was harder for me to choose options regarding things on the ground or options regarding interactions with other people because I had to be really close to them to make a choice but being close made it harder to see what the options were - not game changing though.
- (Visual/Technical) I like that they made choice selection with WASD but I kind of liked the old hold-and-drag method of choosing. It's a small complaint but I wish it were a choice in the option menu.
----------
If you were a fan of Life is Strange and curious about the relationship Chloe had with Rachel, it's SO worth it. I can't recommend this LiS and LiS: BtS enough - two visually stunning games with good stories!

Update - Second episode. Still love it.

The Good:
-A few scenes are quite fun, such as the part where you get to play DnD.
-The Backtalk mechanic is very fun. It's no rewind ability, but it's still a nice staple mechanic.
-The story gives you a bit more of a connection to Rachel
-This game gives you more Chloe.
The Neutral:
-Chloe's new voice actor. Most people would probably put this under "The Bad" catagory, but I personally don't mind as much. It doesn't seem right at all, but Ashly Burch had her reasons, and at least she helped to write Chloe in this.
-Rachel's story is a bit generic. "I'm the happy, popular girl! But oh no! I'm actually depressed! Good thing the protaganist is here to push me through these hard times!". It could have been worse, but oh well.
-It's not made by Dontnod. Very few sequels made by different devs turn out to be as good, and even few turn out better(the only game I can think of that does better under a different team was Fallout: New Vegas). This isn't really a bad thing, but it is undoubtably not a good thing. Lets keep an open mind though.
-We find the origins of "Hella". I'll let you decide if thats good or bad...
The Bad:
-Some dialog(at least at the very start) doesn't quite match Chloe's character. I've mentioned to some friends, at points it seems like the writers thought they were writing for Max, but by the time they realized they weren't, it was too late.(the dialog does slowly fall into place where it should be though)
-Chloe has a too much of an obsesion with Max. I know they were close, and the first game was all about her, but almost every page in Chloe's journal mentions Max in some way, and even talks about her when examining certain items. I love Max as much as the next person, but it was a bit over done here.
-Frank is depicted as a softy. I know he secretly is one(as seen with his dog in the first game), but he's straight up to kind in this. Maybe it will change in later episodes, but this is not the Frank we knew.
-Chloe and Rachel make a cute couple. This pisses me off since Chloe and Max are the OTP.
OVERALL:
If you enjoyed the first game, you might as well get this. It's not a must play though. It's basically here to tide you over if you can't wait longer for the actual Life is Strange 2. I give it a soft 7/10

I used to love this game.
The devs are going the way of DayZ, nerfing everything, never addressing long-standing problems, most of the promises they made early on will never come true, and they completely don't understand what it is that made this game fun and approachable in the first place, and they've made yet another generic crafting/grinding game with occasional PvP that is so laughably one-sided most of the time that its just frustrating for new players to start. They've developed themselves into a corner.
This game also lost its "rustiness" at some point along the way. Look at the early concept sketches and how cool this game COULD have been if they had gone the way they originally intended.
According to the concept materials, Rust was supposed to be a game where you had to scavenge for basic things like boots, springs, little bits of metal, rusty pipes, etc, and craft crude weapons out of them. This game was never meant to have fully functional assault rifles, at least not as a craftable thing. In a world like the original Rust, finding an assault rifle or army helmet would've been seen as godly, in a world where everyone is rocking spears and bows, and the occasional pipe shotgun.
We were meant to be naked, starving, and primitive, with occasional luck finding something from the "old world" that could be used to help us in some way like finding street signs and sharpening them down into weaponry, or fashioning armor out of them, or finding bits of metal, wood, glass, etc and building a shelter out of that.
Now this game is a grind. Get ready for the excitement that hitting trees has to offer. Brace yourself for the blazingly awesome time that is hitting rock after rock after rock for stones/metal/sulfer. Get your camera out and capture the raw beauty that is a janky twig-staircase that was used to bypass any and all security measures you can hope to put down.
You don't play Rust for your own personal benefit/gain, you're just gathering resources for whoever the biggest clan on the server is.
The inherent problem with a game like this is that you're almost required to build a big base, which they will wait until you are offline to raid, and once you're offline, there is NO WAY to know you're being raided, unless you get "lucky" and log in mid-raid. All of the turrets/traps in the world don't matter if you don't have a way to know you're being raided when offline. Base building games are only fun if they are designed that way from the start, and properly thought out from that perspective. Rust is trying to be a PvE survival game, a hardcore PvP game, a base building tower-defence game, and Minecraft all at the same time, and it doesn't do any one of those things really well.
PvP is broken and unbalanced. Base building is a joke in terms of flexibility and design and even more of a joke in defense.  They are slow to help solo players and quick to help the large groups.
Rust was best when it perfectly filled that void between casual game and hardcore game.
Rust should be two different games. One a modern shooter with all the armor and high end guns and focus on big bases/clans that Rust has now, and the "Caveman simulator" a lot of us wanted back when it first came out with spears/bows/scavenged stuff with small, primitive shelters. They'd make more money anyways, and have a bigger over-all community... seems win/win to me.

In a word; dissapointing.
Don't let the hype fool you, this is not an open ended sandbox game. This ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love child of Red Faction: Guerilla, and the Batman Arkham series had some good ideas, but doesn't live up to any of them. What is played off as a series of side quests are actually needed elements to enhance your car and unlock the next type of archangel, meanwhile all the upgrades themselves are pointless, and any buff the flavor text alludes to is non-existant. In a world where seemingly everybody down to the runtiest little cars have plate armor that can withstand multiple blasts. Despite the flavor text saying it will make your car be built like a tank, and prevent 30% damage, you can still be easily taken down by these same runty cars weaving into you a few times, or one good t-bone slam. This problem is further compounded when you try to get back into your car after it's repaired and they slam it back down to half health or less before you can even finish starting it up.
The combat system itself leaves a lot to be desired. From the on foot fisticuff action that encourages you to fight a dozen people at once, but you'll often have trouble managing two fighters. Because every action you take, even a full on body slam of an opponent can be interrupted by the meagerest of punches. That said the variety of enemies in the game is apalling. From the start to the end it's the same swarm of flailing half starved wastelanders in every color of the rainbow.  Even the bosses are resolved to a 'top dog' enemy type with different colored facepaint on their armor, and all wielding the exact same weapon. This sadly extends to the cars as well, each region forcing you to fight the local variety who have their paintjob done up in every variety of neon imaginable, and can resist being harpooned by the same device that literally tears down entire reinforced buildings, yet somehow can't be fired through an open window or into an exposed gas tank.
In the end I just can't reccomend this game, least of all for the full price. Go to any keyseller site and get the game for fifteen bucks at the most if you want a drama heavy brawler with a lot of completionist goals. Drive around, collect shinies, establish a base, break through to the next area, rinse and repeat.

EPISODE 1:
I expected this to to be a lot worse than the original "Life is strange". After all, they couldn't pull the time reversal trick in a prequel because it was all new to Max and Cloe back then , so what other trick is there this time?
Well there isn't realy one. Cloe can foul-mouth (backtalk) people and win arguments that way but that's not really a big deal. Don't get me wrong, it's fun that it's there but it's not as big a deal as the time thing. Far from it..
So, is it worse? Hell no! I loved it! It really feels familiar. Cloe has an awesome sick sense of humor in a few scenes and I totally love that. Rachel too btw. Next to that the game comes with an awesome story (so far), some well played emotions, great acting, great voice-overs. and so on.. The actor for Cloe is not the same as the one from the original game but you don't even notice that.  She's a little different but she's younger here so it actually fits perfectly.
It's also built by a completely different studio and you don't even notice that either. Arcadya Bay looks and feels the same as in the original Life is Strange.
Get this game. So far, it's been really worth it.
EPISODE 2:
A little less great than the first episode but that's usually the case with the middle episode of a trilogy. One really annoying thing of this episode is that the backtalk just didn't make any sense. Everything they explained in the first episode just didn't seem to work in the second one. It's just a lot of guess work now and just hoping you've picked the response that gets you to a success. that seriously sucks. I hope they fix that in the final episode.
Story-wise it's also really the middle one of a trilogy.. Stuff from the first episode gets built upon and seeds are planted for the final episode. the relationship between Rachel and Cloe is getting stronger and that's cool.
I can't wait for the final episode but another part of me is sad that it's gonna be over after that.
I would love to experience more with these two. the chemistry between them is so genuine.
Also, not as much humor and jokes this time.
Still a great episode though (if you don't count the backtalk frustrations) and I enjoyed playing it.
I hope episode 3 gets here fast :)
EPISODE 3:
The 3rd episode is awesome again. It's pretty tough to talk about it without spoiling anything so I'll keep it short. I think story-wise, Before the Storm is even beter than the original Life is Strange. If you liked the original game for the story and not just for the time-thingy, then get this game. Emotions are so important and done so well.. From the first episode I already connected more with Cloe and Rachel than I did with Max, and it stayed like that for the entire game.
It's simply amazing what Deck9 did here and I thank them for it.
Now all there is to do is wait for the special episode with Max. I'm curious about that one.. I'll update for the last time once I've played that.
Hooked. Again! Good job Deck Nine, you nailed it!

Life is Strange: Before the Storm is far better than it has any right to be.  Deck Nine has taken on what literally should have been an impossible task.  As far as I’m concerned Life is Strange is a masterpiece, not just a videogame masterpiece, just a straight up masterpiece.  That’s a pretty high bar to content with.  Added to that is the baggage of the story they are tasked with telling is not a story that needs to be told or probably even one that anyone wanted to be told.  I was utterly baffled when they announced they were going to make a prequel about Rachel and Chole.  It seemed like a horrendously poor decision.  Everyone knows where that story leads, everyone knew the feelings involved, there was no real gaps that needed filling in.  I was expecting the game to be a disaster.
Instead Before the Storm while probably falling short of being as good as Life is Strange, is still just an outstanding achievement in videogames and especially the adventure game genre.  It has its’ problems.  Not having Ashly Burch as Chole really hurts.  Chole is a very complex character and that character needs an extremely talented voice actress.  Ashly Burch pulled it off in the first game, Rhianna DeVries really doesn’t.  She certainly isn’t bad, but she is not at the same skill level of Burch.  It tends to be most egregious in the more intense scenes.  Life is Strange particularly showcases why voice actors should be paid well for their work.  Still I’m quite happy with it overall and Kylie Brown really nails Rachel Amber, so that helps…although if they were both poor voice actresses it might not be as noticeable.  Brown is clearly the stronger of the two.
More surprisingly is that Deck Nine just utterly nails the tone that Dontnod used.  As soon as the game starts and the music kicks in and the opening title screen comes on you know Deck Nine took great care in crafting this game.  Music was literally key to the world Dontnod created for Life is Strange.  Despite not even using the same composer, Deck Nine managed to craft a perfect soundtrack to this game.  The choice of Daughter to compose the music ended up being a genius move.  I really am at a loss for how they managed it so perfectly.  The game sounds like Life is Strange.  The music selections are perfect.  They pull you back into this world and immediately let you know that this is the Arcadia Bay you came to love in the first game.
Deck Nine also adds plenty of small touches that make the world feel familiar.  It uses many of the same camera shots, the same focus on animals and the beauty of nature, the quiet moments you can enjoy, Chole even has a journal you can read and they make it fit her character.  The new characters you meet all feel right at home in this world as well.  I think it’s clear super nerdy girl Steph is the new best character.
I also feel the story is extremely well done, until the end.  I felt episode 2 particularly was very strong.
After finishing this game I strongly feel this should have been 5 episodes, the game felt rushed, the narrative beats needed more time to play out, the last episode particularly needed a lot more time and the plot problems are a tad ergegious.  Still I really enjoyed this game, until about the last 15 minutes, #Worth Any Price…get it because her name is Chole Price, I’m hilarious.

Simulator games!...I love em!
As an older gamer in my mid 30's I remember a time when Simulator games were pumped out ten a penny, sure they were mostly 'war machine' sims such as aircraft, tanks or submarines and every system had them from the early 80's wireframe Spectrum 48k efforts  right up until the naughties full on 3D rendered apachie v havok (00's) but then with the advent online consoles the quality of sims died off in a big way.
Sure we still had a few knocking special ones knocking around, the silent hunter series and microsofts lacklustre (should have been better) combat flight sim series, but most companies now focused on giving us standard cookie cutter clones of console games year after year.
The past few years have however given us a newlease of sim games some great some not so but all withing their rights beautiful, from the oddly popular farming simulator to the even odder goat simulator were now being treated to some proper PC sim love from gaming studios.
And so eventually we come to Euro Truck Simulator 2 or ETS2 to its fans.
Gamers can now live out their dreams as an EU based trucker, buy a truck, pick a job, drive for miles across international borders while avoiding speeding tickets and dodging crap motorway drivers and dodgy AI (since launch AI is vastly improved), its that simple, thats all their basically is to it.
The games engine isnt the best looking by far but its nice enough to look at for hours on end and trust me, you will look at it for hours on end, and the community have taken to the game nicely so theres lots of modding available, from new trucks and trailers, updated true to life road markings and signs for respective countries, a working radio station mod and even an ad hoc multiplayer mode that actually works.
The game plays well, the trucks handle nicely and theres a nice progression system that allows you to form a fleet of trucks of your own and send out AI drivers to complete jobs, theres a good chunk of customisability to your trucks from new paint jobs to lights, wheels, engines ect.
This all may sound pretty boring and in reality it should be, and yet it isnt, its somehow compelling and extremly satisfying as your make sure you slow down for the speed cameras on the M6 en route to Manchester to ensure you dont get a ticket as you run against the clock to get your load of supermarket goods delivered on time..

For the few hours I have played CotW I would definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoys a hunting game and doesn't want to pay extra for Classic.
For people new to the franchise, I would start with CotW. It is the cheaper alternative and delivers for its price range. While Classic may have more animals, gameplay and community features CotW is a more inclusive system. Not nessecarily easier as it comes with its own challenges but the learning curve is more user-friendly.
For people returning from previous theHunter games I believe it would depend on what you want. In a way, CotW is closer to Primal than Classic. There are fewer animals, less trophy diversity and fewer game mechanics but the AI is more advanced and the species don't feel like the same system tacked onto multiple different models.
As for bugs I have only experienced one major one that simply required a game restart. There are several smaller ones that are more annoyances than game breaking, which I am sure will be patched out in the following weeks.
As for the things I don't like, coming from Classic was a bit of a shock and while I know some people would be upset for the change, EW was very upfront that CotW would not be what Classic is. It was sold as a game that would not compete with Classic and some people seem to have forgotten that, or never understood what that ment. After a few hours of playing I grew to enjoy what CotW offers at this moment in time, however, it does feel rather empty. Such large maps with so little diversity.
Despite this, I do think this game is worth buying. Be it now, or in a few months. If you are worried about bugs and missing features I would wait but definitely come back every once in awhile to see how the game progresses.
Good luck and happy hunting!

The slow pace of hunting, the minimalistic UI, the sounds, and gorgeous graphics makes theHunter an impressively immersive experience that manages to be pretty relaxing and thrilling at the same time. The gameplay is in my short experience pretty simplistic, which is probably a necessity given that it's a pretty unique game. You find a trace, you follow it, you shoot the animal, everybody happy. It certainly has depth though, and the world feels very alive, despite pretty much just being you, the land, and the animals. I would attribute this to the AI of the animals combined with the mechanics of the world more than anything, as they'll pretty realistically react to noises, sightings, et cetera.
My main gripes with the game seem to be things that will hopefully be improved upon in later patches. Namely, the tutorial is more or less just text boxes popping up every once in a while. Even though learning through playing might work, there's a good few mechanics that just aren't explained all that well and given how this isn't a common/mainstream type of game, a proper tutorial would really make it easier to get into the game.
Secondly there's a slight lack of polish in some areas. Menus are a bit clunky and there are some smaller graphical bugs. The positional audio could use some work too, it would be an amazing asset to the immersion but there's just something off about it in terms of volume levels and direction.

It's the same thing over and over again. Some fists fights, some car chases, pulling the enemy vehicle apart with your harpoon, and collecting scraps. Rinse repeat.

**Finished game, update below**
It's very much an Avalanche game, meaning you either love their choices and commitment or you don't.
I'm on team Love It.  I think the game plays really well (there are little control and design choices you can nitpick, but it's just nitpicking), has excellent (truly excellent) action--unusually strong for an open world game, and has an incredibly beautiful world.
The game feels gritty and tangible.  You'll run over rocks and stones and dislodge them from the scenery--you feel this in your vehicle handling.  Lightning strikes are loud, hot, dangerous, and scary.  Punches are bloody-wet and bone-cracking--I grit my teeth when I get into a fight.  Your shotgun is powerful, as one is in real life, and is deafening and deadly.
There's a lot of driving, and it handles perfectly well.  There's a lot of exploring.  There's a lot of rationing of food, water, and bullets.  There's scouting.  There's survival.  There's stepping on geckos for a little bit of food and health replenishment when you're desperate.  There are small mementos which remind you of the world that used to be.
This is actually a pretty magical game, really.  It's committed to its source material and its chosen mechanics.  I don't, honestly, have anything to complain about, but if you're looking for non-stop plot and activities that never repeat, you may not love it.  I, however, love it...and I recommend it with gusto.
**UPDATE**
So.  Max and I finished our sordid little affair last night, and my initially glowing review is going to have to be adjusted now...to an even "glowier" review.  This game just got better and better...locations got more and more fascinating and beautiful...mechanics and variability expanded and made the game more and more fun...and the final couple story missions are absolutely incredible.  The story, too, which was an afterthought for me when I first reviewed the game, is terrific; the plot is very simple, but it's told through cutscenes and dialogue that are VERY well-directed and acted.  Please don't spoil yourself thinking the story is unimpressive; toward the end, emotions can run VERY high in this game, if you aren't expecting anything.
Summary follows.
Pros:
1) Spectacular graphics (including very good animation). Also a lot of terrific graphical details, like garbage blowing in the wind or plastic bottles rolling by your feet.
2) Excellent level design; excellent world design
3) Car combat is fun, varied with different weapons and approaches, and well-balanced (you can stretch it out and challenge yourself by chasing, evading, and ramming, or, if you're in the mood to finish up quickly, you can thunderpoon cars [basically a one- or two-hit kill] and put it behind you [not sure why you'd want to do that, though, to be honest])
4) Melee is mostly simple, but rewarding and hard-hitting.  Move upgrades make a world of difference in the tactics you'll use (i.e., the combat evolves).
5) Story is very emotional (don't spoil yourself); plot is straightforward and very much in the spirit of Mad Max
6) Collectibles system (history relics) add a lot to the atmosphere and world.  There's also a ton of them, and they are mostly very interesting.
7) Incredibly well-optimized.  Stutters when auto-saving, and that is IT.  The game ran like a dream, no matter how much action was on screen.
8) Storms.  There are no words.
9) Image editor is so much fun.  It also gives you a great opportunity to explore the world and action up close.  These artists were VERY good...
10) Explosions. Debris.  The best in the industry, hands down.
11) SO MUCH stuff in this game has realistic physical properties applied to it.  It's a lot of fun to hit a random boulder and see fragments chip off and procedurally roll down the adjacent cliff.
12) Shoulder-charging war boys off of ledges or over rails never gets old.
13) Sniping the supports off of the tall guard towers.  Just aim for the red things.  You're welcome.
14) A lot of surprises abound.  Explore and have fun--there's usually a reward.
Cons:
1) You'll spend a lot of time capturing camps and increasing your scrap count, and after a certain point the scrap is fairly useless (this is a very LATE game issue, though).  Granted, game world economies usually always have this problem (see GTA games)
2) Certain tasks can become repetitive, but if you like the gameplay this isn't really much of a con.  It's just something worth knowing before you dive in.
3) Driving at high speeds in narrow areas is frustrating at first (there is a late-game mission where this was particularly noticeable).
4) No way to re-spawn events/camps (as far as I can tell), and no New Game+ mode.
5) One recurring technical glitch I'd have with the image capture mode is sometimes the FOV with the free camera would be very limited.  Seemed too glitchy to be intentional.  Indoors this was common (and expected), but outdoors it would occasionally happen for no reason in particular.
tl;dr PLAY ME, I'M FUN.

This game could have been really cool, but it's designed♥♥♥♥♥backwards, and every mechanic in it is against new players.
Essentially, to be able to live long enough to make a base, you need to avoid players, randomly spawning aggressive animals, and collect a number of materials. If you don't find any food near your (random) spawn, you will die in about 5 minutes. Usually, to find any food means running around a large area, which just so happens to attract aggressive NPCs, like Wolves and Bears. If another player doesn't see you first. Wolves and Bears will kill you in three hits, and make you unable to fight in two. (With no armor). Players can kill you in one hit with a spear. If they don't headshot and instant-kill you, you will die in about 30 seconds to bleedout.
You can occasionally spawn in winter biomes, which will kill you unless you leave or make clothes within a couple of minutes. Stone is extremely hard to find, since it's a competitive resource, and you'll find a lot of other players around any stone spawns. If you can't find stone, your starting tool breaks, and you can't collect any resources until you find more. Including stone. You need stone to get stone. (It *CAN* spawn on the ground so you can pick it up, but in all my time playing I've seen that happen exactly twice).
There is a Voice-chat feature, which will freeze the game the first time you use it. Always.
While the game is already near-unplayable, recently an update came out that makes it quite literally unplayable. At least for me. Essentially, Rust now automatically fetches workshop downloads during gameplay. Did I mention that this game *can't* be played single-player? With my connection, any download (yes, even 16/kbs), makes any multiplayer unplayable. I am unable to interact with the world, pick up any items, or use the text chat without a 10-30second delay. As it turns out, workshop downloads aren't limited by your steam download settings, and anytime you pause a rust download, the game automatically unpauses it.
I was able to play for about 30 minutes today without encountering this issue. Once a download started, it wouldn't stop, no matter what I did. I even maxed out my download speed and waited for it to go through 100mb worth of downloads. It kept going. In that time, I was unable to pick up any items, or move back to safety, so my character was killed and all my items were gone. ...I had finally acquired enough resources to get a gun. Even with minimum downloads, it was so laggy I couldn't open the door on my building to hide.
I've still never used a gun, and when I used a bow I was able to get exactly one shot off before dying to a gun. Recently I found a cave, that was rife with materials, but since I broke my tools inside the cave, I couldn't get any wood to make anything out of it until I died again to get more stone. Also, with every death, there's a 175 second wait before you can respawn to your base.
TL;DR: It's a miracle this game had even temporary success, but hopefully with this terrible update we can finally put it in the trash heap, where it belongs. (Until they fix the massive balancing issues, the unpausable downloads during gameplay, and general inability to do anything without certain items.)
On the bright side, the game is quite well optimized, and at times, even quite beautiful. But the remnants of what I hesitate to call "game design", are worthless to anyone without several teammates. Because that's what this game is designed for. Almost.

Let's get this out of the way. I'm a bit late to the Life is Strange party. I never played the original game until around June of 2017 when the game was offered as a free game for Playstation Plus users. Since then, I have played through the original and all of its episodes.
Life is Strange: Before the Storm is a game developed by Deck Nine Games and is a prequel that takes place 3 years before the events that transpire in Life is Strange. So what's different?
Firstly, unlike the first entry into the series where Max could rewind time; long gone are the days of that feature (at least for now it seems) and has been replaced with Chloe's Backtalk. Backtalking is basically a skill challenge that has the player looking for vital pieces and words in one's dialogue or surroundings to create what I'll call "witty rebuttals"seeing as Chloe plays differently to what Max did in the original game. Also gone are the days of taking photographs in each chapter of an Episode, but instead are replaced with Graffiti. Graffiti allows for the player to search out areas that might not normally go or look to find a spot to tag. Some are in plain sight, while others are hidden very cleverly which I enjoy. Aside from those differences in the mechanics, Before the Storm in my eyes, plays very much like the first game which I welcome with open arms because your actions still have consequences or might affect later outcomes in the game. Unfortunately seeing as this is only Episode 1, there are a few actions that require thought earlier in one's playthrough that might change the outcome later; however, I don't fault the game for it.
In terms of the story, it's hard to describe seeing as it would spoil a mass majority of one's playthrough. As I said above, this game takes place 3 years before the events of Life is Strange and players assume the role of Chloe; however, there is a slew of characters in terms of its cast that reappears from that game into this game including some new faces. Voice acting for the most part, is top notch and while, I can understand why some people were shocked to see that Ashly Burch wasn't returning to reprise her role as Chloe; the voice actress for Chloe hits the role perfectly in my eyes. Chloe being the rebellous teen and just how her lines are delivered are full of emotion and has the right amount of that teenage angst that we've all gone through at one point and time in our lives. While some points in Episode 1's story felt a bit predictable, Episode 1 had the perfect length behind it and honestly has me clamoring for Episode 2 already since Episode 1 leaves off on somewhat of a cliffhanger.
In terms of sound design and the game's soundtrack, I can simply say that it is perfect. The game uses an "indie" soundtrack which fits with the main character and the situations you are put into as you go through Episode 1. While it might not always be my favorite genre of music, I found myself tapping my foot along to some of the songs in certain parts of the game with a smile on my face as I trudged through the game's story.
So is the game worth it for the price? Honestly, I would say yes. I bought the Deluxe Edition of the game a few days after launch and my playthrough ran about 6 hours in total (including the times where I went AFK). While the game might not fully be replayable as of yet (not saying that you can't replay it since the game does offer a Collector Mode which allows players to revisit chapters to collect the Optional Graffiti without it affecting your decisions that you made), it's a breath of fresh air that I quite rather enjoy. Before the Storm is a game that every player should play without a walkthrough on their first pass through the game. Words cannot aptly describe how good of a game this is in my eyes.

This is probably the most thorough review I'll ever write on Steam, so I want to say some things before I start:
I'm only reviewing the first episode in its release state. I don't know yet if I'm going to update.
I'm going to refer to the original game as LiS, to this one as BfS.
LiS was a great game. People are hyped and give BfS 10/10 ratings, disregarding its obvious flaws. I would give it neither a thumb up nor a thumb down, but a "meh" rating.
BfS isn't developed by the same studio and you notice that extremely.
My review will get lots of thumbs down because the review system is broken. Giving a thumb down means telling that the review isn't helpful. People abuse the thumbs to vote down everything that doesn't agree with their opinion while voting up single sentence reviews that don't help anyone.
I'll try to keep spoilers out of my review as much as possible.
Let's take a look at some negative aspects, starting with technical stuff and proceeding into more "relevant" things:
- Graphics
While LiS was based on the Unreal Engine, BfS uses the Unity Engine.
Believe it or not, but the simple graphics are a lot worse. I actually loved the art style of LiS, but in BfS I actually deleted every single screenshot I took (and I take a lot of screenshots) because they just weren't pleasant to look at. Textures often completely lack detail, anti-aliasing is non-existent (even on maxed out AA settings) which is actually a huge problem in this game, even though I usually don't care much about AA. All my screenshots were heavily
pixelated.
- Controls
Remember how you chose an action in LiS by holding the left mouse button and moving the mouse into the direction of the action? In BfS, you hold the left mouse button and use WASD to choose. In other words, in order to look at stuff or interact you need two hands now instead of only one. It's not a big deal, it just makes the game less comfortable at many scenes.
- Voices
You've probably heard already that Chloe has a new voice. You probably still have her accent from LiS inside your head. That's gone. Not a big deal, you could get used to that - the problem is that her new actress just isn't good. At  some points she sounds completely unmotivated and just talks her text down without any motivation at all. Near the end of the game you will also notice heavy breathing and hear clearly that she was standing to close at the microphone.
Chloe isn't the only character with a new voice, for example the famous angry David Madsen sounds really soft now.
- Animations
Lots of animations look really clunky and unnatural. I wanted to call an exorcist when Rachel was turning her head. In dialogues, characters often lack facial expressions. David gets angry and raises his voice, but his soft and calm expression stays. Until BfS I never noticed what a killer missing facial expressions can be.
- Paradoxes and other minor flaws
For example, there's a photo of pirate Chloe and pirate Max hanging in Chloe's living room. However, the Max with the eyepatch on the photo isn't the young Max we know from flashbacks, but the old Max you play as in LiS.
In Chloe's diary entry about a schoolmate she writes something such as "He's exactly like my class schedule. We have history, but no chemistry." You can read this while following the task "Go to your chemistry class."
The game is full of those details.
- Chloe's character
Alright, Chloe's a rebel. But sometimes it's just too much. In the beginning of the game you can look at a knife stuck inside a wooden wall and Chloe says something like "This looks exactly like the knife my mom didn't want to buy me for my birthday." She also likes tossing items just to the ground after using them, even if she borrowed them from a friend few seconds ago. I mean, come on...
- Dialogues
Some dialogues actually make me cringe. I won't go into details here due to possible spoilers. There's a new feature which enables you to argue with people. Everytime you have to persuade someone, just look out for the "arguing" sign and you know that's the way to go. It triggers a minigame like in Monkey Island, where your enemy delivers a statement and you have to counter with a fitting insult. Despite the fact that everyone beyond twelve years of age knows that you basically lose an argument as soon as you just start insulting your opponent, the arguing dialogues are just the worst in the game. They are just completely incoherent. You answer to a statement and suddenly your opponent starts about a completely different matter. After winning the minigame, it always seems to me like people stop arguing because they are annoyed by Chloes inability to argue, not because she "won". But of course Chloe had to be as rebel as possible and so it works in the game's context.
Furthermore, the reactions and answers of characters sometimes don't seem logical at all.
- Other characters
Except for Chloe and Rachel, the characters in this game mostly completely lack depth. You meet them, they start talking about a topic, you choose one or two answers, you go on with the game. I don't even remember what we talked about.
I didn't like Rachel at all until the ending of the episode, but that's just my personal opinion.
- Exploration
Remember how you strolled around in LiS, trying to find out everything about the world and its inhabitants? Trying to find motives for a good photo? It's almost non-existent in BfS. Chloe's a rebel and there's a stage play coming up at school. Everything you'll find are some posters about drug abuse and the upcoming stage play, without giving you any more information. Instead of taking photos, you can draw graffitis at walls now. There's a graffiti in every scene, so you just walk along walls until you find the spot to get your achievement.
Now, some more positive aspects:
+ Clothes
After the intro you have to change clothes. You can choose the outfit you want to wear during the episode. There are two different T-shirts in the base game, you unlock three more outfits if you buy the deluxe edition and you can play as classic Chloe (without blue hair) if you preordered the game.
- I probably don't have to mention that this feature is just a huge cashgrab for Square Enix. It's a neat feature anyway.
+ Soundtrack
Just like LiS, BfS has a nice indie rock soundtrack which fits well into the game.
- Remember the scenes in LiS, where you just enjoyed the scenery and a nice song to it? They are in BfS too, but somehow they don't seem to fit into the game or they were just executed half-heartedly. They are nice to have anyway.
+ Gameplay
Well, the gameplay won't surprise you. If you liked the gameplay of LiS and can live without time travel puzzles, you'll be satisfied.
+ New ideas
After the cool intro and the unfortunately very tedious middle part, the developers suddenly had their own ideas in the end and this is where the game finally shine. This might be a little spoiler, but there's a difference between Max and Chloe. While Max was very calm, Chloe can become very angry. At some part in the game it suddenly gets emotional, and instead of only showing Chloe's emotions, you actually get to live out Chloe's emotions. And it feels great.
The arguing minigame is actually quite exciting, despite it's obvious lack of logic.
For each graffiti, you can choose between two different messages which will also show up in your graffiti diary. Neat little gimmick.
+ The ending
Just like every LiS episode, episode 1 of BfS has a great ending. It didn't only leave me sitting with my mouth open, it actually sent a chill down my spine.
Conclusion:
If it wasn't for the first 20 minutes and especially the last 20 minutes of the episode (3.5 hours in total), I would actually give the game a clear thumb down. I give it a "meh" rating. It has very obvious flaws, but it's quite enjoyable if you're a LiS fan.
