I was a big fan of the original Life is Strange, and have been very much looking forward to getting further insight into Chloe's backstory since this prequel was announced. I was a little worried that it wouldn't turn out well, but am pleased to say I am not disappointed in the slightest after playing EP 1.
I will do my best to keep spoilers out of this review, and to remember to update it after further episodes have been released.
4/5 ★
I don't have particularly much to add that I didn't say in reviewing EP1, EP2 just feels like a continuation, as it should. All the important relationships and characters get expanded upon further yet still leave a lot of room for the next episode.
One problem which has always been present in both games so far is the description of the dialogue choices. However, EP2 seemed to struggle a little bit more than EP1 did at properly summising what Chloe was going to say in the 1-2 words you're given to go off. Consequently it can be quite easy to say something you didn't mean to, by misinterpreting the prompt.
On a similar note, it remains tricky to try and reconcile choices *you* as the player would make vs choices you think Chloe should/would make. Having fallen in love with Chloe's character over the original LiS and then EP1 of this game, I have been trying to make the choices that I believe best fit her character, rather than necessarily what I would do. Combine this with the character Deck Nine have built for her throughout the plot, and the character we know she becomes in LiS, it can be tricky to determine which option to select. You might instinctively pick one option, but know that it's not really what Chloe would have done.
This isn't really a criticism of the game as it's not really resolvable, but more just an element of the genre the LiS franchise sits in.
All that being said, I still love this game and feel I properly connect with the charactes when playing it. Chloe continues to be a complex character, but relatable and very well portrayed.
Still definitely recommend playing this game, but after completing the original LiS first.
4.5/5 ★
This episode focuses almost soley on Chloe and Rachel, without much exploration into other characters, but that is not a problem in the slightest. I feel delving too much into supporting characters would have caused confusion and lessened the experience.
Whilst not perfect, the game does a very good job of portraying Chloe's character, which is one of the main things that anyone who has played the original LiS will take away from playing this. In LiS we obviously saw a lot of Chloe and related to her there, but it was all from Max's perspective. LiS:BtS does very well at connecting the Chloe we know from the outside to the Chloe we see on the inside. She is a complex character, and not always easy to understand. The nature of this game involves giving the player choices to make as to the actions Chloe takes, and the choices that are presented to the player are usually in a summarised format that doesn't alwys indicate exactly what Chloe will do. As such, you can sometimes find that she'll act out of character compared to how we knew her in LiS, and how she behaves throughout the rest of the game. This is the main reason for dropping from 5★ to 4.5★ review overall.
The main issue is that in LiS, Chloe's character wasn't something the player had control over, as we played as Max. Chloe's character was architectured in full by the developers, something not entirely possible in a game set from Chloe's perspective, without removing the whole "choice" aspect.
All things considered however, I can't fault Deck Nine. They had a hard job to do, and pulled it off well. They needed to write Chloe in such a way that the player can understand and relate to her complex character, and all the while not exceeding the bounds of the character we know she will become in LiS. On top of this, the player still needs the ability to feel like their choices have an impact. It was a hard job to do, and they did it well.
I can't write too much here without giving away spoilers, so will keep this section short.
Rachel was always a mysterious character from LiS. As Max, we only ever heard what Chloe said about Rachel, and a few comments from other people. It was very interesting to be properly introduced to her character for the first time. Whilst it's great to see her and learn a lot more about her, I feel her introduction fell a little short of the mark, and caused a chunk of EP1 to feel rushed, almost as if there was part of the story missing. Whilst I've not played the future episodes yet, I have the feeling that maybe this could have done with being a 4 or 5 episode game, and slowing down a bit when it comes to bringing Rachel into the story. This being said, this is does not ruin the game in any way, and does not dissuade me from wholeheartedly recommending this game.
There isn't too much in the way of customisations, but that's most likely because the game was designed to be played in one particular way.
The controls are slightly improved over LiS, options are now selectable via the keyboard rather than requiring you to move your mouse.
I felt the FOV was a bit too close for my liking, but got used to it after a while. No way to change it.
No ultrawide support, again, got used to it after a while, and I'm pretty sure this game is *supposed* to be played in 16:9.

All we can say is wow... Not a review here but an astute observation... This story-driven prequel taps a nerve.  It's an honest homage to the first - A dedication to breakthrough character portrayals made even more epic by the stunning fandom, personal interpretations, and emotional connections already developed and shared by the legions of observers now comfortably entranced by the entire atmosphere and interconnectivity of the realm known as arcadia bay.
Very rarely does interactive media bolster within itself a blossoming social movement like this now multistudio franchise is churning.

As much as Dontnod's original Life is Strange was like lightning in a bottle, with its authentic feeling tale of teenage angst and superpowers and puzzle solving, I wasn't sure that a prequel would really work. That's the problem with prequels. You know how it ends. I wasn't sure how you could even make another Life is Strange game without Max, Time Travel, the storm, and all of the various bits and bobs that made it tick.
I'm glad to say I was wrong. Deck9 has made something that's both familiar and fresh in Before the Storm. It's every bit as engrossing as Dontnod's original title.
Wheras LiS is a game about Max, and things that happen to Max, BTS is a game about who Chloe is. Wheras Max was a blank canvas on which the player was expected to project, Chloe is very much the opposite. Deck9 has taken the opportunity to retread old ground and new. With the help of (the sadly absent from her role due to the union strike) Ashley Burch they've drilled down in to the meat of what a clever, yet troubled teenager really is.
Where Max just tries not to rock the boat until she's thrust in to action by virtue of time travel powers, Chloe's "backtalk" mechanic is innate and familiar to her. There's no awkward phase, the game swiftly tutorializes you, the player in its use, but you're just catching up to something Chloe already knows like the back of her hand.
And that's where Deck9's outing really shines. The original game had a lot of heart, but it was primarily a puzzle solving excercise from the lens of a usually detached, and somewhat morose protagonist. The story worked because of everyone that orbited Max, including in no small part, Chloe herself. BTS, however, places you in the shoes (and internal monologue) of Chloe herself, and that makes all the difference.
Chloe has opinions, feelings, self delusions, and vulnerabilities that feel instantly familiar and real to anyone that was ever on the "bad kid" spectrum at her age. You're not so much defining Chloe as simply choosing what aspects of her you apply to a series of almost exclusively conversation based puzzles and challenges. You have dialog options not so much to define what kind of person you are, but because people are complex and conflicted, and the writing does a great job of carrying this idea through in to gameplay and consequences. Consequences that are, by default, far more impact without the ability to simply rewind time to find the "right answer."
While you may know from having played its sequel what the major story beats are likely to be, it is still profoundly affecting to see the world from her perspective. That's where the real interest lies, not in exploring the limits of cosmic time travel powers, but exploring what lies beneath all that smack talk and cringeworthy pseudo-badassery that all the "bad kids" seem to have.
It's not so much a question of what becomes of her interactions with students, teachers, parents, and Rachel Amber, but who Chloe is. It's so well done I'm perfectly happy to trade control of time and space for really good trash talk, and that's saying something.
If you liked Life is Strange, this is sure to hit the same buttons, in a slightly different way. Highly reccommended.

I wanted to like this game, I really did. The child/succession is a cool idea but, as far as I can tell, is of no consequence to the gameplay. The randomized traits are a great idea, but quickly lose their magic when you realize how few there are. The game's difficulty -- probably it's biggest selling point -- feels artificial, as most of my deaths were caused by the awkwardly generated rooms and the developers' apparent love affair with spikes rather than the enemies that populated them. The gear acquisition and character leveling seemed great initially, but quickly proved to be subject to slow and painful grinding.
The game is clearly intended to be played only with a controller, offering no mouse support and a very bad keyboard setup that can only be minorly customized. (It is of my opinion that very little effort was put into the PC controls. From personal experience, it is very easy and not at all time consuming to add the basic keyboard and mouse functionality that would have made playing the game without a controller a less frustrating experience.)
The reality is, as much as I try to pick apart this game and understand why it is I didn't like it, I can't. The game is hard, but I didn't feel myself getting upset at each death. In fact, I really didn't feel anything. Maybe that's the problem: there was nothing there to keep me playing. Unlike Dark Souls or Spelunky or any of those other "hardcore" games, playing this game just wasn't fun.

Rogue Legacy is difficult, but rewarding, and highly addictive. The general "pattern" of gameplay is that you get as far as you can in the dungeon, die, and start over with a new character. However, you keep upgrades from one character to another, so after a "successful" - i.e. profitable - run, you can spend your gold on upgrades and equipment.
This progression SLOWLY snowballs, and you start to feel powerful (plus, you get better at the game in addition to the upgrades), but clearing whole sections of the dungeons (there are four sections to each: the castle, the forest, the dungeons, and the maya) will take a while to get to. Clearing the entire thing is something I still haven't managed, though I've fully cleared two sections.
The "Genealogical" thing is a bit of a misnomer. Traits from successful heroes don't seem to actually pass down to their heirs, at least in any noticable way. This doesn't matter all that much, because aside from a few really terrible traits (like Vertigo, which flips the screen vertically), most of the time I wound up picking a character because of what class they were rather than what their traits were.
Rogue Legacy is well-suited to any length of time that you might have to play. You can play it for five minutes (if you can stop), or an hour, or an entire day. Each round through the dungeon helps just a little bit, and it builds up over time.
The difficulty scales nicely, and does  so in a good way - lots of games make things more difficult by giving the player less health/damage or enemies more health/damage, but Rogue Legacy makes things more difficult by introducing variants of enemies already seen with new abilities, faster attacks, and more. The game gives you more things to dodge and less time to dodge them in the harder areas,  or puts lots of types of enemies into a single area, making target prioritization a key part of survival.
There are a few flaws. The game somehow managed to be laggy, despite my system specs: a Radeon HD 5800 with 2gb vram, 12GB of ram, a 6 core 3.2GHz processor. My computer's a few years old, but I can run most games on high settings still, or medium at least. This game, though, is 2D. There's no reason on earth why a 2D game should lag with those specs. If you buy it and have a smaller laptop or something, be aware that it might not actually run. Absurd, I know. Also, the difficulty early on was quite frustrating, and I nearly gave up a few times.

First things first: It's obvious that this game does not feature next-gen graphics, two playthroughs took me just around 15 hours and, and by all means, it is quite straightforward. That being said, I loved every bit of it.
Undertale is... Weird. In the most positive way possible in my opinion, but weird.
It has a very special humor, that's for sure.
The characters you'll encounter are really unique in their way of interacting with you, and sometimes I weren't sure if I should laugh or frown about what just happened, or maybe both.
The music is pure art. Just like it was intended, and without any doubt I have to say that Undertale has one of the best soundtracks I know.
But most importantly: It broke me emotionally like nothing I've ever experienced.
I think many of us know this feeling of "Did I beat the game or did it beat me?" Well, both. It comes down to two possible endings, and at the end my first playthrough I shed tears of sadness over the in my opinion beautifully designed background story. The second one however was much harder to finish, because some bosses are quite tough, and in the end I felt a weird mix of pride, confusion, and even more sadness.

First Steam review so bear with me...
The Basics: A hunting "simulator" that drops you into a massive map with a gun in your hand a somewhat helpful voice in your ear. No real setup, just cuts you loose with some very basic and in my opinion decent enough tutorial messages. You could follow the missions that pop up on your huntermate or ignore them. As far as I can tell, nothing is gated behind the completion of any of them. So as soon as you start you can do as you please, unlock outposts, lookout points and other assorted collectibles around the land. Not to mention trying to land your first, of many, kills.
Graphics: Game is gorgeous as hell. Dense forests that give way to open fields, lakes and rivers carving through the hills. Its just a treat to look at. Not to mention the animals are very well done also. Though if I'm honest (and that's the point right?) the animals could maybe use a second albeit small touch up. Nothing a non critical eye would notice. I can't help but feel like this is the way game maps were supposed to be designed from the beginning. It's so great walking through the bushes and branches hoping that you can get a shot on a deer you can barely makeout in the distance. There are a few low texture and blurry bits but I was too awestruck to notice until the five hour mark.
Sound: The sounds are great and not great. Mixed bag. Mainly some are too loud. Some are recycled leading to confusion and some are kind of odd. The rain is an example of excellence. I absolutely love the rain in this game. It truly feels like I am standing in the forest in a storm, and when thunder occurs, I nearly jumped from my seat. Example of bad sound is when for instance, a rabbit takes off from a few feet from you. Not only is it loud as balls, but it makes the same sound as your polyester jacket scraping tree branches. Sounds like this being repeated led to me constantly wondering if a deer responded to my calls, a rabbit got startled, or I'm just molesting a tree. Another positive though, the voiceovers are quite nice. (at least so far)
Gameplay: It's an incredibly simple premise done quite well. You go into the forest and shoot animals. Main drive is to bag the biggest and best you can. It's a very addictive cycle for myself. The game makes it very easy to decide whats worth you ammo. You get experience for better kills ie right tool for the animal, quick kills, and better trophies. You also level up your skill with a particular weapon or tool type which opens up new variants at an oupost. There are perks and skills that allow you to alleviate the difficulty in subtle and so far non game breaking ways.
ETC: The main gripe here with most people is the grind. It takes a long time to begin unlocking things. Me personally though, the gun you start with is more than sufficient and games like these aren't about racing to the end, it's the journey along the way. Other issues are that when playing with a keyboard and mouse it's currently impossible to sneak effectively. No matter the stance you make hella noise moving through any kind of underbrush. And yes, there are reports of quite a few assorted bugs. Missing ammo, scopes not working, animals glitching out. I haven't personally experienced these but I feel for those who are. I trust that given a little bit of time, the dev team will iron these things out and build upon the solid foundation that they have laid. Even the early days of the Hunter classic were an ugly time.
TLDR: Buggy, beautiful, and fun as hell.
When it comes down to it, this game at its worst is miles better than any other hunting game at it's best.

I'm not usually inclined to write a review but i feel i ought to for this game, i will do my best to keep this updated as time goes on.
For those of you that have played thehunter classic i wouldn't recommend it, for those of you that havn't played thehunter classic i still wouldn't wholeheartedly recommend, there are far too many things that the classic has or did better that dont exist in this new release to make it worth buying.
A visual representation of where my view on this game is at the moment.
I don't recommend  | I recommend
[--------------------------//-|--------------------------]
Pros:
- Jumping! brilliant feature! Having the ability to jump up onto rocks above open terrain, go prone and wait for unsuspecting prey is a brilliant feature, personally i much prefer looking at terrain for firing positions than using the pre determined structures.
- Not having to use your Huntermate to track animals, although it does aid you with an easy to follow cone of direction, you can quite happily walk with your rifle in your hands and track animals which helps dramatically in reducing the time to take the shot, nothing worse than cresting dead ground to find the animal standing mere metres away, with only your phone in your hand.
- Having Need zones on the map - whether it be drinking, sleeping  or eating, you are given a time period in which animals of that type will use these need zones,which helps dramatically at ambushing prey and also giving them a less random feel, they live somewhat structured lives.
- A few different ammo types per weapon, allows you to pick and choose which type of arrow or round you would prefer to use, Softpoint or Polymer.
- Easy to see and understand unlockable skills, this gives an RPG feel to the game as you feel you are progressing toward something, it also gives you the choice in which areas you would like to progress, whether it be stalking or ambushing, and perks for the type of weapons you use most.
- Vast expanse of land to hunt on, this game truly does feel vast with two large reserves to hunt on, both with different landscapes.
- The sheer amount of animals on each reserve is staggering and i doubt you have to go particular far in any direction from any position in order to find them wandering around.
- Animals regularly herd together, the most i've seen so far was about 30 odd whitetails wandering together at the foot of a valley, it truly was a sight to see.
- Hunting animals in the same area means animals will start to avoid that area until it has "cooled down", animals with their skittish nature will avoid areas in which they feel threatened, you will still see animals in these areas just less of them, and the more you hunt in the same spot the less animals will wander into it.
- When walking through particular thick vegetation/trees you hear the sound of your nylon jacket, which is incredibly immersive, however rabbits running through the same vegetation appear the make the same noise, i didnt know rabbits were made of nylon (i will admit that after several years of neglecting ear defense this may just be that my hearing is shot and that the two sounds appear to me as the same sound)
- There is a guide available by Daniel which shows you how to make your game less blurry and sharper, im enjoying the game more now that i have wiped the slober out of my eyes.
- No microtransactions - probably the biggest selling point of this game.
- Heart rate and stances effecting weapon sway, this prevents you from being able to run and gun accurately (not that you would neccesarily want to but a good game mechanic to have)
- When in the prone position grass and foliage infront of you inhibits sight picture on target, personally i love this, it requires you to either crawl forward to flatten the grass then crawl back in order to optomise your firing postion, or move to a spot where grass wont effect your sight.
- The ability to turn off tutorials / mission system / multiplayer nametags / downed animal highlight / spotting outline / audio clue visualization / spatial tracking cone / Points of interest / need zone icons / track effects. Turning everything off gives you the ability to hunt with your own hearing and sight.
- Animals leave "channels" in long grass and brush, this helps when stalking or chasing down a wounded animal as an almost perfect trail is left behind.
Cons:
- Graphics, the graphics are OK but are incredibly hard to run for those with dated PCs, i would go as far to say it is heavily unoptimised. Even with the ability to max any modern released game you will be pushing 30 - 60 FPS with medium/high settings in which the foliage will look less than realistic.
- The horrible grind to unlock weapons/lures/etc in the shops - you have to harvest an outrageous amount of animals in order to unlock even the most simple lures or weapon of choice, i feel you should be able to buy any of the kit from get go.
- Animals very rarily spook, you can shoot and harvest one only to walk a short distance and repeat, gunshots/running for the most part dont have a very large spook radius.
- Fast traveling is virtually non existent which is a pain as you have to take time to travel to need zones or particular favourite spots, the ability to put down tents in TheHunter classic sorted this problem.
- No ability to errect your own structures, such as tree stands, 360 stands, ground hides etc, the fact that TheHunter classic has this feature yet the new edition doesn't is a real shame, it feels like a real step backwards.
- By Comparison to TheHunter classic there is very little equipment/weapons/lures available, which i hope with potential future DLC will be expanded upon, again a step backwards.
- The game states that clothes do not have any effect on whether animals can detect you, this again is a feature that is included in theHunter classic with the addition of Ghillie suits, 3D sneaky clothing etc.
- The bugs although not game destroying are rather annoying and with some fairly simple bugs i am astounded that this game was released with them, and that after days after release they still persist is mind boggling.
- According to the games sound indicator, you give the same amount of sound crawling slowly as you do running.
- No ability to range your rifle to anything other than the pre determined 100m.
Overall i feel this game is headed in the right direction but as it currently stands lacks some pretty major components of a hunter game, i feel a mixture between this and TheHunter Classic would be ideal, bring back some of those core gameplay elements whilst also bringing in better optimisation and bringing the grind feeling down to a nice enjoyable level and giving the player more freedom on what to hunt from the get go.
Having said all that i still feel a burning urge to make this review even longer and do a side by side comparison of the two games which would show you just many features/gameplay aspects have been removed for the sake of improving the graphics, there are so many!

Let's get to the meat and list what I DON'T like about the game...

2. Not enough truck accessories. I've seen truckers really deck-out their ride and practically pimp it with mutliple lights, neon ground FX, DVD / TV, game consoles, outrageous stereo systems, interior uphostery upgrades, even compact microwaves and fridges, but nope ... none of that here ... bummer.
3. No animated cut scenes. It really needs some, especially during transit on ferries and trains.
4. Resting process is lame and empty. It needs an actual restroom break and/or a trip inside a convenience store while refueling. Truckers got to have their coffee, jerky, and twinkies ... you know?
5. Headlight and Taillight systems of A.I. traffic is rather dull and dim both in the mirrors and on the highway. This might be hardware related, so maybe we just need a slider adjustment to brighten them and add oncoming traffic lense flare.
6. No functioning radios, No CB chatter whatsoever, not even a check-in for dispatch. The best you can do is to find a stream link to an online scanner or CB repeater and add it to the game's stream player list.
7. No physical viewable damage to anything. The game really needs this to be an ultimate hit.
Things that I like...
1. Love the engine and environment sound FX. Most realistic samples I've ever heard so far.
2. I really enjoy picking up a load from a quarry. It's almost as if I can feel the weight of the trailer tugging on the tractor. Plus the gearing sounds climbing the hill out of there is super awesome too. I'm impressed!
3. More sound FX ... DAMAGE EFFECTS. Those sounds make it fun to deliberately tear up your truck. Just needs some physical damage to go with it.
4. Really like all the city layouts. Some are very spacious.
5. Pedestrians are a nice touch.
6. So many roads to choose from.
7. Scenery is very pleasant outside of towns.
8. The ability to hitch and unhitch at will is very cool.
9. Extra lighting accessories are a big plus. Very helpful for night driving.
10. A.I. vehicles have quality intelligence worthy of being obstacles.
As you can see, I like it more than I hate it. I probably would recommend it.

Let's get this out of the way. I'm a bit late to the Life is Strange party. I never played the original game until around June of 2017 when the game was offered as a free game for Playstation Plus users. Since then, I have played through the original and all of its episodes.
Life is Strange: Before the Storm is a game developed by Deck Nine Games and is a prequel that takes place 3 years before the events that transpire in Life is Strange. So what's different?
Firstly, unlike the first entry into the series where Max could rewind time; long gone are the days of that feature (at least for now it seems) and has been replaced with Chloe's Backtalk. Backtalking is basically a skill challenge that has the player looking for vital pieces and words in one's dialogue or surroundings to create what I'll call "witty rebuttals"seeing as Chloe plays differently to what Max did in the original game. Also gone are the days of taking photographs in each chapter of an Episode, but instead are replaced with Graffiti. Graffiti allows for the player to search out areas that might not normally go or look to find a spot to tag. Some are in plain sight, while others are hidden very cleverly which I enjoy. Aside from those differences in the mechanics, Before the Storm in my eyes, plays very much like the first game which I welcome with open arms because your actions still have consequences or might affect later outcomes in the game. Unfortunately seeing as this is only Episode 1, there are a few actions that require thought earlier in one's playthrough that might change the outcome later; however, I don't fault the game for it.
In terms of the story, it's hard to describe seeing as it would spoil a mass majority of one's playthrough. As I said above, this game takes place 3 years before the events of Life is Strange and players assume the role of Chloe; however, there is a slew of characters in terms of its cast that reappears from that game into this game including some new faces. Voice acting for the most part, is top notch and while, I can understand why some people were shocked to see that Ashly Burch wasn't returning to reprise her role as Chloe; the voice actress for Chloe hits the role perfectly in my eyes. Chloe being the rebellous teen and just how her lines are delivered are full of emotion and has the right amount of that teenage angst that we've all gone through at one point and time in our lives. While some points in Episode 1's story felt a bit predictable, Episode 1 had the perfect length behind it and honestly has me clamoring for Episode 2 already since Episode 1 leaves off on somewhat of a cliffhanger.
In terms of sound design and the game's soundtrack, I can simply say that it is perfect. The game uses an "indie" soundtrack which fits with the main character and the situations you are put into as you go through Episode 1. While it might not always be my favorite genre of music, I found myself tapping my foot along to some of the songs in certain parts of the game with a smile on my face as I trudged through the game's story.
So is the game worth it for the price? Honestly, I would say yes. I bought the Deluxe Edition of the game a few days after launch and my playthrough ran about 6 hours in total (including the times where I went AFK). While the game might not fully be replayable as of yet (not saying that you can't replay it since the game does offer a Collector Mode which allows players to revisit chapters to collect the Optional Graffiti without it affecting your decisions that you made), it's a breath of fresh air that I quite rather enjoy. Before the Storm is a game that every player should play without a walkthrough on their first pass through the game. Words cannot aptly describe how good of a game this is in my eyes.

This is probably the most thorough review I'll ever write on Steam, so I want to say some things before I start:
I'm only reviewing the first episode in its release state. I don't know yet if I'm going to update.
I'm going to refer to the original game as LiS, to this one as BfS.
LiS was a great game. People are hyped and give BfS 10/10 ratings, disregarding its obvious flaws. I would give it neither a thumb up nor a thumb down, but a "meh" rating.
BfS isn't developed by the same studio and you notice that extremely.
My review will get lots of thumbs down because the review system is broken. Giving a thumb down means telling that the review isn't helpful. People abuse the thumbs to vote down everything that doesn't agree with their opinion while voting up single sentence reviews that don't help anyone.
I'll try to keep spoilers out of my review as much as possible.
Let's take a look at some negative aspects, starting with technical stuff and proceeding into more "relevant" things:
- Graphics
While LiS was based on the Unreal Engine, BfS uses the Unity Engine.
Believe it or not, but the simple graphics are a lot worse. I actually loved the art style of LiS, but in BfS I actually deleted every single screenshot I took (and I take a lot of screenshots) because they just weren't pleasant to look at. Textures often completely lack detail, anti-aliasing is non-existent (even on maxed out AA settings) which is actually a huge problem in this game, even though I usually don't care much about AA. All my screenshots were heavily
pixelated.
- Controls
Remember how you chose an action in LiS by holding the left mouse button and moving the mouse into the direction of the action? In BfS, you hold the left mouse button and use WASD to choose. In other words, in order to look at stuff or interact you need two hands now instead of only one. It's not a big deal, it just makes the game less comfortable at many scenes.
- Voices
You've probably heard already that Chloe has a new voice. You probably still have her accent from LiS inside your head. That's gone. Not a big deal, you could get used to that - the problem is that her new actress just isn't good. At  some points she sounds completely unmotivated and just talks her text down without any motivation at all. Near the end of the game you will also notice heavy breathing and hear clearly that she was standing to close at the microphone.
Chloe isn't the only character with a new voice, for example the famous angry David Madsen sounds really soft now.
- Animations
Lots of animations look really clunky and unnatural. I wanted to call an exorcist when Rachel was turning her head. In dialogues, characters often lack facial expressions. David gets angry and raises his voice, but his soft and calm expression stays. Until BfS I never noticed what a killer missing facial expressions can be.
- Paradoxes and other minor flaws
For example, there's a photo of pirate Chloe and pirate Max hanging in Chloe's living room. However, the Max with the eyepatch on the photo isn't the young Max we know from flashbacks, but the old Max you play as in LiS.
In Chloe's diary entry about a schoolmate she writes something such as "He's exactly like my class schedule. We have history, but no chemistry." You can read this while following the task "Go to your chemistry class."
The game is full of those details.
- Chloe's character
Alright, Chloe's a rebel. But sometimes it's just too much. In the beginning of the game you can look at a knife stuck inside a wooden wall and Chloe says something like "This looks exactly like the knife my mom didn't want to buy me for my birthday." She also likes tossing items just to the ground after using them, even if she borrowed them from a friend few seconds ago. I mean, come on...
- Dialogues
Some dialogues actually make me cringe. I won't go into details here due to possible spoilers. There's a new feature which enables you to argue with people. Everytime you have to persuade someone, just look out for the "arguing" sign and you know that's the way to go. It triggers a minigame like in Monkey Island, where your enemy delivers a statement and you have to counter with a fitting insult. Despite the fact that everyone beyond twelve years of age knows that you basically lose an argument as soon as you just start insulting your opponent, the arguing dialogues are just the worst in the game. They are just completely incoherent. You answer to a statement and suddenly your opponent starts about a completely different matter. After winning the minigame, it always seems to me like people stop arguing because they are annoyed by Chloes inability to argue, not because she "won". But of course Chloe had to be as rebel as possible and so it works in the game's context.
Furthermore, the reactions and answers of characters sometimes don't seem logical at all.
- Other characters
Except for Chloe and Rachel, the characters in this game mostly completely lack depth. You meet them, they start talking about a topic, you choose one or two answers, you go on with the game. I don't even remember what we talked about.
I didn't like Rachel at all until the ending of the episode, but that's just my personal opinion.
- Exploration
Remember how you strolled around in LiS, trying to find out everything about the world and its inhabitants? Trying to find motives for a good photo? It's almost non-existent in BfS. Chloe's a rebel and there's a stage play coming up at school. Everything you'll find are some posters about drug abuse and the upcoming stage play, without giving you any more information. Instead of taking photos, you can draw graffitis at walls now. There's a graffiti in every scene, so you just walk along walls until you find the spot to get your achievement.
Now, some more positive aspects:
+ Clothes
After the intro you have to change clothes. You can choose the outfit you want to wear during the episode. There are two different T-shirts in the base game, you unlock three more outfits if you buy the deluxe edition and you can play as classic Chloe (without blue hair) if you preordered the game.
- I probably don't have to mention that this feature is just a huge cashgrab for Square Enix. It's a neat feature anyway.
+ Soundtrack
Just like LiS, BfS has a nice indie rock soundtrack which fits well into the game.
- Remember the scenes in LiS, where you just enjoyed the scenery and a nice song to it? They are in BfS too, but somehow they don't seem to fit into the game or they were just executed half-heartedly. They are nice to have anyway.
+ Gameplay
Well, the gameplay won't surprise you. If you liked the gameplay of LiS and can live without time travel puzzles, you'll be satisfied.
+ New ideas
After the cool intro and the unfortunately very tedious middle part, the developers suddenly had their own ideas in the end and this is where the game finally shine. This might be a little spoiler, but there's a difference between Max and Chloe. While Max was very calm, Chloe can become very angry. At some part in the game it suddenly gets emotional, and instead of only showing Chloe's emotions, you actually get to live out Chloe's emotions. And it feels great.
The arguing minigame is actually quite exciting, despite it's obvious lack of logic.
For each graffiti, you can choose between two different messages which will also show up in your graffiti diary. Neat little gimmick.
+ The ending
Just like every LiS episode, episode 1 of BfS has a great ending. It didn't only leave me sitting with my mouth open, it actually sent a chill down my spine.
Conclusion:
If it wasn't for the first 20 minutes and especially the last 20 minutes of the episode (3.5 hours in total), I would actually give the game a clear thumb down. I give it a "meh" rating. It has very obvious flaws, but it's quite enjoyable if you're a LiS fan.

I was a big fan of the original Life is Strange, and have been very much looking forward to getting further insight into Chloe's backstory since this prequel was announced. I was a little worried that it wouldn't turn out well, but am pleased to say I am not disappointed in the slightest after playing EP 1.
I will do my best to keep spoilers out of this review, and to remember to update it after further episodes have been released.
4/5 ★
I don't have particularly much to add that I didn't say in reviewing EP1, EP2 just feels like a continuation, as it should. All the important relationships and characters get expanded upon further yet still leave a lot of room for the next episode.
One problem which has always been present in both games so far is the description of the dialogue choices. However, EP2 seemed to struggle a little bit more than EP1 did at properly summising what Chloe was going to say in the 1-2 words you're given to go off. Consequently it can be quite easy to say something you didn't mean to, by misinterpreting the prompt.
On a similar note, it remains tricky to try and reconcile choices *you* as the player would make vs choices you think Chloe should/would make. Having fallen in love with Chloe's character over the original LiS and then EP1 of this game, I have been trying to make the choices that I believe best fit her character, rather than necessarily what I would do. Combine this with the character Deck Nine have built for her throughout the plot, and the character we know she becomes in LiS, it can be tricky to determine which option to select. You might instinctively pick one option, but know that it's not really what Chloe would have done.
This isn't really a criticism of the game as it's not really resolvable, but more just an element of the genre the LiS franchise sits in.
All that being said, I still love this game and feel I properly connect with the charactes when playing it. Chloe continues to be a complex character, but relatable and very well portrayed.
Still definitely recommend playing this game, but after completing the original LiS first.
4.5/5 ★
This episode focuses almost soley on Chloe and Rachel, without much exploration into other characters, but that is not a problem in the slightest. I feel delving too much into supporting characters would have caused confusion and lessened the experience.
Whilst not perfect, the game does a very good job of portraying Chloe's character, which is one of the main things that anyone who has played the original LiS will take away from playing this. In LiS we obviously saw a lot of Chloe and related to her there, but it was all from Max's perspective. LiS:BtS does very well at connecting the Chloe we know from the outside to the Chloe we see on the inside. She is a complex character, and not always easy to understand. The nature of this game involves giving the player choices to make as to the actions Chloe takes, and the choices that are presented to the player are usually in a summarised format that doesn't alwys indicate exactly what Chloe will do. As such, you can sometimes find that she'll act out of character compared to how we knew her in LiS, and how she behaves throughout the rest of the game. This is the main reason for dropping from 5★ to 4.5★ review overall.
The main issue is that in LiS, Chloe's character wasn't something the player had control over, as we played as Max. Chloe's character was architectured in full by the developers, something not entirely possible in a game set from Chloe's perspective, without removing the whole "choice" aspect.
All things considered however, I can't fault Deck Nine. They had a hard job to do, and pulled it off well. They needed to write Chloe in such a way that the player can understand and relate to her complex character, and all the while not exceeding the bounds of the character we know she will become in LiS. On top of this, the player still needs the ability to feel like their choices have an impact. It was a hard job to do, and they did it well.
I can't write too much here without giving away spoilers, so will keep this section short.
Rachel was always a mysterious character from LiS. As Max, we only ever heard what Chloe said about Rachel, and a few comments from other people. It was very interesting to be properly introduced to her character for the first time. Whilst it's great to see her and learn a lot more about her, I feel her introduction fell a little short of the mark, and caused a chunk of EP1 to feel rushed, almost as if there was part of the story missing. Whilst I've not played the future episodes yet, I have the feeling that maybe this could have done with being a 4 or 5 episode game, and slowing down a bit when it comes to bringing Rachel into the story. This being said, this is does not ruin the game in any way, and does not dissuade me from wholeheartedly recommending this game.
There isn't too much in the way of customisations, but that's most likely because the game was designed to be played in one particular way.
The controls are slightly improved over LiS, options are now selectable via the keyboard rather than requiring you to move your mouse.
I felt the FOV was a bit too close for my liking, but got used to it after a while. No way to change it.
No ultrawide support, again, got used to it after a while, and I'm pretty sure this game is *supposed* to be played in 16:9.

All we can say is wow... Not a review here but an astute observation... This story-driven prequel taps a nerve.  It's an honest homage to the first - A dedication to breakthrough character portrayals made even more epic by the stunning fandom, personal interpretations, and emotional connections already developed and shared by the legions of observers now comfortably entranced by the entire atmosphere and interconnectivity of the realm known as arcadia bay.
Very rarely does interactive media bolster within itself a blossoming social movement like this now multistudio franchise is churning.

As much as Dontnod's original Life is Strange was like lightning in a bottle, with its authentic feeling tale of teenage angst and superpowers and puzzle solving, I wasn't sure that a prequel would really work. That's the problem with prequels. You know how it ends. I wasn't sure how you could even make another Life is Strange game without Max, Time Travel, the storm, and all of the various bits and bobs that made it tick.
I'm glad to say I was wrong. Deck9 has made something that's both familiar and fresh in Before the Storm. It's every bit as engrossing as Dontnod's original title.
Wheras LiS is a game about Max, and things that happen to Max, BTS is a game about who Chloe is. Wheras Max was a blank canvas on which the player was expected to project, Chloe is very much the opposite. Deck9 has taken the opportunity to retread old ground and new. With the help of (the sadly absent from her role due to the union strike) Ashley Burch they've drilled down in to the meat of what a clever, yet troubled teenager really is.
Where Max just tries not to rock the boat until she's thrust in to action by virtue of time travel powers, Chloe's "backtalk" mechanic is innate and familiar to her. There's no awkward phase, the game swiftly tutorializes you, the player in its use, but you're just catching up to something Chloe already knows like the back of her hand.
And that's where Deck9's outing really shines. The original game had a lot of heart, but it was primarily a puzzle solving excercise from the lens of a usually detached, and somewhat morose protagonist. The story worked because of everyone that orbited Max, including in no small part, Chloe herself. BTS, however, places you in the shoes (and internal monologue) of Chloe herself, and that makes all the difference.
Chloe has opinions, feelings, self delusions, and vulnerabilities that feel instantly familiar and real to anyone that was ever on the "bad kid" spectrum at her age. You're not so much defining Chloe as simply choosing what aspects of her you apply to a series of almost exclusively conversation based puzzles and challenges. You have dialog options not so much to define what kind of person you are, but because people are complex and conflicted, and the writing does a great job of carrying this idea through in to gameplay and consequences. Consequences that are, by default, far more impact without the ability to simply rewind time to find the "right answer."
While you may know from having played its sequel what the major story beats are likely to be, it is still profoundly affecting to see the world from her perspective. That's where the real interest lies, not in exploring the limits of cosmic time travel powers, but exploring what lies beneath all that smack talk and cringeworthy pseudo-badassery that all the "bad kids" seem to have.
It's not so much a question of what becomes of her interactions with students, teachers, parents, and Rachel Amber, but who Chloe is. It's so well done I'm perfectly happy to trade control of time and space for really good trash talk, and that's saying something.
If you liked Life is Strange, this is sure to hit the same buttons, in a slightly different way. Highly reccommended.

First things first: this is a great game.  Some of the critics gave this game average reviews, which I think was undeserved.  The gameplay seems to draw in elements from lots of different third-person open world games in a way that really works.  The game itself is beautiful and really easy to get immersed in.  If you play for long enough you really get that feeling of bleakness and despair driving around the wasteland.
That being said, some of the complaints for this game are fair.  I'm going to point some of these out because if they make a sequel, I hope they improve on some of these aspects:
-The customization is bad.  The game sort of markets itself on giving you the ability to create your very own Magnum Opus.  Unfortunately, there doesn't seem like there's a whole lot of customization options when it comes to designing the look of your car.  You can mix and match different upgrades, but for the most part the cosmetic options are pretty limited.  For a Mad Max game, this is pretty bad.
-Some of the side missions are repetitive and monotonous.  Throughout the game you have to clear out camps, scarecrows, minefields, etc. in order to reduce the threat level in the different areas.  Some of these can be pretty fun, but some of them, such as the minefields, can be pretty tedious.  A lot of the car upgrades require that you reduce the threat level a lot, so you will be forced to do a lot of these if you want the best upgrades.
-The story really only picks up during the second half of the game, mostly at the end.  Sure, there are little side stories when you go to the individual strongholds, but they're not very in depth.  For a vast majority of the game there's not a whole lot of story elements going on, you're mostly running around and taking care of side missions, clearing out camps, scavenging, etc.

Fun game. Plays like a cross between a generic platformer and a side scroller, segueing into bullet hell as you progress.
Classes can be a bit unbalanced but most of them are useful for a specific purpose. The rune abilities and various spells and special abilities add a nice patch of variance to the grindfest. The effects of the traits vary from crippling to distracting to unexpectedly helpful, and are for the most part cleverly devised.
The claim that "every time you die all the gold you've collected can be used to upgrade you manor" is misleading; each upgrade you buy or armor/rune you unlock raises all prices across the board, permanantly, and any leftover coin is taken by Charon as a fee whenever the new generation enters the dungeon. As everything becomes more expensive, you will routinely lose all of the coins the previous generation had amassed because there's simply nothing cheap enough for you to buy. It's an unfortunate bit of artificial difficulty, and it slows down levelling to a crawl (thus effectively slowing down exploration due to level scaling). Expect to go through dozens of generations before you unlock any truly interesting upgrades.

This is my first review of a game, but I though this game deserved a review as it's been getting a lot of negative reviews that are unwarranted in my opinion.
I live in South Africa and have been hunting a couple of times before and it's something I enjoy. What I enjoy about hunting is that you go out into wide open spaces of beautiful nature. You have to patiently stalk your prey, following spoor (tracks), looking at their dung, checking that you're not upwind. It's not easy, and some days you can go the whole day without even getting close to having a shot at your prey.
So in context of this game, I never thought I'd ever find or enjoy any hunting game that gives me the same thrill as I get in real life. But I was wrong. This game does really well in making you feel like you're in this beautiful nature reserve with some of the best graphics and sound design I've seen in a game. It really is stunning. I often just stare at a beautiful sunrise or a strong gust of wind blowing leaves off the trees around me. The beautiful world you get to play in alone is worth the asking price for this game.
The actual hunting part has been done extremely well. In this game I've felt like it really is quite close to hunting in real life. Patience is key. Checking wind direction, following tracks, listening for your prey's sounds, looking at your prey's dung etc. has been really well thought out and implemented. It can take hours to find and hunt the prey you're looking for, but it feels worth it.
I've seen a lot of people complain about bugs in their reviews, and I have seen a couple, but none of them were game breaking in my opinion. If that is what is holding you back from buying this game, then let me assure you, it's not that bad. The bugs aren't that major, and I have to say that it runs extremely well on my machine. My settings are all cranked up and I'm running a GeForce 970, 8GB RAM, Intel i5 2500k processor, and have experienced no lag or crashes.
If you want a game to get lost in, that takes time and patience, that is beautiful and realistic, then give this a go.
I hope they bring out an African map in a future DLC!

tl;dr  I like it, but it is a $30 USD Open Beta at the moment.
The things that work in the game are good.  It feels a lot like theHunter Classic from several years back, but without subscription fees. That's the best thing about the game.  There's more here at launch than the Classic game had at launch, which is also a plus.
The problem is that it is absolutely riddled with bugs, poor design decisions, and a lack of certain features which made the Classic game fun to play for so many years.  It easily could have used another 6 months to a year of development before release. Or at the very least, released it as an Early Access game, because that's essentially what it is at this point in time.
The Good:
1. The hunting is great.  Aside from a few bugs and other minor annoyances.
2. Graphics are really nice.  Easy to immerse yourself in the world.
3. No subscription fee. I've been waiting for a subscription-less Hunter ever since the Classic game released.
4. No microtransactions or other real money purchases. All the weapons and equipment are able to be bought in game without having to pay real money for them.
5. Xbox One controller support.  Seriously this is great. With as much walking and creeping around that you have to do, it's nice to just use the controller and sit back relaxed.  And you can still use the mouse to shoot if you want. I've been using the controller to move, and the mouse for precision shooting.
6. The game is self-contained. No more having to go to theHunter website to setup your hunt and launch.
The Bad:
1. Bugs. Bugs everywhere.  From sounds not being played, to hunting structures not allowing you to build them, to animals getting stuck in the scenery, it is absolutely riddled with bugs.
2. Progression system feels poorly designed.   It takes forever to acquire enough "experience" to unlock new weapons and gear.  13 hours into the release version, I'm level 9 and have unlocked 1 gun, a bullet type, and maybe a caller?  The perks and skills system could use a reworking as well.   Apparently at least one perk doesn't seem to work for anyone.
3. No global leaderboards or competitions.  What's the point of harvesting a great trophy animal, if you can't see where it ranks compared to other people, or enter it into a competition? The competitions are one thing that really gave the Classic Hunter such longevity.
4. The missions.  One of the first missions you get is to "photograph" a deer for a woman's book.  I want to hunt, not take screenshots. Adding to the frustration is that it seems like you have to do this in a very specific area, and at a very specific distance from the deer. Apparently you get more photography missions later, that get even more specific.  Maybe this could have been more fun if they actually modeled the camera like a real world DSLR set up for wildlife shooting. Instead the game's camera is basically the HUD removed, and replaced with a grid. No zoom controls that I could see.  So basically your smart phone from 5 years ago had more features in the camera than this one.
I'm pretty much ignoring the missions right now unless I accidentally trigger one.
Could be Better:
1. A lot of things could use a bit of rework or tweaking.  One thing I'd like to see added is more fast travel options. If I build a hunting stand somewhere, I'd like the option of fast traveling to it like you can do with the outposts.
If the devs don't abandon the game, and continue working on it, it has a lot of potential.  I mostly like what is here now, and I could potentially spend a lot of time with this game.  It wouldn't take a lot to flip the thumbs down to a thumbs up. Mostly fix the glaring bugs and maybe tweak a few of the systems in game. That's not asking much.  I just have a hard time fully recommending the game in its current state.

Once apon a time there was a young boy who wanted to play rust. He got the game from a humble bundle, at a criminal price. The little boy had seen lots of rust, and those who played it. He thought that rust would be a game with common goals for all players. He thought that that common goal would be to have the best base and most guns. He was right, except he forgot about 75% about all of the videos he had seen. He realized that each video had someone being raided, or raiding. He had overlooked this key fact. On the first day, he built himself a nice little shack out of wood. He came back on not 30 minutes later to find out that the entire base had been burned down, and he had been killed. He thought, " Oh well. **** happens. " This continued for days. And the days turned into weeks. Until he just had enough. He thought that if he had played more than an hour on a small server he could get atleast a small unraidable base. He was wrong. Very, very wrong. So he quit rust. But the allure of getting good loot had won him over. So he had enough. He played 7 hours straight until he had a big base. He then logged off for a day. He was blessed that the rust gods had favored him. He had not been raided! He played almost endlessly. All the way until he had raided many, and had many enemies, and allies. At the end of the day he was very proud. What he didn't know about was the fact that the wipe happened the very next day. He was depressed, but he still fought. And to this day, he still plays rust. The End.
Now that the story is over, Rust is a game that has no end to fun. The rage meter is high with this game. Think about the most you have raged at a game, and then multiply that by 5. That is how much you will rage. The game also takes a lot to get used to. But, overall, if you want a game with almost endless fun, then purchase rust. I had gotten rust for 5 dollars in a humble bundle sale. The price that is listed on steam, is still criminal. I do love rust, for the friends i have made playing this game, and i reccomend this to any average gamer, because all servers are not PVP. If you want to sharpen your skills or just build, then join a PVE server. Don't join PVP unless you want to rage like a bull.

An amazing rpg game about real morality; it's system is not based on a karma number where you can gain good karma by donating to a priest, and then be reguarded by a saint by everyone in the world.  Instead it looks at you, and it sees that you were willing to kill beings who inferior to you in most every way just because they were in your way.  This game made me look at every rpg game I've ever played and wonder if every single being i killed truly deserved to be murdered.  This is especially true when I knew i had nothing to gain from killing it and there was no challenge.  Undertale makes its killings feel real.  If you kill something or someone in real life it shouldn't be fun or a challenge you look forward to.  Taking somethings life should have careful consideration; something rpgs never care about you kill without hesitation when playing an rpg because it has never mattered when you killed a stereotypical monster, because monsters are always bad, right?  This game however directly punishes that way of thinking the punishment for killing an innocent isn't 5 points deducted from your good karma meter that you can go donate to a church to regain, it's a permanent mistake that will change the way you live in and out of the game.  People will treat you differently, because you are different you are a killer.  In my opinion that is perfect game design people won't look over the fact that you killed others because of some redeeming act.  Instead it's a permanent scar and it's this factor that makes undertale feel like a real world you can step into.  That is why Undertale is my new favorite game.

This is my first review of a game, but I though this game deserved a review as it's been getting a lot of negative reviews that are unwarranted in my opinion.
I live in South Africa and have been hunting a couple of times before and it's something I enjoy. What I enjoy about hunting is that you go out into wide open spaces of beautiful nature. You have to patiently stalk your prey, following spoor (tracks), looking at their dung, checking that you're not upwind. It's not easy, and some days you can go the whole day without even getting close to having a shot at your prey.
So in context of this game, I never thought I'd ever find or enjoy any hunting game that gives me the same thrill as I get in real life. But I was wrong. This game does really well in making you feel like you're in this beautiful nature reserve with some of the best graphics and sound design I've seen in a game. It really is stunning. I often just stare at a beautiful sunrise or a strong gust of wind blowing leaves off the trees around me. The beautiful world you get to play in alone is worth the asking price for this game.
The actual hunting part has been done extremely well. In this game I've felt like it really is quite close to hunting in real life. Patience is key. Checking wind direction, following tracks, listening for your prey's sounds, looking at your prey's dung etc. has been really well thought out and implemented. It can take hours to find and hunt the prey you're looking for, but it feels worth it.
I've seen a lot of people complain about bugs in their reviews, and I have seen a couple, but none of them were game breaking in my opinion. If that is what is holding you back from buying this game, then let me assure you, it's not that bad. The bugs aren't that major, and I have to say that it runs extremely well on my machine. My settings are all cranked up and I'm running a GeForce 970, 8GB RAM, Intel i5 2500k processor, and have experienced no lag or crashes.
If you want a game to get lost in, that takes time and patience, that is beautiful and realistic, then give this a go.
I hope they bring out an African map in a future DLC!

tl;dr  I like it, but it is a $30 USD Open Beta at the moment.
The things that work in the game are good.  It feels a lot like theHunter Classic from several years back, but without subscription fees. That's the best thing about the game.  There's more here at launch than the Classic game had at launch, which is also a plus.
The problem is that it is absolutely riddled with bugs, poor design decisions, and a lack of certain features which made the Classic game fun to play for so many years.  It easily could have used another 6 months to a year of development before release. Or at the very least, released it as an Early Access game, because that's essentially what it is at this point in time.
The Good:
1. The hunting is great.  Aside from a few bugs and other minor annoyances.
2. Graphics are really nice.  Easy to immerse yourself in the world.
3. No subscription fee. I've been waiting for a subscription-less Hunter ever since the Classic game released.
4. No microtransactions or other real money purchases. All the weapons and equipment are able to be bought in game without having to pay real money for them.
5. Xbox One controller support.  Seriously this is great. With as much walking and creeping around that you have to do, it's nice to just use the controller and sit back relaxed.  And you can still use the mouse to shoot if you want. I've been using the controller to move, and the mouse for precision shooting.
6. The game is self-contained. No more having to go to theHunter website to setup your hunt and launch.
The Bad:
1. Bugs. Bugs everywhere.  From sounds not being played, to hunting structures not allowing you to build them, to animals getting stuck in the scenery, it is absolutely riddled with bugs.
2. Progression system feels poorly designed.   It takes forever to acquire enough "experience" to unlock new weapons and gear.  13 hours into the release version, I'm level 9 and have unlocked 1 gun, a bullet type, and maybe a caller?  The perks and skills system could use a reworking as well.   Apparently at least one perk doesn't seem to work for anyone.
3. No global leaderboards or competitions.  What's the point of harvesting a great trophy animal, if you can't see where it ranks compared to other people, or enter it into a competition? The competitions are one thing that really gave the Classic Hunter such longevity.
4. The missions.  One of the first missions you get is to "photograph" a deer for a woman's book.  I want to hunt, not take screenshots. Adding to the frustration is that it seems like you have to do this in a very specific area, and at a very specific distance from the deer. Apparently you get more photography missions later, that get even more specific.  Maybe this could have been more fun if they actually modeled the camera like a real world DSLR set up for wildlife shooting. Instead the game's camera is basically the HUD removed, and replaced with a grid. No zoom controls that I could see.  So basically your smart phone from 5 years ago had more features in the camera than this one.
I'm pretty much ignoring the missions right now unless I accidentally trigger one.
Could be Better:
1. A lot of things could use a bit of rework or tweaking.  One thing I'd like to see added is more fast travel options. If I build a hunting stand somewhere, I'd like the option of fast traveling to it like you can do with the outposts.
If the devs don't abandon the game, and continue working on it, it has a lot of potential.  I mostly like what is here now, and I could potentially spend a lot of time with this game.  It wouldn't take a lot to flip the thumbs down to a thumbs up. Mostly fix the glaring bugs and maybe tweak a few of the systems in game. That's not asking much.  I just have a hard time fully recommending the game in its current state.

Pros:
- Great visuals
- Immersive sound design
- It could just be because this is my introduction to his type of game, but it was a thrill listening for and tracking down animals to kill.  I look forward to some more difficult targets that will require more time.
- Feels welcoming to players newer to this style of game with a bit more casual presentation.  This of course could be looked at negatively to veterans of this type of game or theHunter Classic.
- Speedy loading times.  I don't even have a SSD, but this game loads from the title screen into the game world very quickly which surprised me considering how large the map is.
- Various challenges, quests, and lore discovery locations are sprinkled throughout the map, giving some extra activities outside of general hunting.
- The two hunting reserve maps are massive in size
Cons:
- The biggest issue right now is that with mouse and keyboard controls you have little to no control over the speed of your movement in each of the stances (walking, crouching, prone).  If you have a controller and test the movement out on that, you'll notice with analog control you can move the stick varying amounts to control your speed and subsequently the amount of noise you make.  Considering how important it is to try and remain silent in a hunting game, this is a pretty big issue at the moment.  Either controller movement needs to have that disabled and rework the amount of noise each stance makes, or keyboard needs an keybinding to slow your pace to a level that makes minimal sound.
- While I've had no crashes (Update: I have experienced my first crash, so this does seem to be a relevant issue for many players), I have had a performance bug which was causing framerate to drop significantly when I was tracking an animal's footprints a lot.  Having too many of these tracking markers will cause the framerate to drop after opening the map or looking at your Huntermate device.  It would fix itself by either putting away the Huntermate or if you killed the tracked animal and collected your trophy.
- Semi annoying menu bug that doesn't let you back out of the menu with escape unless the mouse is hovering over one of the items on the side.
- A few of the animals I've shot seemed like it should have been a clean kill, but they would somehow get away with just a minor wound and run off.  More often than not I found success with my shots though.
- Animal AI was a bit wonky on at least one occasion with a fox that clearly should have been trying to run away, but instead was running circles around me like a friendly pet dog or something.  Perhaps it was being aggresive and trying to attack or something, but it seemed a bit bizarre with it essentially giving me an easy kill.
- Right now it is limited to 12 different animals.  These do have variations to discover, but it would be nice to see some small game targets and birds as well.  I'm assuming we'll see this added down the line at some point when they add some of the planned free and paid DLC content.
- The menus ui and control of them in general just feels like it needs a rework as they look and feel like a placeholder that has been in the game since an earlier state.  There are also some issues with the controls when managing your storage where it just seems to completely break when in that particular menu and you have to back out and open it back up to do anything.

EPISODE 1 Review with Spoilers:
I felt apprehensive of buying this game after hearing about the new developer and voice actor for Chloe. I didn't think that Rhianna DeVries was going to be able to capture Chloe's stubborn and laidback attitude but she did it perfectly. The graphics are amazing and the game runs very well on my computer (which isn't the best in terms of specs). I would say this is better than the first episode of Life is Strange. I actually liked Chloe in this episode. I enjoyed her random comments and really liked the backtalk mechanic. It kept me on edge and introduced an actual time limit on dialogue that Life is Strange didn't have.
Overall, I look forward to the next two episodes of Life is Strange. The ending of episode 1 shows that the acts of Chloe and Rachel are sending ripples through Arcadia Bay. And I can't wait to see what happens with new and returning characters.
EPISODE 2 ADDITION:
This episode really starts to play ball with you now that you are acquainted with Chloe's world. The opening really kicks things off with Chloe being expelled I enjoyed having more of Frank since we didn't see much of him in Episode 1, as well we saw the origins of Chloe's trash pick up truck she later almost rams into Max. There were fewer major choices in this one but they are much more impactful to the story line of the game.
Overall, I really enjoyed this episode and it steps it up from the first episode, with symbolism of Rachel's fire and revenge (in past for the future?) on Victoria and actually seeing Sean Prescott and the GAY. If you liked the first episode, you might like this one much better.

What I think about the first episode:
- Overall the 1st episode is VERY GOOD, the gameplay is like it was in LiS 1, but some stuff changes with the characters too.
- This first episode appealed for our feelings as did LiS 1, however CHLOE AND MAX ARE DIFFERENT PERSON WITH DIFFERENT PERSONALITIES, SO THE GAMES ARE A LOT DIFFERENT TOO, LiS 1 was more calm, strangely nostalgic, even when you play for the 1st time. This game is more like Chloe... Agressive, angry, negligent in some stuff, but it has a lot of fun moments too, because of Rachel.
- Rachel is very sweet and friendly and that's why everybody likes her. Including the players, I think.
- The backtalk mechanism is very nice, but I think there should be more time to decide what's the best option, I do not like to do thinks in a hurry.
There is somethings that don't make sense yet...
1st: Why there are characters that appear in LiS: Before the Storm that do not appear in LiS 1
2nd: How different Chloe is even though she isn't YET what she is was in LiS 1
I really hope this 2 things are explained in the next 2 episodes.
If you liked LiS, and you didn't like Chloe, maybe this game isn't for you then, you need to understand the qualities and flaws in Chloe.

This game had some serious potential. I was a huge fan of the mod, so when I heard about the standalone I was beyond hyped - the development would no longer be held back from the restraints of the Arma II engine... or so I thought. It is no secret that the game is still in it's alpha phase three and a half years after the original release. The original creator of the mod left the development only months after the Standalone was released to work on another game, which has since been cancelled, leaving Dean Hall's original concept to a completely different group.
As for the game itself, there are still many bugs and glitches - I find that whenever I play I can never find any loot, my character ends up starving to death, then rinse and repeat. That feeling that came with finding all kinds of weapons and loot in the original mod is far gone. As updates are sluggish, it seems priorities are put in strange places, such as updated visuals for trees, as opposed to ironing out the many bugs.
In conclusion, the game is in early access and has been for a long time, so I can't really recommend it. I would advise that you only get it if you're aware of the painfully long development time and are fine with it. I've definitely played my money's worth of DayZ, but it's just a shadow of the original mod.

Mad Max is an open world brawler made by the devs behind the Just Cause series. If you've played any of the Batman games you'll be familiar with the combat system as it's very similar, and while it doesn't massively improve upon the formula it does implement it very well. You have your standard light attack, heavy attack, parry and dodge, but on top of that you also have brutal knife finishers which you can perform while carrying knives which are found throughout the game, there are many different kill animations depending on the angle you attack from and they're all very satisfying to pull off and watch. As well as knife finishers you also have Fury kills which are equally visceral and are performed on weak enemies while in Fury mode which is activated once you fill your Fury meter. The combat is definitely the best thing about the game, it's very fluid and just done well, as you upgrade Max you unlock more skills that allow you to pull off even more devastating moves.
As is the trend these days in open world games there are icons all over the map with optional content that add nothing to the game, and even hurts the overall experience I'd argue as tedium does start to set in after awhile, at least it did for me. I would like to see most, if not all of the pointless scrap locations removed if they ever make a sequel, and I would urge the devs to avoid reusing the territory system which is extremely boring, you are basically doing the exact same checklist of objectives over and over just in different zones, it got boring about half way through. Now in stark contrast the side quests and especially the main story are both fantastic and I thoroughly enjoyed them, had the game had more content like that instead of the filler fluff it would have gone from being merely good to great. Another area where the devs really shot themselves in the foot was the Top Dogs who acted as bosses throughout the game, after you kill the first one you're thinking “wow, that was cool” but later you come to realize every Top Dog is exactly the same, just with a different name and a palette swap. If Avalanche make a sequel I would like to see unique bosses instead of the same one recycled 20 times throughout the game.
Other than the pointless fluff content, the biggest issue with the game is the car handling, it's really, really bad. I can't stress enough just how much the car handling hurt my overall experience. Even a fully upgraded Magnum Opus (your car) will spin out of control for seemingly no reason, and God forbid you clip a bucket or something equally insignificant while moving at speed, this will send you into an uncontrollable tailspin. And that's the Magnum Opus, other vehicles you're forced to drive for quests and races handle much worse.
Now the game does do a lot right as well, the cut-scenes are fantastic, helped massively by some top quality voice work. The game also looks stunning, and it runs almost perfectly on PC, I say almost because there is an issue where you will micro freeze for a split second infrequently, I have confirmed this with at least 20 other people who all have the same problem. Other than that blip the game runs at 60fps on max settings without issue, and you don't need a GTX 980 to pull it off, it's extremely well optimised for a wide range of configurations.
In closing I will say I enjoyed the game and I definitely recommend it, maybe not at full price but if it's ever on sale I would snap it up for sure. Just don't get sucked into the fluff content as it will fatigue you by the time you get to the end of the game.

It's easy to take a glance at this game and come away with thinking it just another modern military shooter that glorifies the heroism, as defined by tenacity, persistance, and teamwork, of warfare, but beneath the shades of brown and grey lays a very dark and true-to-life vision of war: it's hell.
This game puts the act of combat under a harsh, harsh, lens and doesn't do it with any filters or restraint. This game will test you more emotionally than it will your skills as a game player. The audio is perfect for the setting, creating a surreal and mesmerizing experience that, at first, seems to want to put murder in the context of a music video or scene from a Michael Bay movie, but you will come to realize is all part of the experience the game dares you to endure.
If there is fault to be found with this game it is sadly in the cover system, a very key element to the game. Shooting, switching weapons, and everything else you can do while prone work just fine, and don't try to do anything novel or new with these systems as they are pretty much as polished as they're going to get in any game. However walking, running, and anything related to moving into, out of, and along cover feels clunky at best and frustrating at worst. Too many times I found myself popping out of cover unintentionally.
However, if you think you can overcome that handicap and want to enjoy a narrative feast, served with viewpoints and beliefs often too taboo to be put in a military shooter, then this is the game for you.
