This review should be prefaced by saying that
.
Borderlands 2 is a game that gets a lot of things right, but gets the core of it wrong, at least in my book. The graphics are great, the writing witty, the characters charming, the story engaging, and the RPG mechanics streamlined. While that's all fine and dandy, the core gameplay, the shooting, is very off. I get that Borderlands 2 is essentially an MMOFPS without the MMO, with regards to mission structure and enemy design, but the bullet-spongey enemies and the constant stream of fetch quests really don't make the core gameplay very engaging. The mechanics
this is actually very good, but you can't have that without having the core gameplay be good.
It cannot be stressed enough that the writing is absolutely fantastic. For most people, the humor is absolutely on point. Some people may find it to be
reliant on memes, but for most, it should work. The story is cliched, but still pulled off in a way that keeps you engaged, and the characters have more depth than the average FPS, which is great. None of the characters are really annoying, and the cast is generally great. I myself get bored of the gunplay, but trudge on through because I find the writing, the story, and the characters to just be
that it outweighs the boredom from shooting sponges.
The RPG mechanics are also great, streamlining what makes an RPG today (loot, quests, stats, buffs, skill trees, etc.) and gets rid of any unneccessary junk. For example, the only loot you can pick up are guns, class modifiers, grenade modifiers, shields, and relics, which provide buffs. You don't have to worry about Random Item #147 to sell back to a vendor: all the loot you can receive are directly related to the core gameplay, which is shooting. The game doesn't pretend to immerse you into a believable world, and so it doesn't need to stock the game world with useless junk just to add backstory: the world they've built has character enough.
While the various guns do feel very different, especially the unique guns, for the most part, they don't convey the power they have well because all enemies, after a certain point, just begin to soak up damage like there's no tomorrow. That itself wouldn't be an issue if they had interesting attack patterns, but most enemies either charge at you or jump around. The AI isn't really attempting to be smart, and combined with the aforementioned bullet-spongey attributes, doesn't make for engaging gunfights, which make up about 99% of the game.
Vehicle segments are present in the game, but are more of just filler content to get you from one place to the next. You have two different classes of vehicle, one being a one-man buggy, and the other a four-man technical, each with two different variants, depending on which turret you want, but it really doesn't matter. The vehicles handle strangely, and in general seems like more could've been done with this.
Compare this with a game I find very similar in terms of gameplay and content: RAGE. Whereas RAGE is developed by id Software, arguably masters of the FPS genre, the gunplay feels smooth, guns feel powerful, enemies are varied and a challenge to fight, and not just because they take insane amounts of damage before falling, and the vehicle segments have some thought put into them, even if they are still relegated to the task of getting you from point A to point B. The only thing RAGE is really missing is a great story and cast of characters, both of which Borderlands 2 does have.
The quests themselves are rather repetitive, of the "go here, fetch
" variety. Sometimes you get a "go here, kill
", but quests are pretty repetitive. The writing behind them, however, is fantastic, which may cover up some of the blemishes and apparent repetitiveness.
I do think bullet-spongey
enemies, weak gunplay, and repetitive quests would have normally been a turn off, but the excellent writing and world building is truly outstanding. There's a lot of Borderlands 2 as well: I'm 60+ hours into the game and still not done. I probably would've been done by now, but I started on the DLC campaigns, so I can imagine at least another 15-20 hours before I'm done, and that's just with one character. You can always NG+ and even play as a new character, which can definitely add to your play time.
Repetitive and boring. Just play Borderlands 1 and that should be enough.

As a huge Mad Max fan I was looking forward to this ever since they announced it many moons ago. It is one of the only games I have ever bought on release day (thanks to the positive reviews on Steam). The last one was probably Citadel for the BBC Micro!
The game itself is great and runs extremely well even on modest PC systems, so kudos to the developers for this! The story is pretty simple and the gameplay revolves around upgrading the Magnum Opus (your car), collecting scrap, helping the locals and pummeling the bad guys.
The driving part of the game is immensely fun, the car feels great to drive and changes according to how you upgrade (go for a speed freak lightly armoured machine or a heavy sluggish tank!). The only letdown is the game does get quite samey but the fun characters, superb car combat and using the harpoon certainly makes up for it. A lot of people complained about the melee combat but I never tied of whacking those desert crazies!
If you are a fan of Mad Max then you will enjoy playing this game and will probably spot quite a few little nods to the film series. Don;t forget to use the in car view sometimes (the V key if I remember correctly), it really adds to the atmosphere! Turn up the sound, put on your scuffed leathers and lay down a rubber road right to freedom!

The story is decent, Chloe is a pretty funny character and I like that some of the choices you make can affect the end result of the game; it makes it interesting and adds replay value. I do like that it's pretty dramatic, and has you feeling lots of feels. Love the feels.
My only complaint is that I wish they would have all of the episodes released at once rather than having us wait so long for the next ones... it just doesn't seem fair, seeing as we've already purchased the entire game. But the suspense is sort of nice, I guess. Maybe a good idea would be to shorten the wait time between episodes, or perhaps make the episodes longer (though I understand this would take a lot more work). Ok guys Im going for the honest no salt review here.  I will also start with the bad because Im hoping it all gets fixed.  Its not a totally negative review so keep reading.
THE BAD - I cant play.  At about ~24 hours in I had found some bugs, most it did not take too much effort to find work arounds but at that 24 hour mark it tanked.  30 minutes into a play session I had my first major crash... game froze, audio loop playing the same half second of audio over and over, and I couldnt even exit to the desktop or use task manager to shut it down.  Had to turn off the PC completely and fire it back up.  The next playthrough the same thing happened in about 5 minutes... rinse and repeat this until I could get ZERO time in before locking up.  I uninstalled/reinstalled and this got me through about 3 hours of gameplay and then all the previous stuff I mentioned happened all over again.  Like I said, I cannot play.  I have a nice set up and really the only thing different from my rig than most others is the SLI.  Im at a loss on this one and its frustrating.
THE GOOD - This game is a plesant mix of sim and arcade.  There are enough moments of "nothing" to make it seem like a sim, but theres also enough going on to keep it from getting boring.... to all the hardcore sim guys out there, hunting for a week in real life not killing anything is still entertaining, doing it in a game is lame and no one would play that.  The graphics are not ground breaking but the lighting, effects, and scale of things make it seem more polished than it probably is (its pleasant walking through the forrest).  As far as the hunter classic went I thought that was a garbage game, I thought it looked like trash, played about the same, and the pay model was a complete rip off.  This game on the other hand is worth the asking price as long as they fix what is above.  Not that it has much competition but it quickly became my favorite hunting game.
THE MEH - The sound, no surround option, why WHY!?  Random light glitchyness and mildly annoying bugs.  The menus, specifically the loadout/store menu is really unpolished.  It also wont save my settings.
THE I WISH - I wish there was a visual difference in the animal racks, not just small and big along with an arbitrary "trophy score" once you harvest the animal.  I wish there was 4wheelers.  I wish small game hunting mattered (cannot harvest upon killing/no XP).  I wish guns were more true to life with their penetration instead of the arcady "weapon balance" to make different calibers arbitrarily matter.  I wish there was a hardcore mode so the sim guys could get their fix along with much more of a challenge.  I wish there was waterfowl hunting... and upland birds... and hunting dogs, please give us some quail and grouse.

To be entirely honest, I had heard a lot of hype from friends and coworkers surrounding Prison Architect. It seemed nearly impossible to live up to the hype, especially for an alpha game.
After playing the game for a while, I have to say it is an excellent game and certainly does live up to the hype! It's fun even when you are losing the game. When your prisoners get irritated enough and riot (mine keep doing it, for some reason), it is very entertaining to watch them slaughter your guards and use their weapons against their fellow officers.

--------------------
- Intro
--------------------
Prison Architect puts you in charge of: designing, building and managing a prison.
You can build anything from cells for your prisoners, offices for your staff, kitchens, canteens, power generators, solitary confinement to yards, work shops, infirmary, CCTV and so much more.
Conduct research to gain access to higher tech, new staff and facility types.
Make daily profit from your prison and cash-in big when selling it off for a bigger balance to start your next prison.
--------------------
- About the Game
--------------------
While the game is easy to learn and after a few attempts you find yourself doing quite well, it is hard to master the bigger facilities and the many prisoner's needs.
The game has a great tutorial which nicely introduces you to the game mechanics, how to build and manage a prison.
Ones you passed the tutorial you are placed on an empty map you can start your prison on. You can either just go ahead and build a small prison you are comfortable with or expand and take on the challenges of high security prisoners and high security techs to help you overview you prison.
During the game you can take on "grands" which are sort of like quests. You get a certain amount of money upfront and upon achieving the outlined tasks get a further monetary reward.
You make money every day from the difference between the money you make from housing prisoners and the money you spend on facilities and staff.
You also can do "research". Some staff when hired or some facilities when build unlock the ability to research new staff roles, facilities or techs which allow you to even further expand your prison and ability to control it.
If you get bored of your prison you can, after some time, have it evaluated and sell it for a nice sum of cash you can use when starting your next prison.
--------------------
- Early Access Note
--------------------
Personally I have not yet come across a major bug in the earlier stages of the game and the stability of the game is very enjoyably.
The only minor bug I came across is when you build a door on a wall before you build the foundation, the foundation will build a wall over the door and you need to remove/re-add the door again but that's nothing to even worry about.
I believe only at the higher end of facilities and staff are there bugs/missing features, such as when hiring lawyers and such, they apparently don't do anything yet for you. Though that is so far beyond the starting point of the game that you will have many hours of fun before you even get there.
You always can sell your prison before you expand to that level and start again with more cash on your next endeavor until the next game patch/update fixes those issues.
Once you figure out how everything works it is a real fun game to build and manage the prison. It only in alpha so I am intested in further update but overall a fun game to play and worth the money.

I went into this expecting to be slightly disappointed, the hype it had received from both friends and press was pretty overwhelming. However, I'm pleased to have been wrong: it was absolutely brilliant.
The core gameplay is your standard cover-based-shooter which you'd get in Gears of War (but with a Call of Duty theme, I guess), but you're not here for the gameplay, you're here for the story. And what a story it is.
This is without doubt one of the best games I've played in the last tweve months. Brilliant. Absolutely brilliant.

By time I finished this game, I was really surprised by how fantastic the story was. I expected a run-of-the-mill shooter, but instead I got a compelling tale of morality in warfare. The voice acting in the game is top-notch, to boot.
As for gameplay, it is a pretty standard shooter, but with some cool sand elements, and some Uncharted-type scripted action sequences that give a nice cinematic feel. In fact, the lack of load screens between chapters also helps to make it feel like you're playing a part in a movie. While the action is nothing new, it is at least well polished for the most part. The only issue I had was the occasional suppressed headshot from my M4 just waking an unaware target up instead of killing him, but the game doesn't really punish you for not be stealthy (even when it recommends it).
In short, I believe this is a sleeper hit, and a top-quality game anyone should play through at least once.

Despite it's flaws, I am still freakin' lit after finishing the first episode. There is much symbolism to explore, some of the usual humor, and you'll see familiar faces if you've played LIS before. You get to play as Chloe, a refresher from playing as Max and you'll see things in her perspective. In a way, I could also identify with her, adding to the realism of her background. To make up for it's shortcomings, there are more comical and entertaining aspects of the game in some of its puzzles, which also feels more like you are involved with the story.
The backtalk feature was an interesting way to explore ways to get yourself out of undesireable situations, getting what you want, or solve other people's problems, and by doing so they create new storylines. As a twist, they are timed against you. This feature is sort of a minipuzzle where you need to be as witty as you can be while using this wit to turn other people's words against them. It can prove useful.
Sometimes, there are some things you can do which cannot be undone. Obviously, because you can't use the famed time travel tool of LIS lore in the original, this is a lot like real life. So it has its challenges the player has to contend with. In fact, because of this, they create new dialogue opportunities you can use to add to a conversation or your backtalk power. Sometimes they can also trigger, what was prominent in the original game, that "actions have consequences".
Speaking of which, this game has many of the basic familiar elements from LIS regardling gameplay. To interact with objects, this is improved by being able to push a button (after clicking it with a mouse) instead of awkwardly dragging the mouse your desired action. With a controller*, it's much easier to navigate. There is also a journal, which Chloe uses as "letters" to Max as a place for her to vent, augmenting how she feels in the game as the story progresses. There is also a summary of the characters for newer people to read about, along with her interactions with them behind the scenes appearing in text messages like Max would do in LIS. In place of photos to collect, Chloe can 'tag' places with graffiti, and you get to choose between 2 different options on what you can write, offering a bit more flexibility. Some of the graffiti opportunities are also sometimes hidden, requiring you to figure out this puzzle to enable it, a little more than what Max did with the hide-and-seek style of finding them. And as per usual, it's not usually counted against you if you explore and converse with more than one character you need to talk to. In fact, there are some that you will be worth the involvement.
While this is literally a throwback to the original LIS, the improvements are also a nice change. In fact, I can say, it makes me appreciate the series more. In fact, I've felt moved For Chloe once again when she had her flashbacks of William, and one particular scene you can observe just how much of a powerful impact he had on her. I've literally cried at that point. That was a huge plus to maintain a reality check for myself that it calls to attention these are devices for character development and important plot points. While it certainly does need some light dusting, I can't dismiss the potential it has to be able to follow in the light and out of the shadows of the success of LIS.
*Although controller use is actually underdeveloped as of this writing, the issues can be easily overcome by enabling the Steam controller feature which will allow the game to deect and support your controller properly.

Ok guys Im going for the honest no salt review here.  I will also start with the bad because Im hoping it all gets fixed.  Its not a totally negative review so keep reading.
THE BAD - I cant play.  At about ~24 hours in I had found some bugs, most it did not take too much effort to find work arounds but at that 24 hour mark it tanked.  30 minutes into a play session I had my first major crash... game froze, audio loop playing the same half second of audio over and over, and I couldnt even exit to the desktop or use task manager to shut it down.  Had to turn off the PC completely and fire it back up.  The next playthrough the same thing happened in about 5 minutes... rinse and repeat this until I could get ZERO time in before locking up.  I uninstalled/reinstalled and this got me through about 3 hours of gameplay and then all the previous stuff I mentioned happened all over again.  Like I said, I cannot play. THE GOOD - This game is a plesant mix of sim and arcade.  There are enough moments of "nothing" to make it seem like a sim, but theres also enough going on to keep it from getting boring.... to all the hardcore sim guys out there, hunting for a week in real life not killing anything is still entertaining, doing it in a game is lame and no one would play that.  The graphics are not ground breaking but the lighting, effects, and scale of things make it seem more polished than it probably is (its pleasant walking through the forrest).  As far as the hunter classic went I thought that was a garbage game, I thought it looked like trash, played about the same, and the pay model was a complete rip off. It's great so far. I was skeptical, like so many others, from both the mixed reviews and the arcadey looking YouTube videos. I've also played the Hunter classic for a long time and have invested many hours in it. I know some of what I'll put here has already been said, but I feel the game deserves another positive review.
The main issue that caused me to hesitate on purchasing was the arcadey look. It mainly comes from the videos having every single visual clue turned on, all of which you can disable. If you simply disable the visual audio clues, and change the track clues to just glow and not the bouncy animation - you are basically right back at the Hunter classic in terms of play. You don't even have that cheat mode of seeing the animal call on the pda and then clicking in the area.  You need to determine from sound direction alone where the call came from. These 2 elements basically remove the arcadey feel just by themselves.
Not sure of all the bugs people claim to be having, I have encountered only a couple in my 12 hours of play and none of them were that serious. One of them required a restart, but that was after 3-4 hours of straight play with no issues. The tracks disappeared.
Graphics look great, it's awesome that the clock just keeps going and you can go all through the day and night if you choose or rest to speed it back up to your desired time. The night time with the moonlight is especially nice.
Don't want to keep going on and on, but again, if your main reservation is the arcadey look - it's worth taking a look for yourself to see, I didn't want to pass it up simply based on other's reviews and I'm glad I didn't.

I could have gone thumbs up or thumbs down with this title, but the sheer enjoyment (mostly) and obvious effort that's gone into the game pushed me (just) to a thumbs up.
Fun up to a point...and then it just becomes tedious. Everything takes far too long to accomplish.
Fill your water bottle? Slow.
Drink from your water bottle? Slow.
Find a hot air balloon? Slow.
Go up in the hot air balloon? Slow.
Get down from the hot air balloon? Slow.
Attack a compund? Slow.
Take down a convoy? Slow.
Loading? Slow.
This game is like peeling an apple - it seems to take AGES to actually get to what you want. Best example of this is the balloons. Riding up in a ballon allows you to spot markers which you can then drive to (slow). But each balloon is a kind of mini-compound where you have to scale walls, press buttons, move levers, find fuel, refuel.....this is just to get to the balloon. Then you spend 10 seconds or so riding the balloon up....leading to you then having to scan the horizon for each and every marker. Then 10 seconds down again. And leave the compound area. And get in your car. Then drive to the marker which is another kind of mini-compound....
10 seconds sounds like nothing, but there are CONTINUAL time wasting little jobs to do that just eat away at the enjoyment and lead you to becoming bored. Shall I traipse around this area to find the one piece of scrap I can't find? Once you finally admit you are bored and give up looking for that one elusive hidden scrap/insignia or whatever, your dedication wanes and your enjoyment drops with it.
I think my main problem is that I'll pick up a game and play it to death. Mordor I played through continually until completing it. But for Mad Max, you'll need to come back and revisit or your mind will melt.
I'll only go back now to blast through the main story - and I hope I don't need to go and collect tonnes of scrap to complete it or I'll just give up. Sad thing is, I enjoyed it until I realised I was doing the same thing over and over again and once I fell off that cliff....
Think Mordor with more timewasting and you'll have this game summed up nicely.
Despite all that - I'll recommend it as it's fun. If you can get past the tedium...

Even though it's in early access, this game is already lots of fun. It's certainly not one of the unplayable pre-alpha moneygrabs that give 'early access' a bad name.
To start with the downsides: Not all features are implemented and there isn't really a campaign. It might take another year or more to implement all this. Despite this, it's already a good game and the devs release a new version every month to make this game even better and more packed with features.
In the beginning it might seem a bit difficult. After playing the opening tutorial, you might still have some questions. Watching some youtube videos might help you to really understand the mechanics. Being spoiled with all the tutorial friendly games on the market, I kinda had to push myself to get through this initial 'what the hell am I supposed to do' phase.
After the rough start you'll soon start to get the hang of it. You'll start building a nice little prison and soon the first inmates will be under your control. Getting a small, peaceful prison with a few inmates will be satisfying, but of coarse you'll soon want to expand. You might want to get your prisoners an education or you'll want to get your prisoners reoffending rate as low as possible. As soon as you start to grow your prison and add features, problems will start to rise and you'll have to manage them or you'll fail. Adding tons of guards isn't the answer to all your problems, so you might have to get creative. You'll have to fight contraband and addiction, but also you'll have to manage the needs of your prisoners without going over your budget. Failing to do so will be the downfall of your carreer as a prison architect.
There will be a few goals set out for the player. In the form of grants you'll want to meet certain requirements to get some extra cash. Right now, besides those grants, you'll have to set your own goals to keep it really interesting. These personal goals won't be too hard to figure out, since managing a prison with 100 inmates is way cooler than managing a 16 inmate prison.
If you enjoy humorous games where you'll have to build, manage and plan ahead a bit: Buy this game. If you want a story driven game about a prison system you might want to wait out the early access phase and check later reviews to see what has come of this.

Various thoughts on the game:
There's a lot to like and some areas that need improvement.
Visuals and audio are both in a good place in my opinion. Performance is alright, though for some reason I cannot get msi afterburner to show up in game.
I do not like the layered progression system, to me it feels like an old RPG-crutch. A matter of taste.
The full UI feels gamey compared to my expectations for a hunting game. I'd like to point towards how Far Cry 2 managed to integrate a more immersive system. Again a matter of taste.
Launch bugs are unfortunate but I fully expect this game to be well supported.
One issue in particular that I hope has high priority is animal pathing. Few things deflate the thrill of the hunt as much as a bear or moose stuck between rocks and glitching wildly.
I recommend this game because I feel it has a good foundation and likely appeal to a fairly wide hunting audience. Despite the various bugs and flaws, I've spent a considerable amount of time trekking and stalking in Call of the Wild. Managing to set up and execute a good shot feels very good.

had been on my wishlist for a long while, and I had never bothered to purchase it until last winter. I do not know why I waited so long. The music, the characters, the gameplay, the...well, the story is honestly a tad predictable, but many character-driven dramas are. You play this game mainly for the aforementioned qualities, but the story is still highly entertaining and did feature several twists that caught me off guard.
You play as a
human child named
who climbs a mountain surrounded by rumor and superstition, and you trip and fall down a hole that leads to the realm of the monsters--beings who once shared the Earth with humans, but were forced underground after a devasting war between the two peoples nearly destroyed them. It is not very surprising, given the circumstances, that friendly faces are few and far between when your humanity is recognized.
features a unique combat/pacifist system that will shape the outcome of your playthrough. Kill even
monster, and there are repercussions. To me, this added a sense of depth and almost realism to the game universe. There are consequences for murder in real life, after all. You start to care about the inhabitants of the Underground, even though they wish you harm. Or, you may treat this game like any other RPG and kill everyone who stands in your way. You may grind for EXP, gold, and HP like any other RPG. There is just one problem with that.
is not any other RPG. You may find yourself becoming more of a monster than the monsters themselves.
I can only describe the gameplay as
meets a bullet hell.
The characters are refreshingly vibrant. Every NPC you meet has a personality, even if it is conveyed only through a single piece of dialogue. There are no duplicated NPC sprites, except for when you are dealing with mutliple members of the same species. The more prominent characters are equally unique, and very entertaining to interact with. My personal favorites are the skeleton brothers, Sans and Papyrus, who are among the first characters you meet after the completing the tutorial/prologue area, as well as Asriel. Why Asriel?
and he's freaking adorable, that's why.
The chiptune-orchestral music fits every area very well, and I am impressed to learn it was composed by one person. The only other one-man-band composer for indie games that has managed to blow me away like Toby Fox is Darren Korb of Supergiant Games (the makers of
and
), and his work is among my favorites where music is concerned. I still have some of the tunes from
's soundtrack stuck in my head, and I enjoy listening to it while I am studying or writing.
Perhaps my favorite part of the game is how even your re-playthroughs contribute to the story, and to the development of one character whom I will not reveal the identity of.
Overall, this is an original and impressive game. My only real complaints are that the Pokémon-esque random enemy encounters can get a tad repetetive in some areas, especially when you are trying to get to the next area or complete a puzzle, and your avatar moves very slowly. Other than that, I very much enjoyed playing
, and I highly recommend it.
P.S. - Don't let the fan hentai and weird YouTube theory videos ruin this game's image or appeal for you. The hype exists for a good reason, it's just channeled in bizarre
ways sometimes, just like with many other fandoms. Heck, just look at Renamon's fanbase...or on second thought, don't.

Various thoughts on the game:
There's a lot to like and some areas that need improvement.
Visuals and audio are both in a good place in my opinion. Performance is alright, though for some reason I cannot get msi afterburner to show up in game.
I do not like the layered progression system, to me it feels like an old RPG-crutch. A matter of taste.

+10 hours since release and im enjoying the game so far. I havent tried the multiplayer yet so this is going to be mostly a single player focused review.
For starters the game launched pretty sloppy for many, including my self, and many of the issues are still prevelent such as graphical glitches, crashes, and AI issues, sound issues. Since launch the game has felt like a unpolished beta rushed to meet a release deadline.
The game over all plays pretty well for those who are a fan of The Hunter and already know what to expect. For new comers to the series It might be the only start to The Hunter they can enjoy since Classic has more of a F2P/P2W business model behind it and isnt very welcoming to new players since they are locked out of 95% of the great content in the game. If you are new to the series i would recommend picking this game up over playing classic first, if you are not a new commer to the The Hunter you might find this game a tad bit lacking in terms of equipment and features (dogs, tents, stands, tripods, scents, callers, birds, ducks, geese, blinds) so it wont fill those voids if you've enjoyed +100 hours with those features in your hunts.
The game offers two reserves to hunt on and a wide array of equipment to use and animals to track and spot, Every animnal you harvest is awarded with XP and cash based on the difficulty of the animal, the weapon used and the shot placement and whether or not the animal died instantly or bled out over time. New features to the game are the new stealth mechanic, sight and sound now play an important factor as well as smell, the noob friendly meters on the HUD will show you how visible or how noisy you are in the environment, i found that the controller utilized these features better than traditional K/M. Progression in The Hunter is very different from other games and very time consuming, and given the unpredictiblity of many animals the game does not reward simple tasks and you will find yourself grinding or side tracked many times. A few new features to the game are "need zones", areas where animals migrate or congregate based on there needs at that specific time of day. NIght time hunting is also a new feature, hunting at night is alot more challenging than during the day you will find yourself wandering the game world following tracks since animals are usually quieter during the night. The new features in CofW are refreshing and a good reason to pick the game up if you like simulation or hunting games. Over all the core elements play well.
The game ran fine on a single Zotac GTX 980 on ultra for the most part with a Gsync display and Vsync turned on for many hours on end so its not a very demanding game if youve still got an older gen card in your machine. I have yet to test the game in SLi but for the most part it runs well without SLi.
In review, The Hunter CotW is essentialy a bare bones experience of The hunter classic with an updated game engine and graphics and some unique gameplay features. I can see this game being polished and packaged really well in the future with a handful of updates and DLCs but for now you will only be getting a fraction of what The Hunter Classic has to offer currently.

I'll skip the introduction and assume that if you're considering this game you've already played the original and know the background.
Gameplay is around 5 hours. I took my time and made an effort to get all the graffiti achievements and explore alternate options in Collector Mode.
Pros:
- Great soundtrack.
- A closer look at Chloe Price, Rachel Amber, and their relationship before Max comes back to Arcadia Bay.
- Extra outfits for Chloe, if you bought the game as a pre-order or the Deluxe edition and an extra mini episode with Max, at some point in the future. Kind of a double edged sword though, making assets which could be key into DLC.
- I enjoyed it.
Cons:
- No tangible graphical upgrades. Textures are rather low res, even with graphic settings maxed out. Some animation aspects (eyes) are largely overlooked. Strange considering how important that area can or could be.
- Virtually none of the original voice actor cast returned for this game. You would think the new developers might want to create some deeper bonds with the old game but not so much in practice.
- Minor bug during Nathan & Football Guy encounter. Chloe's self narration audio was played while the two were arguing. Not show stopping, just annoying.
- Feels short at 5 hours. I spent around 20 or so hours in the original LiS so maybe I'm off in feeling that this is short.
Quibbles:
- Ashly Burch, original voice actress for Chloe, was unable to reprise her role due to the organization of a voice actors strike. 	Rhianna DeVries replaces Burch and does a competent job. Burch was involved in the writing of the game.
- If you didn't take a chance on a pre-order, which I did, you won't get Chloe's classic outfit, not the Max/Chloe episode, which isn't out yet. Annoying but I doubt this will keep a fan away.
Conclusion:
- I recommend the game for Life is Strange fans. I enjoyed it and I'm sure other fans will but this game just left me wanting more. Perhaps that's a testament to how enjoyable it is but... I just feel like some heart or gravitas is missing here. I'm hoping the future episodes flesh things out more and make the world feel whole and more engaging.

This game is a lot like other open world games. It has repetative gameplay. It is full of mini tasks that you can do for hours. You level up your character (and your car). But the game is so polished and fun that I can't harbor any cynisism against it.
The game is anchored by car on car combat and it is some of the most fun car on car combat in any game period. You are given plenty of tools to use, including a rocket powered harpoon that is one of the most fun weapons I've used in a game to date. With the Harpoon you can rip off car tires, tear off car doors, tear drivers out of their own cars, etc. The harpoon also allows you to tear down gates and tiny structures all over the map, letting the harpoon become a consistent part of the gameplay and a very familiar tool for the player. But the car combat is not just made excellent by its weapons, but the feel of a car chase is also spot on. Car v. Car combat is usually not a short thing, especially when other cars start loading up with armor and travel in packs. The durability of all the cars around you makes it feel like you are in a movie, constantly trying to dodge the other cars and often times failing at it. In fact, my most vivid memory of the entire game was when a random group of cars started chasing me and one hit me so hard I spun out and fell down a massive hill, making my car tumble into a fiery wreck that I had to jump out of at the last second before it exploded. I was lucky I managed to jump out of the car, live and run over to my car to see my consistent trusty side kick chumbucket fixing it up. Failing an encounter in a video game is rarely as exciting as it is in Mad Max.
I would also like to point out how good of a job Avalanch studios did at creating such a large open world that is mostly wasteland and yet, it is not boring to explore. There are little shacks and shantys everywhere and each area has its own distinct look to it that is suprisingly seemlessly introduced into the world when just driving around. Some of the smaller on foot environments feel super similar, sure, but then you find stuff like a giant flaming palace that turns out to be a shelter for you or you enter an abandoned airport full of "treasure" (garbage that is rare in the wasteland). Environments more often than not are cool, and considering that this game is graphically excellent, I was generally happy to be exploring the wasteland.
This game has some clear flaws though, once you step outside your car. The hand to hand combat is fine, but not nearly as inspiered as the car v. car combat, using an "Arkham" stlye combat that is not quite as good as the Batman games. I would also say the story in this game is overall pretty bad. In fact, I generally just zoned out during cutscenes during the end of the game. There were a few really cool moments, but not enough to save it. Characters are pretty one dimensional, although well performed for the most part.
I like this game, I like it a lot. The car combat is clearly the reason why I enjoyed this game and I think anyone who likes high tension action sequences will as well.

"Being in the modern military is probably one of the hardest, most trying things a person can do and it's so great to see a game make more of that than a simple power fantasy." -
If you're looking for a mindless, nationalistic military shooter, you're not going to find it here. No other shooters have explored the weight that comes with pulling the trigger in war more than this game has. Although the mechanics are a part of the storytelling, the gameplay isn't as advanced as the current flurry of Call of Dutys, Battlefields, or Medal of Honors but the trade off is worth it. Those games don't even bother trying to touch on half of the things Spec Ops addressed; they actively avoid PTSD to opt for comic book heroics and focus on glorifying and romanticizing war. It's honest, visceral, and engaging in all its literal and metaphorical symbolism.
If you decide to pick this up, and I strongly suggest that you do, experience it for the single-player story. The multiplayer was just an added bonus but don't judge the entire game by it if you decide to try that out first. It'll be one of the most eye-opening gaming experiences you'll ever have. The game trusts you to make your own decisions. Spec Ops: The Line is worth it full price if you think you'd enjoy a military shooter that gives more thought into its story and character development rather than mechanics. Yager really took a risk with this game and it's an experience I will always remember.

As a player who became addicted to this game/mod way back in the ARMA 2 days, it actually hurts to write this.
DayZ standalone has been in a wierd place for a very long time; changing engines and developers over the course of its alpha development stage.
Dean 'Rocket' Hall did a fantastic job of creating the mod and setting the foundations in place for what was then a huge popular zombie survival game but in the early days of the standalones creations, "Rocket" stepped down as lead dev and moved onto other projects. This left DayZ in the hands of a completely new development team and whilst PR suggested that Rocket would oversee and assist on the sideline; the game is still unfinished and STILL in Alpha.
Honestly, this game NEEDS new content! Its been stuck in the same place for a while and even though the stability updates have done a world of good for the game overall; it feels as though without joining an RP server to create your own stories, the content and things to do run out very quickly.

I'll skip the introduction and assume that if you're considering this game you've already played the original and know the background.
Gameplay is around 5 hours. I took my time and made an effort to get all the graffiti achievements and explore alternate options in Collector Mode.
Pros:
- Great soundtrack.
- A closer look at Chloe Price, Rachel Amber, and their relationship before Max comes back to Arcadia Bay.
- Extra outfits for Chloe, if you bought the game as a pre-order or the Deluxe edition and an extra mini episode with Max, at some point in the future. Kind of a double edged sword though, making assets which could be key into DLC.
- I enjoyed it.
Cons:
- No tangible graphical upgrades. Textures are rather low res, even with graphic settings maxed out. Some animation aspects (eyes) are largely overlooked. Strange considering how important that area can or could be.
- Virtually none of the original voice actor cast returned for this game. You would think the new developers might want to create some deeper bonds with the old game but not so much in practice.
- Minor bug during Nathan & Football Guy encounter. Chloe's self narration audio was played while the two were arguing. Not show stopping, just annoying.
- Feels short at 5 hours. I spent around 20 or so hours in the original LiS so maybe I'm off in feeling that this is short.
Quibbles:
- Ashly Burch, original voice actress for Chloe, was unable to reprise her role due to the organization of a voice actors strike. 	Rhianna DeVries replaces Burch and does a competent job. Burch was involved in the writing of the game.
- If you didn't take a chance on a pre-order, which I did, you won't get Chloe's classic outfit, not the Max/Chloe episode, which isn't out yet. Annoying but I doubt this will keep a fan away.
Conclusion:
- I recommend the game for Life is Strange fans. I enjoyed it and I'm sure other fans will but this game just left me wanting more. Perhaps that's a testament to how enjoyable it is but... I just feel like some heart or gravitas is missing here. I'm hoping the future episodes flesh things out more and make the world feel whole and more engaging.

ETS 2 does what it says on the tin. You start off as a poor young truck driver looking to progress in the intricate and complicated world of delivering shipments...
Pros:
- A very relaxing game - you can literally relax for hours on end just playing and progressing
- The locations are modelled on a smaller scale of the real ones - streets and signs are all in the right language, and it's these little details that make the game fantastic
- Upgrades and progressing - you can progress and earn the right to deliver shipments of explosives or hazardous materials - this adds an element of risk and carefulness to the game. Also, you can pimp out your truck and make it really poweful and fast!
- A huge map - there are so many roads, cities, regions and countries that you will never get bored.
- Realism - the graphics are top-notch and there are so many realistic things - indicators, windscreen wipers when it's raining, you can even stream live radio from all over Europe.
Stretching it, it's a bit like GTA in a sense that every little detail makes the game so much more satisfying to play. It's not just driving a truck to your destination, it's the little things along the way which keep you occupied - filling up your tank when it's low, abiding to the real rules of the roads (driving on the left when in the UK, right when in Europe), and even sleeping when your driver is tired. Amazingly, there is only one or two things I'd like to see added to the game. These are:
- Bigger cities - for example, famous Landmarks, mountains etc...
- Continents - I know that the developers would have a tough time with this but if we could drive in Asia, Africa, or South America on the"Death Roads" in Bolivia, that would really be stunning!
So this is my review. If you like driving peacefully and not with 50 police cars behind you or in a race with supercars, then this is for you.

This game is a lot like other open world games. It has repetative gameplay. It is full of mini tasks that you can do for hours. You level up your character (and your car). But the game is so polished and fun that I can't harbor any cynisism against it.
The game is anchored by car on car combat and it is some of the most fun car on car combat in any game period. You are given plenty of tools to use, including a rocket powered harpoon that is one of the most fun weapons I've used in a game to date. With the Harpoon you can rip off car tires, tear off car doors, tear drivers out of their own cars, etc. The harpoon also allows you to tear down gates and tiny structures all over the map, letting the harpoon become a consistent part of the gameplay and a very familiar tool for the player. But the car combat is not just made excellent by its weapons, but the feel of a car chase is also spot on. Car v. Car combat is usually not a short thing, especially when other cars start loading up with armor and travel in packs. The durability of all the cars around you makes it feel like you are in a movie, constantly trying to dodge the other cars and often times failing at it. In fact, my most vivid memory of the entire game was when a random group of cars started chasing me and one hit me so hard I spun out and fell down a massive hill, making my car tumble into a fiery wreck that I had to jump out of at the last second before it exploded. I was lucky I managed to jump out of the car, live and run over to my car to see my consistent trusty side kick chumbucket fixing it up. Failing an encounter in a video game is rarely as exciting as it is in Mad Max.
I would also like to point out how good of a job Avalanch studios did at creating such a large open world that is mostly wasteland and yet, it is not boring to explore. There are little shacks and shantys everywhere and each area has its own distinct look to it that is suprisingly seemlessly introduced into the world when just driving around. Some of the smaller on foot environments feel super similar, sure, but then you find stuff like a giant flaming palace that turns out to be a shelter for you or you enter an abandoned airport full of "treasure" (garbage that is rare in the wasteland). Environments more often than not are cool, and considering that this game is graphically excellent, I was generally happy to be exploring the wasteland.
This game has some clear flaws though, once you step outside your car. The hand to hand combat is fine, but not nearly as inspiered as the car v. car combat, using an "Arkham" stlye combat that is not quite as good as the Batman games. I would also say the story in this game is overall pretty bad. In fact, I generally just zoned out during cutscenes during the end of the game. There were a few really cool moments, but not enough to save it. Characters are pretty one dimensional, although well performed for the most part.
I like this game, I like it a lot. The car combat is clearly the reason why I enjoyed this game and I think anyone who likes high tension action sequences will as well.

"Being in the modern military is probably one of the hardest, most trying things a person can do and it's so great to see a game make more of that than a simple power fantasy." -
If you're looking for a mindless, nationalistic military shooter, you're not going to find it here. No other shooters have explored the weight that comes with pulling the trigger in war more than this game has. Although the mechanics are a part of the storytelling, the gameplay isn't as advanced as the current flurry of Call of Dutys, Battlefields, or Medal of Honors but the trade off is worth it. Those games don't even bother trying to touch on half of the things Spec Ops addressed; they actively avoid PTSD to opt for comic book heroics and focus on glorifying and romanticizing war. It's honest, visceral, and engaging in all its literal and metaphorical symbolism.
If you decide to pick this up, and I strongly suggest that you do, experience it for the single-player story. The multiplayer was just an added bonus but don't judge the entire game by it if you decide to try that out first. It'll be one of the most eye-opening gaming experiences you'll ever have. The game trusts you to make your own decisions. Spec Ops: The Line is worth it full price if you think you'd enjoy a military shooter that gives more thought into its story and character development rather than mechanics. Yager really took a risk with this game and it's an experience I will always remember.

had been on my wishlist for a long while, and I had never bothered to purchase it until last winter. I do not know why I waited so long. The music, the characters, the gameplay, the...well, the story is honestly a tad predictable, but many character-driven dramas are. You play this game mainly for the aforementioned qualities, but the story is still highly entertaining and did feature several twists that caught me off guard.
You play as a
human child named
who climbs a mountain surrounded by rumor and superstition, and you trip and fall down a hole that leads to the realm of the monsters--beings who once shared the Earth with humans, but were forced underground after a devasting war between the two peoples nearly destroyed them. It is not very surprising, given the circumstances, that friendly faces are few and far between when your humanity is recognized.
features a unique combat/pacifist system that will shape the outcome of your playthrough. Kill even
monster, and there are repercussions. To me, this added a sense of depth and almost realism to the game universe. There are consequences for murder in real life, after all. You start to care about the inhabitants of the Underground, even though they wish you harm. Or, you may treat this game like any other RPG and kill everyone who stands in your way. You may grind for EXP, gold, and HP like any other RPG. There is just one problem with that.
is not any other RPG. You may find yourself becoming more of a monster than the monsters themselves.
I can only describe the gameplay as
meets a bullet hell.
The characters are refreshingly vibrant. Every NPC you meet has a personality, even if it is conveyed only through a single piece of dialogue. There are no duplicated NPC sprites, except for when you are dealing with mutliple members of the same species. The more prominent characters are equally unique, and very entertaining to interact with. My personal favorites are the skeleton brothers, Sans and Papyrus, who are among the first characters you meet after the completing the tutorial/prologue area, as well as Asriel. Why Asriel?
and he's freaking adorable, that's why.
The chiptune-orchestral music fits every area very well, and I am impressed to learn it was composed by one person. The only other one-man-band composer for indie games that has managed to blow me away like Toby Fox is Darren Korb of Supergiant Games (the makers of
and
), and his work is among my favorites where music is concerned. I still have some of the tunes from
's soundtrack stuck in my head, and I enjoy listening to it while I am studying or writing.
Perhaps my favorite part of the game is how even your re-playthroughs contribute to the story, and to the development of one character whom I will not reveal the identity of.
Overall, this is an original and impressive game. My only real complaints are that the Pokémon-esque random enemy encounters can get a tad repetetive in some areas, especially when you are trying to get to the next area or complete a puzzle, and your avatar moves very slowly. Other than that, I very much enjoyed playing
, and I highly recommend it.
P.S. - Don't let the fan hentai and weird YouTube theory videos ruin this game's image or appeal for you. The hype exists for a good reason, it's just channeled in bizarre
ways sometimes, just like with many other fandoms. Heck, just look at Renamon's fanbase...or on second thought, don't.

One of my favourite games of 2015.  Note:  You DON'T need to see any of the Mad Max movies to play this.  The most recent film provides a bit of context at best, the prior 3... nope.
If I had to describe the mood... it's somewhere in between Fallout NV and GTA V.  Grim, depressing post-apocalyptic survival where cars, gas and scrap are the source of all power and sway.
A lot of people have compared the fighting mechanics to the Batman games - this is where I disagree.  While yes, they mechanically are pretty similar - in Mad Max they're a lot more satisfying and a lot more responsive (i.e. you're not shouting "I CLICKED THAT WITH PERFECT TIMING, WHY AM I LOSING MORE HEALTH?!")
Don't rush through the main story (even though it's an amazing narrative, much better than its recent movie) and wander around - discovering the Wasteland, trying to figure out what might have happened to it through history relics, scavenging and generally feeling awesome at the well-executed fusion of driving and weaponry - and you'll easily get dozens of hours out of this game.  In my case it was 97 hours until I reached the end of the main quest - and I still have a few things left that I *WANT* to do.
My only criticism is that - as many hours as I got out of it (97 so far) - I wish there'd been more content in terms of side quests for example.  Something perhaps future DLC could address?
Overall Mad Max surpassed my expectations and would highly recommend it to anyone of the post-apocalyptic genre.  I'd give it a 9/10.

After playing a few hours and completing the main story, I feel like writing some relevant points here.
for me was a game based on exploration. The world design is very well done, you can actually feel that you are in an apocalyptic
desert, followed by misery and death from beginning to end.
The graphics are beautiful, especially when it comes to explosions (oh boy!), explosions in Mad Max are key for an enjoyable experience.
Combat system could be better, it is indeed similar to Batman's, but not as smooth or diverse.
Driving around can be annoying sometimes (or maybe I'm just a bad driver) and you will find yourself drifting and having a hard time making turns until those upgrades happen.
In order to make upgrades, you need scrap, and for that you'll catch yourself heading to Scavenging Locations quite often. The first time you do it is fine, everything is new and exciting, but after the 15th time, there isn't much of a difference except for the location. "Collect scrap, kill enemies and repeat." Add "collect upgrade parts and historical relics" to that list in some cases. It feels
.
The upgrade system works great for the car, because they aren't always "100% positive" upgrades, for example: Adding more protection to your car will make it heavier, so you're giving up handling or acceleration.
Upgrading Max abilities in combat will help him considerely and make the combat more diverse (not that much!), it is a shame though that his upgrades aren't more like his car, which means you're not getting heavier and losing mobility.
During my dive into this game, I've encountered a few bugs, nothing that would break the game but doesn't make them any less annoying. Fortunately, it doesn't happen everytime, so you can get away with it and enjoy the game.
+ Graphics
+ World design
+ Explosions
= Easy
= Storyline and sidequests
= Combat system
- Repetitive
- Bugs and glitches
You should play this game and have a good time.

It's late and I don't wanna get into a full review right now, so I might do one later. Who knows.
This game is good. It could have been great, but the end result is simply unpolished. The game is riddled with minor glitches, not gameplay-changing for the most part, but you will definitely notice them, and they are constant. The biggest negative is the sound design; crashes, explosions, gunshots, nothing ever seems to line up with the video if they even play at all, nothing more obvious than in the cutscenes, where the audio is completely detached from what you're looking at. There's nothing wrong with the game that couldn't have been fixed with some extra time in development, but that seems to be a recurring theme these days.
The biggest negatives are out of the way, so let me say this game is fun. It's a lot of grinding, but it's fun grinding. I had fun playing it, collecting scrap, building my car, destroying things in my newly built car, then repeating ad infinitum. The characters were good, although there were major inconsistencies with the accents, but I feel that whole issue is an old one so I won't let it get in the way of the review. There wasn't a lot of time spent on exposition for any of the main characters, but that makes sense because Max is a loner and he doesn't care about other people's problems, or at least really tries not to care. The main quest doesn't have a lot of flow to it, but that may be my fault, since as soon as the open world gets unlocked, I tend to faff about in every conceivable way instead of doing the main missions. I would wager that about 10% of my playtime had anything to do with the main storyline. The random encounters feel like an afterthought, every minor character is voiced by the same two people who say one or two random lines that give you some random task to complete for upgrade tokens, which I'll get to in a bit (this review is getting longer than I anticipated). It seems the real side quests are the races and liberation. Races are straightforward, there's several types of races but they all boil down to: get to location specified while doing some task before time runs out or other racers kill you. These races are fun, but they get repetitive and I wouldn't expect anyone to do all of them unless they're a hardcore completionist, since you unlock a vehicle every time you do a new race. Liberation is a common mechanic in open world games, and this was the bulk of the gameplay for me. You drive around, wrecking stuff and infiltrating bases, killing everyone and destroying everything, and eventually you'll be rewarded with the map turning a greenish-white instead of a red or yellow. Certain car upgrages are locked behind liberation, meaning you'll have to turn everything green before you can unlock everything for your car. It's all pretty straight-forward and overall it's a pretty standard open world grindy game with standard open world grindy gameplay.
The upgrade system specifically for Max's abilities is not the best. In some ways I'd even say it's broken. For every optional additional challenge you beat (most of these are standard. example: 'get a hit-streak of 25 in combat', 'destroy x number of cars from a certain faction', etc.) you'd be awarded a token. This token can then be taken to a magic man named Griffa who is the best character in the game by far, only, if you're like me, you probably won't see him more than 3 or 4 times in the whole game. You get these tokens fast, and there's only so many upgrades you can buy. Once they're gone, he's gone. I recommend visiting Griffa every time you get a token, no more than 5 at a time. Whenever he was in the general direction I was going I would pop in, have an interesting chat, spend my average of 10-15 tokens, then before i knew it I was fully upgraded before mission 2, and this character that I feel is supposed to follow and talk to me throughout the game was gone forever. I'll have to look up his dialogue later because I am actually curious as to what he had to say. Again, this is 'my fault' for playing the game the way I wanted to play it. But there's ways to make sure the player can always get all the dialogue. If Griffa were to still show up even after I Maxed out everything (heh) just to have the dialogue, that would have been preferable. That was my biggest gripe in the game excluding bugs.
I won't get too far in the story because I want to keep this spoiler-free. Again, I might do a full review later, who knows. I ought to stop it here though. Kloveyabye
-Shephard

Utterly brilliant. If you're a fan of shooters and you haven't played this, then you need to.
The game has a unique setting, in a version of Dubai destroyed by sandstorms, which leads to consistently interesting environments and some genuine "wow" moments.
I think the cover system gets more stick than it deserves, too. While it's not perfect (always leaving cover standing is annoying) it adds some nice elements to the standard formula, such as sliding into cover from a sprint, vaulting into an enemy's face, low-profile switching between close pieces of cover, "wild" shooting, where you hold your gun over cover and spray at whatever's on the other side, etc, etc. Getting used to these and combining them together makes for some very fluid and *cough* cinematic moments, and encourages movement rather than static pop-and-shoot.
All that said, the best part of the game, and the reason you need to play it, is the story. The narrative is well written, well told, and uncompromising. The feel of the game is brutal, and the way the events of the game affect the protagonists over time is always engaging. Plus, it has one of the best game endings you'll ever play, which also has a "final choice" mechanic that only makes it better. It's possibly the best-executed game ending since Half Life 2, and that's not something I say lightly. Don't spoil the game for yourself, don't watch a let's-play or anything like that; go in as blind as possible, and if it feels like "Generic 2008 Shooter", keep going, because that's kinda the point.
Oh, and the multiplayer is for♥♥♥♥♥♥ but you're not here for the multiplayer. (Though the game does feature online co-op, which is sweet.)
Play this game.

CONS:
PROS:
The game play is great. The objective is simple: kill your opponents. There are plenty of hazards which aid you in your quest. There are meat grinders, there are falls from sky scrapers, there are subway trains. Beat up your opponents and throw them to their doom! This is all carried out in a wonderfully goofy world populated with strangely dressed jello people who make silly noises and giggle at the misfortune of their opponents. It's incredible.
I play with an Xbox 360 Controller. The default button scheme includes the left stick for movement, A/B/X/Y/LB/RB for control of various body parts. All buttons seem to have two functions: one action for a tap, and another for a hold. In the default scheme, LB and RB control the left and right arms respectively. Tapping punches, holding attempts to grasp whatever is at the end of the player's reach. This is helpful for grabbing and holding opponents. Couple this with Y which elevates the arms, and you can grab and lift an opponent over your head. Additionally, you can kick, headbutt, jump, sit, lay forward, lay backward, and many other combinations like jump kicking or climbing.
While I wholly endorse this game and have had loads of fun playing with my friends, I recognize that not everyone has the option to regularly get together with a group of players in one place and play games. If you are the kind of person who can not easily and frequently get together with a few friends to play, I would caution that you wait until online multiplayer is completely finished. Multiplayer Beta is currently active! Find out how to join
. If you are in a position to be able to regularly get together with some friends and you want to laugh until you puke, check out this game.

I'll skip the introduction and assume that if you're considering this game you've already played the original and know the background.
Gameplay is around 5 hours. I took my time and made an effort to get all the graffiti achievements and explore alternate options in Collector Mode.
Pros:
- Great soundtrack.
- A closer look at Chloe Price, Rachel Amber, and their relationship before Max comes back to Arcadia Bay.
- Extra outfits for Chloe, if you bought the game as a pre-order or the Deluxe edition and an extra mini episode with Max, at some point in the future. Kind of a double edged sword though, making assets which could be key into DLC.
- I enjoyed it.
Cons:
- No tangible graphical upgrades. Textures are rather low res, even with graphic settings maxed out. Some animation aspects (eyes) are largely overlooked. Strange considering how important that area can or could be.
- Virtually none of the original voice actor cast returned for this game. You would think the new developers might want to create some deeper bonds with the old game but not so much in practice.
- Minor bug during Nathan & Football Guy encounter. Chloe's self narration audio was played while the two were arguing. Not show stopping, just annoying.
- Feels short at 5 hours. I spent around 20 or so hours in the original LiS so maybe I'm off in feeling that this is short.
Quibbles:
- Ashly Burch, original voice actress for Chloe, was unable to reprise her role due to the organization of a voice actors strike. 	Rhianna DeVries replaces Burch and does a competent job. Burch was involved in the writing of the game.
- If you didn't take a chance on a pre-order, which I did, you won't get Chloe's classic outfit, not the Max/Chloe episode, which isn't out yet. Annoying but I doubt this will keep a fan away.

After 54 hrs of solid gameplay here's what I think about Mad Max.
First of all
Performance: This game might just be the best optimized game to date, not only did it run well on my pc, but it ran on 60 fps on a Evga gtx 670 2gb card; not many recent games could run at all on my pc let alone at a solid 60 fps, but somehow this game managed to utilize my little card and perform better then I could have hoped for. Now that was on high, and 1080p. But I ended up ordering a new card in the middle of playing this game, upgrading to a Gigabyte G1 980ti and I cranked it up to Max and had it on 4k resolution and it still stayed at 60fps and never went below that on either cards.
Graphics and terrain: The Graphics in Mad Max are very beautiful, they aren't the best but they are very nice. there are a few things here and there that aren't as detailed as other things but that never really bothered me as I was too busy taking in the view and having a blast. The art style is very nice and although the colour pallet is very orange and yellow it never gets old! Same with the terrain, you would think that the desert gets old, but somehow the devs pulled off something that I could not have imagined possible the terrain is quite the same but at the same time it isn't it never really gets old like you think it would. There are plenty of hills, caves, Gullies, cliffs and other terian that just works and gives that feeling of variety.
Gameplay: The gameplay in Mad Max was over all quiet satisfyingly balanced, not to easy not to hard. A lot of the games mechanics were for myself quiet enjoyable but repetitive, same with the side quests which were very repetitive but that’s kind of what most side quests are in games these days, BUT... it was the okay kind of reparative, the kind you went "oh god, I may as well 100% this thing" and after about 10 you start to stop paying much attention to what’s happening. The story could have been done better but overall was okay, the ending was VERY unsatisfying for me, and didn’t really accomplish anything at all. Also something that bugged me was the terrible mouth movement in and out of cut scenes honestly for a triple A title you'd expect that they would be able to hands down own this but it was very disappointing to watch the models mouths when they talk. I will say though that i really did enjoy customizing the car and max himself but the car had more vaiety and was more fun.
Over all this was a fun game and Worth the $30 Aud I purchased it for, I would reccomend this game but not at full price. Even if you get 40 + hours of gameplay it still is mostly doing repetitive side quests that takes up most of that time.

Borderlands 2 is a first-person shooter that randomly generates the guns you find, varying damage values, clip sizes, accuracy, and even how many bullets they fire at once. It's built like an RPG: you level up by killing things, improve your character's abilities, and find higher-level guns to kill higher-level beasts and bandits on a rocky, backwater planet.
That was already compulsive in Borderlands 1, but here the formula's been tweaked to ridiculously addictive effect. I think I had one or two guns I really liked in Borderlands, and the rest were necessary but uninspiring situational alternatives. In 2, I have a full loadout of weird, powerful and satisfying weapons I love, and an entire 'alternate' set in my backpack that I switch in and out to compare potency.
I've become a gun scientist. Sometimes I fill all four weapon slots with different types of shotgun and throw myself into a nest of Skags – as one does – to take notes.
The Jakobs has the numbers – 24 pellets at 600 damage each – but it's an ammo hog, and the Hyperion's bigger clip makes it better against mobs. But it's hard to bench the Tediore, because when it's out of shells, you can throw it at someone and it explodes and a new one teleports into your hands. And goddamn it, I've run out of Skags.
This is the game, and it makes Borderlands persistently fresh in a way other shooters never are. So it's weird that they kick it off with a painfully slow introductory segment that strips the game of everything that makes it good. It's ages before the first randomised gun even drops, and for ages after that, it's all useless inaccurate trash. And although the quests later become a highlight, in the first hour they're a maddening drag. You spend most of your time trying to figure out why your robot guide Claptrap has stopped following you, and backtracking to unstick his sloppy scripting.
It matters more than most ♥♥♥♥♥♥ intros, because you'll probably go through it more than once. Even if you stick to one class, you can start the game again after you complete it, taking your levelled character into a mode with new high-level enemies and loot. And if you don't, of course, there are three more classes to try.
The Commando can throw down a turret, a play style that needs some planning: you can execute satisfying pincer movements, but it doesn't help you escape if you screw up.
The new Siren can temporarily suspend a single enemy in the air, and her skill recharges rapidly enough to be used in every fight. It's spectacularly cool to leap into the air to get a perfect shotgun critical on your hovering victim.
The Gunzerker can enter a rage that lets him use two guns at once, regenerating health and ammo as he goes. It's fun, but the perks he can unlock as he levels up are less interesting: mostly percentage increases to this or that.
The Assassin can cloak, leaving a hologram of himself to keep enemies focused on his former location. I stuck with him for my main character, upgrading to give myself lots of buffs shortly after every kill. The ultimate skill in that tree let me maintain stealth if my melee attack killed someone in one hit. I could prey on groups by taking out the weakest first, invisibly eliminating each until only the toughest was left.
More than in the first game, those abilities fit together nicely in co-op: the Gunzerker can be more reckless with friends around to revive him, the Assassin benefits hugely from distracted enemies, and it's a relief for everyone when the toughest enemy in a fight is suddenly plucked into the air by the Siren.
The interface for joining a co-op game is much nicer this time, and it's better at handling how quests are shared. But we still couldn't connect to each other without some port-forwarding faffery, and we still had to argue among ourselves about who got what loot.
More than the class abilities, it's the enemy design that keeps the combat fresh. The Goliath might be my favourite. Facing two of them in a bandit camp, I shot one in the head. At first he just seemed surprised. Then he got angry – angry enough to turn on his friends. He turned to the other Goliath and screamed: “Ever been strangled with your own intestines?” then projectile vomited a stream of caustic acid into his face.
His victim was baffled. “Why are you so mean? ” he said, dripping in acidic sick, before fighting back.
This is already sterling entertainment. But there's a twist: if the Goliath kills his friend, he levels up, getting stronger still with every kill. If you just want a distraction while you slip by, that's perfect. If you actually need to kill him, you have to be strategic about how much damage you let him do first.
Then there are the robots. I was dubious about how much fun it'd be to shoot metal instead of flesh, which now that I write it down doesn't make me sound like a particularly great person. But I needn't have worried. You can't headshot robots, but their joints are weakspots. If you're taking a lot of damage from a particular droid's weapon, you can aim and blow that arm off.
Flying repair droids try to fix the others in the field. Jet Loaders transform from humanoids into fighter jets, and bombard you with missiles. Bull Loaders can drop their shield to the ground and ram you like a bulldozer. And Constructors churn out a slow but endless stream of new bots until they're killed.
Best of all, the robots, the bandits and all of the world's gargantuan wildlife hate each other. Luring a giant stealth bat into a battle with a squadron of killbots is exactly what I want to be doing with my life.
The robots belong to Hyperion, whose CEO Handsome Jack is the main quest's verbose antagonist. The dialogue in that is mostly funny, but sometimes clangingly misjudged: every time it tries to properly demonise Jack or glamorise your friends, it resorts to being needlessly cruel or gratingly smug.
The sidequests are a different story. Because they're not about saving the world, they have room to have fun with the whims of the characters, who are always the strong point in Borderlands.
I set up a tea party for a 13-year-old girl. I took photos to inspire a garage mechanic's terrible poetry. I had a mission objective to endure a boring party. I had a three-way shootout with two other bounty hunters looking for the same long lost gun stash. I helped a malfunctioning robot delude himself into believing he was human. I tried to solve a murder, and shot the wrong guy. I was chased by Skag-riding cops five levels too high for me as I hunted for a cursed gun. And I took an assassination contract to kill myself – and completed it.
The effort and invention that's gone into this stuff is a constant pleasure, and the sheer amount of it is overwhelming. The majority of the game is tied up in these side quests, and it's mind-bogglingly huge. I probably found half of them, and the game took me 30 hours to complete.
The main quest takes you to some cool places, but it's often marred by disproportionately tough bosses. Dying in a boss fight also undoes all the damage you've dealt, wasting all that time and ammo. I once made the mistake of using the nearby fast-travel station to get to a shop to restock. Turns out you can't travel back to that particular beacon, so I had to do the whole mission again, with all enemies respawned.
Luckily, you can level up by doing side missions first, where these problems generally don't come up.
It's generally well-adapted to the PC: graphics options, an FoV slider, some sensible control tweaks, and most importantly smooth and responsive mouse movement. My only issue is that levels load before the textures are ready, so everything's hideously blurry for a moment.
The Verdict
90/100

Spec Ops: The Line, to me, is an underrated game because it tells one hell of a story. While it doesn't offer a lot of innovation in terms of gameplay, the story truly makes up for everything it lacks. Set in a future, sand-ridden Dubai, you and your 2 Delta Force comrades are sent in to investigate the disappearance of a group of U.S. soldiers stationed in Dubai. What you and your team discover is something darker than expected and nothing ever goes the way you want it to. The way this game delivers the story is truly fantastic and story is truly gritty and will leave thinking about certain aspects in life. If you ever want a modern 3rd person shooter with a great story, get Spec Ops; you won't be disappointed. The gameplay is similar to many 3rd person shooters but like I stated previously, it's the story that makes this game truly shine.

This is not what you think.  Its a life lesson wrapped up in a video game.  Its smacks you upside the head and tells you to wake up.  Everyone owes it to themselves to play this game.
I've never been quite so attached to the "story" in any military shooter.  It's always shoot 10,000 nameless bad guys and come home the hero.  Thankfully this game changes the formula.  It takes the normal military shooter formula and punches it in the gut.
The basic premise is you and your squad are sent in to a natural disaster area to investigate what happened to an entire army battalion.  Once the story starts, all hell breaks loose and you are apparently the good guy that can stop it.
Many, many professional reviewers simply didn't understand this game.  It was never at any point in time supposed to be a CoD or Battlefield competitor.  Its a story wrapped around a very normal shooter.  The gameplay is good and engaging but used to enforce the narrative rather than make you want to keep blowing stuff up.  In fact, soon you start actually questioning what you (as the character) are doing.  For all intents and purposes it is designed like a standard shooter but it is so much more once the game really begins.
Play this game.  Final Grade: A-
