Mad Max is a, for the most part, enjoyable open world game set in a desert wasteland and full of unholy beings. Storywise, the game is great. The driving and combat are, in my opinion, also quite great. Being able to customise the Magnum Opus to suit your driving and upgrading Max's gear for the Arkham-like combat system leads to a decent amount of progression to these mechanics throughout the game. However, it is the progression of the story (not so much the story itself) that is the downfall of what could've been one of the best games of 2015. At times I felt as though I was meerly just running errands for people, something even Max notices, which makes him qutie Mad (it had to be done)... What I mean by this is that in order to progress you would have to upgrade your vehicle, which often meant reducing the threat in a region or gathering scrap... lots and lots of scrap... Yes, there is a lot of loot in this game, and you will need to be collecting as much of it as you can.
But overall, this game was quite enjoyable. For a game set in a desert it is quite a pretty game, and the voice acting and characters found in the game are quite special. The world of Mad Max is truly something that you need to experience for yourself if you're a fan of racing games and third-person action games (similar to Shadow of Mordor and the Arkham series developed by WB as well).
Enjoy! :D

It's hard to give a fair accounting of Spec Ops: The Line because listing what makes it worthwhile is pretty much damning with faint praise. Is doing a war game with better accounting of moral consequences than other military shooters an accomplishment?
If games are to be judged by the extent to which they achieve their filmic ambitions, SOTL is a Michael Moore flick: Well presented and touching on important points but nothing new to anyone who pays attention and by its very reputation unlikely to reach the people who might be exposed to a new idea. The overwrought praise for SOTL more or less damns it to never be played by fans of the dudebro shooters whose conventions SOTL seeks to upend.
SOTL isn't going to blow your mind and its cover shooter mechanics are pretty humdrum and workmanlike -- think the Mass Effect series stripped of its RPG elements.
That said, it still has Hollywood ambitions in its presentation and visuals. Its storyline, while not deserving of the hype it receives, is still enjoyable and a nice break from the spiritual and moral poison of your typical rah-rah army shooters.

There are commonly two perceptions of war, according to writer James Shea: ritualistic, and survivalistic. Ritualistic views are those that glorify the art of conflict, shine it up and fill it with stirring tunes and noble ideals, and create heroes and colourful legends from the men and women who participate in it. See Call of Duty, Battlefield, and Medal of Honor for examples of this.
Ritualistic perceptions are those that focus on war's darker side: the ambiguous morality of it, the dark passions involved in it, and the terrible things a soldier must do to survive it. They are the ones that try to instill in the viewer the realization that sometimes, the best intentions often result in the very worst outcomes. And Spec Ops: The Line is perhaps the finest example of what happens when you adopt this approach when creating a shooter that is commonly used to achieve the opposite effect.
From the beginning, to the end, Spec Ops tells a story most war-gamers won't want to hear. That most studios studiously ignore, and most glorified portrayals of war seek to bury. And, as we follow a squad of initially well-intentioned U.S infantrymen on their journey through the eerie, sand-blasted ruins of a once-opulent Dubai, and see them break down as they confront the utterly horrifying acts they are forced to commit in order to 'save the day', we get to see one of war's most traumatizing truths laid out in all its razor-sharp, unearthly simplicity.
"I...I didn't mean to hurt anybody!"
"No one ever does, Walker. No one ever does."
A dark, troubling, fascinating game, which tells a story that for too long has been ignored by the gaming industry. In a standard Modern Warfare game, when a console comes up letting you fire missiles at an unspecified area, you gleefully eviscerate the baddies, confident that they deserved to die because they hated your freedoms. Spec Ops lets you do the exact same thing: there are no auto-cues or context-specific actions – but also shows you the brutal aftermath of what happens when you carelessly pull the trigger, or press the button. Sometimes, going in all guns blazing damages more than just the evil-doers. And then you’re forced to stop and think, could I have done it a different way? A better way? Could I have avoided doing what I did, now that I’ve seen the consequences? And as the bodies lie smoking round you, the blood trickles gently into the shifting sand, and the hanging corpses swing unnervingly from the street-lights illuminating the way to what was once a seven-star hotel, you ask yourself;
Am I actually the bad guy?
But there’s gunfire in the distance, your squad-mates hoarsely yell at you to move, and you’re swept relentlessly into the next confrontation, as the edges of your world fray with the stress of doubting every action you make, every bullet that comes out of your rifle, and even your own sanity. Is this real? What am I doing? Why am I here? What's going on? Why can't I stop it? Am I killing the wrong people?
But the guns keep firing, the sandstorms keep roaring, the blood keeps flowing, and you're forced to keep moving.
Do you feel like a hero yet?

I rate this game a 2/5, and this is coming from someone who gives the first season 5/5. I'm just going to list the problems with this game:
- Bad voice actors: most actors from the original game are gone because of the strike, so the characters are voiced by subpar actors. The voice actors don't know how to sound sad so they just talk really slow.
- Bad writing: The writing throughout the game is incredibly cringy and just bad. Season 1 had its share of cringy dialogue but doesn't come close to the awfulness of the writing in Before the Storm. The plot goes nowhere throughout the game; the end of each episode makes me feel like I'm back where I started. There are weird dream sequences that don't help the story and just feel awful to play/watch.
- Little interaction/puzzles: This game lacks the puzzles present in Season One. This game feels like a movie with a few meaningless choices. There are no elements that make this a game rather than a movie. The first game had the rewind power which allowed the developers to add puzzles for the player to solve. The only attempt at a puzzle in this game is the boring "backtalk" challenges.
- No "strange" elements: This game should just be called "Life: Before The Storm." Without a supernatural element, nothing is strange about this game, and makes it just boring teenage drama.
- Backtalk: Many of the backtalk interactions make little sense, and why am I only given a few seconds to think about my choices in a game about decision making?
- Bad characters: Chloe is constantly mean to people, especially David, despite their efforts to be nice to her. Chloe is incredibly annoying in this game which makes it hard to watch. Other characters are also poorly written, but I won't go into detail for sake of spoilers. Elliot is also a totally meaningless character, and his scene in episode 3 is so bad I was laughing the whole time.
- Lacks content: This game doesn't contain nearly as many conversations or places to explore as the first game. It also only has three episodes. In the original game, Max could walk around every area and talk to people and examine objects. In this game I had little control over Chloe's movement and conversations.
- Bad ending: Choices made throughout the game have no significant impact, and the final binary choice isn't a tough choice like the one presented in Season One. On the other hand, to get an important scene at the end, a very specific sequence of choices needs to be made, which only 8% of people have managed to do at the time I finished the game. For such an important scene, it feels like it shouldn't be reliant on choices.
- Poor use of music: While Daughter composed some great music for this game, it was poorly used in the game. Much of Season One's charm, for me, was the use of music. In this game, there is no music playing during most scenes, making the conversations seem even more awkward than they already are and it highlights the poor writing. The ambient guitar music, and the great licensed songs in Season One were essential and it's what brings the first game from a 4/5 to a 5/5.
To summarize, this game is horribly written, and is clearly just a cash grab from Square Enix to make some money and maintain interest while we wait for DONTNOD's Season Two. Deck Nine just were not able to recreate the elements which made Life is Strange so great.
I wish this game contained a superpower or other supernatural elements, and I wish it was better written and had better usage of music.
Here's hoping that the Farewell episode and DONTNOD's Season Two will be better than this.

I'm only about two hours into the game, but initial impressions are very positive.
The Good:
Graphics are lovely, foliage density, lighting, weather--it's all on point.  I have brought my binoculars up multiple times checking if that movement in the distance is an animal, only to find a blowing branch or moving shadows. This really added to the immersiveness for me.  Branches and grass bend as you stalk past.
Playing the game with maxed settings (albeit at 1080p) with a constant 65fps, optimization seems solid, CPU/GPU temps both stayed well within reason.  intel i5 3.4GHz / gtx 980
Sound is on point as well, highly directional, underbrush crunches, animals chirp, hoot, hollar and otherwise immerse you in the living environment.
Core gameplay is solid.  Tracking, stalking, and shooting make for a fun formula.  I like that the hunting help (glowing tracks, directional assistance) are customizable, letting you play at the level of attention-to-detail you desire.  There seem to be plenty of progression options: weapon choices, different scopes, lures, binoculars; as well as a leveling skill/perk system.  And yet, the starting rifle feels plenty suitable for the game i've encountered thus far, so I don't feel rushed to level or worry about that stuff yet.
The Bad:
As some of the other reviews mentioned, the menu controls are kinda strange at times.  Either they occasionally hang so that you can't back out entirely, or there is some element of the selection that is somewhat tricky/unclear.  It hasn't caused me any major setbacks as a combination of escape and selecting the settings menu has allowed me to resume each time.
There don't seem to be many 'visual' character customization options.  Character presets  are pretty limited as are outfits.  This doesn't matter to me right now, but may become more important when I try out the multiplayer gameplay options.
The To Be Continued:
Haven't tried the multiplayer.  As that is the primary reason I was anticipating this game, I will have to update once I've had a chance to do so.

Hands down the best local multiplayer game on steam. It's very different from other local multiplayer games on steam largely because everything is based on manipulation of the physics engine. Other games require memorising different weapon and action combinations (e.g. Duck Game: knowing about the chain saw slide or the sniper shooting through windows). In Gang Beasts you can manipulate the body of your beast, and you use that to get the other players out of the map, or into the fire, or something similar.  That's it. You just learn the ways that your character moves - you learn, for instance, that you can jump and flop at the same time (A to jump, X/B to flop forward/backwards) and that allows you to dropkick people. It's not a combo of random buttons that does a prefab animation, it's entirely the manipulation of your character. That means that there's basically no skill cap - you just keep learning more stuff about how to do things. It's absurdly fun.
Things that need to be done:
* General bugfixing (like the ability to survive underwater sometimes, or the massive glitching out of the character mesh sometimes).
* Campaign mode - this is off to a good start already.
* More optionality over settings - we need to be able to select different map cycles, for instance.
Tons of fun and builds on your own skill.

Look, I was expecting a hard game. I was expecting difficult-to-kill zombies. I was expecting a murderous community hell-bent on stripping me of everything I have. I was expecting scarce loot.
What I was not expecting was entire cities with literally no food. The current loot tables make this game, at least for me, unplayable. Now, I know about apple trees and I know about chickens and I know I need to head north to get better stuff, but I can't even find any damn chickens or apple trees. They too are impossible to find. Scarce loot is to be expected in a post-apocalyptic game. But when entire city blocks contain less than 5 items, we have a problem. I've found more melee weapons than I have food and drink.
If I stay by the coast, I starve. If I go north, I starve. If I stick to the cities, I starve. I tried. The game is ridiculously hard, and that difficulty is created solely by scarcity of resources. It's not fun. I'm not asking to find an AK47 inside every house, I'm asking to maybe find just enough food to survive. As a long-time survival horror veteran, I'm fine with having to manage my supplies, but this takes it to an extreme I can't tolerate. Couple this with crappy hit-boxes for items and poorly designed zombies and this game simply isn't good.
I've only played two hours though, so I guess maybe I don't know what I'm talking about. Normally I'd play several more hours before writing such a scathing review, but guess what? If I play for less than two hours, I can get a refund. At least there's that.

Spec Ops: The Line, or as I like to call it, "War Crimes - The Game", is a pretty standard third-person shooter. The main difference is a focus on the storyline, which deconstructs the military shooter genre and shows the ugly side of war.
All in all, a pretty decent game, especially if you can get it for under ten bucks, as I did. It's nothing too special, but if military shooters are your thing, this game serves all that up with a fairly decent storyline, to boot. Good for a weekend of shooting big guns, friendly fire, and crimes against humanity.
Play this game. Now. Seriously, Spec Ops has the best storyline I've seen in a shooter in a long, long time.

There's a lot to like about this game. It takes a fairly tired genre (third person corridor shooter) and gives it some life with its interesting story, location, and set pieces. I've never seen a game set in Dubai before, and not only that but a post-apocalyptic Dubai. The art direction, with the super-modern architecture submerged in sand, and at odds with the war tearing the city apart, is very well done. The gameplay is designed to be disturbing- you mostly just kill other American soldiers, playing as an American soldier, and are forced to make hard decisions, and kill civilans in terrible ways, in order to achieve your goal. The set pieces somewhat reminded me of Bulletstorm, in that you frequently rope between the rooftops of 50 story buildings, or slide down collapsing skyscrapers, that sort of thing. It's very Heart of Darkness inspired in terms of the story, and in testing the morality of the main character. I would recommend a play, but it's worth picking up on sale for its short length, 6-7 hours.

A few things before I write my review:
: $9.99 (was on sale during the Steam Summer Sale).
: Alpha 21
: Alpha (Early Access)
Prison Architect is one of those games that I could probably play hundreds of hours, due to it's Sandbox gamestyle and nearly endless possibilities. Players play as a third-person controller on a top-down one-level prison, and have the freedom to customize their prison into many different configurations. While not fully accurate to a real prison, the game does have more immersion than the typical sandbox game. For example, players need to wire up their lights to a power generator, and all of their plumbing needs to be hooked up to a water station.
If you've never played a game like this, think of it sort of like the Sims, but in prison; diverse building options, unique people, and different services you can call on, either permanent or emergency. By unique people, I mean every prisoner is unique; they all have different backgrounds, families, prison sentences, and personal needs to keep them happy, or at least from rioting.
The Steam Workshop is enabled for PA, and there are quite a few mods out already. Many of the language packs were made by other players. I don't speak another language, so I can't speak to that, but it's definitely a plus if you're a modder or like to mod in general.
A couple things I think might be worth saying for this stage (not necessarily all bad):
* There are bugs. If you don't know what Alpha or Early Access means, please look it up before buying. Most of the bugs I encountered are graphical bugs (prisoners facing the wrong way when eating, clipping issues with certain objects, etc), but I don't doubt that there are gameplay issues as well.
* The tutorial is not fully immersive or broad enough to cover all the basics. While it covers some things such as power, a lot of what you might want to know will come with trial and error or looking up popular builds. For example, plumbing is not explained, nor is the Bureaucracy option. I personally like figuring out the different options and settings as part of the adventure, but other might not. Expect this gap in explained material to increase as more content is added.
* There is an "upgrade tree" in the game. I noticed it after hiring my Warden under the Bureaucracy menu, and "upgrades" do take time. I haven't gone through the entire tree yet, but so far the upgrades have been very useful and game-enhancing, versus 'upgrades for the sake of upgrades'. At the same time, don't expect to start a new game, build the perfect prison within the first 10 minutes, and then quit. Building is a process, and the game overall is a process.
* Unless you just copy successful prisons, it is a learning process. As of right now, I've designed two prisons, and both of them ended up failing on some level (albeit not completely fail in the sense of 'game over'). Prisoners escape, you hit your spending limit, you need riot police to come keep the order. But you just add a few more doors, hire a few new guards, and don't get afraid of locking down your prison.
Overall, I only forsee this game to get better. I'm pretty happy with the features already in-game and can't wait to see where they take this.

As I died screaming between a wolf’s jaws, collapsing in the snow that dusts the top of the mountains while listening to it gnaw through virtual flesh, I had a realization: survival games are fun as long as they are about the threat of death.
Death itself is underwhelming: a gateway to an ever-increasing set of chores and tasks that you must repeat in order to recover your lost progress. Inevitably, the process eventually repeats, and the to-do list gets longer and less fulfilling, which sounds a little bit like hell and a little bit like a parable about the human condition. Rust [official site], the multiplayer survival game from Facepunch Studios, seems comfortable with both analogies.
If you’re not familiar with Rust, or if you only know it as the Survival Game with Lots of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it’s actually a weirder and more interesting game than it first appears to be. You wake up in a strange landscape, cold and naked with nothing but a torch and a rock to your name. Then, after a few minutes of trial-and-error exploration of Rust’s wilderness, you can start building crude tools out of loose materials, then using those tools to harvest more material to build better tools, etc. The tech tree runs from Stone Age materials all the way to automatic weapons and heavy body armor. Survival in Rust can become a fairly comfortable survivalist’s fantasy if you stay alive long enough… but death comes swiftly and with little warning.

1. Optimalization. What a perfect optimalization!
... forget on Batman´s epic fail. On the highest settings the game runs like a Swiss watch. Many thanks to Avalanche studios for really good job.
2. Wasteland. What a atmospheric wasteland!
... really big, really large and variable.
3. Details. What a impressive details!
... fortresses, various locations, points of interests and more.
4. Sandstorms. What a real sandstorms!
... I can´t remember better processed video games sandstorms. Maybe in Spec Ops: The Line, but in Mad Max sandstorm appears randomly in two variants.
5. Ride. What a rough ride!
... feeling of riding is really enjoyable. Not only in Magnum Opus.
6. Combat system. What a brutal combat system!
... simple but effective. You know his older and better brother from Arkham series.
7. Visualization. What a sexy visualization!
... nice graphics, effects of explosions, mentioned locations.
After 15 hours of gameplay, Mad Max caught a second wind, gets momentum and simply will not let you go. Despite the fact you´re doing the same thing all the time.
I´d like to support devs by purchase upcoming Just Casuse 3. They deserved it in times of terrible console ports.

I bought this game expecting......well I don't know what I was expecting actually but It was a suprisingly fun and made me crank 56 hours into it within the two weeks I owned it.
I can honestly say I've never seen brown and blue look as good as it has in this game and makes pretty much any other desert setting look bland.  The detail is pretty good and runs very well on high on mid range computers (I still have my old HD 6970) and only got choppy at one or two spots which almost seemed like a bug as it had nothing to do with rendering.
The combat I can best describe as Batman 1.5 fighting as it is essentially almost all mouse based BUT you can't just teleport to enemies as you could in batman games.  There are a few mechanics which adds to it and makes it a little more complex than that but fighting in Mad Max is actually VERY satisfying and at many points it somehow felt new again.  That being said there isn't a lot of variety in enemies (for example all the "mini bosses" were all just reskins) and could have been added to make the combat more difficult.  The car combat however is actually the best I've ever personally done and I just wish there were more convoys to take advantage of it.
My final note is every camp I went to and most scrap locations were unique and while one or two camps were a little mazelike it made taking over the camps the best part of the game.

To start off with, this is an absolutely beautiful game. The environment is stunning and the texturing and animations for the animals are incredible. The sounds are amazing. They've definitely done an excellent job with creating a visually spectacular game. However, I don't want a hunting game that's just pretty to look at, and that's just about all this one is so far - pretty.
It is essentially a very dumbed down version of theHunter: Classic. While they improved certain mechanics such as the tracking system - making it so you don't have to have the HunterMate in your hand in order to track animals - and a visual wind direction right on the compass, they drastically oversimplified others. Size/rack variations are practically non-existant from what I've seen thus far, small game other than coyote is present, but not able to be harvested, there's no trophy shots (although you can always just take a photo manually prior to harvest), skill progression is global rather than per-species, and is based on general XP gain rather than skill-specific XP, and many of the points of interest which say they grant skill/perk points do not actually do so.  Overall it feels like they've gone the way of a Cabela's game - going from a simulation heavy title to an very arcade-like experience.
Hopefully a lot of those issues can be handled by an update. Until then, if you're looking for something close to theHunter: Classic, this simply isn't it.

As you can see by my playtime, I have played quite a bit of Undertale. Now, after beating the game for the third time, I can safetly say that the game is not as good as everyone says it is, however, I still recommend it. Now, before you go burning down my house for not loving or hating Undertale, just listen, or, in this case read. However, if you haven't played the game, don't bother reading, just play, you will be spoiled.
The First Playthrough:
I already knew quite a bit about the game, so of course, first I went on a Neutral Run. I killed here and there, and didn't do any of the side events. And the ending, made me see how I did all the wrong decisions. I also had several moments of difficulty, where I spent weeks being stuck. Now, If this was all there was to the game, I couldn't recommend or not recommend it. However, my next play though, changed it.
The Second Playthrough:
This time, I went pacifist, spared everyone, and made several friends. I enjoyed this Playthrough, the most. While it didn't change my opinion of the characters,as I still liked some *cough*Papyrus*cough* and still hated some *cough*Alphys*cough*, it was a much more satisfying game, as I had to solve puzzles to try and spare these monsters, and I got into their motivations. However, The True Lab was annoyingly difficult, and the fact you couldn't actually die in the final fight sucked, but was made up with it with a better ending.
The Final Playthrough (Yes, I just  Majora's mask'ed you):
This Playthrough, the genocide one, was my least favourite. Now, several people would disagree with me, but just hear me out. All the genocide Run added was two new boss fights (which I have to admidt, were pretty good) and endless grinding. In this Run, you have to kill a certain amount of enemy's, so it was just waiting for them to encounter me. It was boring and not fun. Plus, that route, prevented me, from getting the great pacifist ending again.
Overall:
This game is pretty good. The netutral Run was alright, the pacafist was amazing, and the genocide, not as much. But I will give it this, the game has some increadible music, and sucky graphics. And Alphys. Worst character in the game.

Look, I was expecting a hard game. I was expecting difficult-to-kill zombies. I was expecting a murderous community hell-bent on stripping me of everything I have. I was expecting scarce loot.
What I was not expecting was entire cities with literally no food. The current loot tables make this game, at least for me, unplayable. Now, I know about apple trees and I know about chickens and I know I need to head north to get better stuff, but I can't even find any damn chickens or apple trees. They too are impossible to find. Scarce loot is to be expected in a post-apocalyptic game. But when entire city blocks contain less than 5 items, we have a problem. I've found more melee weapons than I have food and drink.
If I stay by the coast, I starve. If I go north, I starve. If I stick to the cities, I starve. I tried. The game is ridiculously hard, and that difficulty is created solely by scarcity of resources. It's not fun. I'm not asking to find an AK47 inside every house, I'm asking to maybe find just enough food to survive. As a long-time survival horror veteran, I'm fine with having to manage my supplies, but this takes it to an extreme I can't tolerate. Couple this with crappy hit-boxes for items and poorly designed zombies and this game simply isn't good.
I've only played two hours though, so I guess maybe I don't know what I'm talking about. Normally I'd play several more hours before writing such a scathing review, but guess what? If I play for less than two hours, I can get a refund. At least there's that.

It's very hard to hype this game up. You get into a truck with some cargo to deliver and hit the road accross a scaled down version of Europe. Over time you gain experience for things, like longer distances, more valuable cargo, etc. You can eventually buy your own truck(s), hire other drivers and expand your trucking empire and stuff.
But basically, it's about driving heavy, sluggish trucks. I am having difficulties putting into words
any of this is fun. Perhaps fun isn't the right word at all.
It's relaxing most of the time, satisfying, and sometimes tense.
There's something in there about small moments. The moment where you pull out of the loading dock with your frozen peas or whatnot and find the highway. The moment where the countryside changes and you cross borders. The moment where the signs change and the language is different. The moment where you know you're almost there and are about to arrive. The moment where somewhere in the middle, it rained for a while, or got really dark. Or both. The moment where you missed your exit somewhere in belgium. The moment where you discovered you could listen to actual internet radio from within your truck, from a station that matches the country you're gently passing through.
This is probably not something you'll want to sit at for multiple hours, but if you're anything like me, you'll keep coming back to it, running a delivery once in a while, because it's relaxing, and the moments are tantalizing.
Oh also, there's a multiplayer mod. It's all of this except once in a while you will pass another guy going in the opposite direction. You'll both cheerfully honk your horns in greeting, then continue on your respective ways. I guess that's also another moment.

As I died screaming between a wolf’s jaws, collapsing in the snow that dusts the top of the mountains while listening to it gnaw through virtual flesh, I had a realization: survival games are fun as long as they are about the threat of death.
Death itself is underwhelming: a gateway to an ever-increasing set of chores and tasks that you must repeat in order to recover your lost progress. Inevitably, the process eventually repeats, and the to-do list gets longer and less fulfilling, which sounds a little bit like hell and a little bit like a parable about the human condition. Rust [official site], the multiplayer survival game from Facepunch Studios, seems comfortable with both analogies.
If you’re not familiar with Rust, or if you only know it as the Survival Game with Lots of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it’s actually a weirder and more interesting game than it first appears to be. You wake up in a strange landscape, cold and naked with nothing but a torch and a rock to your name. Then, after a few minutes of trial-and-error exploration of Rust’s wilderness, you can start building crude tools out of loose materials, then using those tools to harvest more material to build better tools, etc. The tech tree runs from Stone Age materials all the way to automatic weapons and heavy body armor. Survival in Rust can become a fairly comfortable survivalist’s fantasy if you stay alive long enough… but death comes swiftly and with little warning.

At the beginning I have to admit that Mad Max is very stereotypical game, contains a few unimportant bugs, the plot is not the best (but not the worst) and unfortunately the potential has not been excavated to the maximum which this open-world game totaly deserves.
But, you know what.. Let me introduce you seven fundamental reasons why the game forces you to play it!
1. Optimalization. What a perfect optimalization!
... forget on Batman´s epic fail. On the highest settings the game runs like a Swiss watch. Many thanks to Avalanche studios for really good job.
2. Wasteland. What a atmospheric wasteland!
... really big, really large and variable.
3. Details. What a impressive details!
... fortresses, various locations, points of interests and more.
4. Sandstorms. What a real sandstorms!
... I can´t remember better processed video games sandstorms. Maybe in Spec Ops: The Line, but in Mad Max sandstorm appears randomly in two variants.
5. Ride. What a rough ride!
... feeling of riding is really enjoyable. Not only in Magnum Opus.
6. Combat system. What a brutal combat system!
... simple but effective. You know his older and better brother from Arkham series.
7. Visualization. What a sexy visualization!
... nice graphics, effects of explosions, mentioned locations.
After 15 hours of gameplay, Mad Max caught a second wind, gets momentum and simply will not let you go. Despite the fact you´re doing the same thing all the time.
I´d like to support devs by purchase upcoming Just Casuse 3. They deserved it in times of terrible console ports.

Mad Max for me is my favorate Post Apocolyptic universe. The movies really help transport you to a Post Apocolyptic universal plainly built on gasoline and brutality.
The game, allows you to get a upclose and personal look at the world of Mad Max. Build the ultimate car, and drive the waists of Australia. Take down outposts, fortresses and camps to lower threat levels in territories, or chase down a convoy and destroy it to take out Gas towns supplies. Enter Death Races to win vehicles to add to you collection.
Mad Max over all is one hell of a fun ride. The land scape is vast and intresting. The storms are powerful and beatiful. Car building and customazation, although limited, engaging and worthwhile.
Only big flaw thats brakes emersion is the crappy "survive" mechanic where you need food and water to heal and bullets which is suppose to be a rare commonity. But, max out 1 fort and you will have infinate water, gas, and bullets. Just quick travel when ya start running low. Not to mention, is scattered pretty heavily across the waists. None of the "rare" stuff, has been hard to find. I find myself leaving it, cause theres so much.
I do recommend giving this a playthrew though. Its a very fun and strangly addicting game. Any fan of Mad Max will adore what this game offers.

I bought this game expecting......well I don't know what I was expecting actually but It was a suprisingly fun and made me crank 56 hours into it within the two weeks I owned it.
I can honestly say I've never seen brown and blue look as good as it has in this game and makes pretty much any other desert setting look bland.  The detail is pretty good and runs very well on high on mid range computers (I still have my old HD 6970) and only got choppy at one or two spots which almost seemed like a bug as it had nothing to do with rendering.
The combat I can best describe as Batman 1.5 fighting as it is essentially almost all mouse based BUT you can't just teleport to enemies as you could in batman games.  There are a few mechanics which adds to it and makes it a little more complex than that but fighting in Mad Max is actually VERY satisfying and at many points it somehow felt new again.  That being said there isn't a lot of variety in enemies (for example all the "mini bosses" were all just reskins) and could have been added to make the combat more difficult.  The car combat however is actually the best I've ever personally done and I just wish there were more convoys to take advantage of it.
My final note is every camp I went to and most scrap locations were unique and while one or two camps were a little mazelike it made taking over the camps the best part of the game.

A great improvement on TheHunter Classic. The graphics are better, the sounds are better, the environment is better, and the animals are better - especially the rabbits hiding in the underbrush. It's just better. There are also visible trails of bent grass where the animal you're tracking travelled, which is awesome and makes tracking much more intuitive than the search patterns you probably learned to do in theHunter Classic, and the render distance isn't capped. That's right you can shoot out beyond 200 meters now - there's even a 400m kill achievement!
At release the menus are pretty clunky, but you can work with them. I haven't experienced any major bugs except having to switch to the map screen to exit a menu. Once they patch it up this will be a solid title.
If you're a stalker-type hunter, like me, you'll probably want to know that if you use a controller with analog sticks there is a range of movement speeds that will allow you to move while walking and crouching without alarming nearby animals. If you use a M+K setup only the WASD keys have you moving at maximum speed and you'll alarm the animals even when crouching. I use an Xbox One controller to stalk then switch to my M+K to shoot because aiming with a controller is way too hard. Hopefully the devs add a movement speed toggle for M+K, but until they do stalking is really only possible with a controller.

There are nods and thematical tie-ins with the original trilogy, and, watching Fury Road after the game's completion, there are definite stylitsic similiarities and prequel elements to the latest installment that add more depth to locations, factions, and characters that remain as mere plot points in the movie without the game's  (admittedly sparse) story. Car combat is great, and the convoy chases and explosions feel straight out the film. Less faithful is the ground combat: Max can disinterestedly take out dozens of enemies with his bare hands, a stark contrast to the brutal ferocity that he would, in a more realistic way, need to focus on single enemies in the movies (yeah yeah, it's a videogame). You'll also never have to contend with mis-firing shotguns, and will almost always have ample fuel. As such, it's not The True Mad Max Experience, but at least give it points for coming close.

I almost feel obligated to make this review seeing the low scores that this game is getting for no apparent reason, so here we go.
I'm not gonna dwell on the story cause it's just there to be there and to give you a purpose. Nothing special to it
The gameplay is where this game shines, you have a car with a massive list of parts that you can upgrade you have three main aspects to it: Speed, handling and strength. You can either have a car that is good at all of them or a car that is great at two and weak at the other. the customization is also complex and fun, it's not just you trying to max out every category, you also have to keep in mind the down side to every upgrade.
Upgrading Max himself is also just as fun. Learning new combat moves never felt like I'm wasting scrap (the currency in the game). Each move felt unique and useful from reversals to wall slamming to limb breaking. The game is also VERY violent and gory which makes it even better for me. You'll face different types of enemies that will require you to use most of you moves along the game.
The open worlds of this game is one of the best I've ever seen in any video game. All the roads connect to each other and it's extremely nonrestrictive which is a huge plus. Each area has a big balloon where you can spot landmarks and "Threats" that you need to lower in order to unlock new upgrades for you and your car
The graphics in this are superb, especially when it comes to lights, shadows, tire and footstep trails. The game looks pretty colorful and well done. Can't ask for much more than this
The sound isn't up to the game's standard. I often found myself not being able to precisely pinpoint where the sound is coming from, but overall it's serviceable.
For the most part this game is bug free, though I did find myself getting stuck on minute objects but there isn't a persistent bug worth mentioning.
Overall this game is one of the best games I have played this year and it baffles me that it's getting these low scores. I definitely recommend you purchase this game at full price, you won't be disappointed.

Life Is Strange: Before the Storm has somehow managed to match the emotional intensity, character connectivity, tone, and overall atmosphere of the original game, something not often said of a prequel/sequel. Let's dive into some simple pros and cons:
PROS:
- Relatable characters. From rebellious Chloe to mysterious Rachel Amber; from nerdy Steph to jock Drew North, everyone will relate to at least one character presented.
- Backtalk challenge. A new risk/reward conversation minigame to Life Is Strange, this minigame requires the player to use some wit to make clever backtalk remarks in order for Chloe to achieve a more favorable outcome in a situation (getting out of trouble from the principal, for example).
- Animations. Deck Nine really did a fantastic job of bringing characters to life with natural-looking animations. There are a few janky animations, sudden changes, but nothing worth serious criticism. The lip sync in this game is dramatically improved over the previous game too.
- MUSIC. MUSIC, MUSIC, MUSIC! Daughter did an INCREDIBLE job with the soundtrack of this game. The echoey yet emotionally heavy guitars mixed in with ambient audio (like a rusty car hood creaking when Chloe puts her hand on it) exponentially improves the atmosphere of the game. You feel completely immersed and connected to the world through the music alone.
- Beautiful scenery. By this I mean graphics of course---the lighting, artsy textures, etc. Those things are nice, yes, but the design of Arcadia Bay, the return to Dontnod's original work while creating entirely new additions to the small fictional Oregon town we know and love creates a rich and diverse world that, once again, completely immerses you in the world of Chloe. Through the combination of well-written dialogue, beautiful music and excellent audio effects, and immersive scenery, you truly feel and experience what Chloe feels and experiences. You almost feel like a guardian angel standing over Chloe's shoulders, subtly influencing her destiny, instead of feeling like a gamer moving a mouse and clicking on a keyboard.
- Symbolism. Game theorists who made tons of theories in the first game: you'll be put to work diving into symbols and theories again. Keep a close eye on the appearance of ravens, glyphs on tucked away walls, etc.
- Journal. The journal is back again and it has a creative twist on it. Instead of a diary like Max had, Chloe's journal is a collection of letters written to Max that she never sends. If you played the first game, yes, that is as heart-wrenching as it sounds. Read the letters, they're very humorous at times and really brings you closer with Chloe's character. You won't end episode one with 40 pages like the original either; they're short and sweet.
- Player Choice. Choices really seem to matter this time around, in the short term and long term. For example, stealing the shirt in the beginning (like the demo showed) and wearing it will result in people talking to you about the sketchy concert Chloe got it at. There are quite a few of small choices like this that seem to be bigger in the long run, but for the sake of avoiding spoilers, I'll leave it at that.
CONS:
- Few janky animations. This is largely unavoidable, but it was annoying a few times to see a scene ending with Chloe stopping mid-conversation animation and walking away, or other slight things of that nature.
- Voice actor changes. This is in no way Square Enix or Deck Nine's faults, but it was quite jarring to hear known characters from the first game with completely different voices. Most of the repeating characters however did have voice actors that nearly perfectly matched the personality and face of the characters presented in the original game, however some just sounded completely off. If you're new to the series and don't want to play the original, this won't bother you as they're talented actors. Returning players though, you'll notice it. David doesn't sound as tough or gravely, and Principal Wells sounds much younger.
- Audio glitches. I noticed in my playthrough of episode 1 that sometimes audio lines would be cut off abruptly and the next character in line to speak would start doing so. I like to play without subtitles on my first playthrough of games like this for immersion's sake, but this caused me to turn them on. If you play without subtitles, it will only be an occaisional minor annoyance, and I imagine this will get fixed.
BOTTOM LINE:
If you enjoyed the original Life Is Strange, you will absolutely enjoy this game. It is much more than a "fan fiction" as some claim it to be; it is truly a work of art worth its own game.
To newcomers: you will experience a truly tragic yet also heart-warming story in this game (in episode 1 and the others to follow), and you will find relatable characters that will stick with you for a life time; and above all else, you'll have a great time experiencing this wonderful game. (And of course I recommend you play the first game!)

TL;DR: Spec Ops: The Line is an amazing story, told through an okay FPS.  I think it's certainly worth the ten bucks I paid for it.  If you don't think it's worth buying even on sale, I suggest at least watching a Let's Play of it someday, because the story is awesome.
The gameplay is your standard cover-based shooter, which might make a kind of sense once you finish the game, but will still be fairly boring if you're not into FPS action for it's own sake.  The game isn't that long, so if you're just playing for the story you can turn the difficulty down and forge ahead with little trouble.

I almost feel obligated to make this review seeing the low scores that this game is getting for no apparent reason, so here we go.
I'm not gonna dwell on the story cause it's just there to be there and to give you a purpose. Nothing special to it
The gameplay is where this game shines, you have a car with a massive list of parts that you can upgrade you have three main aspects to it: Speed, handling and strength. You can either have a car that is good at all of them or a car that is great at two and weak at the other. the customization is also complex and fun, it's not just you trying to max out every category, you also have to keep in mind the down side to every upgrade.
Upgrading Max himself is also just as fun. Learning new combat moves never felt like I'm wasting scrap (the currency in the game). Each move felt unique and useful from reversals to wall slamming to limb breaking. The game is also VERY violent and gory which makes it even better for me. You'll face different types of enemies that will require you to use most of you moves along the game.
The open worlds of this game is one of the best I've ever seen in any video game. All the roads connect to each other and it's extremely nonrestrictive which is a huge plus. Each area has a big balloon where you can spot landmarks and "Threats" that you need to lower in order to unlock new upgrades for you and your car
The graphics in this are superb, especially when it comes to lights, shadows, tire and footstep trails. The game looks pretty colorful and well done. Can't ask for much more than this
The sound isn't up to the game's standard. I often found myself not being able to precisely pinpoint where the sound is coming from, but overall it's serviceable.
For the most part this game is bug free, though I did find myself getting stuck on minute objects but there isn't a persistent bug worth mentioning.
Overall this game is one of the best games I have played this year and it baffles me that it's getting these low scores. I definitely recommend you purchase this game at full price, you won't be disappointed.

First of all let me point out what is awesome about this game. Atmosphere! Oh! The atmosphere! If the movies did it well, then so too has this game captured the bleak-yet-beautiful nature of the wasteland. The skies, the weather, the STORMS!
The great addictiveness of Mad Max is perfectly executed in 3 things:
1) The development of your car - the Magnum Opus (a wasteland mistransaltion of the Greek - Magna Opus - Great Work of Magnificence)
2) The development of stronghold projects for benefits - every project is a mission and every project is a reward.
3) Collection of vehicles - who needs cards these days when you can collect cars?
Summary of things I loved:
The majetsy of driving and fighting in the vehicle.
The intensity of the physical fighting and great dynamic moves
Did I laready mention atmosphere? I'm sure I did.
The sandiest sandbox I have ever played in.
Australian accents made by a real Australian. No-one can do a real Aussie accent . Seriously. You can't. We can tell. Also, right hand drive. Get used to it.
Now this game peaks on so many levels and it is well worth whatever you decide to spend on it, but that said - I do have a few gripes. A lot of peeps complain that the gameplay can get repetative, and whilst that is a little true, it also offers up a big variety of things for you to do - so when you are getting bored of busting bases, you can race, and when you get tired of that there are wastelander missions, scrap looting missions, convoys, minefields or just bombing around in your recently stolen vehicle admiring the scenery non-missions to do.
The intro could have been playable.
The ENDGAME could have been playable - but no - all we are given is a cinematic. VERY unsatisfactory.
I don't want to spoli the end, but I'll say this:
Poor storyline at the end. Very poor in a way that makes you question whether the writers just couldn't care about putting any effort into the endings. The storyline is written to force you to fail - at EVERYTHING - and I don't care for it. It made me feel like the wiorters were just too damn lazy. I also felt very cheated on the outcomes of the major characters, both friend and foe. But, let's put that aside for a moment.
Neutral things:
The car collection you can achieve is nice, but not particularly engaging unless you are a screenshot ♥♥♥♥♥ (and yeah - I find that fun). For all you other screncap ♥♥♥♥♥s, there is a nifty in-game feature to let you get your own caps and vid - and that's a very cool thing. Car collection? Well - I guess it might be what you make of it.
Races - well, very musch a lot of fun if you want to compete amongst friend or be the bestest of the bestest. A good addition.
Overall - this game certainly rocks!
My advice - Don't get too caught up with the storyline - get your V8 early-ish and have fun blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up!

Life Is Strange: Before the Storm has somehow managed to match the emotional intensity, character connectivity, tone, and overall atmosphere of the original game, something not often said of a prequel/sequel. Let's dive into some simple pros and cons:
PROS:
- Relatable characters. From rebellious Chloe to mysterious Rachel Amber; from nerdy Steph to jock Drew North, everyone will relate to at least one character presented.
- Backtalk challenge. A new risk/reward conversation minigame to Life Is Strange, this minigame requires the player to use some wit to make clever backtalk remarks in order for Chloe to achieve a more favorable outcome in a situation (getting out of trouble from the principal, for example).
- Animations. Deck Nine really did a fantastic job of bringing characters to life with natural-looking animations. There are a few janky animations, sudden changes, but nothing worth serious criticism. The lip sync in this game is dramatically improved over the previous game too.
- MUSIC. MUSIC, MUSIC, MUSIC! Daughter did an INCREDIBLE job with the soundtrack of this game. The echoey yet emotionally heavy guitars mixed in with ambient audio (like a rusty car hood creaking when Chloe puts her hand on it) exponentially improves the atmosphere of the game. You feel completely immersed and connected to the world through the music alone.
- Beautiful scenery. By this I mean graphics of course---the lighting, artsy textures, etc. Those things are nice, yes, but the design of Arcadia Bay, the return to Dontnod's original work while creating entirely new additions to the small fictional Oregon town we know and love creates a rich and diverse world that, once again, completely immerses you in the world of Chloe. Through the combination of well-written dialogue, beautiful music and excellent audio effects, and immersive scenery, you truly feel and experience what Chloe feels and experiences. You almost feel like a guardian angel standing over Chloe's shoulders, subtly influencing her destiny, instead of feeling like a gamer moving a mouse and clicking on a keyboard.
- Symbolism. Game theorists who made tons of theories in the first game: you'll be put to work diving into symbols and theories again. Keep a close eye on the appearance of ravens, glyphs on tucked away walls, etc.
- Journal. The journal is back again and it has a creative twist on it. Instead of a diary like Max had, Chloe's journal is a collection of letters written to Max that she never sends. If you played the first game, yes, that is as heart-wrenching as it sounds. Read the letters, they're very humorous at times and really brings you closer with Chloe's character. You won't end episode one with 40 pages like the original either; they're short and sweet.
- Player Choice. Choices really seem to matter this time around, in the short term and long term. For example, stealing the shirt in the beginning (like the demo showed) and wearing it will result in people talking to you about the sketchy concert Chloe got it at. There are quite a few of small choices like this that seem to be bigger in the long run, but for the sake of avoiding spoilers, I'll leave it at that.
CONS:
- Few janky animations. This is largely unavoidable, but it was annoying a few times to see a scene ending with Chloe stopping mid-conversation animation and walking away, or other slight things of that nature.
- Voice actor changes. This is in no way Square Enix or Deck Nine's faults, but it was quite jarring to hear known characters from the first game with completely different voices. Most of the repeating characters however did have voice actors that nearly perfectly matched the personality and face of the characters presented in the original game, however some just sounded completely off. If you're new to the series and don't want to play the original, this won't bother you as they're talented actors. Returning players though, you'll notice it. David doesn't sound as tough or gravely, and Principal Wells sounds much younger.
- Audio glitches. I noticed in my playthrough of episode 1 that sometimes audio lines would be cut off abruptly and the next character in line to speak would start doing so. I like to play without subtitles on my first playthrough of games like this for immersion's sake, but this caused me to turn them on. If you play without subtitles, it will only be an occaisional minor annoyance, and I imagine this will get fixed.
BOTTOM LINE:
If you enjoyed the original Life Is Strange, you will absolutely enjoy this game. It is much more than a "fan fiction" as some claim it to be; it is truly a work of art worth its own game.
To newcomers: you will experience a truly tragic yet also heart-warming story in this game (in episode 1 and the others to follow), and you will find relatable characters that will stick with you for a life time; and above all else, you'll have a great time experiencing this wonderful game. (And of course I recommend you play the first game!)

Spec Ops The Line is a game I find it difficulty to accurately explain. On the surface, it's just another below average third person cover based shooter with nothing to set it apart from the hundreds of similar games on the market these days. Once you dig in a little, once you look at what is beneath you find a game that pushes the boundaries of video game narrative and tells you to look inward and feel a little ashamed.
It would be hard to call Spec Ops The Line a fun game, because it isn't, the generic shooter mechanics grow old after about 2 hours. But it's not a game that's trying to entertain you. It's a game that wants you to feel bad, to get angry, to get sad. It's a game that talks to you, as a gamer, and just to the protagonist you play as.
As you start off the game it is the classic scenario, something has gone terribly wrong in a middle eastern country and you are in command of a small special forces team that has to go in there and see what's happening. The specifics, Dubai has been encompassed by a gigantic sandstorm that pretty much ate the entire city and it's population, a US battalion disobeyed orders and went there trying to evacuate the civilians but haven't been heard from since.
As you go through the opening motions the game fills you with the classic stereotypes, you and your team makes crude jokes as they walk past bodies of those that didn't make it out in time and quickly enough you run into a bunch of locals with guns and find yourself shooting your way downtown. With a great degree of subtlety however the game quickly changes as things get progressively darker and more grim without you being able to pinpoint exactly where things went off the rails.
Spec Ops The Line is a game I would recommend that everyone plays, even if just to see how a video game narrative can potentially evolve. I doubt Spec Ops The Line will become that great of a success story. I even doubt it will have that much of an impact on how games are made. But it is still a very important game because it does something that you have never experienced before and that is rarity these days.

WARNING: SOME SPOILERS AHEAD (long review)
I'll try to be as spoiler-free as possible, because going in blind (like myself, somewhat) REALLY helps with your enjoyment of the game.
Having played all 3 routes, overall it's good. Be warned- it's one of those "artistic" games that value story over the gameplay. If that doesn't appeal to you, go look for enjoyment somewhere else. Of the 3 routes, I rank 2 of them as good. 1 of them is the pits.
Story- Undertale does a remarkable job in building its characters and world. A lot of them are very likeable (Toriel and Papyrus spring to mind) and it's honestly interesting to learn about the world and its inhabitants. Bonus points to its deconstruction of video game troupes (save for two, but I'll get to them). This comes at a cost- you'll only get this if you do a pacifist or neutral. If you do a GENOCIDE run, you get next to NOTHING. It's just a slog to the end, where you finish off the last monster. No character development, no world building, no nothing. To be fair, it is spooky (likely the intention), but it's still not interesting.
Presentation- I dig the "retro" look. The sprites are very well designed and some of them just make you say "WTF?" I like this because that's how I felt when I played Earthbound (one of my favorite games and an inspiration for Undertale) for the first time. However, I kind of wish that the monsters had some damn color in them when in battle. They're just black and white (with one exception). It is unique, but at times I kinda wish they popped out more. But this is a nitpick. The music, like Earthbound, is phenomenal. ASGORE, Megalovania, and Metal Crusher spring to mind as some of my faves. I actually kind of recommend buying the soundtrack, too (although the no looping thing sucks). Really, anything that's a boss theme is ♥♥♥♥ing incredible. Easily one of my favorite soundtracks for an indie game.
Gameplay-The pacifist and neutral routes are the 2 fun routes. The gameplay is very unique and fairly enjoyable. It's a bullet hell- think of it like "Asteroids" or some other space shooter like that. You control your SOUL (represented by a heart), dodging enemy attacks. If you're skilled enough, you won't get hit at all. Be warned- you will have a miserable time if you don't like this style. Undertale does a damn good job making every fight feel different and unique (especially bosses). One of them only lets you move your SOUL on a set of three bars. It's sort of like the 5 bars on sheet music. Another only lets you move your heart via jumping, making dodging him harder. Another requires you to turn its attacks against it, making it angry. Battles are in a turn-based system, and you have 3 options- run away, fight them (via timing your attacks like a QTE) or showing mercy. The final option is dangerous as you'll have to spend a few turns to figure out how to get the monsters to stop fighting. The reason you'll want to do this instead of running all the time is because if you do this, you still get gold like you would if you just killed them.  Honestly, this and dodging attacks are the most fun you'll have with combat.
If you do the final route (GENOCIDE), you have to kill EVERYTHING THAT MOVES. And THIS IS THE WORST. OMG, it is so BORING. You wander in circles until you exhaust a counter that gives you a set amount of monsters to kill. To it's credit, it is unsettling (something Undertale is very good at), but it's ungodly boring. The only positive I can say for the gameplay in the Genocide route is the final boss. However, you'll spend probably 10 hours just wandering in circles to get to him. (This decision confuses the hell out of me). Overall, it's good ('cept the Genocide the hell with that), but I think it could've been a bit more engaging. I'll say again- the neutral and pacifist route gameplay is good enough, even if it could be a bit better.
If you've noticed, I've criticized the hell out of the Genocide route, and before any fangirls or boys start threatening me, I know the Genocide route is the way it is because that's the point. You want to be serial killer? Fine, go ♥♥♥♥ yourself. You can't have fun.
Here's the deal- I play games to HAVE FUN. Not to have it scold me for my ethics (if I wanted that, I'd go to church lol I kid). AND THEN, just to be a total♥♥♥♥♥♥ if you complete a Genocide run, it's impossible for you to get the best ending ever again on subsequent playthroughs. I'm not kidding (unless you ♥♥♥♥ with the game's files there's guides on google that can show you how to do that).  And it made me go through all of that, just because I wanted to see what the game had. Some might say that's a brilliant deconstruction- I think it's just a LITTLE pretentious. Because ♥♥♥♥ me for just wanting to see what Undertale had to offer, right? I know what I'm going to say sounds like I'm a sociopath, but gameplay shouldn't be sacrificed just for getting a message across. People who do a Genocide run should have just as much fun as someone who does a pacifist or neutral run. Instead of letting the inactivity and amount of death in the Genocide route speak for itself (imo, that would've been more powerful), it constantly guilt trips you for just seeing everything Undertale has.
Final verdict- Undertale is a solid game overall. I enjoyed the pacifist and neutral routes, their gameplay and the characters and world. The presentation's great, and I love how it explores it's themes. Except for killing is wrong and your actions have consequences where I feel it gets its head up its♥♥♥♥♥ The genocide route sucks, except for the very end. I can see myself playing it again, but it will NEVER be a Genocide route because you know why.
8.5/10. I think it's worth $10. Give it a shot if your curious.

Quite a nice simulation - you can enjoy hours and hours of nice driving in European landscape.
The deliveries and the economic model - simplified from reality enough to be comprehensible and quite fun, although in late stage (if you purchase some garages and hire drivers) you'll earn more money than you can spend, even if you drive your truck like a lunatic and have to repair it frequently because of all the crashes.
Pros:
Nice landscape and scenery, the real distances are "scaled" down 25:1, so 100 km of road in real world is compressed into 4 km of road in game, while preserving the scenery and the look that can be seen in the road in real life.
Moddability: game support mods and the modding community is quite active, so you can download more trucks (there are more european trucks, but also russion or american trucks), more roads (russia. alternative roads in Alps region, even Nurbugring if you want :)), etc ...
Cons:
The traffic is quite stupid. Blindly obeys any speed limits (50 speed limit = everybody will drive exactly 50, unlike real world where 50 = most people will drive between 40 and 60, few of them faster) and is generally incapable of handling human driver errors. If you park you truck so that 30 cm of your truck stands out into lane - traffic won't drive around you, just stay there and honk. If you fail to give way to traffic on main road, they notice you too late and ram you instead of trying to brake or drive around you. Same when overtaking, if you fail to judge the distance needed for overtaking correctly - they won't try to move even a bit closer to the side of the road to avoid a collision. Well, maybe this is how the real world would look like once most of the cars will be computer-driven :)
Also, when you drive from minor road to a main road, in real life you look to the left and right to see if there is some traffic before you. In the game it is difficult, as you cannot map some keys (or hat switch directions?) on your wheel to quickly look 90 degrees to the left/right, so you have to take one hand from the wheel and use mouse to look around.
Physical model: if you drive too fast into a bend, the truck will never drift, but always will start toppling over. Even without a trailer and on wet road. While this is not exactly a racing game, perhaps the physical model may be more realistic in this regard - the game now does not feature icy roads and snow, but if it would, you should drift into a ditch instead of toppling over if you go too fast through a bend.
The game is actively developed, so perhaps one day there will be a patch addressing these minor issues, making the game much more fun. Even with these issues, I recommend the game if you like driving a truck :)

Inital review:
This game is clearly in an unfinished state, mainly problems with menus and keybindings, graphic glitches and so forth.
I was hyped for the game for a long time since i have 400H played in the hunter classic.
In this game like in so many other as a day one buyer you feel like a beta tester thats a real shame, at least mark it as early access then.
I will change my review when the game is in a playable state since you could get a lot for your money here when it finaly works.
EDIT: Since this review somehow made it to the top of the reviews i kinda feel obliged to add a little bit more so people see more then just a day 1 rant for their first review.
Like stated above the games menus and configuration is what causes the most problems for me those are things that are easily fixable however and might depend on what hardware specs you use so here a mine for a little more insight. My pc is build by myself and is all new from January 2017
CPU: i5 7600K @ 5.0GHZ MOBO: Asrock z170 Extreme 4 GPU: Powercolor Red Devil RX480 8GB RAM: 16GB Corsair Vengeance @ 3000 CL15
With that pc i do not have any problems running the game in 1440p fps wise but i still encounter random crashes that can not be attributed to anything in particular, sometimes when i press esc sometimes when i just press E to respond to a call.
The mouse sensitivy setting seem to take no effect i got a logitech G402 but other people have also brought up this issue in the steam forums.
Keybinding is a nightmare its unresponsive and never unbind you mouse buttons or you cant restore them unless you scroll down to the end and do a reset to default, if you want to bind mouse 4 or 5 (side buttons) the game crashes instantly.
The animal AI is not very clever, the pathfinding is just not done well enough, they run into things all the time and get stuck, also once they run away from you they will only remember your last postion, so you can make them flee into your arms when you spook them a second time, kinda funny but anoying.
Also HoorCairs a well respected community member did say on his Youtube lets play that the best way to shoot deer is to run trough the woods an go after them when they flee since its the easiest way to track them, thats true and shouldnt be like that.

Original review:
Extremely bugged and bad optimization(GTX980 1440p 40fps). The game wouldn't save some settings after restart. Have to click 60 times to decrease mouse sensitivity from 80 to 20, why there is no SLIDER?! Still mouse moves too fast, and the game resets setting for me every time! Sometimes it's impossible to exit in-game menu (only to desktop), pressing the button does nothing. Once I lost the progress on the map, and so on.. Considering return because of that.
Graphics look good, especially close vegetaion and foliage. But on the distance not very impressive. Reminds me the same old classic hunter, which I have played for more than 1000 hours total..
I disabled all arcade elements I could. Still there are signs and pointers flying everywhere. The game is very easy, the main goal is to kill everything that moves(or stuck). In the classic game I enjoyed walking a long distances through beautiful environments, searching for a monster buck, trying to avoid other animals, almost never shot does and small bucks. There was a leaderboard, daily events, personal galleries, trophyshots, and we could discuss our trophies, and so on. For me this was the main point of the game. It was fully focused on quality, not quantity. Here we have another story - kill 'em all, this is how you get xp and money to unlock unlocks, so you can unlock more unlocks even faster. All antlers look the same, there are no unique racks, no scoring system, no trophyshots, no reason to play after everything has been unlocked. I'm not interested in just shooting the same animals over and over again, when there is nothing to discover.
Wouldn't recommend at this point, at least because of bugs. As for the gameplay - may be they will improve it later, but I doubt it.

I recommend this title, but really mainly for people who have played (and loved)
. Because the writers were able to draw from the characters and locations in the original, they could cut corners in developing the world and in creating an emotional connection to Chloe.
In other words, it's less of a free-standing story, more of an Arcadia Bay Nostalgia Tour.
On those terms, the developers have done a creditable job filling in the back-story of a character and a town many of us already care about.
If I were to pick nits, I might call out the clunky "skill challenge" system, the sometimes stilted dialogue, and the fact that the setting lacks much of the richness and the wonder of discovery that characterized the original.
But I guess I'm content to take the Nostalgia Tour and hold my peace.

At first glance, Spec Ops: The Line is a by-the-numbers third person shooter. The game utilizes a cover-based combat system as well as the ability to order basic commands to the two other soldiers in the squad.
The game stars Captain Martin Walker of Delta Force along with his squad mates Lieutenant Adams, a heavy weapons expert, and Sergeant Lugo, a wise-cracking sniper in a ravaged yet eerily beautiful city of Dubai.  The squad is sent in to track down and rescue the 33rd Battalion who were on a rescue mission to evacuate civilians in the ruined city. Among the missing soldiers is Walker's mentor, Colonel John Conrad (a nod to author Joseph Conrad, author of "Heart of Darkness," which the game is based on).
The story starts with a turret sequence in a chopper as Delta Force is pursued by other helicopters trying to shoot them down. The sequence showcases the setting as bullets shatter into the beautiful and extravagant skyscrapers and helicopters crash and burn by the handful.
Delta crashes and thus begins The Line's campaign. This is where the game and its lead writer, Walt Williams, takes the player on a journey that gets not only to the heart of darkness of war and Walker, but the person playing the game as well.
The plot and writing sets Spec Ops apart not only from previous games in the Spec Ops franchise, but from nearly every game in the market. The story gets progressively darker and darker as the Delta squad continues their hopeless mission.
The squad does come into contact with the 33rd early in the game however with results much different from what they were expecting. The battalion has been seemingly brainwashed into a cult-like death squad who kill and terrorize the devastated civilians in Dubai with white phosphorus (similar to napalm) strikes. The men appear to be controlled by the Radio Man (voiced by Jake Busey), a maniacal former journalist who taunts Delta Squad through an elaborate speaker system that has been set up throughout the city.
Walker's squad mates, Lugo and Adams both have distinct personalities and react to the horrors they encounter with believeable and relatable reactions.
The graphics in the game come with mixed results. The player models have been fantastically designed with great detail as Delta's bodies become bloodier and more injured. The setting is at times beautiful with the gaudy buildings and at times haunting as players encounter hundreds of bodies of civilians. However, the explosion effects look downright awful, there are only a couple of noticeably different looking enemies and the weapon sound effects are weak.
The game features an execution system where Walker can put down a dying enemy with a variety of brutal and at times disturbing kill moves. The player is then rewarded with extra ammunition. The fact that it's possible to do this reward based feature is slightly unsettingly as the hordes of enemies you encounter in the game are your own countrymen.
That being said, the execution feature, the hordes of American soldiers the player gets to kill as well as Walker's actions are all explained by the ending which will hit the player in the gut. The game's creaters at Yager Development take a much more "meta" approach to the story as the ending questions the player.
The game will take about six hours to complete and has a thrown-in multiplayer as well as a co-op mode that was given in a free patch. The game comes highly recommended not for its gameplay, but for its powerful story that wil leave the player thinking for days.
The game is rated M for Mature for blood and gore, intense violence, and strong language.

Life Is Strange: Before the Storm has somehow managed to match the emotional intensity, character connectivity, tone, and overall atmosphere of the original game, something not often said of a prequel/sequel. Let's dive into some simple pros and cons:
PROS:
- Relatable characters. From rebellious Chloe to mysterious Rachel Amber; from nerdy Steph to jock Drew North, everyone will relate to at least one character presented.
- Backtalk challenge. A new risk/reward conversation minigame to Life Is Strange, this minigame requires the player to use some wit to make clever backtalk remarks in order for Chloe to achieve a more favorable outcome in a situation (getting out of trouble from the principal, for example).
- Animations. Deck Nine really did a fantastic job of bringing characters to life with natural-looking animations. There are a few janky animations, sudden changes, but nothing worth serious criticism. The lip sync in this game is dramatically improved over the previous game too.
- MUSIC. MUSIC, MUSIC, MUSIC! Daughter did an INCREDIBLE job with the soundtrack of this game. The echoey yet emotionally heavy guitars mixed in with ambient audio (like a rusty car hood creaking when Chloe puts her hand on it) exponentially improves the atmosphere of the game. You feel completely immersed and connected to the world through the music alone.
- Beautiful scenery. By this I mean graphics of course---the lighting, artsy textures, etc. Those things are nice, yes, but the design of Arcadia Bay, the return to Dontnod's original work while creating entirely new additions to the small fictional Oregon town we know and love creates a rich and diverse world that, once again, completely immerses you in the world of Chloe. Through the combination of well-written dialogue, beautiful music and excellent audio effects, and immersive scenery, you truly feel and experience what Chloe feels and experiences. You almost feel like a guardian angel standing over Chloe's shoulders, subtly influencing her destiny, instead of feeling like a gamer moving a mouse and clicking on a keyboard.
- Symbolism. Game theorists who made tons of theories in the first game: you'll be put to work diving into symbols and theories again. Keep a close eye on the appearance of ravens, glyphs on tucked away walls, etc.
- Journal. The journal is back again and it has a creative twist on it. Instead of a diary like Max had, Chloe's journal is a collection of letters written to Max that she never sends. If you played the first game, yes, that is as heart-wrenching as it sounds. Read the letters, they're very humorous at times and really brings you closer with Chloe's character. You won't end episode one with 40 pages like the original either; they're short and sweet.
- Player Choice. Choices really seem to matter this time around, in the short term and long term. For example, stealing the shirt in the beginning (like the demo showed) and wearing it will result in people talking to you about the sketchy concert Chloe got it at. There are quite a few of small choices like this that seem to be bigger in the long run, but for the sake of avoiding spoilers, I'll leave it at that.
CONS:
- Few janky animations. This is largely unavoidable, but it was annoying a few times to see a scene ending with Chloe stopping mid-conversation animation and walking away, or other slight things of that nature.
- Voice actor changes. This is in no way Square Enix or Deck Nine's faults, but it was quite jarring to hear known characters from the first game with completely different voices. Most of the repeating characters however did have voice actors that nearly perfectly matched the personality and face of the characters presented in the original game, however some just sounded completely off. If you're new to the series and don't want to play the original, this won't bother you as they're talented actors. Returning players though, you'll notice it. David doesn't sound as tough or gravely, and Principal Wells sounds much younger.
- Audio glitches. I noticed in my playthrough of episode 1 that sometimes audio lines would be cut off abruptly and the next character in line to speak would start doing so. I like to play without subtitles on my first playthrough of games like this for immersion's sake, but this caused me to turn them on. If you play without subtitles, it will only be an occaisional minor annoyance, and I imagine this will get fixed.
BOTTOM LINE:
If you enjoyed the original Life Is Strange, you will absolutely enjoy this game. It is much more than a "fan fiction" as some claim it to be; it is truly a work of art worth its own game.
To newcomers: you will experience a truly tragic yet also heart-warming story in this game (in episode 1 and the others to follow), and you will find relatable characters that will stick with you for a life time; and above all else, you'll have a great time experiencing this wonderful game. (And of course I recommend you play the first game!)
