My first prison I started was a modest one. I did not have enough funds to build individual cells, so all of my prisoners were stored in the holding cell. After overcrowding, they started to riot; the special SWAT units were no match for the prisoners and most of them escaped. They took my prison away, forcing me to start over.
On my second attempt, I made a conscious effort to build jail cells with every new incoming prisoner. I learned about grants that I could use for extra funds in these endeavors. For a while, I was successful. However, overcrowding became an issue, I was constantly in the red (DANGER), and I couldn't keep up with the demand for prison space. They rioted, killed, and my prison ended up barren. I could not recover.
My third attempt is where I started to succeed. I learned that you could actually turn off the flow of prisoners and accept different types of prisoners. I learned that if you connect two power stations, the entire prison blacks out. I learned that, even though it is expensive, feeding high quality, high quantity meals to your prisoners goes a long way towards keeping them in line. Through work, they can reform and even make you a profit! I am still on this prison, with it being worth over $1 million and having $400,000 in reserves.
This game is about learning. There is no tutorial that teaches you the tips and tricks. After the game opening, you are plopped into a plot of land for you to do whatever you want or can. The fun in this game comes from the failures, it comes from the satisfaction of finally building everything correctly and having a fully-functioning prison that works without you having to lift a finger. There's always something new to learn in this game. As fun as it is now, I can't wait to see where it goes.

**** CONTAINS SPOILERS ****
If there is one word that I can use to sum up this game is its “FUN”. This game is “FUN” to play, and unfortunately it’s a rare thing in games these days.
The good stuff …
I thoroughly enjoyed this game from start to finish. The music, sound effects and graphics are just gorgeous. The atmosphere of the game made me actually feel like I was Max in the wastelands, I actually watched Mad Max 1 and 2 during breaks from the game, and went out and bought Mad Max Fury Road on Bluray just because I really got in to this game. The story was engaging throughout and it actually made Max’s actions in the game meaningful. With me playing as Max, I actually felt like I had a purpose.
Yes the side quests were very, very repetitive in terms of what you had to do but they were engaging in my opinion and you could see the progress you were making in the strongholds and map which I liked. Vehicle combat was just a blast … dare I say it was THE most entertaining aspect of the game. Taking out convoys what the best part of all. I really like how the upgrade to the "Magnum Opus" actually made a difference to the vehicle physics. I actually spent a couple of hours just messing around with different upgrade / downgrade combinations. I also got engrossed by Chumbuckets biblical quirkiness, he actually “made” the game for me, and without him I don’t think it would have been as enjoyable. Chumbucket was a great side kick to me.
The negative stuff …
**** START SPOILER ****
The game does have its faults however, the biggest one for me it was the ending. It was a bit of an anti-climax, and it didn’t take much to bring down Scrotus in the end. After battling him in Gastown I was expecting the last battle on the cliff to be an epic one, but it wasn’t, it was about as challenging as squeezing out a fart. The final ending felt like it was rushed, like there wasn’t any meat to the suspense.
Another big disappointment was having to kill Chumbucket, he was my sidekick, my buddy, my personal black-finger, why the F$%k did he have to die? I know Max is a loner and will hurt others to achieve his goals, he’s an anti-hero so I can see how this fits into the game, but it’s Chumbucket!, He was with me the entire game as a loyal follower of the “Saint” why kill him? I realise it was for the deaths of Hope and Glory, but I didn’t feel as connected with them as I was only "with" them in a few cut-scenes, where as Chumbicket was with me the entire game. I think to have a greater impact on me they needed to be there along for the whole journey as well.
**** END SPOILER ****
Further to the ending, but not as big of an issue are the Boss fights, they were “Meh” once you learn how to beat the first one, and although I didn’t think it was a big issue, the side missions are very repetitive, but overall it was ok as you knew it was a one small cog in an engine.
To the developers …
I would have liked “Griffa” to have played a bigger role in the story, rather than just be the mystic dude that grants you skill boosts in exchange for tokens. I feel he was wasted in the game, he could have made an interesting character to interact with throughout the game, even give Max missions to help uncover Max’s past and unlock his future. He is an intriguing dude and I was begging for more insights from him. I think it would be great if he is part of the next story and plays a much bigger and deeper role … oh please let there be another story! Also Hope and Glory should have played a bigger role, there just wasn't enough time spent with them to make me feel like I cared that much for them as portryed in the story / cut-scenes.
Overall ...
This game is probably the rare game I find where I was presently surprised at just how good it actually was. Despite the end battles and Chumbucket (Oh Chum … why Oh why!??) this game has left me wanting more. I hope, I seriously hope, there is a pre-sequel or sequel or both coming.

Wearing the trappings of a modern military shooter, a genre that has become the industry's main enemy of creativity and thoughtful exploration of important thoughts on the hero fantasy and graphic violence, Spec Ops: The Line works its deep cover with such intensity and unflinching honesty that it demands the attention of any gamer who takes games as an art form seriously. I almost passed this one by due to its superficial premise and appearance, but I am very glad I did not.
Following in the footsteps and perfecting the ugly tenor of games like Kane & Lynch and Far Cry 2, this brutal exploration of PTSD, gaming's indulgence in violence, and the cost of war pulls no punches in challenging the player to confront what--if any--redemptive or meaningful value there is in parading through a foreign landscape as a hero of war. Forced to make ugly decisions that will demand you square with the game on an emotional level and shouted down for every mistake you will inevitably make, this is the slap in the face an industry drenched in blood and rewarded violence needs. Marking a new era in mature gaming, Spec Ops: The Line is a challenge to us to return from our thoughtless murder and enter into a new era of self-aware, meaningful interactive experiences.
You will come out of this a changed man. For good... or for bad. Either way,♥♥♥♥♥♥s ♥♥♥♥ed.

I have well over 500 hours in Borderlands 2 and plan to play much more. Why? Because the game is HUGE and incredibly fun.
A defining winner from the Borderlands franchise, this game presents everything that made Borderlands so successful, but turns it up to 11! It amazes me how well they transformed the Borderlands style into this game. The maps, characters, DLCs, NPCs, skins, gun variety and comedy are mixed together in a unique way that no other game can offer to the public. Everything is tied together very nicely, from the detailed map layout to the extremely hard raid bosses. I recommend this game to almost anyone who has played the first one, or is looking for a game that is offering all of the mentioned above.
You probably already know that this is shooter with RPG elements - but reduced to minimum. Level up, pick loot, create the craziest builds and go from there. There is no time for deep interaction or complex puzzles. Quest indicator shows you clearly where to go and what to pick, so you don't waste time looking for hidden stuff and can keep shooting.
All the quests are only a pretext to trigger dialogs full of GREAT humour. Pretty much everyone on Pandora is insane and, moreover, likes to record their delusions for you to find. Voice acting in pretty much the strongest part of the game and there's so much of it, so funny! Not only player characters and NPCs have lots to say, but also enemies. Oh, enemies - there's a great variety of them and they're just amusing. Nomands, Goliaths, Midgets, Rats have multiple voice lines and they're always funny to listen. I pretty much never stop smiling. While burning enemies to death, or blowing them up.
Ahh, it's a shooter after all. With DLCs you get 6 playable characters with multiple skill trees, all of which give you dozens of ways to build very different ways to kill enemies. On top of that you get hundreds of unique weapons and items, many very hard to find, with procedurally generated variants. Diversity of guns is astounding and scoped shotgun are nothing special after all. Thrown weapons, weird firing patterns, secret bonuses and odd gimmicks are all here. Everyone will find something suitable for himself, and something to explore over hundreds of hours.
The gear progression is good and fast, you often discard purples and legendaries to pick up better greens - this was solved perfectly. It can become tiring in a fact, as quests won't level up with you until you're level 50 after TWO playthroughs for each character, and then comes Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode - which is third playthrough where finally al enemies and rewards level up with you, but takes forever to reach max level 72. This is where the game starts for good and feels comfortable, which unfortunately takes a lot of time. A big drawback is that to fully enjoy the potential of Borderlands 2 and jump into DLCs you need to complete main story line at least twice. And it's quite lengthy, with non-skippable cut scenes. I recommend to start play this game step by step and don't run for best and rarest rewards since beginning, as it might become tedious and unsatisfactory.
And yes, it's great for coop. You can play solo and coop alike, no balance issues here. However there have always been some coop connection issues. Sometimes, I can connect to someone in the US better than someone in my city.
All in all, Borderlands is a very polished game with tons of content, certainly one of best games ever made. Go get it and explore in your own pace.

Before I got this game I read a lot of reviews about it and there was one word that seemed to be particularly recurring. "Toxic." I figured it was just a word used by this game's community to describe anything and everything they don't like, but then I played the game.
Does not really matter what server you play on, the players will fight for their own selfish desires. I feel like "toxic" is a strong term. The community that this game has cultivated definitely makes the game harder, but that is also the culture that the developers have in mind as they continue to improve the game.
This game is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and you can't trust anyone, but it's fun. You'll spend your first 100 hours farming and building, and you could lose it ALL at any time. Then you'll start from scratch again maybe on a different server and repeat the cycle for the rest of existence.
Now that's said about what the game is, I want to mention what the game could be.
There are mechanics in this game that give it potential to be the single greatest civilization simulator in gaming history, and I don't think anyone realizes it. There are countless faction minecraft servers and things similar, (Shout out to Civcraft) but they are all modded to be that way. Rust naturally has many elements from them. It is convenient to claim property and lock doors. Before a recent update, you could even see the owner's name of an item so you could actually track people using evidence. The new vending machines make very convenient offline trading. These things and more give Rust amazing potential, There are only 3 things that would make it complete as a civ sim.
1. Servers that lasted longer than a month. All servers wipe at least once a month because the clients get outdated.

Life is Strange which is actually the sequel to this LIS: BTS game, was actually pretty strange..its a strange game that starts all of as a Normal teenage game, but takes on a different route with a series of Dark events...
Life is Strange ; Before the Storm is no exception on that part, it just starts of with a Character we know very well (If one has played LIS) or A character we are interested to know if one is playing for the first time .
Chloe Pricefield...
She seems to be someone who has a big mouth, loves to get into a fight, and has a lot of personal issues, at the start we can see her risking her life and getting into trouble.
This episode is a clear cut message on whats going on with Chloe and how something starts to change with the entry of character in her life all of a sudden ; Rachy.....sorry I mean Rachel Amber
As a player of the Original LIS ; Season 1 (If your wondering why I say Season 1 , coz the original studio who developed LIS [Dontnod Studio] have confirmed they are working on LIS Season 2 , [Thus Deck nine were hired to make this prequel])
I saw this game from a different prespective from a fresh player and made comparisson with the previous LIS
+ tives....
-Optimization is bang on, coz I ran this game maxed out (Hella High settings) on My Nvidia Geforce GTX 850M - giving approx 67-75 Fps overall , No stutters, glitches lags whatever
So Kudos to Deck 9 studio
- The story in the beginning is an intense introduction to Chloe, so one knows something is up with her..... Characters have been rendered pretty well, and characters that were younger in this prequel have been graphically represented well.
- Music is spot on , one must get the Deluxe edition to use the mixtape mode for the wonderful relaxing music (Especially the song in the Train by Lantern on the Lake - song - ''Through the cellar door''
- Rachel looks awesome, she was a mysterious character in LIS, where her tragic event about her was revealed at the 4th episode of LIS season 1,
- Voice acting has been surprisingly good, despite Ashley Burch (The original LIS voice for Chloe) not giving her voice for Chloe due to the Voice actors strike, and another artist giving her voice, she has done a Marvellous job !!
- Chloe's main power of her smartass cocky answers to get things done helps us a lot in the events of the stroy which seems to be a nice addition unlike Max of LIS who had a power to rewind towards the past.
- Lots of emotion displayed and nice insight into the main characters complex and sad life
- Negatives
- Environment kept asking for more to be done, like more to explore and interact around
- The sprinting animation was a bit lackluster, didn't find much use
- The game is Kind of too easy where we can easily see whats to be done.
- Main issue Fov (Field of View) - !!! - it can't be adjusted ?! I get its a Interactive game, but it is hard to play on a ultrawide screen with an unadjustable Fov ....
- Some characters had very limited interaction unlike LIS S1, so not much can be known about them if one is new to this franchise...
Overall;
Deck 9 ....WHat a Marvellous job you have done !!!! (You can see my excitment in my speech Lol ;)) , loved your version of LIS,
I bet Dontnod Studios and Square Enix will appreciate this work !!

Well.. I have spent 13 hours with Mad Max and that apparently was enough. I just finished game. Did I leave a ton of side objectives to do? Yes, Yes I did. I did not feel encouraged to do them in the least.
Mad Max if it had came out 3-4 years ago might of been game of the year material, except it didn't. I am forced to compare this game's open world to those of other games I have played recently. The two that stand out in my mind is The Witcher 3 and Metal Gear Solid 5.
In terms of open world, Mad Max IS a beautiful game, the concept of a wasteland has never looked better. The thing that stands out to me the most is when a sand storm would blow in. It was truly something to look at and was super fun to try and survive in while collecting scrap.
Other than that this open world is nothing spectacular. We have literally done and seen and played these kinds of objectives dozens of times in the past. I think I honestly would of preferred a long extended linear story to the open world style game we got here. Thats not to say its BAD, its actually pieced together quite well, however it isnt spectacular. As I have said nothing felt new about it, nothing truly stood out other than what I have already mentioned.
Mad Max himself as a character has always been a weak basis. However the forced voice acting in this just really made me not give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about Max or what he is going through. His past, his future. I never really felt connected to him or his plight. Thus I felt nothing during the climax of the game when Max is forced to go through something pretty bad. I didn't care about him, or the other characters. Hell the only one I felt anything for was Chumbucket and that was just annoyance. His constant mouthing off for no reason seemed forced and added nothing to his character or the game in general.
The one thing this game does decently is customization. Max and the Magnum Opus do have alot of options however these are really none options. You will constantly get upgrades for both of them and it is linear, the only TRULY customizable things are the car paint colors and Max's hair/beard configuration. Other then that it would really be a waste to use anything except the highest level of whatever it is you are currently trying to upgrade. So I guess you could just think of it as a linear progression as opposed to any true customization. Maybe that was what was intended but to me I would of preferred to make real choices instead of binary ones regarding Max and his car.
There are several areas in the game to explore, however they are visually not very distinct from each other with the exception of one of the last areas you go to with the underdune, the drive leading up to it is the most visually distinct because it is a pure desert in the classical sense of nothing but dunes.
The melee combat in this game is about on par with any of the various batman games that have come out recently, if you liked that style of 1 guy taking on an obscene number of guys via hitting a button to parry and pounding on the group until they all go down you will like this. The animations for combat are all very well done and the finisher animations are satisfying. I again felt no need to fully upgrade Max's melee ability because of lack of general interest of seeing more of the game.
The car combat is annoying really, the car controls in general seem a bit floaty to me even with a pretty upgraded car it would seem to go out of control much easier than you would expect. Having to use the Harpoon constantly is just annoying. You basically are forced to whittle down enemy car's armor until you can harpoon a key component and then rip that component off rendering the car dead effectively. Its fun for awhile but it gets old rather quickly.
The side objectives that are available again are just things we have seen before, and they get old very quickly because there is nothing introduced into them once you get beyond the first zone. Tear down this... search that... go kill everyone in a camp...
The boss fights are very boring because they are just a dodge fest. Boss does a huge telegraphed move you avoid it and just wait for the parry prompt to come up or otherwise lead him into hurting himself on some sort of environmental hazard such as spewing fire or gas tanks.
Also the whole gas thing, it is a none issue. I never once came anywhere close to ever running out of fuel at any point in the game rendering that entire thing just pointless, just another UI element that became totally ignored. The fuel cans just became bombs I could use at that point.
It might sound like I am dogging on the game, which I guess I am. However the game IS very well put together, it runs great and looks great and what it does do it does very well for the most part. If you are looking for a decent open world game to kill some time while we wait for other bigger releases to come out than this might tide you over if you want to dive into it. Just plowing through it its only about a 10-15 hour game. If you do alot of the side objectives it could probably easily be a 50+ hour game if you let it. I however will not be spending that much time in it.
If anything I would say this game would be a steal once it goes on sale around the holidays. Currently I don't feel its worth its full price tag but somewhere around the 25-40 dollar region would fit it just nicely or just give it a year or two when its on sale for 80% and then it would be a 100% buy.
It was a decent attempt and I can appreciate the craftsman ship here but there are other games out there that just top what it is trying to do.

As a long time Mad Max fan, I was pretty stoked on the Mad Max video game. I'm not sure if anyone here has played the original Mad Max video game for the NES, but gameplay essentially consists of driving, picking up fuel, getting out and killing some baddies, and repeat. Well, it has been 25 years since that original Nintendo game was released, and not much has changed. A carnage filled intro cut-scene leads to a very slow intro to the "story". Early on the game is a beautiful, mesmerizing open sandbox (literally) where I had a blast tooling around and exploring in Max's "Magnum Opus", a phrase in which you will soon loathe hearing everytime your hunchbacked mechanic spouts it out of his mouth. The game quickly grew boring, as the main goals are to infiltrate enemy camps and destroy fuel pumps, collect scrap to improve your car, and go do tedious missions to collect scrap and project materials. As the game progresses the camps you must destroy get more challenging. Not new challenges to face or more difficult enimies, but just more and more quantities enemies. Every so often you will encounter a "boss", essentially a big brute you need to defeat. But as I faced the second boss I made a horrible realization: every boss was EXACTLY the same. At this point I was already growing bored with the game, and though I sent in a request, I had too many play hours on the game to return it to steam. I trudged on, each boss and enemy and side mission becoming more of a nuisance than the last, to the point that I essentially said, "screw it" and just decided to finish the story. Speaking of which, the story really doesnt start until a 1/3 of the way through the game where you meet some slave lady and her daughter that wants to marry you or something and you are supposed to feel connected or attached to. They die and you need to get revenge. Anyway, finishing the story led to a pathetic boss "fight" and Max getting his Interceptor back. The ONLY reason to continue playing after the credits was to drive around for a few minutes having fun driving the classic Pursuit Special around, which ultimatley led me to drive to the edge of the map, fall off a cliff and die.
On a good note, the vehicle combat was pretty fun, right up until you could just launch your thunderpoons at cars and blow them up, offering little to no challenge at all.
IF you want to still play, save your money 'till this game is clearanced. I really wish I had that $60 back right now, as my car in real life could use a full tank of gas.

Wearing the trappings of a modern military shooter, a genre that has become the industry's main enemy of creativity and thoughtful exploration of important thoughts on the hero fantasy and graphic violence, Spec Ops: The Line works its deep cover with such intensity and unflinching honesty that it demands the attention of any gamer who takes games as an art form seriously. I almost passed this one by due to its superficial premise and appearance, but I am very glad I did not.
Following in the footsteps and perfecting the ugly tenor of games like Kane & Lynch and Far Cry 2, this brutal exploration of PTSD, gaming's indulgence in violence, and the cost of war pulls no punches in challenging the player to confront what--if any--redemptive or meaningful value there is in parading through a foreign landscape as a hero of war. Forced to make ugly decisions that will demand you square with the game on an emotional level and shouted down for every mistake you will inevitably make, this is the slap in the face an industry drenched in blood and rewarded violence needs. Marking a new era in mature gaming, Spec Ops: The Line is a challenge to us to return from our thoughtless murder and enter into a new era of self-aware, meaningful interactive experiences.

After using as much of my free time as possible (and probably most of the time i should've spent on college homework), I finished the story line and probably about 60% of gameplay in just under 40 hours. My review won't be reflecting graphics quality as i've had issues running a lot of my games since a current update to my OS i'll be working with. But the gameplay itself was rather solid.
pros:
-extremely sizable open world
-single player (a nice almost relaxing change if you're burnt out from online games and need a break)
-you get to see and use your progress through the game. Something felt rather satisfying seeing more people join the strongholds as it grew (as did my scrap wallet)
-explosions, lots
mehs:
-from my gameplay quality i'm unsure of how well optimized the game has been, in my lower framerate range i noticed it varying a lot
-for all of you batman arkham series fans, the battle mechanics are near identical with less controls to worry about
-enemy AI seem always vigilant, making my total count of sneak kills about 3 by this review.
-unless I'm missing something, (and granted i should have gone and checked before writing this review, will check and edit this part once I do) the possibility for griffa tokens seems to be incredibly unbalanced to the max total you can use on him to max your stats. This could be so that players can play to their style and still hopefully rack up enough to max their stats but with going around and simply doing story missions and most of the death races You'd more than likely have more than enough without doing intel quests/whatever else with all the killing you'll be doing just to get to the next story mission
cons:
-Even after patch 3 i've noticed numerous audio bugs, which for me was a dissappointment after the rather high-quality audio from the arkham series.
-mouth movement in cutscenes often didn't match up with the audio (could probably be added to the previous con)
-scrap locations.... if you are one to 100% a game, then have at it, but I believe the creators set these up to gain avg. gameplay hours from their players. You'd gain as much scrap taking out 3 cars as you would in some of the scavanging locations. The only vital scrap locations are maybe the pallets and the stronghold items which i found ammo (storyline) and cleanup crew to be some of the most useful ingame, the scrap crew is nice for being away but i've seen little advancement with it vs. the regular stronghold profit.
and the big one, the story. I won't go into detail as to not spoil anything for newcomers.
The most irksome thing to me in the story is the bonding of the characters. To me it seems like they wanted max to continuously push away those around him yet his actions and talks with griffa constantly betray this main plot idea. Maybe more that Max just isn't being honest with himself. Later in-game bonds begin to form with what I assume the creators wanted to be major characters instead of minor characters but their role by this point was undeveloped and felt half-baked. Max is meant to continue on alone, he is the modern lone ranger, I get that. However, I feel like a lot of the game's story could've gone more fluidly. A game with straight-forward linearity can be nice, but being able to make some slightly pertinant decisions to characters or situations in the game, allow the player to feel attached to part of the game, making the sensation deeper and gaining a better experience from the player. Mad max was more a "I'm gonna tell you to go here, go here, kill, blow stuff up, and in return you get chunks of metal to slap on your car like you can make a fully functional engine out of the 300 superchargers and 200 radiators you've scavanged across the great white."
All negative points aside, in the end I actually very much enjoyed it, and plan on continuing to play and clear out the rest of the camps and such. It may not be suitable for everyone and I'd suggest watching a playthrough or something of it if you are unsure, don't waste your money if you dont know if you'll like it. But I certainly enjoyed it, and I would still reccomend this game. Some of the hiccups can be fixed, and I hope they offer some sort of story DLC to the game as I think it could use a little more support to the backbone of the game.

*Note: this review comes from the perspective of a big Life is Strange fan*
I'll admit I was skeptical at first about this new prequel. New studio, new actors - I was legitimately concerned that this new game would tarnish all my beloved memories and feelings for the original series.
The game began a bit rocky with a small controller bug, but after switching to a different controller things picked up significantly. Deck Nine's passion for the original series is on full display with every little detail - from the opening title, to the UI, to character quirks, music and most importantly, the overall vibe.
I ended up absolutely loving this first episode. Chloe's new voice actor honestly put all my fears to rest, and there are definitely moments of vulnerability that she absolutely nails. Arcadia Bay feels alive and well, and I really enjoyed the new Backtalk system - makes you think on your feet in a way that really meshes well with Chloe's personality. Speaking of meshing with her personality, the music hits those same LiS nostalgic beats while maintaining a bit edgier/punk feel at times to help convey that this is a story about Chloe, a girl searching for meaning in her life after the tragic loss of a loved one.
Overall, a tremendous first effort from Deck Nine and a welcome entry to one of my favorite series.
Edit: After finishing the final episode, I can safely say this is an absolutely beautiful and memorable game. Deck Nine forgoes supernatural elements in favor of a much more intimate story, and I'm glad they did. The passion the studio put into this work shines through in every facet of the experience they've crafted. Amazing voice acting, music, characters, and a story that, much like the original, will stay with you long after the credits.

After using as much of my free time as possible (and probably most of the time i should've spent on college homework), I finished the story line and probably about 60% of gameplay in just under 40 hours. My review won't be reflecting graphics quality as i've had issues running a lot of my games since a current update to my OS i'll be working with. But the gameplay itself was rather solid.
pros:
-extremely sizable open world
-single player (a nice almost relaxing change if you're burnt out from online games and need a break)
-you get to see and use your progress through the game. Something felt rather satisfying seeing more people join the strongholds as it grew (as did my scrap wallet)
-explosions, lots
mehs:
-from my gameplay quality i'm unsure of how well optimized the game has been, in my lower framerate range i noticed it varying a lot
-for all of you batman arkham series fans, the battle mechanics are near identical with less controls to worry about
-enemy AI seem always vigilant, making my total count of sneak kills about 3 by this review.
-unless I'm missing something, (and granted i should have gone and checked before writing this review, will check and edit this part once I do) the possibility for griffa tokens seems to be incredibly unbalanced to the max total you can use on him to max your stats. This could be so that players can play to their style and still hopefully rack up enough to max their stats but with going around and simply doing story missions and most of the death races You'd more than likely have more than enough without doing intel quests/whatever else with all the killing you'll be doing just to get to the next story mission
cons:
-Even after patch 3 i've noticed numerous audio bugs, which for me was a dissappointment after the rather high-quality audio from the arkham series.
-mouth movement in cutscenes often didn't match up with the audio (could probably be added to the previous con)
-scrap locations.... if you are one to 100% a game, then have at it, but I believe the creators set these up to gain avg. gameplay hours from their players. You'd gain as much scrap taking out 3 cars as you would in some of the scavanging locations. The only vital scrap locations are maybe the pallets and the stronghold items which i found ammo (storyline) and cleanup crew to be some of the most useful ingame, the scrap crew is nice for being away but i've seen little advancement with it vs. the regular stronghold profit.
and the big one, the story. I won't go into detail as to not spoil anything for newcomers.
The most irksome thing to me in the story is the bonding of the characters. To me it seems like they wanted max to continuously push away those around him yet his actions and talks with griffa constantly betray this main plot idea. Maybe more that Max just isn't being honest with himself. Later in-game bonds begin to form with what I assume the creators wanted to be major characters instead of minor characters but their role by this point was undeveloped and felt half-baked. Max is meant to continue on alone, he is the modern lone ranger, I get that. However, I feel like a lot of the game's story could've gone more fluidly. A game with straight-forward linearity can be nice, but being able to make some slightly pertinant decisions to characters or situations in the game, allow the player to feel attached to part of the game, making the sensation deeper and gaining a better experience from the player. Mad max was more a "I'm gonna tell you to go here, go here, kill, blow stuff up, and in return you get chunks of metal to slap on your car like you can make a fully functional engine out of the 300 superchargers and 200 radiators you've scavanged across the great white."
All negative points aside, in the end I actually very much enjoyed it, and plan on continuing to play and clear out the rest of the camps and such. It may not be suitable for everyone and I'd suggest watching a playthrough or something of it if you are unsure, don't waste your money if you dont know if you'll like it. But I certainly enjoyed it, and I would still reccomend this game. Some of the hiccups can be fixed, and I hope they offer some sort of story DLC to the game as I think it could use a little more support to the backbone of the game.

It's a SimCade; it has equal parts of simulation and arcade to please both seasoned and new players. Unlike most "Simulators" on sale, it's very well made and accessible.
You start as a truck driver without a truck; complete some deliveries for others and get some loans and soon you have your own truck (and even your own company); the freights will lead you across the roads of a scaled version of western Europe while carrying a nice variety of goods; from chemical substances to cars.
The landscape is beautiful but the cities are rather simple (not really a big deal though since you spend most of your time on highways).
Simulation is more on the arcade side, with the possibility of adjusting many parameters to increase the simulation level. With some practice, anyone should be able to drive well. It's highly recommended to play this game with a steering wheel or a controller.
Pacing is very relaxing; you'll spend most of your time managing the truck speed and route. Play your favorite song or podcast and enjoy the travel.
The modding community is awesome; you'll be able to completely overhaul your experience with more realism, cargo variety, truck models and maps, but the vanilla game should provide you many hours of fun.
In conclusion, it's a game for those looking for a different experience where fun does not come from the challenge but the gameplay itself.

Very fun and addicting game. Can be played alone or with friends; either experience is perfectly fine. Combined FPS and RPG elements make for a very immersive game, and the writing is rather humourous. Play styles are not restricted by character classes, it really is just about having as much fun as possible while shooting your way through enemies. Become a sniper with the Gunzerker, charge in with a Siren, make your Assassin into a shock trooper; do whatever you want, the classes just add flavor to the fun. With the amount of guns available, you're kind of guarenteed to try different things.
Does get somewhat repetitive at times, namely when your objective asks you to go back and forth between two areas, forcing you to keep re-killing the same enemies over and over again. It's a flaw found in a lot of RPGs, but the main storyline missions are worth it. It's genuinely pleasing to fight bosses, as the challenge is proportional to the satisfaction you feel afterwards.
Don't need a high end rig to play this. While certainly perferred, Borderlands' art style allows for lower quality visuals to feel acceptable. Adjust the settings a bit, and the game flows very well with consistent frame rates and no crashing.
So yeah, the game is fun. Like, I'm honestly thinking about buying some DLCs to play after finishing the campaign. Go ahead and get it, it's worth the money. It's fine if you're a complete introvert and have no friends, the game plays perfectly without them. But hey, shooting people is always more fun with friends.

Usually, when a game is made out of a movie, extreme caution is advised, most of them being utter crap ! However, in this case we got a nice exception.
First thing worth of notice are the landscapes. Gorgeous, as much as ruins of civilisation buried in the sands can be. This game will make you feel its post apocalyptic setting more than any Betheda's "Fallout" ever did.
Second thing you'll quickly realise is that well crafted wasteland is a theme park where you unlock zones and inside them find plenty of challenges and local figures to help, in order to upgrade both your character and its precious car the "Magnum Opus" and incidentally make the story progress.
I personnaly haven't found this too artificial or redundant yet at some point it became a bit repetitive. ...
Still the fun is there ! Ridin' into bad boys convoy brings the same feeling of chaos and mayhem than in the "Fury road" movie. Once out of your vehicle, it'll be all about brawling. And that ground combat feels raw and satisfying .As brutal as you could imagine in such a universe.

I was skeptical to a prequel to Life is Strange. The original is probably my favorite among all Telltale-likes out there, any sequel or prequel have a lot to live up to and Deck Nine doesn't have the backlog of games that made me think they could pull it of. But as of the first episode it feels like they mostly did just that. The story center on and fills out Chloe and Rachels relationship, aswell as the ones with most of the cast from the first game. The writing is strong, it's emotional, funny and it might actually win some of the "I hate Chloe" people over with the more fleshed out characterization of her. The new voice actress for Chloe also did a great job. But there is less to do this time around. The conversations are shorter and there are less things to look at in the enviroments.
They also borrow heavily on the mechanics and styles of the first game, almost too much. Max had a camera, Chloe has a marker to tag things with. They both have a journal that function the exact same way. The music is in the same style (even thou I think slightly harder rock music would fit Chloe more). The end where various characters stop what they are doing and look at something is exactly the same as the first one... If nobody told you it wasn't made by the same developers, I'm not sure you would have noticed. Max timelord powers where a stronger mechanic but I can totally see why they didn't have a supernatural power for Chloe, instead relying on a mechanic called Backtalk, that's pretty much using wit to get your way in conversations. It's not a entirely new concept, but works fine even if some of the isults you throw back are really cringy.
It doesn't have as strong a mystery as the first one with the storm dream and time powers to hook you from the begining, but what we got is enough to keep me interested. The recommendation of this game is easy, did you like the first one or not? You will probably enjoy this one if you did, but there is nothing here to convice you if you didn't. If you haven't played the first one, play that first.

The return to Arcadia Bay was pretty cool, but it didn't have nearly as much of an impact as the first episode of the original.
The best thing about this game would certainly be that Chloe, while younger and not quite as punk yet, is still Chloe. She's witty, she's confrontational, she's self-centered, and deep down she's a complete nerd with a kind heart. They got the character 100% right in my opinion (apart from the voice issue). I simply enjoyed being her for 3 and a half hours. Other than that, there are some pretty funny jokes, the seeds of a mystery and beauitful visuals and music.
The worst thing about this game, as much as it pains me to say it, is Rachel Amber. The reason the first game worked so well on me was because I cared about Chloe right from the start. This attachment to her character was the driving force behind the entire story and is what made the game so powerful. In this game, Rachel takes Chloe's place as the best friend to the player's character, and I'm not feeling it. Sure, Chloe seems to like her, but I feel it's mostly because the script needs her to. The connection is not nearly as powerful this time. Who knows, maybe she'll grow on me, and maybe we haven't seen her true self yet, but so far I'm not impressed.
Other issues:
- The "backtalk" conversation mode is quite meh. There are some witty lines delivered in there, but it always feels like the person you're arguing with is trying really hard to set up your punchlines. It feels very scripted. Also, choosing the right response was terribly easy (didn't get it wrong even once), which makes the whole "risk/reward" aspect of it quite pointless. It's just reward, unless you actually try to fail.
- Chloe's voice. I'm sorry, I really tried,  and I thought it would grow on me as I play and I'll get used to it, and I even argued with people who are boycotting the game because of it, but I just can't bring myself to like it. Chloe sounds WRONG, and it's annoying and distracting.
- There's no sense of risk. No matter how hard I screw things up, I know it's all gonna work itself out because this is a prequel. The devs claimed that removing time travel would make your choices feel more impactful, but they don't, because this is a prequel and I know that no matter what I'm gonna say, Chloe and Rachel are going to end up together and everyone is going to be fine. This is always a problem with prequels, of course, and was always gonna be the case. Still, it's a negative point for the game.
Overall, if you're a fan and you want more of Arcadia Bay and Chloe Price, this is a nice window into their lives before the events of the original. The characters feel the same and the town is still beautiful.
But if you're looking for a story as powerful and as thrilling as the first one - So far, Before The Storm doesn't deliver. Lets hope episode 2 packs more of a punch.

So I couldn't wait for the 1st of September, the day when it was going to be released. And straight away, it didn't disappoint me. It never did. There's a TON of stuff to collect, a decent amount of missions to complete and the combat (both in car and on foot) was great, at least according to me. Loved it all.
The story is barebones. Max lost his car and gets help from a character called Chumbucket to retrieve it, but in order to do so they need to build a new car first - the Magnum Opus - and then he can go out for his revenge on the person called Scrotus (play the game and you'll know why he is called that). On the way he meets some characters who is more or less likeable, including an elderly woman in a AWESOME wheelchair.
Well, here I am, 56 hours later (spread over 25 days, I completed the game on the 25th of September) and I could say that this is the game of the year. But I won't. Well, if I would be looking at the amount of content, this game would be GOTY. But even though it was a great game all the way through... it's gonna end at that.
TL;DR. Do you like open world games? Action filled games? Driving games where you get to do combat with other vehicles? Go for it, buy this. You won't be disappointed.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is that rare thing, a strong sim tethered to a strong game. Where other vehicle-obsessed devs seem to take player motivation for granted, Czech studio SCS understand that a pleasingly modelled steed needs a pleasingly modelled environment to shine.
On this occasion that environment is a swathe of Europe stretching from Plymouth in the west to Wroclaw in the east, from Aberdeen in the north to Milan in the South. The tangle of motorways and major roads is stylised and condensed, but feels massive. After a splendid week of non-stop trucking the stats screen tells me I've still only seen 50% of it.
There's satisfaction in exploring new routes, seeing new golden been-there-done-that squiggles appearing on the in-game map, but it tends to be the promise of cold, hard cash that gets you out of bed in the morning. Like Farming Simulator, ETS2 has a simple yet resonant economic sandbox at its centre.
The only time when the game itself loses concentration is when attempting to evoke certain regions and sounds. The further you get from central Europe the less convincing the landscapes become. No one seems to have told SCS's countryside crafters that rural Britain features long green things called hedges. Cities are often depicted with the shortest of visual shorthand – a few warehouses, the odd landmark if you're lucky. Don't expect to see a favourite local roundabout, slip-road, or speed camera in this highly-recommended HGV-driver RPG.

These are my views of the game. This is pretty long, so read at your own risk :P
Well done Deck Nine! We all had our worries, but I think you just proved yourselves with this episode. The first video I watched had me pretty worried about everything from the animations to the voice acting and dialog, but I was extremely happy to see all my worries put to rest.
First things first: Chloe's voice actor. We were all very skeptical and worried when we found out that a new voice actor was to take the role, especially myself. Comparing the early videos to the finished product, I can happily say that Rhianna DeVries improved and delivered an amazing performance. Obviously she doesn't sound exactly like Ashley Burch's Chloe, but it didn't need to be as the voice acting was able to properly bring Chloe back to life. She used to have Chloe sound like she had a hard time finding to right words to say to the point where she would almost stop in mid sentence (from what I remember), but now it's still there but toned down a lot. The sentence are more fluid, but still retains Chloe's way of speaking. I'm not sure if this was worked on since, and it could just be my mind tricking me after hearing her talk throughout the game, but going by the last video I saw of the garage scene with Chloe and David, it seems like Rhianna's inner voice dialog has improved as well. It no longer sounds like it is trying to "be" a thought, but rather Chloe talking to herself for the most part. If anything could be improved on in this aspect, then it would be voice inflection. Every once in a while the thought feels a little.....off. Chloe's attitude is portrayed better too. It doesn't feel like she is trying to sound rebellious now. Either way, the point is, it has improved a lot from the first time I heard it. [EDIT] I took out a critique about tempestuous voice acting. After watching the part again, I realized that I did not remember the scene correctly. Chloe pleading with Rachel to stay was well acted.
I would also like to say that Kylie Brown did a fantastic job with Rachel. To be honest, I was really worried after watching the junkyard scene video, but like with Chloe, I was happy to be proven wrong.
The dialog between two characters has improved as well. It no longer feels like voice actors taking turns reading from a script. It now feels like they are having a conversation with each other. To kind go along with character interaction, this episode focused on Chloe and Rachel primarily, which is to be expected, with a few side character making small introductions. In the next episode, I would like to see a lot more character development for all the characters.
The art direction is noticeably different. It still retains the original's feeling but still manages to give this game its own uniqueness. Your team did a wonderful job at making each place feel very "lived-in", with very detailed environments. Posters, graffiti, papers, objects all "litter" each environment. In a good way that is. I spent a lot of time just looking around. I only find one repeated graffiti asset in the mill on two of the pillars. I caught you, haha. Still though, I really like when developers give me a reason to take in the scenery.
Character animations were executed beautifully. Everything from a character's idle animation to their walking animation. My personal favorite are the facial animations. The eyes and lips to be exact. I love the attention to detail, and this really helped create believable characters full of emotions.
I really enjoyed the cut scenes and camera work that was implemented throughout the game. They really made for a very cinematic experience.
I think sound design was handled pretty well during this episode. The highlight being the mill scene with the band playing. I do think you use the "compressed" sound (as if you are listening through someones phone speakers or from their earbuds) transitioning to "uncompressed" high quality sound a little too much. An example of that would be when the campus guard shows you his demo.
When it come to the clothing decision and graffiti game play mechanics, I actually enjoyed them. I think one one of my guilty pleasures is character customization; from facial design, to outfits. As for the graffiti, I found myself somewhat looking for places to write on while I was exploring and was always happy when I did. I originally thought of them as things that really did not need to even be implemented, but after playing, I am glad that they were.
Okay. Time for some tough love:
-I did notice a bug where Chloe's dialog would start twice when attempting to leave an area when I wasn't supposed to.
-I think you guys really need to do something about the loading screens. They are very abrupt and almost completely kill the moment. A very good example would be the first dream Chloe has. Any impact that would have had gets cut short when that loading screen appears. There needs to be a better transition to keep the emotion created from the first scene lasting though to the next scene.
-I have noticed that Rachel's character model sometimes has "bug" eyes. An example of that would be during the drama room scene when she is in costume. It is a little creepy. It was really good though throughout the rest of the game.
-In my honest opinion, I think that the relationship between Chloe and Rachel escalated a little too fast. They have, presumably, only known each other for less than a day, and yet Chloe already has feelings for her. My choice ultimately, I know, (to be honest, I kind of felt obligated to pick that response for fear that I would not get the ending I wanted) but as soon as they got on the train you can easily tell there was something there. They looked like they were going to kiss at any moment. This combined with the scene in the junkyard made the whole outcome feel rushed and really awkward, kind of negating the emotional impact that was intended for me. If there was a segment before the party that established Chloe's current relationship with Rachel and what she thought of her, this could help set up the decision that was made in the junkyard scene, and would make it seem less sudden and rushed. [EDIT] After watching the junkyard scene again, I'm a little conflicted with my previous statement. When picking the friendship option, the scene plays out A LOT better. Especially with the reasoning Chloe gives for not wanting her to leave. When picking the other option, the scenes that play out after don't seem to work together well with the lover option. So the tempo rush may have been my fault actually. I might have misinterpreted the train scene as well. Upon watching again, I can see it more as Rachel trying to break Chloe out of her shell a bit. Trying to be extra caring and friendly to make Chloe feel more safe and less uncomfortable.
All in all, I enjoyed this episode very much and I believe it was a very wise decision for DONTNOD to give your team the reigns on this project.

I LOVED IT. Seriously. I knew it wouldn't disappoint to go back to Arcadia Bay, but it's even better than I expected. Just like in LiS1, the soundtrack is amazing, the characters are well-defined, and the story is touching. I liked Max, but I might like Chloe even better.
What meant a lot to me, though, was the representation of Chloe's trauma caused by her dad's death. It felt real to me. At times she'd be angry with him, or angry with the entire world, or angry with people who had absolutely nothing to do with her father or his death - but she was just angry, and that's accurate, because that's how these things work.
Personally, Chloe's flashbacks were a punch in the gut for me, but in a good way?
I lost my mom when I was 10. I still get flashbacks about it. When Chloe said she had trouble finding out what was real and what wasn't, that some parts of her real life would sometimes sneak into her nightmares... I was like, I FEEL YOU SO MUCH. SAME SAME SAME.
So. TLDR; great game and i'm shook by the amazing representation of chloe's trauma. This was even better than I expected.

:
The side-scrolling action RPG combat and exploration bring back fond memories of golden era GBA, DS, and Playstation Castlevania games, which Konami seems happy to have forgotten about. At the outset, your character is a weak little thing that can barely survive a couple of rooms. Before you know it, though, you’re curb stomping bosses and flying through the castle like you own the place.
Roguelikes are famous for their borderline frustrating level of difficulty. Rogue Legacy manages to balance the difficulty with the opportunity for advancement in such a way that evaporates much of the frustration. While you can explore and loot as much as you want, you really can’t get stronger until you die. Death is even sometimes a welcome relief from the current expedition, in some cases.
By placing the ability to upgrade yourself past the game over screen, there’s always an impetus to continue, to play just one more life and see where this next one takes you.

I Really hope Deck Nine reads all of these. I would like to hear feedback from them, myself
These are my views of the game. This is pretty long, so read at your own risk :P
Well done Deck Nine! We all had our worries, but I think you just proved yourselves with this episode. The first video I watched had me pretty worried about everything from the animations to the voice acting and dialog, but I was extremely happy to see all my worries put to rest.
First things first: Chloe's voice actor. We were all very skeptical and worried when we found out that a new voice actor was to take the role, especially myself. Comparing the early videos to the finished product, I can happily say that Rhianna DeVries improved and delivered an amazing performance. Obviously she doesn't sound exactly like Ashley Burch's Chloe, but it didn't need to be as the voice acting was able to properly bring Chloe back to life. She used to have Chloe sound like she had a hard time finding to right words to say to the point where she would almost stop in mid sentence (from what I remember), but now it's still there but toned down a lot. The sentence are more fluid, but still retains Chloe's way of speaking. I'm not sure if this was worked on since, and it could just be my mind tricking me after hearing her talk throughout the game, but going by the last video I saw of the garage scene with Chloe and David, it seems like Rhianna's inner voice dialog has improved as well. It no longer sounds like it is trying to "be" a thought, but rather Chloe talking to herself for the most part. If anything could be improved on in this aspect, then it would be voice inflection. Every once in a while the thought feels a little.....off. Chloe's attitude is portrayed better too. It doesn't feel like she is trying to sound rebellious now. Either way, the point is, it has improved a lot from the first time I heard it. [EDIT] I took out a critique about tempestuous voice acting. After watching the part again, I realized that I did not remember the scene correctly. Chloe pleading with Rachel to stay was well acted.
I would also like to say that Kylie Brown did a fantastic job with Rachel. To be honest, I was really worried after watching the junkyard scene video, but like with Chloe, I was happy to be proven wrong.
The dialog between two characters has improved as well. It no longer feels like voice actors taking turns reading from a script. It now feels like they are having a conversation with each other. To kind go along with character interaction, this episode focused on Chloe and Rachel primarily, which is to be expected, with a few side character making small introductions. In the next episode, I would like to see a lot more character development for all the characters.
The art direction is noticeably different. It still retains the original's feeling but still manages to give this game its own uniqueness. Your team did a wonderful job at making each place feel very "lived-in", with very detailed environments. Posters, graffiti, papers, objects all "litter" each environment. In a good way that is. I spent a lot of time just looking around. I only find one repeated graffiti asset in the mill on two of the pillars. I caught you, haha. Still though, I really like when developers give me a reason to take in the scenery.
Character animations were executed beautifully. Everything from a character's idle animation to their walking animation. My personal favorite are the facial animations. The eyes and lips to be exact. I love the attention to detail, and this really helped create believable characters full of emotions.
I really enjoyed the cut scenes and camera work that was implemented throughout the game. They really made for a very cinematic experience.
I think sound design was handled pretty well during this episode. The highlight being the mill scene with the band playing. I do think you use the "compressed" sound (as if you are listening through someones phone speakers or from their earbuds) transitioning to "uncompressed" high quality sound a little too much. An example of that would be when the campus guard shows you his demo.
When it come to the clothing decision and graffiti game play mechanics, I actually enjoyed them. I think one one of my guilty pleasures is character customization; from facial design, to outfits. As for the graffiti, I found myself somewhat looking for places to write on while I was exploring and was always happy when I did. I originally thought of them as things that really did not need to even be implemented, but after playing, I am glad that they were.
Okay. Time for some tough love:
-I did notice a bug where Chloe's dialog would start twice when attempting to leave an area when I wasn't supposed to.
-I think you guys really need to do something about the loading screens. They are very abrupt and almost completely kill the moment. A very good example would be the first dream Chloe has. Any impact that would have had gets cut short when that loading screen appears. There needs to be a better transition to keep the emotion created from the first scene lasting though to the next scene.
-I have noticed that Rachel's character model sometimes has "bug" eyes. An example of that would be during the drama room scene when she is in costume. It is a little creepy. It was really good though throughout the rest of the game.
-In my honest opinion, I think that the relationship between Chloe and Rachel escalated a little too fast. They have, presumably, only known each other for less than a day, and yet Chloe already has feelings for her. My choice ultimately, I know, (to be honest, I kind of felt obligated to pick that response for fear that I would not get the ending I wanted) but as soon as they got on the train you can easily tell there was something there. They looked like they were going to kiss at any moment. This combined with the scene in the junkyard made the whole outcome feel rushed and really awkward, kind of negating the emotional impact that was intended for me. If there was a segment before the party that established Chloe's current relationship with Rachel and what she thought of her, this could help set up the decision that was made in the junkyard scene, and would make it seem less sudden and rushed. [EDIT] After watching the junkyard scene again, I'm a little conflicted with my previous statement. When picking the friendship option, the scene plays out A LOT better. Especially with the reasoning Chloe gives for not wanting her to leave. When picking the other option, the scenes that play out after don't seem to work together well with the lover option. So the tempo rush may have been my fault actually. I might have misinterpreted the train scene as well. Upon watching again, I can see it more as Rachel trying to break Chloe out of her shell a bit. Trying to be extra caring and friendly to make Chloe feel more safe and less uncomfortable.
All in all, I enjoyed this episode very much and I believe it was a very wise decision for DONTNOD to give your team the reigns on this project.

I LOVED IT. Seriously. I knew it wouldn't disappoint to go back to Arcadia Bay, but it's even better than I expected. Just like in LiS1, the soundtrack is amazing, the characters are well-defined, and the story is touching. I liked Max, but I might like Chloe even better.
What meant a lot to me, though, was the representation of Chloe's trauma caused by her dad's death. It felt real to me. At times she'd be angry with him, or angry with the entire world, or angry with people who had absolutely nothing to do with her father or his death - but she was just angry, and that's accurate, because that's how these things work.
Personally, Chloe's flashbacks were a punch in the gut for me, but in a good way?
I lost my mom when I was 10. I still get flashbacks about it. When Chloe said she had trouble finding out what was real and what wasn't, that some parts of her real life would sometimes sneak into her nightmares... I was like, I FEEL YOU SO MUCH. SAME SAME SAME.
So. TLDR; great game and i'm shook by the amazing representation of chloe's trauma. This was even better than I expected.

It's a SimCade; it has equal parts of simulation and arcade to please both seasoned and new players. Unlike most "Simulators" on sale, it's very well made and accessible.
You start as a truck driver without a truck; complete some deliveries for others and get some loans and soon you have your own truck (and even your own company); the freights will lead you across the roads of a scaled version of western Europe while carrying a nice variety of goods; from chemical substances to cars.
The landscape is beautiful but the cities are rather simple (not really a big deal though since you spend most of your time on highways).
Simulation is more on the arcade side, with the possibility of adjusting many parameters to increase the simulation level. With some practice, anyone should be able to drive well. It's highly recommended to play this game with a steering wheel or a controller.
Pacing is very relaxing; you'll spend most of your time managing the truck speed and route. Play your favorite song or podcast and enjoy the travel.
The modding community is awesome; you'll be able to completely overhaul your experience with more realism, cargo variety, truck models and maps, but the vanilla game should provide you many hours of fun.
In conclusion, it's a game for those looking for a different experience where fun does not come from the challenge but the gameplay itself.

It even does a good job of simulating the monotony of delivering goods to various cities in a way that will actually keep you playing the game. Definitely a game for a targeted audience, but if you like driving sims that add the complexity of handling a large vehicle on many small European highways and tight secondary routes added with good business management side, this could be a good game for you.

DayZ Standalone is a simple game of luck. If you spawn in an area near a town your chances of survival are ok, if not you'll die from starvation or dehydration. Then there is the multiplayer only aspect that destroys all hope of a fun time in game. If you are with friends it is a pain to find one another. Then you have to find enough provisions for you and them; which due to poor loot spawn one will have to kill the others just to stave off starvation. If you are not with anyone then all the loot is yours untill you run into another player. At that moment it turns into a battle for each others inventory. Despite all of of that one will still have to survive the environment. the game has so many internal errors that vaulting over a fence may send you flying into a tree to where if you a re lucky only your legs break, if your unlucky you die. Same situation with ladders and stairs; one may be climing a ladder to get to the top to realize that your character falls back down to certain death. Stairs you glitch through and fall under the map where you die. Then there is the biggest problem this the game poor tick rate. The servers update at such a low rate you can search a ten building village to get a message stating "No Message Recived for # Seconds" Which means you'll get booting or just leave on you on accord. wait a minuet join back to find that the last 20 min. have been wasted, and you have to search the town all over again. Fowling up with that I have never experienced a pin over 300 every now and then no matter what sever where it is every 30-40 min. the my pin just skyrockets wile staill having perfect internet conection.  Then the game just chrashes, to where you hope that the game didn't lose your character save file. Which is a major problem if someone works hours upon hours to scavenge the best supplies to have the server screw up and delete all of your work. Finally the worse part is that for years Bohemia Interactive has stated the game is a work in progress; after a dozen or so updates I can tell you one there is no difference in gameplay from when I played this game when it first came out. The only difference is there are more official servers. Which does not affect gameplay because connecting to them is still a pain. In the end the game itself is poor quaility, not worth the money, the in game multiplayer just destroys any chance of realy progressing in the game, and the severs, internet connection, and gliches futhers the problems DayZ has. Do not get the DayZ standalone there is more fun to be had in the Arma Mod where it came from.

I hate this game.
I hate the way it made me feel like my choices mattered in a way where I regretted every dialogue option.
I hate the way the stunning visual design of the pacific northwest took me back to the dark places in my own childhood.
I hate how much Rachel and Chloe's interactions made me look back on my own life and kick myself for being so stupid, for making all the wrong choices I have made.
I hate that there is a significant populus who won't play these games out of some sort of principle, as if they aren't "games", and that an inability to be defined so simply as a "videogame" makes this unplayable because it's existence is somehow some kind of false advertising.
I hate that those people may not understand that, though the aquisition of accomplishments and/or milestones is one way to be a captivating game, there are other ways, and Life is Strange and other similar walking simulators, when done right, can also captivate us in raw and paradoxical ways.
I hate that I had doubts about this game before launch, that I thought there was no way deck 9 could pull off what dontnod did, that it was doomed to fail.
Of course, by now, you know that I love this game.
The first line was a lie.
I'm not sorry.
I have spent an exorbitant amount of money and time on new game releases these past few weeks, and though I liked many of them I loved none.
None but this game.
If you liked Life is Strange, this does not disappoint. If you did not, then don't look here for your fix.
And if you're new to the show, please for the love of Talos play the first game first.
I guess so far my only gripe has to be the minor one that this game sucked me in so relentlessly that it is now nearly 4 in the bloody morning and I have a three day concert in the neighboring town and now I won't be doing it on any sleep because I need to replay this episode with a "the choices I would have made knowing the spoilers" playthrough.
Because, while there are may healthier and more mentally reinvigorating choices I could be making right now, I'm gonna follow my instinct and make this one. Because it is the choice I love.
This is Bucket, signing off. For now.

I will admit that, at first, I was very much into this game. But as time went on I noticed many small glitches and problems and annoyances that built up to such a degree as reccomending is impossible. And to put it bluntly - it's because the game feels like it needs you to work for it. It's hard to explain, but it consistently wants effort from you as the player [and buyer of this game] to learn everything from the outset rather than use a more in depth tutorial than it currently has.
Reasons why - it's functional, but buggy. Seriously, I can't count how many times workers have got trapped on a tiny corner of wall which everyone else can pass just fine. This could be overlooked, except that for this kind of game there needs to be SOME kind of tutorial. And I'm not talking about the completely pointless ten minute one which shows you the basics - no, we need an ADVANCED one!
For the last eight hours or so I've been practically trying to teach myself this game because all the important parts, like, say, the grants that are given for your prison to establish itself or maybe knowing where the button to turn off the constant barrarge of prisoners even though there is barely enough room to keep them or maybe giving away SOMEWHERE in the tutorial how education facilities can be set up or other programs implemented. And when there isn't anything to use to help or refer to, gaming doesn't become fun, it becomes a chore and nothing less than boring.
All that the player is given is one letter from the Warden or whoever the hell the random tutorial fairy is called and a short introduction which barely explains anything about the game at all because there are advanced parts which are never explored. Yes it's all very nice that you made up a small cutscene in the intro but that never happens again! There isn't any campain! At least, not since I've started playing.
Now I can understand that some of you might be suggesting small titbits, such as the wiki that they happily put on the game menu. And after the first hour leading me straight to said page, I found out that this CAN ONLY BE SEEN IF YOU HAVE REGISTERED ON THEIR WEBSITE. Seriously, guys? It's not enough that I've supported your small indie project for making more interesting games than crouching tiger hidden wall simulators, but I have to supply my email address and password as well? Are you trying to annoy me and make me do all this leg work for a game which I would only consider mediocore at best?
And that's what this is. Mediocre at best, and yet this game consistenly punishes you for hard work and doesn't offer any input or direction as to the actual game that has been created. I'm giving it an early bad review because I don't want to register myself to a website that I don't really know just to understand a game that I have already bought and therefore should have some kind of TUTORIAL TO!
Although I'm not angry, if anything, I'm just annoyed by this game and everything which it has thrown [and has failed to throw] at me. Usually I enjoy hardcore games, Banished especially, but there needs to be a little more direction than this game is offering than just - building, camera and really obvious basic game mechanics. In Banished [taking this as an example] there are really deep tutorials which informs the player of each aspect. And guess what - where PA has a whole team working on it, that game only had one. Somehow this makes it 10000x better - which just about sums up the gaming developers at this moment in time. There needs to be something more advanced which players can understand and use when building their prisons.
I've seen plenty of reviewers easily comment that they've mastered the game in less time than I, and I suspect that they've registered and looked at the wiki unlike me who is striving not to do this. DOING SO IS BUSY WORK FOR A GAME NOT WORTH IT AND CERTAINLY NOT WORTH YOUR MONEY.
In honesty, there are many better city builders out there which have intact tutorials and don't actually waste your time with this constant insanity. Go for one of those, a cheaper one at that.
[ps - I realise that there are some people who understand this whole thing and have made amazing prisons and posted them online to the applause of one person; but I'm not like that and I'm generally♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at being treated like a moron when I just want to be taught the damn game I just bought!]
UPDATE: Now that I've worked out how to play, amazingly it's really fun. But that doesn't detract from the other points that I made. Help in a game should be made avaliable in the game when its bought and not be exclusive for people who sign up for a bloody website! It's ridiculous!

What meant a lot to me, though, was the representation of Chloe's trauma caused by her dad's death. It felt real to me. At times she'd be angry with him, or angry with the entire world, or angry with people who had absolutely nothing to do with her father or his death - but she was just angry, and that's accurate, because that's how these things work.
Personally, Chloe's flashbacks were a punch in the gut for me, but in a good way?
I lost my mom when I was 10. I still get flashbacks about it. When Chloe said she had trouble finding out what was real and what wasn't, that some parts of her real life would sometimes sneak into her nightmares... I was like, I FEEL YOU SO MUCH. SAME SAME SAME.
So. TLDR; great game and i'm shook by the amazing representation of chloe's trauma. This was even better than I expected.
