This is probably (it is) the best truck simulator ever made and the perfect game for all of us, who always dreamed about being a trucker. But most people are not made for this kinda job, because you're always on the road and don't come home very often. But now, we all can be on the road AND being at home at the same time!
I clearly remember, when I first played something similar to this truck simulator . It was, when I played the "hauling missions" in GTA: San Andreas, this was the first time I had huge fun driving a big truck and delivering cargo over long distances. The only difference in ETS 2 is, you don't have all of the cops of San Andreas on your♥♥♥♥♥;).
The game is just very beautiful, especially the graphics, it's very detailed, you don't have just the roads you're driving on, but also very detailed landscapes with meadows & bushes, fields, trees & forests, mountains, lakes & rivers and also cities and villages you are passing by, construction sites, rest stops, gas stations, industrial areas, wind turbines, electricity pylons as well as birds, airplanes and hot air balloons decorating the sky. Further you can see lots of other things beside the road, like working people and machines, cows & horses. The graphics also contains beautiful light- and shadow-effects, reflections and a nice weather system with sun, rain, thunder & lightning, fog and more.
You have several countries of Europe to explore, such as Germany, England, France, Italy, Scotland, Wales, The Netherlands, Belgium, Poland, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Austria and Switzerland, with thousands of kilometers of roads to drive along. On the map you have over 80 european cities to see with lots of recognizable sights and places.
The gameplay is also very well done, you just feel, like you are really driving a 40 ton truck, even when you, just like me, never driven a truck yourself. It is not very easy at the beginning, but when you progress in the game, you get better and better as you understand the mechanics of the game and get to know the different handlings of the trucks better and get more experienced in driving them.
But you'll always have to pay attention to the road, because there is always something happening. If it's a slow truck trying to overtake another slow truck, someone before you has to do an emergency braking, because there's an accident on the road, you can't see far ahead, because of the heavy fog laying over the road or some moron cuts you, doesn't give way or changes lanes, when you're right next to him, which often results in an accident. But you don't just have to keep an eye on other vehicles, but also on the road itself, that you don't damage your cargo, when you are parking your truck backwards or have to  take a tight turn, especially when it's raining, then the roads are slippery as hell. Cause if you drive too fast into a tight turn, your truck will overturn!
Furthermore you'll have to observe the traffic regulations, otherwise you must pay fines for speeding, driving without light, causing a collision, crossing a red light, driving on the wrong side of the road or driving the wrong way.
Then you have a huge variety in the game, not just many different road surfaces, like concrete, several types of asphalt or sometimes gravel roads, but also lots of various cars on the roads other than tucks. And although the cars are not licenced, you will recognize BMW, Mercedes, Mini, Land Rover, Volkswagen, Opel and many more.
You have 7 different truck manufacturers in the game like Scania, Iveco, Renault, Volvo, MAN, DAF and Majestic, which represents Mercedes. But all trucks are very detailed and look like the real trucks. You can also drive to a nearby workshop, where you can modify your trucks in lot of different ways, like engine, transmission, tyres, exhausts, sun visors, interiors, RHD/LHD, lights, chassis, many different painjobs and so on. If your truck is damaged, you can get it repaired there, too.
What's kinda funny, is when you first go to England and forget to drive on the other side of the road and wonder, why is there oncoming traffic on the RIGHT side, which in England is the WRONG side. But even funnier is to drive with a RHD-truck on the left side, feels like everything is mirrored.
At the beginning of your trucker career you start with nothing and have to take jobs from other companies to earn money for your future emerging business. It takes a while, before you have enough money to buy your first little garage and your first own truck, but from this day on, you run your own company! At first, you're just a one-man-business, but now that you are a independent trucker, you can earn more money, buy new trucks at a local truck dealer, extend your garage, buy new garages and most important of all, hire drivers for your company, when visiting an employment agency near you.
With every job, that you deliver, you'll receive experience points (XP), the better the job, the more valuable the cargo, the longer the distance, the more XP you'll get. When you have collected enough XP, you will rise in your rank. With every new rank, you can gain skill points in several skills, like ADR, long distance, high-value cargo, fragile cargo, just-in-time delivery and eco driver. With the acquisition of a skill point, you will receive better jobs to deliver, either more hazardous material, longer distance deliveries or cargo of higher value. Additional you will get more XP with every skillpoint you achieve respectively increasing your fuel savings with eco driver, which also saves money on the gas station. And of course, you can also level up your drivers, as they collect enough skillpoints to reach a higher level, so that they bring in more money and increase your company's income.
In my nearly 200 hours of gameplay so far, I'm currently at week 20 of my career, driven over 120.000 kilometers, explored 92% of the map and reached rank 44. I own 17 large garages and one small garage, 86 trucks and have 86 employed drivers, 48 men & 38 women, my 7-day-profit amount to 3.000.000 € (3.426.300 $). Although I played this game for so long, there is still ONE city, I haven't been yet. It's Dijon in France, will visit it soon.
Concluding I can honestly say, this is one of the most enjoyable games I have ever played, because it's just so much fun, even after 200 hours of playing. This is another good thing about this game, it's a long term game to play, because there is so much to see and to explore. Of course, europe isn't rebuilt in scale 1:1 with all roads and stuff and the cities are not full accessible, but that was never the goal of the game, it is about delivering cargo across europe over long distances to lots of different cities, that's why you only have the most important routes in there and the important areas of the cities, where the big companies are. That is what you do, you deliver cargo from one company in one city to another one in another city.
And even though the game ist out for over 2 years now, the developers are still bringing new content to the game to make it even better and bigger, with regular updates and fixes and also a new DLC of scandinavia coming up. I also hope, that they will add the other missing parts of europe, so that we on one day can go all across europe, to every single country and almost every big city.

Citizens of Dunwall, please accept my apologies. I was a hop, skip and a slide away from the Lord Regent's chamber when this seriously compelling lorry sim sped into my life. Suddenly, stealthy vengeance seems far less important than ensuring a load of new JCBs gets to Bratislava on time.
Euro Truck Simulator 2 is that rare thing, a strong sim tethered to a strong game. Where other vehicle-obsessed devs seem to take player motivation for granted, Czech studio SCS understand that a pleasingly modelled steed needs a pleasingly modelled environment to shine.
On this occasion that environment is a swathe of Europe stretching from Plymouth in the west to Wroclaw in the east, from Aberdeen in the north to Milan in the South. The tangle of motorways and major roads is stylised and condensed, but feels massive. After a splendid week of non-stop trucking the stats screen tells me I've still only seen 50% of it.
There's satisfaction in exploring new routes, seeing new golden been-there-done-that squiggles appearing on the in-game map, but it tends to be the promise of cold, hard cash that gets you out of bed in the morning. Like Farming Simulator, ETS2 has a simple yet resonant economic sandbox at its centre.
The only time when the game itself loses concentration is when attempting to evoke certain regions and sounds. The further you get from central Europe the less convincing the landscapes become. No one seems to have told SCS's countryside crafters that rural Britain features long green things called hedges. Cities are often depicted with the shortest of visual shorthand – a few warehouses, the odd landmark if you're lucky. Don't expect to see a favourite local roundabout, slip-road, or speed camera in this highly-recommended HGV-driver RPG.

Okay, before everyone jumps on me and calls me a hater and says that I am giving this game a negative review just because everyone else loves it hear me out. I don't completely hate this game. I love the art style, the game looks amazing lets just get that out of the way. And the game functions just fine for me but, in most other aspects the game is just disappointing.
The gameplay itself just doens't work for me. The controls are decent but nothing has any weight to it. I get that that is the point but to quote the immortal yatzhee "THEN WHY AREN'T I LAUGHING?" I admit that it's funny for a little while but it just lost me along the way.
Also a major focus of the game is the multiplayer. I'm not really much of a multiplayer guy, but I do indulge in the pleasures of multiplayer now and again. But the problem is that this game is made for local multiplayer, and if you're like me then you just don't have the ability to get a bunch a friends over to play. So naturally there's online multiplayer right? Right?
Wrong.
The online multiplayer is still a work in progress and barely anyone has access to it. Adding the multiplayer would make this game INFINITELY more replayable, but so far there's just no incentive for people like me to play.
Also the player vs. npc mode has a single map to play on and it is easily the most boring map in the game.
I don't like this game and don't recommend this game in its current state but you should DEFINITELY keep an eye on it because it has so much potential and can only get better from here. I'll definitely buy the game again when online modes are added but until then, keep the 20 dollars and use it to buy other complete games like Shovel Knight, or Dust: An Elysian Tail which are complete and well worth your money.

Allright, for starters: I absolutely adore the entire Mad Max franchise, and been a fan for years. This game captures the feel of the old trilogy quite well.
Now, for the pros and cons:
1.Pros
-Good "feel"
-Chumbucket! (Although, he could use some more on-screen time)

-ENGINE SOUNDS. My God, how can this get done sooo wrong? V6 sound like some supercharged straight engine, and is super tiresome at any longer trip but...
V8 Sound is a travesty. Sounds a bit meatier than V6s, but come on... If you want the MEAT from Road Warrior or Fury Road, forget it. They're just bland and weak.
-Nitrous working like a rocket engine. In the middle of air and need some extra elevation? Nitro!
- SPOILER LOADING SCREENS: I don't know who thought it would be a good idea to show you important NPCs or how future upgrades look on the loading screens, but they deserve a special reward.

As far as driving games, go, Euro Truck Simulator 2 is one of the most ambitious. Euro Truck Simulator 2 sets a new definition for large scale maps in driving games (with the exception of The Crew, which is a close competitor). Deliver cargo all around Europe as you build up your truck and garage into a huge network of truckers. The scenery is very beautiful, and although some elements are copy-and-paste, the landscape varies a lot and never ceases to amaze me. I can't help but stop and take photos, even do sight seeing, and bask in it beauty. You may think that sounds a little funny, but come on, just look at those views! :P
The game does have it's flaws, but SCS is a small independent game development company, and the products they have been able to release are incredible feats. They are getting closer to releasing American Truck Sim, which looks awesome. The AI can be a bit buggy, the economy a bit lacking, but you can easily spend hours playing this game, and with a ton of DLC (both current, and upcoming) you'll have a lot of opportunities to expand.
The one thing I absolutely love about this game is the detail on the interior of the trucks. It's very immersive. The team at SCS have done an incredible job creating the realism of the trucks, both inside and out. Overall, the entire game just looks good. The addition of game wheels and Oculus Rift are a plus... even though I'm currently not lucky enough to own either.
If you like driving games, driving sims, or exploration games, Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a good purchase.

The simulation game all simulation games strive for. The game is boring, but addicting and exciting at times. This reminds me of those crappy Facebook games where you level up stuff and build an empire...of trucks. Trucks are nice looking, trailers are nice, and there is even live radio from Europe to listen to.
Bad thing is that the AI cars are stupid...like in real life. Some of the cars are way too polite, and I end up getting stuck at an intersection. Also, speeds posted on the Nav are different than the speed limit is in some places. For example, the 2 motorway crossings at Rotterdam, Netherlands list the speed as 50 mph, when it's actually 31 mph.
This game also has a ton of mods, ranging from different trucks, different cargos, map extensions to places like Northern Africa, and various reskins. Just a word of advice, when using mods, you are at your own risk for the game not working, so get a program like WinZip and zip up your save files before playing a mod. Some mods also have a ReadMe file, so read those too. Also, every time the game updates, you need to download a new version of the mod to keep up with the version of the game. If you wern't going to get into mods, download the Multiplayer Mod. It's tons of fun driving with other people in the world...except when your ping gets high and you are kicked.
Overall, fantastic game. Wait a little bit more until the Scandinavia DLC comes out, and get a discounted bundle with this game and 2 pieces of DLC: Scandinavia and Going East!, which includes Poland, Czech Republic, and Romania, which I recommend. At the time of this review, Scandinavia hasn't come out yet, but very soon it will.

Before the Storm has gotten off to a great start. At first I was hesitant about even getting this game since A: the same developers from the first game didn't work on it, and B: I wondered what even the point of a prequel to L.I.S. proved to serve since we know what's going to happen already.
Well, my concerns about the devs was unfounded considering they've written a great story and script so far. I'd even say that the writing is even better than the first in a lot of regards. The animations have improved as well - no longer do characters have flat, expressionless faces. These devs definitely gave this game some tlc when they worked on it.
As for my concerns about a L.I.S prequel? Well...that remains to be seen. The story has been compelling enough so far that I want to find out what happens, but since I know what happens to a lot of these characters already, I can't help but feel wary.
All in all, I'd recommend it, especially if you're a fan of the first game. I can't wait for the other episodes to be released.

-The Wasteland of the game and all the bizarre characters who inhabit it really capture the look and feel of the recent movie. The map is huge and your let loose to try and attack Scrotus' camps and structures to weaken his influence over the Wasteland.
- The Magnum Opus can be customized with different weapons like flamethrowers or a ramming grill for example as well as improving things like wheels and engine. Which is great because the Magnum Opus feels more like your own vehicle than some generic vehicle. The vehicle combat in game is a lot of fun too.
-The graphics in this game are great though you'll need a powerful rig to get them at their max. (No pun intended)
Bad points:
- This game has a lot of collectibles and you'll spend a lot of time gathering scrap to improve the Magnum Opus and Max.   This gets very repetitive and while i didnt mind it so much at first i was sick of it towards the end. Unfortunately since you need certain upgrades for some of the story missions it'sunavoidable to some extant.
- The combat is similar to that of other WB games like the Arkham series and Shadow of Mordor. It does feel a bit too easy at times as it's just one button to attack and another to counter. There isnt much enemy variety either.The one thing i liked about the combat was how visceral and real it looks. Rather than fancy acrobatics or martial arts the fights look more like a pub brawl and just as brutal.
While some might see the freedom to explore as you will with occasional story mission as a plus, i felt the game could have done with more structure as it would have helped it avoid becoming a repetitive experience. I have decided to recommend it because i did really enjoy the game for the first 15-20 hours and it still is a decent game overall. However if you cant stand loads of collectables and repetitive gameplay this might not be for you.

It's a SimCade; it has equal parts of simulation and arcade to please both seasoned and new players. Unlike most "Simulators" on sale, it's very well made and accessible.
You start as a truck driver without a truck; complete some deliveries for others and get some loans and soon you have your own truck (and even your own company); the freights will lead you across the roads of a scaled version of western Europe while carrying a nice variety of goods; from chemical substances to cars.
The landscape is beautiful but the cities are rather simple (not really a big deal though since you spend most of your time on highways).
Simulation is more on the arcade side, with the possibility of adjusting many parameters to increase the simulation level. With some practice, anyone should be able to drive well. It's highly recommended to play this game with a steering wheel or a controller.
Pacing is very relaxing; you'll spend most of your time managing the truck speed and route. Play your favorite song or podcast and enjoy the travel.
The modding community is awesome; you'll be able to completely overhaul your experience with more realism, cargo variety, truck models and maps, but the vanilla game should provide you many hours of fun.
In conclusion, it's a game for those looking for a different experience where fun does not come from the challenge but the gameplay itself.

I regret breaking my one rule. I told myself that I’d never preorder a game – not on my life. It’s not how the game industry should run, I told myself. But Life is Strange – one of my favorite games of all time – it had such a place of respect in my eyes, I let myself do it. How wrong of me.
Why was Life is Strange so good? This should be the question anybody that wants to follow up on it asks. The characters, the dialogue exchanges, the simple moments of just laying next to a character you like and letting time pass – or not. These made LiS great. Chloe and Max were both expressive, and deep, and voice acted brilliantly. You could feel their emotion through the screen.
This wasn’t anywhere near my experience with Before the Storm. The writing has its moments, with some meaningful silences and obeying the hot-topic-cold-prose rule almost to a T, but, more often than not, Chloe is awkward, the dialogue is on-the-nose, and people bring up weird non-sequiturs that seem grossly out of place in the middle of conversations. The greatest offenders being the “talkback” options – these sequences where they try to fill the gap left by a missing time control mechanic – that try to paint Chloe as some “badass” who can talk her way through anybody, but in actuality show more of how out of touch the writers are with reality. The displeasure of having to sit through these moments cannot be overstated. Granted, the effective moments it has just about even out with the cringeworthy ones, but it isn’t enough – if you had to be force fed dog♥♥♥♥♥♥to be able to eat a few cookies, would you take the offer? Especially when you have to pay for it?
Rachel, however, is a bit more expressive. Her presence also builds context for the original – meaning that we finally learn why she’s so great a person that Chloe spends the entire first game looking for her. Her voice actress did a great job of carrying emotion with her intonation, unlike that of her friend, Chloe. After some brouhaha over not getting the original studio to make this game, Deck Nine failed to get her original voice actress. This is off-putting at first – the new one seems just a bit more nasal than the former. The more problematic fact of this is that it seems similarity to the original was prioritized over actual talent. The new girl delivers her lines in a monotone, and Chloe becomes dull and lifeless. Perhaps this isn’t entirely on the studio casting the roll poorly – perhaps it is because the voice actress tries too hard to sound like the original (maybe because the studio told her to do so), and this doesn’t let her give us the full range of her own voice. Whatever the reason, it’s hard to listen to, and makes the Chloe less believable.
On the topic of believability, I don’t buy the expressions and character designs for a moment. Every asset was just copy-pasted form LiS – which, while not horrible, wasn’t exactly eye candy. A few new characters had to be made, and they don’t look any better. I remarked to myself once while looking at a face close-up; “I think I know that brush… What’s it called in Blender again? Clay strips?” Yet, this slightly-under-par visual composition is nothing compared to the horrendous animations. Half the time the character’s faces don’t even seem to move, and the other half the time they look like poorly made android replacements of people. What I will say is that the previews on this page are fairly accurate – uncanny and janky movements, not helped by the low-poly graphics and pixelated textures. Though, the lighting is weirdly good – the color selection and ray rendering are out of place in their quality.
There is probably something to be said about time control not being present. I do think that added a lot to the story of LiS – and provided a solid second mechanic to fall back on and contrast with when the characters had said all they could. There seems to be something missing here – now all we really have is the dialogues. If they were a little better written I might say that’s all we need, but as it is, it leaves much to be desired, and the endless conversation starts to wear thin without something else to take the load off once in a while. It would be nice if there were more sequences like there are at the end of episodes – where there is little to no talking, and much of the story is conveyed through body expression, imagery, and the music that overlays it. Like the original, BTS is good at letting the sound design, visual theme, and cinematography do the talking. Yet, this happens such a small portion of the time that it almost isn’t even worth mentioning. I wish there had been more of this – it could have provided the contrast this story needed.
Now that I mention it – missed opportunities are something this shares with LiS. The main mechanic of both games is the ability to make choices, and have those choices show up at a later date. This means that if you steal money from a guy in the fist episode, you will – get this – have somebody mention it in a later episode. Is your mind ♥♥♥♥ing blown yet? Of course not. Such a mundane difference is almost offensive when the advert is that “choices matter”. I remember there being about two choices in the original that mattered in any significant amount – when you interact with Kate in the middle of the second episode, and the final choice in the last episode. Yet, anyone who has played that game more than once can tell you how little actually changes with all the little decisions (save the one at the end, but that actually completely undoes the scene with Kate and makes every earlier choice absolutely meaningless, so it doesn’t get much credit for that). BTS has a similar number of options that actually make a significant difference. But just a few is not enough – I don’t want to have to play the exact same story twice just to see a character wind up with a slightly different hat or something later on.
Other people here have made the statement that the story cuts a little short. I hazard to agree, and it really doesn’t explain how Rachel got to the dark room (although I don’t personally think that matters, since we more or less found that out in the original LiS), or provide much closure. There is supposedly a “bonus” episode that will be released later that you get with the deluxe edition, but I don’t hold much hope that it’ll do much to save the first few episodes.
By and large this game had potential, and it choked. It wasn’t worth the preorder, nor the deluxe upgrade. What it needed was someone on the writing team who had interacted with human beings before, a voice actress that actually had a voice, and an art director who wasn’t blind. Every once in a while, the original LiS’s quality shows through, but it isn’t worth putting up with the rest. Save your money, and your respect for the characters and story. Let it die a hero.

I felt a bit cagy going into this episode. But although this sequel is not made by the same people as the first entry to the series, I quickly learned that the people of Deck 9 have a keen eye for what made the first game great.
The time travel mechanic isn't present anymore, but imho the new game mechanic is equally gripping, while succesfully engaging you with the situations in which it is used.
What stands out when you compare the first episode to its predecessor is the dialogue. Some people didn't enjoy the sequel to this game, because some of the diaolgue made them cringe. You won't find that in this game. The exchanges develop naturally and almost always hit the right tone.
The staging and music selection is  as great as it was in the first game.
Together staging, dialogue and music create those perfect little moments, that would suck you into the first game and make you linger.
This story driven game won't please people, who get their joy from mastering game mechanics. But for people who love a well-told story and the heightend emotional engagement well placed moments of fitting interactivity can offer, Life is Strange: Before the Storm is off to a great start.
For people who like numbers, I guess the first episode would be a 9/10 to me.

In order to understand what I expected from Life Is Strange: Before the Storm one has to know what I liked about the first Life Is Strange.
For me the most important point of art (yes I do think that these games belong to the art category) is to transport feelings and emotions. The genre of the art determines the direction of the feeling (e.g. rock vs. classic). At the end of the first part of the first Life Is Strange you're sitting with Chloe in her room, while Santa Monica Dream (I knew the song before and was really happy hearing it in this setting) is playing from the old stereo and the dust scattered the late afternoon sunlight, tinting everything in a warm orange. Her room is trashed just like her mind and you realize that she just wants to be loved.
For me this was the best moment of the first game, after this the actual plot started and thing still where good but not this touching. Maybe because I can more relate with a broken teenager who whats to be loved as with someone who gets to decide who lives and who doesn't.
The commercialism of the new Life Is Strange was deterrent for me, preorder bonus, and delux editions feel like they want to bleed this cow dry like every other one. Despite this I bought it. If you can get some good emotions its worth a try.
Within the backtalk feature you do have a time limit to decide what to say, I would have liked it without this limit, the first game worked completely without time pressure and it was a relive.
Some of the critics wrote that they missed some more complex puzzles, actually I can't say this of myself. Solving artificial problems that someone else made seems kind of pointless to me, I'm here for the story not for the challenge. So I am fine with the lack of puzzles.
I wanted a game (do you realize how unfitting this description has become) with this mellow warm feeling to it, were the plots task is to connect the images. The first part of Before the Storm gave me exactly this. It was grate and in the end it had me thinking for two days about the game.

Ive been playing truck games since hte early versions of 18WOS and as a kid, that series was brilliant. But the advances in programming technology, SCS have done a fantastic job with ETS2! As a single player simulator, the game offers a challenge to build up your company, hire drivers and buy trucks, putting you in the management seat as well as th driving seat. With the addition of the multiplayer mod, the game was bought to life and has since exploded in popularity in my opinion. ETS2MP bought the world of virtual truckers together, enjoying the game together, driving in convoys, working for virtual trucking companies and generally having even more fun than single player!!
Overall, the game on its own is fantastic, but with the addition of official DLC's it is becoming an incredibly immersive environment, and some of the mods you can download really make the experience unique to the player. Ive truly not seen a better truck simulator than Euro Truck Simulator 2.
But dont take my word for it, my hours are good, but i know a few people with 500+ hours on the game!! Creating an experience that good is most certainly something for SCS to be proud of.
Now, no game review is complete without pointing out some of the bad points. ETS2 itself has been out for a while and technology has advanced greatly since its initial release, therefore the physics engine could be improved. eg. why not have the road become slightly slippy when its wet during/after rain? However, I know that SCS are working on improving various elements of the sim whilest creating new exciting DLS's at the same time.
The ETS2MP Mod (the most popular unofficial mod) shares similar downfalls as many other mass multiplayer games (Call of Duty, Battlefield, GTA Series) whereas the servers become filled with people just wanting to ruin your day by not playing the game properly. It was suggested by an ETS2MP admin that new players should be made to "take a driving test" before being able to play on hte main ETS2MP servers, however I dont think this will take off.
I hope this review is helpful, I truly think SCS will one day create something better than their capabilities, but that hasnt, and wont happen with ETS2. WELL DONE SCS SOFTWARE!!

Undertale is a fun and unique RPG game that allows the player to do something that most games do not.
Have you ever wondered, why in many RPG games, you have to kill everything, and you have to seek getting as much EXP as possible? Why do you have to kill everything? What if you could befriend them, and learn their story, instead?
In Undertale, you play as a human who has fallen into Mt. Ebott, somehow surviving their fall by falling into a bed of golden flowers. During this time, tensions are strong between humans and monsters, as the humans and monsters are involved in a war. The humans had sealed the monsters into the underground, trapping them with a barrier.
As you explore the Underground, and as you progress in the game, you will meet new friends, new enemies. you will meet many different kinds of monsters. Some hostile at first, and some friendly, each monster in Undertale seems to have a different and unique personality.
You can be either a pacifist or genocidal, but I prefer only taking the pacifist route, as the pacifist route of the game is heartwarming and uplifting, and it allows me to hear more about the Monsters and their perspectives and their story in Undertale, and also, well... if you're like me, you'll get quite attached to these charming characters. (I have played the Pacifist route four times, and the game is still super fun and charming!)
In Undertale, as you explore, you will also see all sorts of cool environments, and hear the game's acclaimed great soundtrack.
Every character in Undertale has their strengths and weaknesses, and their flaws and their good traits, too. With their unique and varied personalities, many of Undertale's characters have become relatable for quite a few fans of the game, and I admire games that put so much care and attention into its characters and its writing.
Although the game can be creepy and foreboding at times, the game also has many moments of humor, fun, and silliness!
Undertale, in its pacifist run, has been one of the funniest, most uplifting, emotional, and heartwarming games that I have ever played. I have no complaints about the game, and I would encourage anyone to play! Don't mind the fan-base, and give Undertale a try. In my eyes, it is essential that you go into this game blind, and not let yourself uncover spoilers, as the game has its share of surprises and events! ^.^

Euro Truck Simulator. Three words which, in isolation, seem innocuous enough, but which when spoken in sequence can put even the most ardent gamer to sleep.
If you’re still reading this, then that means you’re still awake. You passed the first test.
If my tone seems cruel and mocking now, that’s because when I first heard about ETS, I did cruelly mock it. Trucks? Boring. Simulation games? Boring. That’s what my STUPID brain thought when I read the title, and it relayed the various commands so that I might signify my condescension. Fake yawn, patronising shake of the head, roll the eyes. Fart a little bit - my bottom pleading to be involved somehow.
And so I ignored it, for about a year after its release, until I read an article (I forget where, or by whom) which said that even though it sounds like it’ll be boring, it actually isn’t.
It is. It is a bit boring, but in a
.
First, the meat. ETS is a game where you drive a truck and deliver goods around Europe. You start off doing freight jobs in loaned trucks, but will eventually earn enough to buy your own, which is when you’ll see real money coming in. You’ll continue earning money until you can rent premises, hire people and buy more trucks for them to deliver goods in, earning you even more money. That’s it, really. There’s not much to the business management side of things, so once you’ve got your own truck you could just ignore that aspect entirely. Control options are fairly customisable, which is nice. I play on a 360 pad (very “casual mode”) with all the assists turned on and automatic gearing and whatnot, and it’s lovely. Relaxing. But if you want you can have 50 different buttons on the keyboard devoted to different functions and really take control. The holy grail, of course, is playing with a wheel and decent pedals, but I doubt I’ll ever get the chance to try that out.
After I played the demo until about 3am, I decided to buy ETS. I couldn’t say that I had had a lot of fun, precisely, or that I’d learned anything about what it is to drive a truck, or any other aspect of trucking. But as the rain fell upon my cab in Calais, and the wipers swished hypnotically back and forth, back and forth, I had felt tremendously involved. In that time I’d gone from Manchester to London, then all the way to Scotland on some slow, winding roads, and then belted back down south and across the channel. I’d signalled properly, watched my speed, and stopped at the lights like a good boy. Is this even a proper
? Where are the zombies?
Often, when we talk about games we talk about atmosphere. How does this game conjure the atmosphere or exploring an underwater wreck, or how does this one make you feel like you’re in the middle of a war, running for your life. ETS has an amazing amount of atmosphere: you really will feel like you’re sat in traffic on the M56. And if that sounds mundane, fair enough, it probably is, but somehow this game seeps into your pores and you start to care. You want to make your delivery on time, and you want your cargo to be undamaged, and you want to ease the trailer into the bay like a boss (your first time around this will seem impossible). It can be tremendously satisfying to get things right, and very stressful when things start to go wrong. I remember driving past my exit somewhere in Germany and having to take a huge detour. Pressed for time and with my truck running on fumes, I started driving faster, more recklessly. That job cost me a lot of money, and in real life, would have earned me some serious jail time.
Speaking of jail time, the way fines and penalties are handled in this game is a little odd. There are no rozzers to speak of, and when you, for example, hit another car or run a red light you will automagically be fined a set amount of money, curse under your breath and continue on your way. That’s it. It’s a bit disappointing to me that even if you careen into a mini at 100mph, there will be no real negative consequence to that. A small fine, that’s it. Worse still is the infuriating way speed cameras are handled. If you’re doing 31 in a 30 zone as you pass one, you’ll get a fine. Shouldn’t there be a bit of leeway, like in real life? I’m not sure what the game is “simulating” in that situation.
The AI in this game is hilarious at times, too. I remember once a car flashed me to let me out of a busy junction, and I thought that was great. It didn’t seem like a scripted response at all, and I honked my horn in approval. That’s only even happened once in about 60 hours. More often than not you’ll see drivers stopping dead on the sliproad for no reason, or entering a roundabout in the wrong lane at the wrong time as you pull 22 tons of furniture in their path. I remember one particularly determined driver who got himself wedged under my trailer as he tried to change lanes. I got a big “collision” fine for no reason, and he put his hazards on, pointlessly. I’d like to say this stuff is rare, but usually you’ll see some crazy AI behaviour on every job you take.
Look, I love this game. It’s what I love to play when I want to unwind. Undeniably, it is repetitive. Even if you’re going somewhere new - and on a map this size you often are - you’re still essentially going through the motions. But, like taking a big dump, these motions are very satisfying, and the odd glitches and quirks of the AI add to the charm somehow. It’s a big achievement that a simulation game, such as it is, has managed to find quite so broad an audience. Give the generous demo a try, and I think you’ll soon be seduced by its shiny, chrome encrusted charms.

One of the best games I have ever purchased on steam, a lot of people will say negative things about the fact you die too much or that everything gets really expensive quite fast. The dying is a main, if not essential part of the Rougelike Genre of games. This game utilises dying to improve your "legacy" whether it be a new class to choose from, an upgrade to a class you already have or a stat boost, the game makes every upgrade a little more expensive each time you buy one but thats the equivalent to the lowest value coin found in the castle. It is a bit slow to start off with as you lose every last piece of gold you earned to re-enter the castle.
Story wise this game doesn't really have much. You have the tutorial and the log entries, which provide some background to the start of the game. Its not brilliant, but it does provide you with the reason behind the actions done in the tutorial.
This game also has your heroes with "traits". These are actual known medical conditions (to some extent) and affect your hero in different ways like I.B.S which makes your hero fart to things like vertigo which flips the games screen upside down. Each hero can have up to 2 different traits and may very rarely have none.
The castle is randomly generated each time, unless you decide to get an upgeade that allows you to "lock it down". Which allows you to practice bosses or try to reach that chest you couldn't reach last time. These chests can provide runes, which can give you different benefits and come in 5 varieties (for each main piece of equipment you have), you can only have 1 rune in each piece of equipment and you can also get equipment blueprints, which allow you to spend your gold after you die to unlock and maybe even equip (providing you have the weight allowance that is).
The enemies have 3 different tiers basic, advanced and expert, but you won't come across any expert tier enemies till you have beaten the game twice, but they still can spawn and you will be facing expert enemies a lot after you beat it for your first time, the bosses and mini-bosses are a nice challenge aswell as they need you to think ahead. After you beat a boss you can find its "obol" (except the 5th one, you just need to beat all the remix bosses to be able to find its obol) which allows you to face its remixed version where you use a specific preset character, these are a true test of skill and will take many attempts and beating them all gives you a real sense of accomplishment, once you beat the final boss you are sent into New Game + mode, where you do it all again with harder enemies and the enemies are all now at the advanced tier (expert if its NB++ onwards)
I know I have recommended this, but if you don't like games where you die a lot, or games that get repetitive quite fast then this game isn't for you.

I regret breaking my one rule. I told myself that I’d never preorder a game – not on my life. It’s not how the game industry should run, I told myself. But Life is Strange – one of my favorite games of all time – it had such a place of respect in my eyes, I let myself do it. How wrong of me.
Why was Life is Strange so good? This should be the question anybody that wants to follow up on it asks. The characters, the dialogue exchanges, the simple moments of just laying next to a character you like and letting time pass – or not. These made LiS great. Chloe and Max were both expressive, and deep, and voice acted brilliantly. You could feel their emotion through the screen.
This wasn’t anywhere near my experience with Before the Storm. The writing has its moments, with some meaningful silences and obeying the hot-topic-cold-prose rule almost to a T, but, more often than not, Chloe is awkward, the dialogue is on-the-nose, and people bring up weird non-sequiturs that seem grossly out of place in the middle of conversations. The greatest offenders being the “talkback” options – these sequences where they try to fill the gap left by a missing time control mechanic – that try to paint Chloe as some “badass” who can talk her way through anybody, but in actuality show more of how out of touch the writers are with reality. The displeasure of having to sit through these moments cannot be overstated. Granted, the effective moments it has just about even out with the cringeworthy ones, but it isn’t enough – if you had to be force fed dog♥♥♥♥♥♥to be able to eat a few cookies, would you take the offer? Especially when you have to pay for it?
Rachel, however, is a bit more expressive. Her presence also builds context for the original – meaning that we finally learn why she’s so great a person that Chloe spends the entire first game looking for her. Her voice actress did a great job of carrying emotion with her intonation, unlike that of her friend, Chloe. After some brouhaha over not getting the original studio to make this game, Deck Nine failed to get her original voice actress. This is off-putting at first – the new one seems just a bit more nasal than the former. The more problematic fact of this is that it seems similarity to the original was prioritized over actual talent. The new girl delivers her lines in a monotone, and Chloe becomes dull and lifeless. Perhaps this isn’t entirely on the studio casting the roll poorly – perhaps it is because the voice actress tries too hard to sound like the original (maybe because the studio told her to do so), and this doesn’t let her give us the full range of her own voice. Whatever the reason, it’s hard to listen to, and makes the Chloe less believable.
On the topic of believability, I don’t buy the expressions and character designs for a moment. Every asset was just copy-pasted form LiS – which, while not horrible, wasn’t exactly eye candy. A few new characters had to be made, and they don’t look any better. I remarked to myself once while looking at a face close-up; “I think I know that brush… What’s it called in Blender again? Clay strips?” Yet, this slightly-under-par visual composition is nothing compared to the horrendous animations. Half the time the character’s faces don’t even seem to move, and the other half the time they look like poorly made android replacements of people. What I will say is that the previews on this page are fairly accurate – uncanny and janky movements, not helped by the low-poly graphics and pixelated textures. Though, the lighting is weirdly good – the color selection and ray rendering are out of place in their quality.
There is probably something to be said about time control not being present. I do think that added a lot to the story of LiS – and provided a solid second mechanic to fall back on and contrast with when the characters had said all they could. There seems to be something missing here – now all we really have is the dialogues. If they were a little better written I might say that’s all we need, but as it is, it leaves much to be desired, and the endless conversation starts to wear thin without something else to take the load off once in a while. It would be nice if there were more sequences like there are at the end of episodes – where there is little to no talking, and much of the story is conveyed through body expression, imagery, and the music that overlays it. Like the original, BTS is good at letting the sound design, visual theme, and cinematography do the talking. Yet, this happens such a small portion of the time that it almost isn’t even worth mentioning. I wish there had been more of this – it could have provided the contrast this story needed.
Now that I mention it – missed opportunities are something this shares with LiS. The main mechanic of both games is the ability to make choices, and have those choices show up at a later date. This means that if you steal money from a guy in the fist episode, you will – get this – have somebody mention it in a later episode. Is your mind ♥♥♥♥ing blown yet? Of course not. Such a mundane difference is almost offensive when the advert is that “choices matter”. I remember there being about two choices in the original that mattered in any significant amount – when you interact with Kate in the middle of the second episode, and the final choice in the last episode. Yet, anyone who has played that game more than once can tell you how little actually changes with all the little decisions (save the one at the end, but that actually completely undoes the scene with Kate and makes every earlier choice absolutely meaningless, so it doesn’t get much credit for that). BTS has a similar number of options that actually make a significant difference. But just a few is not enough – I don’t want to have to play the exact same story twice just to see a character wind up with a slightly different hat or something later on.
Other people here have made the statement that the story cuts a little short. I hazard to agree, and it really doesn’t explain how Rachel got to the dark room (although I don’t personally think that matters, since we more or less found that out in the original LiS), or provide much closure. There is supposedly a “bonus” episode that will be released later that you get with the deluxe edition, but I don’t hold much hope that it’ll do much to save the first few episodes.
By and large this game had potential, and it choked. It wasn’t worth the preorder, nor the deluxe upgrade. What it needed was someone on the writing team who had interacted with human beings before, a voice actress that actually had a voice, and an art director who wasn’t blind. Every once in a while, the original LiS’s quality shows through, but it isn’t worth putting up with the rest. Save your money, and your respect for the characters and story. Let it die a hero.

The staging and music selection is  as great as it was in the first game.
Together staging, dialogue and music create those perfect little moments, that would suck you into the first game and make you linger.
This story driven game won't please people, who get their joy from mastering game mechanics. But for people who love a well-told story and the heightend emotional engagement well placed moments of fitting interactivity can offer, Life is Strange: Before the Storm is off to a great start.
For people who like numbers, I guess the first episode would be a 9/10 to me.

Undertale is a fun and unique RPG game that allows the player to do something that most games do not.
Have you ever wondered, why in many RPG games, you have to kill everything, and you have to seek getting as much EXP as possible? Why do you have to kill everything? What if you could befriend them, and learn their story, instead?
In Undertale, you play as a human who has fallen into Mt. Ebott, somehow surviving their fall by falling into a bed of golden flowers. During this time, tensions are strong between humans and monsters, as the humans and monsters are involved in a war. The humans had sealed the monsters into the underground, trapping them with a barrier.
As you explore the Underground, and as you progress in the game, you will meet new friends, new enemies. you will meet many different kinds of monsters. Some hostile at first, and some friendly, each monster in Undertale seems to have a different and unique personality.
You can be either a pacifist or genocidal, but I prefer only taking the pacifist route, as the pacifist route of the game is heartwarming and uplifting, and it allows me to hear more about the Monsters and their perspectives and their story in Undertale, and also, well... if you're like me, you'll get quite attached to these charming characters. (I have played the Pacifist route four times, and the game is still super fun and charming!)
In Undertale, as you explore, you will also see all sorts of cool environments, and hear the game's acclaimed great soundtrack.
Every character in Undertale has their strengths and weaknesses, and their flaws and their good traits, too. With their unique and varied personalities, many of Undertale's characters have become relatable for quite a few fans of the game, and I admire games that put so much care and attention into its characters and its writing.
Although the game can be creepy and foreboding at times, the game also has many moments of humor, fun, and silliness!
Undertale, in its pacifist run, has been one of the funniest, most uplifting, emotional, and heartwarming games that I have ever played. I have no complaints about the game, and I would encourage anyone to play! Don't mind the fan-base, and give Undertale a try. In my eyes, it is essential that you go into this game blind, and not let yourself uncover spoilers, as the game has its share of surprises and events! ^.^

This game surprised me in so many ways. My initial impression after completing the demo was a boring and generic third person cover based shooter with little that interested me. Now that I’ve sunk some hours into it, I can safely say my first impression was so wrong!
Spec Ops: The Line is actually one of the most moving games I’ve ever played. The setting, the characters, the overall story and decisions, it all comes together to form such an unforgettable experience. Instead of mindless violence, the player sees the effect each enemy encounter has on the main characters. There’s a progression in the attitude of the characters towards both the enemies and each other. Few games manage to successfully pull this off without making it look outright cheesy.
The sandy Dubai setting and unique back story make Spec Ops: The Line even more interesting. No more generic military desert country with “insurgents” and mud huts. Dubai really does feel like Dubai and the problems that exist there feel genuine and make you want to find out more. It’s safe to say that there are plenty of decent twists throughout the story line.
The only problem I’ve noticed with Spec Ops is the gameplay which (although fun and addictive) could be improved upon. Enemies moving around and suddenly popping up from cover looks unnatural and the ballistic and particle effects look rubbish (when you shoot walls, fire your weapon). It’s still fun to use all the different weapons and basic squad tactics though. Seeing the look on the main character’s face as he gets shot at is priceless :D
Spec Ops: The Line is one of the most surprising games I’ve ever played and I feel truly humbled to have found such a gem amongst a year of generic shooters that seriously lack story. The developers at Yager studios put their heart and soul into making The Line what it is and it shows (the same can’t be said for the absolutely terrible multiplayer, but that was made by another studio so who gives a ♥♥♥♥).

I purchased this game on a Steam Holiday sale for 10 bucks and it was well spent.  I actually would have gotten the game for more, looking back in hindsight.  The game is a shooter and at first you might think that it is like any other shooter out there.  You will soon realize that the game does have the typical shooter elements but the direction of story and choices you have to make will get you to think about how war can be in reality.  I will not say much more for fear of ruining the story but it was a good 10-12 hour ride.

Spec Ops: The Line can be summed up in one word: FUN. There is nothing innovative about this game. Everything is straightforward and quite linear. The choices you make along the way have almost no impact on how the story unfolds. These choices, however, will prompt you to act on your instincts.
SO:TL is a third person cover shooter yet the covering system is unreliable at times, and it will guarantee to annoy on Suicide Mission and Fubar difficulty. Vaulting over cover has to be precise or a melee command will be executed instead. Imagine being fired at and you suddenly pop out of cover to elbow the air followed by a "You Died" message.
Technical issues aside, Spec Ops: The Line is a satisfying cover shooter. Events and story pacing is superb. The guns are varied. Switching firing modes or a grenade attachment adds a bit of tactical depth to the gunplay.
If you are looking to play mutilplayer online matches, look elsewhere. Invite only co-op can possibly add another 2 to 3 hours of gameplay on top of the 6 to 8 hours required to complete the campaign. Spec Ops: The Line is an underrated gem that deserves more attention. Buy it on sale and enjoy the ride.

Having just completed the first episode (the only one out so far), I can say that the game is incredibly true to some of the angst that many of us felt as teenagers.  It accurately depicts the poor reasoning decisions we often made.  Rachel seems destined for a tragic end and Chloe seems as if she's in an adventure that she'll never forget, for better or worse.  As with the first installment, the graphics aren't special but the music is perfect for the mood, the voice acting is authentic and the game is filled with some of the most regrettable decisions someone could ever make.  I personally loved the tone and appreciate the story the developers are telling here, and I think you will too.  The decisions are varied, though I haven't had multiple play-throughs to see what other outcomes are possible.  In much the same was as the Dream Fall series, this series of games should make for some very memorable experiences.

Deeply flawed game, imo. It's beautiful, Dubai is a great setting with incredible vistas and amazing interiors, but then you spend a lot of your time in ho-hum corridors and rooms.
You have a wide variety of powerful weapons that take down enemies in a few bullets, but even so you're constantly struggling to conserve ammo because the game is so stingy with it.
The much-ballyhooed story aspect fell totally flat for me. The Big Bad Thing you do that's supposed to make you feel bad is another one of those "you have no other options" things. You can't choose NOT to do it. Same for the "you're killing American soldiers!" broohaha. Every single one of those soldiers attacks YOU first, so it's pure self-defense. It doesn't bother me as a gamer-hell, it wouldn't bother me as Walker himself. The 33rd open fire on US soldiers, therefore they are traitors.
That said, the story is told well, and it's very well represented visually, and especially through the incredible voice acting work from the three main characters.
I think this would have done better as a Splinter Cell type of game. Instead, the devs chose to make it Gears of War, and it just hinders the seriousness of it all. I mean, here's three guys mowing down literally a thousand enemy soldiers, and I'm supposed to take it seriously and think on what they're doing? it's like the devs couldn't figure out what kinda game they wanted to make.
All in all, it's a pretty, but utterly bog-standard third person shooter with a pretensious story that fails to deliver, and it's over in ~ 6 hours.  Get it when it's on a cheap sale.

For fans of both Metroid-vania style games and permadeath rpgs with persistent progress,  this game is absolutely fantastic! It blends to the two concepts flawlessly.
Reminiscent of Symphony of the Night, though with a more comical, light-hearted narrative, Rogue Legacy is a wonderful indie title, and clearly a labor of love.
I strongly recommend.

There have been a lot of games lately that have been bland in times of their colour scheme so Rogue Legacy is definitely a welcome change. It's a good old side scroller with a bit of bullet hell sprinkled in and involves a randomly generated castle so you'll never (If not rarely) go through the same rooms twice to build up the amount of gold you have which can be spent on armor, adding to your mansion (Aka your HP up, MANA up, Strength and so on. Usual rpg type elements) and paying a certain person to lock down the castle after you have died (In case you want to go straight to a boss without having to look for it). Of course you will die. It's just a matter of when you die and when you do, you better hope you racked up a lot of gold because you'll need it. It has a very dark souls feel to it where even enemies you can now breeze through will mess you up if you underestimate them. Upgrading yourself is key to taking on the bosses.
I definitely recommend this game.
Fun game, I suggest it.

I bought this game thinking it would just entertain me for a couple hours since it was on sale for a pretty good deal, but I actually ended up really liking it. Rogue Legacy does a really good job of creating a challenging game, but not making it so challenging to the point where you want to punch your computer screen. It can be hard starting out but once you start clearing out the castle more and beating a boss it feels so rewarding. There are so many diverse classes to choose from that all have a different take on your approach at the castle keeping the game fresh and not just doing the same thing over and over again. It is also very amusing with the different disabilities like IBS or Color blindness. If you would want a platforming beat em up rpg style game then this game would fit your needs very well and I would highly recommend it.

Pros

+Customisablility of Max and your vehicle
+Beautiful enviroment to explore
Cons
-Some people can find it repetitive exploring the plains of a desert all the time
Overall I would recommend this game to anyone, I for one don't enjoy racing game or car games in general, but Mad Max feels different, maybe because of the added fighting and exploration but I don't know, I just really enjoy it.

Is Mad Max a perfect game? No. Is it a fun game? Most definitely.
If you enjoy driving around the desert and blowing stuff up, you'll enjoy this game. It also has an Arkham-style ground combat but with stricter timing and spacing and absolutely brutal animations. Upgrading your car feels like natural progression and as a result is very satisfying.
However, the game, like most open world games, has a lot of collectibles and checklists. If you don't enjoy that, it will hinder your enjoyment of the game. There is a bit of variety in the various activities, though, meaning you can extend your playing time. There's also a lot you can do while driving around, or you can simply ignore it.
Finally, this game works like a charm on PC. Couldn't ask for a better port.
Overall, I found this game to be quite enjoyable. If you like the idea of a post-apoctolyptic driving combat game, this is for you. If you hate open world games and collecting stuff, I'd stay away.

Undertale is a fun and unique RPG game that allows the player to do something that most games do not.
Have you ever wondered, why in many RPG games, you have to kill everything, and you have to seek getting as much EXP as possible? Why do you have to kill everything? What if you could befriend them, and learn their story, instead?
In Undertale, you play as a human who has fallen into Mt. Ebott, somehow surviving their fall by falling into a bed of golden flowers. During this time, tensions are strong between humans and monsters, as the humans and monsters are involved in a war. The humans had sealed the monsters into the underground, trapping them with a barrier.
As you explore the Underground, and as you progress in the game, you will meet new friends, new enemies. you will meet many different kinds of monsters. Some hostile at first, and some friendly, each monster in Undertale seems to have a different and unique personality.
You can be either a pacifist or genocidal, but I prefer only taking the pacifist route, as the pacifist route of the game is heartwarming and uplifting, and it allows me to hear more about the Monsters and their perspectives and their story in Undertale, and also, well... if you're like me, you'll get quite attached to these charming characters. (I have played the Pacifist route four times, and the game is still super fun and charming!)
In Undertale, as you explore, you will also see all sorts of cool environments, and hear the game's acclaimed great soundtrack.
Every character in Undertale has their strengths and weaknesses, and their flaws and their good traits, too. With their unique and varied personalities, many of Undertale's characters have become relatable for quite a few fans of the game, and I admire games that put so much care and attention into its characters and its writing.
Although the game can be creepy and foreboding at times, the game also has many moments of humor, fun, and silliness!
Undertale, in its pacifist run, has been one of the funniest, most uplifting, emotional, and heartwarming games that I have ever played. I have no complaints about the game, and I would encourage anyone to play! Don't mind the fan-base, and give Undertale a try. In my eyes, it is essential that you go into this game blind, and not let yourself uncover spoilers, as the game has its share of surprises and events! ^.^

A rare occurence of a state where, so far, I can state that the 'sequel/prequel' took the lessons from the previous iteration, and improved upon it. The storyline, based on your choices is so much smoother. I played through The Walking Dead extensively, and the original puts what I thought was a great entry into this genre and puts it into the dust. The game takes that even further, polishing the overarching experience, making almost every social option feel like it has meaning (versus one options is 'perfect', while the rest feel hastily added in for 'fluff'). If that wasn't enough, they iterated on the social options, creating a game of the 'challenging. As Chole, we all know how aggressively she challenged anyone and anything she didn't with which she didn't agree. In this game, you have the option, during certain conversations, where you can basically begin a social challenge with the other character, choosing responses that could win or lose you points torwards a successful verbal challenge. Also, to add onto that, while the 'best' choice is minorly obvious to me, it definitely doesn't feel like it's HEY PICK ME, and it does feel like they did a great job in making at least 2/3 options feel viable on a majority of the conversations. This particular aspect could use a little polish, but for a first iteration this is definitely incredible, worth the purchase!

I was so wrapped up in the game and so utterly convinced that i was still playing LiS 1, that It felt wrong.
But it was oh so good.
The acting is mostly great
The voice actors, while not all are the same, were on point...especially Chloe's
There are plenty of "have a seat and think" moments that feel natural, as well as tagging opportunities that are used to mimic Max's -take a photo- moments.
You get options on what to write in graffiti and they are all hilarious.
You see some familiar faces, which made me especially giddy.
Of course the music is on another level. You cant have LiS without a stellar soundtrack, and this soundtrack is exactly that. It's themed around Chloe's music choice, which is refreshingly more punk instead of Max's Indie scene music.
It all works. It works so incredibly well that you would think you were playing Season 2.
Just play it already.

Mad Max reviews panned its story for being practically non existent. Fair enough, its not that complex. Max has his car stolen and is left for dead, he is assisted by a Blackfinger who has been spying on him and admires his driving skills. Max wants his car back but is told its been destroyed for parts so they go on a quest to build the greatest four wheeled death machine ever, he grudgingly helps some people and alot of people die. Some of them, for me, very important. I'll get to that later though.
It took me forty-five hours to get the V8, partially through the gated requirements to get to that point of the story but mainly due to the fact of the sheer enjoyment derived from the vehicular combat, or personal conveyance jousting if you will. The fisticuffs aren't up to the Arkham games standard but once Max's skills are fully upgraded it's sufficient enough to provide a disparate experience that can be enjoyed if you're into the type of videogame violence that is straight forward and brutal rather than flamboyant but effective. I'm sorry, I got tired of dancing around bad guys with the skills of a Ninja and the finesse of a ballerina in the Arkham games eventually.
The vehicular combat is the meat and bones of this game and it deserves recognition as probably the best exponent of this style of gameplay I have ever experienced. There are four vehicular weapons employing projectile, explosive, incendiary and breaching mechanics. The shotgun speaks for itself as the projectile weapon and the Thunderpoon as seen in Fury Road should be self explanatory. The Sideburners are as you would expect jets of flame that spout from the side of the car setting adjacent cars on fire and the Harpoon is where the breaching mechanic comes into play once you start going up against armoured vehicles so you can remove the hardened layer before tearing the soft insides out. The soft insides being the War Boys or Buzzards by the way. Adding to those are the vehicle armour which is exceedingly useful, the ramming grill which you can use to bludgeon other vehicles to death and the Rim spikes that tear through armour and the chassis eventually. You can even chain sideswipes for extra damage and there's the sniper rifle for long range fun,
Both the Magnum Opus and Max can be upgraded, with Max it's straight forward, the more upgrades the more formidable he becomes. Where as the Magnum Opus can be augmented to increase its effectiveness in varied situations or playstyles aswell as six different chassis if you have The Ripper DLC to get a desired look but that would take a further three to six paragraphs to go through so I'll not get into that because I want to get back to the story or in some peoples eyes the lack there of. Yes, this game is full of busy work so to speak, whether it be tearing down scarecrows, clearing out camps, murdering snipers in your own personal way, defeating convoys in order to lower threat within an area and upgrading Strongholds to reap the benefits. All of these take time and lead to unlocks, story progression or both. Each can also lead to emergent gameplay as you head to an objective and something happens like getting attacked by a war party and so on, I guess the thrill for me was in the hunt and the reward was provided by explosions, car wrecks and scrap. Some of these objectives and unlocks are related to story missions and wasteland missions aswell but if you go straight for the story missions you'll get the same outcome experienced from Fallout 3 in that playstyle. Yes, you'll have to do some sub-missions in order to get to the next story based mission but you'll miss out on so much of the world and character building context so that it all falls flat.
Unfortunately, Mad Max doesn't have the depth of Fallout 3 when it comes to the world creating aspects provided by the terminals and the characteristics of each vault. It's a massive open wasteland and it looks unique through its portrayal of desolation. However, it steps above Fallout 3 by providing one instance I didn't see coming but looking back now I should've. Some eighty-five hours into my play time I completed Act 4 and was met with something as tangible as having to kill The Boss in Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater, for all its critic espoused deficiencies its managed to portray characters I actually cared about. Maybe it's just me but the attention paid to the portrayal of the characters physical movements in cutscenes and the combination of having great voice acting meant that I now feel a need to murder Scrotus that has no relation to the Interceptor anymore.
I still haven't finished the game and I'm looking forward to an awful lot more hours stalking the wasteland of Australia.
To possibly be continued....

So, where do I begin? I'm a really big fan of Mad Max movies, especially the classic first and second movie. Although, the game and the new movie gives us a little bit of a different view of things, this is a welcomed change. The game itself has an astonishing atmosphere. The looks of the wasteland, the background music and the kinda sorta big world makes even roaming interesting.
The tasks on the other hand getting a bit repetitive after an amount of time. Clearing out all camps, tearing down all the scarecrows and such can get a bit boring. The story and side missions (called wasteland missions) are fun. The only downside is there not much of them.
Customizing the car to your style of playing is a nice addition. In early game I thought getting more armor and bigger fenders are the key. Then I realized speed and firepower is everything. You can also choose from various car bodies and paintjobs. So the car can and will look anyway you want. Well, in it's boundaries at least.
The game can be completed on a basic level in 35 hours and to max it out with Max (pun intended) you'll have it to work with it around 50 to 60 hours I think. It's worth it. You can fool around with the photography mode, which is a really cool screenshot maker and editor, that gives at least +50% fun factor to the game.
Now I wait for the Bullet Farm DLC and hopefully some kind of multiplayer combat arena, at least a destruction derby. Too bad it's not gonna happen.
PROS:
- Large, fully discoverable world
- Widescale customization of your ride (and Max himself)
- Interesting missions and tasks
- Awesome looking wasteland with all of it's detail
CONS:
- After a time some tasks can get a bit repetitive
- Minor bugs, nothing game breaking
- Storyline is short, way too short

Initially when you start out the game, there are not a lot of ways to collect scrap metal, which is used to upgrade your car and character. There are these "scavenging points" you can go to, however these points will often only give you like 10 scrap. However, once you start taking over camps and embracing the storms, scrap starts rolling in. So this is quite a slow start in scrap collecting when you just started the game.

On foot is pretty much the Arkham style combat. Only without the range of weapons to use. You use your fists, and maybe and occasional melee weapon, and just mash M1 and an occasional M2 to parry. While the hits does feel like you are bashing your enemy's skull in,  and there are upgrades to give marginally more variety (press E to shatter the shield) it does get stale after awhile.
These are the bane of my existence. This is one of the many types of "camps" you can find in Mad Max, and are supposed to clear out. You are supposed to find around 6-9 transfer tanks within the camp and explode them. However, these are not marked unless you are quite close to it, so you can be assured that you will be wandering around the camp, trying to find this one last tank to blow up. It is especially worse if it is at night, and the camp is like a damn maze. (spent about half an hour wandering around in one until I said "♥♥♥♥ it" and looked at a playthrough, only to know it is hidden behind a god damn white fence.
This entire game is almost like Far Cry 3 and Batman Arkham City had a baby, only with a badass car and badass car fights. Basically you are supposed to clear these "camps" to lower the threat of the enemy in your ally's territory. There are these hot air balloons that serve as vantage points where you can see the entire region. Is this the new meta now? Vantage points and liberating camps?
My review for this one is pretty mixed, although the fantastic vehicle combat has me recommending it. It DOES get repetitive after awhile, So taking breaks between each session of Mad Max is a necessity or it just gets so mind numbingly dull.

You might have a look at the screenshots or watch a gameplay video and think "Man, that game must be incredibly dull and boring".
And you wouldn't be wrong, at first. Yet, that is also what makes it so relaxing. If you've ever driven for a long time and ended up "in the zone", where you're basically on auto-pilot, calm and focused, this is the kind of feeling you'll also get while playing this. That doesn't mean there is nothing to do, but once you're immersed, it's hard to get out.
Of course, you can also play the game like a, well, game, and micro-manage every aspect of your growing empire, hiring drivers, upgrading your truck, taking the best paying jobs, leveling up, and all that. I'm sure some people enjoy playing it that way. But personally I just like taking a random job that will make me drive across a few countries and enjoy the ride.
You should definitely not expect too much from ETS 2, though. In the end, the gameplay is somewhat limited (there's not much else to do other than drive a truck, after all), the jobs can get repetitive, and the map could use some more variety and details. But if you enjoy driving because it's relaxing, ETS 2 can be a good way to experience that at home.
On a side note, there's a multiplayer mod that's fairly advanced. While it lacks some features (no cars on the road, no synchronization of stoplights), it gives the experience a whole new aspect. Honking at another player going the other way to greet them in the middle of a snowy road at night gives a pretty unique feeling. Also, traffic jams are a sight to see.
Very good game, but I don't recommend driving like it's GTA if you want to really do well

Few studios are bold enough to challenge the conventions of entire genre with one game. Yager was. Spec Ops: The Line is a frighteningly well-constructed blend of narrative and gameplay that towers over the rest of its genre, and a game that everyone who cares about storytelling in video games must play. You will never look at military shooters the same way again.

While the third person shooter setup is clunky, and the cover mechanic can be utterly frustrating at times, the game itself is amazingly well written. It provides not only questions about shooters as a gamer, but takes a critical look at the US' involvement in conflicts, with a healthy dose of skepticism and lets you make the decisions. In short: it could be better, but this is what Vidja Gaems should aspire to do.
An unique shooter experience; highly disturbing and memorable.

Do you feel like a hero yet?
This is the fundamental question this game asks. How far can you descend into abject evil while still being convinced that you're the good guy? How far do you trust yourself to have the right information when making moral choices? How can you even define morality in the pure horror that is war? This game asks these questions and delivers a truly horrific experience.
You won't enjoy this. If you do, there is something wrong with you. But I challenge you to ask - at what point do you cross the line that's in this game's title? If you do everything accurding to your morals, how long do you really hold out?
This is a game that could well trigger a revolution in game writing. If only more play it.
