Well, here's a real pickle.
Spec Ops: The Line is a very, very mature game. And this shows on several levels.
Let's start with gameplay. In it's essence, this is a third person shooter with a cover system. A large amount of the weapons have an alternate state. For example, the M4A1 carbine has a silencer you can equip, while the AK47 can switch from full-auto to burst shot.
This here is where I want to warn you. In theory, there are about three to four moments where you'll really want a silenced weapon. But in general, you'll always have an oppertunity to get your hands on one before such a moment arrives. So holding on to a weapon simply because of it's silencer is usually a waste.
You are also restricted to two weapons, sidearm or not. So choose wisely.
The variety is not bad, but holding on to a specific weapon because you like it may throw up issues if you are playing on Veteran. (the toughest difficulty that you don't need to unlock)
Ammo of different weapons are not interchangable, so opting for a lesser weapon because of it's frequency may be advisable.
The story is...unusual. Or should I say, unexpected? Whatever you do, don't spoil it for yourself through Youtube. This is one story you'll want to experience unspoiled. If you want my guarantee that it will surprise you until the very end, rest assure. It will. I did not expect it, and I catch on to cliches pretty fast.
Moral choices are present, but not always as obvious. This game doesn't give you a left or right choice, or an A or B choice in matters. Action and inaction are the choices you can make, and they will be noticed and mildly felt. I myself, even felt guilty for a moment.
Other reviewers didn't lie. Spec Ops: The Line will make you question your allegiance, your perspective and your morality. At several points you'll question whether you really are a savior or actually the villain. Even the tips in the loading screens are genius and, at times, surprisingly offensive (in a non-insulting way) when they are appropriate.
This is something you must experience in person, and any other media other than the game can not provide you the experience. Don't say I didn't warn you.
Overall, the gameplay is tough and challenging, maybe even infuriating at times. What I mean by that is... when you, storywise, are facing impossible odds, the game will very much make you feel that. But, if you pay enough attention to the lessons learned (take cover, you moron!) and your teammates, you may very well overcome these impossible odds with a sense of accomplishment.
The hints your teammates give are sensible but scripted. So they usually are at moments when the designers feel you'll probably need that vital hint. It's not always easy to realize that you should flank or circle a turret pinning you down.
In single-player, you can only give two commands to your teammates, and that is to attack the enemy your reticule is aimed on (they'll light up red). The other being, if the enemy is pinning you down with heavy fire, you'll get an option to have them throw a flashbang.
Their AI isn't the smartest, a still living curse in videogames, but their not too foolish either. Just get used to their quirks, and they shouldn't dash ahead in enemy fire. Accustom to them as they get accustomed to you.
Not much to say other than to heartily recommend the game. It's an experience that manages to tell a story well, I have to say. I finished the game in one go, because it was hard for me to let go of it.

The Dubai environments look original and interesting, especially some of the luxury hotels. The character models are excellent. Sound design pretty good. Gunplay works fine (I played it on easy). General atmosphere... almost surreal, shootouts playing out to distorted rock tracks. The story, and what we're supposed to take from it... whatever, man. Modern Warfare 1, or for that matter the first Call Of Duty, had more useful things to say about war than this. Overall, not sure I would recommend, certainly not at the full price I paid for it. And reading the credits... jesus, really, it took that many people to make this? AAA development has gone crazy.

A rare occurence of a state where, so far, I can state that the 'sequel/prequel' took the lessons from the previous iteration, and improved upon it. The storyline, based on your choices is so much smoother. I played through The Walking Dead extensively, and the original puts what I thought was a great entry into this genre and puts it into the dust. The game takes that even further, polishing the overarching experience, making almost every social option feel like it has meaning (versus one options is 'perfect', while the rest feel hastily added in for 'fluff'). If that wasn't enough, they iterated on the social options, creating a game of the 'challenging. As Chole, we all know how aggressively she challenged anyone and anything she didn't with which she didn't agree. In this game, you have the option, during certain conversations, where you can basically begin a social challenge with the other character, choosing responses that could win or lose you points torwards a successful verbal challenge. Also, to add onto that, while the 'best' choice is minorly obvious to me, it definitely doesn't feel like it's HEY PICK ME, and it does feel like they did a great job in making at least 2/3 options feel viable on a majority of the conversations. This particular aspect could use a little polish, but for a first iteration this is definitely incredible, worth the purchase!

Mad Max is a solid open world experience, creating an immersive environment through ambient sounds and visuals from the Avalanche Engine (notably found in Just Cause series). A pre-release review labelled the game as "exhilarating, fast, violent, and fun" and I'd have to agree to that. The game puts heavy emphasis on vehicular combat, in which around 60% of the game requires the player to drive their car to fight against enemies.
After a global collapse of civilisation and society, followed by an intense nuclear skirmish, Max's journey to the Plains of Silence takes an unexpected turn when a group of War Boys (run by warlord Scabrous Scrotus, psychotic son of Immortan Joe) run him off the road and steal his clothes, his supplies, his weapons, and his car before leaving him to rot in the desert sun. Traversing the wasteland in search of his prized Interceptor, Max meets a hunchback mechanic named Chumbucket, an overzealous individual that's hell bent on crafting the perfect vehicle, the Magnum Opus. After giving Max hope of exacting vengeance on Scrotus, the two form an unlikely partnership and set out in the base of the Opus in search of food, water, allies, upgrades, and redemption in a world devoid of sanity.
The two downfalls to the game are the controls and the fighting capabilities. Controls make the game feel cheap, constant big HUD reminders for which key to press, and normally you have to
the button down rather then just press it. It doesn't seem a huge issue, but gets incredibly frustrating the more you invest time into the game. Fighting capabilities are somewhat slim, with just a couple different buttons to use to fight and defend Max. I was really hoping for something along the lines of the Batman series in terms of combat mechanics, but was mildly disappointed. However, the violent nature of Max and his different styles of taking out opponents somewhat makes up for this.
On a huge plus, this game makes you feel like the wasteland is alive. Constant threats driving around and notorious weather changes can drastically alter your initial plans. Its also extremely refreshing to find a game that doesn't include regenerating health, which makes scavenging for food and water supplies a nice change. The camera mode is superb and instantly reminds me of the one found in Shadow of Mordor, easily allowing you to capture your best images the way you want - with different vignettes/filters to apply and tweak your shots with. You will probably find yourself continuously busy in Mad Max, and with that said you will more then likely be rewarded around every corner of doing so, normally in the form of scrap (the games currency used to upgrade Max, vehicles and strongholds).
Finally, the car combat is absolutely fantastic and really shines over the negative points mentioned. Numerous occasions I found myself wandering off of missions in hunt of enemies & loot. You will find yourself ramming, shooting and harpooning every vehicle/structure you find, not forgetting to mention lone snipers trying to pick you off at range. The ability to customise your vehicle (& character) to your liking is a personal favourite of mine and therefore lets you explore the wasteland as the Mad Max that you want to be. It all makes for a forward moving and overall fun experience.

Euro Truck Simulator. Three words which, in isolation, seem innocuous enough, but which when spoken in sequence can put even the most ardent gamer to sleep.
If you’re still reading this, then that means you’re still awake. You passed the first test.
If my tone seems cruel and mocking now, that’s because when I first heard about ETS, I did cruelly mock it. Trucks? Boring. Simulation games? Boring. That’s what my STUPID brain thought when I read the title, and it relayed the various commands so that I might signify my condescension. Fake yawn, patronising shake of the head, roll the eyes. Fart a little bit - my bottom pleading to be involved somehow.
And so I ignored it, for about a year after its release, until I read an article (I forget where, or by whom) which said that even though it sounds like it’ll be boring, it actually isn’t.
It is. It is a bit boring, but in a
.
First, the meat. ETS is a game where you drive a truck and deliver goods around Europe. You start off doing freight jobs in loaned trucks, but will eventually earn enough to buy your own, which is when you’ll see real money coming in. You’ll continue earning money until you can rent premises, hire people and buy more trucks for them to deliver goods in, earning you even more money. That’s it, really. There’s not much to the business management side of things, so once you’ve got your own truck you could just ignore that aspect entirely. Control options are fairly customisable, which is nice. I play on a 360 pad (very “casual mode”) with all the assists turned on and automatic gearing and whatnot, and it’s lovely. Relaxing. But if you want you can have 50 different buttons on the keyboard devoted to different functions and really take control. The holy grail, of course, is playing with a wheel and decent pedals, but I doubt I’ll ever get the chance to try that out.
After I played the demo until about 3am, I decided to buy ETS. I couldn’t say that I had had a lot of fun, precisely, or that I’d learned anything about what it is to drive a truck, or any other aspect of trucking. But as the rain fell upon my cab in Calais, and the wipers swished hypnotically back and forth, back and forth, I had felt tremendously involved. In that time I’d gone from Manchester to London, then all the way to Scotland on some slow, winding roads, and then belted back down south and across the channel. I’d signalled properly, watched my speed, and stopped at the lights like a good boy. Is this even a proper
? Where are the zombies?
Often, when we talk about games we talk about atmosphere. How does this game conjure the atmosphere or exploring an underwater wreck, or how does this one make you feel like you’re in the middle of a war, running for your life. ETS has an amazing amount of atmosphere: you really will feel like you’re sat in traffic on the M56. And if that sounds mundane, fair enough, it probably is, but somehow this game seeps into your pores and you start to care. You want to make your delivery on time, and you want your cargo to be undamaged, and you want to ease the trailer into the bay like a boss (your first time around this will seem impossible). It can be tremendously satisfying to get things right, and very stressful when things start to go wrong. I remember driving past my exit somewhere in Germany and having to take a huge detour. Pressed for time and with my truck running on fumes, I started driving faster, more recklessly. That job cost me a lot of money, and in real life, would have earned me some serious jail time.
Speaking of jail time, the way fines and penalties are handled in this game is a little odd. There are no rozzers to speak of, and when you, for example, hit another car or run a red light you will automagically be fined a set amount of money, curse under your breath and continue on your way. That’s it. It’s a bit disappointing to me that even if you careen into a mini at 100mph, there will be no real negative consequence to that. A small fine, that’s it. Worse still is the infuriating way speed cameras are handled. If you’re doing 31 in a 30 zone as you pass one, you’ll get a fine. Shouldn’t there be a bit of leeway, like in real life? I’m not sure what the game is “simulating” in that situation.
The AI in this game is hilarious at times, too. I remember once a car flashed me to let me out of a busy junction, and I thought that was great. It didn’t seem like a scripted response at all, and I honked my horn in approval. That’s only even happened once in about 60 hours. More often than not you’ll see drivers stopping dead on the sliproad for no reason, or entering a roundabout in the wrong lane at the wrong time as you pull 22 tons of furniture in their path. I remember one particularly determined driver who got himself wedged under my trailer as he tried to change lanes. I got a big “collision” fine for no reason, and he put his hazards on, pointlessly. I’d like to say this stuff is rare, but usually you’ll see some crazy AI behaviour on every job you take.
Look, I love this game. It’s what I love to play when I want to unwind. Undeniably, it is repetitive. Even if you’re going somewhere new - and on a map this size you often are - you’re still essentially going through the motions. But, like taking a big dump, these motions are very satisfying, and the odd glitches and quirks of the AI add to the charm somehow. It’s a big achievement that a simulation game, such as it is, has managed to find quite so broad an audience. Give the generous demo a try, and I think you’ll soon be seduced by its shiny, chrome encrusted charms.

Few studios are bold enough to challenge the conventions of entire genre with one game. Yager was. Spec Ops: The Line is a frighteningly well-constructed blend of narrative and gameplay that towers over the rest of its genre, and a game that everyone who cares about storytelling in video games must play. You will never look at military shooters the same way again.

While the third person shooter setup is clunky, and the cover mechanic can be utterly frustrating at times, the game itself is amazingly well written. It provides not only questions about shooters as a gamer, but takes a critical look at the US' involvement in conflicts, with a healthy dose of skepticism and lets you make the decisions. In short: it could be better, but this is what Vidja Gaems should aspire to do.
An unique shooter experience; highly disturbing and memorable.

Do you feel like a hero yet?
This is the fundamental question this game asks. How far can you descend into abject evil while still being convinced that you're the good guy? How far do you trust yourself to have the right information when making moral choices? How can you even define morality in the pure horror that is war? This game asks these questions and delivers a truly horrific experience.
You won't enjoy this. If you do, there is something wrong with you. But I challenge you to ask - at what point do you cross the line that's in this game's title? If you do everything accurding to your morals, how long do you really hold out?
This is a game that could well trigger a revolution in game writing. If only more play it.

Well, here's a real pickle.
Spec Ops: The Line is a very, very mature game. And this shows on several levels.
Let's start with gameplay. In it's essence, this is a third person shooter with a cover system. A large amount of the weapons have an alternate state. For example, the M4A1 carbine has a silencer you can equip, while the AK47 can switch from full-auto to burst shot.
This here is where I want to warn you. In theory, there are about three to four moments where you'll really want a silenced weapon. But in general, you'll always have an oppertunity to get your hands on one before such a moment arrives. So holding on to a weapon simply because of it's silencer is usually a waste.
You are also restricted to two weapons, sidearm or not. So choose wisely.
The variety is not bad, but holding on to a specific weapon because you like it may throw up issues if you are playing on Veteran. (the toughest difficulty that you don't need to unlock)
Ammo of different weapons are not interchangable, so opting for a lesser weapon because of it's frequency may be advisable.
The story is...unusual. Or should I say, unexpected? Whatever you do, don't spoil it for yourself through Youtube. This is one story you'll want to experience unspoiled. If you want my guarantee that it will surprise you until the very end, rest assure. It will. I did not expect it, and I catch on to cliches pretty fast.
Moral choices are present, but not always as obvious. This game doesn't give you a left or right choice, or an A or B choice in matters. Action and inaction are the choices you can make, and they will be noticed and mildly felt. I myself, even felt guilty for a moment.
Other reviewers didn't lie. Spec Ops: The Line will make you question your allegiance, your perspective and your morality. At several points you'll question whether you really are a savior or actually the villain. Even the tips in the loading screens are genius and, at times, surprisingly offensive (in a non-insulting way) when they are appropriate.
This is something you must experience in person, and any other media other than the game can not provide you the experience. Don't say I didn't warn you.
Overall, the gameplay is tough and challenging, maybe even infuriating at times. What I mean by that is... when you, storywise, are facing impossible odds, the game will very much make you feel that. But, if you pay enough attention to the lessons learned (take cover, you moron!) and your teammates, you may very well overcome these impossible odds with a sense of accomplishment.
The hints your teammates give are sensible but scripted. So they usually are at moments when the designers feel you'll probably need that vital hint. It's not always easy to realize that you should flank or circle a turret pinning you down.
In single-player, you can only give two commands to your teammates, and that is to attack the enemy your reticule is aimed on (they'll light up red). The other being, if the enemy is pinning you down with heavy fire, you'll get an option to have them throw a flashbang.
Their AI isn't the smartest, a still living curse in videogames, but their not too foolish either. Just get used to their quirks, and they shouldn't dash ahead in enemy fire. Accustom to them as they get accustomed to you.
Not much to say other than to heartily recommend the game. It's an experience that manages to tell a story well, I have to say. I finished the game in one go, because it was hard for me to let go of it.

The Dubai environments look original and interesting, especially some of the luxury hotels. The character models are excellent. Sound design pretty good. Gunplay works fine (I played it on easy). General atmosphere... almost surreal, shootouts playing out to distorted rock tracks. The story, and what we're supposed to take from it... whatever, man. Modern Warfare 1, or for that matter the first Call Of Duty, had more useful things to say about war than this. Overall, not sure I would recommend, certainly not at the full price I paid for it. And reading the credits... jesus, really, it took that many people to make this? AAA development has gone crazy.

A rare occurence of a state where, so far, I can state that the 'sequel/prequel' took the lessons from the previous iteration, and improved upon it. The storyline, based on your choices is so much smoother. I played through The Walking Dead extensively, and the original puts what I thought was a great entry into this genre and puts it into the dust. The game takes that even further, polishing the overarching experience, making almost every social option feel like it has meaning (versus one options is 'perfect', while the rest feel hastily added in for 'fluff'). If that wasn't enough, they iterated on the social options, creating a game of the 'challenging. As Chole, we all know how aggressively she challenged anyone and anything she didn't with which she didn't agree. In this game, you have the option, during certain conversations, where you can basically begin a social challenge with the other character, choosing responses that could win or lose you points torwards a successful verbal challenge. Also, to add onto that, while the 'best' choice is minorly obvious to me, it definitely doesn't feel like it's HEY PICK ME, and it does feel like they did a great job in making at least 2/3 options feel viable on a majority of the conversations. This particular aspect could use a little polish, but for a first iteration this is definitely incredible, worth the purchase!

Rust.... Wow. What an incredible game.
I have easily played more hours in rust than any other game I have on steam.
If you love surival, love having freedom to do whatever the heck you want to do, rust is for you.
So what's the catch?
Rust in currently at a state, which it has been for months, where playing on an official server simply is not an option.
Official servers don't have admins, and because of rust's incredibly poor in-built hacker detection/prevention, official servers are ruled by hackers.
Hackers have an endless and abundant supply of explosives as they can take down the helicopter at will. This means that no matter how much effort you put into making your base, mitigating risk of being raided by making multiple bases, you are never safe, they always have enough to not just raid your base and get your loot, but completely wipe it off the face of the map (this has happened to me multiple times).
There are thankfully a lot of servers that have admins, this means that hackers can and will get banned off of these servers. Unfortunately, as an Australian, there isn't a viable option for a monthly wipe administrated server. If you are able to dedicate a lot of time to the game, or have a very large group, playing on a fortnightly wipe or weekly wipe will generally be okay. If you don't fit into either of those two categories, you slip through the cracks. You WILL NOT last on a server like Rustraliasia, and you WILL NOT be able to play an official server for reasons outlined above.
Rust is a game that relies completely on it's community. There is no PVE, this game is all about humans players against other human players. Facepunch don't seem to recognise or care enough about this fact. Many players are being turned away from the game because they don't fit into the categories I outlined.
Facepunch if you care enough to take the time to read this review here are some EASY fixes to the problems I have outlined:
Hackers can snowball by taking heli. They take heli within what? 30 seconds of engaging it? I'm betting most damage is from a single player. I'm sure even the most experienced players are not capable of this. Why not study this and confirm this suspicion? If indeed true, why not automatically permanently ban a player who does that much damage to a heli?
A similiar story for headshots, if a player hits headshots consecutively in a fully automatic burst from range with a high recoil (or spread) gun (ak or even pump), this player should be at the very least flagged for investigation.
Yes, investigating and playing the role of admin on official servers is going to take time, resources and money. But remember, hackers spend money on their hacks and their accounts, they buy your game. If they are getting banned within 5 minutes of playing they will surely stop bothering.
If you don't want to invest the time to improve the automated hacker prevention/dectection, or don't want to invest money to do it manually with an admin... Create official servers that have play time minimums. Hackers get banned eventually (although it takes far too long), creating this extra time hurdle, maybe 250 hours, should aid in curbing this issue.

When I first heard of this game I ignored it out of
Simple. Because war shooters tend to suck. Not saying they all do, but in my eyes its sub-genre that has more generic shooters than others sub-genres. Each year new Call of Duty with minimalistic changes, yet another failed attempt to reboot Medal of Honor series...its a mess.
From my friends I heard great things about this game so I decided to pick it up and oh boy was I surprised. Fitting soundtrack, easy to use yet engaging squad command system and one thing I have been lacking lately...engaging game-play. If I were to go into graphics, which I really don't like to do because when looking at games graphics are on last place for me, BUT if I would, I would say they are beautiful.
Now you might think "fine, good shooter so what?". I will tell you "so what". This game it does something games don't tend to do so much. It tries to attack your emotions. Mind you, I most often play all sorts of games as an maniac, trying to steal everything, shoot everything, then loot the thing I shot, and then shoot it again. But this game actually made me think. And not in a good way, in an depressing way. It made me actually care about events of the game. It made me fear the monstrosities that are happening.
I am playing the game on second hardest difficulty out of four (fourth is available only after you finish the game on second hardest one), so logically I was sneaking around to not get shot in my beautiful coconut. And how I was sneaking I heard 2 soldiers talking (to not glorify the game too much, I didn't hear much dialogue between NPCs in this game). They were talking about how its actually beautiful in Dubai, when they have little peace from all the war that is going on, and how the melody of the wind remind one of the soldiers of his home. Of course then I threw an grenade and they were flying with their beautiful wind...but it got me thinking again. I had to kill them, I couldn't continue without it. And I guess that is main beauty of the game it makes you think.
tl;dr : Buy it, play it, finish it, and if you want proceed to weep after that.

The gameplay is very fun. I was hesitant to get this game after hearing that it is repetitive, but I found that I experienced none of that. The customizing of the Magnum Opus is fantastic, and I was always excited to get it upgraded further. Edit:
DayZ and PUBG are completely different. The only real similitary is that you get guns and shoot eachother on a large map.
PUBG gives you a set goal, and it does not offer anything less or more than the necessities to finish that goal. In this case, the necessities being weaponry, and armor, etc, and the goal being to win the game of battle royale. This makes development somewhat easier compared to a much more expansive game like DayZ SA.
Now DayZ on the other hand, the players get to choose their goals, either it be one of the things I mentioned, or simply killing other players for loot. This requires a lot more development to implement features to accomplish these goals.
Think of it this way;
More content = More development time
PUBG offers one objective; kill everyone and come out on top, using weapons, armor, vehicles, etc in a set amount of time, before you are forced to encounter another player.
DayZ offers many objectives; fishing, hunting, PVE, camping, etc. You can even survive by never stepping foot in a town.
How can you compare a game with one linear objective to a sandbox game where you are free to do whatever, when only a few aspects of each games are the same?
TL;DR 2: PUBG is nowhere close to being the same as DayZ

With so many upgrades available to the player-character, a NewGame+, and "secret" bosses available, this game has tons of replay value (or at least keep-playing value).

In a sea of permadeath progression games, Rogue Legacy hits a really cool and versatile niche that both hardcore enthusiasts and newcomers can enjoy. Whichever protagonist you choose out of three randomised options, know this: you will die eventually, be it to traps, minibosses, the area-bosses or the varying fauna in any of the four zones you must explore. Fear not, however, because your family's lineage will be furthered by each respawn, and the gold you hoard on every adventure can be spent on stats and equipment improval. Every run is different, and both the personal traits of your heroes (varying from drawbacks such as myopia to perks like regaining mana from breaking miscellaneous items) and the ever-shifting dungeon architecture get randomised into interesting scenarios that demand different approaches, clever tactics and quick reflexes. Alternate boss fights, New Game+ content and hidden classes will add quite a few hours to an incredibly addictive experience coated in a toon fantasy setting that looks pretty much like a cross between Prehistorik and Castlevania.
Buy it if you:
Enjoy indie Metroidvania titles with RPG elements sewn in
Like riding the line between dying and progression
Prefer light humor and nostalgic sidescrolling misadventures to the cinematic polish of modern AAA titles
DO NOT buy it if you:
Get easily frustrated and think dodging should be done via quick-time events
Expect an elaborate narrative
Want 3D in your games

If you've ever driven for a long time and ended up "in the zone", where you're basically on auto-pilot, calm and focused, this is the kind of feeling you'll also get while playing this. That doesn't mean there is nothing to do, but once you're immersed, it's hard to get out.
Of course, you can also play the game like a, well, game, and micro-manage every aspect of your growing empire, hiring drivers, upgrading your truck, taking the best paying jobs, leveling up, and all that. I'm sure some people enjoy playing it that way. But personally I just like taking a random job that will make me drive across a few countries and enjoy the ride.
You should definitely not expect too much from ETS 2, though. In the end, the gameplay is somewhat limited (there's not much else to do other than drive a truck, after all), the jobs can get repetitive, and the map could use some more variety and details. But if you enjoy driving because it's relaxing, ETS 2 can be a good way to experience that at home.
On a side note, there's a multiplayer mod that's fairly advanced. While it lacks some features (no cars on the road, no synchronization of stoplights), it gives the experience a whole new aspect. Honking at another player going the other way to greet them in the middle of a snowy road at night gives a pretty unique feeling. Also, traffic jams are a sight to see.
Very good game, but I don't recommend driving like it's GTA if you want to really do well

After each succesfuly delivery you'll receive exp, once you level up you can upgrade one of your drivers skills (hired workers will auto choose based on the training method you pick) which vary from long haul to get even longer distances jobs, ADR training to deliver dangerous stuff like gasoline tanks or acids, fragile or high value cargos, optimize fuel spent or just in time deliveries which some of them doesn't even give you enough time to rest on the way.
The driving mechanics are very well done, but also a pain if you don't own a game wheel + pedals so i just play with keyboard and mouse and automatic transmissions, if you go too fast your cargo will shake and you might flip over, which you can solve by buying a 6 wheel truck.
There's not a lot of trucks, barely 1-2 truck variations per truck brand, altho in the shop appears to be a lot because they set presets of each, you can just pre-order a truck with the upgrades you want for less, spoiler Volvo is the best.
Achievements are quite easy to get in this game, except one or two, which you'll need going east dlc for them to increase map size and to get longer distances jobs for more money and the 2200km delivery achievement.
The AI is completely brain dead imo, i once was driving at 90km on the highway when suddenly two cars switched lanes at the same time and collided with each other, causing me to crash into them and lose a lot of money on repairs and penalties on the delivery.
Overall a good game to relax a bit.

Undertale is THE indie game. And what helps it be that is the fact that it offers an experience even AAA games cannot match. Other games from bigger teams in the same genre have not innovated or even bothered to try and tackle gameplay and story in the way Toby Fox has here with Undertale.
Soundtrack
The sound design is perhaps the best part of the game. Every peice of music is tailored to the exact moment of the game it plays in and it makes for a simply moving experience. The main theme is remixed into various versions in this game and it works beautifully. It also hepls make it that much more memorable. This is the soundtrack to destroy my old Halo 2 soundtrack CD. The only other CD I think anyone would own of video game music and be proud to rock it. It's that good people.
Gameplay
The gameplay is beyond anything I was expecting. It plays out a lot like Mother or as most people know it Earthbound. The dialoge with characters changes as the story progresses. It changes according to how you treat the characters in the game. Not only the dialoge but the music and the settings. It's ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant and beyond anything I've seen before. The fights are challenging in the way that donkey kong country is challenging. Meaning that the reason you fail although sometimes frustrating just can't be blamed on the game. You know in your heart if you die, it's your lack of execution/skill . It even goes beyond just using what has been dubbed the "bullet box" by adding the options to talk or run. Sure run isn't an exciting part of the game but the fact that it ties into the story so well and has been altered to be more than a box with a randomized chance of letting you out of a fight shows that this game is not just out to offer a single mechanic to keep you entertained for it's 8 hours. The amount of things that the creator has thought up for the game to surprise you with is absolutely ♥♥♥♥ed. From witty text when examining objects to a comment on how you decided to reload your save in order to prevent a death. From the fourth wall breaks. To the mouse. I swear I've never looked forward to saving a game more than I have in this one in my life. Every single character you run into has something interesting to say to you and the puzzles in this game, get this, are actually decently challenging!
Story
The premise of Undertale is an interesting one. Undertale takes place in the Underground, a massive subterranean cave where monsters, who once lived harmoniously with humans on the surface, have been banished after losing a war with humanity. The Underground is sealed from the surface world by an uneven magic barrier created by humanity's most powerful wizards. A human child falls into the Underground and this is where the player takes control. And from here the player goes through a rather generic story with a few twists. The thing about Undertale however is that it's more about everything else around you that supplements the story rather than the main plot points. Those just advance a simple narritive while exploring around and talking with the inhabitants clues you into a much more grandiose tale. That's the beauty though. Your interactions with the game world are just as important as the main narritive it seems. Dialogue changes everywhere based on seemingly insignificant actions. It's bloody brialliant. Either way, the Undertale is well done.
Graphics
There really isn't a reason to talk about graphics other than the fact that this game is a shining example of gameplay over graphics. It's just a big middle finger to every single dev out there that says no we want to make sure it looks good while you do it. Fair to a point, but it's that mentality that brought on a Halo title without splitscreen.
I could go on and on and on with this game to redundancy. It's one I would and do recommend to anyone I know who games. And it could be recommended and played by those who don't. It's a fantastic game. I would actually pay more money for it if I could. One of the greatest I have played in my lifetime.

In a sea of permadeath progression games, Rogue Legacy hits a really cool and versatile niche that both hardcore enthusiasts and newcomers can enjoy. Whichever protagonist you choose out of three randomised options, know this: you will die eventually, be it to traps, minibosses, the area-bosses or the varying fauna in any of the four zones you must explore. Fear not, however, because your family's lineage will be furthered by each respawn, and the gold you hoard on every adventure can be spent on stats and equipment improval. Every run is different, and both the personal traits of your heroes (varying from drawbacks such as myopia to perks like regaining mana from breaking miscellaneous items) and the ever-shifting dungeon architecture get randomised into interesting scenarios that demand different approaches, clever tactics and quick reflexes. Alternate boss fights, New Game+ content and hidden classes will add quite a few hours to an incredibly addictive experience coated in a toon fantasy setting that looks pretty much like a cross between Prehistorik and Castlevania.
Buy it if you:
Enjoy indie Metroidvania titles with RPG elements sewn in
Like riding the line between dying and progression
Prefer light humor and nostalgic sidescrolling misadventures to the cinematic polish of modern AAA titles
DO NOT buy it if you:
Get easily frustrated and think dodging should be done via quick-time events
Expect an elaborate narrative
Want 3D in your games
Timeless.

Rogue Legacy is a roguelike platformer where you play as the offspring of your previous character, with varying abilities and quirks in the hopes of conquering the castle and claiming your birthrite.
I completed Rogue Legacy, while doing a YouTube playthrough on YOGSCAST Nilesy, in around 22 hours. The game is incredibly fun and self-aware, leading to a super fun and enjoyable experience.
My favourite part of the game were the character quirks: one character may be an Endomorph, so maybe they can't be knocked back, or an Exomorph who is very likely to be knocked back, another can only see in black and white, another is a Dwarf and thus a shortened version of the others, and many, many others. The character quirks lead to immediately engaging gameplay, as every time you start the castle you are forced to play dependant on the character you have.
The seamless interaction between character quirks and skill level is perfect and balanced, leading me to consider this to be one of the best current roguelikes on the market.
The humour in the game is also fantastic and witty. The story is a little obvious and a little contrived, but the game is fully aware of the fact, and feeds off of it to deliver a poignant and satisfying conclusion.
I should add that JUST after my 22 hour completion, the developers added a major content patch which added a hell of a lot of new content, so if you're a new player there will be tonnes for you to do.
Highly recommended.

Classic FPS that can have a high entertaintement/hour value with replayable storylines, scaleable enemies, with better and better loot as you go. There are three main types of BL2 players I've seen. You have the diehard, the casual, and the barely interested. The diehards love doing the playthroughs, they love farming bosses and loot, they love the skills; they are great players and they have above 1k hours in the game, they can talk shop about this game all day but they're a dying breed because the game does have a half life for how interesting it is; the diehards will buy the game when it comes out, they don't need a steam sale, they'll buy all the DLCs and they bought TPS (the pre-sequel) for $60 the day it came out and already have 50 hours on it. The barely interested will wait for the steam sale, they'll wait for a few friends and they'll play up to level 30, maybe 60, they'll buy only the GOTY version, and theyll have 40 hours and be done with it. The hard part is figuring out if you're a casual player since you've never played the game.
The best way for a casual player to play is to select the most interesting character to you (first time favorites: commando, siren, assassin) and you play them through until you finish all the storylines, challenges, achievements, sidemission and do level 1 to 72 to op8, that will take about 200-300 hours. Then you normally don't want to do another complete playtrhough of a couple hundred hours so you get powerleveled through to op8 on the other characters and you can go through the storylines easier, you can play with the skills and see how the skills work and even more fun see how the skills work with all the loot, most likely duped loot. Most of your playtime then will be helping others get there missions done, doing raid bosses, a little farming and the game will reach its half life, that will take another few hundred hours and you'll be finished with the game.

There I was, I had just put some money onto my Steam Wallet to prepare for the amazement that is the Steam Summer Sale, I was pondering for many moments, browsing the front page. I knew I wanted a game but which game. I'm on a Mac you see so not many games are available. Prison Architect was there though. I was questioning my mate  (I later found out that he had no previous experience with the game) and he just said "If you want." I responded with, "Of course I want!" And thusly proceeded to acquire Prison Architect in the usual fashion.
I ordered a pizza and let the game download, presuming it would take my 'terrible' internet a while to download. I was surprised to find that the game was simply 150 MB in size and my 'terrible' internet was able to download it in a matter of minutes. I went onto it. Tried to change around with the settings, being in a Skype call and having the game sounds blaring into your ears wasn't the greatest thing. With that tweak well and truly sorted I moved on to play the game.
The first thing the game asked me to do was to build an execution room and I was already excited. Have you always wanted to build a room to kill all those that wronged? Then this is the game for you! Having completed the introduction I thought I was ready to move onto larger and greater things... I've never been so wrong in my life before.
I went onto load up a world in all it's default gloryness. Built the usual holding cell, office, canteen and kitchen. Proceeded to hire a warden, one million guards and two cooks. Then the normal risk prisoners arrived.
I was there in all my naivety believing the guards would able to handle these prisoners... again, I've never been so wrong in my life before.
Trying to pimp out the kitchen when a red sign pops up saying '1..2...3...4..5...6...7 prisoners escaped'. I immediately scanned the area, spotting out the escapees and bringing them back to justice. Turns out, the guards would rather fight a guy inside the holding cell as opposed to capturing those who flee. It was a dead end and I had to plow on.
In the end, I just turned out to be really bad at the game and as much as I found it difficult it truly is an enjoyable game. I do recommend you buy it this sale or if not buy it whenever.

The first hour of Rogue Legacy is frustrating. You don't have the power needed to overcome the huge amount of enemies. But when you start to learn the monsters patterns, collect gold and equip your characters, the game becomes much more enjoyable. Yes, there's permadeath here, but the gear you buy stays with you forever.
Levels are randomized, but you can lock them if you want. It's good for practice, but bad for looting, because when you "lock the castle" you need to pay a high fee, so you'll earn a lot less gold. I recommend to do this only if you found a boss area and feel confident to fight him (you can teletransport to the boss area since the beginning).
So, you might be thinking: "how I'm gonna beat all the bosses and finish the game with the same locked castle, earning almost no gold?". The answer is: thankfully, when you beat a boss, you don't need to lock the castle. The game register that you've already won that fight, even playing with different castles over and over again. With this feature, you can play with no pressure to beat all the bosses in one sitting.
All in all, if you're seeking for a great challenge and enjoy games like Castlevania and Ghouls'n Ghosts, you should play Rogue Legacy. There's a long and tough way to go, but I'm sure you'll enjoy the ride as much as I do.

Undertale is THE indie game. And what helps it be that is the fact that it offers an experience even AAA games cannot match. Other games from bigger teams in the same genre have not innovated or even bothered to try and tackle gameplay and story in the way Toby Fox has here with Undertale.
Soundtrack
The sound design is perhaps the best part of the game. Every peice of music is tailored to the exact moment of the game it plays in and it makes for a simply moving experience. The main theme is remixed into various versions in this game and it works beautifully. It also hepls make it that much more memorable. This is the soundtrack to destroy my old Halo 2 soundtrack CD. The only other CD I think anyone would own of video game music and be proud to rock it. It's that good people.
Gameplay
The gameplay is beyond anything I was expecting. It plays out a lot like Mother or as most people know it Earthbound. The dialoge with characters changes as the story progresses. It changes according to how you treat the characters in the game. Not only the dialoge but the music and the settings. It's ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant and beyond anything I've seen before. The fights are challenging in the way that donkey kong country is challenging. Meaning that the reason you fail although sometimes frustrating just can't be blamed on the game. You know in your heart if you die, it's your lack of execution/skill . It even goes beyond just using what has been dubbed the "bullet box" by adding the options to talk or run. Sure run isn't an exciting part of the game but the fact that it ties into the story so well and has been altered to be more than a box with a randomized chance of letting you out of a fight shows that this game is not just out to offer a single mechanic to keep you entertained for it's 8 hours. The amount of things that the creator has thought up for the game to surprise you with is absolutely ♥♥♥♥ed. From witty text when examining objects to a comment on how you decided to reload your save in order to prevent a death. From the fourth wall breaks. To the mouse. I swear I've never looked forward to saving a game more than I have in this one in my life. Every single character you run into has something interesting to say to you and the puzzles in this game, get this, are actually decently challenging!
Story
The premise of Undertale is an interesting one. Undertale takes place in the Underground, a massive subterranean cave where monsters, who once lived harmoniously with humans on the surface, have been banished after losing a war with humanity. The Underground is sealed from the surface world by an uneven magic barrier created by humanity's most powerful wizards. A human child falls into the Underground and this is where the player takes control. And from here the player goes through a rather generic story with a few twists. The thing about Undertale however is that it's more about everything else around you that supplements the story rather than the main plot points. Those just advance a simple narritive while exploring around and talking with the inhabitants clues you into a much more grandiose tale. That's the beauty though. Your interactions with the game world are just as important as the main narritive it seems. Dialogue changes everywhere based on seemingly insignificant actions. It's bloody brialliant. Either way, the Undertale is well done.
Graphics
There really isn't a reason to talk about graphics other than the fact that this game is a shining example of gameplay over graphics. It's just a big middle finger to every single dev out there that says no we want to make sure it looks good while you do it. Fair to a point, but it's that mentality that brought on a Halo title without splitscreen.
I could go on and on and on with this game to redundancy. It's one I would and do recommend to anyone I know who games. And it could be recommended and played by those who don't. It's a fantastic game. I would actually pay more money for it if I could. One of the greatest I have played in my lifetime.

Incredibly addictive 2D platformer with retro-style graphics, random levels and a great replay-factor. Every run of the game consists of a single life, where you make your way through a semi-randomly generated tower to hunt down a number of bosses. When you die, the world is wiped-clean (barring any bosses you've already slain) and you play your character's child - which is randomly generated from a number of entertaining traits. This makes it fun to pick your next child (you get a choice from 3 variations) - who might be a dwarf warrior, a giant mage, or an exceptionally strong rogue type.
While death is permanent, you get to spend your loot on permanent upgrades that give you a good sense of progression between runs. There are hundreds of incremental upgrades, so there is always something new to purchase and look forward to. However, you have to make sure you spend your gold before your next run, otherwise Charron will take his hefty share for letting you back into the tower. Each run typically lasts between 5 and 15 minutes, which means that it's a lot of fun to just pick up and play a few runs at any time and feel like you're making progress.
On the down-side, if you don't get hooked by the mechanics, I could see the game becomming a tad repetitive. You make your way through the same 4 regions of the tower over and over and while I found this a lot of fun, it's a little tedious given the fact that, before you buy the upgrades from dying 50 times, you are probably simply just not strong enough to take on certain bosses / regions.
Overall, this is an excellent game if you like retro-style platformers with a high-tension feel (think Ghouls and Ghosts on steroids). The graphics are colourful and fun, the audio seemed to fit and never felt out of place and, while a little on the repetitive side, the amount of variation in the characters you play, the abilities you get through the various classes and the spells you can cast - means you can easilly play this game for a few hours on end before realising the time that's slipped away!

Welp…I finished this game a long time ago. Looking back on it, I’m going to attempt to give a helpful, mostly unbiased, sorta concise review.
The Music:
I love music; I have played countless games based on hearing the soundtrack first, from SMRPG to this one (I actually heard a Megalovania cover first and really liked it). Undertale has a great mix of 8 bit and full orchestra music. Honestly, I feel like the music conveys half the emotions in the game. If you like video game/movie soundtrack music, you might want to buy the Undertale + soundtrack bundle.
The Designs:
Clever….very clever. The character designs range from cool to humorous to weird. Just look at the pictures on the store page… it’s a mix of black and white representations of characters (in battle) and more detailed sprites (in normal gameplay). Most of the backgrounds, characters, objects, etc. are pretty creative.
The Story:
I feel like this one is kinda on the border of good and ok. The story is emotion-filled and the actual ideas presented in the game are new and creative. For instance, sparing characters, exiting before saving, dying, and killing characters all have major impacts in the game. Undertale goes to great lengths to remember everything you do, including previous play-throughs. The dialog between characters and the ending of the game depend on what you do, and I enjoyed seeing a lot of the possible outcomes to each fight.
Buttttt, for all of the emotion and creativity, the story is…weird. The game breaks a lot of RPG stereotypes, but the characters themselves feel stereotypically “funny”, “bitter”, “awkward”, etc. (although some characters have a good amount of emotional depth). I also feel like the game has a bit of a creepy, sometimes annoying undertone (no pun intended), even when your character’s actions are “good.” I actually prefer some of the stories present in fan comics more so than in the game itself (but that might just be a personal preference). If you just want a good story, it’s there though.

Actual Gameplay:
I would say that this is a story-based game more than anything; if you’re looking for challenging combat or anything like that, it’s not here. If you’re new to bullet hell games, however, then the battles can be pretty interesting. It’s not your typical “hack n slash” RPG game (it’s barely an RPG actually), so I thought it was unique, but not as much emphasis is placed on battling. There are also a couple of puzzles and 6-7 dogs to keep you interested.
Game Length:
I think it took me about 6 hours to complete the first play-through, so it’s not that long. However, the game is meant to be played over at least one or two more times. I have a total of 35 hours from about four play-throughs. The game does a good job of keeping things entertaining through several play-throughs.
Overall:
It’s worth the money (it's only $10... if you really want to try it, just skip a meal at Chipotle or something). I was skeptical about buying it at first, but I'm glad that I did. Undertale has a strong emotional impact. It’s entertaining even during its awkward moments, and I think that’s what counts.

The whole retro-gaming thing is getting out of hand. I picked this up because it was only $5 on sale, and it looked like a nice casual break from other games. I immediately felt cheated. I have never wanted a refund so badly before. The feature of your descendants carrying on after you die sounded very cool, but the implementation is simply this: every time you start, you get to choose from only three characters with random traits and classes. The characters don't really have anything that ties them to the previous generation. Let's talk about the retro aspect of the game. What this means is it is very hard and repetitive. If I was playing with a controller, I would be constantly throwing it across the room. Progress is extremely slow and unrewarding. The worst part is, you cannot persistantly chip away at the game. Any progress can only be gained by massively successful rounds. This is because every time you upgrade your character, the cost increases. Combine this with the fact that every time you re-enter the castle, you forfeit all your gold. The impact of this game design choice is that you make ZERO progress over and over and over again, unless you have an amazing round. Then you are rewarded by increase perhaps one stat by 1 out of 100, or something like that. I cannot stress how much I hate this game.

On the whole, not a bad game.
Orginality is scant here, particularly if you have played any of the Batman Arkham series (not surprising as it is a WB game), although the world is much more open.
The openess does come with a downside, as sometimes it can feel that the game has, as a victim of it's open world design, been forced (almost slavishly) to have the need to travel great distances to accomplish a task. I'd suggest getting a few of the fast travel points unlocked as you will benefit greatly from them, especially during the latter stages.
The missions are engaging, but can be repetitive, and once you have upgraded Max to the...max....you will find it incredibly easy to beat even large numbers of enemy. A small tip is to bust as many camps as you can early on so that the scrap tribute will mount up quickly. Also, choose at least one stronghold to upgrade completely to help you out if you are low on fuel/ammo/health/water etc.
Without wishing to give too much away, the ending is a little depressing. However I really would have much preferred to fight Scrotus hand to hand in the final battle.
A small, but annoying (for me) part was when you fast travel, you always end up with the magnum opus. Don't fast travel with scrap cars from camps, or you will NOT get the scrap. This goes for archangels as well. You don't fast travel with an archangel, even if you were in it when you entered fast travel.
On the whole, the game is good, and there is enough left after you finish the main story to keep you occupied for a while.

2. PC porting is just fantastic. I don;t have decent gaming PC but Mad Max was smooth as ♥♥♥♥ and looked gorgeous. The best optimization I've seen so far.

Cons:
1. Story missions are good, but there are not many. Game play can be stretched out quite longer if you play those meaningless missions, but they are not interesting after doing them for a couple of hours.
2. Too easy. Combat mechanic has potential to be "simple to learn, difficult to master". However, there is very little reason to master it. Only few Stank Gum camp missions were actually challenging.
3. Collecting scraps is painful. They should've made collecting animation nuch shorter.

Spec Ops would likely be regarded as a fairly average 3rd-person cover-based shooter in a world that's already inundated with the genre, if raw gameplay were the only factor. The real draw is the decidedly grim and muddled story, which isn't quite Apocalypse Now: The Video Game, but it's still surprising that the game got made at all. Each mission strings the player along to a series of choices, simple to execute but  damning in consequence. These crucial moments feel organic, urgent, unlike other games that freeze the action and give you a button prompt that basically says "Shoot this guy, or don't." Spec Ops is worth playing just to witness these threads come together, and the characters' responsiveness to their bad situation as it continues to worsen. I hope more games incorporate this kind of storytelling in the future.

I didn't really mind this as it kept things engaging but unfortunately the level design is so bland and AI is so awfully predictable that after a few camp clears it's just not fun anymore.
Also... story just plain sucks. You feel like nothing is really happening half the time other than the constant reminder to make your car better... simpleminded got to make it better to get back at the warlord. However, towards the end things kind of pick up and some degree of character development happens. You become invested in them but it's already the end, credits roll.
While I didn't mind that the plot was directly linked to your enjoyment of your car, I did mind there was a lot of upgrade gating. 80% of the upgrades are tied into you reducing the threat level of various zones in the Mad Max world. The camps are the worst repetition for this because A) you get out of your awesome car B) combat is snooze after a handful of times and you got like 40+ camps to clear! Destroying scarecrows, sniper nests, and convoys are probably the most fun objectives to reduce threat but don't provide as much. I have around fourty some odd hours into the game and it was mostly spent in the time sink of trying to get upgrades for my damned Magnum Opus.
You'll love the environment and driving portion though. Man I can't forget the sandstorm sequence from Fury Road and it was crazy to not only witness it in the game but to be in one! You just got to hunker down and hope the debris doesn't kill you because the lightning storms might lol. Driving around is fun as hell. The V6/V8 engine sounds viseral and you can't help wanting to rock out while pedaling to the metal, I was super impressed! Combine that with the heat haze effect in your interceptor cruising in the desert with buzzards on your tail... now thats immersion.
Ultimately a lot of Mad Max is forgettable shallow experience with exception to the driving. If you're a big fan of the franchise and new to open world games then you'll have a blast. For veterans, you should pass.

Spec Ops would likely be regarded as a fairly average 3rd-person cover-based shooter in a world that's already inundated with the genre, if raw gameplay were the only factor. The real draw is the decidedly grim and muddled story, which isn't quite Apocalypse Now: The Video Game, but it's still surprising that the game got made at all. Each mission strings the player along to a series of choices, simple to execute but  damning in consequence. These crucial moments feel organic, urgent, unlike other games that freeze the action and give you a button prompt that basically says "Shoot this guy, or don't." Spec Ops is worth playing just to witness these threads come together, and the characters' responsiveness to their bad situation as it continues to worsen. I hope more games incorporate this kind of storytelling in the future.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is an incredible game. That's right, a simulator that is worthy of being called a game. It is still a simulator, and quite a good one at that, but unlike many other simulator "games" out there, this one is enjoyable. It creates a very satisfying experience out of something that you would at first believe to be boring.
First of all, the game looks good. The sounds compliment this and, if you're getting tired of listening to the roar of your engine as you roam the roads of Europe, you can play your own MP3s from your computer through the in-game radio. Even better is the ability to stream internet radio stations through the in-game radio, which, when I first discovered, I was very pleased about it!
So what do you do in ETS2 exactly? Well, you can start off working for other trucking copmanies, taking valuable cargo from point A to point B, earning some money and experience points along the way. Once you start earning enough money (or decide to get a loan from the bank), you can then purchase your own truck instead of using other people's vehicles, allowing you to earn more money and even more EXP. EXP is what allows you to "level up", which gives you skill points that you can allocate to various different skills, e.g. improved eco-driving or being able to take jobs that involve fragile cargo (better-paying jobs).
With the rest of the money you make, you can buy more trucks, upgrades/paint for said trucks, and most importantly employees who will work for you (and garages to place them in). Soon enough, you will be running the best trucking business in all of Europe, which is ultimately the aim of this game (to build up your business and have fun doing it!).
But what is the actual driving aspect of the game like, you might ask? Well, as I said before, you drive cargo from point A to point B and earn money whilst doing so. This may sound tedious and boring, but what makes it such a grand experience is a) the scenery (as you drive through a scaled-down version of Europe), b) the excellent vehicle physics and mechanics, and c) what you do with it all: are you going to play seriously, making sure to follow all road rules and never commit a speeding offence? Or are you just going to play casually, listening to your internet radio stations and free-roaming Europe without any cargo at all? Or perhaps you'd like to muck around with some friends on multiplayer (requires a mod), crashing into things and having fun doing it?
ETS2 is truly a magnificent experience that seems to offer little yet offers so much! I thoroughly enjoyed my time with this game and will most likely revisit it in the future. All I can say is this: if you want to drive around Europe in a truck, earning money and buying trucks as you do so, this is the game for you. And if you're skeptical, trust me, I was too. After playing it, though, I can tell you I had no regrets with it.
Enjoy! :)

This game is a gem which unfortunately has to tumble through the simulation genre with the rest of the ordinary boring rocks. Many other simulation games out there give the genre a bad name, but this game is truly incredible not only to the genre of simulation but to gaming as a whole.
This relaxing, addictive game is for anybody. Simulator enthusiasts. Gamers. Children. Adults. Men. Women. Anyone. It's potentially captivating to such a wide range of an audience, that it's definitely worth downloading the demo to see if you like the flesh of the game. And if (when) you do like it, you can buy the meat.
Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a game where you lead a trucking company, at first making money fairly slowly doing freelance jobs for random people (using their trucks) until you can afford your own truck. The quickjob part of the game shows you the flesh of what's going to come within the rest of the game, it lets you get to grips with the mechanics of driving the trucks in game, and gives you a general feel as to what you're going to be doing.
When you get your own truck, the real meat of the game starts to show as you can make much more money from jobs which can then be used to do a series of things:
The main things here are buying more trucks and hiring the workers. Once you've hired your first worker, you realise "Actually, this is turning into a company, old turbo Joe himself is under my command in his fresh little pimp mobile. I'm gonna make the big bucks."
And that's how it goes, you do more jobs, get more money, buy more trucks, hire Turbo Joe and Rod Stewart to drive your trucks, and voila, you have an exponentially growing company.
There is also a leveling system in the game, which gives you a skill point for each level. This leveling system allows your to get longer distance jobs, hold fragile cargos, get bonuses for driving economically, getting to your destination earlier bonuses, and other things. The leveling system is good, but it doesn't add much to the content, just allows you to make more money for each individual job.
Okay, so you don't want to splash the twenty buckaroos on Turbo Joe trucker Sim 2 because you're worried you won't find enjoyment in the game?
Here's what I'd suggest.
Play the demo for an hour or two, see if you find enjoyment in the driving mechanics of the game, if you find it satisfying to haul a load of heroin (or potatoes) across Poland. If you enjoy these two key things that make the flesh of the game, the meat of the game is going to add to the experience tenfold as it gives you big goals to go towards, but doesn't make them impossible to get.
I feel like the sexiest thing on earth when I haul that big load straight into the delivery point. And you will too (if you don't think you will, try that god damned demo).
Seriously though, this is an incredibly relaxing game. I find it really good for winding down after a long day at college and suchlike. You don't have to pay too much attention, just enough to stay in your lane and to know when to turn off. The game proposes a constant low level difficulty, meaning that it's easy to play and you can be great at it as soon as you start, but this constant low level difficulty means that you've got to balance between relaxing and fully enjoying the game and keeping your eyes on the road. In my opinion they've done a really good job with this.
I currently find myself coming home and playing this over WoW, which tells me the devs have done a really good job at giving the game a pull factor, making you want to come back to it time and time again.

The Euro Truck Simulator 2 Multiplayer mod makes the game a different experience, replacing all of the virtual traffic with real life players driving across europe completing similar missions to yours. When driving long distances, you may go a long distance without seeing anybody, which may make the game slightly lonely for you but when you do see somebody, the humble honk of the horn that you exchange makes it all worth it. In other journeys however, the roads teem with over players, all trucking away individually but the united cause of mothertruckers makes everyone united in away.
The winter mod is pretty much just a mod that makes everything snowy, and does a damned good job at it too. The snowflake textures that stretch on the windscreen aren't great in my opinion, but that's my only criticism of the mod. The Multiplayer mod runs this during the holiday period.
This game is for anybody. Simulator enthusiasts. Gamers. Children. Adults. Men. Women. Anyone. In spite of the mediocre ratings from critics, this game is a masterpiece. Not because "Spec Ops: The Line" is a bad game, but because it shows war and violence in a way that is gut-wrenching and terrifying.

At a glance, you could easily dismiss this game as another generic military shooter. It is and it isn't. The mission structure is by the books Call of Duty style: move forward, stop, kill a million enemies, move forward a bit and do the same. However, what elevates it above other military shooters is the story.
You're deployed to Dubai -- or what's left of it -- on a mission to locate survivors of a cataclysmic sandstorm. Simple enough, right? It would be, if not for the war raging within. As you explore the ruins of Dubai, questions are raised. How far is too far? Is the pursuit of your mission worth it, in spite of the casualties along the way?
If a thought-provoking story is of interest to you, I strongly recommend Spec Ops. On the other hand, if you are simply looking to kill people with abandon, you're best to look elsewhere. Whilst the shooting is solid, it can't carry the game and actually becomes tedious towards the end.

A brilliant and surreal protrait of war and war-based gaming in the modern age. Without giving too much away, this game is more than it seems. Based upon the book Heart of Darkness by Joseph Conrad (at least thematically) and, more directly, the Heart-inspired Vietnam flick Apocalypse Now, Spec Ops: The Line is one of the greatest narrative achievements in gaming. By offering genuinely fun dudebro shooting (think Gears of War with a Call of Duty paintjob) but a skewed, critical perspective upon the nature of itself, the game becomes something entirely unique. If you like shooters, play this game. If you like shooters and mindscrews or intelligent, analysis-friendly psychological fiction, play this game.
I will not give any more away. Play this game. It will change you.

Undertale is a good game. I'm going to say the right off the bat, that being said, reading this review will probably make the game less enjoyable. Undertale is a game best enjoyed when you don't understand how it will be good; that being said I don't want anyone to miss out on the awesome-ness that is undertale, so if you're still undecided I hope reading this review will help make your mind. The first time I saw the game, I was skeptical. The game seemed shallow; a retro rpg with a strong moral focus. I felt like it would be boring because the only aspect of the game originally presented to me was the moral choices and so I felt like that was all the game had to offer. But, due to the constant good reviews I decided to buy it. My first reaction was of interest, The game seemed to be doing moral choices well, with an actual reason to kill things rather than just making it a decision for a different ending. But my interest tapered in the beginning as the game gave up it's most powerful asset: the character. I was roaming a dungeon completing rather boring and generic puzzles, but soon the game takes a turn as the gameplay is switched up to a more interesting choice of focusing on the characters, making it so that their choices affect you as much as your choices affect them. This form of story telling give depth to the characters, giving you legitimate reason to be invested in each one as they help, backstab and trust you. The puzzles and their solutions aren't for the sake of the puzzles themselves but for furthering your relationship and understanding of the characters involved. The storytelling is really well done, it makes you feel the situation which leads to the reason why I think that undertale is good: YOU are the protagonist. The game does everything in it's power to help you feel yourself as the main character, the characters are friends with YOU for the decision YOU made. The gravity of the situation really weighs on YOU. When the game presents a new situation, you feel as if you have a personal stake in the game, because you do. This game isn't about the world or the main character's struggle and arc through it. It's about you and the relationships you make along the way.

Follow the story of our hero, Max, as he seeks revenge against the bandit clan leader who stole his life away.  Mad Max has a lot of entertaining and fun aspects, but also contains a lot of boring and repetitive actions.  The story is decent, the controls are good, the graphics are very beautiful, and the environment is very well done.  The gameplay is rather simple, and even without upgrading your character's abilities or gear you can do very well in a fight with minimal experience, but the true enjoyment of this game does not occur on foot, but in your car.  With your trusty mechanic and harpoon shooter in the back, you take the wheel and fight head to head against other drivers, often with tricks up their sleeves.  The car combat is very fun, and it's worth upgrading your ride to handle some of the difficult challenges that await you in the wasteland.  Overall I would recommend it if you can find it for less than $25, but I would not say that it is worth much more than that unless you enjoy exploring a vast and open wasteland picking up scrap metal for hours on end.  A scavenging location can yield anywhere from 2 pieces of scrap to 50, but you need thousands of scrap to get a few of the upgrades for your car, and that takes a lot of time to grind out.
TLDR: Overall, a good game, but be prepared for a lot of grinding if you want 100% completion on it.

Boy, oh Boy - where do I even start?
First of all - I absolutely LOVE Life is Strange. I think it is an experience everyone should play and enjoy. (...and cry their eyes out, like I did...)
Secondly - This game is HELLA dope - let me explain you why:
Story -
"Gee, why does it have to be a prequel - we already know how it ends anyway" - While this might be true - it is definitely not entirely true. If you get involved and immersed in the people and stories around Arcadia Bay, you DO want to know everything, right? How where those guys before the "main game", what changed? How did Chloe change, what did she go through to become the person we know and (and might or might not) like in the maingame), Who is Rachel, whats the deal about her? And the most important question though - will Frank be getting his beloved beans again? Seriously though - there is a lot more to it than just the inevitable and already known end. My opinion is - it only makes it more heartbreaking and gutwrenching, knowing what lies ahead, in the future.
Atmosphere -
It just feels like coming home after a long and seemingly endless trip. Its just awesome to see the already known people, hear and read what chloe thinks about them and if they were different in the past of the maingame. If you liked "exploring" and checking out stuff in the first game, you will definitely like it here, too. I mean, come on! Its Chloe! Sure she has her very own opinion and view points at almost everyone and everything. (Protip/possible Spoiler - If you get to the plaza of blackwell, do yourself a favor and join in the D&D Game, its freaking hilarious.)
Music/Sound -
While the Main game already has awesome tunes fitting perfectly to each and every scene, its almost impossible to improve on that. (Listening to the mainscreen-music for hours and almost every track in the game is still one of my weekly rituals). When it comes to sound and music, Before the Storm is awesome too. The Music brought in by Daughter fits the mood of the Game and its main-character perfectly. It changes from chilling, relaxing tunes to rocky, exciting tracks perfectly and provides a rememberable and definitely buy-able Soundtrack thats top notch in my eyes. (Especially at the ending, chills everywhere!)
Voiceacting -
Im going to be honest here - when I found out that noone will voice their character from the maingame, I was worried that the experience would be crippled entirely because each and every VA in the main game was absolutely awesome and perfectly fitting. I thought it would be hard to get used to the new voices, especially because Ashly Burch was slaying as Chloe in the main game. As soon as I heard the Voice of Chloe in a gameplay/trailer, I liked her voice and found it to be fitting to a younger chloe. And while it might be a bit odd in the first minutes, you will get used to the new voices pretty quick. Chloe and Rachels VA's are doing an amazing job here!
Decisions & Chloe's "Power" -
When it comes to decisions, I kind of feel they are not worth/changing very much in the story - at least in the first episode. I didnt try out every possible outcome, but the ones I tried and changed while getting the Achievements have seemed to change nothing (yet.)
Same goes with Chloes Power - While the "Power" itself is awesome and you get to choose how she will roast the one shes talking to, I dont feel any consequences here yet either - and going with the aggressive chloe should seem to be the more reckless and "get in more trouble" path, However, I did not experience any of the trouble so far. It might come in the next episodes, though.
TLDR: This Game is Hella Dope, every Life is Strange and "Wants to be" Fan should definitely go and buy it. Deck Nine has created a masterpiece here!
