Alright, here we go. This is all around a great game, its filled with tons of action and explosions that we've come to expect in the Mad Max francise, but there are some problems. When i first go the game i was impressed by how good it looked, but the way that everything looks in this game still makes it look a little washed out, but that more of a realistic point of veiw that i dont really mind much, it was expected coming from a WB game. As you may know many critics who review this game usually grade it poorly but when you start looking at it from a proffesional veiw, you see that they can be right. When you first get the game you have so much fun doing every thing that could be done, but as you start to play it more and more, you start to sense the repetiveness in it. There seems like a lot to do, like building up strongholds, improving the Magnum Opus, taking over camps, and knocking down Scrotus' influence, but all it really boils down to is you collecting scrap. Its a never ending cycle of "go here, fight these people and collect this scrap", and it does get really repetitive.
As far a combat goes, there are two types in this game, foot-combat and car-combat. Foot-combat is the same kind of reaction based combat that we've come to love in games like the Arkham Trilogy, and Shadow of Mordor. but it just doesn't have the viriaty that those other games have, and you notice they try to make up for it with abillities, but there is such a little pool of them that its easy to make each fight a Block-and-Stab just like the other fights. Max only has his fist, a shotgun, and some shivs, but compare that to all the gadgets of Batman, or the Wraith powers of Talion. It does take a slightly more realistic approach  with the resources that are present in the Mad Max universe though.
Car combat is the next version of combat we have. The way that WB incorperated the combat with cars it actually pretty well done in my opinion, though it does come with its quirks. Its easy to become overpowered with the car, but only if you have the best of the best upgrades, anything less and your practically drive a tin can with rollarblades for wheels. There is a wide gap of how good you car is in the upgrade list, on teir two your armor can take three good hits before you explode or have to jump out, but the next level you basically become godlike to the point you dont have to worry anymore.
How the upgrades works is that you have to collect scrap, lower Scrotus' influence in certian areas, and do certain side quest to unlock upgrades for your car, but a big problem ist that it doesnt tell you how to start the side quest or any information about unless the name of the quest. Making you either run around doing numerous "go-fetch-this" quests which tends to get tiresome eventually, or look it up in a Wiki which feels like cheating. these just get old after a while and starts to become repetative like most everything else in this game.
Upgrades to Max's Legend are all but useless, you'll only need to upgrade four items that are actually worth while. One big problem there is, is that there are no upgrades to the water flask, there is a upgrade you can get to help you get more water out of water spouts, but that doesn't matter when you have to drink the whole flask twice just in order to get 3/4 of your health back. Couldn't they have an upgrade to haver the water heal more? Or maybe to have the Flask actually hold more water instead of spending 2 minutes by a water spout constantly refilling your bottle to get your health back.
Now I know that i just basically trash talked this game and called it a repetative mess but all in all, from a regular person's point of view it is a fun and enjoyable game. the story it pretty well written and it does seem like something of the Mad Max legend, the action is fun and enjoyable, filled with slowmotion bits, eplosions, and reactiveness. I do recommend this game if you're just playing it to have fun, and if you like repetitiveness, but if you play for critism of the game, then it does deserve a lot. It is a fun game and i really do love it, even if it does have its flaws.

You start as a low-skilled, truckless lorry jockey, forced to take work from established haulage companies. At a glance, you could easily dismiss this game as another generic military shooter. It is and it isn't. The mission structure is by the books Call of Duty style: move forward, stop, kill a million enemies, move forward a bit and do the same. However, what elevates it above other military shooters is the story.
You're deployed to Dubai -- or what's left of it -- on a mission to locate survivors of a cataclysmic sandstorm. Simple enough, right? It would be, if not for the war raging within. As you explore the ruins of Dubai, questions are raised. How far is too far? Is the pursuit of your mission worth it, in spite of the casualties along the way?
If a thought-provoking story is of interest to you, I strongly recommend Spec Ops. On the other hand, if you are simply looking to kill people with abandon, you're best to look elsewhere. Whilst the shooting is solid, it can't carry the game and actually becomes tedious towards the end.

A brilliant and surreal protrait of war and war-based gaming in the modern age. Without giving too much away, this game is more than it seems. Based upon the book Heart of Darkness by Joseph Conrad (at least thematically) and, more directly, the Heart-inspired Vietnam flick Apocalypse Now, Spec Ops: The Line is one of the greatest narrative achievements in gaming. By offering genuinely fun dudebro shooting (think Gears of War with a Call of Duty paintjob) but a skewed, critical perspective upon the nature of itself, the game becomes something entirely unique. If you like shooters, play this game. If you like shooters and mindscrews or intelligent, analysis-friendly psychological fiction, play this game.
I will not give any more away. Play this game. It will change you.
This game may have given me PTSD.

Which also makes it ten times more fun as playing alone is sort of boring, unless of couse you've discovered how to use Dev mode, which, on this particular game, is about as much use as a knitted condom.
I wouldn't say the game is perfect. The lack of online multiplayer makes multiplayer in general extremely hard. "Yes, you and your mates can play this game together, but they have to drive down to wherever the ♥♥♥♥ you happen to live in order to do so" Unless you live near your best mate, live near your Siblings r at least have a sex slave locked away in your basement, multiplayer can only be accomplished when the second, thid and fourth player are in the same room as you, playing on the same PC.
Also, this game is buggy. Not just the sort of buggy where there's that one part of that one map where you can walk through a wall, but the sort of buggy where you look down to see that your leg is halfway up your♥♥♥♥♥♥buggy. The character models seem to have a feud underway with the laws of physics, as characters tend to just randomly dart in one direction, as if someone's just landed a roundhouse kick on their left testicle. However, despite the game having more bugs than a Dog with worms, the charming way in which the game is styled makes me unable to refuse its' shiny, colourful, seizure-inducing fun that I get from playing it. If I was going to say anything about this game, I'd say it's probably better to approach it as someone who's played many Indie games before. When I first heard about this game I was given the impression that it was an RPG first and a platformer second.
...the people describing the game like that need to stop right now, this is a rogue-like platformer with an upgrade system.
If you don't like platformers, this isn't your style of game; you can go ahead an stop looking into the game.
However, if you DO enjoy plaformers, let me talk about this little gem for a bit. Rogue Legacy is a game with an outstanding feel and contrastingly mediocre enemy design. The swinging of your sword feels like swinging a sword should, responsive and fluid, and the jumps are completely in your control as they reach their acceptable peak. These are the basics and extremely responsive basics at that. It just feels good to control, something that certain games fall limp on.
Customization is a particular aspect Rogue Legacy strives on. By exploring the castle in its hundreds of forms, you can come across runes, money, and equipment to improve your future kin's chances of survival. Equipment is rather straight forward, better swords and pieces of armor provide boosts in strength but some lines of equipment have perks and disadvantages to go along with them (for example, the guardian line has great defense but heavy weight and weak attack). Runes are a little more unique, you get to have one rune per piece of armor and they provide extra skills such as extra jumps, dashing, vampirism, magic regeneration, floating, etc. Nothing ground breaking, but it lets you experiment a bit to keep you entertained. However, nothing could progress without money. Money is used for everything from improving base stats to unlocking new character classes to actually allowing you to use the equipment and runes you've found during your exploration.

There's next to nothing for story aside from journal entries from the villain, but the game is built around the gameplay and that's what will keep you invested in the game. Rogue Legacy can be a breeze if you just focus on finishing the game, but for all you completionists out there, there's a neverending new game+ cycle (I'm on new game+17 right now) and revamped bosses to keep you busy with unlockables in postgame activities and the game become exponentially more difficult.
I should mention the child system in this game. When your character dies, you don't start over with that same character, you venture into a new, randomly generated castle with one of you character's kids (hence the "Legacy" part of the title). Each offspring will have a class and specific traits that change how the game actually functions (you can be color blind, have vertigo and play the game upsidedown, you might be a compulsive swearer, it's randomized and that's the fun of it (although you have a choice between three successors)
If Rogue Legacy sounds like fun to you, I wholeheartedly encourage you to try it out, it's worth your time and there's a great sense of exploration and achievement to come along in the quirky, crazy game.

MEDIOCRE at best.
In what seems to be an alternative universe of the Mad Max Fury Road (2015), Max once again loses his car, stripped of his gear, and left for dead. But at least this time you get a dog right? Nope sorry not after the first half hour. Aided by a hunchback you, Max, are on the path of petty vengeance; going on great lengths to pimp his ride and get even with the warlord / main villian.
Unfortunately, the game formula is identical to most cookie cutter open world games from last generation. It's hard to stand out when majority of your game is copy pasta from Farcry, Deathrally, and Batman. The combat is very much like Batman series close quarter combat with your very limited shotgun and shivs as your backup weapons. I didn't really mind this as it kept things engaging but unfortunately the level design is so bland and AI is so awfully predictable that after a few camp clears it's just not fun anymore.
Also... story just plain sucks. You feel like nothing is really happening half the time other than the constant reminder to make your car better... simpleminded got to make it better to get back at the warlord. However, towards the end things kind of pick up and some degree of character development happens. You become invested in them but it's already the end, credits roll.
While I didn't mind that the plot was directly linked to your enjoyment of your car, I did mind there was a lot of upgrade gating. 80% of the upgrades are tied into you reducing the threat level of various zones in the Mad Max world. The camps are the worst repetition for this because A) you get out of your awesome car B) combat is snooze after a handful of times and you got like 40+ camps to clear! Destroying scarecrows, sniper nests, and convoys are probably the most fun objectives to reduce threat but don't provide as much. I have around fourty some odd hours into the game and it was mostly spent in the time sink of trying to get upgrades for my damned Magnum Opus.
You'll love the environment and driving portion though. Man I can't forget the sandstorm sequence from Fury Road and it was crazy to not only witness it in the game but to be in one! You just got to hunker down and hope the debris doesn't kill you because the lightning storms might lol. Driving around is fun as hell. The V6/V8 engine sounds viseral and you can't help wanting to rock out while pedaling to the metal, I was super impressed! Combine that with the heat haze effect in your interceptor cruising in the desert with buzzards on your tail... now thats immersion.
Ultimately a lot of Mad Max is forgettable shallow experience with exception to the driving. If you're a big fan of the franchise and new to open world games then you'll have a blast. For veterans, you should pass.
Why Angel of Combustion have you forsaken me with this arduous journey?

You take the role of Mad Max and meet a character called Chum Bucket early on. You then spend the time together helping out allies by destroying enemy landmarks and capturing camps. As you progress you earn scrap that can be used to upgrade your car and Max himself.
You spend a lot of the game in your car, which you would expect, and the battles you have with other road users seem to work well with Harpoons and your Shotgun being essential gear.
The story itself is short and sweet, and It is in addition to the film and allows you to delve into Max's world even deeper. As you are in a fairly open world you can also compete in races, collect relics or farm scrap to your hearts desire. Boy, oh Boy - where do I even start?
First of all - I absolutely LOVE Life is Strange. I think it is an experience everyone should play and enjoy. (...and cry their eyes out, like I did...)
Secondly - This game is HELLA dope - let me explain you why:
Story -
"Gee, why does it have to be a prequel - we already know how it ends anyway" - While this might be true - it is definitely not entirely true. If you get involved and immersed in the people and stories around Arcadia Bay, you DO want to know everything, right? How where those guys before the "main game", what changed? How did Chloe change, what did she go through to become the person we know and (and might or might not) like in the maingame), Who is Rachel, whats the deal about her? And the most important question though - will Frank be getting his beloved beans again? Seriously though - there is a lot more to it than just the inevitable and already known end. My opinion is - it only makes it more heartbreaking and gutwrenching, knowing what lies ahead, in the future.
Atmosphere -
It just feels like coming home after a long and seemingly endless trip. Its just awesome to see the already known people, hear and read what chloe thinks about them and if they were different in the past of the maingame. If you liked "exploring" and checking out stuff in the first game, you will definitely like it here, too. I mean, come on! Its Chloe! Sure she has her very own opinion and view points at almost everyone and everything. (Protip/possible Spoiler - If you get to the plaza of blackwell, do yourself a favor and join in the D&D Game, its freaking hilarious.)
Music/Sound -
While the Main game already has awesome tunes fitting perfectly to each and every scene, its almost impossible to improve on that. (Listening to the mainscreen-music for hours and almost every track in the game is still one of my weekly rituals). When it comes to sound and music, Before the Storm is awesome too. The Music brought in by Daughter fits the mood of the Game and its main-character perfectly. It changes from chilling, relaxing tunes to rocky, exciting tracks perfectly and provides a rememberable and definitely buy-able Soundtrack thats top notch in my eyes. (Especially at the ending, chills everywhere!)
Voiceacting -
Im going to be honest here - when I found out that noone will voice their character from the maingame, I was worried that the experience would be crippled entirely because each and every VA in the main game was absolutely awesome and perfectly fitting. I thought it would be hard to get used to the new voices, especially because Ashly Burch was slaying as Chloe in the main game. As soon as I heard the Voice of Chloe in a gameplay/trailer, I liked her voice and found it to be fitting to a younger chloe. And while it might be a bit odd in the first minutes, you will get used to the new voices pretty quick. Chloe and Rachels VA's are doing an amazing job here!
Decisions & Chloe's "Power" -
When it comes to decisions, I kind of feel they are not worth/changing very much in the story - at least in the first episode. I didnt try out every possible outcome, but the ones I tried and changed while getting the Achievements have seemed to change nothing (yet.)
Same goes with Chloes Power - While the "Power" itself is awesome and you get to choose how she will roast the one shes talking to, I dont feel any consequences here yet either - and going with the aggressive chloe should seem to be the more reckless and "get in more trouble" path, However, I did not experience any of the trouble so far. It might come in the next episodes, though.
TLDR: This Game is Hella Dope, every Life is Strange and "Wants to be" Fan should definitely go and buy it. Deck Nine has created a masterpiece here!

Follow the story of our hero, Max, as he seeks revenge against the bandit clan leader who stole his life away.  Mad Max has a lot of entertaining and fun aspects, but also contains a lot of boring and repetitive actions.  The story is decent, the controls are good, the graphics are very beautiful, and the environment is very well done.  The gameplay is rather simple, and even without upgrading your character's abilities or gear you can do very well in a fight with minimal experience, but the true enjoyment of this game does not occur on foot, but in your car.  With your trusty mechanic and harpoon shooter in the back, you take the wheel and fight head to head against other drivers, often with tricks up their sleeves.  The car combat is very fun, and it's worth upgrading your ride to handle some of the difficult challenges that await you in the wasteland.  Overall I would recommend it if you can find it for less than $25, but I would not say that it is worth much more than that unless you enjoy exploring a vast and open wasteland picking up scrap metal for hours on end.  A scavenging location can yield anywhere from 2 pieces of scrap to 50, but you need thousands of scrap to get a few of the upgrades for your car, and that takes a lot of time to grind out.
TLDR: Overall, a good game, but be prepared for a lot of grinding if you want 100% completion on it.

Rogue Legacy is a 2d (sprites) pseudo-Roguelike action platformer focusing on the acquisition of statistic upgrades / new abilities for your manor and your lineage of heroes. Its basic physics are somewhere between a NES or SNES platformer and a Metroidvania.
Each individual hero you send into the dungeon will stay mostly as-is and will not be getting noticeably stronger as they fight. The primary resource you need to accrue is gold, obtained from destroying objects, killing enemies, and in much higher quantities from treasure chests and minibosses. (Or real bosses.)
When you die, your character's "last words" will be a game tip to help you find your way around the game and do better next time (unless your character has compulsive swearing in which case their last words will be grawlix swears.) You will then be asked to pick an heir from one of 3 randomized options. The game will also let you scroll back to see every hero you've ever used in this playthrough right up to the prefab tutorial hero.
After picking an heir, you will spend however much gold your last hero acquired on expanding your family's mansion / castle, forging new equipment with your blacksmith, or unlocking new runes with your Enchantress. These unlocked upgrades will then apply to every subsequent hero in your lineage.
After you have decided on your upgrades, Charon will take everything you've got left before letting you into the castle again - thus, you have to get enough gold for your desired upgrade(s) in one run, until you get the upgrades that reduce his toll. You can also get an item in the dungeon that will skip his toll on your next entry only.
Throughout the game, you will occasionally stumble on rooms containing journal entries, which will explain the goal of the game by showing a past adventurer taking the same route: The castle grounds have four biomes, each of which have one boss, and you need to take them all out to fight the final boss, who is always accessible from the first room. If you kill a boss, he stays dead - you don't need to fight them all with one hero (I'm not sure if that's even possible.)
You will also occasionally bump into minibosses, who are easily identifiable by their dramatically increased size and their ability to kill you very quickly. Defeating these bosses will give you better chests than usual that will almost always contain a blueprint or a rune. If not, you'll get diamonds (lots of money.)
You can find Strange Rooms, one of which contains a statue you can pray to for a bonus item. You can carry one item at a time. If you find another item room, you will lose the previous one if you pray.
You may also encounter two NPC's in the dungeon.
Booyan is a clown who will give you either an axe or a dagger accuracy game. If you get the highest score (10 or less targets left with axe or destroying all targets with dagger) he will give you about 450 gold and a miniboss chest.
Miserly Elf will offer to take 25% of your gold and let you pick one of three chests. If you pick the correct one, you get triple your investment (multiplied by your Bounty boost), otherwise you get nothing. If you pick a Hero with a vision disorder and get the Nerdy Glasses elsewhere in the dungeon, you can see which chest contains the gold (i.e. cheat.)
Finally, you will occasionally find rooms containing Fairy Chests, which will open if you can reach them after fulfilling a certain bonus condition (or will close permanently if you fail a bonus condition.) These will always contain runes.
MISC. PROS:
- Has New Game +. You can stack them, getting a new perk every time you beat the game. However, each New Game + will also make all of the enemies harder.
- Some of the hero perks are purely for hilarity, e.g. if your character is bald, the castle will generate with "Balding..." instead of "Building..."
- You can use the Architect to keep your last run's dungeon layout, which means you can retry failed Fairy Chests et al. The drawback? -40% to your gold multiplier, which becomes meager once you can boost your multiplier up to 200% and beyond.
MISC. CONS:
- The four main bosses are nothing more than souped up regular enemies, even behaving extremely similarly to them. The fights are monotonous and frustrating, even more so when you fight the remix versions.
- You can only pick from 3 randomly rolled heroes each generation, and sometimes will get 3 of the same class you don't like. This is mitigated partway through by an upgrade that lets you discard these and get 3 more random heroes, once each generation.
- You can't fight the same boss twice in one playthrough, except if you give Charon a token to unlock its EX mode... which is not only much much harder but gives you a prefab'd character to do it with.
- Only characters with the Flexible perk can change direction after you've pressed the attack key. Be careful!
- You can't jump during a dash (but you can dash multiple times in midair.)
MISC. TIPS:
- Knight (Paladin) is far and away the easiest class. Consider using him on gold runs until you have Spelunker (not Miner.)
- Enemies scale to your level, which is determined by your various lineage upgrades. The Curse and Grace runes will add or subtract levels to or from this scale, and I presume one Curse and one Grace cancel each other out.
- You can only get the Nerdy Glasses (and thus cheat at the elf's game) if you have a vision disorder, which the glasses will heal. This includes vertigo, colorblindness, and nostalgia.
- For "Don't look" Fairy Chests, face away from them and dash backwards into them. The condition will say complete as soon as you touch the chest, so you don't need to worry about overshooting and failing it.
- Dwarfism allows you to slip into secret passages in walls that other characters can't enter.
- Certain classes are better against certain bosses. Lich Royal w/ Crowstorm + full set of Siphon Runes = dead forest boss.
- You get a damage multiplier for subsequent "pogo" attacks without landing. You can upgrade this multiplier in the manor.
- After you get Increased Invulnerability Time, highlight it. Press Up. Get that.
All in all, Rogue Legacy is a wonderful, hilarious, and sometimes very frustrating game. Definitely advise to give it a shot.

This game takes an approach to roguelikes that I didn't really see before - for one, you will die a LOT early on, most bosses are nearly unbeatable before you get anywhere. But when you die you get to upgrade, to pick a new hero, to explore a new dungeon.
The trick is to accumulate as much gold, blueprints and runes as you can early on (remember to spend as much gold as you can as it gets taken away from you when you enter the dungeon again). Get to learn the controls, the enemies and the patterns of the various rooms that there are. Purchased upgrades, runes and blueprints that you found gets carried over to your next hero, so with each run you will be a little stronger.
If you like roguelikes I can only recommend this game, definitely. But don't expect to make a no-deaths speedrun - it's as close to impossible as it can be.

While the cover alludes to an experience akin to Modern Warfare or Battlefield, this game is anything but.  You assume the role of Capt. Walker, leading a small group of Delta Force into what is to be a simple mission. But what you end up with is a downward spiral into insanity in a Dubai-meet-Apocalypse-Now setting. While the gameplay is nothing ground-breaking, the narrative is particularly strong. It sets out to have you question your own actions as the situation becomes increasingly dark. "Do you feel like a hero yet?” a loading screen taunts me, mocking the FPS genre in the process. No, I don't - I've seen the horror of war, and blood is on my hands. "You are still a good person", another tries to reassure me. This is not a fun game as such – but I’d highly recommend it. By the time the game draws to a close you’ll understand why this is called "The Line". You’ll have crossed it too.
Ghost Recon / Rainbow Six meets Apocalypse Now

It elegantly kicks modern war shooters in the teeth, showing them it's possible to have a great story, which also depicts a gritty reality of war's consequences and the shell socked human psyche.
Add great visuals and pretty solid mechanics in the mix, and you have a hell of a game.

The premise is rather straightforward - drive a truck around Europe. The beauty of this game is in its great application of detail and simplicty where each matters. Once you get started you pick up delivery contracts, customise your truck inside and out, keep it repaired, refueled, and make sure to get yourself some rest on long hauls. While it is a lot to keep track of the game makes sure everything is easy to do, with everything being accessible from either an always available pause menu, or from simply pulling into a stop.
The game is very lenient with mistakes and accidents, with relatively light penalties for doing the wrong thing that encourage you to do better without making you feel like quitting in frustration. It provides just enough of a challenge to keep you casually engaged while not being so easy as to become dull and boring.
If you want to sit down, relax, and zone out to some music, Euro Truck Simulator 2 has you covered.

If you liked original Life is Strange, you will very likely enjoy it.
If you tought Life is Strange is kinda cheesy/gringy, even then you will very likely enjoy it.
The thing is, many were afraid it doesnt live up to expectations, but first episode actually is really great- i'd say this miniseries has even potential of becoming even better than original. I mean yes, you dont have rewind, but backtalk ability is actually even more interesting. Writing quality has also increased and game does offer quite a few rather unexpected things. All in all, at least on launch of episode 1 (meaning time of writing this review).
Oh and emotions. You still can laugh (Chloe can be deviously witty), but there are obviously tear-jerking moments, although so far (again, im writing this only as of episode 1) not so much as in original- but im comparing full season to just 1 episode so thats hardly fair play- especially considering original didnt really kick off in that regard until ep. 2.
Atmosphere still hits the spot on as well, still allowing you to have calm moments.
So in case you wondered if its gonna be worse (because lets be honest, its kind of trend with spinoffs/sequels to new franchises lately, especially when given to another studio), then have no fear- if anything, this shapes up to be even better game (and original LiS is one of my all-time favourites).
EDIT (Episode 2 launch)! Well, my prediction was correct- it definetly removes most mistakes LiS did and dares to experiment with new ideas in way that actually fit the game. And it makes most of those changes. Its just absolutely incredible game. Though it might be tad better for people who played original (although at same time, maybe not)
EDIT 2 (Episode 3 launch).
Holy. Hella. Hell. Who said prequels cant be good, well, that person should play this. I can sit back and appreciate all the continuous effort that has gone into the development of Rust. I think it is an excellent game if you can play it on your terms; beyond that, everything goes south.
This game is a very apt statement on the direction game development is currently going and it's almost as bad as micro-transactions. Long story short, will this game ever come out of early access? I find it rather hard to belive that a major vendor like Steam allows every small developer and his camel to swiftly fire out an absolute turd of a game under the moniker of "Early Access" and charge whatever they like for it, without pre-requisite for ensuring the game's 'investors' will get a return by providing any sort of development roadmap. All we get forewarned of is that the game "may be buggy". Credit where credit is due though, a lot of work has gone into this game over the best part of 4 years now...
I have played this game since day dot actually, despite minimal hours as a ratio to its existance. It's gone from strength to strength, but more notably, weakness to weakness. At one point it was absolutely unplayable due wholly to being saturated with cheaters.
The most important issue is the community itself and it is a lesson that if you give people the power of anonymity, nobody can be trusted. After very little thought, because that's all it took, the reason for this is that the game does not enable any sort of reward or benefit to be taken advantage of by cooperating with any random person (except where clans take advantage of an economy of scale). There are so many toxic knuckle-dragging community members that just unrealistically expect more and more PVP due mostly to the fact that Rust is portrayed in a very skewed, inaccurate and glorified way by popular YouTube channels. The last thing Rust needs is more PVP. As if it's not hard enough already to get on your feet in a server that hasn't been freshly wiped, enter gangs of thugs that kill on sight, setting you back HOURS for no reason. That's not fun, and it's not a productive comminuty.
Building mechanics are great, minus the exploits, and allow for creative thinking. Unfortunately if you're a one-man-band, time and resource economy are overwhelming parts of the early game. Defending yourself is very difficult if you encounter anything other than a one-on-one with similar weapons, otherwise because of reasons previously mentioned, there is a 99% chance that the outcome will only be bad for you. Most of your time will be spent gathering enough resources to increase the raid resistance of your house, which becomes increasingly futile the longer you spend on the server.
Monuments are so irradiated that they're impossible to explore without protection which can often only be found within the radiation zone itself. You'll get tired of literally cooking your balls for terrible loot in no time! (I still think it's funny that you wake up confused and disoriented, completely naked, hungry and cold; have only a rock and...a Geiger Counter!) Also, if you go near any of these monuments, review your life insurance policy because the likelihood of being killed on sight increases three-fold.
If you find youself in an empty server, you can be in awe of the fantastic visuals of the game and get a handle on getting ahead in the early game if you ever dare step foot into hacker-ville.
Take it easy out there...

Rust is a promising, ambitious game that tries to do everything, and unfortunately fails to do anything especially well. It's disappointingly shallow in most aspects, which is especially concerning given how long this game has been in development.
I picked up Rust in a Humble Bundle about a year or so ago, and had never gotten around to playing it. Since it had been released in early access several years prior to THAT even, when I stumbled across it in my library a couple days ago I expected a fairly polished product (or at least something that really showed that this game has been in development for years.
The first thing I noticed upon spawning in was how horribly unoptimized this game is. I have an excellent gaming rig, and I nearly had to bottom out the graphics settings just to get it to run smoothly. I've heard great things about the graphics when they're maxed out, but the fact that I can play much prettier games at full bore while being forced to lower my graphics substantially to play this is pretty telling.
The next thing I noticed is that the persistent building mechanics make every world a massive mess. Literally anyone who logs on to a server can build, and those buildings stay there until the server is wiped, which oftentimes happens several times a week on a given server. There is hardly a patch of clear ground in the servers I tried - and the poor building mechanics and the need to make your base as hard to raid as possible (more on that later) means that most structures are an absolute blight to look at, and very out of place. It's a pretty disappointing system, in that there are so many crappy structures that there's very little to explore - and even if you like building, your structure will be gone in a couple of days anyway and you'll have to start from scratch.
Speaking of starting from scratch, I hope you have hours upon hours to spend grinding out quality materials, because if you don't,
. Yes, you heard that right, when you leave to do other things, you can still get raided, your stuff stolen, and killed. If you want to come back and pick up where you left off, you better hope you fortified your base with top-tier or near top-tier materials before you log, which takes several hours of straight grinding to achieve. Even then, a committed team can still break down and destroy the most fortified structures, so you're really just crossing your fingers that no one well-equipped enough stumbles upon your base. Additionally, you're forced to make your base as convoluted as possible to discourage raiders - which makes it a huge eyesore and difficult to navigate. There's also little-to-no functionality to remove structures you've built after you place them - meaning a wall or floor placed wrong means you need to either start completely over, blow up with top-tier explosives, or spend a massive amount of time breaking it down with tools.
The combat seems to be the main selling point of Rust, but it lacks the same punch as games like DayZ or the Culling. In DayZ, everyone had guns, it was a piece of cake to find them, and always ended up making engagements fun. In the Culling, melee weapons were able to contend with firearms because guns were scarce, had little ammunition, and were difficult to use. In Rust, you hope that the people who have been playing longer don't randomly kill you, because there is absolutely no way you can contend with firearms if you're still using low-tier weapons. There's very little logical progression either - you go straight from spears and sticks and rocks to rifles and machine guns. Despite the fact that this game has been in development for
, there's very few weapons to choose from at all.
There are so many aspects of Rust that I really, really like. I love the hunting, I love the base building, I love the friend-or-foe interactions with other players - but none of it is really that good. There are few animals to hunt and there's no way to sneak up on them, forcing you to do the same chase-shoot-chase action every time. The base building is clunky, there aren't enough options, and it looks awful in the world. The interactions are generally poor because the game is so shallow, there's nothing to do but kill people once you hit a certain point.
I really want to like Rust, and maybe it'll blossom into an amazing game some time in the future. I just don't count on that, given how long it's taken them to reach where they are now.

Holy Hells. Playing this game is like being punched repeatedly in the gut and then forced to watch someone strangle a puppy. In the best way possible.The game is simultaneously a self-aware critique of modern shooters, an "Apocalypse Now" for the new generation, and as I've described it to several friends: the feel-bad game of the decade. Do not play this game for the gameplay. The gameplay was very good in my opinion, but I do not play many 3rd-person cover-based shooters, and people who do that I have talked with tell me that it is not particularly good on that front. No, instead play this game for the emotional, mentally crushing kick to the groin that it delivers very slowly over the course of a six hour single player campaign. I don't think any other game has made me physically sick with this unique cocktail of revulsion, guilt, and cognitive dissonance. I believe it was somewhere around the point when the loading screen asked me "Do you feel like a hero yet?" and I replied simperingly out loud "No, no I just want to go home, please," that I realized what a real work of art this game was. So, if you're just looking for another mindless CoD or Battlefield clone, please, avoid this game, it probably isn't for you. But if you are instead looking for a game that will make you rethink the nature of morality, war, and sanity, give this game a go. You won't be dissappointed.

What is this game?
Mad Max is a post apocalyptic open world action game. It involves a lot of driving around in the barren wastelands, and finding camps to take down, scarecrows to destroy and many more things. The games main character is Max. Max is a man who lost it all. After your car is destroyed, and you have nothing, you meet Chumbucket. A lunatic liing in the wasteland, worshipping a divine spirit called the "Angel Combustion". Together with him you upgrade your Magnum Opus (A car) and your final goal is reaching the Planes Of Silence.
Pros and Cons
Pros:
+Great driving mechanics
+Good combat
+Storyline is good as well
+Super good optimized (i could play it at 30 fps with my geforce 840 m)
+The capture mode
Cons:
-Game can get a bit repetitive after you completed the story and side missions
-Chumbucket talking to you with the same lines over and over

I really enjoyed the story, as i think it was thrilling to watch Max become less the mad man he was. There is also an issue i have with this game. You never really feel that you'll run out of water. You never feel that you'll run out of gas. It doesn't really make you feel like you're in a dire situation. After a few hours of playing this game, i could just teleport to a stronghold, and get water. I really enjoyed this game, and i really recommend it. Finally Warner Bros. didn't come out with a game only half finished. Nice job!
If i had to rate it would be a 9/10!

After beating Life is Strange (LIS) and realizing it's one of those rare games I genuinely love, I knew I wanted more but didn't really think I would get it. So when Before The Storm (BTS) was announced, I pre-ordered the deluxe version as soon as possible.
So how did it turn out? Well, I’ll separate my review with a summary and then the full detailed review.
The summary is that it’s a good game, but highly flawed.
The game starts strong with episode 01, but weakens dramatically with each episode. By the end, it meanders along weakly with what feels like shoehorned subplots and far too much drama from too many different angles. I didn’t feel like the game focused as much on building the relationship between Chloe/Rachel as it should have and it ended up feeling unnatural.
Aside from that, there were technical issues. Controllers never worked properly and the game had an issue with dialogue cutting out near the last one or two words. This was present in the first episode, but got worse in later episodes.
Overall, I recommend Before The Storm only if you’ve played and are a fan of Life is Strange. Unfortunately, the game just isn’t strong enough to stand on its own and a big part of its appeal lies in its connection to the first game. As a game, I would rate it perhaps 6/10.
Now then, that is the summary, I’ll now provide the detailed review.
I want to talk about the gameplay first. Much of Before The Storm (BTS) remained unchanged from Life is Strange. The graphical quality, the method of story telling, and the gameplay mechanics are all very similar. There are some notable differences, though.
The biggest of this is that there is a new gameplay mechanic called ‘Backtalk’. The original LIS uses time travel as a gameplay gimmick, but BTS uses Backtalk -- a title for her simply becoming verbally aggressive and argumentative in order to get her way. What happens is that when players initiate 'Backtalk', they then have to direct the conversation using word cues as clues in order to help Chloe achieve her aim. The conversation is time-limited so players do have to make a choice quickly.
Personally, I'm not a fan of the new 'Backtalk' mode. Generally, when playing story-driven games, I absolutely do not like being rushed for any reason when deciding the flow of conversations. Furthermore, it’s unfortunate, but much of the Backtalk dialogue is a little childish. This, I suppose, is the point due to the main character being a young teen, but it wears thin quickly.
So, for me, 'Backtalk' mode is actually more of a negative.
Now the other thing I wanted to touch on that is different from LIS is, of course, the story. BTS is now focused on what was the deuteragonist of LIS, Chloe Price, and the story now revolves around her life and how she met LIS' mystery character, Rachel Amber. I've wanted to learn about Rachel for a while, so this was a big positive for me. Plus, some of LIS’ other characters make an appearance and it’s a real treat to see how they differ.
However, I’ll be frank here. The story is weak.
It starts strong with episode 01 which presents a good premise, introduction, and builds up suspense/characters, but then the story weakens significantly by episode 02 then weakens even further with episode 03.
This isn’t entirely Deck Nine’s fault. Unfortunately, they’re heavily constrained by the fact that this is a prequel and it must connect with the future story, so they can’t be too outrageous with in-game events.
However, what is their fault is that the game’s plot had been greatly weakened due to a meandering plot featuring subplots which seem to go nowhere. Furthermore, I think the game made a mistake by trying to push drama buttons from too many different directions instead of focusing on the development of Chloe/Rachel. By the end, I actually felt like the relationship between Chloe/Rachel still feels kind of forced instead of natural. They didn’t get enough development between each other.
The ending was one of one of the worst aspect of the plot, but I won’t talk about it due to avoiding spoilers. I will say, though, that it completely lacked any strength.
Finally, the last issue I had that really brought the game down. The technical issues. Now it seems like everybody had some kind of issue with the game, but the issues I had were limited to two aspects: The controller and audio.
The first issue and the one that drives me up the wall the most is the lack of proper controller support. Unlike almost every other game, BTS does not properly support xinput controller (e.g. Xbox controller). Instead, what you have to do is configure Steam’s controller support to use a controller and, even then, not all functions are supported.
That is outrageous. Games been coming with controller support since 2011~ and the original LIS also had proper support. How is it that this game does not? Deck Nine had released a patch that tackles the issue, but it seems to have made no difference at all.
Another issue I wanted to bring up is the sound. That is there appears to be an issue with some conversations cutting off (last one or two words) near the end. It doesn’t affect all conversations, but enough of them for you to notice that it’s a problem. This was present in all episodes, but it actually becomes worse with newer episodes.
That is even more outrageous. As a narrative game – a game you play almost entirely for the story and characters – dialogue is literally one of the primary aspects of the game. It should be one of the main things that developer pay attention to and absolutely ensure it is working 100%. If it doesn’t, it should be fixed as soon as possible.
Now, I’ve been experiencing both of these issues since the beginning, but I was patient and kind enough to decide not to judge the game on these complaints until all three episodes were released. That gave the developer some four months to get the issues resolved.
However, when the final episode was released, the issues remained present, and that brought my judgment.
So overall, BTS is a decently good game that has a lot of problems which I mentioned above. Do I regret pre-ordering it with all the goodies I can get? No.
I said that I loved the original LIS and I genuinely wanted to learn more about the story and characters. So even if I had knew beforehand I would have these issues, I would have bought it (even the deluxe edition) anyway. Probably for the same price anyway.
However, this doesn’t mean BTS earns my full recommendation. I can only recommend this game to others who also loved the original Life is Strange. This game really isn’t strong enough to stand on its own.
Ultimately, I would rate it a 6/10 on a scale.

This is going to be a very unorthodox review, because I firmly believe that the less you know about the content of this game, the more you will enjoy it. The biggest mistake I ever made in Undertale was choosing to watch a playthrough of it on Youtube.
I'll start with a little history behind this game. Undertale was released in Fall 2015 and developed almost exclusively by Toby Fox. He loves Earthbound and this game was somewhat inspired by it. Since its release it has gained what I can only describe as a die-hard cult following. This game has had a much bigger effect on people than anyone expected. It got rave reviews from several gaming publications, and Destructiod and IGN both gave it a perfect score. It went on to win the Gamefaqs user-driven "Best Game Ever" award, beating out many timeless classics and popular games like GTA 5 and Skyrim. There are endless amounts of Undertale related fan art, comics, videos, songs, and other tributes all over the web.
Anyway, enough about that.

When I first saw the MS Paint graphics of this game, I was disgusted. I skipped past Undertale in my Steam queue thinking it was just another piece of indie garbage. About a year later I was convinced to actually try the game. I was wrong about the graphics. They are perfectly fine, and don't hurt the game at all. In fact, I've grown rather fond of them.
The soundtrack is pure genius  and I love it. Toby does some things with the music in this game that are just crazy. You have to play through the whole thing to understand what I mean. I would be more specific in explaining why I love it so much, but that would spoil the surprize.
Undertale fixes everything wrong with turn-based battle systems. Having a normal text-based menu plus the ability to dodge attacks makes it so much more engaging, since you actually get to
during your opponent's turn. Try out the demo and see for yourself. The overworld is a typical overworld for the most part.
The story is at the heart of this game, and it is wonderfully integrated into all of the above categories. The basic premise of the story, if you don't know already, is this: there is a human world and a monster world. One day, a human child accidentally falls into the monster world, known as the underground. They begin a fantastical journey through the underground, and meet people along the way. I'll stop there, because spoiling this story is like telling a four year old there is no santa claus.

Rogue Legacy, is a rogue-like which means - permadeath, randomly generated content, being hard-as-nails.
Is it good?
Indeed it is. It's a 2-d platformer in which you must defeat 4 bosses to face the last one.
But you won't be able to do that with the first of your line...
You will die, and when you will die - you will choose your heir, choosing them by class and traits, as they are the ones the you will play as next.
You collect gold, and when you die, you will be able to upgrade your castle, armour and equip runes to help your next character survive. Better spend it all, because the gatekeeper guarding the door to your goal, will take the rest ( or a significant amount if you leveled a specific section of a castle ).
Game is hard but fair, simplistic but still challenging and very often it invokes the "just one more run" aspect.
It also is very tongue-in-cheek.
Recommended, that's for certain.

There are a lot of interesting things to be said in favor of, or against war. Sadly Spec Ops: The Line does neither, opting instead for the childishly obvious: War is hell, people die, corpses are ugly. Dr Phil would be proud.

Many have dissected, analyzed, and downright devoured Spec Ops: The Line. Many theories have been concocted regarding the game's complex and incredibly disturbing narrative. But only one thing is certain: The Line is the most mature, intelligent, and introspective video game ever created. I would go as far as to call it the first post-modern video game ever made.
It is, thus far, the only video game in existence that manages to ask so many questions of the player in such unbelievably subtle and imperceptible ways. It may be the first video game that truly is about something. And not only is it the only video game that truly made me question my perception of reality, it's also the only video game that made me truly question the ending I chose. But did I actually choose at all?
Well, whatever Spec Ops: The Line is, it's well worth the price of admittance. The gameplay can be lackluster, at times (it's still very much playable and enjoyable, though), but the profound and compelling story more than makes up for any of its faults.

Excellent story that makes you think about the consequences of war combined with difficult moral choices and great action. On the down side: Campaing only lasts about 7hrs but it does have some replay value since you have multiple ways of dealing with situations.

A pretty average shooter altogether. A couple weapons, a very limited squad tactical feature, and a brilliant yet underused mechanic including sand - explosions lift sand clouds that make it really hard to shoot precisely, sandstorms make targeting near impossible, environment allows you to bury your enemies - so many options, yet I saw so little of it. A shame. The gameplay is enjoyable, but not innovative or fantastic in any way. But it's not the gameplay you should be looking at: it's the story and character development that's groundbreaking. To say anything would ruin your experience, but let's leave it at "While it starts as a normal TPS, there's a clear turning point after which this game will repeatedly make you question yourself as a gamer and, maybe, as a person.". Character development of this magnitude in a genre like this is one of a kind. Pay attention to Cpt. Walker. Not just his looks, but his attitude, even during gameplay.Yes, this game takes the care to show you story and character not only during cutscenes. By the end of the game, you will be shocked at the change. By the way, the sand-filled landscape of Dubai is drop-dead gorgeous.
It's difficult to talk about this game without spoiling it's major selling point. EVERYTHING has a meaning not immediatly evident. Even the STOP sign you see at the beginning of the game. I don't care if you put this game on Easy and brush through it in 4 or 5 hours: just play it. Pay attention. And once you're done, think about it.

This is without a doubt my pick for best action game of 2012 and easily top 5 games of 2012 overall. The negative reviews for this are ridiculous and alot of them have to do with the admittedly tacked on multiplayer which actually is decent if you can even find a game. This is the best story in a video game since Bioshock and if this game was a movie, every scene would be remembered as iconic. The characters are written flawlessly, the dialogie is top notch and the environment which is in itself a character is beautiful and always has something to take your gaze which is saying a lot seeing as how the game is set entirely in a desert. The clever use of sand as a weapon or even an equalizer in the form of a blinding sandstorm to transform an open area into a tense close quarters nerve-fest are innovative and show just how skilled the level designers are at making excellent level after excellent level. The graphics are eye-candy and run very well on my mid-grade laptop at high settings. the controls are the only thing i would mark this off for as some things like using space bar to run and cover with no easy way of canceling mid-sprint a-la Mass Effect stink of clumsy console port but they aren't game breaking as the difficulty on normal is just forgiving enough to make you want to avoid bullets like they were... well bullets  but still make you feel your failures. Luckily though, checkpoints are frequent enough. All in all if I were in the business of giving numerical scores this would get an 8.5/10 from me marked down only because of slightly clumsy controls and a tacked albeit decent but dead multiplayer mode. One last word of advice: the story is the best part of this game so try not to look up any spoilers. This game will make you feel real emotion and have you make very difficult decisions that will result in multiple endings and the choices are varied enough that I played through several times to experience each outcome and loved every one.

What is this game?
Mad Max is a post apocalyptic open world action game. It involves a lot of driving around in the barren wastelands, and finding camps to take down, scarecrows to destroy and many more things. The games main character is Max. Max is a man who lost it all. After your car is destroyed, and you have nothing, you meet Chumbucket. A lunatic liing in the wasteland, worshipping a divine spirit called the "Angel Combustion". Together with him you upgrade your Magnum Opus (A car) and your final goal is reaching the Planes Of Silence.
Pros and Cons
Pros:
+Great driving mechanics
+Good combat
+Storyline is good as well
+Super good optimized (i could play it at 30 fps with my geforce 840 m)
+The capture mode
Cons:
-Game can get a bit repetitive after you completed the story and side missions
-Chumbucket talking to you with the same lines over and over

I really enjoyed the story, as i think it was thrilling to watch Max become less the mad man he was. There is also an issue i have with this game. You never really feel that you'll run out of water. You never feel that you'll run out of gas. It doesn't really make you feel like you're in a dire situation. After a few hours of playing this game, i could just teleport to a stronghold, and get water. I really enjoyed this game, and i really recommend it. Finally Warner Bros. didn't come out with a game only half finished. Nice job!

If you're thinking about getting DayZ know these things:
1.) What's the point?
There's not really a "point" or "goal" to this game. Once you get yourself decently kitted out with military grade equipment, you'll regularly find yourself asking, "What do I do now." Your options are somewhat limited. You can survive, try and repair a car (which requires one to scoure the map for parts - none of which are ever found in one city), PK, or get PKed - neither of which (PKing or getting PKed), mind you, carry any sort of meaningful consequences or reward.
If you find yourself getting PKed, typically, it will occur not long after you spawn a new character. Being slain as a Bambi (fresh spaw) wouldn't be so frustrating if you were reasonably geared. However, those PKing you are almonst never fresh spawns, they are players who have obviously exerted some effort to acquire the game's "high-end" gear. I guess that's the "ego" reward for some people - i.e. - the feeling of beating up on fresh spawns that haven't the slightest chance of countering your attacks. The game offers some interesting options for capturing or "toturing" players, but if you get captured (handcuffed, tied up, etc..) you might as well just respawn because you're basically dead. All this to say, currently, it's not very fun.
2.) Combatting the combat controls.
Fresh spawn combat is tenuous, at best, and frustratingly annoying, at worst. Hit mechanics for melee weapons, which is what you'll find yourself with as a fresh spawn, have extremely frustrating and non-intuitive range of motions. This frequently leads to situations where you are fighting the controls more than other players or zombies. Until you come to grips with the awkward melee combat, swinging where your reticle is pointed, is not only futile, but will regularly cause you to die. Even when your attacks appear to be spot on, you'll still miss either because of distance, or angle. Gunplay is not much better, if you're in the third person mode, you might as well pray and spray, because you don't have a chance. First person is slightly better, but still not that great.
While the zombies are not especially hard to kill, if you managed to attract the attention of one, inadvertently, and you have no weapon to defend yourself, be prepared to run. When I say run, you're running for a good 2 to 3 minutes, if not longer, before they drop their lock on you. You can try to hide, and sometimes you can, but while you're running and/or hiding your vitals - hunger, thirst and warmth, will slowly begin to tick down.
3.) Suriving is half the battle.
You are required to eat, drink and stay warm. Food is somewhat of a rarity. If you're lucky, when you spawn, you'll be nearby some apple trees to get a quick blast of food and some liquid. Apples, like some of the canned foods you can find in the game, provide both food and water. They are a good first point for fresh spawns, but not always in abundance. If you are unable to find a well, apples or other source of food, you may find yourself with a food borne affliction because you had to drink pond water, or you had to eat worms.
Currently, there are no ways to shake food borne illnesses even though there are antibiotic bottles and vitamins that spawn all over the map. If you are lucky and contract a food borne illnes once you are established, you can sometimes shake it off if you are well fed and hydrated. However, eating worms and drinking pond water are not the only ways to get food borne bacteria. If you undercook, or stupidly, overcook your food (chicken for instance) you're gonna get sick. The only way to tell if a chicken breast is grilled to perfection is by the color of it. The only way to know what color you should be aiming for is to look online for information. There are so many crafting recipes, it's nearly impossible to know them all, making "alt+tab" one of your most important key combinations in the game.
4.) Looting and navigation.
There's lots of loot in the game, but none if it is especially well explained. Want to learn how to craft items? You better get ready to "alt-tab." Likewise, want to know how to get to an army base? Better get ready to pull up a map from the internet. I understand to some extent (realism factor) why these knowledge of these things are not included. However, there's a difference between what's fun on paper, and what's fun in practice. Having to constantly pull yourself out of an immersive experience to understand how to make a fire, which you will have to do if you get wet from rain or want to cook meat, know where you're located, or any number of other things, could have been facilitated in game. The devs created the toys, so let us have fun with them in a way that doesn't constnatly require removing yourself from the experience to check third party websites.
5.) Last thoughts.
Admittedly, there is a lot of potential with this game, and it's still in Alpha, so how critically you want to take my feedback is up to you. Maybe there are grander plans that we are not privy to yet.
Some things that I would like to see implemented:
*Make  being "good" or "bad" meaningful in some manner - If there was some sort of incentive for people to be, or not to be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s (reputation, stat bonuses, something...) it would be a great improvement. There are some servers that have safe/trade zones. These are quite fun to play in, but they still regularly get their fair share of fresh spawn slaying. I'm all for creating your own adventure, but even in the earliest days of MMORPGs, Ultima Online specifically, there consequences and bonuses that shaped your interactions with the world and with other players around you. For instance, if you are PKer, you'd be flagged with a red name, to give players an idea of your standing in the world. You'd also earn "glamour titles" to reflect your playstyle - "notorious," "blood-thirsty," etc...people could have bounties placed on them, and it would also affect your interactions with npcs. While I know there are no npcs and this is not an MMORPG, perhaps there could be some consequence for how the zombies interact with you, or animals of the world respond to you.
*Get rid of the useless items and abilities - teddy bears, books, gardening, charcoal tabs, lockpicks? They curently do nothing for the game. Unless there's a robust implementation plan for these items, cut the crap and add features that will be meaningful and fun for players. There may be plans for these items in the future, but if there are, they have not been explained.
*Improved melee combat - If you are handicapped at the beginning and are forced to interact (read: battle) with players with better gear, at least make hitting someone with a fireaxe as devastating as getting shot with a handgun. Not many people I know could survive a hit with the sharp end of an axe, but a bullet seems much more reasonable to survive. It comes down to risk reward - you're taking much more risk going in with a melee, so make the reward (damage) higher to reflect this.
In spite of all this criticism, I still play DayZ with somewhat regular frequency. In it's current state, I can't really recommend it to anyone, as games like Battlegrounds: Players Unknown are just better. However, do look forward to the future and hope the devs add content that will provide the best experience for players.

Awesome wasteland simulator 2015! Ride shiny and chrome into Valhalla with the Magnum Opus V8!

I expected explosions, I expected epic car combat, I expected brutal combat and a harsh world, I got it all.
Gameplay feels very solid, performance is GREAT, you can litterally run this on max with a potato, graphics fits very well with the wasteland feel. I had tons of fun with this game with a few nitpicks which I will write below.
You start out with nothing, your legendary v8 Interceptor is stolen from you and you want it back! You drive around the wasteland scouring for scraps and blueprints to upgrade your new car, the Magnus Opus. To get car upgrades, rewards and good amounts of scraps, you will have to do certain things like destroying scarecrows or wiping out camps in the different areas. This can get a little repetive but the locations all have different designs, and by doing said things you get some badass upgrades for your Magnus Opus which makes it rewarding.
Pros:
+Excellent Performance.
+Great graphics.
+Great gameplay.
+Sandstorms are epic.
+Races with leaderboards and different modes
+Convoys are great fun, feels very much like mad max.
+The world has many interesting locations, specially in a certain sandy area.
+History Relics are interesting and I really enjoyed the dialogue that max says when he looks at the photos.
+Photo mode for screenshot enthusiasts ♥♥♥♥♥yeah).
Mixed:
-+The tasks in the zones feel a bit repetive, but they are all designed differently which makes most of them interesting.
-+Story is a bit shallow early on but I got very engaged towards the end, nice buildup and imo a great conclusion.
-+Thunderpoon makes the game feel super easy.
-+If you have the friendly camps fully upgraded, you will refill all your ammo, fuel, health, water every time you fast travel or visit a friendly camp which removes a bit of the survival feel of saving your bullets and eating maggots to survive.
Cons:
-Minefields.
-Random people you find in the world that you talk to, they feel shallow and when speaking to them you are frozen and can't move, so be prepared for yourself and the other person to get pancaked into the dust over and over again.
-Scavenging locations, there are like 3-4 locations that I remember after finishing the game, (I did them all) they just feel like a grind.
-Some areas can be a maze, mountain areas in particular, where you have locations that are hidden inside a mountain and you need to drive around 10 times to find the entrance.
Is the game worth a buy? definitely, I've had tons of fun with this game and would recommend it to anyone who asks.

Despite the name, it's difficult to call this game a "Roguelike" as the only things it has in common with Rogue is that the dungeons are randomly generated and you die a lot. That said, it's one of the most enjoyable hack-n'-slash platformers I've ever played and for anyone who enjoys that style of gameplay you simply can't pass this one up!
Awesome, fluid gameplay, good music, well designed, plenty of character features and upgrades, several classes to unlock, none of which are horribly unbalanced, very simple to use system for equipment and special abilities, legitimately difficult bosses.
Extremely difficult overall, somewhat repetitive, doesn't really have the "loot" aspect you would expect from a dungeon crawl (not to the same extent of randomly generated items anyways), occasionally you'll be forced to play as a character with lousy attributes.

A Rogue-LITE SHMUP/Platformer meatgrinder.  This is not a true to form roguelike...even on the level of FTL or Binding of Issac where each playthrough is a self-contained journey to greatness or fatalistic doom where knowledge gained is the progression.  On the contrary,  your past heroes directly fund future hero successes.  And you will be stacking dead heroes a mountain high before surmounting the dungeons and taking on the grand foozle.

Rogue Legacy is great, great great great. Its one of the few games where you can genuinely just play for 5 minutes a time or sit and play through for hours, mainly due to dying/restarting on a nicely regular basis without it being an annoyance (aka, like all good rogue-likes). Its a challenge and a half, for the first 5-10 hours it is just crushing apocalyptic despair of the game just crushing you into the floor whenever it gets a chance, that's basically every time you think you've got used to an area then you head somewhere else and it's a whole new hammer being smashed across your face.
One downside is personally I feel once completing the game, if you want to carry on playing still the challenge is cranked up by about 900%, the old hit once and its dead enemies take many many hits to bring down it brings the learning curve to an overhang as nothing in the game (except bosses) are as strong as the enemies are now.
However up until that point the game feels well implemented in terms of the challenge vs. the overall learning curve, so overall, really great!
Did I say it was great? Well it was.
10/10 buy it now

This is a game that after beating the first episode, the next thing that passes through your head is "♥♥♥♥ it, lets beat it TWICE". The choices of this series of Life is Strange feels more respected than the first chapter (Max Clauflield as protagonist), the transition from Unreal to the Unity engine was executed perfectly; the game's frame per second and the monitor's 60Hz refresh rate pays off nicely, the cartoon-ish textures still look beautiful (even improved), the lip sync annimations have completely been overhauled, which was one of the things that was criticized a lot from it's predecessor (or successor since it's a prequel?)
While I'd like to talk about the characters, I feel like it's too early to make a conclusion out of it yet, since it's only one episode of out three. While yes, you could look at the first game, but of course, Chloe was not the protagonist.
Overall, the episode is a fantastic start to an already promising franchise. This game will NOT disappoint you.
9.8/10
Pros
+Smooth transition from Unreal to Unity Engine
+Those who said a prequel wasn't neccessary were proven spectacularly wrong
+Overall improved environment, in about every aspect
+Great effort to keep the same voice of Chloe, with a different actor.
+Better lip sync annimations
+Choices you make have concequences, finally.
+Replay value
+Less amount of millennial style language (The first series, omg :/ )
+Great characters
Cons
- idk
Conclusion: Sorry if I sound biased, but trust me, you'll love the game. :DDDD

From the perspective of pure gameplay, Spec Ops: The Line is merely a decent cover-based shooter, with a variety of weapons and conveniently placed chest-high walls aplenty. However, from a narrative perspective I do believe it is one of the few (and perhaps the only) military shooter that forces the player to come face to face with the most dreadful and frankly nauseating consequences of their actions.
I am sorely tempted to spoil it for everyone reading this because it had -that- much impact, however I don't want to lessen that selfsame impact for those that will play the game. And you -should- play this game, because it has something to say.
This is one of the few shooters that doesn't make you feel like a cartoon character fighting faceless evil and if you have a heart it will be broken.

This is definitely one of my top games of 2012, and probably the most compelling singleplayer campaign in a purely shooter game I have ever seen. I think the lousy metacritic rating is ridiculous, but you should definitely pick it up!

I've been playing this game for a while now (granted having played since little more than a year is nothing compared some others, as well as 250+ hours of play time). It started as a game I bought just to have something to play with my friends (who were having the wildest adventures to listen to in TeamSpeak). I had no idea what I was up to, not even knowing what DayZ was all about other then it beeing a Survival-Type of game (with Zombies). "If you die, you lose everything" I've been told (It's true). After a rough start, many encounters with other players (most of them tried and managed to kill me), many many many deaths through various reasons and said 250+ hours of staying in Chernarus I've decided to give my opinion about this game (current Patch 0.62).
Pro:
+ Huge world with (almost) no boundaries.
+ Though it seems to be simple the System itself is very complex (Health, Hunger, Thirst, Bone-Stats, Shock, Loot-System, Shooting) [I recommend to check out WOBO's Youtube-Channel*, he helped me a lot to understand how DayZ works].
+ Fairly good view distance (though details drop off very quick).
+ The Immersion is great despite those Zombies (Light- and Soundeffects, Wind and its effects on trees and smoke for example [Since 0.62]).
(+ If there's any value to it: Sometimes it's so calming and peaceful just wandering around)
Con:
- Slow development Cycle (It's true, a good wine needs time to age well, but this doesn't apply to games while still beeing alpha).
- KOS (Kill on Sight) is still prevalent, even though I feel like more and more people tend to be friendlier (what doesn't mean they won't kill you, but rather they talk to you and then kill you if they think you've got something of interest - C'est la vie).
- Still full of glitches, buggs and lag-spikes (It keeps improving and YES it's just normal in an alpha but still ...[I hate this damn apple glitch, it makes survival way easier if you don't need to worry about finding food and water - as apples give both - and just run up to the next appletree])
- Beginners will have a hard time getting the hang of it (If it hadn't been with my friends, my first hours of the game would've consisted of me starving, dieing of thirst, and generaly have no idea what to loot and how to shoot [No seriously, only thanks to DayZ I practised shooting in videogames in general]).
In all honesty now that I'm writing this review, I understand, why many are drawn away from DayZ. Promisses not keepen, tiny evolution steps compared to a slow development, KOS, glitches, buggs and yes sometimes just running around looting or sitting and waiting for something to happen (for someone to come around so you can shoot them for example) can and will be boring. This game needs a lot of work until it's finished.
And still I have to say, the most boring moments in gaming to me happend in DayZ, but also the most exciting ones as well (alone and together with friends). It's undescribable, how thrilling it is to have a gunfight with other players, or to be curing your illness (in my case: Cholera) sitting within a forest just to hear a car driving by followed by gunshots.
Why i still recommend this game?
Not only for its potential, but for what it has become in the (granted short) time that I've been playing it. I look at ArmA3 Mods, at other (Zombie-)Survival-Games, but to me DayZ (despite its flaws) makes so much right, that I'm willing to stick through another wave of KOSers, glitches, running around for hours and uncounted deaths, so that I can once more feel the thrill and joy of surviving all this and I wish for others to have the same amount of fun like I do, too.
Give DayZ a try, you won't regret it, I surely didn't.

I expected explosions, I expected epic car combat, I expected brutal combat and a harsh world, I got it all.
Gameplay feels very solid, performance is GREAT, you can litterally run this on max with a potato, graphics fits very well with the wasteland feel. I had tons of fun with this game with a few nitpicks which I will write below.
You start out with nothing, your legendary v8 Interceptor is stolen from you and you want it back! You drive around the wasteland scouring for scraps and blueprints to upgrade your new car, the Magnus Opus. To get car upgrades, rewards and good amounts of scraps, you will have to do certain things like destroying scarecrows or wiping out camps in the different areas. This can get a little repetive but the locations all have different designs, and by doing said things you get some badass upgrades for your Magnus Opus which makes it rewarding.
Pros:
+Excellent Performance.
+Great graphics.
+Great gameplay.
+Sandstorms are epic.
+Races with leaderboards and different modes
+Convoys are great fun, feels very much like mad max.
+The world has many interesting locations, specially in a certain sandy area.
+History Relics are interesting and I really enjoyed the dialogue that max says when he looks at the photos.
+Photo mode for screenshot enthusiasts ♥♥♥♥♥yeah).
Mixed:
-+The tasks in the zones feel a bit repetive, but they are all designed differently which makes most of them interesting.
-+Story is a bit shallow early on but I got very engaged towards the end, nice buildup and imo a great conclusion.
-+Thunderpoon makes the game feel super easy.
-+If you have the friendly camps fully upgraded, you will refill all your ammo, fuel, health, water every time you fast travel or visit a friendly camp which removes a bit of the survival feel of saving your bullets and eating maggots to survive.
Cons:
-Minefields.
-Random people you find in the world that you talk to, they feel shallow and when speaking to them you are frozen and can't move, so be prepared for yourself and the other person to get pancaked into the dust over and over again.
-Scavenging locations, there are like 3-4 locations that I remember after finishing the game, (I did them all) they just feel like a grind.
-Some areas can be a maze, mountain areas in particular, where you have locations that are hidden inside a mountain and you need to drive around 10 times to find the entrance.
Is the game worth a buy? definitely, I've had tons of fun with this game and would recommend it to anyone who asks.
