The genre of this one is RPG roguelike 2d platformer. I have seen so many reviews of people comparing this to the Binding of Issac. ♥♥♥♥ those reviews, this is nothing like that game. The only thing they have in common is that each run is different.
In Rogue Legacy, you are basically running around in a castle collecting as much money as you can (for your legacy) and killing monsters (for yourself). Each time you enter the castle, it is different inside. Once dead, you must choose a new heir (1 of 3) to explore the castle. Everyone is different. Everyone has a unique name, a class, a gender, and random attributes that make them unique. The money you earn goes to that heir and is used for purchases of items/upgrades/unlocks and must be used before going into the castle. What you choose to purchase stays for every character (equipable items can be switched/unequipped). Everyone gets 1 life to live. There are some small exceptions to things I've mentioned, but that's via unlocks anyway.
Get a controller for this game! This game definately rewards you for playing it often.

Like the name implies, Rogue Legacy is basically a rogue-like platformer. Let me state now that if you get frustrated easily or are an impatient individual, then this is NOT the game for you. However, if you enjoy a challenging, difficult/semi-casual game, then you should definitely check out this game. The best feature of this game to me is that most of your time is spent earning gold to upgrade your characters. So basically never-ending character progression. It is scaled though in that every time you buy an upgrade or piece of equipment, the other upgrades you didn't initially choose very slightly increase in price. It is in this way that Rogue Legacy promotes a setting that allows you to continuously work harder to get better, one little upgrade at a time that does not seem impossible or overwhelming.
The game does have a nice balance feature to it. Before you go into the next randomized Dungeon, you must pay up the gold you have left in your possession after upgrading to "Charon" (he really looks a lot like a cloaked grim reaper...). This is necessary unless you buy a few upgrades to where you only have to pay a significant portion but still keep some of your gold upon entering. Also, you can stabilize the dungeon by acquiring an architect in the game, but this will cost you 40% of the gold you would normally earn within the dungeon to do so. Therefore, the game presents a nice challenging cost/benefit scenario to the player. Lastly, I'd like to address the characters you will be playing as and their unique abilities/features. Every time you die, he next child in line will be who you ultimately play as in the next dungeon run-through. However, you can select from 1 of 3 various and randomized characters. Now when I say random, I mean it. Gender, abilities, spells, physical features, mental aspects, etc.--ALL randomized. You could have a gay female paladin who has irritable bowel syndrome with a blade summoning spell to a male assassin with dwarfism and hypergonadism (look it up), with a spell that throws giant spike balls at enemies (the irony is thick). What I'm trying to emphasize here is that every single playthrough is inherently different, and the player must adapt and change their gameplay style to match what they judged to be the best character they selected for the next dungeon runthrough.
With so many choices available to the player, you can expect Rogue Legacy to accrue several hours of play time in your daily lives. If you like Indie games with intentional imbalance aspects (such as the Binding of Isaac), then I believe you will quite enjoy Rogue Legacy as well. I found myself feeling a mixture of humor, frustration, anxiousness, excitement, and joy as i played. So essentially this is highly addictive, adaptive, challenging, and a ton of fun. So what are ya waiting for? It's time to start poppin' out the most random heroes the fantasy world has ever seen nonstop for generations to come.
This game is HARD, but in a good way. Each playthrough gets more addicting than the last, and earning more money than your previous run is satisfying. Just expect to die, A LOT.

I liked this game enough to play it 70+ hrs and get every achievement. Having paid full price on pre-order, I still feel that I got most of my money's worth out of it in enjoyment. That being said, if you get the game on discount you will probably feel better about the purchase afterwards.
The themes of post-apocaliptia, scavenging for limited resources and exploring the ruins of a bygone era all things that appeal to me as a fan of the Mad Max world. The added bonus of vehicular mayhem with a somewhat customizeable car certainly adds alot of potential fun factor.
What this game does right:
- Stylistic atmosphere and graphics (lighting, smoke effects, wind and dust, explosions... good stuff)
- Crazy car vs. car combat with limited adherence to real world physics makes for a fun arcade feel
- Varied, but not overly difficult ground combat, with multiple ways (with skill upgrades) to eliminate enemies in gloriously brutal fashion
- Colorful and interesting NPC character models
- Varied enemy types and their respective combat techniques and day/night appearance of alternate enemies keeps fights from feeling overly repetitive
- Making each location to explore unique enough that the numerous "fetch-quests" give you reason to really explore the open world provided without it growing too stale
- Opportunity to race your car in "Death Races"
- Mostly good in-game engine cutscenes
- 60fps highly optimized PC Port (with minor menu flubs)
Where this game falls short:
- This game is crazy easy for any mildly experienced gamer
- No pressure for survival as all resources are abundant and/or need is completely nullified through game progress
- Limited story provides no real opportunity to become attached to main character or any NPC
- Apart from achievement, no reason at all to do "Death Races" since rewards are nil/laughable
- Mixing and matching car upgrades is pointless... best is best, period
- In-game currency of "scrap" is so abundant and easy to acquire that intermediate character and car upgrades could easily be bypassed for top quality gear too early in gameplay providing no feel of progression
- Limited or no tutorialistic explanation of simple game elements (how to quickly abort a failed race run or progress in the story) leads to avoidable web-searching frustration
- Major bosses feel extremely "cookie-cutter" in a boring way
- One really stupid and nonsensical cutscene (if you play, you'll see it)
Overall, the game had a fair balance of pros & cons that neither made nor ruined the game for me. Play this game for the atmosphere and the arcade style simplicity. Don't play this game for the story or the survival aspect. This is a casual game with ZERO replayability. Purchase with hefty discount is reccomended.

Prison Architect is 'different' to most strategy games out there. It is still an alpha (15/06/2014) however the game seems almost completed! The game has so much potential-some of which it has already forfillled. The glitches, such as prisoners remain seated and act as normal when a deadly fire is in the room, make the game hilarious and laughable. Even if it is an alpha it does what a game is ment to do; entertain you. It isnt severly incompleted. Eveything in the game works flawlessly-most of the time-and you forget it is an alpha. Also there are fun glitches/things, e.g. the prisons sit on the blade of a saw in the workshop as they are using it, the prison jail doors get overwhelmed with people trying to get through and the guards can't open it for them so for hours your prisons are waiting at a door!
The gamemakers (introversion softwere) also go very in-depth with detain in some parts of the game. An example of this is the attention to detail to the prisons. Each is given a name, picture, list of convictions e.g. how many years served (and what for) and how many years to serve(and what for), also family, security level, #ref number, recent status, activity, mood, condition, experiance, punishment/security grading, bio and more. You can also make your own character by purchasing the 'Name in Game' upgrade dcl which allows you to create your own character which could even be based on you with your name!
The only complaint I have is the price, especially of the 'Name in Game' upgrade dcl. I find that £15 for your name and bio in-game isnt worth £15. And that's just for name in the game, if you want the game as well it is just short of £35. The game (only) is £20. This game does not have good graphic qualitly however for a game like this you don't want nor need it as the graphics suit the game perfectly.
Overall, it is a great game and introversion have done well-so far. I would reccormend you buy this games as if you like strategy, organisation and building this game is perfect. It is worth the £20 sale price. I would also highly recommend you upgrade the game with the 'Name in Game' dcl ONLY DURING A SALE(personally £15 is over-expensive). This is an exellant game with everything I would expect in it and more. I cannot wait to see what the game developers have instore in the next update! (Alpha 22) Great game-buy it!

Idk what to write, so here is a recipe on fried Human...
INGREDIENTS
4 tablespoons kosher salt
3 tablespoons freshly ground black pepper
2 tablespoons ground cayenne pepper
2 teaspoons garlic powder
2 teaspoons onion powder
1 teaspoon dry mustard powder
2 cups all-purpose flour
8 chicken drumsticks
4 cups buttermilk
Canola oil, for frying
DIRECTIONS
Mix the salt, pepper, cayenne pepper, garlic powder, onion powder and dry mustard powder together in a bowl. Divide the spices evenly between 2 mixing bowls. Add the flour to 1 of the bowls, mix well, and set aside.
Rub the Human drumsticks with the reserved spice mix. Poke all of the pieces with a fork a few times to let the flavors seep down into the meat. Set aside.
Pour the buttermilk over the Human, and cover the bowl with plastic wrap. Refrigerate for at least 1 hour. Cook's Note: You can also let the Human marinate longer, even overnight.
Add the flour mixture to a large re-sealable plastic bag. Remove the humanpieces from the buttermilk and in batches, drop them into the bag, shaking them to make sure they become heavily coated.
In a large heavy-bottomed saucepan, pour enough oil to fill the pan about a third of the way. Heat over medium heat until a deep-frying thermometer inserted in the oil reaches 360 degrees F. (If you don't have a thermometer, a cube of bread will brown in about 3 minutes.)
Drop the coated human drumsticks into the hot oil. Turn the pieces as they brown and do not let them touch each other while frying. Work in batches, if necessary check the underside of a piece by lifting it with tongs. It should be a deep golden brown. Cook the human until the pieces are crispy and brown, about 15 minutes, turning occasionally.
To test for doneness: Cut into the thickest part of a drumstick. The juices should run clear and the meat should be opaque throughout. If necessary, pop the  human into a preheated 325 degree F oven, until they are fully cooked.
Transfer the fried  human to a paper towel-lined baking sheet to drain the excess oil.
Transfer the drumsticks onto a serving platter, or put into a bucket. Serve the human hot, room temperature, or cold.

Another of my favorite games on Steam. This game has everything I like all wrapped up into 1 game. It is a roguelike game, so expect to die a lot. I usually don't like roguelikes, but this game added the most important part of enjoyment for me; being able to upgrade your character after every run. You have a castle that you upgrade with all the gold you earned from your last run. These upgrades consist of making your character's statistics better and all sorts of different things related to the game. This makes every run feel worthwhile to me, instead of having to start at basically nothing everytime I start a new run.
Theres a lot of equipment and abilities to find in treasure chests. Your character's visual appearence will change with each new piece of equipment you put on (I love games that do that). The storyline is also simple, but I really like how the game told it. There are a lot of interesting journal entries that I recommend reading to add to your gameplay experience. It really puts what your character is doing into perspective.
The boss fights are all excellent. None of them are cheap and all of them are expertly designed. If you can't beat them at first, then just focus on trying to find more chests with equipment and upgrades, or finding more gold to upgrade your castle.
After beating a boss, you will be able to challenge the remix version of that boss. These are the same bosses that you fought while going through the castle, but they have all been changed to make the fights more difficult. They are A LOT more difficult. You will use a specifically made character for each fight, instead of the one you have been using throughout the game. Levels and equipment effect nothing. Its all about your skill for these fights. Look at how low the Steam percentages are for the remix boss achievements. They are still a ton of fun trying to beat though.
The music is also great in this game. I have a couple new favorite songs now after playing this (I'm looking at you title screen and ending theme). The game will last you around 25 hours and you can go through New Game + as many times as you like. Everything keeps getting harder the more playthroughs of the game you complete.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is one of those weird games that you end up with, thinking 'I'm going to spend like an hour on this, then get bored and leave it to rot in my library.' However, that is not the case with this game at all.
Do you know how satisfying it is to crush cars under your wheels when you turn into the wrong lane? Are you aware of the amazing, euphoric state of gunning it about 20km over the speed limit and not getting fined? If you'd like to know these pleasures, then I would reccommend this game without a moment of hesitation. In fact, I'd reccommend this game ANYWAY without a single doubt.
My friends think I'm sad for playing this game. I mention it and they say, 'Really? This stupid truck simulator again? God, get a life.' But they don't understand. Trucking is my dream job: and it can be yours too.
You begin as a single driver, working your way through the grueling task of upgrading your company through quick deliveries. Your aim? The overall gameplay is solid, and everything works wonderfully. The problem comes when you start to realize that the game has you doing the same menial chores over and over in order to pad out the gameplay hours. Mad Max looks and sounds absolutely perfect. Voice acting is believable, and the sounds of cars ramming, exploding, and tearing are suitably raucous. On Ultra, Mad Max looks absolutely stunning, with some of the best explosions I’ve ever seen in games.
There’s a fortune of content here, but so much of it relies on repetition that I doubt many will get a full 100% game completion. There are issues with Mad Max and it certainly isn’t a game that will win many awards, but it is a really enjoyable game, where you can in the end overlook what are, at the end of the day, pretty minor issues in the grand scheme of things.

- Great atmosphere and beautiful graphics with low system requirements.
- No mindless "Pinball-Combat" aka Shadow of Mordor / Batman series. Some negative reviews didn't get it that you have to move Max in order to block properly. Also unlike other games, enemies will attack and not wait till it's their "turn".
- Nice feeling of progression.
- Upgrades that are at least as meaningful as in any other game.
- Unlike Shadow of Mordor: Items and NPCs won't re-spawn directly in front of you each time you move 2m away and you don't have to kill the exact same enemies you did one minute ago.
- Much to do (of the same type). But you don't have to.
- Runs great on a PC and that at release date (should be normal, but isn't).
- No DLC grinder at release.
- Ingame screenshot editor for creative players.
- Only a few female characters. :)
- No motorbikes. :(
- Boss fights in camps could be more interesting.
- Side-missions lack variety. As in many other games.
- Car controls are horrible, if you don't have upgrades. So at start you get frustrated easily.
- Only a few female characters. ;)
Great game, but not without flaws. Apart from the car combat, nothing really new that stands out. But that isn't a bad thing, when the package is done right. Had a lot of fun with the game. I don't give much about paid reviews or reviews that make judgements on debug code.
Worth a buy? - For me: Yes, but not for the price on Steam. You can get it much cheaper from third party sites.

Storytelling in video games isn't dead, it's just not profitable to do. No, the reason we can't have nice things is because of the reviewers who praise Call of Duty and disregard Spec Ops, possibly because of what the game says about them. And you for wanting to be the hero.

Spec Ops is a game intended to be in the same theme of Heart of Darkness and Apocalypse Now, a sobering and introspective take on the typical war shooter genre, just as Apocalypse Now was meant to be a thematic counter to the jingoism of Hollywood's depiction of the Vietnam war. I feel that it succeeds at this, quite effectively throwing a spanner into the works of the modern war game industry by playing off the typical player response to glory-killing games and starkly contrasts it with a dose of reality. Accompanied by an extremely well-done soundtrack which really brings the mental anguish of combat to life, the game left me feeling disturbed and thoughtful.
There's a lot of criticism surrounding this game as being "forced" in its' portrayal, and that it fails as being meaningful in its' linearity. There's no way to "win" at the game, everything you do will inevitably lead to things getting worse. Critics point out that the effect of being left feeling horrific is ruined by this lack of choice. However, I believe that this was an intentional design choice - it's probable that the writers wanted to emphasize the idea that war can never lead to good, only ruin.
Overall, I consider Spec Ops to be a very good game, but this is primarily because of the storytelling. It paints a picture and it does it well, but in no way could it be considered your typical game. If you're a fan of art in media, especially the works which the game was inspired by, then I would recommend this to you in a heartbeat.

Rogue Legacy manages to take the fun core mechanics of a 2D Castlevania game and make them addictive and replayable. Add to that the variety and humor from the random character differences, and what you get is nothing short of an excellent game.
I've always been a fan of the Castlevania/Metroid genre, and I buy a lot of indie games that mimic the style. I'm usually not disappointed, but these types of games are short (5-10 hours) and usually don't offer much in the way of replayability. Rogue Legacy is the exception. It offers all the charm of the genre, but somehow I've managed to sink some 50 hours into it. The characters change, the castles change, and all the while you collect upgrades and items so you're always progressing. Even once you do manage to get all the way through the castle there's a new game+ and a new game++ and a new game +3, and  that's as far as I got, but I'm pretty sure it'll just keep giving you a harder castle if you keep playing. Now if you'll excuse me there's a level 300 Dwarf Lich Queen with irritable bowel syndrome and my name on it. Happy hunting!

The overall gameplay is solid, and everything works wonderfully. The problem comes when you start to realize that the game has you doing the same menial chores over and over in order to pad out the gameplay hours. Mad Max looks and sounds absolutely perfect. Voice acting is believable, and the sounds of cars ramming, exploding, and tearing are suitably raucous. On Ultra, Mad Max looks absolutely stunning, with some of the best explosions I’ve ever seen in games.
There’s a fortune of content here, but so much of it relies on repetition that I doubt many will get a full 100% game completion. There are issues with Mad Max and it certainly isn’t a game that will win many awards, but it is a really enjoyable game, where you can in the end overlook what are, at the end of the day, pretty minor issues in the grand scheme of things.

- Great atmosphere and beautiful graphics with low system requirements.
- No mindless "Pinball-Combat" aka Shadow of Mordor / Batman series. Some negative reviews didn't get it that you have to move Max in order to block properly. Also unlike other games, enemies will attack and not wait till it's their "turn".
- Nice feeling of progression.
- Upgrades that are at least as meaningful as in any other game.
- Unlike Shadow of Mordor: Items and NPCs won't re-spawn directly in front of you each time you move 2m away and you don't have to kill the exact same enemies you did one minute ago.
- Much to do (of the same type). But you don't have to.
- Runs great on a PC and that at release date (should be normal, but isn't).
- No DLC grinder at release.
- Ingame screenshot editor for creative players.
- Only a few female characters. :)
- No motorbikes. :(
- Boss fights in camps could be more interesting.
- Side-missions lack variety. As in many other games.
- Car controls are horrible, if you don't have upgrades. So at start you get frustrated easily.
- Only a few female characters. ;)
Great game, but not without flaws. Apart from the car combat, nothing really new that stands out. But that isn't a bad thing, when the package is done right. Had a lot of fun with the game. I don't give much about paid reviews or reviews that make judgements on debug code.
Worth a buy? - For me: Yes, but not for the price on Steam. You can get it much cheaper from third party sites.

When you say "Theme Hospital", I say - GIMME GIMME. That's how I got hooked on idea of playing Prison Architect, game that lets you be Tim McManus of OZ. Plus all the architectural wonders.
"Prison Architect" is a great indie game with a great idea - it's a prison simulation that you can make as casual or as hardcore as you want. Your task is to obtain and maintain complete control over your prison - from setting up the basic foundations to cells, canteens, kitchens, visitation rooms, offices, even execution rooms, to hiring personnel, creating programs for your inmates, fulfilling grants, grabbing money and so on. It's a fun and detailed game and although learning curve is not easy, you'll get the hang of it, just peek at some awesome guides waiting for you on Workshop (I warmly recommend Rutger's one).
You'll face riots, fights, drugs and every single beautiful prison occasion you already saw in your favourite movies. I would like to see race wars, rapes and so on, just to make it more grusome, and hopefully it will happen soon enough.
BUT, there's always a BUT issued by a BUTT such as me... I cannot recommend this game at this particular moment. There is a gamebreaking bug that doesn't allow you to even try out the full potential of alpha - and believe me, I've tried everything, from following guides, installing modes to check out other people configurations, reinstalling game, playing on two different computers... nothing helped.
At certain point in the game, workmen, your main force that helps you build your prison JUST STOPS WORKING. There is no way to force them to work - your orders stay queued up, but they don't move. They don't build, they don't bulldoze, they don't dump nor dismantle stuff. It becomes truly frustrating when you already wasted a few hours into planning. I've tried canceling orders, giving 'em again, quitting game, entering the game again. Nothing.
With this furious bug that destroys all the enjoyment, I can't recommend the game at this phase (written during month of Alpha 21). When it's squashed, I'll change my grade because I REALLY, REALLY, REALLY WANT TO PLAY THIS ONE.

Storytelling in video games isn't dead, it's just not profitable to do. No, the reason we can't have nice things is because of the reviewers who praise Call of Duty and disregard Spec Ops, possibly because of what the game says about them. And you for wanting to be the hero.

Spec Ops is a game intended to be in the same theme of Heart of Darkness and Apocalypse Now, a sobering and introspective take on the typical war shooter genre, just as Apocalypse Now was meant to be a thematic counter to the jingoism of Hollywood's depiction of the Vietnam war. I feel that it succeeds at this, quite effectively throwing a spanner into the works of the modern war game industry by playing off the typical player response to glory-killing games and starkly contrasts it with a dose of reality. Accompanied by an extremely well-done soundtrack which really brings the mental anguish of combat to life, the game left me feeling disturbed and thoughtful.
There's a lot of criticism surrounding this game as being "forced" in its' portrayal, and that it fails as being meaningful in its' linearity. There's no way to "win" at the game, everything you do will inevitably lead to things getting worse. Critics point out that the effect of being left feeling horrific is ruined by this lack of choice. However, I believe that this was an intentional design choice - it's probable that the writers wanted to emphasize the idea that war can never lead to good, only ruin.
Overall, I consider Spec Ops to be a very good game, but this is primarily because of the storytelling. It paints a picture and it does it well, but in no way could it be considered your typical game. If you're a fan of art in media, especially the works which the game was inspired by, then I would recommend this to you in a heartbeat.

There are very few games with the emotional depth, artistic ambition or moral maturity of Undertale.  This is the game that is, by turns, hillarious, thrilling, terrifying, tragic and throughtful.  At a glance, the characters are silly, but most of the cast reaveals the depth of their persons in due time.  Characters who seem at a glance, relentless killers, reveal courage, tenderness and insecurity if befriended.  Characters who seem at first, laughable caricatures of social awkwardness harbor dark secrets, guilt and depression.  Thematically, this is a game driven by the struggle to survive an often inhospitable world without resorting to violence.
Well, it is the way I played it.  Maybe it'll be different for you.  Your choice between violence and pacifism will determine where this story goes, and I won't spoil anything else about the game (there are plenty of other people on the internet who are all too happy to do just that.)
While Undertale is very much driven by its characters and story, the gameplay itself is enjoyable.  The puzzles aren't like to keep you stuck for very long, but the combat can be challenging if you are unused to bullet hell games.  Striving to evade enemy attacks you have never seen before is likely to keep you on edge, and if you try to resolve fights pacifistically, be prepared to spend some time thinking through the solution.  There isn't much strategic depth in the equipment available, but the richness of the story and the action more than make up for it.  A must-buy.

This sounds like your average run-of-the-mill dungeon crawler right? Wrong! Where as in most games like this the enemies you encounter are little more then cannon fodder, the monsters of Undertale are given dialogue and behaviour that gives them bits and pieces of personality. The minor monsters might have some quirky dialogue that will bring a chuckle out of you or some wierd behavior that will make you pity them or get annoyed by them, while the named reccuring monsters will have an entire personality mapped out.
"Oh a game, where the npcs have personality, I've never seen that before." True, this isn't exactly an earth shattering breakthrough in gaming. Here's the thing though: I
the characters of Undertale. Seriously, I freaking love all of them soo. Very. Much. To be honest I can't remember ever getting this attached to npc characters before, they are witty, hearthwarming, ridiculous, tearjerking, awesome and I just want
. For me the writing is the strongest point of Undertale.
You didn't think that was the only point though, did you? To sum up the next point: Undertale gameplay is
. First of, it scraps the conventional rpg style fighting where you take turns selecting different atacks to throw at each other. Instead you have to make it through a bullet hell minigame everytime after you perform a action. Don't worry, the game won't be throwing Touhou level♥♥♥♥♥♥at you, even as someone who have never been too much into bullet hell games I throughly enjoyed Undertale through and through. Without spoiling much I will say that the game also gets creative with the
of bullet hell it throws at you. You fight a frog and it will be throwing flies at you that buzz eratically across the screen or you fight a dog  and it will try to stab you with sweeping knives moving across the screen.
Where Undertale
stands out from the rest of the crowd though is the forth wall breaking. As you continue to play the game you get the feeling that the game becomes increasingly aware of
, the player, sitting behinf your desk, pushing your buttons. Here's the thing: Most story driven games requires a certain suspension of disbelief. When your playing as Link and fighting Ganandorf and he beats you? The game is over right? Ganandorf won! But the game just says "Nonono, that didn't happen, do-over!" and you get to start the fight again and you just have to pretend that defeat never happend. Yay, you totally beat Ganondorf and saved all of Hyrule, those 20+ deaths was just a bad dream!
Undertale says "Yes. That
happen." And then just kinda leaves it one the table like that. What is usually constantly challening your suspension of disbelief, Undertale takes it and makes it part of the game, which I think is why you can become so increadibly immersed into it. The fact that the game outright acknowledges these breaks in logic allowed me to feel connected to the game in a way that very few games has made me feel before, and never to this degree.
Finally, the third and last major strong point of the game that I want to bring up is the music. If you think the fact that I'm putting this last means it is the part I was less impressed with you are
. It's just that I have to put these points in some kind of order, I would have all three of them with overlapping text, but reading this review might become an issue then.
Anyway, the music is great. It's awesome. It fits the mood perfectly at every turn just nailing it again and again, be it a upbeat tempo during a fight, a slow comforting composition while you're in a safe area, a melancholical tune as your truding through the rain in the darkness and pass a lonely statue, or a heartwrenching melody for "those" moments.
Undertale is one of the best games I've ever played and I can't recommend it enough. Maybe it's not your type of game, but from my own experience and from the overwhelmingly positive feedback this game has gotten from the gaming community. . . there's a very good chance it is. If you have
kind of disposable income I recommend you try this game! Chances are, it will be worth your time.

Figured I would write up a quick review as this game is deserving of some praise.  First off, the game is a well optimized one and tends to run very well on a wide range of systems (thats a nice plus right off the bat).  Flawless, this game is not.  The main story is weak at best, many bosses are quite similar to one another  and the rate at which corpses, destroyed vehicles and other “decals” disappear is so fast it will make your head spin (Blow up a car, turn around, its already gone).  But as far as major gripes go, that’s about all I have so far (10 hours in).  As for story, this sandbox world seems to be sufficient enough for you to write your own leaving the actual main story as more of a side note.  The world (while desolate) is strikingly beautiful with great draw distance and nice texture work (The clouds are the best I’ve seen in a game so far (Sorry Witcher)).  Partially destructible environments add to the gameplay too.  This game world is also massive, which is nice as most of the time you are driving (on foot, the world might be to big to even cross).  Combat is strong (if a bit “Batman-like”) and there are plenty of side tasks to take on.  Voice work is very good in some areas, merely passable in others but overall is just fine.  Best feature in my opinion is the day/night cycle which actually takes time!!  In too many games its dusk only 10 minutes after dawn and that needs to stop.  Real-time might be off-putting of course but Mad Max finds great middle ground where from dawn till dusk can take a solid hour and night lasts just as long.  Overall, a great game for those who do not require an amazing main story line.  As for how “movie-like” it is, Mad Max gets the tone and atmosphere right but the brutal car battles from the latest movie are not fully realized here.  The car combat is good, but its not drop-dead insane.

First thing I should say about this game is that it bears little resemblance to roguelikes at all.
Second thing I should say is that I'm entirely fine with that, quite pleased in fact.
Really is quite the fun and addicting game though, definitely. The caste's layout is randomized every time and there's a huge number of possible rooms (hundreds of them, for sure; 30 hours in and I still occasionally found a room layout I'd never seen before). And each area has its own set of enemies as well (though the areas all tend to share the same room layouts, which can make them a tad indistinct on any new game plus runs). So if you're worried about there not being enough to keep you coming back, quell those worries now.
The second thing to say is that the game is quite hard. For a good while at the start you'll spend most of your time dying every few minutes, but after a while and a lot of generations later you learn the skills to help you survive, and generally you'll be able to get a fair number of upgrades after every run as well. It's a tough, but fair difficulty. Very rarely does the game present you with something decisively unfair (and usually it's only on new game plus runs as well.) The five bosses all offer something different as well, helping to keep the gameplay diverse. While the game itself technically isn't very long at all, just exploring the castle itself can keep you busy for a good long time, especially since it's rather enjoyable. The "grinding" in this game is about as exciting as grinding will ever get and I'm quite glad for that.
The game is also a lot more about platforming than combat, too; most roomss have enemies, true, but a lot of it comes down to learning how to dodge their attacks *and* not get hurt by the environment as well. Because rarely is the arena you fight in something as simple as an empty room with a smooth floor. No, often you're dealing with some combination of spikes, spike traps, fireballs, and spikeballs bouncing around. A lot of the challenges for fairy chests can really put platforming skills to the test, as well. The game does surprisingly well to sate my platforming hunger as a whole and I much prefer this approach to a mainly combat-focused one; it makes the game as much about skill as it does leveling and gear.
A few minor gripes I have are mostly restricted to side-content; one of the remixed bosses is excessively difficult and generally feels more luck-based than anything. Probably one of the few times I actually got angry with the game, and possibly needs to be toned down a bit, because even compared to the other four remixed bosses he's way too difficult. Also, the rate of the carnival bonus room appearing is frustratingly low; I spent 5-6 hours at one point just trying to get the room to appear /once/ (and naturally when it did it was the harder of the two carnival games, of course.)
These really don't detract from the experience as a whole though, just nag at the achievement hunter in me. All in all it's a great game that's worthy of anyone's time. Just don't expect it to be easy.

There are very few games with the emotional depth, artistic ambition or moral maturity of Undertale.  This is the game that is, by turns, hillarious, thrilling, terrifying, tragic and throughtful.  At a glance, the characters are silly, but most of the cast reaveals the depth of their persons in due time.  Characters who seem at a glance, relentless killers, reveal courage, tenderness and insecurity if befriended.  Characters who seem at first, laughable caricatures of social awkwardness harbor dark secrets, guilt and depression.  Thematically, this is a game driven by the struggle to survive an often inhospitable world without resorting to violence.
Well, it is the way I played it.  Maybe it'll be different for you.  Your choice between violence and pacifism will determine where this story goes, and I won't spoil anything else about the game (there are plenty of other people on the internet who are all too happy to do just that.)
While Undertale is very much driven by its characters and story, the gameplay itself is enjoyable.  The puzzles aren't like to keep you stuck for very long, but the combat can be challenging if you are unused to bullet hell games.  Striving to evade enemy attacks you have never seen before is likely to keep you on edge, and if you try to resolve fights pacifistically, be prepared to spend some time thinking through the solution.  There isn't much strategic depth in the equipment available, but the richness of the story and the action more than make up for it.  A must-buy.

Figured I would write up a quick review as this game is deserving of some praise.  First off, the game is a well optimized one and tends to run very well on a wide range of systems (thats a nice plus right off the bat).  Flawless, this game is not.  The main story is weak at best, many bosses are quite similar to one another  and the rate at which corpses, destroyed vehicles and other “decals” disappear is so fast it will make your head spin (Blow up a car, turn around, its already gone).  But as far as major gripes go, that’s about all I have so far (10 hours in).  As for story, this sandbox world seems to be sufficient enough for you to write your own leaving the actual main story as more of a side note.  The world (while desolate) is strikingly beautiful with great draw distance and nice texture work (The clouds are the best I’ve seen in a game so far (Sorry Witcher)).  Partially destructible environments add to the gameplay too.  This game world is also massive, which is nice as most of the time you are driving (on foot, the world might be to big to even cross).  Combat is strong (if a bit “Batman-like”) and there are plenty of side tasks to take on.  Voice work is very good in some areas, merely passable in others but overall is just fine.  Best feature in my opinion is the day/night cycle which actually takes time!!  In too many games its dusk only 10 minutes after dawn and that needs to stop.  Real-time might be off-putting of course but Mad Max finds great middle ground where from dawn till dusk can take a solid hour and night lasts just as long.  Overall, a great game for those who do not require an amazing main story line.  As for how “movie-like” it is, Mad Max gets the tone and atmosphere right but the brutal car battles from the latest movie are not fully realized here.  The car combat is good, but its not drop-dead insane.

It would be easy to nit-pick Mad Max to death for its repetitive design, flimsy plot, sometimes painfully slow upgrade progress, and Max’s pathetic little jump. However, when the chips are down you have a game that is just a lot of fun to play, even when you are doing the fairly mundane side tasks. The game plays well, runs well, and doesn’t make you worry about whether you should really be spending thirty minutes chasing down a convoy in place of going off to do the next story mission. Instead, it actively encourages you do deviate from the main path, and you will probably find yourself gleefully doing so, constantly getting distracted by scrap-transports, camps, convoys and scavenging locations; even when you tell yourself its finally time to drive to the next story quest marker.
As a side note, I'll mention that I probably enjoyed MM more than Far Cry 4, Shadow of Mordor and Arkham Knight which are all more critically acclaimed. The game is just wierdly, compulsively addicting and fun to play.

Nobody told me this is Heart of Darkness: The Game. Absolutely amazing, epic, grim story about horrors of war where you'll be asking yourself - am I the bad guy or the good guy? Set in post-apocalyptic Dubai flooded by desert this is a gem of gaming story-telling. Gameplay itself is Gears of War: Modern Warfare but that's really secondary to an incredible emotional experience I didn't expect when buying this title.

Spec Ops: The Line
PC GAMER's Headline: "A generic shooter with lots to say. Spec Ops: The Line trades quality gaming for quality narrative and interesting characters".
And I agree with it completely. Strong story, narrative, voice acting, music and especially the graphics, the character models, the Dubai Skyscrappers and level design are all very impressive.
As for the CONS, weak clunky gameplay mechanics. The game plays like a Gears of War clone except with poor cover mechanism. The guns feels weak most of the time, the ammo is more than scarce; like you have to be on the move all the time searching for more ammo. Lots of cheap shots from enemies!
I haven't tried MP nor Co-Op but won't bother!
Overall, fun story mode with weak cover mechanics. Get the game on a nice deal!

Rogue Legacy is a game that I might not play every day but I do find myself returning to on a regular basis. The game can be punishing at times and as I mentioned before, the 'legacy' hook that has you playing a different member of your lineage each time you start a new game isn't as impactful as I would have liked it to be, but it does what it sets out to do very very well. If you like slow burning, action-oriented rogue-likes, Rogue Legacy is a sure bet.

Rogue Legacy is a roguelike indie platforming game with bullet hell elements that get more and more apparent the further you progress into it. You play as a member of a family whose wish is to conquer the castle guarded by charon and save the kingdom. You'll gather gold and stat increases (which are permanent as well as cross-character), and upon death you can purchase upgrades in the form of ability and class upgrades. Keep in mind that your character will have traits and drawbacks, such as seeing in black-and-white, farting randomly, and walking on the ceiling. Each class also possesses a special ability, such as a renamed skyrim-shout, a ninja substitution technique, and more. There are four bosses, one in each area of the map, and as you beat them you'll get permanently closer to the final boss. Unless you beat a boss on a given life, you haven't really made any progress aside from the stat increases and upgrades.
It gets very, very tough, since you can new game+ over and over again, with increasingly higher challenge (you reach a point where everything can shoot through walls eventually), but it's loads of fun :3

Story is you are Max, left stranded for dead, vehicle taken and dismantled to scraps, and left with nothing but your clothes.
Now full of vengeance and teamed up with your hunchback sidekick Chumbucket, it is now your destiny to rebuild a better machine called the Magnum Opus, something that the wasteland will tremble in fear from decades to come.
That is basically it as you will have to travel the wastelands going into uncharted territory to build and upgrade your new vehicle from scrap all the way to making the Scrotus clan eat your deadly wheels as you will have to fight to survive by gathering food and water, taking over enemy clans camps, and racing your way to collect scrap as you upgrade.
The vehicle has much to offer as you upgrade everything from wheels with better traction, harpoons to destroy enemy vehicles, paint job, armor, and all the works.
You can also upgrade Max as well from his looks to his uniform to upgrade in combat as well, combat system kind of reminds me of Batman, only with shotguns and plenty of satisfying German Suplex's to even make Brock Lesnar jealous.
Other form of combat comes from your vehicle as you the other half of the time you will come across gang of other vehicles looking to demolish, this all comes in handy as you can use your shotgun to shoot the enemy fuel tank in on kill or be strategic and use your harpoon to take off portions of the vehicle or lasso the driver out and flip him to oblivion.
Now this may not be a popular opinion and I do apologize but to me, the racing and the driving controls in general were just way too stiff and clunky for me, I know you can upgrade for better traction but even half way through the upgrades my vehicle still felt like it was swimming through Crisco. Also, good luck with racing in the game, if you even as much get hit and swerve into the rocks while driving, you might as well restart the race because it takes forever to catch up to your enemy drivers while avoiding hazards to make sure your vehicle does not spontaneously combust while skating through the crisco wasteland. That may not happen to others, I don't know but that is my opinion.
The other little minor issue I have is the weak ending. Throughout the game you will also have your share of boss battles which they all fight in the same pattern pretty much, either dodge out of the way to avoid their powerful attack or click the mouse to counter their attacks and lay into them with a series of punches and kicks as you will also go into fury mode which turns you into a ninja and you become a buffed up one man wrecking crew..but yeah the bosses were kind of weak, especially the ending boss, oh god the ending boss, which made the ending feel anti climatic..
I mean here is the build up for the Lord of the wasteland called Scrotus, built up to make him look like a complete bad a**, and what do they do? Oh let's just put him into a car playing scaredy cat as we toss like 3-4 harpoons at him..and thats it..thats the last boss. Also the ending story just came out of nowhere as I felt like it was rushed, once again, maybe it was just me but they could have done something more to it.
Other than that, graphics are great, I love traveling through the desolate wasteland to the creepy tunnels.
Music and everything else is pretty good.
So on this game it is kind of in the middle for me, but I do recommend it, just let the price go down a bit and then see what you guys will think. It is a good game with a decent length of 15-25 hours of gameplay depending on how many missions you go on.
So yeah, a little repetitive but still something worth checking out.

In Mad Max we saw disabled characters equally represented, their presence in the film world was a given, they weren't just tropes for evil or disabled in some way to show subservients (ie, Chumbucket). Fury Road had the women in the right light and showed every swinging♥♥♥♥♥♥how badass a female lead can be without being reduced to a sterotype. I don't think Max would ever refer to a man helping him out as "that hunchback", nor do I think Max would accept the role of personal Jesus for the guy either. It seems awkward, forced and trying to make Max someone the character just isn't. There are women present in various roles (which is cool) you have the gas huffin junkee fighter, you have the wheelchair bound faction leader and then you have the damsal in distress, just when you thought that it was going to be a different kind of game. In the same vain as Max being a casual jerk to Chumbucket, Max's weird infatuation with the character of Hope is kind of off. Max is a broken man, his wife and kid (good old Sprog) are long dead thanks to Toecutter- I think love and family are behind him, and that through his eyes we are vicariously meant to view the Wasteland- without any input from Max- because he has, aside from some sense of humanity, ZERO ♥♥♥♥s left to give. Mad Max is a collection of great ideas poorly tied together and capably (but not perfectly) executed.  It's shallow gameplay is outstnding fun when taken in small doses.  Just don't plan on powering your way through this game in a few sittings; if you do, the lack of polish, disjointed story, and repetition (oh lord, the repetition!)  will kill your buzz all too soon.
Mad Max has been compared and found wanting to Assassin's Creed and Batman: Arhkam games (and rightly so while on foot), but the best part of Mad Max takes place behind the wheel.  The car chases (enemies chasing you and vice versa) and convoy battles will stick with you and drive you to play even more  ...at least while they last.  Unfortunately, there are only a limited number of convoy missions (and no free-roam convoys), which is a shame since this seems to be every player's favorite activity.  There are still randomly spawning enemy vehicles roaming the wastes, but they seem fewer and fewer as the game progresses, and enemies flat out run away once your vehicle becomes moderately equipped.
If you're looking for a good gap filler - a game to play when the latest MMO has become stale, but before another massive time-sync game - this is a great place to start.  Just don't be in a rush to finish.

Here's how my viewpoint changed after the updates.
**ORIGINAL POST IN WHICH I LEFT A THUMBS UP**
Amazing game! Hours of laughter, definitely reccomend if you have siblings. I play with my younger brothers, and they still beat me because of how unpredictable it is!
Really, the game keeps us laughing the WHOLE time. It's sooo much fun!

POSSIBLE SUGGESTION:
Allow the ripping off of limbs if two people pull you apart? Or when you grab onto two objects that are moving away from eachother.
It would be HILARIOUS watching your friend run away with your arm!
**END OF NEW POST IN WHICH I LEFT A THUMBS UP**
**NEW POST**
I think the devs are going in the wrong direction with the updates. My personal favorite part of the game, having epic battles while climbing all over the map, was removed. Also, knocking out other players is a bit more difficult, but the worst part of the new updates is that you can no longer laugh your lungs out attempting crazy shenanigans up in extreme heights. I can only imagine that the devs removed this ability so the game is more "simple" and "age friendly", but I have to say that it hasn't made it any simpler. I, a skilled gamer, found this game very fun, as it is hard to master the tricks you can pull off. My 8 year old brother enjoys it more than I do, and he is fully able to scale walls as well. Finally, my second brother, who is 6, also knows how to climb walls, and pulls off stunts that I probably couldn't do if I tried. My point is, the game was perfect for all ages, as it was easy to use but hard to master. Now, the game is just easy to use. I'm just about to search the web to find out whether I can revert my update or not. I respect the devs and absolutely love this game, but I have to leave a thumbs up simly because of the restricting update.
Here's what I think the devs should work on:
-Adding new, interactive maps
-Adding powerups (Superpunch? Grapple Ability? Hypermode?)
-Adding random yet rare occurances like pulling another player's limb off
I hope the devs listen to the community and make changes accordingly.
**END OF NEW POST**

Rogue Legacy is a roguelike indie platforming game with bullet hell elements that get more and more apparent the further you progress into it. You play as a member of a family whose wish is to conquer the castle guarded by charon and save the kingdom. You'll gather gold and stat increases (which are permanent as well as cross-character), and upon death you can purchase upgrades in the form of ability and class upgrades. Keep in mind that your character will have traits and drawbacks, such as seeing in black-and-white, farting randomly, and walking on the ceiling. Each class also possesses a special ability, such as a renamed skyrim-shout, a ninja substitution technique, and more. There are four bosses, one in each area of the map, and as you beat them you'll get permanently closer to the final boss. Unless you beat a boss on a given life, you haven't really made any progress aside from the stat increases and upgrades.
It gets very, very tough, since you can new game+ over and over again, with increasingly higher challenge (you reach a point where everything can shoot through walls eventually), but it's loads of fun :3

In this game you will die. You will die a lot.
But it is not just because the game is insanely hard (although it is a little bit), but death plays a very fundamental role here.
When you die with a character, you won't be able to play with it again. Instead, you will have to choose among three of his or her heirs. Every character is randomly generated, with classes and traits that directly affect gameplay in very interesting and clever manners. The map also changes for every generation, so you'll have new challenges, treasures and secrets after every death.
The point is that every generation will be more powerful than its predecessor, once you'll have the opportunity to buy status, equipment and abilities with what was found in the castle by the previous character. So there is going to be a very clear feel of progress even if you die a lot in the beggining of the game, being able to survive a little bit more with each character generated.
So don't get frustrated when you die. Don't give up, because this game is totally worthy! Every single element was pretty well planned and applied, like the controls, graphics, sound, music etc. A really enjoyable, fun, addictive and remarkable game. Without a shred of doubt this is a must-have to all fans of the metroidvania genre.

Do you like having hours of your life eaten away by something incredibly addictive? Well, if you're going to allow that to happen, it should probably happen in the most fun way possible.
Rogue Legacy combines the classic gameplay mechanics of Metroid, Mega Man and Castlevania with some charming, modern RPG nuances to give a fresh experience in a tried and tested formula. While the gameplay and controls are simple, its what is going on behind the scenes that makes Rogue Legacy a keeper. The biggest draw is the inherent replay value that comes with the inevitable death of each heir you choose, when you are offered a new selection of three, randomly generated and distinctly different characters to select. Once your choice is made, you venture forth into the randomly generated castle, which changes with each playthrough (with one exception) and kill and break as many things as you can, to collect as much loot as possible before your death. This brings players back to the heir select option, and the game branches from there.
The gold has a two-fold value: firstly, players are offered to upgrade their keep to provide stat and skill bonuses, new classes and class upgrades, and NPCs, all of which will combine to make the next playthrough run that much longer. Next, the gold can be used with said NPCs as players unlock the Blacksmith, Enchantress and Engineer. The smith, as expected, offers gear upgrades, though the trick is you need to discover the blueprints within the castle's depths, first. The enchantress will provide you with runes, which can be slotted within each gear spot, but again, you will need to locate them before she can offer them! Lastly, the engineer offers an unique, though costly, service in saving the castle layout from your previous playthrough. The value here comes from knowing what enemies and treasures are where, and even allowing you to practice against a particular boss that is giving you a tough time. Beyond these upgrades, gold serves no other purpose expect to move you to tears as you part with it before entering the castle with each playthrough.
Now, if all that customizability and such was not enough to freshen the experience, there is the randomness in the hiers. Not only does each of your three selections comes with a random class and magic combination, they are also given random traits, more often than not, which will add new dynamics to your gameplay strategies. While in one playthrough you may be an assassin who is small in stature (dwarfism) and has a noticeable blur around the immediate vicinity of the sprite (near-sighted), the next you could be a barbarian who will fart at times (IBS) and has to play the entire playthrough with the map upside-down (vertigo)! The excitement that comes with each playthrough, wondering what combinations you'll have to choose from, and what new blessings, or curses, you may discover drastically increase that 'just one more life' mentality of the game.
All of the above is presented in an incredibly well-designed package, as the art direction is pretty fabulous in the game. Well-detailed sprites litter every corner of the castle and its grounds, with a vibrant colour palette that harkens back to gaming's earliest days. Furthermore, the music is incredibly solid, adding just the right arcadey touch to the atmosphere, and without becoming mind-numbing due to the repetitive nature of the title. The music is really quite catchy and helps to push you further into your playthrough.
Really, I have little ill to say against this game, except that I found that, sometimes, the controls can be somewhat less than tight, which is really a shame in a playstyle that requires fine-tuned reaction times. However, these instances are pretty few and far between, and largely, the game runs smooth like so much warm butter.
If you're looking for a game with an epic storyline and easy gameplay that will make you feel godlike, then go elsewhere. Want a challenge? Want to earn levels, not through grinding, but through refined skill? Want to discover just how much of a sailor's cussing mouth you have? Then look no further than Rogue Legacy, my friends. Money, and time, well spent.

Bom jogo. Em diversos momentos exagera na nerdice como personagens com miopia, glaucoma, não enxergar cores, ficar de cabeça pra baixo, etc nada ver isso. Tem uma hora que isso tudo começa a enxer o saco. As músicas são boas, dando um clima legal a alguns temas porém com notas também meio nerds e acaba enjoando. É claramente um jogo feito de nerd para nerd, bem no melhor estilo de desenvolvedor indie deprimido que usa de um cansativo humor nerd o tempo todo dentro do jogo. A jogabilidade é ótima, super precisa, pecando apenas quando o personagem está se movendo muito depressa pois acaba perdendo um pouco da sensibilidade no controle. Os inimigos são bem feitos e desafiadores. Os efeitos sonoros são ótimos, com destaque pro som de pegar os tesouros, que é excelente e dá realmente vontade de continuar pegando-os pra continuar ouvindo o tlimtlim das moedas e sacos de ouro. Os gráficos são bem definidos e bonitinhos. O jogo tem um valor replay maneiro pois te faz querer jogar e zerar mais algumas vezes pra abrir algumas coisas novas e catar mais itens, abrir achievs. Mas fica quase tudo igual (apenas mais difícil) e isso podia ter sido mais bem elaborado. E o final do jogo eles deixam você passar algumas partes mas obrigam vc a ver o momento mais nerd do jogo, que são os créditos finais, com os nomes de quem fez o quê do jogo, com um desenho nerd do lado de cada nome - claramente fizeram isso querendo se promover e isso eu achei bem escrotinho, princaipalmente pra quem vai zerar duas, três vezes - Finalizando: o jogo podia ter muito mais conteúdo mas vale a pena dar uma jogada e depois largar pra sempre. De qualquer maneira vou recomendar. Se tivesse o voto nulo, eu votava assim. Saudade de um Wonder Boy de verdade ..

Loved the Mad Max movies as a kid and adult.
Love the world it is set in.
When I saw the chance to actually play in this world, in an open world game, I was more than excited!
Then I saw the critic reviews upon it's release I was so disheartened.
I had given up hope.
One day I opened Steam, saw it's banner at the top and clicked.
The user review rating was Overwhelmingly Positive.
I then started wondering why I had placed so much faith in critics? Why had I not trusted the people of Steam?
So based purely on this rating I clicked buy.
Game downloaded and installed - fired it up.
An unknown number of hours later I stopped to look away from the game at the clock - it was 1:30AM. Time for bed!
Next time I play, again hours later I look up - 1AM. Time for bed!
Not many games have had me so completely engrossed that I lose track of time.
This game has, and continues to.
Yes it has repeatitive aspects (like every game)
Yes it takes its combat from Batman - but in my opinion improves on it. It feels more raw and involved.
Driving is great fun.
The upgrades are not linar and feel like they make a difference.
The graphics are exceptional and it runs smooth and flawlessly!
The many many side missions do tickle my OCD - must clear all zones!
I do feel like it doesn't quite fit into the movies, yet - I haven't finished the main story and don't plan to for quite some time. Saying that the story and characters do feel great. The people I cross paths with feel real.
Ultimately I am enjoying the game immensely. I can recommend it without a doubt!

I finished with shellshock... It's a meta anti-war game where violence is depicted as ugly and chaotic as it is in real life. Man's grotesque fallibility is perfectly offset by an almost painterly art design rendering both the rich environments and the aftermath of slaughter in unflinching detail; to witness the transformation of the men from every battle into callous psychopaths is a remarkable feat. And that a mainstream game studio would put out an action-packed, smart and cancer black meditation on the horrors of war is even harder to believe. This is a grueling, beautiful and absolutely extraordinary descent into the haunted heart of PTSD. If you could only ever play one military shooter let it be this. It will stay with you long after it's finished.

Amazing, I love this game. The attention to detail is phenomenal, the skin textures, the subtle facial animations, every nick and scratch; there is just so much attention to detail in this game. I've played this game at least seven or eight times and I still find something I didn't notice before.
While some say the gameplay is a bit dated, I say that it is perfect fit for the over all experience.  This game is a drama, too much action or fun would ruin this game just like a gunfight in each episode would ruin Breaking Bad. This is game was not meant to compete against games like COD or Modern Warfare, but to provide contrast.
The story is where this game true shines, I've never seen a video game focus on what the reality of war does to a person.  This game doesn't pull any punches, it covers the parts of war that other games shy away from such as the lack of moral certainty, consequence free violence, civilian death tolls, and PTSD. It's truly a mature game, not in the juvenile way most “M” rated titles are, with their gratuitous nudity and violence. It's mature in as in it take the topics it covers seriously and with respect.
Simply put, it raises the bar of what a video game can be.

Here is one of my first reviews here, after 80 hours i think i am able to write a good and honest review
Mad Max is a third-person action-adventure vehicular combat video game set in an open world environment and based on the Mad Max film series.
The game’s opening introduces you to the mechanic called Chumbucket who builds you the bare bone of the Magnum Opus, a replacement for the movie's iconic Interceptor. To achieve this you're set loose in a vast, hugely populated map, pulling off missions for various minor warlords and trying to lessen the grip of the dominating Scrotus gang by destroying its bases, minefields, totem-like scarecrows and other displays of power.
Early on it’s all a bit directionless with such an arbitrary overall objective: you’re trying to make your car better by completing missions to… um, make your car better. With such a woolly heading, the first 4-5 hours become a formless muddle among the wealth of things to do, making it easy to get lost or find yourself in trouble above your level.
Once you get past those muddy first hours however, the world opens up and Mad Max becomes a seriously enjoyable realisation of the character. The plot, already more a distraction than a directive, becomes secondary to the pure dusty joy of driving around looking for trouble. Forget that main mission, the wasteland is the game. Whether that’s ramming convoys off the road or fighting your way through camps - this is all about the journey, a perfect setup for the original Road Warrior.
Shortly said-
pros;
-Furious car-based combat
-Satisfying close-quarters brawls
-Atmospheric wastelands with plenty to do
-Captures the spirit of the films
Cons;
-Too reliant on repetitive activities
-frame rate dips and audiobugs

Life is Strange: Before the Storm is far more
to its predestor, Life is Strange.
I'll start with possitives, which unfortunatelly aren't so many:
- better lip sync than in the first game
- still clinging to beautiful and fitting soundtrack
- better controls; you are now pressing buttons instead of dragging your mouse towards options in the dialogue sequences
Now I shall review each episode while trying to avoid huge
, but still, there are gonna be some:
:
So far probably the best one. Maybe it was all thanks to having to wait for so long for another interactive movie, but I simply liked it much more than the rest. But even if this one is my favorite, it is far from perfect.
First aspect of the game is its dialogue - which I know wasn't perfect in the first game - here you get some dose of cringe and awkwardness in the very first chat you have, with the bouncer of Firewalk. You may feel for Chloe, especially if you also lost someone in your life, but her constant nagging and rebelious attitude feels way too forced. I don't know if it was the voice actress or if producers just chose her to be like that and talk with that monotoneus voice the whole time, but frankly it because quite annoying. If they wanted me to like Rachel Amber, they couldn't have done worse job. Rachel was introduced poorly, I didn't get to know much about her, except that she has daddy issues, hides her true personality behind the mask of 'perfect girl and student', everything that again was pretty much apparent from the first game. Ending of this episode made me believe that she may have some supernatural powers and that maybe this will get better each episode.
:
In this episode, they decided to show you triviality and uselessness of your choices. After talking to principal you
. And whatever you've done in the previous episode has almost no effect on how this one plays out. You'll spend like 15 minutes in the junkyard polishing your car and then you go to Blackwell. Again, choices don't matter. You can learn something
from Frank, but that won't have any consequence. When you break into the dorms you are greeted by Damon, a thug and drug dealer. You get to choose again and Illuminati sign is looking at you in the left corner of your screen, a symbol of dire consequences you would need to feel later. It's a lie. There won't be any.
In the middle of this suffering, you'll get to kiss Rachel if you played your cards well before. Yay, fan service! The rest of this episode goes down hill again. Spending another 15+ minutes in Amber's residence will give you nothing. Time will drag even more because you'll learn that their household is boring and quiet. I felt very uneasy at that point. You'll experience great plot twist at the end! Kidding. It won't be great. And if you paid attention and thought about things thoroughly, it becomes quite obvious.
:
Say hello to the worst episode. If previous episode didn't show you how inconsequential your choices are, this one will break it to you. Whole episode is dragged, gives you no option to really play the game, you just talk with others. Seems alright given what this game is. But the talking is completely useless. You'll learn nothing, you won't laugh or cry. Perhaps emotionless and effortless are the best words that could summerize this one. They put a fight in and it wasn't really satisfying. It just didn't suit it. It felt extremely rushed and pointless. I know that many people blamed the first episodes and perhaps that is why producers didn't feel that motivated, but this was a joke of an episode.
What was I expecting:
I wanted story of how Chloe and Rachel tried to escape. It was nice watching them bond and get closer, but it honestly didn't satisfy me when I know how Rachel ends up anyway. There was nothing you could do to prevent the events from first game to happen. So I really don't see the point of showing us this for such price.
I expected to see Mark Jefferson. If they made the third episode to be 2 years later from the first one, it would've been amazing. I needed to know how Rachel got involved with him and then Nathan. How she got closer to Frank. None of that was covered in this game and it is a shame. The third episode especially made me upset.

I followed this game from the moment I saw the very first teaser trailer however long ago that was. It was on the edge of my radar for months and months before it ever was released. It's been a long time now, and for some reason the devs still claim this game is in alpha. Is that bad? Absolutely not. The game is incredibly complete, very addicting, and yet they keep putting out more and more stuff every month. And when I say every month, I mean you can count on an update to this game being released with new content and features once a month. Presumably for a long time.
Okay, now to the actual review part.
Ive put a few long hours into the game and its pretty much a sandbox prison sim where you can choose to control your own pace. You can choose to have prisoners arrive when there are enough rooms, or you can just turn on the fire hose and intake a random number or prisoners every morning. Each has its own play syle.
Taking prisoners as you build rooms allows you to plan ahead a little better and control your population, while taking in a random amount each day will have you constantly building rooms to handle the intake. However, from my experience you will face a colony collapse at some point no matter which route you go. Once a prison reaches a certain population you face the challenge of keeping them all content, which can be pretty tough.
I've literally had games where the prisoners riot almost constantly, forcing you to have to call in your riot police over and over, and it never ends up pretty in the end. These moments can be pretty frantic, and have you pulling out all your staff members to save them, hoping to keep as many people as you can alive. The aftermath is just as calm as the riots were violent, as the ambulance comes and takes away all the corpses.
The one thing that makes this game great is that the battle you face against the AI prisoners is exactly what you could imagine a real wardon faces every day, but perhaps on a more extreme scale. Every prisoner is always testing the limit of what they can get away with, and they're always pushing the boundries of your prison. If you don't have enough guards or walls, they will try to escape. If your guards arent watching closely enough, prisoners get hurt or killed. They are constantly making weapons or bringing in contraband. It really is you versus them. Because of this you'll probably scrap your prison and start over with a new idea in mind to counteract what you did wrong last time, only to find a new flaw in your system.
Another great thing is that prisoners all have their own personalities. Most are calm and go through the motions of daily life in prison, but there are always those few trouble makers that need constant attention. I had a prisoner who would craft a shiv from the food warmer in the mess hall every day and attempt to bring it back to his room. Out of the 50 prisoners in my prison at the time, he was one of the few I learned his name, his criminal history, and I could always pick him out of the crowd. I usually spent the lunch period watching him act suspicious, and then promptly telling a guard to search him.
This is the core gameplay of Prison Architect. There are plenty of bugs, and it is still an alpha, but there are hours and hours of gameplay just waiting to be had. Normally I might not review a game so "early" into its development, but the core game is great, and just when I think that its amazing, the devs slip in another facet of running a prison I hadn't thought of before. It will only get better from here on out, and based on how much game is already here, I can't imagine how great the finished product will actually be.

It's quite a challenge for the developers to make a game that lives up to the incredibly well-written, beautiful, and atmospheric game that the original Life Is Strange is, and they just flat wowed me in the first episode of the prequel.
If there's one word that captures what I think of the LIS, it is thralldom. You can just sit in front of the monitor for hours and take in the serene Arcadia Bay in the title screen. It gives you the feel of snuggling on the sofa when it rains outside. You don't have to do anything but feel. Feel the perfectly designed world around you, feel the warmth of your body, and feel the moment that nothing can keep you from relishing. Then there's the story, the super power, the characters we've come to love and hate, and the hard choices we have to make along the way. There's a lot that can be said about these more concrete elements of the game, but, as Susan Sontag puts it, "Interpretation takes the sensory experience of the work of art for granted, and proceeds from there." And it is the sensory experience of LIS that makes the "content" potent enough for us to emphasize with and, deservedly, a work of art.
Now fast forward to Before the Storm. I do miss the subtler and softer vibe the original game has, but the more cut-to-the and cynical feel works extremely well with the story it is telling. It felt kind of weird playing Chloe for the first half hour, but as you got to know her a bit more, I was starting to find I resonated with her more than Max. In BtS, Chloe is living with and trying to understand loneliness, budding sexuality, personal loss, grief, misunderstanding, and other abstruse emotions that are beyond the age to make sense of. And this hodgepodge is built up through the seemingly mundane interactions that affects Chloe in one way or another, culminating in the amazingly affecting junk yard scene where she finally can't ignore or take any more of it but is forced to confront those feelings in a very personal way. The game ends with a cliffhanger soon afterwards.
Though I can't wait to find out what happens next, finishing the game, I got the same feel as I did watching the Netflix adaptation of 13 Reasons Why. Both are amazing emotional rollercoasters with incredible depth and distinctive style of presentation. Both put me on a journey to relive some of my confused adolescent life and understand and appreciate more the struggles I and everyone around me have been through. Both, in the end, instill in me the appreciation for the random acts of kindness I receive everyday and life and humanity. It's beautiful how a game, a movie, a play, a tv show, or any piece of art can give people an opportunity to experience what might have not been experienced so people can understand the world more and thus have such a great influence on its audience.
I wish there's always cultural products like Life is Strange when the world is shrouded in chauvinism and bigotry.
Buy this game. You will not be disappointed.

Going into the the sequel of Life is Strange, there are some initial concerns that I have beforehand in regards to Before the Storm. First of all, with such success that Life is Strange has already achieved over the past year, fans are going to have high exceptions exploring the game. And I think it is safe to say that unlike other triple A titled E3 games, Before the Storm delivers, and here’s why.
I thought that taking away beloved character Max was a risky move after seeing the E3 demo, not only it is going to be a somewhat disappointment for those who really enjoyed play as her, also it indicates that there’s not going to be any rewinding time, which will change the game mechanics drastically.
Instead of going back to time, Before the Storm offers an aggressive arguing style that Chloe Price uses to achieve certain goals in the game. It’s designed as this really fast paced “lightning round of choices” which the player gets to pick whatever Chloe is going to say next based on characters’ previous replies in limited time. Even though picking what you wanna say is nothing new in LIS, and players have already been doing that throughout the whole game. But I think it is a solid replacement of time rewinding. Choices now weight heavier, considering you can’t just go back and fix them, and the gameplay itself is just more engaging with these mini QTEs that you have to choose. Also, it is a great way to really reflect Chloe Price’s personality as the ruthless teenage that she is.

Mad Max is a third-person action-adventure vehicular combat video game set in an open world environment and based on the Mad Max film series.
The game’s opening introduces you to the mechanic called Chumbucket who builds you the bare bone of the Magnum Opus, a replacement for the movie's iconic Interceptor. To achieve this you're set loose in a vast, hugely populated map, pulling off missions for various minor warlords and trying to lessen the grip of the dominating Scrotus gang by destroying its bases, minefields, totem-like scarecrows and other displays of power.
Early on it’s all a bit directionless with such an arbitrary overall objective: you’re trying to make your car better by completing missions to… um, make your car better. With such a woolly heading, the first 4-5 hours become a formless muddle among the wealth of things to do, making it easy to get lost or find yourself in trouble above your level.
Once you get past those muddy first hours however, the world opens up and Mad Max becomes a seriously enjoyable realisation of the character. The plot, already more a distraction than a directive, becomes secondary to the pure dusty joy of driving around looking for trouble. Forget that main mission, the wasteland is the game. Whether that’s ramming convoys off the road or fighting your way through camps - this is all about the journey, a perfect setup for the original Road Warrior.
Shortly said-
pros;
-Furious car-based combat
-Satisfying close-quarters brawls
-Atmospheric wastelands with plenty to do
-Captures the spirit of the films
Cons;
-Too reliant on repetitive activities
-frame rate dips and audiobugs
Loving it already.
