This game is one of the few games that embraces the concept that their player is going to die and is going to die on a regular basis.  The game is built around you building your family legacy and the acceptance that not every character is the hero you control in other games.  People are going to die. I followed this game from the moment I saw the very first teaser trailer however long ago that was. It was on the edge of my radar for months and months before it ever was released. It's been a long time now, and for some reason the devs still claim this game is in alpha. Is that bad? Absolutely not. The game is incredibly complete, very addicting, and yet they keep putting out more and more stuff every month. And when I say every month, I mean you can count on an update to this game being released with new content and features once a month. Presumably for a long time.
Okay, now to the actual review part.
Ive put a few long hours into the game and its pretty much a sandbox prison sim where you can choose to control your own pace. You can choose to have prisoners arrive when there are enough rooms, or you can just turn on the fire hose and intake a random number or prisoners every morning. Each has its own play syle.
Taking prisoners as you build rooms allows you to plan ahead a little better and control your population, while taking in a random amount each day will have you constantly building rooms to handle the intake. However, from my experience you will face a colony collapse at some point no matter which route you go. Once a prison reaches a certain population you face the challenge of keeping them all content, which can be pretty tough.
I've literally had games where the prisoners riot almost constantly, forcing you to have to call in your riot police over and over, and it never ends up pretty in the end. These moments can be pretty frantic, and have you pulling out all your staff members to save them, hoping to keep as many people as you can alive. The aftermath is just as calm as the riots were violent, as the ambulance comes and takes away all the corpses.
The one thing that makes this game great is that the battle you face against the AI prisoners is exactly what you could imagine a real wardon faces every day, but perhaps on a more extreme scale. Every prisoner is always testing the limit of what they can get away with, and they're always pushing the boundries of your prison. If you don't have enough guards or walls, they will try to escape. If your guards arent watching closely enough, prisoners get hurt or killed. They are constantly making weapons or bringing in contraband. It really is you versus them. Because of this you'll probably scrap your prison and start over with a new idea in mind to counteract what you did wrong last time, only to find a new flaw in your system.
Another great thing is that prisoners all have their own personalities. Most are calm and go through the motions of daily life in prison, but there are always those few trouble makers that need constant attention. I had a prisoner who would craft a shiv from the food warmer in the mess hall every day and attempt to bring it back to his room. Out of the 50 prisoners in my prison at the time, he was one of the few I learned his name, his criminal history, and I could always pick him out of the crowd. I usually spent the lunch period watching him act suspicious, and then promptly telling a guard to search him.
This is the core gameplay of Prison Architect. There are plenty of bugs, and it is still an alpha, but there are hours and hours of gameplay just waiting to be had. Normally I might not review a game so "early" into its development, but the core game is great, and just when I think that its amazing, the devs slip in another facet of running a prison I hadn't thought of before. It will only get better from here on out, and based on how much game is already here, I can't imagine how great the finished product will actually be.

Rust is a game developed and published by Facepunch Studios, the same people behind the sandbox game; GMod
Rust can be a very fun survivial game, especially with friends which I don't have. It can sometimes feel very slow pace on the official servers, so If you want to quickly build and join in on the action, I'd suggest a modded server with faster crafting and gathering
The good things about Rust are that players can host their own servers off of their computers for free, or pay to have it hosted on a local server. Rust offers an intricate and fun base building system. The hunting/gathering portion is fun and Rust offers a day/night cycle with an ever changing weather system
The game is moddable with frequent updates and development blogs. The game offers a procedural generated world which gives you a sense of paranoia and generated biomes which include desert, snow and grass
However, Rust has loads of issues in its current state. The game tends to lag if too many people are connected to the server and uses a lot of RAM with framerate and crashing issues. Rust, surprisingly runs on the Unity engine, making it not the best for optimization, but the development team is managing to fix it and also animals don't follow rules of physics, such us running up walls if they feel like it
One thing I absolutely hate in Rust is the sleeper servers. Even when you log off you are still in-game, and able to be killed. Pretty much forces you put in time to build a stable base before leaving the server or risk being killed which takes time and patience
Overall, if you have the money, I'd suggest looking into buying this game. It is currently in Alpha, so really look into it before purchasing. However, I wouldn't whole heartdly recommend it in its current state

Rogue Legacy is a game where you play as a lone knight with a big sword and a single spell. You enter a randomly generating castle that changes based on your own skill level and results after dying. Every time you die, you start as one of your heirs, which have their own attributes that add to how the game is played(like being colorblind, unable to see in 3 dimensions, having dyslexia, and vertigo.) Every time you die, you also have a chance to upgrade your own manor with the gold you gain during your last playthrough and you can gain people to help you, like a blacksmith that sells you weapons and armor, an enchantress to give your stuff magical attributes, and someone who can set the castle to only one form for the price of 60% of your gold. Speaking of gold, be sure to use it as much as you can after every playthrough, because you lose it when you re-enter the castle(until you get upgrades where you only lose a high percent of it.)
The game itself is very fun and platforming and controls are solid. There is genuine progression through how well you do and the constantly changing difficulty. You always get better with every try, no matter how bad you are at "hard" games like this.
The only flaw I can see is your attacks. There are only 2: a swing, and a down-stab, which is mainly used for activating platforms. The attacks do have a decently wide range radius-wise, but both only cover about half of your hitbox, so there will be times where damage can't be avoided.
Aside from that, the game is still a lot of fun, challenging, and rewarding. Definitely one of the better time-consumers.

Going into the the sequel of Life is Strange, there are some initial concerns that I have beforehand in regards to Before the Storm. First of all, with such success that Life is Strange has already achieved over the past year, fans are going to have high exceptions exploring the game. And I think it is safe to say that unlike other triple A titled E3 games, Before the Storm delivers, and here’s why.
I thought that taking away beloved character Max was a risky move after seeing the E3 demo, not only it is going to be a somewhat disappointment for those who really enjoyed play as her, also it indicates that there’s not going to be any rewinding time, which will change the game mechanics drastically.
Instead of going back to time, Before the Storm offers an aggressive arguing style that Chloe Price uses to achieve certain goals in the game. It’s designed as this really fast paced “lightning round of choices” which the player gets to pick whatever Chloe is going to say next based on characters’ previous replies in limited time. Even though picking what you wanna say is nothing new in LIS, and players have already been doing that throughout the whole game. But I think it is a solid replacement of time rewinding. Choices now weight heavier, considering you can’t just go back and fix them, and the gameplay itself is just more engaging with these mini QTEs that you have to choose. Also, it is a great way to really reflect Chloe Price’s personality as the ruthless teenage that she is.

Spec Ops: The Line is a fully functional third person shooter with cover mechanics that you might enjoy. But that's not point. The point is, that through its story, it's one of the few games that asks you to reflect upon your actions and view them in a different, far more mature way, revealing their true dark qualities. And that is where the real enjoyment comes from.
Do you have friends? Do you like punching your friends in the face, knocking them out and throwing them off of a truck? Buy this game.

Rogue Legacy is a game where you play as a lone knight with a big sword and a single spell. You enter a randomly generating castle that changes based on your own skill level and results after dying. Every time you die, you start as one of your heirs, which have their own attributes that add to how the game is played(like being colorblind, unable to see in 3 dimensions, having dyslexia, and vertigo.) Every time you die, you also have a chance to upgrade your own manor with the gold you gain during your last playthrough and you can gain people to help you, like a blacksmith that sells you weapons and armor, an enchantress to give your stuff magical attributes, and someone who can set the castle to only one form for the price of 60% of your gold. Speaking of gold, be sure to use it as much as you can after every playthrough, because you lose it when you re-enter the castle(until you get upgrades where you only lose a high percent of it.)
The game itself is very fun and platforming and controls are solid. There is genuine progression through how well you do and the constantly changing difficulty. You always get better with every try, no matter how bad you are at "hard" games like this.
The only flaw I can see is your attacks. There are only 2: a swing, and a down-stab, which is mainly used for activating platforms. The attacks do have a decently wide range radius-wise, but both only cover about half of your hitbox, so there will be times where damage can't be avoided.
Aside from that, the game is still a lot of fun, challenging, and rewarding. Definitely one of the better time-consumers.

It took me 36 hours to completed Mad Max, that includes completely upgrading Jeets base, getting certain areas down to 1-0 threat level so I could obtain certain upgrades etc, all the side story quests and upgrading the Magnum Opus with several top tier upgrades including the largest motor (which does take a lot of scrap!)
It was a great game, not your typically bad movie to game experience, they've actually done this well. It has decent combat both vehicular and on foot, story is enough to keep you pushing forward to the next confrontation/the next mod/the next upgrade. Graphics are nice, sound is nice.
The game CAN be grindy and repetitive to a degree, hunting around for scrap for your next upgrade can take a while sometimes. Clearing threat is also somewhat grindy, though there are several things you need to do in order to clear an area so it keeps changing things up and you can pick and choose which you'd like to do as you go along.
'Discovering' new areas also feels like I'm climbing those towers in Assassin's Creed to get to the eagle eye point or whatever it was called.
Experiencing the sandstorms was pretty awesome also, the ferocity of the winds, the thunder and lightning the scrap metal flying at you etc whilst out in the storm is certainly something worth trying to live through, taking cover behind a large rock/cliff face or inside a base to hide all adds to the atmosphere of the game.
I'd definitely recommend it if you're looking for something fun to play or love the whole Mad Max experience, even if it can be a little grindy. Certainly glad I got to play through this one.

- Very well optimized. Running 50 FPS on a HD6950 with very few dips
Cons:
- Alot of small glitches like falling through the world, opponents not taking damage at random, own car taking damage for no reason, enemies disappearing mid-combat, etc. Nothing gamebreaking. Just odds and ends.
- Story is good and compelling... right up to the end. Whoever wrote the last 4-5 missions of this game should be fired... out of a cannon... into the sun.

Overall this is a good, solid game with many hours of fun and entertainment. You'll be emmersed into the world of Mad Max and live the legend, drive the car and smash the f*ck out of insane opponents. There are a few things that should have been done differently on the drawingboard and some glitches that should have been fixed before release. A solid 8/10.

It took me 36 hours to completed Mad Max, that includes completely upgrading Jeets base, getting certain areas down to 1-0 threat level so I could obtain certain upgrades etc, all the side story quests and upgrading the Magnum Opus with several top tier upgrades including the largest motor (which does take a lot of scrap!)
It was a great game, not your typically bad movie to game experience, they've actually done this well. It has decent combat both vehicular and on foot, story is enough to keep you pushing forward to the next confrontation/the next mod/the next upgrade. Graphics are nice, sound is nice.
The game CAN be grindy and repetitive to a degree, hunting around for scrap for your next upgrade can take a while sometimes. Clearing threat is also somewhat grindy, though there are several things you need to do in order to clear an area so it keeps changing things up and you can pick and choose which you'd like to do as you go along.
'Discovering' new areas also feels like I'm climbing those towers in Assassin's Creed to get to the eagle eye point or whatever it was called.
Experiencing the sandstorms was pretty awesome also, the ferocity of the winds, the thunder and lightning the scrap metal flying at you etc whilst out in the storm is certainly something worth trying to live through, taking cover behind a large rock/cliff face or inside a base to hide all adds to the atmosphere of the game.
I'd definitely recommend it if you're looking for something fun to play or love the whole Mad Max experience, even if it can be a little grindy. Certainly glad I got to play through this one.

Likes:
A focus on vehicle combat. The cars have a good amount of weight to keep you engaged but simple enough to control to keep the focus on the action. Car chases, escapes and convoys are definitely the highlights of the game providing lots of exciting moments.
The world is huge and captures the feel of the Mad Max universe very well. It's also very detailed with endless amounts of places to explore, some large and some small, each of which feel unique and carefully made.
Loads to upgrade, from Max to the car to the strongholds. A lot of the upgrading for the car isn't linear progression either, as choices need to be made to decide between speed and strength.
Most of the characters are interesting, especially your sidekick who is probably one of my favourites from a videogame.
The visuals are great, managing to make a barren wasteland actually quite picturesque. The weather effects add to this, looking great while providing lots of interesting moments.
A massive amount of things to do, even if you're not a completionist.
Capture mode: the serial screenshotter's dream tool.
This has been said to death by others but the optimisation of Mad Max really does raise the standards and should be noted in every review.
Dislikes:
At the moment there are bugs here and there, particularly towards the end of the game. I haven't come across any game breaking ones but there are annoyances.
Balloons; Mad Max's version of Ubisoft's radio tower obsession. They're not particularly interesting and frustratingly slow to use. Having a tricky driving section up a tall hill or something could have been much more fun.
The fighting, while decent, barely evolves throughout the entire length of the game but takes up a big part of it. It's not bad, it just becomes "something you have to do" by the time you get to the end of the game so it feels like a missed opportunity.
Bosses and Top Dogs are all identical with their move set which I feel was, again, a big missed opportunity.
Signposting isn't particularly good in some places while being excessive in others. For instance, it doesn't tell you your severe scrap shortage can be alleviated by building certain projects, but it will highlight "secret" entrances and access points in big yellow paint.
Conclusion:
I'd definitely recommend it; I don't play many games until completion these days but I had a blast with this. You'll especially appreciate it if you have any interest in the Mad Max movies or even muscle cars, rat rods or vehicular combat.

Uma das grandes surpresas dos últimos anos, Spec Ops: The Line é um jogo que usa as convenções de jogos de tiro militares em 3ª pessoa para "enganar" o jogador, passar por "genérico" e de repente, puxar o tapete e pegar o jogador de surpresa com decisões fortes, uma narrativa psicológica e uma crítica direta aos outros jogos de tiro militares modernos. É um jogo *sobre* guerra, não *de guerra*; é o Apocalypse Now dos videogames, e não um filme do Michael Bay como Call of Duty. Já virou um clássico cult, e todo mundo que gosta de games precisa experimentá-lo, mesmo que não goste de jogos de tiro.

I generally don't enjoy Rogue-style games, but this was a pleasant exception for me. It allows you to continually improve your character by basing the game around a family tree. Gold, equipment, and other factors are transferred over at the point of death. Then you get the chance to spend any gold you've made to improve your character before spending most (if not all) of the gold you have left to give the castle another go. Its a little different from your average rogue title, but I believe rogue fans will enjoy it as much if not more than I did.
The controls feel great especially considering the various different characters and runes one can use to modify the movement. The game does a great job of teaching you how to deal with the various enemies, and does so without over reliance on a tutorial. The tutorial that is in game is short, sweet, and effective (though I think it could stand do away with the text all together).
The music is decent though it can get repetitive if you spend too much time in a given section. Despite this I never found it grating or annoying; it blended well into the background. The leveling system is well suited to the game, but it does allow you to quickly out level bosses. While that annoys me slightly I give credit to the leveling system for being engaging without being overly complicated. As for playtime I feel like I am getting my money's worth, and the new game + option offers some replayability.
Everything in the game looks great, and the suddle changes in your armor are pleasing to watch as you progress. I absolutely reccomend this game, and give it a 8 out of 10. This title is a creative take on the rogue-genre that I think most people will enjoy.

Likes:
A focus on vehicle combat. The cars have a good amount of weight to keep you engaged but simple enough to control to keep the focus on the action. Car chases, escapes and convoys are definitely the highlights of the game providing lots of exciting moments.
The world is huge and captures the feel of the Mad Max universe very well. It's also very detailed with endless amounts of places to explore, some large and some small, each of which feel unique and carefully made.
Loads to upgrade, from Max to the car to the strongholds. A lot of the upgrading for the car isn't linear progression either, as choices need to be made to decide between speed and strength.
Most of the characters are interesting, especially your sidekick who is probably one of my favourites from a videogame.
The visuals are great, managing to make a barren wasteland actually quite picturesque. The weather effects add to this, looking great while providing lots of interesting moments.
A massive amount of things to do, even if you're not a completionist.
Capture mode: the serial screenshotter's dream tool.
This has been said to death by others but the optimisation of Mad Max really does raise the standards and should be noted in every review.
Dislikes:
At the moment there are bugs here and there, particularly towards the end of the game. I haven't come across any game breaking ones but there are annoyances.
Balloons; Mad Max's version of Ubisoft's radio tower obsession. They're not particularly interesting and frustratingly slow to use. Having a tricky driving section up a tall hill or something could have been much more fun.
The fighting, while decent, barely evolves throughout the entire length of the game but takes up a big part of it. It's not bad, it just becomes "something you have to do" by the time you get to the end of the game so it feels like a missed opportunity.
Bosses and Top Dogs are all identical with their move set which I feel was, again, a big missed opportunity.
Signposting isn't particularly good in some places while being excessive in others. For instance, it doesn't tell you your severe scrap shortage can be alleviated by building certain projects, but it will highlight "secret" entrances and access points in big yellow paint.
Conclusion:
I'd definitely recommend it; I don't play many games until completion these days but I had a blast with this. You'll especially appreciate it if you have any interest in the Mad Max movies or even muscle cars, rat rods or vehicular combat.

It has it's flaws here and there, and some people may feel like exploration doesn't reward enough but I feel the strengths of the pros heavily outweigh the cons.

- Listening to the waycryer telling me that he's sorry for all the things he yelled at me and that I shouldn't kill him. But then I was curious what this little crank that was connected to his chain did.
- Boosting off cliffs and taking little to no damage most of the time. "Nailed it!"
- The storms were pretty cool. Although, one time I was sitting inside of a hut while I was waiting for the storm to pass and then my body starting flipping around like a ragdoll, I then got glitched into the wall for a minute or two, unable to move, and once the storm passed I was magically pushed on top of the hut. How can I give that a con? It was pretty funny.
- I was a few missions into the game and it was already giving me missions really far away, but I barely explored anything around me. I felt like they did a poor job at slowly guiding you to the "end location." I just ignored it and had fun lowering the threat of the bottom areas first before progressing.
- I didn't like how many little cinematic things they had to show me doing simple things. I don't really want to watch Max eat dog food or maggots. Kinda gross. I got used to it though, so it's not a big deal.
- I honestly didn't know there was a jump button in this game until I looked up the controls. Usually the controls are self explanatory, but left ctrl for jump? That was a bit weird. I bet I looked a little odd just rolling around in the dirt everywhere.
- Bringing down the scarecrows seemed pointless and it made a ton of metal pieces go everywhere, causing you to try and maze your way through them to pick up the scrap pieces. Now just think about how silly I looked trying to roll my way over these pieces when I didn't know there was a jump button. *Sigh*
- I really wish there was more stealth abilities in this game. I always felt like I was just running right at a group of enemies like I was trying to go give them a hug. They never liked that.
- Many times I found myself ramming an unmanned vehicle over and over just to get it to explode so I could pick up the scrap pieces. It would have been nice to have a way to blow it up faster (without wasting my ammo because it is limited) or have chumbucket go out and take pieces off the car; sort of like what happens in real life if you park your nice car in a bad neighborhood. Wait, was that racist? Oh well,
- The historic relics were a bit weird and I found myself just ignoring them most of the time because I didn't care. They served no purpose in the game really.
- The balloon rides were really time consuming. They could have easily simplified this with a cinematic that automatically finds the spots near you. Far Cry did a great job at this. I had to mark a few things, back out to the map, use my binocculars again, and then back out until I was able to mark everything.

I'm not sure what those who negatively reviewed the game were expecting to get out of it. Mad Max clearly isn't trying to reinvent the open world genre. I've played over 60 hours and feel I got my money's worth. While far from perfect, it's a solid open world game that I would definitely recommend buying on sale.
Graphically and soundwise, it's a fine achievement. It's beautiful to look at and the ambient sounds go a long way in creating an immersive world. From the environments to the characters, it perfectly nails down the atmosphere of the Mad Max universe. Technically, it's also a very smooth experience and I've yet to experience a single crash, freeze, or gamebreaking bug.
As far as gameplay is concerned, it uses the same formulas as many Ubisoft games (Assassin's Creed, Watch Dogs, Far Cry). You're dropped in a large map filled with optional objectives in addition to a couple hours worth of story missions.
Car combat is fun but also fairly simple, as are the rest of the game's mechanics. However, simple does not necessarily mean boring. Streamlined mechanics don't keep you from actively playing the game and exploring the world. You're constantly doing something in Mad Max and at every turn you're rewarded in some small way, whether it's exploring and finding a new upgrade for your car, character or strongholds, improving your car and seeing the effects of the changes during combat, participating in races and unlocking new vehicles, liberating a fort that will grant you more ressources, etc. It all makes a for a forward-moving, rewarding and overall fun experience.

Let me start by saying this, in order to get anywhere in Rogue Legacy, you have to die, and die you will. In Rouge Legacy you control your children in a long line of sometimes afflicted family members who are trying to atone for the past sin of your ancestor. You'll brave a castle filled with a number of powerful bosses in different areas, all ready to send you to a very easily earned death, though you'll have to find them in the castle first. Each time you die, you get to select one of your three children, all of different size, class, gender, and other factors that can affect gameplay.
While this game does require a certain level of skill, in the end, it's a grind, but a fun grind if you can enjoy this sort of thing. Your character grows by leaving all of the gold they've gathered in the castle to their children, which they can spend on stat upgrades, equipment, and special runes that can give you abilities. Be warned though, until a certain upgrade is earned, you'll loose all of your unspent gold when entering the castle again (there's a skill that when a large sum of gold is invested into, you can keep upwards to 50% of your gold when going in the castle).
However, once one of your children decides to brave the castle, they'll find it isn't what their dad or mom went through. The castle randomizes its layout each time you enter, unless you pay to have the layout locked down at the cost of potential rewards (good if you decide to work on fighting a boss). This can definitely keep you interested while you throw your children into harm's way just so their children after them can have a few more hitpoints to survive the next area.
All in all, I've had a lot of fun with this game, and still play a bit on NG+ ever now and then. It may not be worth 15 bucks to a lot of people (though I think it is, but was lucky enough to get it as a gift), but if you see it on sale and want a Rogue-lite Castlevania-esque game, pick it up!

Since Steam doesn't provide a stars or points rating system for games the only way to downrate Rogue Legacy is not to recommend it. What is my problem with this game?
I know myself that I am not the best platform gamer. I do not play that sort of games very often so I knew to some extent that RL would be a challenge for me. Of course the main reason for me to buy RL was its game principle. Dying is not bad at all and it's even a central part of the game by investing earned money, blueprints and so on after death.
So I liked this refreshing idea which I miss in a lot of blockbuster titles nowadays. When I started playing this game there was a big motivation to become better. In this respect it is good that skills cost more for each purchased level. However, the rise of the cost is too much and the fact that the overall character's level is part of the formula is the decisive knockout for me. I know that a lot of platform indie gamers and developers emphasize a hardcore gaming experience - but sorry, in the end this is too frustrating for me.
Apart from that there could be a greater repertoire of enemies. Some are just a bigger version of the previous ones, throwing more fireballs or whatever. And I think a COMPLETELY randomly generated dungeon is not that good. It causes balancing problems and sometimes it is nice to have a little storyline (RL journal entries are not enough). And it makes more fun to explore a well-designed world than walking through meaningless rooms. Only partially generated would be fine. Having randomly generated traits is funny, but often they don't mean that much for the gaming experience and because the character dies so fast there is too less identification with your traits or the hero.
I'd say overall 7 of 10 points, 6 of 10 if you are not a hardcore platform gamer.

NOTE: This is a review of Alpha 20. I will update this review as new versions are released.
Prison Architect is an amazing game. I've played 25 hours at the time I'm writing this, and I confidently expect to reach triple digits.
Gameplay is exactly what you see in the trailers. You build a prison, and you deide whether it's a hellhole with armed guards at every turn or a relaxing, communal environment where prisoners occupy themselves with education and playing pool. I found the process of building blueprints a little unintuitive, especially when they add on to an existing building, but you should be able to construct all manner if prisons in no time. If you just want to jump in a muck around, there are prisons and mods you can download from the Steam Workshop. You can also upload your own prison and share it with the masses.
The prison theme is also one worth discussing. While the devs have said that they don't wish the game to take a side, and that there should be functional ways to play all prison styles, you still notice little in-game events that can stay with you after you close the game. In a very early prison, I didn't build phones or visiting rooms fast enough, and the prisoners rioted because they missed their families. Unfortunately, at present the prisoners feel largely interchangeable, with most of them only being noticed if they manage to pass advanced workshop courses and make money for the prison. However, more interpersonal elements are going to be added in future builds, most notably gangs.
This does bring up that "early access" tag that you see on the store page. While the game is enjoyable as it stands, it is definitely not complete. Bugs range from amusing (inmates tearing off their clothes and gleefully streaking through the halls to the showers) to annoying (workers walking through walls and sometimes getting items they carry stuck there) to baffling (trees suddenly growing in the middle of my kitchen, only to be dumped in a garbage bag and thrown away). There is also a certain amount of optimization to be done. The devs have said that they plan to drop the price upon full release, so if that's a major consideration for you, then I'd suggest waiting for release or at least a sizeable sale. I bought it myself on the last sale for about $10, and it's easily worth the full, current price to me.
In summary, if you enjoy simulators at all, I urge you to check this game out. I highly doubt you'll be disappointed.
UPDATES:
Alpha 21: Drug addiction is a good addition to the game. It doesn't feel really fleshed out at the moment, though, and is more of an annoyance than anything else. My prisons generally don't get to the point of riots, but I'm glad that those mechanics are more subtle now.

While some could argue however that this is not a positive aspect to it (which wouldn't exactly be wrong since again, this is very subjective), I do find it a little problematic when story writers try to make some that is, or at least should be, simple into something complex in a attempt do add, or make it look like, it has "depth" to it. Most often than not to me such action ends up just making the narrative confusing and in some cases, nonsensical.

Yet, despite its simple presentation there is some good and funny creativity here (most noticiably on
this world works and how people make by and live on it). Your faithful ally Chumbucket and his crazy religious beliefs and lines is an (funny) example of it.

The things only start to frail a little when we enter the voice acting department, some are good and others.. eh. While I certainly don't expect every single line on every single occasion to be delivered as if Laurence Olivier was behind it, there were some moments (and not exactly few) that were bellow the average of what you would expect from it. Most noticeably it happens when you talk to random NPC's around the map that give you intel/scrap/whatever.
Not much to say really - it is a very good one on almost all aspects. For more detailed info;
.

However I did noticed a very small/rare problem. Despite the game running at 60 FPS pretty much always there are times every hour or so where the game freezes for a second and then goes back to 60. The pattern looks to be completely random and I've seen it happen on some people videos/streams a few times and there were others talking about it. If I were to take a very wild guess here, the blame lies on the (already cracked) Denuvo DRM (for more info on why it would be the DRM, google on how this thing works).
I guess they will never learn.
This will be a tricky part. But if you want my personal opinion, there is a not so small problem(s) with it.

And the problem is that if we remove travel times and focus solely on the action parts THAT ACTUALLY MATTER, be it on a minor or major way inside the game (i.e outpost capture, random quests, main quest, etc), we have 60% on foot combat and 40% car combat. Now, when you also consider that the melee combat is 100% based on the already overused Batman-like system of 2 button presses with the occasional 3rd one.. Well, I guess your experience will depend on how you personally view said combat system.

The thing is, when we compare to other games that use the very same style like say for example, Shadow of Mordor, we can still conclude that what we have here is a fairly inferior one. While playing SoM there was at least some sort of "variety" to it, be it on the superior character skill customization and combat combos, more weapons with each allowing for different approaches during gameplay, much better weapon customization (runes) where you can build your arsenal in such way that it complements/enhances the way you have built/play with your main character skills, and lets not forget of course all the effin amazing fatality animations we do during combat (If by the way you have a personal problem with Orcs, that game will be your perfect stress reliever).
Also as a final note here.. Sometimes you will have to face mini-bosses, the so called "Top Dogs". And the interesting thing here is that they all LOOK THE SAME AND FIGHT THE SAME WAY - that is just lazy.

As for the car part of the game.. There is definitely a certain charm in building the Magnum Opus to your liking, seeing it evolve from the pile of junk you start with it and later on becoming your Symphony No. 9.

I won't say that there's little variety in this department but when you really get down to it, there's also not that much. You get a set amount of parts where some are straight upgrades from the others so you won't find much reason to go back and grab a "lower" one - if we were then to forget the body of the car (which there is a selection for you to choose from) and focus on a max performance-only build, most player cars will pretty much use the very same parts all around and end-up being the "same".
If you ask me, we definitely need more customization options here, both when it comes to looks and when it comes to performance/gadgets. Also as a side note, you can collect cars on the wasteland and use them, although I never ever felt the desire to do so.

But what about the big booms? The dirty in-your-face car combat? When you get to the thick of the action it is fun. You have a selection of weapons you can use and most of the time you can target specific parts of your enemies. The explosions and the sound are well made and the debris fly around almost in a poetic manner. There is also a variety of enemies here with each having their own strategies to try to take you down (not that many though mind you, this also should really be expanded).

I feel however that the game really drops the ball in the convoy system and that a great opportunity was lost here, both on the action department and in the metagame aspect.

What should be (to me) an intense RACE against the clock to try to stop a cargo from reaching its destination, ends up becoming a very simple hit-n-run-wait-for-repair-and-repeat mission. Convoys drive in circle, on the very same route, 24/7 non-stop despite being under attack or not. What do you do then? Start your run, kill 2-3 cars, fallback (if you leave the leader alone, they wont chase you), repair and catch up or just stand still and wait for them to come back in the very same route.

This is a
on several levels. Convoys should carry a very important cargo (what they carry barely matters), they should go from point A to B as fast as possible (adding to the tension, action and making SKILL play a bigger role) and it would be on your best interest to stop them not only for the loot but because if they do end up completing their run point B would become stronger making then your life on the world more difficult (this is what we call metagame). I really, REALLY wish they upgrade this system down the line.

Hey guess what Undertale is a great game.
Some of the best writing I've seen in games, incredibly lovable characters, and a personality that bleeds through every aspect of the game, both humorous and occasionally disturbing.
Undertale is a game having a conversation with the player. The game does not reveal everything about itself, and asks you to unfold the story and setting on your own. There is no genocide of pacifist run, at least not naturally. You go through the game organically, facing the consequences of your actions while the game assumes your being honest. But it also knows when you're simply going through the motions for a certain ending. It knows when you're only focused on "unlocking" everything, on seeing everything the game has to offer, when you just want to see that one cool fight and what happens to the characters be damned.
It knows if your being dishonest in your conversation with it, and uses that fact beautifully.
Me personally, I've only ever had two runs of this game, neutral and "pacifist", and I've seen enough to know I'm satisfied with my time in the world of Undertale. I had a wonderful conversation with the game, and politely said goodbye when I knew I saw what I felt I needed to see. If you play Undertale in a different way, I have nothing against you, as everyone should play a game as they see fit. However, I recommend that you close that wiki, that you come in cleanly as possible (which I know is difficult due to this game's popularity), and simply sit down with the game and see where the conversation goes.

-Mods. Not really necessary, but why not? More stuff.
What I don't like:

Spec Ops is a rare game: a military shooter thats actually fun. Gameplay is a standard 3rd person shooter, with regenerating health and chest high walls. Weapon variety is good, although negated slightly by only being able to carry 2 at a time. Your squad AI is mostly reliable. This is honestly one of the best games I have ever played this year. The story is very intriguing and it keeps you wanting to progress through the story! The game features a very well-balanced fighting system similar to the Batman Arkham series and Shadow of Mordor. As you may have expect, there are also weaponry available. But ammo is scarce and can only be obtained by either scavenging areas or looting defeated enemies. The game features a very large open-world atmosphere where you can explore and scavenge many areas available in the world. Cars are essential to survival. You will be able to customize your own car with a great number of customizations to select from. You may choose to customize your vehicle with more attack power, more speed, more defence, or a balance. You will also be able to customize Max as well. With all that said, there are also some drawbacks. As you start to play the game, you will start to realize that the activities and the scavenging component becomes rather repetitive. Majority of them require you to collect a different number of scraps, crew scrap parts, and/or history relics. This can be very time consuming. Activities requiring the Magnum Opus (your vehicle) are also quite repetitive, but rewarding. Although I appreciate the challenge that random enemy encounters on the road can bring, the likelihood of them occuring is high. Most of them, you can't bypass an area without having to fight them. This can be very fustrating. The story is great and easy to understand, but unfortunately, it is very short. Do not expect to achieve 30+ hours just by completing the story alone. With all the positive and negative components out of the way, the game is still worth purchasing, The game is very enjoyable, especially if you enjoy racing games, but with a side of killing! And did I mention that it is very optimized out of the box? I recommend!

This is not your average "America saves the world from Terror"-crap story that most military shooter bring us today. No, this is not sir, this is an engaging tale of survival amidst the "Heart of Brightness in Dubai", exlporing themes commonly overlooked
in other games of the genre. Here "The Line" is definetely getting crossed and in the end there was never any other choice than the way we advanced to the climax.
While some players may be complaining about certain events in the game that might make you feel bad, it should make you think about war and what's going on - or better what is/may/might happen in a warzone. Thus Spec Ops The Line becomes one of those rare to find "anti-war" titles. An arousing story that shouldn't upset us but  make us think.

Yet another favourite title, Spec Ops: The Line is pretty much the video game equivalent of Apocalypse Now with the same sort of descent into madness which the player character, Captain Martin Walker, and his two squadmates are subject to. It sucks you into thinking it's another generic shooter but it is in fact, a complete deconstruction of the otherwise stagnant genre as it is today. Well worth taking a look at, at least.
This game, is not  very fun, It's actually fairly . . . crushing? I guess that's the word. The gameplay is lacking, but solid. The story, Is amazing, and that's why you should buy it.

Spec Ops: The Line is a reboot of the old Spec Ops franchise which last game was released a decade ago. Despite being lauded for its "accurate" portrayal of the military life, The Line still plays like your typical third person cover shooter.
Its cookie cutter mechanics aside, one thing The Line will certainly be remembered for is its dark and gripping plot. The player assumes the role of Captain Walker, one of three Delta Force soldiers tasked with locating a missing battalion.
On top of the many twists and turns, the game will also ask the player to make several moral choices. Unfortunately, these moments are far in between, even in a game as short as 6 to 7 hours, and their impacts aren't played out to their fullest potential.
In a game where the biggest threat comes from American soldiers and civilians, Spec Ops: The Line bends the expectation of modern shooters. Sadly, with its short campaign, subpar mechanics and dead multiplayer, full price is a tad too much.
Grade: B-

There is a very impactful image in game (I didn't take a screenshot, but I am sure you can find it in the steam game stream), of a mother and her baby.  If I take anything away from this game, it will be that.  There was a huge disconnect between the graphicness of the image, versus how little setup, follow up, or caring about it in the aftermath.  It felt very shock-driven.

This is honestly one of the best games I have ever played this year. The story is very intriguing and it keeps you wanting to progress through the story! The game features a very well-balanced fighting system similar to the Batman Arkham series and Shadow of Mordor. As you may have expect, there are also weaponry available. But ammo is scarce and can only be obtained by either scavenging areas or looting defeated enemies. The game features a very large open-world atmosphere where you can explore and scavenge many areas available in the world. Cars are essential to survival. You will be able to customize your own car with a great number of customizations to select from. You may choose to customize your vehicle with more attack power, more speed, more defence, or a balance. You will also be able to customize Max as well. With all that said, there are also some drawbacks. As you start to play the game, you will start to realize that the activities and the scavenging component becomes rather repetitive. Majority of them require you to collect a different number of scraps, crew scrap parts, and/or history relics. This can be very time consuming. Activities requiring the Magnum Opus (your vehicle) are also quite repetitive, but rewarding. Although I appreciate the challenge that random enemy encounters on the road can bring, the likelihood of them occuring is high. Most of them, you can't bypass an area without having to fight them. This can be very fustrating. The story is great and easy to understand, but unfortunately, it is very short. Do not expect to achieve 30+ hours just by completing the story alone. With all the positive and negative components out of the way, the game is still worth purchasing, The game is very enjoyable, especially if you enjoy racing games, but with a side of killing! And did I mention that it is very optimized out of the box? I recommend!

I can’t overstate how great this game is. This might be one of my favorite games of all time. It’s incredibly challenging yet deeply rewarding. You will find yourself dying over and over again yet you are happy to come back for more punishment. The idea of having to pick a character – each with their own strengths and weaknesses – from a randomized gene pool is a great concept. Sometimes you will simply have to concede defeat and sometimes you will luck out and prepare yourself for a long run into unknown worlds. The randomized castles are a great mechanic that provides a fresh experience every time you restart. The ability to unlock power ups and game-changing mechanics is unique and fresh and allows for much more gradual difficulty curve. Eventually you should be able to beat the game; the question is how many hours will it take? It took me just under 20 hours to beat the final boss. The game is hard but not Spelunky hard.

An interesting indie game that utilises an incredibly intriguing central game mechanic; you are part of an increasingly stupid, or honourable family. Upon death in this wonderful rogue-like RPG the game isn't over, yet far from it, instead you choose one of three children that the recently deceased adventurer produced at some undetermined point before entering Castle Hamson, which each descendant enters for some reason far beyond my understanding, despite the fact countless ancestors have perished upon entry, they continue until you achieve victory.
The castle changes each time you enter, unless you employ the talents of the Architect, who 'locks' it in place, leaving the place just how your ancestors found, minus the loot and with returned monsters, so there are constantly new skeletons, flying-cloaked-fire/ice-spitting-wizard-thingys, walking suits of armour, and floating eyeballs to kill, yielding gold which you use to upgrade your manor that rests right outside the castle, (convenient, huh?) which in turn improves your chances of defeating endless foes on your way to the four minor bosses, and I'm assuming the one big boss (haven't faced it just yet). What makes the integral mechanic of this game even better is the way in which each child is different; each is one of a different class group, has different traits, like dyslexia or vertigo, and has a different spell. For instance, one of my more interesting characters was a bearded lady who was a lover of the ladies (literal lesbian description) and suffered from vertigo, and could summon fireballs (how she ever had three children in medieval times is also beyond my comprehension).
The sound for the game is nothing to lose your pants over, yet serves its purpose; setting the mood wonderfully, which is in contrast with the controls, which when used effectively can see the most pathetic character succeed better than any tougher characters, and seem to be a product of great design. The graphics are quite charming, Cellar Door takes great advantage of its' resources, by creating charming effects in line with the traits characters experience.
Overall I'd give the game a 9/10. Everything feels great when you get into it, yet a few minor problems with the overall vibe of the game just irk that last point from my score. Definitely buy.

This is not your average "America saves the world from Terror"-crap story that most military shooter bring us today. No, this is not sir, this is an engaging tale of survival amidst the "Heart of Brightness in Dubai", exlporing themes commonly overlooked
in other games of the genre. Here "The Line" is definetely getting crossed and in the end there was never any other choice than the way we advanced to the climax.
While some players may be complaining about certain events in the game that might make you feel bad, it should make you think about war and what's going on - or better what is/may/might happen in a warzone. Thus Spec Ops The Line becomes one of those rare to find "anti-war" titles. An arousing story that shouldn't upset us but  make us think.

Yet another favourite title, Spec Ops: The Line is pretty much the video game equivalent of Apocalypse Now with the same sort of descent into madness which the player character, Captain Martin Walker, and his two squadmates are subject to. It sucks you into thinking it's another generic shooter but it is in fact, a complete deconstruction of the otherwise stagnant genre as it is today. Well worth taking a look at, at least.
This game, is not  very fun, It's actually fairly . . . crushing? I guess that's the word. The gameplay is lacking, but solid. The story, Is amazing, and that's why you should buy it.

Spec Ops: The Line is a reboot of the old Spec Ops franchise which last game was released a decade ago. Despite being lauded for its "accurate" portrayal of the military life, The Line still plays like your typical third person cover shooter.
Its cookie cutter mechanics aside, one thing The Line will certainly be remembered for is its dark and gripping plot. The player assumes the role of Captain Walker, one of three Delta Force soldiers tasked with locating a missing battalion.
On top of the many twists and turns, the game will also ask the player to make several moral choices. Unfortunately, these moments are far in between, even in a game as short as 6 to 7 hours, and their impacts aren't played out to their fullest potential.
In a game where the biggest threat comes from American soldiers and civilians, Spec Ops: The Line bends the expectation of modern shooters. Sadly, with its short campaign, subpar mechanics and dead multiplayer, full price is a tad too much.
Grade: B-

I bought this game on a whim. Although was expecting it and had seen pre-release material, I wasn't too hopeful, given movie tie-ins and was planning to wait reviews. After a weekend of a music-festival-turned-unplanned-Mad Max-cosplaying, I decided to buy the game, my face still covered in chrome spray.
Just like Fury Road to original three Mad Max films, this game follows its own continuity of sorts (although the ending suggests it might actually be a prequel to Fury Road).
First off, the game looks *amazing* and is incredibly well optimised to PC. This is a statement I had seen in reviews before I bought it and thought it was just people struggling to find compliments for a bad game ("Damned by Faint Praise") but it really looks good and runs very smooth. The distances show very well, there is little to no flickering, I have not encountered any obvious glitches. I had only one spot where the framerate dropped significantly. Flames and thunderstorms in particular look sublime.
Gameplay is fairly solid. Nothing too exciting if you have played AC or Batman, as elements of both are readily apparent. Controls are a bit off. Some of the default key mapping puts commands in odd places but you can re-map them. As a whole, the gameplay is fairly shallow. Most commands are reliant on holding the E button. Or mashing the E button. Or mashing the E button while mashing mouse keys if you're fighting. Controls are stable and it is fun to fistfight, use your gun, shiv or weapons. No real issues stick out.
Car controls vary but overall tend to lack handling, though nowhere as badly as the cars in Watch_Dogs did and they depend on the car you pick too. Still, without dedicated handbrake buttons and the like (though the vehicle slam button can substitute as one in some situations) the vehicle mechanics feel fairly shallow. Nitro boosts, harpoons and other abilities on the Magnum Opus make this a bit more enjoyable, almost to the expense of other vehicles. I honestly fail to see why you should even step in any other vehicles if Magnum as around. Given the abundance of interesting vehicles around, this is bit of a shame.
The pre-release material touted the game's survival element quite a bit. You would need to make sure you eat and drink to avoid starving/dehydrating and would be on the hunt for guzzoline like in the hunt for Mad Max: The Road Warrior. These never really come into play. You come across food (in the form of dog food cans with a reference to The Road Warrior, lizards and rats you can kill and eat or maggots on corpses) but they are all effectively static health pickups. There isn't a real hunger mechanic or picking up and hoarding food or spending hours in the wastes looking for it. Same with water. You can carry it in a canteen and it replenishes your health. Max will comment about thirst if canteen is empty but doesn't actually suffer for it. Most camps tend to have some gas canisters and locations where the gas is part of the objective they regenerate. Bullets are rarer and easier to run out and is effectively your only resource to keep an eye on. However if you fully upgrade allied camps, you will rarely be lacking resources.
Both Max and the Magnum Opus can be upgraded and customised, using scraps as resources. Most of the customisations improve abilities but some are purely cosmetic. Throughout the game, you also come across a wastelander called Griffa who has some cryptic conversations with Max, which lead to additional upgrades for Max's abilities. This allows for a degree of customisation and especially on-foot sections will challenge you even if you are fully upgraded. On vehicle, most of the fighting is fairly balanced, if prolonged. Once thundersticks are unlocked, they become a cakewalk.
Thoughout the game, there are many small camps/ as well as a number of bases belonging to Gastown. Most side missions involve taking these out for scraps, history relics, upgrades for friendly fortresses. Destroying Gastown bases also reduces the threat level in the region, reducing Gastown patrols and enabling you some of the upgrades. Taking all of these out can get a bit tedious and repetative. There are many camps that are just mooks + loot with nothing specific to flesh the world a bit more (other than some history relics). The more interesting places don't really appear until later in the game (especially in the Buzzard territories) and are still rare and in between. Most Gastown bases follow the same formula with no interesting sidequests (rescuing people for instance. There are many corpses in cages. Why can't some be alive to be rescued?) The %100 completion chase can sometimes kill any momentum, as the devs seem fond of showing how clever they are by putting things in really obscure spots. As a whole, this is the weakest part of the game and I enjoyed it a whole lot more once I got them out of the way. Outside these, there are the occasional wasteland encounters (mostly wastelanders with something to tell you and occasional questgivers with very simple quests) and a racing circuit that makes things a bit more interesting.
The setting and locations are a bit more interesting. As stated before, you play around the Wasteland surrounding Gastown and despite it being a desert wasteland, the creators went to some effort to make things varied. Jeet and Gutlash's territories used to be the ocean and there are plenty of reminders as you drive into a cave and notice all the dried corals or take shelter in grounded ships, giving a clear idea how messed up the world is. Heading inwards, you see go through old highways and abandoned towns. Eastwards, there are dunes which look empty but have a whole city that was buried beneath. Finally, the area around Gastown is a polluted wreck. So, kudos to to making the different locations a bit more varied. The history relics you collect give a sense of how things became the way they did and probably go into more detail about the nature of the apocalypse than any other Mad Max production so far. After a while, they don't say anything you didn't already know and could be a bit more detailed but are still a nice touch.
I initially didn't have much hopes of the story but it actually didn't turn too bad. As his is getting ready to travel to the Plains of Silence, Max is waylaid by Warlord Scarabus Scrotus (son of Immortan Joe, introduced in a Fury Road tie-in comic) and loses the Interceptor, gravely injuring the Warlord in the process. Max then comes across Chumbucket who is looking to create his own vehicle, the Magnum Opus. Believing Max to be a Saint of his strange religion, he enlists Max who only helps him looking after a new car. As they look to build it, they encounter settlements that have come under attack from the Warlord scouring the wasteland, gradually leading up to Gastown itself in pursuit of a V8 engine. The earlier parts of the story are fairly standard but as it develops, it goes more and more into Max's demons and his fears of attaching to people in fear of losing them just as he lost his Wife and child and these issues come pretty heavily later in the story. Between that and the optional encounters with Griffa, the game actually goes into a lot of detail regarding Max's solitude and survival guilt. Not going to spoil a lot more but there is a reason why I feel the game is a prequel leading up to Fury Road.
You won't find the charm and crazy-fun of Fury Road here. I doubt even the film sequels will have that. The characters aren't as memetic or memorable either, although the makers clearly tried to and Chum, Crow Dazzle and the Outcrier shine among the rest.
As a post-apocalypse game taking place in the Mad Max universe, this is a good, solid game that will keep you busy, so definitely buy it, though you may want to wait for a discount if you have doubts. I almost regretted a Day 1 purchase but it grew on me as I progressed, so I am glad I bought it then.

Simple, but surprisingly addictive game. If you enjoyed SimTower, you will enjoy this. Prison Architect puts you in a position to design a prison, hire staff, and survive the inmate population growth over time. Logic and strategy have to be applied to your design to ensure rooms/resources are accessible, and prisoners don't escape.
Your first few games will be failures, because the game's tutorials don't cover every concept. You don't have much money to prepare a big enough prison to handle constant growth. After a while, you learn how to lay out your building and prepare for prisoner needs. The zoning of rooms and layouts of utilities are similar to SimCity, with the construction aspect closer to SimTower.
Tips: Learn how to turn off incoming prisoners in your report. On a new game, hire your warden and all the workers you can. Get an immediate building complete to use as office space to get your warden to work on researching Maintenance and Medicine. You want a Janitor and Doctor as soon as possible. Once the office is done, spend all your time and money building as big of a prison as you can. As long as you have the cash on hand for the materials (building, lights, walls, beds, toilets, utility lines), you can spend all the time you want building it with no incoming prisoners. Once you're ready for your first batch, allow low or medium risk prisoners. Once they arrive, you will have a higher daily budget, use that to hire guards to get them in immediately. Future added budget should go to admin staff to research more skills.
Ultimately, you may get bored playing vanilla, and that's where cheating comes into play. The save file is in plain text, and you can edit the cash you have on hand. Reload the save, and then build as much as you want with unlimited money. It gives you a longer insight into the gameplay and may help you play vanilla in the future.
Caveat: The game is definitely unfinished. AI logic and interaction with objects can be flawed, and that can lead to negative impacts on your game. Hopefully the functionality improves significantly over development, as the MSRP is fairly high for something this early.
The surprises the game has for you (escape attempts, attacking staff, riots) are interesting and keep you on your feet. I can easily play this game for hours on end with no consideration for time. It's literally like being in prison. It may not be worth MSRP, but if you can get it on sale, definitely pick this up.

Until you see reviews indicating that the devs have managed to put some depth into the game, I would advise against buying it.
I was very excited when first playing, but after not too long, you run out of new things to discover and learn, apart from optimizing your prison.
Did I get my money's worth? Probably, the game is not awful. It's just not very replayable.

I thought I knew what to expect after reading the description and watching the trailer. The first impression it made on me was that it would be a fun and quick little way to kill some time. I figured it would be a casual game. Boy was I wrong.
Pros:
This game offers just enough challenge to keep me hitting the proverbial try again button while saying 'I know I can do better'. The random level generation works! So far I have never felt like I was just replaying the same thing (unless I wanted to ;)  ).
Key mapping is also a great feature. I like being able to customize what keys control what movements.
I really like having the ability to re-enter the exact same castle layout. It is really handy for if I died too quickly, or I came across a spot that my current character couldn't enter. In fact, it's actually nice to see that the physical and personality quirks that each character has, not only adds some neat little dynamic to the next playthrough, but also can have a genuine use. While it's fun to run around as a gigantic barbarian, smashing all in my way repeatedly with my sword, sometimes, to access little hidden areas, I need to be the tiniest of men, or women, and I love that!
Another thing I like IS just the variety of character options! With so many classes, it's fun to play around with the various randomly generated character options. Even though they aren't given to you at the beginning, I feel it's actually better that way. I liked working to earn the coin to unlock them. However, I will admit that it was almost painful sometimes, when chosing what to unlock.
I really enjoy reading the journal entries and I can't wait to find out more of the back story. While it is agonizing to have to hand so much coin over to Charon at times, I understand the necessity. I think that the game did a great job explaining why it is present. An unlockable that you can get later on  is really nice though and I admit I don't feel bad about haggling with Charon to keep some of my hard earned gold. (Honestly, best job in this game is Charon's XD )
The sound track is phenominal. In fact, I have actually started the game and just left it running so I could listen.
I'm a really big fan of pixel art and I have to say Rogue Legacy did a beautiful job with it. The characters and environments are nicely detailed and look fantastic.
Cons:
I was led to believe that, while I could pick a new character from a selection of three options, I could also go back and pick one of my previous characters. I don't know, maybe I missed something, but I honestly thought I could go back and pick a character I had already played as. I understand why this is not an actual feature though, because it could be abused and defeat the purpose of playing as the "child" of your now dead character. Still though, it was a little disappointing when I went back to play as Sir Taco II, only to find I couldn't.
Some of the descriptions on items that you can unlock, are either unclear, or too vague. I have used the gold I earned to purchase power ups that ended up not doing what I thought they would. For example, I was led to believe that through purchasing a certain power-up, I would be able to fly (aka pressing the action button would allow me to "fly" upwards), if for a very limited amount of time. In truth, what I did was stay in place in the air for several seconds (which didn't help me when I was falling after attempting to make too large a jump, thinking that I would be able "flap my wings" to reach it).
While most of the upgrades and power-ups boost general stats, some of them unlock other branches, which may contain playable classes. The problem is, sometimes the branch unlocked doesn't make any sense compared to what unlocked it. Unfortunately, I found myself having to put coins into things I didn't necessarily want, just so I could unlock a new branch and hopefully find a new playable class, or something else useful (which means I would have to just keep throwing myself at castle after castle for more gold, that I could spend on the new thing). Considering how difficult it can be to accumulate large sums of money, I didn't really like having to spend it on something I didn't feel a need for.
I think that while the enemies' increase in difficulty as you level up, works, the steep rise in how much it cost to unlock things seems kind of unfair. Especially compared to each coins individual worth. Sometimes I feel less like an adventuring hero out for glory and vengeance, and more like a peasant struggling to pay the resident lord.
Even though it may seem like I have a lot more negative criticism for the game, I truly do love it. This game can, through great will power (rarely frustration) on my part, be a casual quick time killer. However, I find myself coming back to it again and again because I keep telling myself 'I can make it this time', or I'm enticed by the promise of a new layout.
Needless to say my death count, or rather "portrait count" is quite extensive.
I whole heartedly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a nice pixel-visual and musical accompanyment; and has the patience to die a thousand deaths.

Mad Max is one of my favorite film series, and this game really feels like Mad Max to me.
There is plenty of stuff to do although it gets really repetitive really fast.  You spend most of your time grinding for scrap for the numerous upgrades for your car as well as Max himself,  these come in the form of demolishing enemy camps, searching old wrecks and buildings, clearing minefields, etc.  The story is good but short and it forces you to complete a lot of these scrap grinds in order to upgrade enough to advance.
The melee combat feels a lot like the Batman games, and the whole game plays a lot like Shadow of Mordor.  The game is really repetitive with it's tasks but it is very satisfying driving around in your overloaded car getting into road battles and fist fights.
I would highly recommend it for fans of Mad Max but I could see how some people would get bored with it easily.

I'm just sitting here, still in awe of how well these new developers understood the complex character of Chloe Price. Going into this, I honestly wasn't sure how the story of Life is Strange would hold up when expanded with a prequel, but all of my worries were unfounded. So far, they've nailed absolutely everything. Episode One was hella amazing!

Life is Strange: Before the Storm starts with an emotional firework. You play as Chloe Price, known from Life is Strange, and her befriending Rachel Amber - also known from Life is Strange.
Both are building up a tight relationship, which makes the characters talk about their plans for the future. This makes the story very depressing, as the future of both characters is known for players of the first game. In addition, Chloes struggle with her father's loss is depictured more intense than in Life is Strange and explains why Chloe is who Chloe is.
Instead of a time travel mechanism, Chloes ability is to argue with people. Here you have to use the correct responses to people's talking. Even though you go through talks only, the story is intense and ends with a big "OMG" in the end.
If you are fan of Life is Strange, you don't have to be scared of playing Before the Storm (maybe you think, that nothing can replicate the feelings or quality of Life is Strange. That is wrong. Before the Storm can). But you don't have to. Put tissue paper on the desk. Get ready for the feelings.
10/10

It is no easy feat to follow up a game that is beloved by fans. It's even harder to meet the expectations that fans have for the game when it launches. LIS is very important to many people including me and I was sceptical at best for what Deck 9 could pull off, not that it would be a bad game but could it evoke the same emotions that LIS could pull out of my cold dead heart.
As of now BTS is everything I could have asked for in a follow up. I have some gripes with parts of the game but nothing is perfect and when BTS gets it right it gets it right. Now we are only at episode one so things can change and maybe my gripes will get worse or maybe they will go away, but the price of entry is worth it just for one scene in particular IMO. That feeling that only LIS could evoke in me and that I was semi positive would never happen again was reached and I couldn't be happier.
BTS has opened from the gates strong and while it's anyone's guess how good it will end up, if they follow suit with how episode 1 played out I don't think it would be a bold claim to say BTS we be equal to LIS.

I feel much the same way about this game that I did about the original Dead Island.  A beautiful and realized setting with enjoyable and meaty combat hampered by poor execution on the story and gameplay flow.  The story just doesn't connect though the base themes are powerful and enjoyable.  Characters are not given the time to be fleshed out and the player isn't given time to CARE about them before tragedy strikes.
A large number of side activities flesh out an otherwise barebones game, bringing me in at over 40 hours to feel that I had 'finished' the game (didn't finish the races because insisting that I have to drive THEIR setup instead of my own is idiotic).  You're certainly getting your money's worth if you do all that you can but people speeding through will be disapointed in the meat of the game.
TLDR - I game I heartily recommend, though it lacks a bit in the story department and non 'collect everything under the sun' people may find it a bit short.

Borderlands 2 is spot-on in every way.
From the hilarious characters with brilliantly written dialogue to the enticing loot to the zany, phrenetic combat, every aspect of the game is perfectly executed. Gearbox took a risk in casting four (six) new vault hunters to replace those from the original Borderlands, but the new characters fill in their positions excellently. In addition, Lilith, Mordecai, Brick and Roland all play major parts in the game as NPCs, and their presence is welcome. Claptrap returns as well, as humorously moronic as before.
The four new vault hunters, Axton (Commando), Zer0 (Assassin), Salvador (Gunzerker), and Maya (Siren), are racing against Handsome Jack, president of the Hyperion Corporation, to reach and open a new vault. In addition to the main four vault hunters, there are two DLC characters, Gaige the Mechromancer and KRIEG the Psycho, who are definitely worth purchasing if you are into the game. They are included in the Game of the Year Edition.
The story is entertaining throughout, with plenty of fun side missions to complete if and when you finish the main game. There are also three DLC bonus campaigns which are all extremely fun.
In conclusion, Borderlands 2 is a rare 10/10 in my book. It's one of those games that is just plain old fun, without sacrificing a clever, well thought-out story and excellent character design.
