Euro Truck Simulator 2 is all about living the dream that is professional trucking. Euro Truck Simulator 2 is too serious. The game even tells you as you begin that this is your dream job. With more than enthusiasm, players begin their adventure humbly with a little garage in the home city of their choice, and a company with no trucks.
The player begins by taking jobs for other companies, earning money from one city to another, with an eye toward earning enough cash and purchasing a truck. An owned truck means more freedom, with higher paying jobs that require more responsibility. When working directly for the player company, cargo is waiting at a select shipping yard and must be hitched to the truck before it can be taken to its ultimate destination. The next step from there is to start upgrading the garage, hiring other drivers to bring in more income, and eventually building a trucking empire that spans all of Europe.
The more you go, the more there is to do. Want to expand quickly? You can take out loans that need to be repaid. Want specialized drivers? They each level up the same way you do, and you can dictate the way they do. Of course, you also have to be mindful of expenses, be they repayments to the bank or fuel consumption by employees looking for work. There are a lot of ducks to get in a row, but the interface is user-friendly and information is constantly provided so nothing ever feels hopeless.
More than a game about driving, Euro Truck Simulator 2 boasts some role playing elements to keep things interesting. Successful jobs earn experience, which gives skill points. Skill points can be spent upgrading one's proficiency in certain types of jobs, unlocking new types of cargo, or even investing in fuel efficiency. Improving personal abilities and building a business from one lone driver to an entire fleet.
Driving trucks is as realistic as possible. Offering a huge map of Europe, there's plenty of time to be spent on the open road, and lots of distance to cover. Although you won't be undertaking journeys in real-time, a decent paying job is still quite the investment. I often found myself able to only play one job at a time.
There are a variety of controls and settings allowing for significant flexibility in terms of personal comfort. You can choose how complex your controls are, with automatic settings keyboard and set up a wheel. Whatever your available input, Euro Truck do a great job of covering you and ensuring you get into the game easily.
A tutorial guides for newcomers, and the essential GPS is easy to understand, as is its clear and simple route map. My first job was a decided disaster, with me getting the trailer stuck a number of times, managing to tip the vehicle over, and even call for emergency rescue.
Traffic lights, speed cameras, and the ever-present need to keep one's eyes on the road can always trip up an overconfident player, and as relaxing as long country drives may be, the pressure to avoid mistakes is present throughout. It's very easy to start getting speeding along a motorway without regard to other drivers and strict speed limits. Every mistake translates into a financial penalty, damaged cargo reduces the payday, and suffered by an owned truck will have to be paid for at service stations.
When a mistake occurs, it's almost always our fault, but there are some moments where the computer controlled road users face an issue. But they're few and far between, and experienced drivers will be able to avoid many of the hazard that lead to such trouble. Despite the occasional pressure to perform jobs well, Euro Truck Simulator 2 is still a largely cleansing experience. There's a driving through a variety of countries, a sense of joy as you get closer to your destination, and a sense of accomplishment in performing such boring tasks as refueling at gas stations and finding parking stops at which to grab some sleep. As you build your business up from nothing and take on more of managerial duties, it's hard not to feel pride over rewards well earned.
Although most visually advanced game, Euro Truck's believable presentation of Europe's roads and cities and atmosphere of the backdrops, there's a sense of individuality to each new territory you uncover, and the trucks themselves are lovingly recreated with an intricate level of detail. Owned trucks can be repainted and upgraded with all manner of parts, and as the player levels up, the potential for personalization expands.
The most fun aspect of Euro Truck Simulator 2, however, comes in the form of its music. With the simple tap of the "R" key, you can open up a menu packed with European Internet radio streams as well as your own Music and Radio streams. Providing a wide variety to listen. There's also the option to queue up music from one's own PC.

Rogue Legacy has everything you want in a game.
There's challenge, humor, really catchy songs, and interesting mechanics. The family tree element is put to excellent use, allowing you to choose your successor, which isn't as easy as it sounds, as they all have advantages and disadvantages.
The challenge also lies in the randomly generated castle, which you can later choose to "lock down" and head in to the same castle over and over again. That is, so long as you aren't too fond of gold.
I personally found it to be more difficult with they keyboard, and opted to play with a controller instead, which, in my opinion, greatly improved my overall experience.
Back to the castle for a second, I did run into similar or near exact replicas of rooms multiple times (though never in one playthrough), but this was no huge issue. The challenge was still there, and this was quite the infrequent occurance.
The writing contains brief glimpses of humor, in the descriptions of surroundings and charactes, though the story is slim, or non-existant if you choose not to read the journals scattered throughout the castle. If you do choose to invest yourself in the story, the game makes you work for it, as you never know where you'll end up.
All in all, great game with hours of gameplay and tons of replayability. For only $15, why wouldn't you give it a chance?

I can't talk about Borderlands 2 in 2017 without talking at least a little about Gearbox Software's shady business practices.  This game benefits greatly from the draining of money away from Aliens: Colonial Marines, another Gearbox project which was sabotaged to give BL2 a boost.  And in the years since the release of BL2, Gearbox and Randy Pitchford have done all they can to prove that they never deserved success in the first place, partnering with a company called &quot♥♥♥♥♥quot; (ed: wow, Steam censored my use of this company's name), cramming as much scummy DLC into their games as possible, and mouthing off at every opportunity about how they would have changed all the things fans love about their games, given the chance.  BL2 comes with a host of baggage in this regard.  Even if you can ignore the industry politics surrounding the game, there is a LOT of pointless cosmetic DLC in this game, and the pause menu will advertise all of it to you.
It also comes with a built-in chest that dispenses vastly-overpowered gear for your current character's current level, using a currency shared by ALL characters (gold keys) that can only be earned by entering codes gained outside the game, by participating in now-defunct social media promotions (or entering them from a list you can find online).  Once you're out of gold keys, no more loot from that chest for you, ever again.  For ANY of your characters.  While this isn't a massive complaint, it speaks to Gearbox's overall scummy, mobile-esque, ad-heavy, DLC-nickel-and-diming strategy that they really went all-in on starting with this game.  While (spoilers) I do think it's worth buying the game even so, you need to know what you're getting into ahead of time.  If you find this stuff as distasteful as I do, you may want to think twice.
In terms of game design, if you think of Borderlands 2 as Diablo from a first person perspective, you won't go far wrong in how you approach it.  The focus here is the loot, not the story, although the story does try pretty hard to be interesting (your mileage may vary on whether you agree or not).  I definitely found the villain of the piece, Handsome Jack, to be eminently dislikeable in a good way.  I wanted to put bullets into this guy, so as the villain, he's doing his job pretty well.  Much of that is down to his voice actor, Dameon Clarke, who paints a really fantastic picture of a sociopathic corporate ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in Jack with his flippant, arrogant, pseudo-casual delivery.  Spot on, "pumpkin".  In any case, the story has its share of problems, but it primarily exists to ferry you from one loot arena to the next, and it does what it's supposed to do.  When the writing isn't veering off into wackytown, I actually found a lot of the intended emotional beats resonated with me, and the more understated instances of humor didn't fall flat.  This is a game that thinks it's a lot funnier than it is, though, so be forewarned.  The tone is all over the place.
Anyway, on to the loot.  The weapon types are pistols, shotguns, submachine guns, assault rifles (of which miniguns are a subtype), sniper rifles, and rocket launchers.  Each is randomly generated from a pool of manufacturers and parts that lend them particular characteristics, with stats determined by a dice roll.  You can also find grenade mods which determine the characteristics of the grenades you throw, and shields (in the Halo sense of a personal energy deflector) for defense.
This is a massive game, especially with all content DLC installed, and you can easily play it for hundreds of hours without really being "done" with it, even on a single character.  So, how you spend the bulk of your time will end up being a personal choice.  You could level as fast as possible and focus on fighting raid bosses with online friends/strangers for the highest-end loot you can.  You can play through all the stories and call it quits (which alone will take you probably 50-80 hours depending on DLC).  You can try and complete every sidequest in the game.  You can aim for completing the main story in each of the unlockable difficulty modes.  When you wake up on the glacier at the start of the game, it's hard to wrap your head around the sheer size and length of the journey ahead of each new character.  There is a lot more here than meets the eye.
The playable characters have some nice variety to them, although they grew on me a bit slower than did the heroes of the first game's cast.  BL2 went all-in on the characterization of everyone except the main characters, and it shows that they were designed with mechanics in mind first and foremost.  Zero, for instance, plays like a combination of the siren and sniper from BL1.  Axton plays like they had a chance to redesign Roland and iterated on his mechanics.  Salvador is Brick, but with guns instead of fists.  Maya's power (the new Siren) is the only entirely new, original idea in the cast, and it's on the one who's a carbon copy of a character from BL1 in physical design.  These don't feel so much like character traits as they do a list of patch notes.  The 2 DLC characters, the Mechromancer and Psycho, both have better personal characterization as well as really fun mechanics.  I recommend purchasing them both.
I also recommend acquiring the content DLC, starting with the Tiny Tina module, then adding Captain Scarlett.  If you enjoy those and just want more BL2, grab the rest.  They all come with a variety of new enemies to shoot, loot to find, and bosses to fight.  Be advised that, if you don't intend to play online with others, BL2 contains several bosses that are designed to be fought in a group and that have particular mechanics that make them prohibitively difficult to go at it alone.  Think of them as raid bosses in an MMO.
So, okay.  Enough faffing about.  Is Borderlands 2 fun?  Yes.  It feels good to play.  Shooting the guns is nice, they have impact.  The enemies scream and writhe around satisfyingly.  Elemental effects are impressive.  The visual style is fun, different, and nice to look at.  It drags a bit in the early game, especially very early on before your characters get their defining ability, but everything up to arriving at Sanctuary can be pretty boring and eminently linear.  However, once you're farther along, BL2 blossoms into one of the best Diablo-like loot-focused slot machine type games available.  There's a reason it's still so active on Steam multiplayer even in 2017.  It's very very good.  Just be advised going into it that it comes from a very scummy company, and is tainted by their shotgun approach to DLC.  Don't get suckered by them and you'll have a great time.

I like Mad Max. About 12 hours in I got a solid feel of the overall game.
The important thing to know about Mad Max is that it's fun. And that's the whole point.
It is far from perfect, lacks in many departements but it also has a lot of positives which make it a good enjoyable game.
The over the top action makes you want to play a little bit more all the time.
Completists will have their hands full.
The game focuses a lot on driving and does it well, there are so many upgrades for your vehicles, and so many of them.
The on-foot action is also good, fighting is a little simple (like batman) but its fun nevertheless. I do wish there was more weapons and customizations for them. It is very thin in that department, and you barely find any ammo in the game so you practically never use your shotgun.
The acting is good but the story is week. You don't feel like you're switching gears between the main story and side missions, they both feel the same, so you don't get that change of pace that breaks the monotony of tasks.
The game feels a little sand boxy but that doesn't take away form the fun of playing it.
The worst issue of the game is the character animation and movement. It's horribly done. The jumping in particular is the worst I've seen in any game the last 10 years, super clumsy. And the falling animation feels like you're a floating leaf.
They really needed to work on that departement to make max feel heavier, with the ability to jump and grab etc. All of which aren't there and hurt the gameplay.
The Positives:
-Great Atmosphere overall. Enviroments are spot on and so is music.
-Fun gameplay, fighting, driving and effects are satisfying.
-Tons of upgrades and mods.
-Lots of things to do.
-Pretty good acting.
The Negatives:
-Weekish Story. Even main mission feels like a side mission.
-A Little repetitive at times.
-Abysmal character movement for a current gen game. Jumping in particular is terrible.
Still, you will get a good 60-70hr atmospheric fun and thrilling gameplay out of this game.

I funded the game in about Alpha-2, and have seen it grow over time but here is my opinon.
Graphics:
-The graphics from this game are not from your AAA Shooter, (Battlefield, Call of Duty) Nor is it in 3D. However, they sprites may be simple, but they are well designed.
-Several minor graphics issues as of Alpha 20
Gameplay:
-The tutorial itself is not very sound and is not very good, however the devs have stated to change that in the future.
-The gameplay is basic but challanging for those who have never player before. (Like any other Introversion game)
-The current endgame of the game is a bit, bland. Once you have figured how to sucessfully run and manage a prison, you lose much of the current, "Fun" of this game.
-Many disaster features have only been partially implemented and or broken. (Ie; Fire in the game spreads, but water will only stop fires from spreading and not extingush the fires themseves.)
AI:
-Pathfinding: While many optimisations were made, the game itself still has framrate issues on lower end computers due to the amount of calculations needed.
-AI gets stuck on corners at times.
-Pathfinding importance: The game orders the jobs in by time assigned, and sometimes you will have ridiculous failures like cooks not washing foodtrays and prisoners cannot eat; thus causing a riot.
Community:
Forums- The main forums are here:

The fourms are where most of the activity takes place. However, there are certain members in the forums who tend to fight over the slightest provocation; so it is generally advisable to watch what is posted there.
Mods- Modding right now is pretty much limited to graphics and scenarios. You cannot change the basic features in the game or add new ones.
Pricing:
The game it self has a very high price tag for a open alpha game. The developers have stated that main reasons for that were to keep out people who bought the game and instantly expected it to be finished; and finding out that it isn't proceed to flame in the forums.
Developers:
The devolpers have a pretty good trackrecord as of far.
-Game Updates: They are released usually at the start of the month as there is pretty much one person coding the game, (Chris Delay). Leading to one or rarely two new features an update. Many other games have more content included within one patch due to the fact there are mutiple coders working on the game.
Code:
-Coded in C++ if I am right with the developer's engine from their game Subversion. (Currently on hold.)
-Scenarios are scriptted with LUA
-Uses OpenGl for compatability between Windows, Linux , and Mac OSX.
End thoughts:
Don't get me wrong, I loved the other games by the devolpers, but right now the game just feels bland and unintresting after you have gotten the hang of building and running a prison.

What if Castlevania: Symphony of the Night and a roguelike had a baby? Well, that baby would be monstrous, but its name would be none other than Rogue Legacy. In RL, you attempt to trudge through a randomly generated castle, collecting as much money as possible, beating back baddies, gathering up blueprints and runes, and hopefully taking out a boss or two.  The goal is to take out the four main bosses from the five different areas of the castle, then proceed to the main antechamber where you’ll fight the final bosses.
Of course, you won’t survive. Neither will your child. Or your children’s children. And so on. What gives? Well see, the only way you improve is by spending money outside the castle to build up your fort and buy new equipment and runes…but once you enter the castle, you don’t leave.  Your children will take your place when you die, first starting at the fort to build stuff up, then arriving at the castle to start the journey over again anew.
With all the ridiculous classes, traits, skills, equipment, and all the rest, the game constantly presents itself as an original challenge each time and is addictive as hell. If you like roguelikes, SotN, or both, you owe it to yourself to pick this up.

Part RPG, Part Rogue-like, and Part-Platformer, Rogue Legacy pleases on many levels but still leaves something to be desired. That's not to say its not worth your time, just that it's the mix of many different aspects which don't have the depth and variety to make them AMAZING. It does however compel you to keep hacking and slaying through the generations and it's a fun ride to the end boss. While it's a great twist on the permanent death paradigm this game doesn't have much puzzle or tradtional rogue-like challenge to it. Instead, you're greated with fantastic platformer gameplay more dependant of well timed jumps, strikes, dodging and button mashing. Couple that with a solid RPG level/skill system, a variety of classes, and a procedually generated dungeon and you have a really fun game. Still, it's not as punishing as many rogue-likes - there are major limits on spells, no inventory, non-item-specific enchantments (just swappable stat/game modifiers labeled enchantments), and no decisions to be made that alter the outcome of the ending (not that there isn't atleast one different ending). You can't really make a bad decision other than getting hit too much. Perhaps its just as well, because instead they focus on creating 4 distinct level types, a whole host of increasingly difficult baddies, and just enough items to keep it from getting boring. If you decide to buy the game, which I encourage you to do if you like RPGs and side-scrolling platformers, know that in Legacy+1,+2,+3, etc. I got another 10-15 hours of enjoyable gameplay before it got old. Also, maybe it's just me not understanding the story but there's a sick king and some sort of cure in this castle - how does getting it generations later help? Oh well, I haven't got a 5th go around in me so perhaps I'll never understand what the goal is... other than beating all the bosses. Cheers!

Life is Strange was my favourite game of 2015. So I came into this with huge expectations and I must say they were met.  Deck Nine really nailed the atmosphere and setting of Arcadia Bay, I love their take on the LiS universe. I'll keep editing my review after each episode comes.
Straight off the bat I will say the new VA for Chloe made the voice her own. She sounds exactly like how I pictured a young Chloe would. The game while being in the same universe and same art style as LiS, feels really different and I love it more for it. For those of us who are fans of the game and are attached to the characters, this game is amazing. But if you haven't played LiS, you may not like it. Personally I'd say go for it, and if you can buy and play LiS before this. That will make the game so much more better. The music is as usual phenomenal. The setting, the storyline, character dynamic almost everything about Episode 1 was flawless to me. I can't really say anything else without spoiling the story so I must say try the game for your own. You won't regret it.
This episode was phenomenal! Lots of callbacks to the original LiS and great character developments for Rachel. The episode had everything: amazing storytelling, amazing music, hard choices, romance, comedy, drama, fan service and a twist ending leaving everyone with desire to play more. Deck Nine are really doing LiS justice.
There were a few inconsistencies since they had to keep the story cannon with the main game. That and Rachel's mother's lackluster voice acting aside overall this was a solid episode.  Life is Strange was more about the journey than the ending, this is also similar. Before the Storm is even more so about the journey because if you have played the main game, you know what tragic fate befalls upon Chloe and Rachel. Deck Nine did a great job continuing and honoring the brilliant story that DONTNOD created. I'm really looking forward to both of these developers' future works.

which reveals the character development is solid.

I like Mad Max. About 12 hours in I got a solid feel of the overall game.
The important thing to know about Mad Max is that it's fun. And that's the whole point.
It is far from perfect, lacks in many departements but it also has a lot of positives which make it a good enjoyable game.
The over the top action makes you want to play a little bit more all the time.
Completists will have their hands full.
The game focuses a lot on driving and does it well, there are so many upgrades for your vehicles, and so many of them.
The on-foot action is also good, fighting is a little simple (like batman) but its fun nevertheless. I do wish there was more weapons and customizations for them. It is very thin in that department, and you barely find any ammo in the game so you practically never use your shotgun.
The acting is good but the story is week. You don't feel like you're switching gears between the main story and side missions, they both feel the same, so you don't get that change of pace that breaks the monotony of tasks.
The game feels a little sand boxy but that doesn't take away form the fun of playing it.
The worst issue of the game is the character animation and movement. It's horribly done. The jumping in particular is the worst I've seen in any game the last 10 years, super clumsy. And the falling animation feels like you're a floating leaf.
They really needed to work on that departement to make max feel heavier, with the ability to jump and grab etc. All of which aren't there and hurt the gameplay.
The Positives:
-Great Atmosphere overall. Enviroments are spot on and so is music.
-Fun gameplay, fighting, driving and effects are satisfying.
-Tons of upgrades and mods.
-Lots of things to do.
-Pretty good acting.
The Negatives:
-Weekish Story. Even main mission feels like a side mission.
-A Little repetitive at times.
-Abysmal character movement for a current gen game. Jumping in particular is terrible.
Still, you will get a good 60-70hr atmospheric fun and thrilling gameplay out of this game.

Rogue Legacy is a platformer roguelike combined with RPG elements. During each run of the castle, it is possible to find new equipment and bonuses that are permanent. The next run through the castle you normally can buy a new stat or skill or some piece of equipment.
The best way to find rare blueprints for the good equipment is by using a shrine in hopes to get a compass that will lead to a otherwise invisible room with 1 or 2 blueprints. However, this shrine also gives out CURSE OF THE HEDGEHOG. This curse causes you to lose hundreds of gold every time you take damage. If the gold doesn't land on spikes or impossible to reach places, it can be picked up again. When you receive this curse, the best thing to do unfortunately is to suicide on a monster while trying to pick up as much of your gold as possible. If this occurs in a low level area, it is even more annoying if your character has a lot of hit points left and a good armor rating.
There is no mod to get rid of this "feature" and the game doesn't have steam workshop. The only way to advance your character is with gold, after you die. If you try to continue playing through a run with the curse on, it will not be a good use of your time or fun picking up tons of gold every single time any damage is taken.
If the game was patched so that when instead of getting CURSE OF THE HEDGEHOG your character just lost 10% of his gold and instantly died while a big middle finger was displayed on the screen it would be an improvement.
When running the game on OSX operating system, exiting the game will not shut it down. It has to be force quitted, or will continue running in the background and steam will record it as time played. The OSX version also suffers from periodic freezes or stutters. These usually aren't too bad, but it can mess up a boss fight or tricky jump.
Other than that the game is fun and has a good soundtrack. It is fun to finish a run and go back into the castle with a new character and try out a new combination of gear. Hopefully the bad things are patched out at some point.

If you enjoyed Castlevania, Ghosts and Goblins, Megaman or any of the classic side scrollers... this side-scrolling, tongue-in-cheek platformer is definitely for you. This game is one that can very quickly cause immense frustration in the gamer; especially for those of us that haven't played a game like this in a while. The humor in this game is fantastic, and the classic artwork of the castle will not get old before you have an rage induced violent episode. This game manages to be both very forgiving and back breakingly punishing; by that I mean that the first few deaths (they're inevitable unless you're the wiz) are mostly inconsequential, but as your lineage becomes larger... each death becomes progressively more punishing as you notice that skills are becoming increasingly expensive. At that point, if you're having a hard time with the game it will scale out of control really fast and you'll likely not have an opportunity to upgrade the first few levels.
All of that being said, this is simply remedied by starting a new legacy once you've gotten more in the groove of the game. The learning curve is not horribly steep, and once you figure out the game and the system you'll find yourself living significantly longer as your character literally farts along the screen.
If you're not a hard core side-scroller fan... I'd recommend waiting till this game goes on sale to purchase, even for casual fans of side-scrollers this game can be a good bit of entertainment. If you're a hard-core fan, this game is worth full value.

I have spent a little bit of time with the game and have just completed it.  Overall, I would say it was a pleasant experience and I can and cannot see why critics gave it mediocre reviews.  Below are the pros and cons I experienced during my time:
PROS
-The game looks very, very good.  The weather effects look awesome; the landscape is beautiful; the key characters have good detail.
-The story gets pretty good, once you get to Gastown -- given all the criticism given to the game in regards to lack of story, makes me wonder whether critics just gave up on the game before getting to the climax portions.
-The combat is fun and brutal -- if you like Batman style combat without any restraint on killing people, you will like this.  I liked how the shotgun can be used during combat and how you could eliminate troublesome enemies quickly with it.
-Overall, the car combat is quite fun and, once you get your rocket launcher (exploading harpoon), it becomes a blast
-Using the harpoon on the Magnum Opus is very fun during car combat, as you can do lots of things, like pulling off the wheels of cars and harpooning land pedestrians and flinging them halfway across the map (Just Cause style)
-The upgrade system for the car and Max are good, if not standard now for these kinds of games
-Some of the setpieces and battles are pretty cool (e.g., going into an abandoned burried airport or church, with enemies surprising you in the dark)
-The atmosphere is very bleak, which suits the character
-The game ran well on my low end gaming PC.  Optimized to a "T".
-The voice acting was really good and I enjoyed Max's stern reserved hero characterization.  The actor did quite well.
CONS
-The majority of the gameplay revolves around doing very, very repetative missions.  There are 4 major territories in the game, each with 4 sections with things that need to be cleared and scrap to be found.  All the territory clearing missions consist of the same 5 types of missions (searching for mine fields, taking down totems, clearing bases, destroying a carravan of bad guys, or killing snipers) and random scrap bases.  If you are like me, and like to try to get 100% clear in zones, you will find yourself getting worn out by the time you even get to Gastown.  By hour 40, I was really slogging away, starting to get burnt out of doing the same things over and over again.  This seems like really lazy gamplay design, and quite common for this genre. If it weren't for this aspect, I am sure the average critic review would have been over 8 easily.
-Because of the above, the game has no replay value.  Who would want to do all those same, boring, side missions again?  There is no game + mode either.  Once you are done with this game, you are most likely done.  That said, I got 60+ hours out of the game, which isn't bad value.
-The game is too easy.  There was little challenge in the game, except for one racing mission.
-The cars handle pretty poorly.  For most of the game I didn't realize how poor the cars handled until a mission where I had to race on a real enclosed racing track. Then I realized that driving the car, even with all the upgrades in the game unlocked is like driving on ice.  You will find that when you run over a rock or barely clip a wall your car will ALWAYS spin around, stop and face the opposite direction of the one you were facing previously.  This can be pretty frustrating during races.
-There is a notoriously bad racing mission in the game that comes out of the blue and took numerous tries to beat, not because it in itself was hard, but because the very poor car handling controls made it hard.
-You need a controller for this game.  From what I can tell, the game is pretty awkward using a keyboard and mouse.
-There is basically no character development until you are almost done with the game.  Probably the most regrettable flaw of the game is the lack of story throughout the game.  The story content that is there is superb, but it only makes you realize how empty the rest of the game (the majority of the game) was.
-There are bugs in the game. I found myself at times when trying to pick up scrapped warping through floors.  Some climbing locations are not marked with yellow, like every other climbing location.  Some scrap was not labled like every other.  The UI suddenly disappeared sometimes.  The fast travel and summoning Chumbucket was very inconsistent in working.  And more.  Overall, it was pretty smooth experience, but beware of bugs.
-The sandstorms that randomly occur in the world are cool the first two times, as they look neat, kick your butt and are a great source for scrap.  HOWEVER, the rest of the game they are super annoyance.  They are annoying because you cannot fast travel while they occur and they take 10 MINUTES!!! So, if you are on your way to just complete a basic mission to clear a zone and sandstorm occurs, be prepared to just run around trying to live and wait it out.  This became increasingly frustrating as I was trying 100% zones.  Sometimes I would just come into the game and leave a base and it would immediately tell me beware of a sandstorm... if that occurs, just go back into the base or leave the game and come back in and the storm will be gone.
-The day night cycle TAKES FOREVER!  You probably won't notice the day/night cycle, except its aesthetics, for most of the game, until you get to two sidemissions that require you to do something at night and it is daytime.  There is no way to speed up the clock and, if you log out, and come back, the cycle will be at the beginning of whatever part you were at previously.  Thus, if you log out during the day, it will be morning.  Therefore, the only way to get to these missions and make it night, is either go off and do something else in the game until it turns night or just sit there with the game out and check back later.  Given that these missions occur near the end, and, if you had been clearing stuff out as you went along with little else to do, this will be a bit frustrating.
-The combat was fun, but it didn't feel as smooth as some of the other Batman Arkham type games.
-Some of the bleakness was a bit over-the-top, especially in regards to the "relics" you find, which are pictures from the world prior to the apocalypse.  For example, you will find a cheerful picture of a little kid with some stuff written on the back about the kid being turned into "raspberry spray" and then Max will make some depressing remark about how we are in hell.  I guess this fits the world he lives in, but the "doom and gloom" of every comment does grate on you after hours and hours of play, especially once you start to realize that he is making the same comment over and over again with just new words.
-There is car collecting in the game, but I didn't see the point of it, as every other car in the game pales in comparison to your main vehicle, as they don't have harpoons and the like.  They tell you when you get in the car that you have some sort of stealth towards a faction, but it hardly works and usually as you drive past that faction, they will realize who you are in about 5 secs, if not before.
Though I do have a lot of negatives, and I probably wouldn't touch the game again in the future, I did have a fun experience and it was worth the discounted price I paid.  The story at the end was pretty moving and and it saved the game from a lower score. This is a game that takes its cues from roguelikes and celebrates a long trail of dead grandpappys and gam-gams as one of its main selling points.
The developers, Cellar Door Games, have dubbed the genealogical mis-adventures of the Rogue family a "rogue-lite." Similar to other recent roguelike games such as Binding of Isaac and Spelunky, Rogue Legacy features an ever changing dungeon filled to the brim with ridiculously lethal monsters and flagrantly unfair traps, all presented with a perversely masochistic glee. Where it differs from it sadistic peers is its sense of continuance. While each hero may only have one life to live (and impale upon a spike), the treasures and items he or she accumulates is passed to their next of kin. Bizarre elements foreign to the roguelike mindset, such as stat upgrades and ability expanding items, enter the mix.
Unlike Isaac where the entire game is a mission to see the end (or at least how far you'll get), Rogue Legacy has more of a gradual slope. You know it's unlikely you'll take your first few heroes all the way to the end, or maybe even to the first boss. But that's okay, because success in Rogue Legacy isn't just determined by how far one gets, but what they amass and pass on.
It's a lovely blending of genres that, like many blindingly brilliant ideas, is so amazing that it somehow becomes obvious in retrospect. Of course someone had to make a game like this. It's the perfect entry point for a new audience just dipping their feet into roguelikes.
Despite the fluffy exterior of being a new audience friendly "rogue-lite", it's still damn tough. For such a cute looking game, there is a lot to learn and a lot to screw up. I played the absolute hell out of Rogue Legacy and made my fair share of boneheaded errors and dumbfounding revelations figuring things out.
If you like good games, you should play Rogue Legacy.

So you can easily die in a few hits, but for a game that demands you go on quite long runs this just makes me want to give up early.  The down-attack is clunky and the control scheme for it is not designed well which is unfortunate because there are a lot of platforms you have to down-attack in a time-critical manner.  The down-attack is very low damage for a difficult-to-use move, is short-lived, and often damage is taken when jumping down platforms where you can't see an enemy, taking away a huge chunk of your life.  Is a fun game when not dealing with these flaws.

Before the Storm is, after Episode 1 at least, a beautiful return to Arcadia Bay. It sets the stage for Chloe's emotional reaction to the premise of the first game and it handles the hugely emotional relationships teenagers feel really well. The characters feel like they -would- have the sort of dynamics they do, and as always LiS handles queer relationships tastefully, and in a way that doesn't feel forced or token.
Mechanically speaking - It's hard to really talk about the mechanics of a game like this but it feels right. Chloe doesn't have the tricks Max does, but she has a system to get her way, for sure. The game feels like your decisions have even more weight as you can't travel back in time to change them - short of restarting a whole section of the episode. Which is great when you consider the premise of the story.
This is a hearty recommendation from me.

Just finished Episode One and I'm so happy to be back in Arcadia Bay! Here are my toughts on why I enjoy Life is Srtange: Before the Storm and why I'm excited for the future episodes.
WHAT'S THE SAME AS THE FIRST GAME?
Seeing familiar faces and meeting new characters just feels natural as you step back into the artsy asthetic from Life is Strange. Chloe doesn't feel like a new character. She is still the hard-hearted, badass chic we all know and love and it's great to hear her speak again, even if the voice actor is different. All in all, the controls are all the same and the conversation mechanics work very similarly to that of the original game. The character development is still very natural and I immediately cared about everything Chloe was feeling even though it's been a while since I've played the first game. And finally, the art style is gorgous as always and I took probably a thousand screenshots cause every scene had something beautiful to offer.
WHAT'S NEW?
Where Max had her Time-Travelling mechaninc that allowed her to manipulate events and conversatoins, Chloe (being more down to earth and less sci-fi) has an argument function called Backtalk that allows her to verbally fight anyone she disagrees with, making the player suddenly read everyone's dialogue carefully for clues on how to corner them. I found this mechanic to be a pleasant surpise, since I was wondering how Before the Storm would make up for having no time travel. HOWEVER, because there is no time travel, every choice you make in this game is undoable! This means you can't screw around like you may have in the first game, expecting not to have consequences attached.
I learned playing though it a few times that Before the Storm feels much more realistic than the first game. Emotions are much more raw, which I think is just what this story needs and I look forward to future episodes.
My favorite change has to be the music! The music has gone from indie folk to indie punk, but it still works and continues the trend of really feeling like it's organically a part of the Pacific Northwest!
I'm glad this game didn't try to outdo its predecesor, because that would have made it feel out of place. I was so worried that Deck Nine wouldn't be able to capture the same magic as Dontnod did in the original Life is Strange, but it's unreal how perfectly they captured the same charm and envoirnment. I honestly feel like I'm comparing Ocarina of Time with Majora's Mask! They're both near perfect games in my opinion (despite the technincal flaws that both games are riddled with) and I'll be on the edge of my seat, waiting for the next installment!
PS: One last thing, I wont spoil excactly what the achievements in this game are related to (the first game had you take pictures of various items and people), but I was franctically trying to find them all, going back and replaying the episode just to find ones I missed.

Prison Architect is one of those games that you see a lot of on Youtube on let's plays and such, and you're not really sure if you'd have much fun with it if you got it. I thought originally that it wouldn't be that fun for me in the long run, but when it went on sale a couple of weeks ago, i went ahead and got it. It's one of the most entertaining alphas I've ever played. The begining of a prison is always rocky, because you have to judge (often inacurately) how big you cans start off.  I had built a pretty awesome starting prison one time, but somehow neglected to build a kitchen, resulting in all of my maximum security prisoners (which I thought I could handle) rioting and escaping becasue they were♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that they didn't have any food. Basically, the early game is really fun and suspensfull, with pretty much any way you start. With people sneaking weapons into their cells, shanking other inmates, and digging tunnels under their cells.
Another strong point in the game is the feeling of total power over your prison. You can set the schedule, rules, punishments for breaking those rules, security patrols, and obviously the building of the actual prison. The only problem I have with this game is, things seem to get way too predictable and unexciting later in the game, because once your superb security is set up, and you find the right schedule to where every prisoner is happy because you meet their needs, nothing really happens. I understand the game is in alpha, and that is why I'm not really dissapointed that much about it. I just wish there would maybe be elaborate escape attempts, or ocassional instances where maybe a staff member falls in love with a prisoner and tries to help them escape or something. That being said, I do really enjoy this game, and definetley reccomend it to anyone who'd like to be a warden/architect of a prison.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is all about living the dream that is professional trucking. Euro Truck Simulator 2 is too serious. The game even tells you as you begin that this is your dream job. With more than enthusiasm, players begin their adventure humbly with a little garage in the home city of their choice, and a company with no trucks.
The player begins by taking jobs for other companies, earning money from one city to another, with an eye toward earning enough cash and purchasing a truck. An owned truck means more freedom, with higher paying jobs that require more responsibility. When working directly for the player company, cargo is waiting at a select shipping yard and must be hitched to the truck before it can be taken to its ultimate destination. The next step from there is to start upgrading the garage, hiring other drivers to bring in more income, and eventually building a trucking empire that spans all of Europe.
The more you go, the more there is to do. Want to expand quickly? You can take out loans that need to be repaid. Want specialized drivers? They each level up the same way you do, and you can dictate the way they do. Of course, you also have to be mindful of expenses, be they repayments to the bank or fuel consumption by employees looking for work. There are a lot of ducks to get in a row, but the interface is user-friendly and information is constantly provided so nothing ever feels hopeless.
More than a game about driving, Euro Truck Simulator 2 boasts some role playing elements to keep things interesting. Successful jobs earn experience, which gives skill points. Skill points can be spent upgrading one's proficiency in certain types of jobs, unlocking new types of cargo, or even investing in fuel efficiency. Improving personal abilities and building a business from one lone driver to an entire fleet.
Driving trucks is as realistic as possible. Offering a huge map of Europe, there's plenty of time to be spent on the open road, and lots of distance to cover. Although you won't be undertaking journeys in real-time, a decent paying job is still quite the investment. I often found myself able to only play one job at a time.
There are a variety of controls and settings allowing for significant flexibility in terms of personal comfort. You can choose how complex your controls are, with automatic settings keyboard and set up a wheel. Whatever your available input, Euro Truck do a great job of covering you and ensuring you get into the game easily.
A tutorial guides for newcomers, and the essential GPS is easy to understand, as is its clear and simple route map. My first job was a decided disaster, with me getting the trailer stuck a number of times, managing to tip the vehicle over, and even call for emergency rescue.
Traffic lights, speed cameras, and the ever-present need to keep one's eyes on the road can always trip up an overconfident player, and as relaxing as long country drives may be, the pressure to avoid mistakes is present throughout. It's very easy to start getting speeding along a motorway without regard to other drivers and strict speed limits. Every mistake translates into a financial penalty, damaged cargo reduces the payday, and suffered by an owned truck will have to be paid for at service stations.
When a mistake occurs, it's almost always our fault, but there are some moments where the computer controlled road users face an issue. But they're few and far between, and experienced drivers will be able to avoid many of the hazard that lead to such trouble. Despite the occasional pressure to perform jobs well, Euro Truck Simulator 2 is still a largely cleansing experience. There's a driving through a variety of countries, a sense of joy as you get closer to your destination, and a sense of accomplishment in performing such boring tasks as refueling at gas stations and finding parking stops at which to grab some sleep. As you build your business up from nothing and take on more of managerial duties, it's hard not to feel pride over rewards well earned.
Although most visually advanced game, Euro Truck's believable presentation of Europe's roads and cities and atmosphere of the backdrops, there's a sense of individuality to each new territory you uncover, and the trucks themselves are lovingly recreated with an intricate level of detail. Owned trucks can be repainted and upgraded with all manner of parts, and as the player levels up, the potential for personalization expands.
The most fun aspect of Euro Truck Simulator 2, however, comes in the form of its music. With the simple tap of the "R" key, you can open up a menu packed with European Internet radio streams as well as your own Music and Radio streams. Providing a wide variety to listen. There's also the option to queue up music from one's own PC.

Spec Ops: The Line - War really is Hell.
[WARNING:SPOILERS - No, seriously, reading this entire review will likely ruin the impact of some key moments in this game]
War is hell. We've all heard this particular turn of phrase. Hell, for some of us, we've heard it so many times it's lost all meaning. For people who don't believe in hell, what's it supposed to mean in the first place? For those of us who've never been to war, what do we have to compare it to? What frame of reference would I have, aside from that vaguely haunted look when my dad would politely decline to discuss his time in Vietnam, or how he prefers not to watch movies based on real wars.
I think the closest thing I've seen yet, at least for the most part, has come as quite a surprise. I have a habit of picking up Call of Duty games because I played the first one way back in the dusty days of the early 'naughties when they had intense single-player campaigns and the multiplayer was decent but not the main focus. They were really trying to show you how hard it was being a soldier at first. Nowadays, it's 'MERICA FK YEAH except for the scenes with the charmingly amoral SAS soldiers. Don't get me wrong, Captain Price is a total badass, but a believable character he's not.
Spec Ops: The Line is not the first in its series, but it's the first I played. I'd never heard of the series before this one, and wouldn't have picked it up if not for the good words of two critics I respect, a well-done demo on Steam, and Amazon having a summer sale of 50% off on a game only released maybe a month prior with a key redeemable on Steam.
To get the technical aspects out of the way, because those will surely not be the focus, the gameplay does not carry this one at all. I can't imagine people will be flocking to the multiplayer, as the land of chest-high walls makes an appearance here, along with his best friend, Mister Cover-Based-Shooting. It's average gameplay at best. I hesitate to say the Call of Duty franchise does it better, but that's not where it shines.
I was truly taken aback by the story. I went in expecting a gung-ho John Rambo-style, check your brain at the door experience, with the ever-popular Delta Force as the main characters. That was not what was delivered. The game starts out, innocently enough, as you're tasked to investigate a distress call from a military commander of a unit, the 33rd, that stayed behind after Dubai was swallowed by massive sandstorm with people still living in the city. What follows is several episodes of standard shoot-em-up combat with a surprisingly hostile US Army force. Just as you get over questioning why these supposed friendlies are firing on you and you start to get into the rhythm of counter-attacking, the game drops a huge moral choice in your lap.
You encounter two men suspended from a bridge. You're told that one man, a civilian, was stealing water to help his family. The other, a soldier, was in the process of apprehending the man and used excessive force, resulting in the death of the man's family. You're then advised, by the very man who sent the distress call, to shoot one of them. You cannot simply refuse, as there are four snipers with their weapons trained on you from behind cover. Refuse, as I did, and you are forced to take the snipers out, resulting in the two men both dying in the exchange.
OK you say. That's not too bad. A play on a common theme. It gets worse. At one point, the 33rd launch a white phosphorous mortar strike on a group of insurgents sponsored by the CIA that you're only meters away from.
White Phosphorous, or as it's colloquially known as Willy Pete, has valid uses. It burns obscenely bright, as far as illumination, and can produce a solid smokescreen for obscuring movement. Loaded into a mortar, as in here, and almost nothing better defines "Death From Above." An airburst of WP burns and poisons, and can cause death from multiple organ failure if you don't die from shock first. The few times it's been used in combat have been wildly controversial to say the least, and it's been addressed under Chemical Warfare conventions.
You have to walk through the burning and dying remains to reach your next destination. This comes back to haunt you later as you reach the outskirts of a 33rd outpost that simply could not be breached on foot, due to the sheer number of soldiers and weaponry. Unfortunately for them, they've left their own white phosphorous mortar lying unattended. It was about this point that gnawing in the pit of my stomach started growing into something ugly. It didn't go away, as the next few moments left me shaking, when my character realized there had been civilians in the encampment. Approximately 40 of them.
The game takes a decidedly "Heart of Darkness" turn towards the end, in the only real stumbling outside of the slightly clumsy third-person cover shooting. You finally, after the painful ends of your team, reach the tower where the voice on the radio has been waiting. You are saluted by the remaining squad of the Damned 33rd, and told you are now in command of Dubai. After climbing a few staircases into a posh, almost spotless loft, you come face to face with Konrad, who continues talking to you even after you find his corpse slumped in a chair with a gun hanging out of his cold, dead hand. In a scene straight out of Fight Club, the reflection of Konrad holds a gun on you and you relive key points in the game that are not how you remembered them, such as Konrad's voice never actually coming through the radio, and the two men strung up on the bridge being long-dead, and you're faced with the option of shooting your reflection or Konrad's. Or not firing at all.
The game's writers throw a saving pass when you shoot Konrad, as you're allowed a post-credits playable sequence as the window shatters, and Konrad says "You can still go home.."
He's right. Cut to Army Humvees making their way to you, as you're slouched in front of Konrad's tower with an AA12, in Konrad's uniform. Your actions, and yours alone dictate what happens. As the soldiers approach, do you open fire on them? Or do you drop your weapon and allow them to take you home, admitting that the city defeated you.
The statement of "War is Hell" has been captured perfectly here, to the extent few stories of any other medium have captured it. The narrative forces you to feel the toll that hard decisions can take on a man, while at the same time giving us a warning that even the hardest and best of us could break under extreme situations. What makes you think you could be any stronger?
Highest recommendations, if you can pick it up for less than full price.

This is Apocalypse Now.

Borderlands 2 is spot-on in every way.
From the hilarious characters with brilliantly written dialogue to the enticing loot to the zany, phrenetic combat, every aspect of the game is perfectly executed. Gearbox took a risk in casting four (six) new vault hunters to replace those from the original Borderlands, but the new characters fill in their positions excellently. In addition, Lilith, Mordecai, Brick and Roland all play major parts in the game as NPCs, and their presence is welcome. Claptrap returns as well, as humorously moronic as before.
The four new vault hunters, Axton (Commando), Zer0 (Assassin), Salvador (Gunzerker), and Maya (Siren), are racing against Handsome Jack, president of the Hyperion Corporation, to reach and open a new vault. In addition to the main four vault hunters, there are two DLC characters, Gaige the Mechromancer and KRIEG the Psycho, who are definitely worth purchasing if you are into the game. They are included in the Game of the Year Edition.
The story is entertaining throughout, with plenty of fun side missions to complete if and when you finish the main game. There are also three DLC bonus campaigns which are all extremely fun.
In conclusion, Borderlands 2 is a rare 10/10 in my book. It's one of those games that is just plain old fun, without sacrificing a clever, well thought-out story and excellent character design.

Prison Architect is one of those games that you see a lot of on Youtube on let's plays and such, and you're not really sure if you'd have much fun with it if you got it. I thought originally that it wouldn't be that fun for me in the long run, but when it went on sale a couple of weeks ago, i went ahead and got it. It's one of the most entertaining alphas I've ever played. The begining of a prison is always rocky, because you have to judge (often inacurately) how big you cans start off.  I had built a pretty awesome starting prison one time, but somehow neglected to build a kitchen, resulting in all of my maximum security prisoners (which I thought I could handle) rioting and escaping becasue they were♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that they didn't have any food. Basically, the early game is really fun and suspensfull, with pretty much any way you start. With people sneaking weapons into their cells, shanking other inmates, and digging tunnels under their cells.
Another strong point in the game is the feeling of total power over your prison. You can set the schedule, rules, punishments for breaking those rules, security patrols, and obviously the building of the actual prison. The only problem I have with this game is, things seem to get way too predictable and unexciting later in the game, because once your superb security is set up, and you find the right schedule to where every prisoner is happy because you meet their needs, nothing really happens. I understand the game is in alpha, and that is why I'm not really dissapointed that much about it. I just wish there would maybe be elaborate escape attempts, or ocassional instances where maybe a staff member falls in love with a prisoner and tries to help them escape or something. That being said, I do really enjoy this game, and definetley reccomend it to anyone who'd like to be a warden/architect of a prison.

Just finished Episode One and I'm so happy to be back in Arcadia Bay! Here are my toughts on why I enjoy Life is Srtange: Before the Storm and why I'm excited for the future episodes.
WHAT'S THE SAME AS THE FIRST GAME?
Seeing familiar faces and meeting new characters just feels natural as you step back into the artsy asthetic from Life is Strange. Chloe doesn't feel like a new character. She is still the hard-hearted, badass chic we all know and love and it's great to hear her speak again, even if the voice actor is different. All in all, the controls are all the same and the conversation mechanics work very similarly to that of the original game. The character development is still very natural and I immediately cared about everything Chloe was feeling even though it's been a while since I've played the first game. And finally, the art style is gorgous as always and I took probably a thousand screenshots cause every scene had something beautiful to offer.
WHAT'S NEW?
Where Max had her Time-Travelling mechaninc that allowed her to manipulate events and conversatoins, Chloe (being more down to earth and less sci-fi) has an argument function called Backtalk that allows her to verbally fight anyone she disagrees with, making the player suddenly read everyone's dialogue carefully for clues on how to corner them. I found this mechanic to be a pleasant surpise, since I was wondering how Before the Storm would make up for having no time travel. HOWEVER, because there is no time travel, every choice you make in this game is undoable! This means you can't screw around like you may have in the first game, expecting not to have consequences attached.
I learned playing though it a few times that Before the Storm feels much more realistic than the first game. Emotions are much more raw, which I think is just what this story needs and I look forward to future episodes.
My favorite change has to be the music! The music has gone from indie folk to indie punk, but it still works and continues the trend of really feeling like it's organically a part of the Pacific Northwest!
I'm glad this game didn't try to outdo its predecesor, because that would have made it feel out of place. I was so worried that Deck Nine wouldn't be able to capture the same magic as Dontnod did in the original Life is Strange, but it's unreal how perfectly they captured the same charm and envoirnment. I honestly feel like I'm comparing Ocarina of Time with Majora's Mask! They're both near perfect games in my opinion (despite the technincal flaws that both games are riddled with) and I'll be on the edge of my seat, waiting for the next installment!
PS: One last thing, I wont spoil excactly what the achievements in this game are related to (the first game had you take pictures of various items and people), but I was franctically trying to find them all, going back and replaying the episode just to find ones I missed.

This game has been getting a lot of mediocre to bad reviews, and frankly, I'm baffled. It almost seems like some of the reviewers were just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that they didn't get to review the new Metal Gear Solid or Mario Maker, and they took their disappointment out on this totally solid, fun game. In other cases, the reviewers are clearly just tired of Far Cry/Assassin's Creed-style open world games, so Mad Max didn't have a chance. And it does suffer in comparison to last year's Shadow of Mordor, which was similar in structure but brought something fresh to the genre. But all that being said, for what it is, for what it's trying to be, Mad Max is a dang good time.
The bottom line is that the core action loop is rock solid: the car combat is blazing fast, metal-crunching fun, especially the convoy battles; melee combat is a pared-down Arkham--not as good, but solid and satisfying in its own right; the car customization adds a nice twist to the open world genre, and provides a compelling motivation to conquer enemy forts and complete other tasks; each enemy fort has a unique design, with more than one way to approach it; and collectibles are kept to a minimum, and you can either skip them or they actually help you in some way (there are no AssCreed feathers!). In fact, I can't think of any tasks that I didn't like that I was forced to do. I didn't really like the races, but I think only had to do two. Finding and disarming minefields is dull, but you never had to do it.
Which brings us to the bad parts: The boss fights are lame--not hard, just boring and repetitive. The story is mostly lame, especially towards the end when they hamfistedly try to tug at your heartstrings. Some of the writing and voice acting is terrible, especially the random quest and information givers you encounter in the world, Some of Max's reactions to the "history relic" collectibles--which are usually just old photos with messages written on the back--are also awful. The relics themselves are often poignant and provide some needed context for what happened to the world, and often Max doesn't even say anything. It would have been better if he never commented on them.
And I have some nitpicks, like how gas is never really an issue--I literally never ran out, or even came close, so what was the point of including that mechanic? And I didn't really like Max's customization, none of the upgrades to his appearance actually made him look cooler or more interesting. The game can also be really awkward in how it surfaces information. For instance, it took me a long time to understand what the Archangels even were (it turns out that they're just car archetypes, suggested builds depending on what kind of car you want--light, fast, low armor; heavy, high armor, low acceleration; etc.). And they totally squander the role of your faithful dog by relegating him to the minefield missions, which require that you drive a totally different car, one that you would never otherwise drive. Speaking of squandering, the Griffa character is one of the most interesting in the game (think the Outsider from Dishonored, but with more personality), but you only meet up with him a few times, and once you've unlocked all of his perks, you never see him again.
There are two other things I loved that I should mention--this game is absolutely gorgeous, from the changing sunlight to the vehicle damage to the raging sand storms, it's a veritable screenshot factory. And then there's Chumbucket, your companion throughout your journey. He's easily the best character in the game, and provides the only real empathy in the story. His dialogue is well written and his voice actor (Jason Spisak) gives him just the right amount of humor mixed with pathos.
In the end, the vast majority of what you do in this game is very high quality fun. If you like open world games, it's a no-brainer. If you like car and melee combat, this is your game. If you're a Mad Max fan, you might want to give it a try, it does a decent job of presenting that world. Don't listen to the grumpy old critics...who are likely younger than I am, but whatever!

I got Mad Max for 18 bucks and I still feel that I wasted my money and time. First of all I would like to comment on the graphics, not that I think that graphics really matter as much as people make it out to be but the fact that everyone is praising the game for looking amazing and running so well. The game does not look good. The textures and models look closer to something from the PS2/3 days and the only reason it looks kind of nice is because they heavily rely on shaders and blur to hide the fact that things just don't look very good which leads to why the game runs so well. It runs well because there is basically nothing going on. I was able to pull a minimum of 80fps and a near constant max of 100fps @ 1080 with my frames being limited to 100 as that is the refresh rate of my panel on my laptop. There are no complex models or detailed places to find while the game is supposed to be a barren wasteland I feel that they could have done it so much better. It just feels cheap and quick which is consistent with the rest of the game. The story line is crap, but who expected anything out of that department really? The fighting mechanics are the rehashed batman mechanics we are all too familiar now except that this feels much easier. I can't put my finger on it but the combat is just so damn easy that it feels like a chore you need to get through rather something you need to concentrate on and have some fun with. When I am fighting I find myself trying to think about other things and paying little attention to the actual task at hand because it is so boring and so easy. The vehicular combat holds up about the same as the hand to hand combat. It just feel uninspired and empty. You do the same basic things a couple times each time you meet a car or convoy and without much thought you win whatever it was you were after., There is no real reason to change your tactics or even think about what you are doing. Need to hit something perfectly every time with a weapon? Just hold a button and press another button and you hit home every damn time without any skill or thought. The rest of the game is like the combat, nothing special, repetitive and super easy. You do the same things over and over and over and over and over and over and over again it gets quite ridiculous. The initial fun that the game offers quickly turns into a quagmire of thinking to yourself... why am I still playing this? The game is so repetitive that I had to wait a few days between game sessions just to build up the want to go back and do the same things again a few times over. After 14 hours of game play and at least 6 hours of asking myself the question, why am I still playing this, every time I played I finally uninstalled it. I think the best feeling during this whole fiasco was the feeling of finally committing to uninstalling it and moving over to something more fun.
6/10 for a PC port done well, but a totally lacklustre and uninspired game.

I never thought I'd get hooked on one of these "Euro Sim" games, but I did. There is something very Zen about just driving along the countryside, with your lead foot and the beautiful landscapes around you. If you've ever travelled Europe by rail or car, this game can be a very nostalgic and dramatic experience.
My only complaint is that sometimes the game "lurches" -- that is, when you are driving at a constant speed, the truck periodically slows down and then catches up again. During the lurches, the framerate does not seem to drop, so it seems that something else is causing it to bottleneck. I'm playing on a GTX 980 with a 3Ghz i5 CPU and 8Gb RAM, so I doubt my system is to blame. At any rate, the lurching doesn't occur constantly and it doesn't really detract from the driving experience, but I still hope that it gets sorted out in a future update.

Life is strange is one of my favorite game series, so going into this, I had extremely high expectations.

I wasn't entirely blown away with the beginning. The original series suffered from a slow start as well, but this seemed a tad slower. Although I love the series, I found myself asking the question "Alright, nothing here has drawn me in besides the fact that it's more LIS." That's when the second half of the episode hit, and boy was I blown away. I found myself more and more drawn in after every conversation. Every time something happened, I just kept hoping that the episode wasn't over. When it finally was, I immediately tried to find the episode two release date because I was so hungry for more.
Closing thoughts. I loved it. It did start a bit slow but it's totally forgiven. I was originally scared because this was a different company, but they more than delivered. I got the same feeling I had when I played the first series; I'm pulled in. I want to know more, I feel for the characters. I can't praise it enough. I love it, and I think you will too

As obnoxious as the fandom may be, it's a very worthwhile game. It's all around a pretty great experience and I absolutely recommend this game to anyone. Challenging and original turn-based conflict, charming writing, the soundtrack has some instant classics, and the visuals are appropriate and high-quality. Lore is deep and story is complex enough to keep you intrigued in the world and denizens of Undertale.
I'm going to get into my major cons about the game first because I think they're very important, but I will get into the pros afterward because, cons aside, these pros are what make the game an otherwise very worthwhile play. But the cons are important.
I will offer my insight, why my experience was unsatisfactory going into the game blind, and why, despite that initial poor impression, the game has grown on me and utterly earned my respect. I will also be as concise as possible.
My major con would be that the content you get for playing however you want/killing things vs the pacifist content is very distant in quality, with a pacifist run having an obvious amount more work and love put into it. You are essentially punished for playing the game any other way with a watered-down experience. This punishment comes with no obvious notice, and with only one save slot
, you will have to endure an entire run (which may be worthwhile anyways, again, for
) if you save after missing a flag or anything else critical.
I understand that having a better plot is a reward for playing the game "correctly," but this is different from a "good ending" or "bad ending" style of reward and punihsment. Undertale will still put you through hours of gameplay that is actually very bland when you do not follow the pacifist route. Some of the content that you experience on these other playthroughs can be interesting and significant to lore, but those are very far and few. Still, I respect the developer for allowing the game to be completed rather than offering a simple "Game Over" when something is done "wrong" or off-course for the pacifist route. At the end of the day, it would require so many different playthroughs to get all off the lore, you probably
get on the wiki to learn lore that you may have missed. I started going on the wiki after I did my first playthrough (completely blind), and that's when I was disappointed to discover that I was somewhat punished for playing the game how I wanted to play it. It did address my confusion as to why I did not think the game was good, despite all of the hype (played through on launch-week, the hype was real). I actually felt like I was being ignored by a narrator -- like the narrator stopped watching and providing commentary because I stopped doing what it wanted to see me do.
The rest of the content is great. I'd say look up the steps for getting the true pacifist playthrough, and go with that. Going through the first playthrough blind honestly felt like a lot of friction on me and a real drag on my personal time as I was not really enjoying it. Otherwise, everything is very socially respectful and inclusive, while not being overly SJW, though pacifist run did get a bit distastefully preachy. I believe that morals should be recognized beyond the binary too; there can be circumstances and perspectives that support Frisk's employment of violence and opposition, whether it be something plot-related or a character-flaw (that can be more drawn out) on Frisk's end. Otherwise, allowing the player to make Frisk act as such and not offer a validating reaction from the world can be a detriment to immersion. Sorry, I'm getting into cons again.
I have to reiterate -- despite all of the cons that I have listed, I think it's a fantastic game. The incredible consistency that you only get with a small team of developers is present and the quality of all pieces of the media for this title are immaculate. The love and work that went into this game is deep, and the fandom mirrors that. People have gone into the code of the game to learn more plot and lore, with the developer playing along. This hasn't been earned without merit. If you have time, do a blind playthrough initially, then wiki stuff and do a true pacifist run. You can do a true genocide run if you want too, but it's a long and dry road. Maybe just read up on that one if you don't have that much free time on your hands.

I'm going to invent a new syndrome now: Bulletstorm Syndrome (BSS from now on). Games that suffer from this syndrome exhibit the following symptoms:
- generic visuals that look like a tech demo
- copycat gameplay mechanics, like squaddie runs or "press A to cover"
- screenshots and trailers that make the game look like "another so-and-so but in a different setting"
- crap marketing campaign that does nothing to emphasise the real value of the game
- the game will hardly sell any units, because of all the above
Sadly, BSS also has one last important, but unfortunate symptom: THE GAME IS ACTUALLY PRETTY DAMN BRILLIANT.
You see, Spec Ops suffers from BSS. It looks like a crappy Gears of War clone, whereas in reality it's a very clever 3rd person shooter, that's leagues beyond and above GOW, or any recent 3rd person in fact.
It's a fantastic tale of how soldiers eventually crack, amidst all the death and suffering they see and inflint, they are, afterall, just humans.

I'm going to invent a new syndrome now: Bulletstorm Syndrome (BSS from now on). Games that suffer from this syndrome exhibit the following symptoms:
- generic visuals that look like a tech demo
- copycat gameplay mechanics, like squaddie runs or "press A to cover"
- screenshots and trailers that make the game look like "another so-and-so but in a different setting"
- crap marketing campaign that does nothing to emphasise the real value of the game
- the game will hardly sell any units, because of all the above
Sadly, BSS also has one last important, but unfortunate symptom: THE GAME IS ACTUALLY PRETTY DAMN BRILLIANT.
You see, Spec Ops suffers from BSS. It looks like a crappy Gears of War clone, whereas in reality it's a very clever 3rd person shooter, that's leagues beyond and above GOW, or any recent 3rd person in fact.
It's a fantastic tale of how soldiers eventually crack, amidst all the death and suffering they see and inflint, they are, afterall, just humans.
