As obnoxious as the fandom may be, it's a very worthwhile game. It's all around a pretty great experience and I absolutely recommend this game to anyone. Challenging and original turn-based conflict, charming writing, the soundtrack has some instant classics, and the visuals are appropriate and high-quality. Lore is deep and story is complex enough to keep you intrigued in the world and denizens of Undertale.
I'm going to get into my major cons about the game first because I think they're very important, but I will get into the pros afterward because, cons aside, these pros are what make the game an otherwise very worthwhile play. But the cons are important.
I will offer my insight, why my experience was unsatisfactory going into the game blind, and why, despite that initial poor impression, the game has grown on me and utterly earned my respect. I will also be as concise as possible.
My major con would be that the content you get for playing however you want/killing things vs the pacifist content is very distant in quality, with a pacifist run having an obvious amount more work and love put into it. You are essentially punished for playing the game any other way with a watered-down experience. This punishment comes with no obvious notice, and with only one save slot
, you will have to endure an entire run (which may be worthwhile anyways, again, for
) if you save after missing a flag or anything else critical.
I understand that having a better plot is a reward for playing the game "correctly," but this is different from a "good ending" or "bad ending" style of reward and punihsment. Undertale will still put you through hours of gameplay that is actually very bland when you do not follow the pacifist route. Some of the content that you experience on these other playthroughs can be interesting and significant to lore, but those are very far and few. Still, I respect the developer for allowing the game to be completed rather than offering a simple "Game Over" when something is done "wrong" or off-course for the pacifist route. At the end of the day, it would require so many different playthroughs to get all off the lore, you probably
get on the wiki to learn lore that you may have missed. I started going on the wiki after I did my first playthrough (completely blind), and that's when I was disappointed to discover that I was somewhat punished for playing the game how I wanted to play it. It did address my confusion as to why I did not think the game was good, despite all of the hype (played through on launch-week, the hype was real). I actually felt like I was being ignored by a narrator -- like the narrator stopped watching and providing commentary because I stopped doing what it wanted to see me do.
The rest of the content is great. I'd say look up the steps for getting the true pacifist playthrough, and go with that. Going through the first playthrough blind honestly felt like a lot of friction on me and a real drag on my personal time as I was not really enjoying it. Otherwise, everything is very socially respectful and inclusive, while not being overly SJW, though pacifist run did get a bit distastefully preachy. I believe that morals should be recognized beyond the binary too; there can be circumstances and perspectives that support Frisk's employment of violence and opposition, whether it be something plot-related or a character-flaw (that can be more drawn out) on Frisk's end. Otherwise, allowing the player to make Frisk act as such and not offer a validating reaction from the world can be a detriment to immersion. Sorry, I'm getting into cons again.
I have to reiterate -- despite all of the cons that I have listed, I think it's a fantastic game. The incredible consistency that you only get with a small team of developers is present and the quality of all pieces of the media for this title are immaculate. The love and work that went into this game is deep, and the fandom mirrors that. People have gone into the code of the game to learn more plot and lore, with the developer playing along. This hasn't been earned without merit. If you have time, do a blind playthrough initially, then wiki stuff and do a true pacifist run. You can do a true genocide run if you want too, but it's a long and dry road. Maybe just read up on that one if you don't have that much free time on your hands.

Spec Ops does the shooter thing just differently enough to carve out its place in a crowded genre. The combat is decent, but the story and characters do enough interesting things to make this a valid purchase for anyone.
Is it worth the $50 or whatever that it's going for now? Probably not. Still, it has an excellent singleplayer campaign with a good, dark story in the vein of Heart of Darkness.

Spec Ops The Line is an Intense third person shooter with a serious focus on story telling and gruesome actions. The game uses a solid cover system that many people thought was too sticky but I quite liked. The way the character vaulted and moved from cover to cover or out of it was quite smooth. The shooting mechanics in the game were solid and much better than most of the competition (Gears Of War). The story in it is about 4 soldiers who enter Dubai after it has been ravaged by storms in a rescue mission. As they go into Dubai they find how wrong everything is and have to make tough choices. The game itself can get to be quite gruesome but lots of fun and really interesting. The multiplayer seemed to be dead when I tried it but it may have been somewhat fun just don't count on it to keep you coming back to this game. The campaign will last you around 4-7 hours. I recommend this game to any story lover or anyone interested in a solid third person shooter. 90/100

Rogue Legacy is a rougelike game made by Celler Door Games, who also made Don't **** your pants and Tribal Tallies. So you're thinking this won't be a great game based of their previous games. It isn't. Rogue Legacy brings in some very unique gameplay that makes it fun and enjoyable. You play as a hero with a class as they enter the castle looting and killing baddies until they die. They will be remembered by how well you played in the castle and each time you die, your descendants will continue where you left off, or at least do better than you did. And sometimes they can have good or bad traits depending on what the RNG gives you. But each time you enter the castle. You have to pay a fee with Cheron before you can enter and each time you enter, the castle will randomize itself, so you always expect different results each time (unless you use the architect to keep the castle the way it is).
There are RPG elements added in the game to beef off your heroes. Such as increasing stats and gaining new classes and abilities in the manor. You can also gain runes and blueprints for equipment in the castle for your son/daughter to wield the next time they enter, some giving them unique abilities when equip. There's also a training dummy to see how strong your attacks are. Sometimes there will be fairy chest challenges that will be needed to be done before you can obtain the runes and later stats upgrade once you obtained all the runes. Some are nearly impossible to do and others are really simple if you have the right tools or you know what you are doing. There are minibosses you can fight too for bluepritns and stats upgrade too that appear rarely. So it's worth it to fight them if you have enough health to withstand their attacks.
The story is simple. The tutorials give you a hint on what happened before you entered the castle with your heroes and later near the end explains what happens. It may not be heavily story based, but the story seems to work well with the game.
There are also minigames you can play too, such as carnival games and pick the right chest to gain profits or lose it all. They are hard, but with the right tools and strageties, you can earn some neat stuff.
There are negative stuff to be had too. One, this game is really frustrating. Expect to die alot from careless mistakes or not being lucky enough. It even sucks when the characters you choose will have really bad traits and can't trade them in (until you get a upgrade that allows you to reroll your children). And second, it's a grindfest. If you want to beat bosses and enemies and last longer in the castle, get alot of money for upgrades. Usually Cheron takes all your money, but upgrading the haggle skill allows you to keep some money for later purchases, which is good.
All in all, this is a wonderful game. It has neat graphics, cool soundtracks, and it's addicting to play. But the frustrating levels and the hardcore grinding makes it hard to really love this game when it's not being evil to you.
Rating 8/10

If you looking for a game to relax while listening music,cruising with the traffic,watching the landscape flow after a session action,survival,shooting,horror game then in Euro Truck Simulator 2 you will find that peace.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is all about living the dream that is professional trucking. Euro Truck Simulator 2 is too serious. The game even tells you as you begin that this is your dream job. With more than enthusiasm, players begin their adventure humbly with a little garage in the home city of their choice, and a company with no trucks.
The player begins by taking jobs for other companies, earning money from one city to another, with an eye toward earning enough cash and purchasing a truck. An owned truck means more freedom, with higher paying jobs that require more responsibility. When working directly for the player company, cargo is waiting at a select shipping yard and must be hitched to the truck before it can be taken to its ultimate destination. The next step from there is to start upgrading the garage, hiring other drivers to bring in more income, and eventually building a trucking empire that spans all of Europe.
The more you go, the more there is to do. Want to expand quickly? You can take out loans that need to be repaid. Want specialized drivers? They each level up the same way you do, and you can dictate the way they do. Of course, you also have to be mindful of expenses, be they repayments to the bank or fuel consumption by employees looking for work. There are a lot of ducks to get in a row, but the interface is user-friendly and information is constantly provided so nothing ever feels hopeless.
More than a game about driving, Euro Truck Simulator 2 boasts some role playing elements to keep things interesting. Successful jobs earn experience, which gives skill points. Skill points can be spent upgrading one's proficiency in certain types of jobs, unlocking new types of cargo, or even investing in fuel efficiency. Improving personal abilities and building a business from one lone driver to an entire fleet.
Driving trucks is as realistic as possible. Offering a huge map of Europe, there's plenty of time to be spent on the open road, and lots of distance to cover. Although you won't be undertaking journeys in real-time, a decent paying job is still quite the investment. I often found myself able to only play one job at a time.
There are a variety of controls and settings allowing for significant flexibility in terms of personal comfort. You can choose how complex your controls are, with automatic settings keyboard and set up a wheel. Whatever your available input, Euro Truck do a great job of covering you and ensuring you get into the game easily.
A tutorial guides for newcomers, and the essential GPS is easy to understand, as is its clear and simple route map. My first job was a decided disaster, with me getting the trailer stuck a number of times, managing to tip the vehicle over, and even call for emergency rescue.
Traffic lights, speed cameras, and the ever-present need to keep one's eyes on the road can always trip up an overconfident player, and as relaxing as long country drives may be, the pressure to avoid mistakes is present throughout. It's very easy to start getting speeding along a motorway without regard to other drivers and strict speed limits. Every mistake translates into a financial penalty, damaged cargo reduces the payday, and suffered by an owned truck will have to be paid for at service stations.
When a mistake occurs, it's almost always our fault, but there are some moments where the computer controlled road users face an issue. But they're few and far between, and experienced drivers will be able to avoid many of the hazard that lead to such trouble. Despite the occasional pressure to perform jobs well, Euro Truck Simulator 2 is still a largely cleansing experience. There's a driving through a variety of countries, a sense of joy as you get closer to your destination, and a sense of accomplishment in performing such boring tasks as refueling at gas stations and finding parking stops at which to grab some sleep. As you build your business up from nothing and take on more of managerial duties, it's hard not to feel pride over rewards well earned.
Although most visually advanced game, Euro Truck's believable presentation of Europe's roads and cities and atmosphere of the backdrops, there's a sense of individuality to each new territory you uncover, and the trucks themselves are lovingly recreated with an intricate level of detail. Owned trucks can be repainted and upgraded with all manner of parts, and as the player levels up, the potential for personalization expands.
The most fun aspect of Euro Truck Simulator 2, however, comes in the form of its music. With the simple tap of the "R" key, you can open up a menu packed with European Internet radio streams as well as your own Music and Radio streams. Providing a wide variety to listen. There's also the option to queue up music from one's own PC.

At first, I was EXTREMELY unsure whether or not I would be able to play this first episode and come away from it with a "I actually really enjoyed this." Life is Strange remains one of my top 5 favorite games, and while Before the Storm is good, it's definetely more of a nostalgia trip along with a plethora of new (mostly) interesting characters.
As you will see, most of the negative reviews for this game are because of the crashing during playing, failure to start up, or not optimized for controller settings. A very select few of them are for the game itself, which is surprising to me, but also not, depending on if they even played the first game at all.
That being said; if you did not like Chloe in LiS, you will NOT like her here. It's pretty self explanatory.
I was underwhelmed, to say the least, when I saw the game reveal because of the change in voice acting. Not just Chloe is different, I mean EVERY SINGLE CHARACTER you liked, right, they're a different voice now. (Though I could be incorrect on Nathan, I can't quite remember.) This may not impact you, but for me loving the original so much, it was a step in the wrong direction, I miss Ashly Burch immensely here. The new VA is great, don't get me wrong, it's just hard to get used to. My only other problem would be Rachel and Chloe sounding almost TOO alike in some scenes, but again, I was surprised at not being too annoyed with this decision.
Making Rachel an actual, living, breathing character instead of an unknown entity guiding you, was one of my other concerns, but surprisingly, I like her. She's everything you thought she would be, yet everything tortured and so... imperfect than the vision Max had of her. I won't say any spoilers, but the depth provided in the first episode alone is enough to make me crave more.
Being a gay woman myself, obviously this factors in on how much I'm enjoying this new beginning. Chloe is one of my favorite characters, for obvious reasons, and her struggles are very relatable to me. She's dealing with a lot of grief here, so if you expected everything to be more calm and lighthearted, or even more relaxed than the original, you're dead wrong. The romantic subtext helps ease the mood, and though I do quite like the vibe they have going, knowing how it all ends makes me dread each decision that much more. In fact, there were actually some jokes that made me smile, or even laugh a bit, which gets a few bonus points for appealing to my emotions. Yet, despite Before the Storm already having a canon ending, I can't help but want to go back and try the things that I didn't, just to see how much I can mess it up.
Backtalk was a new and very interesting way to revise the time traveling mechanic, and while it may not have that Life is Strange-esque feel, it's something I love to push my luck with (and I haven't failed yet!) It was a wise decision adding this, and I feel if the game didn't have this, I may not even be listing BtS as recommended, truthfully.
All of this is coming from an avid LiS fan, crazy conspiracy theories and all, but each game has it's faults, and I won't deny that I was EXPECTING to be disappointed, which is no good for a game. I'm betting that a lot of people have felt the same way, but I do encourage you to give it a try, because it wasn't as bad as I predicted it would be (and I love Max dearly, so you can imagine how I felt.)
Even so, if you didn't like LiS, here are some big improvments I noticed:
-the animations!! Finally the voice lines up with the mouth movements. Faces are much more expressive, legs and arms aren't jittery. Obviously LiS had it's own, endearing way of hair clipping through hoodies, but I do enjoy the jigglebone feel when Chloe moves her head around.
-character design. This may be a little vague, but if you payed close attention to earlier models, a lot of them were... cut and paste. I felt a bigger sense of realism when interacting with other people, even animals. The squirrels are different sizes now, the people have their own busts, and there's a wide range of them to look at. (I honestly love squirrels a lot so seeing a chubby one with a skinnier one made my day.)
TLDR : So. If you are on the fence about purchasing this game due to Reasons, here's what I have to tell you: give it a try. I was one of those people, and I do not regret spending my money on this game. I look forward to more episodes.

Go ahead and scroll through the reviews. Take a look a deep look at the points laid out in all the negative reviews. You will see a lot of "unbearable bugs" and "game will never be finished" and "devs are lazy". It is easy to slander a hardworking group of people from behind a keyboard and screen, but it only takes a little thinking to make the decision about whether or not you should purchase this game, which is of course why you are reading these reviews.
Look at the hours some of the reviewers have put in, despite their rage at the state of the "game". Many of these have hundreds and sometimes thousands of hours devoted to playing and leave the most negative reviews.
Why? Well, they are frustrated with the pace the game is developing at, they are upset that milestones have not been met on time and they feel as though bugs havent been fixed, or have been replaced by other bugs. They aren't wrong about these things, but they are wrong about how precisely purchasing an Early Access "game" works.
Lastly, let us do some cost/benefit analysis to understand whether and why you should or should not purchase. Remember those reviews you looked at?  Let's assume for the sake of it that you only play a game for enjoyment. If you play a game for X hours, then you continue to play because you are getting Y hours of enjoyment out of it where Y is equal to or less than X amount of hours you have played. If you spend $35 on a game, and get 35 hours of enjoyment out of it, that is one dollar per hour of fun. If you play for more hours, your investment in money becomes much more efficient.
Therefore, if you play for hundreds, or thousands of hours like many of these reviewers and then say "don't get it, its not worth it" you are saying "Don't invest, because despite the fact that I have played for 50 or 100 or 1000 hours, I am unwilling to admit that this project (which is still in development) was not at all worth my time". Its up to you to make the decision on how many dollars you are willing to pay per hour of enjoyment, but it is pretty foolish to say "Excellet game and its potential ruined by lazy and incompetent developers" (sic) when you have played for 1500 hours, and only paid 0.00067 dollars per hour of enjoyment.
Where else is fun that cheap? Nowhere. But don't make the mistake of buying this project and expected a full game to appear before you. It's not, and it won't. If you are willing to make an *INVESTMENT* in a game project, however, and you want to feel your heart pound in your chest as you creep through the military camps at night, surrounded by hostile players, do so. If you aren't willing to deal with unpolished bits and parts for the sake of the greater experience, then do not purchase. It's not done yet, and if you are the kind of person that doesn't want to invest their money in an imperfect experience (despite the many hours of enjoyment it has CLEARLY provided to the greater Steam community) that is 100% your prerogotive.

Do you like random generation in characters and areas? Do you like retro graphics? Do you like recolored enemy sprites? If so, Rogue Legacy is the game for you. Although not perfect, Rogue legacy is still greatly enjoyable, and is worth the $15 for sure.
Pros:
-Randomization
Randomization is pretty much the #1 requirement for Roguelites, as it keeps each run fresh and fun, and Rogue Legacy pulls this off spectacularely. Although many of the randomization for rooms is just a set room with different enemies scattered about, the number is very high, and due to all the different possible room types this works well, but rooms aren't the only random thing here. As clearly stated above, Rogue Legacy features random "children that you choose to take up your throne, although they won't necessarily turn out how you would like. To put it in simple terms, there are several classes that can be chosen from, each with unique stats, and once upgraded, abilities. Each child wilol also get one unique spell, chosen from a fairly small list, but it is not the numbers that matter here, as each one is extremely different.  Aside from their class and spell, another role is their traits, most of which are diseases or disabilities such as Gastro-intestinal disorder, P.A.D., ect. All of these are varied and quirky, not to mention mix up the gameplay, this helps out a great deal as you will not always get what you want, and forces you to cope with things you may not like, and I like that.
-Gameplay
Rogue Legacy is supposed to call back to old adventure games, and it does so with flying colors. All enemies you encounter are very different, and as opposed to some games, feel meaningful. As there are many different things to do and plenty of devious traps to encounter, it truly feels meaningful as you travel through the many different parts of the cursed castle, on your quest to end a Rogue Legacy. Every time you play a new castle is generated, making sure you don't know what to expect, and keeping the experience fresh, no matter how many times you play. Add this to some superb boss figts and you get yourself one heck of a fun game.
-Control
Ever play a game with clunky controls that make you want to throw down the controller? Rogue Legacy is not one of them. Despite all the different upgrades available to you that effect your movement the control in Rogue Legacy is superb. Your sword slashtakes a second to wind up for slight stragety, your jump feels meaningful, yet not floaty, everything about how you control is very fluid and works perfectly with the various obstacles you encounter, to make each death fell like your own fault.
-Music
Typically, games do not have a great soundtrack, fitting? Yes, fun? Yes, but so far very few games have as good a soundtrack as rogue legacy. Just by listening to the trailer, you know you'll have something worth listening to while playing the game. Each area has a soundtrack fitting to it's dark, yet adventurous tone. Wether it's the grim garden, now a savage wood, or the tower standing atop the castle, now a place of mystery and death, each track is pleasant and catchy. But wait, better yet than the area music are the boss theme, a boss theme is supposed to pump you up for whatever you are facing, but Rogue Legacy has boss themes that do much more. Each theme gives you a good theme of what you are up against, be it the horrendous gatekeeper that will kill you in an instant if you lose focus, or the panic-inducing beast of the dungeon, the boss themes are truly superb. Couple this with one of, if not my favorite title theme of all time and you have some catchy tunes. If you are not a fan of rogue-likes, at least but the soundtrack, trust me, you will not regret it.
Cons:
-Graphics
Don't get me wrong, I like the style of this game, the 16-bit look keeps it feeling retro, but some things just don't work. I will ocasionally see a graphics error that is just irritating, though it is rare. However, my largest problem here are the enemies, I stated above that each enemy is ubique, and yes they are. But, what I did not say is that there are 3 copies of each enemy, each stronger and different in some ways,  and they work well for the most part, except that they are just bigger and are a palette swap. Many things in this game are either just a pallet swap or stretching/squishing a sprite. Considering the massive amount of effort that went into the games it annoys me how lazy this is, and I'm fine with enemies sub-types looking similar, but simply changing size and color is very lazy, and I really don't like this.
Overall Rogue Legacy is easily one of the best indie games there is, up there with the likes of The Binding of Isaac and Super Meat Boy. Although it does have one flaw, the game is still superb, and I love every pixel of it. If you like adventure games, platformers, Rogue-Likes, you know what? Screw it, the game isn't perfect, but it is just amazing despite it's one flaw. If you like games, get this game, but you probably do to have made a Steam account, so buy this now. I mean it. Or I'll murder you.

I can't talk about Borderlands 2 in 2017 without talking at least a little about Gearbox Software's shady business practices.  This game benefits greatly from the draining of money away from Aliens: Colonial Marines, another Gearbox project which was sabotaged to give BL2 a boost.  And in the years since the release of BL2, Gearbox and Randy Pitchford have done all they can to prove that they never deserved success in the first place, partnering with a company called &quot♥♥♥♥♥quot; (ed: wow, Steam censored my use of this company's name), cramming as much scummy DLC into their games as possible, and mouthing off at every opportunity about how they would have changed all the things fans love about their games, given the chance.  BL2 comes with a host of baggage in this regard.  Even if you can ignore the industry politics surrounding the game, there is a LOT of pointless cosmetic DLC in this game, and the pause menu will advertise all of it to you.
It also comes with a built-in chest that dispenses vastly-overpowered gear for your current character's current level, using a currency shared by ALL characters (gold keys) that can only be earned by entering codes gained outside the game, by participating in now-defunct social media promotions (or entering them from a list you can find online).  Once you're out of gold keys, no more loot from that chest for you, ever again.  For ANY of your characters.  While this isn't a massive complaint, it speaks to Gearbox's overall scummy, mobile-esque, ad-heavy, DLC-nickel-and-diming strategy that they really went all-in on starting with this game.  While (spoilers) I do think it's worth buying the game even so, you need to know what you're getting into ahead of time.  If you find this stuff as distasteful as I do, you may want to think twice.
In terms of game design, if you think of Borderlands 2 as Diablo from a first person perspective, you won't go far wrong in how you approach it.  The focus here is the loot, not the story, although the story does try pretty hard to be interesting (your mileage may vary on whether you agree or not).  I definitely found the villain of the piece, Handsome Jack, to be eminently dislikeable in a good way.  I wanted to put bullets into this guy, so as the villain, he's doing his job pretty well.  Much of that is down to his voice actor, Dameon Clarke, who paints a really fantastic picture of a sociopathic corporate ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in Jack with his flippant, arrogant, pseudo-casual delivery.  Spot on, "pumpkin".  In any case, the story has its share of problems, but it primarily exists to ferry you from one loot arena to the next, and it does what it's supposed to do.  When the writing isn't veering off into wackytown, I actually found a lot of the intended emotional beats resonated with me, and the more understated instances of humor didn't fall flat.  This is a game that thinks it's a lot funnier than it is, though, so be forewarned.  The tone is all over the place.
Anyway, on to the loot.  The weapon types are pistols, shotguns, submachine guns, assault rifles (of which miniguns are a subtype), sniper rifles, and rocket launchers.  Each is randomly generated from a pool of manufacturers and parts that lend them particular characteristics, with stats determined by a dice roll.  You can also find grenade mods which determine the characteristics of the grenades you throw, and shields (in the Halo sense of a personal energy deflector) for defense.
This is a massive game, especially with all content DLC installed, and you can easily play it for hundreds of hours without really being "done" with it, even on a single character.  So, how you spend the bulk of your time will end up being a personal choice.  You could level as fast as possible and focus on fighting raid bosses with online friends/strangers for the highest-end loot you can.  You can play through all the stories and call it quits (which alone will take you probably 50-80 hours depending on DLC).  You can try and complete every sidequest in the game.  You can aim for completing the main story in each of the unlockable difficulty modes.  When you wake up on the glacier at the start of the game, it's hard to wrap your head around the sheer size and length of the journey ahead of each new character.  There is a lot more here than meets the eye.
The playable characters have some nice variety to them, although they grew on me a bit slower than did the heroes of the first game's cast.  BL2 went all-in on the characterization of everyone except the main characters, and it shows that they were designed with mechanics in mind first and foremost.  Zero, for instance, plays like a combination of the siren and sniper from BL1.  Axton plays like they had a chance to redesign Roland and iterated on his mechanics.  Salvador is Brick, but with guns instead of fists.  Maya's power (the new Siren) is the only entirely new, original idea in the cast, and it's on the one who's a carbon copy of a character from BL1 in physical design.  These don't feel so much like character traits as they do a list of patch notes.  The 2 DLC characters, the Mechromancer and Psycho, both have better personal characterization as well as really fun mechanics.  I recommend purchasing them both.
I also recommend acquiring the content DLC, starting with the Tiny Tina module, then adding Captain Scarlett.  If you enjoy those and just want more BL2, grab the rest.  They all come with a variety of new enemies to shoot, loot to find, and bosses to fight.  Be advised that, if you don't intend to play online with others, BL2 contains several bosses that are designed to be fought in a group and that have particular mechanics that make them prohibitively difficult to go at it alone.  Think of them as raid bosses in an MMO.
So, okay.  Enough faffing about.  Is Borderlands 2 fun?  Yes.  It feels good to play.  Shooting the guns is nice, they have impact.  The enemies scream and writhe around satisfyingly.  Elemental effects are impressive.  The visual style is fun, different, and nice to look at.  It drags a bit in the early game, especially very early on before your characters get their defining ability, but everything up to arriving at Sanctuary can be pretty boring and eminently linear.  However, once you're farther along, BL2 blossoms into one of the best Diablo-like loot-focused slot machine type games available.  There's a reason it's still so active on Steam multiplayer even in 2017.  It's very very good.  Just be advised going into it that it comes from a very scummy company, and is tainted by their shotgun approach to DLC.  Don't get suckered by them and you'll have a great time.

The Line thus far is the biggest sleeper hit of 2012. On the surface it looks like nothing more than a standard military-centric shooter and to a degree (in terms of actual gameplay) this is completely true. However The Line has a sinister undertow to it that takes the premise of Joseph Conrad's late 19th century novella Heart of Darkness (which inspired Francis Ford Coppola's Apocalypse Now) and applies it to a fictional Dubai which has been laid desolate by sandstorms. This game has some truly wrenching moments and events that make things like Modern Warfare 2's "No Russian" level look like Sesame Street yet The Line never becomes exploitative - it's brutality and darkness effectively communicating the game's larger message. I highly recommend this game to anyone who's even the slighest bit interested in it and can appreciate a very mature gaming experience.

The last and biggest problem was with one boss battle I had. I feel bad for saying this but I stopped playing because that one fight was too hard. I really enjoyed the game prior to that point, and wanted to know how it would continue, but several times I would sit down and spend an hour or two just trying to beat that one fight, failing repeatidly and feeling terrible. Ultimatly I desided that the game was no longer fun, and would only make me feel miserable. If this game was like dark souls, where its whole purpose is to be hard, I wouldnt mention this because it would just mean the game wasn't for me. Undertale isn't like that though. It is made to be cheerful, make you laugh, make you feel good, and for the most part it is great at that, but this one fight made me completly miserable when playing and prevented me from playing the rest of the game even though I'm sure it was spectacular.

Prison Architect. Well, where do I begin? If, like me, you're quite nostalgiac when it comes to gaming, then the time management, maintenance and building-block type games will be very familiar to you. Remember Theme Park, Theme Hospital and the original Sim City? Well this is an updated version of all of those games set around a prison. And it's been made wonderfully! The level of detail put into this game actually surprised me. The fact you actually have to plumb the water system around the prison as well as electrical cables to make sure the facility is kept running is quite impressive, not to mention all the different rooms and sections of the facility you can actually create in order to make your very own supermax. This game is incredibly fun and addictive and you can easily find yourself hibernating in a darkened room, headphones on and playing this well into the early hours of the morning. If when you first play it, you're put off by failing your first prison, don't let it discourage you. It won't be until your fifth or sixth prison where you actually start to flow into prison building and adding all the essentials and actually having a functioning and beautifully constructed penitentiary. This game is well worth the money and well worth playing if you're into these types of games. I'm glad I bought it and backed it up and I'm happy it has it's own place on my games list.

Go ahead and scroll through the reviews. Take a look a deep look at the points laid out in all the negative reviews. You will see a lot of "unbearable bugs" and "game will never be finished" and "devs are lazy". It is easy to slander a hardworking group of people from behind a keyboard and screen, but it only takes a little thinking to make the decision about whether or not you should purchase this game, which is of course why you are reading these reviews.
Look at the hours some of the reviewers have put in, despite their rage at the state of the "game". Many of these have hundreds and sometimes thousands of hours devoted to playing and leave the most negative reviews.
Why? Well, they are frustrated with the pace the game is developing at, they are upset that milestones have not been met on time and they feel as though bugs havent been fixed, or have been replaced by other bugs. They aren't wrong about these things, but they are wrong about how precisely purchasing an Early Access "game" works.
Lastly, let us do some cost/benefit analysis to understand whether and why you should or should not purchase. Remember those reviews you looked at?  Let's assume for the sake of it that you only play a game for enjoyment. If you play a game for X hours, then you continue to play because you are getting Y hours of enjoyment out of it where Y is equal to or less than X amount of hours you have played. If you spend $35 on a game, and get 35 hours of enjoyment out of it, that is one dollar per hour of fun. If you play for more hours, your investment in money becomes much more efficient.
Therefore, if you play for hundreds, or thousands of hours like many of these reviewers and then say "don't get it, its not worth it" you are saying "Don't invest, because despite the fact that I have played for 50 or 100 or 1000 hours, I am unwilling to admit that this project (which is still in development) was not at all worth my time". Its up to you to make the decision on how many dollars you are willing to pay per hour of enjoyment, but it is pretty foolish to say "Excellet game and its potential ruined by lazy and incompetent developers" (sic) when you have played for 1500 hours, and only paid 0.00067 dollars per hour of enjoyment.
Where else is fun that cheap? Nowhere. But don't make the mistake of buying this project and expected a full game to appear before you. It's not, and it won't. If you are willing to make an *INVESTMENT* in a game project, however, and you want to feel your heart pound in your chest as you creep through the military camps at night, surrounded by hostile players, do so. If you aren't willing to deal with unpolished bits and parts for the sake of the greater experience, then do not purchase. It's not done yet, and if you are the kind of person that doesn't want to invest their money in an imperfect experience (despite the many hours of enjoyment it has CLEARLY provided to the greater Steam community) that is 100% your prerogotive.

NOTE: This review contains spoilers. If you don't want to be spoiled then.. Go do something else.
When I got this game, I thought it was amazing. I loved the story, the characters and I felt it was one of the best games of the year (Just look at my list of aliases on my profile)
That was old me. Now, I look back at this game and realize that it's not that good of a game. In fact, I don't even think it is a good game anymore. And no, this review will not take the community into consideration because everyone already knows how... Interesting it is.
-The Good?-
Believe it or not, I do still find some good in this game. Let's discuss that!
1) The music is actually pretty good. A lot of the tracks are catchy, interesting and pretty varied for such a short game. Each area's music really complements it (For example, Snowdins track reminds me of winter, the Core's track reminds me of that feeling of "You're almost at the end.") and some of the tracks (Particularly Sans, Undyne and Asriel's) are really deserving of their praise. This is the one aspect that is really always going to be a positive.
2) While the story isn't really as great as everyone makes it out to be, it is still a nice twist on most recent games, and I appreciate that. I love the morality system and how if you act particularly "bad" or "good" some events and dialogues are different.
-The Bad.-
1) First and foremost, the game itself is not fun to play. The combat gets repetitive real fast, I didn't enjoy pressing the dialogue options and hoping that I chose the right one on my first playthrough, and I didn't find spamming the correct options on my subsequent playthroughs fun either. Back then, I didn't mind though because I thought "well, the game is focused on  the story so the combat wont be so good." But sometimes the game just expects you to be psychic. For example, in the normal run of the game, Undyne is the third boss of the game, and just like the boss before her (Papyrus) you can't run away. That is until she starts running out of dialogue options, and then you are able to run.. How is anyone actually meant to know that on their first time? I've seen a lot of people's youtube playthroughs, and almost all of them got confused by that part. A lot of people think that it goes with the "Ohhh. That's what.." attitude the game presents. It doesn't. It's just annoying.
The game was made in a freeware game making application, and it shows. The graphics are..presentable, but I feel that 8-bit "New-Tro" games are becoming stale now. Also, it doesn't help that you can't move in some directions while holding multiple buttons, but you can in others. Also, you can hold up, down and right while against a wall on the  X axis to walk really fast. Nice bugfixing.
2) The final bosses. Oh dear. I will count asgore because he is portrayed as one until the "twist."
Omega flowey is the only one I actually enjoyed fighting, as it actually switched up the gameplay. Instead of "dodge the slow projectiles and make friends with the enemy" approach you were used to you had to actually dodge some pretty difficult stuff while slowly gaining enough power to defeat him. It was enjoyable, and I was satisfied when I beat him.
Asgore was just a harder toriel. Though I really liked the idea of him destroying your mercy option, but other than that he was literally Toriel with more projectiles and one new attack.  Nothing else to say.
Asriel was built up fairly well, but his fight was probably the worst, bar one. The whole thing is ruined since you can't lose. Whenever you die, you simply restart the battle from a certain point when you die. This makes it really boring to play because there's no punishment. It's been a long time since I played the game, but when I last did I remember Flowey crashed your game when you lost to him, which meant losing was a restart of the whole fight, not just the current section. And his fight was hard, which meant dying was actually a threat. In Asriels fight it's just a chore. And it's really a shame because he has both my favourite theme in the game and my favourite attacks in the game.
And now Sans. Everyone overrates the hell out of this fight. The main gimmick is because sans is "the weakest enemy" and "only has 1 hp" and "can only do 1 damage"  he should be the hardest fight in the game. It's bad enough that I hate the "The underdog is the strongest" gimmick anyway. His fight is completely unfair (Which is similar to another genocide run boss: That being Undyne)  and intentionally designed to make you give up out of frustration. The game doesn't want you to be evil, it wants you to be the best you can possibly be. So why not make the final boss super difficult and hope that they just reset? Because it's boring. I did beat him, but I wasn't satisfied because the genocide ending (like the run itself) was terrible. It doesn't help that I hate Sans and Papyrus's characters the most out of any of them. Originally they were my favourite. But why is that?
3) Sans is the most boring "He's the lazy guy but is secretly a ninja" type character. His puns and jokes aren't funny and feel like they're only there so he can get meme cred. And Papyrus.. Isn't as bad, but I hate how all his dialogue is basically to try and turn him into a meme. It's lazy, if I'm being perfectly honest. But at least their dialogue matches their name (Papyrus for Papyrus, and Comic sans for sans) which I did find pretty clever. But that doesn't save them.
4) The last thing, and the biggest problem I have with the game. This is similar to the first point, but is the other half of the problem. And it is significantly larger. The first point was how the game isn't fun. This point is simple.
The game is boring.
Really boring.
You basically have two ways to play this game. And those ways are:
A) Not killing anyone, making friends with every enemy and beating the game twice just to get the true ending
or B) Grinding every area and kill enough enemies in each area before progressing in a long and boring process where the only boss fights you actually do are really cheap and intentionally made so that you drop the run.
And there is absolutely no reason to do a neutral or Genocide runs because of a few main reasons.
Firstly, neither ending is the best ending. That's the simplest way of putting it.
The genocide run is deliberately made to be boring: You start one-shotting every enemy and the whole thing is the very definition of a grindfest: You can end up spending upwards of 20 minutes just killing the same few enemies with the same few attacks and it ends up being boring. The only two bosses in this run that actually count are both boring and cheap, they last for a long time and are purposely made so you quit playing and restart.
As for a neutral run.. The game doesn't reward or punish you for doing it.. It just ends.
So as a result the game is essentially forcing you to play through it one way: The pacifist way. To put into perspective how bad this really is: Imagine an MMO with two warrior classes and a ranged one. You wouldn't play the warrior classes as they were slow and weak, so everyone ended up playing the ranged class unless they forced themselves to play one of the others. It's the same thing.
-Overall-
This game isn't very good at all. It lacks polish, and once you've played through it once, you've played through it all the times you need. I've actually played through this game three times, and I never want to touch it again. If I want to listen to the music, I'll buy the soundtrack, or just go on youtube.
Get it only if you really, really want it.

Since I got this game, I have been unable to unglue myself from my computer. In Rogue Legacy, you control a character, exploring a procedurally generated castle in search of riches and adventure. When your character inevitably dies, their child will come along to take their place as your next character, and this cycle continues.
When you first start out, you'll find the game a bit unforgiving, especially when you see that you have to fork over all your gold from your previous character's run whenever you play as a new heir. On the other hand, once you get into the groove of the grind, there's no going back. The factor that keeps this game fun is that your new heirs (characters) come in a variety of classes with a slew of traits.
For example, you can have a character that's a Mage (magic user, regains mana with every kill) but has his Health and Mana swapped. Suddenly that large mana pool turns your mage into a pretty decent tank, along the lines of a Barbarian. You might come across a character in your legacy that is afflicted with Dwarfism, rendering their swings short but allowing them to fit into tight spaces and access secret treasures.
So far, I have been playing for a few days and only now plucked up the courage to face and defeat the first boss. When I finally did it, there was a feeling of great satisfaction that can only be garnered from knowing you overcame a difficult obstacle, as opposed to being handed the victory.
There are all kinds of upgrades and item customizations in the game, as well as magic rune effects that add either passive traits to your character or allow you to perform certain extra skills, such as midair dashes or double jumps. Mash all these options together and you'll find yourself, as I am, formulating the "perfect class builds" that I would hope for when I select my next heir, such as "Lich King" class (adds 4 to max HP cap, increasing every kill) with the trait that gives him a crippling fear of chickens, allowing me to kill them as well to add to my HP cap, and then topping it all off with Vampirism runes and Blood Armor to allow for health siphoning while I'm killing things to boost my health cap.
This game doesn't look it from the outside, but it's DEEP, and for the price, more than a bargain. GET IT!

I have some serious - and I mean SERIOUS - issues with collision detection in this game. Mainly when I jump and press down + attack, whether it pops the small portable bridges or not. This could be improved.
Having said that, this game is still super fun. I'm finding myself lost in it for hours at a time. The entire day today has literally slipped away from me. The only thing I wish I had more of was money - I'm terribly bad at this game, and the game penalizes you greatly for being bad at it. There's a point reached where the gold you make can no longer buy you items or skills, making your only choice for advancement to get lucky enough to survive long enough to make a wise purchase with your coin before doing it all over again.
That's part of what a Roguelike is supposed to do I suppose, but this game could be a bit more forgiving and friendly with regards to coin issuance and/or skill cost. Prison Architect. Well, where do I begin? If, like me, you're quite nostalgiac when it comes to gaming, then the time management, maintenance and building-block type games will be very familiar to you. Remember Theme Park, Theme Hospital and the original Sim City? Well this is an updated version of all of those games set around a prison. And it's been made wonderfully! The level of detail put into this game actually surprised me. The fact you actually have to plumb the water system around the prison as well as electrical cables to make sure the facility is kept running is quite impressive, not to mention all the different rooms and sections of the facility you can actually create in order to make your very own supermax. This game is incredibly fun and addictive and you can easily find yourself hibernating in a darkened room, headphones on and playing this well into the early hours of the morning. If when you first play it, you're put off by failing your first prison, don't let it discourage you. It won't be until your fifth or sixth prison where you actually start to flow into prison building and adding all the essentials and actually having a functioning and beautifully constructed penitentiary. This game is well worth the money and well worth playing if you're into these types of games. I'm glad I bought it and backed it up and I'm happy it has it's own place on my games list.

Mad Max is a completely competent open-world action game with a story that is  short and shallow, but
Mad Max.
Mad Max ticks all the open-world action check boxes. You destroy towers (scarecrows) and take over forts to gain influence in each region. You fight against other factions in a Batman-light-style hand to hand combat and an excellent vehicle-combat that includes harpoons, thunderpoons, flame-throwers, depth-charges, ramming bars, boarding spikes, and wheel-shredders.
In addition to playing through main missions (of which there are only a handful - really, by the time you realize there is a narrative, the story is in its last few missions), there are a lot of side missions that you will run for various demented characters throughout the wastelands.
The game is beautiful. It also performs very well, showing what you can accomplish when you put effort into your platform optimization. On an i7-4790k with 16GB RAM and NVIDIA GTX 970 SLI system, we see consistent framerates in excess of 140fps at 1920x1080. Even with almost every setting maxed-out and while doing a live streaming session (usually disastrous for framerate on an SLI system due to the way streaming applications capture frames), we hit well-above 100fps.
Other than a shallow and fairly short story, Mad Max doesn't suffer any great failures on any one aspect. Yet, it does not quite seem to be greater than the sum of its parts. It is very entertaining. It has a lot of thoroughly enjoyable aspects, of which vehicle combat is probably the best. But it is also wears out its welcome, by the end. You've eventually had enough sand, screaming crazies running at you, and flame-shooting cars side-ramming you. You've had enough scrap collecting and busy-work -- which this game is riddled with.
It is competent; not groundbreaking.
But this should not be a bad thing. And it also does help us to understand why the reviews have been all over the place for this title. It isn't mind-blowing, but it isn't bad. I bought this game for just over half price, just before launch. Due to the discounts we saw everywhere, I was certain they were trying to dump the game while they could and had low expectations. Instead, I found a thoroughly good game for which I have no quarrel having paid half price. At full AAA launch price? Well, I'm not sure it would quite have lived up to that . . . but I wouldn't be disgruntled over it. I would be interested in a sequel to this title, if they make one. They have a solid foundation, here.
It is difficult for me to say that I do or do not recommend this game. I enjoyed it and feel it was worth what I paid for it. I would not be upset, but perhaps a little disappointed, if I'd paid full price. So, ultimately, I'd have to suggest that if you are a huge Mad Max fan and you can't stop playing open-world games, it may be worth full price. If you just love Mad Max or just love open-world games, then pick it up for half price and you'll probably be very satisfied and surprised.

Easily the best party game I've ever played in 2015. Gang Beasts is essentially Super Smash Brothers with a robust physics engine. I bought this for $15 as a New Year's Eve Party game, and my friends and I played it for 4 hours straight, laughing and cheering loudly as fights were constantly coming down to nail-biting and hilarious finishes. I've never yelled so loudly (in anger OR joy) at a game so much.
Gang Beasts is still in early Alpha, and despite this, comes with a TON of physics-based levels, with some (like "Trucks") standing way above the rest. I'd say watch a few videos online to see if it's your cup of tea, but honestly, you don't really "experience" Gang Beasts until you invite a few friends over and get a match going. You will have an asbolute blast, and probably lose your voice from all the yelling and cheering. It's that good.

Make sure to read this on-point review as well:
POSITIVE

+ Nice graphics and physics:

NEGATIVE
- Plenty, PLENTY of game braking bugs:
Game mechanics, mouse cursor bugs, random glitches, random char dying, etc
- Bad console port regarding keyboard controls:
Using the same damn key to ignite or refuel using a fuelcan is depressing!
There is no stealth elements, no options to walk, crouch, etc
- Bad mission design:
I ran into problems several times because of unlocking or using items in the open world which conflicted with some missions...
- Lifeless world:
convoys just loop in circles, random patrols etc very repetitive, people in towns just idle all the time
- Boring, repetitive and/or depressing gameplay design:
The game becomes repetitive VERY FAST. attacking camps, destroying oil pumps, searching locations for items - it's basically all the same.
Attacking an convoy can become impossible duo to the never-ending amount of patrols interrupting your attack. The frustration gets even bigger as you don't get any resources for taking out those enemy cars (they loose about 5-10 scrap on explosion)
- Motivation:
I find it very hard to motivate myself to go around and search for loot. When you collect scrap, you get about 5-10 scrap in one location.
Low items cost around 100-200 scrap, better ones cost between 300-900. This makes you rather hope to get some special items or reward during a mission than scavange the wasteland.
Rating: 4/10

A very good, high quality truck simulator.
Giant map (even without Going East DLC), different types of goods (precious, fragile, explosive) and deliveries (long distance, just-in-time), possibility to create your business with purchasing garages, hiring drivers, buying trucks: leasing, trade-in, credit money - it is all there.
Player earns experience points, which allow for getting more expensive deals and powerfull trucks.
The graphics is on the top level: sceneries are quite minutely drawn, cities correspond somehow to their real life prototypes. Trucks are modelled with love to details and look great in- and outside. Good drive physics is available (unfortunately no crushy crushes though:(, only dry numbers of damage percentage).
Interestingly that, the game doesn't get boring even having quite a monotonous gameplay (get deal, drive through, sleep, tank, manage company, get deal, drive...) - there is a lot to do till you become King of the road.
Recommended.

I never thought I'd get hooked on one of these "Euro Sim" games, but I did. There is something very Zen about just driving along the countryside, with your lead foot and the beautiful landscapes around you. If you've ever travelled Europe by rail or car, this game can be a very nostalgic and dramatic experience.
My only complaint is that sometimes the game "lurches" -- that is, when you are driving at a constant speed, the truck periodically slows down and then catches up again. During the lurches, the framerate does not seem to drop, so it seems that something else is causing it to bottleneck. I'm playing on a GTX 980 with a 3Ghz i5 CPU and 8Gb RAM, so I doubt my system is to blame. At any rate, the lurching doesn't occur constantly and it doesn't really detract from the driving experience, but I still hope that it gets sorted out in a future update.

You can upgrade and modify your truck, and work your way to own small or huge fleets. The game looks nice, and the developer actively supports and expands it, which is also a huge plus.

Even though I know it's my fault, I still blame the other drivers.

This is a fun game, no question. But at the time being it is very clearly an alpha game.
It's showing a LOT of potential. There's a lot of customisation options for your prison, in that you can build it with your own little touch. Not as much as I'd like, but I'm sure more will be added as time goes on.
You really do feel like you've accomplished a difficult task when you get a large prison going though. It's just really satasfying looking after 70 maximum security prisoners, managing their shedule, making sure they have no escape attempts, or that any riots break out, and just keeping all that in check is suprisingly engaging.
It has it's flaws. The AI is very, VERY stupid, the Art Style is a little bland at the moment, I find it slightly annoying how you never see the staff/prisonsers actually USING about 80% of objects put into the prison, and some minor bugs that I'm sure will be fixed as tome goes on!
I look forward to following Prison Architect throughout it's development process - this project has so much potential that I'm just ecstatic to see how it turns out!
TL;DR - It's good, but clearly not a finished product and has issues, like buggyness and an art style that isn't fully realised yet. The idea has so much potential though that I can't dislike it. If it's this much fun now, when it's finished it could be something truly fantastic.

The only really good parts for me were the music, the pretty art, and especially the introduction of ...

This is a fun game, no question. But at the time being it is very clearly an alpha game.
It's showing a LOT of potential. There's a lot of customisation options for your prison, in that you can build it with your own little touch. Not as much as I'd like, but I'm sure more will be added as time goes on.
You really do feel like you've accomplished a difficult task when you get a large prison going though. It's just really satasfying looking after 70 maximum security prisoners, managing their shedule, making sure they have no escape attempts, or that any riots break out, and just keeping all that in check is suprisingly engaging.
It has it's flaws. The AI is very, VERY stupid, the Art Style is a little bland at the moment, I find it slightly annoying how you never see the staff/prisonsers actually USING about 80% of objects put into the prison, and some minor bugs that I'm sure will be fixed as tome goes on!
I look forward to following Prison Architect throughout it's development process - this project has so much potential that I'm just ecstatic to see how it turns out!
TL;DR - It's good, but clearly not a finished product and has issues, like buggyness and an art style that isn't fully realised yet. The idea has so much potential though that I can't dislike it. If it's this much fun now, when it's finished it could be something truly fantastic.

It is difficult to begin a review of this game that accurately captures both its awesomeness and appeal. Fans of hack-and-slash games, dungeon crawlers, and RPG's alike will find themselves pouring hours and hours into this game. You explore a massive castle, with each new area revealing new enemies and evolutions of previous ones. You scour the castle for gold to upgrade your abilities in order to defeat the bosses in each area. When you die, you keep your gold, and your next character spends it on permanent upgrades like health and damage, new equipment (which you must find blueprints for in the castle) and 'runes' to attach to your equipment (which you also find in the castle, but must complete a challenge to obtain). However, you must spend your gold wisely, as you lose it all upon re-entering the castle! This is a great example of one of the many ways this game is brilliantly balanced. Another is the castle layouts. Each time you die, your next character explores a whole new layout. Unless, of course, you agree to give a percentage of your gold to one of the characters in front of the castle so that he can keep the layout the same! Finally, you do not get to choose your character and customize them complete. Instead, when you begin a new character, you can choose from one of three, each with their own unique traits and class and magic. This may sound like a bad thing, but it often instead leads you to discover the use of a class you have not used much, and how to deal with some of the more difficult traits in the game.
All in all, this is a game that will continue to draw you back death after death, Sometimes your best character will meet an untimely death, and sometimes your worst will make you the richest hero alive. Never knowing what will happen next is half the fun, and the further you get the less predictable things become, even as more abilities become available to you. While this game is quite challenging, I would recommend it to anyone, as it is a top-of-the-line model when it comes to games of any kind.

POSITIVE

NEGATIVE
- Plenty, PLENTY of game braking bugs:
Game mechanics, mouse cursor bugs, random glitches, random char dying, etc
- Bad console port regarding keyboard controls:
Using the same damn key to ignite or refuel using a fuelcan is depressing!
There is no stealth elements, no options to walk, crouch, etc
- Bad mission design:
I ran into problems several times because of unlocking or using items in the open world which conflicted with some missions...
- Lifeless world:
convoys just loop in circles, random patrols etc very repetitive, people in towns just idle all the time
- Boring, repetitive and/or depressing gameplay design:
The game becomes repetitive VERY FAST. attacking camps, destroying oil pumps, searching locations for items - it's basically all the same.
Attacking an convoy can become impossible duo to the never-ending amount of patrols interrupting your attack. The frustration gets even bigger as you don't get any resources for taking out those enemy cars (they loose about 5-10 scrap on explosion)
- Motivation:
I find it very hard to motivate myself to go around and search for loot. When you collect scrap, you get about 5-10 scrap in one location.
Low items cost around 100-200 scrap, better ones cost between 300-900. This makes you rather hope to get some special items or reward during a mission than scavange the wasteland.

Eventually, I overcame this downside and have taught myself how to farm quickly to protect my precious loot. The best part about the game is that once you make a base, you can die and farm back up way faster and It feels like you have a little bit of challenge, power, responsibility, and instincts that all sandboxes should make you feel which makes you feel like you matter on your server. In conclusion, If you don't mind the occasional bit of pvp, than rust is a great open world survival that you need so bad.

After 50+ hours sunk into this game (single playthrough!!), I can tell you this: A very small number of games managed to captivate me this much in terms of its setting and subsequent possibilites. Here is the main positives gist version:
- The vast desert, strongholds, wrecks, open sand dunes, they all create a desolate world so sO SO worth exploring,
- Customization (both character and car) is off the charts for an open world title.
- Graphics range from above average to HOLY SHEET!, depending on the scenery. Overall it is truly eye-candy in terms of art direction and color palette, I honestly loved it.
- Sound is sweet as hell if you have the appropriate sound system. With a 7.1, the gunshots, punches (Fury mode !!) and engine sounds were a true treat. Obviously hearing authentic australian accents is a plus too:)
- Car/fist fights. The core of the game. And yes, AAA action game/movie caliber. I dare anyone to dispute this.
- And last, but not least: it runs like a dream. Seriously. Knife through butter kind of smooth. This is how games are supposed to ship in the first place, so take note everyone else. But nevertheless, Avalanche did a stand up job here!
The story is passable, but then again, I did not expect Witcher/Mass Effect complexities in the 1st place. It is simple, with a few turns here and there. Enjoyable. I might have expected a bit more variation in the side quests or available stranger stuff, but I honestly cannot fault this game for that, as practically every other open world has the same, if not worse issues. No biggie, its the story + setting + options that count. And in this, Mad Max truly succeeds. My darkhorse for 2015 is exactly that. Bravo !

Great storytelling. That's what Spec Ops is about. Don't mind the shooting, it's generic and many other games have nailed that aspect in a better way (sand isn't as important as it seems). But that's not what Spec Ops is about. It takes you and two squadmates on a journey through Dubai, resulting in total chaos. The way your character becomes more insane as you play through the game is done in a brilliant and, above all, realistic way. I can't say any more really, I would risk spoiling the story for you. Believe me, that would be a shame.
The graphics are very good; there's lot of detail and the environments keep the game from being grey(ish) and colorless. The voice overs are great, really great. The other sounds and music are also very well done.
It's a short game; I clocked in in about 5 hours, so it's a steep price to pay. Buy it or don't buy it, just make sure you have at least played it once.

Spec Ops: The Line is a few things. It's graphics are dated, and its gameplay and multiplayer are par for the course of the FPS genre. It's saving grace, though, is its top-notch campaign. It is a psychological thriller inspired by The Heart of Darkness and Apocalypse Now, and it delivers one of the most haunting and compelling stories I've ever seen in a shooter. When you aren't running-and-gunning, you are faced with moral conundrums which are left open-ended. There is no "right" or "wrong" decision, it's just what choices your made and what effects they have. And as the story pans out, you will see that your character - Cpt. Martin Walker - and his squad aren't the only ones in a sandstorm ravaged Dubai who are struggling not only to survive, but to reconcile their decisions. 9 out of 10.

Although the game itself is fairly generic in the gameplay department (duck behind cover, shoot, loot, find ammo, find more cover, shoot), the story, visual effects and soundtrack combine to make a powerhouse blockbuster. If you're interested in a dark descent into the human psyche, and  even into your own emotions, this is worth checking out.

- Sound is sweet as hell if you have the appropriate sound system. With a 7.1, the gunshots, punches (Fury mode !!) and engine sounds were a true treat. Obviously hearing authentic australian accents is a plus too:)
- Car/fist fights. The core of the game. And yes, AAA action game/movie caliber. I dare anyone to dispute this.
- And last, but not least: it runs like a dream. Seriously. Knife through butter kind of smooth. This is how games are supposed to ship in the first place, so take note everyone else. But nevertheless, Avalanche did a stand up job here!
The story is passable, but then again, I did not expect Witcher/Mass Effect complexities in the 1st place. It is simple, with a few turns here and there. Enjoyable. I might have expected a bit more variation in the side quests or available stranger stuff, but I honestly cannot fault this game for that, as practically every other open world has the same, if not worse issues. No biggie, its the story + setting + options that count. And in this, Mad Max truly succeeds. My darkhorse for 2015 is exactly that. Bravo !

I was hesitant about picking up Mad Max simply because it's one of my all time favorite movie series, well, except that POS Beyond Thunderdome. It's typically hit and miss when a Developer tries to adapt a movie franchise as a video game (anyone remember The Thing?) so I thought I'd wait for others to influence me on this one.
What video I'd seen prior to purchase made it look beautiful (as beautiful as a wasteland can anyway) and fluid from a gameplay standpoint.
Around this time a fellow Member at Band of Others picked up the game and was raving about it so I thought I'd give it a try.
Not expecting much, I was  completely blown away by Mad Max.
It's an exceptionally well done port, plays very fluidly, has great sounds, terrific environments and in oddly fun. Vehicle combat is very satisfying particularly when you're trying to take down trade routes and the Arkham style combat is done well.
The game is a bit light on story but given the fact Max isn't exactly what you'd call a story driven franchise it doesn't seem to detract from the game much, if at all.
The environments are absolutely amazing and surprisingly diverse as are the camps you'll need to infiltrate to complete objectives.
The one area I'd like to address though is the critique toward the looting system. Reviewers have been a bit negative toward this citing that you don't get a lot of scrap for completing loot areas or destroying vehicles (for example). I just don't understand this critique as how much scrap do you think you can get off a destroyed vehicle, it's destroyed?
Also, it's a post apocalyptic wasteland so can you really expect there to be scrap lying around everywhere?
I feel those reviews completely miss the point about what this story is about so don't let it guide you into not playing the game. In fact, the game does a good job of helping you collect scrap once you build up certain projects within strong holds.
I'd go as far as to say that at this point the scrap system goes too far because it becomes too easy to collect scrap.
Of course one can also pick issues here and there such as the game having fetch quests and that some elements are repetitive. Personally I think this is also reaching a bit as it's the recipe most Open World Games use so it's little different in this regard.
Honestly, this is a very well done game that is overall just a blast to play.

Spec Ops: The Line is a few things. It's graphics are dated, and its gameplay and multiplayer are par for the course of the FPS genre. It's saving grace, though, is its top-notch campaign. It is a psychological thriller inspired by The Heart of Darkness and Apocalypse Now, and it delivers one of the most haunting and compelling stories I've ever seen in a shooter. When you aren't running-and-gunning, you are faced with moral conundrums which are left open-ended. There is no "right" or "wrong" decision, it's just what choices your made and what effects they have. And as the story pans out, you will see that your character - Cpt. Martin Walker - and his squad aren't the only ones in a sandstorm ravaged Dubai who are struggling not only to survive, but to reconcile their decisions. 9 out of 10.

There's always the fear that when a prequel comes along, it will cheapen the original material. Whether it's with weak characterization or telling a story that does not need to be told.
This is not the case with Life is Strange: Before the Storm.
What the Life is Strange team has done is craft a deeply engrossing, emotional, and intimate story that honors and improves upon the world laid out in Life is Strange.
Chloe and Rachel are excellent characters, and the moments they share together are so touching and wonderful. I found myself teary-eyed the whole time, eager to see what happened next.
This game has improved upon the previous game in just about every way. The animations are more detialed, the writing is miles better, the voice acting, even without Ashly Burch, is phenomenal.
I do not know how I am going to be able to wait for Episodes 2 & 3. I am so glad this game series exists.
Great game, looking forward for the next episode!

NO SPOILERS!
Update for episodes 2 & 3, prior to the Bonus Episode:
This game is shockingly close to being better than the original; it's not perfect--the third episode has one section where a mechanic pulled me out of the game while I tried to figure out what object to click on to perform an action--but the issues are so minor that I can't help but applaud the overall project. The story manages to set up for the original LiS *regardless of what your interpretation of Rachel was* by letting you see her in the light that fits your playthrough.
I'm also hugely impressed by their use of themes--specifically, pondering why we lie, and whether or not it is ever good to lie to someone. I am moved by the story and thrilled to have more thinking to do about it, to unpack it more completely.
Original Review:
I'll update this review as the remaining episodes drop, but having playing the first episode thoroughly with one tactic, I'm absolutely thrilled. Deck Nine has impressed me much more than I expected was possible in a prequel from a new developer.
The story relies on the elements that made LiS its best self: emotional depth and relatable content. From the bullies and baddies who clearly have their own problems and redeeming qualities, to the realistic looks at differing reactions to pain, I was glad to see that LiS is back.
But to address the elephant in the room: The voice actors are fine, and in fact, I really enjoyed the game's use of them. Just like in the original LiS, what appears out-of-context to be choppy dialogue (c'mon, folks; LiS had cheesy dialogue and, in some cases, not-excellent voice acting) actually melds together into believable conversations and satisfying narrative beats. There are cringe-worthy moments, but that's to be expected... and to be honest, some of them felt like intentional homages to the first game's "charm" (quality issues).

Although the game itself is fairly generic in the gameplay department (duck behind cover, shoot, loot, find ammo, find more cover, shoot), the story, visual effects and soundtrack combine to make a powerhouse blockbuster. If you're interested in a dark descent into the human psyche, and  even into your own emotions, this is worth checking out.

The game has very smooth and responsive controls, which is one of the most important parts of a platformer. The game progression and other RPG elements are great. You really get the sense that your bloodline is slowly growing stronger through the generations.
The game has immense replay value in the NG+ system and hidden extras. The enemies and environments are varied and diverse enough to prevent the game from getting stale, but only in your first or second playthrough. Once you get into NG+3 territory you'll have mastered every enemies patterns and behaviour and be looking for more. The 5 extra bosses added in the 1.2 patch go great lengths to fill that void though. The extra bosses expand on the previous ones, but require near perfect player skill and a deep understanding of game mechanics to defeat. As a result this was probably the most satisfying game to get 100% of the Achievements in and it feels like a real accomplishment of skill to do so.
This game manages to appeal to both the casual and hardcore gamers at the same time. Less avid gamers will enjoy the light-hearted humor, the sense of growth and character development from the castle improvements, and the plethora of options and combinations to choose from. Hardcore gamers will enjoy the tight controls, difficult but fair gameplay, the replayability, and the late game challenges. If any of those things appeal to you, you'll find something to enjoy in this game.

The open roads of western Europe and the UK scaled to 1:15 of the real size is the setting for the base game of ETS2. Kitted out with real trucks from such manufacturers as Scania, DAF, Iveco and Magestic, you are presented as a truck driver dreaming of one day owning his/her own logistics company complete with a fleet of vehicles and drivers to drive them.
In the begining your role is to freelance, driving other people's trucks moving cargo from city to city. From the position of the driver seat, above, behind or side views, you need to ensure you obey all the road rules and avoid any crashing. Thats right this is a simulator after all so you need to ensure that you stay in your lane, indicate to turn or change lanes, stop at red lights, keep under the speed limit, don't exceed your maximum driving hours and keep your truck fueled. Luckily there are ample stops and gas/petrol/refueling stations available along the way so that shouldn't be too hard. Just watch out for those 550  euro speed cameras in the UK, Ouch!
If you are unimpressed with GTA's driving realism and want something a bit more non-fiction, then ETS2 is for you. Driving a truck is more addictive than at first glance. Sure you are hauling cargo on roads, but its more than that. You are trying to kickstart your own trucking company, so you need moolah to get there.
If in doubt wait for a sale, but honestly even at the full price its worth it. Especially with the mod support.
