Regardless of what people say, Undertale is a very well made game. The story boils down to "I fell down a hole and i'm not trapped in the underground... How do I get home?" So there's not much story here. It's a nice take on the typical RPG which instead of cutting down every enemy you come across it allows you to show mercy to your foes while still letting you kill them if you wish. Everyone will most likely say "PLAY THE PACIFIST ROUTE" since the game thrives on it's characters. However by killing them of course you don't really find out much about them which is why people say to play that route, but they do offer fun and challenging fights on the Genocide route. Better soundtrack in my opinion too. Did I mention the soundtrack? That's really good. The combat is also something new to RPGs and very fun. As rather than watching your character attack and dodge, you're actually in control. You have to time your strikes and when the enemy attacks you, you have to dodge the attacks. However since a certain website discovered the game the fanbase can be quite "special" and has made some serious damage the community. So avoid looking anything up about the game other than remixes of the songs.

Even though I haven't finished the game yet, I've seen enough of it to put my thoughts in writing.
is pure bliss.
The first thing you'll notice is, of course, how absolutely gorgeous it looks. This is one of the best-looking games ever made, and it performs flawlessly even on middling hardware.
The sound design matches the visual quality and enhances the wasteland's hostile atmosphere.
Melee combat is heavily inspired by the likes of the
series and
, which to me is a good thing, but some may find overly simplistic.
But obviously what sets this game apart from other open-world action titles is vehicular combat, and it's as fun and enjoyable as you'd expect from a game set in the
universe. Your car - or should I say, the "Magnum Opus" - itself is a weapon (with which you can ram and grind enemy vehicles), but as you progress in the story you'll equip it with a grappling gun, a sniper rifle and a makeshift rocket launcher, making it the ultimate dispenser of death and destruction.
There is, however, a distinct lack of motorcycles and larger, truck-sized "war rigs", such as the ones seen in
and the recent
.
Open-world games have been criticized lately for excessive reliance on inconsequential side-missions and collectibles, something that has been referred to as the "Ubisoft school of open-world games".
has side-missions, collectibles, strongholds, camps: the whole nine yards. But none of them feel like fodder. Every little place you visit has its own unique design and backstory, giving a sense of immersion that is sadly quite rare these days.
Throughout your adventures you'll be assisted by Chumbucket, the horribly disfigured hunchback mechanic. I won't call him a sidekick because he's every bit as important as Max himself, and is really the heart of the game.
And he's just one of many interesting characters you'll meet. Friends and foes are all equally well designed and voice-acted. It helps that the dialogue is great, too.
Anyway, there's so much else I could say, so let me be perfectly clear and be done with it: this is not just a recommendation. It's a ringing endorsement.

UPDATED SOLO REVIEW
Devblog 175:
The rust of today is not the Rust anyone remembers, and to be honest that’s a very good thing. Sense its initial launch, this game it has gone through many changes with the vast majority of changes good while the minority falling on their face.
The game itself is getting prettier and prettier all the time, the mechanics continue to improve and gameplay continues to get flushed out with memory leaks getting patched and new content continuing to make its way onto the game like the addition of the armored-personnel-carrier (APC)
Developers of Rust continue to focus on features for team play or clans play while ignoring the needs of solo players. Devs clam that what helps clans inevitably helps the solo player. As a solo only player I can tell you that this is a load of ****. If you’re a solo player and your new to the game you are going to get wrecked, eventual it’s going to happen.
I recommend moded or community servers with 0 to really low pop count are the servers for new solo players with no experience in games like rust, or moded/community servers that are dedicated to solo or PvE only for solo players.
However, if you have skill and you got ice for blood, then a vanilla server will get your heart pumping from the moment you wake on a cost line, until the day of the monthly wipe, when you start all over again and it can be fun.
Overall the game is solid and continues to improve. Content is good and getting better. At this point I can recommend this game with confidence for people who are solo players thanks to the improvements made by the devs and the support of moded and community servers.
Original Solo Revue Devblog 158:
What we have here is a game that has gone far, far away from its point of origin that made it a game to be excited about.
The devs continue to work on optimization while adding features and gameplay. However, if you’re expecting a game setup for solo survival, you’re going to greatly disappointed. With an emphasis on clan play (or zergs), the game-devs continue to create feature and tools for large clans that dominate a server or servers. in a game where a solo favoring person could once have played for the fun of it, now needs to be in a team to survive, host a server that they can enjoy the PvE game play, or find a solo only server with an admin that enforces solo play for a solo player to enjoy the game.
Clans, however, now face no problems as the dev team has recently add new game changing features that brake the rules as it has been for so long. Now, no structure or base is safe from anyone and the rule book has been shattered.
Where I once would have highly recommended this game, the game is no longer worth getting into.

First things first, which also seems to be the thing everyone is talking about, this game is one of the best optimized games I have ever played. This thing could probably run medium settings on an intel HD 4000. Either way, my 370 runs this thing at high at an almost constant 60 fps. It also has nearly every graphical adjustment setting you can imagine. So, from a techincal standpoint it is awesome.
The world is beautiful as well. It may be a desert, but it is a very pretty desert. Everything looks good in this game, characters, vehicles, explosions, vehicle explosions. Driving is a lot fun, and the vehicular combat is what keeps this game going. That and the entertaining modifications you can make to your car.
The problems with this game are mostly story related. I don't really know what exactly the plot of this game is. It just seems that your main companion decides to work with you because your the saint. And nothing more is really explained of that and you have your companion who by rights seems to be the smartest person in the wasteland. This game is also extremely repetitive. After about three hours of gameplay you have probably done every different task there is to do, and you will realize you are just going to repeat these tasks over and over till you acquire all your car parts. Now, there is something really charming and comforting about doing these repetitive tasks. It's kind of odd, really. Driving around the desert acquiring scrap and punching war boys to death just works.
Worth the money if you enjoyed Shadows of Mordor at all.   The upgrading your vehicle aspect, and overall dreary beauty of the wasteland is awesome.

One episode in, and I already think I'll enjoy Chloe's series more than the original.
In terms of gameplay, it's still the same storytelling mechanic from the original series, except with Chloe's own unique feature of being able to "backtalk" someone into getting what you want. There's also a cool minigame of sorts if you are into table-top games!
The Max's series had the drawback that the developers were still trying to iron out how to use Max's powers in a storytelling game, which led to some weird and sometimes annoying mechanics in the first two episodes. However, by the end, Max's mechanics had been fully fleshed out, and gave a great ending to the series.
I feel like Deck Nine had already known what went right with the first game, and built upon it. The soundtrack is amazing, the storyline is more involving, and the new backtalk feature feels more exciting than Max's ability did. Just like the original, each character has a unique look and langauge that makes them mean more to you than their cartoonish apperance shows. I'm sure I'm about as far away from the demogrpahic that the developer was targeting as you can get, yet Chloe's story still makes sense and is interesting. Really looking forward to the next episodes.

Some notes:
- The new voice for Chloe is good! The recasting due to the voice actors' strike doesn't bother me at all. It's a good and believable replacement for the younger Chloe.
- The character writing is good as well, both for Chloe's lines and thoughts.
- The chemistry between Rachel and Chloe feels the way the original Life is Strange makes you think.
- There obviously is no time travel, but they introduced a fun "special power" Chloe has, and it fits her character and the game really well.
- Revisiting known locations and characters was perfectly woven into the debute episode, as well as references to Max and some iconic character traits that will be referenced "later" in the original.
- The first episode was longer than I expected!
- The music is great!
- Overall, the game really has a soul, which is probably what made us Life is Strange fans fall in love with it in the first place.

I've played Rust since Legacy w/ Zombies.  I've been here through all the major changes and the Beta of 'Current Rust'.  I've seen BP system go away, Experience System go away, Component System changes, Explosive Ammo Raiding get nerfed, Raid Towering go away (and then brought back this patch), and I've stuck through it all.
However this last patch is a game killer.  My clan of 18 players, which normally has 9 people at a time (half Euro, Half US), has 0 people on right now.  This patch killed the game for not only us, but several of our allied clans that play on other servers.  The ability to thatch onto other people's bases without TC access allows anyone to bypass all security.  It has effectively gotten rid of "Big Raids".
Normally, our clan would raid 20-ish bases between Thur (wipe day) and Sat.  They were offline for the most part and "Economy raids", and then we would find the biggest group on the server to "Big Online Raid" on Sunday.  It was fun building massive compounds, towers, and walls and then going out in groups of 4-6 finding trouble or taking down Helis/chasing down Air Drops.  This new change however isn't fun anymore.
A group of 3 people can now effectively raid any base they see with very little effort.  All Helk did was change the way people build (instead of tall towers, it would become mathematical formulas for "width protection vs height protection".  You'll see double-stack AIDS bases that are 40 rockets to the core and 40 rockets from the ceiling, and it will take a group of 20+ to build it (and not be able to do much manuevering once inside of it...)
If Helk had made it so only ladders were placeable within TC range, it wouldn't have been a game killer.  It would have actually been a good change in some regards.  But to be able to place down Thatch to climb up and over any base, is ridiculous.
After 4,169 hours in Rust, through all the changes... I'm finally done with Rust.  Maybe this was Helk's intention.  The real money is in mobile games.  Perhaps he is forcing Rust to die out.  In any case, I got my money's worth and met some cool people over the years.  Time to find another game to occupy my time.
If Helk removes the thatch building and leaves the ladder placement, I would come back, but it doesn't appear to be his intentions now or ever.

I discovered Rogue Legacy off the back of a Destructoid Podcast recommendation and the gimmick alone perked my interest enough to warrant looking it up.
The game has a similar feel to many other Roguelike, Metroidvania games but also carries its own distinctive charm in the form of genetic imperfections your new character develops every time you die. Some give you bonuses (too light to set off traps, too heavy to be knocked back) and some will impede your progress (swapping your MP and HP bars, being unable to use your map) and some are just plain useless but still amusing (baldness, farting every time you jump). The one thing all of these traits do, along with the randomly generated castle, is guarantee a slightly different game every time you play. Add to this a reasonably robust upgrade system, along with a slightly lacklustre loot/ability system, and there is plenty to keep you coming back.
The game initially felt extremely punishing, for me at least, and in my first few attempts I struggled to make it more than three or four rooms. Upgrading my stats and unlocking things like double-jump and dash abilities did mean I started to progress further, but as well as that you learn that, unlike the more recent Castlevania titles, just running in and slashing away isn't really an option. The game rewards patience, and timing your attacks and movements correctly. Once I got into the rhythm of the game it felt extremely satisfying to weave in and out of enemy attacks; exploiting their blind spots and taking advantage of the environment.
There are a few issues I have with the game, though, one being that a lot of the later enemies, and the bosses to a certain extent, have some pretty cheap attacks that are almost impossible to dodge, especially when you're being overwhelmed by everything else in the room, but because you're constantly evolving your character, eventually I was strong enough that I could just take the hits and barrell through them. The controls can also be a bit fiddly at times --again, especially when you're being expected to focus on several different things at once-- and I occasionally found my character running backwards slashing at the air instead of the enemies that were in front of him. Finally, the random element of the castle layout means that, on rare occasion, my character got stuck in a room it was impossible to get back out of. This only happened once or twice, though, out of literally hundreds of runs, so it's absolutely not a common problem.
All in all, this is a great game with a ton of personality, at a great price, and what few foibles it does have never become frustrating enough to be a dealbreaker; especially when you can just die and re-roll your character and the castle layout until you find something more to your tastes.

Rust. The No. 1 Sandbox-Survival-Shooter-Multiplayer game that is out there right now.
The developers of Rust are constantly pushing out new updates, fixes and events to suit the requests and needs of the rapidly-growing, creative player base. Recently, these have included nerfs, the release of the Vending Machine, the release of the Muzzle Break and the Rust Olympics (3rd Instalment).
I really like the open-world, rustic survival feeling that Rust is emitting, even when you come about the occasional ground of rowdy bandits or clan members looking to ruin your day. The weapons and their skins are very accurate to the general theme of the game, and even the terrain and buildings are very dishevelled-looking, adding to the game.
I also liked how well-engineered communication was in the game. Push-To-Talk transmits your voice clearly and without interruption to surrounding players, whilst the Chat function represents simple text communication to the whole server. There are certain servers that are 'Modded', meaning that they take the initial rules of Rust (stack limits, travel speed, crafting speed) and change them, thus resulting in many different game modes.
Game modes that I really enjoyed were Hunger Games, Rust King of the Hill, Hide and Seek and Deathmatch. These can be found either on official Facepunch servers or on public community servers.
Out of 10, I would rate this game 9/10. This is because whilst I feel that every important aspect of gameplay and community is covered, the game should and could be optimised a little more in order to suit every players' PC needs (Note that I have a perfectly functioning PC and that I am including that for people I have played with).

What a ride.
Despite slightly repetitive gameplay, this game is undeniably beautiful. The LOD distance detail makes this game increadibly immersive. Fantastic car sounds. Great slomo effects when fighting. Great writing. Such a satisfying combat system. I'd say it's a cross between Dirt 3 and Assassin's Creed, minus the parkour.
Although the menu upgrades and "bio" style lore delivery are a slight burden, they do end up being cool if you're patient to go through them.
It's a great game if you are a completionist, and even though things can get repetitive, they are still so damn fun, and varied just enough to keep the interest moving. No two strongholds and bases are the same. Each have their own flavour and vibe.
Lastly, this game has some of THE BEST LIGHTING mechanics you'll come across. The skybox is quite organic in nature, and moves naturally. Dust, sand, wind, storms, lightning, sunsets, ambient occlusion, everything is perfect.
I give it a well-deserved 8/10. -2 pts because of repetitive elements and overburdened menu content/lore delivery method.

Rogue Legacy is a game that has more content and replayablity than most big budget AAA titles on the market right now. Rogue Legacy is about your decendents as you search Castle Hamson for treasure and other reasons.

People are too fast and can easily avoid your melee attacks in this game.  Now let's talk about mobility.  Walking to places in this game takes so ♥♥♥♥ing long. I love games that punish me for not playing perfectly. Things like Super Meat Boy, Spelunky, Super Hexagon, and Limbo are some of my favorites. And when I started Rogue Legacy, it felt like heading back down into the mines of Spelunky. But as I kept playing, that changed a bit. This game is hard on you, but it's not unforgiving because, even when you fail, you make progress.
I hesitate to call this a rogue-like because it moves almost all progression from the game to the meta-game; you don't power up at all (except for one or two rare exceptions) while you're playing, and when you do, it's permanent. Contrast that with Spelunky, FTL, Binding of Isaac, Desktop Dungeon, etc., where failure means a complete restart, and you get a much different experience - a nicer, kinder experience.
This rogueish-like (rogue-likeish? rogue-like-like?) gameplay is perfectly complimented by smooth platforming mechanics, very solid controls (though I would recommend a gamepad), a good variety of enemies, and a great soundtrack. Toss in the descendent and trait gimmicks and this you've got yourself a well-designed, highly replayable, very polished experience.

This is the game for people who like dying both in and out of game.
Right off the bat I have to say that this is my current favorite game. Yeah I've played others more, but have I talked about them to the extent that it nearly cost me one friend and the ones who are slightly more tolerant are still rolling their eyes? No. I am almost willing to bet that I have a bounty on my head. "Kill this person!" someone has said. "They won't stop talking about this game!"
To make things crazier, the thing I'm willing to risk my own life for also involves a cuss-ton of death. I've literally gotten an achievement for dying so much.  The fact that you will die is a given; the biggest draw of the game is in the very title. This is a story about your legacy. Your lineage. Yes, you have to start at the beginning of the game when you die (albeit with much more power and better items and stuff). But maybe this time your kid will have some cussing useful traits, like not having a pulse in their feet, or a really awesome memory. Of course, they could also have any number of vision problems (which will cuss with you like you won't believe), or maybe they'll be upside down for their entire life. With a good hero, you'll be rooting for them not to die. A bad one practically has you throwing them in front of the monsters.
While the "rogue-lite" setup is draw in and of itself, I found myself sticking around for the awful (and by awful I mean hilarious) humor. References abound. Naruto, Skyrim, an internet meme or two. References aren't your thing? The characters you'll come across are among the most sarcastic you'll meet in gaming. None are afraid to openly mock you for being very, very awful at Rogue Legacy. Even the training dummy joins in: "Dost thou even hoist?" he sneers. If sarcasm is also not your thing, it's easy to be delighted by the random things you'll find in your exploration of the dungeons in this game. Jukeboxes, random carnival games, and for those who just literally have no sense of humor, the pieces of a (mostly) serious journal that tell a grim tale when read together.
I recommend this to anyone with a lot of time to spare (you'll need it), a mountain of patience, and a love of platformers. A controller is optional (the keyboard controls work well, and some even say they work better, though I disagree). Thinking price-wise, I got this on sale, but would have paid the full price if I knew how much fun I was going to have playing it. The only complaint that I can even vaguely form is that there is no multiplayer/co-op. This is probably a good thing, because if there was I would likely force my friends to play it with me and then they'd hate me even more than they already do.
I'm not saying you should get this game, but you should definitely get this game.

Full review:
Ahh, Rogue Legacy. My favorite rogue-like game, although it also served as my introduction to the genre. Even after playing a lot of others from the genre now, I still look back on Rogue Legacy as my favorite out of the bunch.
The game is presented in a pixel fashion, making use of some nice looking sprites for the various people and enemies you will meet along your journey. This style fits well, especially for a game of this genre. Come to think of it, I don't think I've played a rogue-like that was not in this style, and I've played several of them over the past several months. Can't really complain either, there's nothing wrong with it and I'd actually prefer this style in a rogue-like game, although I may be a bit biased there (heh).
Rogue Legacy's niche is the rebirth mechanic. Upon dying as one character, you'll have the choice as to which of the three offspring of that character you'll play as next. The interesting thing about this mechanic however, is that each child has separate traits, disguised as real world disorders and conditions. These can either be in your favor or against it. ADHD, for example, works in your favor in that your character will move 30% faster than usual. My favorite defect is vertigo, which mirrors the screen vertically. Yes, everything, including menus. Vertigo is a pain to deal with as I cannot rotate my monitor upside down, forcing me to play upside-down.
Aside from that gimmick, the other half of the game is the immense class and upgrade system. You'll start off with no skills, playing as the default class, the knight. Upon death, the opportunity to choose offspring with a different class is presented. The basic classes to choose from contain classes such as: mage, knave, knight, barbarian, shinobi, miner, etc. Each class can be upgraded, getting a name change in the process. The shinobi, for example, changes into the hokage, my favorite class. Each class has its own advantages and disadvantages, keep that in mind.
The shinobi/hokage has the benefit of upgraded strength (175% to be exact), but at the cost of only having 60% HP, 40% MP, and not being able to take advantage of critical hits. I never really used the game's spells, so the MP cut didn't have much of an effect on me, but the HP and critical hits were quite the drawback. Even so, whenever I was given the opportunity to play as a hokage, I always took it. You can't beat 175% damage. I found it crucial to defeating some of the game's bosses. I actually defeated the forest boss (the second one I took on) without getting hit as a hokage, quite the achievement.
On top of the classes, there's also a plethora of upgrades to choose from each time you die. The upgrades are laid out in a branching format, with certain upgrades unlocking others. The first one made available is Smithy, the blacksmith. Once purchased, you'll be able to purchase both armor and weapons from him. There's also an architect (who can keep the last layout of the castle if you choose to not want the game to randomly generate another castle again) and an enchantress, who sells runes, which can be equipped to provide various abilities (like the ability to jump while in air).
The other upgrades consist of class upgrades (like barbarian -> barbarian king) and stat upgrades. This consists of mana, health, and equip upgrades. Equip upgrades allow you to carry more weight and is required if you ever want to wear good armor. There's plenty of other upgrades to base skills (attack up, magic damage up, armor up, etc.) and a few unique ones, like "death defy" and "haggle". Death defy, as you can probably tell, allows you to defy death (1.5% everytime the upgrade is purchased). Haggle, on the other hand, lowers Charon's toll when entering the castle.
The game's map is divided into five zones: the front "safe" area at the entrance to the castle, the castle, the maya (above the castle), the dungeon (below the castle), and the forest (to the right of the castle). Each area (aside from the safe area) has its own boss that needs to be defeated if you want to unlock the golden door at the entrance of the castle. These bosses are very difficult if you're not properly equipped (I did tell you about my love for the hokage class, right?). Each time you die and want to re-enter the castle, you'll have to give up all of your funds earned during the previous run to Charon, who guards the entrance to the castle.
Rogue Legacy is a fantastic game overall. The sense of progression is really profound and it just feels really, really satisfying to defeat the bosses and open that golden door. Now that it's only $15, why not give it a shot?

*Now Spoiler Free!*
Life Is Strange:Before The Storm is a choice-based story game about a teenager who is an "outsider". Someone with not many friends, and a troubled past causing grief and torment in her everyday life.
This is the story of Chloe Price and how she met the one person that changed her life.
*Important notes
-It has Denuvo for DRM
-It is NOT made by Dontnod (makers of Life Is Strange), it is made by DeckNine (Formerly Known As Idolminds)
Everything outside of the demo footage is not as cringy or out-of-character as what had been shown. Granted, there are totally a few things to make me question inconsistencies.. Overall, most of what I had played was alright. I never had any performance issues except for achievements not working.
The story is *alright* I guess. There's a lot of concern with the demystification of a certain character that was key to the first game - but it's still an interesting story nonetheless. There's drama, a bit of action, romance (that I feel is forced), and quite a few mysteries and hidden meanings. Half the fun of games like this is speculation between and after episodes, and there's quite a few loose ends to make you wonder what it is that will happen with your choices.
In terms of choices and action/consequence, there are a lot of things you can choose from but you won't *really* see the effects until the next episode that you play. There's a few cases where it effects you in the same episode, but for the most part it isn't seen right away. The game offers you quite a few ways to play though.
-The demo parts are sometimes hard to get through. There's dialogue that just seems either out-of-character (admittedly, only for brief moments) and Chloe seems super b*tchy compared to the first game. She wasn't perfect in the first game, but it's hard to sit through at times. A perfect example is the demo-footage of her and David. I won't spoil it, but we get it. We know how she feels for him. Does this really need to be said with every line? Does this *really* need to be brought up all the time? At least in the first game it wasn't this annoying - and I'm saying this as someone that has been in Chloe's position and acted like her at times.
-Various other characters seem to both be written differently and the voice acting being completely redone is sometimes not that great. I get that this takes place when everyone is younger, but there are two very specific "vortex club" members that I find very hard to imagine them acting this way.
-On top of odd characters, there are some scenes that are pretty stupid and overdone to try and seem cool. I feel like they're trying to live up to the first game and are constantly overdoing themselves. It isn't a huge problem, but it's certainly noticeable at times.
-Some of the animations are awkward and kinda weird at times. Some of the facial animations are a little odd as well.
-For being this demanding in PC specs, the game looks way worse (in my opinion) than it did in Life Is Strange (the original). They only really put a lot of detail into the main characters. I find it funny how a game this demanding is nowhere near the art style or graphically better. Maybe that's just me not wrapping my head around the requirements jump (probably just the engine switch), but it's still kinda funny to me.
-The ending is very over dramatic, and people are totally not reacting the way people would normally. One of the key characters are actually the most over dramatic and really... "questionable" in this scene. There's  few things that I feel are overdone in the episode, but this is by far the most annoying for me on  personal level.
-Achievements did not work until the 4th re-installation of the game.
I'm mad that they can't get the old voice actors as I feel there was not much emotion behind these characters when it came to speaking sometimes. That's a pretty big deal and a noticable change for anyone that has played the original "Life Is Strange".
This genuinely does feel like a fan-fic that Square Enix said they "needed".  I know that a head at Dontnod had mentioned in an interview that they felt they didn't want to touch Max or Chloe again because they felt the story was perfect where it was.
To add on to that, knowing Rachel Amber and seeing her/what she does with Chloe kind of ruins the mystery of "Rachel Amber" which was one of the major elements to the first game.
I *guess* it's a decent game if you can look past some of this, but I'm hoping the other episodes are better.
This episode wasn't bad, the characters are heavily relatable if you've been in some of their shoes, but I'm nowhere near impacted as I was with the original game. I wish I could treat this game as a solo experience, but it's not possible.
It is moving at times, and it can be emotional... but there's times where it just looks like you're watching a cheesy TV drama. It just feels like a video game adaptation of a fan-fiction story that tries to follow a pre-made world/story. Sometimes, it doesn't work and feels forced on you.
*Released as of 10/19/2017!*
Let me start by saying that "Brave New World" is much better episode in my opinion. It's still pretty slow, and not much *action* happens. Most of what happens here is just character development. In the first episode, we met everyone and got to know the state of "past-arcadia bay". With this new episode, it kind of goes into exploring what we learn in the first episode in order to give us some insight as to why things appear the way they were and are in the first Life Is Strange. For the most part, it is pretty interesting. You actually get a fair bit of answers to everything in Episode 1, but there isn't much that left me questioning anything in this episode. The only things I'm really wondering about are things you learn at the very end of the episode, which isn't much.
Now,
...
There's still some issues with animations seeming very dramatic but the voice not matching the dramatization of the animations. There's also a bit of a problem for me with how a few people talk, and a few minor details that ultimately aren't game-ruining unless you're looking for them.
In the end, I'm pretty pleased with this episode. I feel like it was a step up from the last and I'm extremely happy that the decisions seem more "realistic" so to speak. They seem reasonable and are choices that I actually feel work and make me care about what I'm doing. This is a great improvement, at least in my opinion.
Hell Is Empty is a pretty... interesting episode.
This episode causes some lore problems, at least from my perspective. There's a lot that happens which should be mentioned in LiS 1, but of course that can't happen since that game is already made and we are all here.
Anyways, for what it's worth, the game DOES move in some very interesting directions in terms of what we're used to in the LiS world. Things are more violent, but sometimes a bit cheesy and unrealistic feeling. The ending is a little "meh", but that's most likely just the way I played out certain situations. Overall, it had some pretty great moments.

Undertale released September 15th, 2015 to PC. It was funded by a successful Kickstarter and took almost 3 years to develop. The game is written, designed, and composed by Toby Fox. As such, Undertale is an indie game.
Story:
The story follows a child who falls through a crevasse into the underground world of monsters. Monsters and humans fought long ago, the humans emerged as the victors and banished the monsters underground, sealing them beneath with a magic spell. You control the child as you attempt to find your way to the surface.
Along the way to the surface, you meet many monsters, some just for battles and some for the story. However, these aren't just typical video game monsters. All of the monsters you meet have personality and can respond to the player either in or out of battle. Due to this, the player isn't lonely and has plenty of conversations with monsters during the journey to the surface.
Gameplay:
Undertale takes a unique look on battles. It looks like a typical older RPG. Battles are turn-based and you select your options from a menu while you face a pixel monster. If you attack a monster, you time your attacks to maximize damage, such as you would in Super Mario RPG or the Mario and Luigi series. When a monster attacks, the player is put in a brief top-down shooter style mini-game, similar to Raiden or Galaga. Getting hit damages your HP. Killing a monster gets you XP and gold.
However, you never really have to kill monsters in Undertale. Each monster has personality and can speak, as stated earlier. You are often able to speak or perform some sort of action to the monsters that you are in combat with. If you manage to strike up a conversation or placate your opponent, you are given the option to spare the monster instead of killing it. Sparing a monster nets you gold, but no XP.
Why then, would you want to spare monsters? The short answer is that Undertale's story and characters are very reactive to what the player does. In fact, one of the main draws to this game is that the developer seems to have thought of everything. Dialogue will change based on many different factors and multiple endings are possible. It is entirely possible and in fact very likely that even after having played through the game 3 times that you could watch someone else follow the same path as you, yet receive different dialogue.
Undertale takes things a step further, however, by even offering different dialogue after the completion of the game. This game is around 6 hours long, but due to multiple endings and altered dialogue, it should be played at least twice to explore at least half of what Undertale has to offer.
The largest strength this game has is the ability to portray its characters as if they are real. It also truly attempts to dissolve the disconnect between player and character. Meaning, in any other game, you would treat your character as a separate entity. For instance, in any open world RPG, you'd do as you please because no consequence could ever come to the person holding the controller, however, Undertale has a unique way of directing the dialogue directly towards you, rather than your character. Undertale acts like it is a living entity.
In terms of exploration, Undertale is mostly linear. The main path will only very temporarily split for items typically. There are plenty of secrets to be found though, most of which is dialogue, NPCs, or rooms rather than items.
Graphics:
The art style heavily resembles Earthbound when outside of battle. In battle, the character sprites and attacks are mostly black and white. Character sprites are made of pixels and aren't particularly high quality. Monsters can be quite expressionate despite the pixel medium, often having many different facial expressions or even having their models shift around a bit in combat.
The art is very clean and unintrusive. You don't ever really mistake something for something else. There is good use of colors and contrast. Text is always readable, characters are distinct, and it's clear where you can and cannot go. While not being a graphically intensive game, the graphics are perfectly fine.
Sound/FX
Music is also quite fluid and expressionate much like the graphics. A lot of the music seems to reference other songs within the game. Even within the very first encounter in the game, the music does some pitch shifting to represent the tone or mood of the situation at hand. Many character have specific theme songs, which is a great thing that most games seem to lack. In addition to the fantastic theming the music adds, much of it is very memorable and fun. Much of the music seems to be inspired by the chiptune genre, though the music mostly just goes its own way.
Final Thoughts:
As a whole, Undertale isn't very difficult, but it is extremely interactive in the way you fight and dodge attacks as well as being extremely reactive to the decisions you make. The music is very expressionate and memorable. The characters have a lot of personality and are very fun to interact with. And while the game is short, it does have a fair amount of replay value.
If anything, I think Undertale could have been more challenging with its puzzles and battles, but it's not so easy as to detract from the experience. This game plays upon the player's notions of how RPGs work, and as such, I'd recommend this game to anyone who is familiar with RPGs or anyone who likes retro-styled games.

Full review:
Ahh, Rogue Legacy. My favorite rogue-like game, although it also served as my introduction to the genre. Even after playing a lot of others from the genre now, I still look back on Rogue Legacy as my favorite out of the bunch.
The game is presented in a pixel fashion, making use of some nice looking sprites for the various people and enemies you will meet along your journey. This style fits well, especially for a game of this genre. Come to think of it, I don't think I've played a rogue-like that was not in this style, and I've played several of them over the past several months. Can't really complain either, there's nothing wrong with it and I'd actually prefer this style in a rogue-like game, although I may be a bit biased there (heh).
Rogue Legacy's niche is the rebirth mechanic. Upon dying as one character, you'll have the choice as to which of the three offspring of that character you'll play as next. The interesting thing about this mechanic however, is that each child has separate traits, disguised as real world disorders and conditions. These can either be in your favor or against it. ADHD, for example, works in your favor in that your character will move 30% faster than usual. My favorite defect is vertigo, which mirrors the screen vertically. Yes, everything, including menus. Vertigo is a pain to deal with as I cannot rotate my monitor upside down, forcing me to play upside-down.
Aside from that gimmick, the other half of the game is the immense class and upgrade system. You'll start off with no skills, playing as the default class, the knight. Upon death, the opportunity to choose offspring with a different class is presented. The basic classes to choose from contain classes such as: mage, knave, knight, barbarian, shinobi, miner, etc. Each class can be upgraded, getting a name change in the process. The shinobi, for example, changes into the hokage, my favorite class. Each class has its own advantages and disadvantages, keep that in mind.
The shinobi/hokage has the benefit of upgraded strength (175% to be exact), but at the cost of only having 60% HP, 40% MP, and not being able to take advantage of critical hits. I never really used the game's spells, so the MP cut didn't have much of an effect on me, but the HP and critical hits were quite the drawback. Even so, whenever I was given the opportunity to play as a hokage, I always took it. You can't beat 175% damage. I found it crucial to defeating some of the game's bosses. I actually defeated the forest boss (the second one I took on) without getting hit as a hokage, quite the achievement.
On top of the classes, there's also a plethora of upgrades to choose from each time you die. The upgrades are laid out in a branching format, with certain upgrades unlocking others. The first one made available is Smithy, the blacksmith. Once purchased, you'll be able to purchase both armor and weapons from him. There's also an architect (who can keep the last layout of the castle if you choose to not want the game to randomly generate another castle again) and an enchantress, who sells runes, which can be equipped to provide various abilities (like the ability to jump while in air).
The other upgrades consist of class upgrades (like barbarian -> barbarian king) and stat upgrades. This consists of mana, health, and equip upgrades. Equip upgrades allow you to carry more weight and is required if you ever want to wear good armor. There's plenty of other upgrades to base skills (attack up, magic damage up, armor up, etc.) and a few unique ones, like "death defy" and "haggle". Death defy, as you can probably tell, allows you to defy death (1.5% everytime the upgrade is purchased). Haggle, on the other hand, lowers Charon's toll when entering the castle.
The game's map is divided into five zones: the front "safe" area at the entrance to the castle, the castle, the maya (above the castle), the dungeon (below the castle), and the forest (to the right of the castle). Each area (aside from the safe area) has its own boss that needs to be defeated if you want to unlock the golden door at the entrance of the castle. These bosses are very difficult if you're not properly equipped (I did tell you about my love for the hokage class, right?). Each time you die and want to re-enter the castle, you'll have to give up all of your funds earned during the previous run to Charon, who guards the entrance to the castle.
Rogue Legacy is a fantastic game overall. The sense of progression is really profound and it just feels really, really satisfying to defeat the bosses and open that golden door. Now that it's only $15, why not give it a shot?

A great RPG platformer, a lot of the fun comes from continually building up your abilities and such and the rest of it comes in typical platforming fighting stuff. There's lots more to explain about the game, but theres not much point in me doing it as you can probably find a video about it online or find other reviews. The main thigns I'm going to talk about is the use of the word roguelike or rogue-lite. Many people will insist that a game isn't a roguelike unless it's turn based, tile based systems or has a few other feature and I may be inclined to agree with them, but thats not what I want to talk about. What I want to talk about is even calling this game a rogue-lite, a rogue-lite or like implies that when die you'll be losing all your character and your progress, but in Rogue Legacy you don't lose your "character" whatsoever. Sure your name changes and you get a new set of advantages and disadvantages along with a new class but you essentially keep all your stats equipment and abilities with a few minor tweaks so your "character" just keeps progressing like in any standard RPG which isn't a bad thing by any strech of the imagination, just different. You can even choose to not lose any progress in the dungeon you've made by payign a bit of money and no matter what your progress with boss fights is never lost, which again is not exactly a bad thing. The only thing left that you could argue makes it a roguelike is the randomly generated characters and dungeon, but randomly generation doesn't really make something a roguelike.

With illusive revere, i'm going to illustrate my thoughts of Life is Strange: Before the Storm which is created by Deck Nine. First of all i would like to thank to all Deck Nine members for this astonishing creation. Most of the fans were worried about it. But i guess they're gonna be grateful to them. Though this is an intensive and mind captivating creation. Now let me share my thoughts on few aspects like Story, Gameplay, Visuals, Impressions and Performance.
Story, the most momentous feature of any Life is Strange titles and so for this one. Before the Storm tells you the eariler story of the most beloved person, Chloe Price. Like what happened before Chloe reunited with Max in season 1. So i could say, this is how a prequal story should be created. Actually you'll know more about Rachel Amber alongside Chloe Price. Like how they met and became so close which binded their bonds intensively. Also you're gonna love Chloe more than ever after knowing her previous story. You kinda know what happens to their relationship if you're experienced with season one. But still you'll be more augmented to know more of her previous story than present. The story illustrated actual emotions of Chloe and Rachel. Also core of their beautiful and passionate love story. Although i loved it more when moments turned into more romantic. So this is what makes it something more than just a word called perfect.
Gameplay isn't really matters in these titles. Because these are story based titles. So i would like you to avoid extreme gameplay experience. All you have to do is walk to your destination then point and click to interact which is really simplistic. So that's all i got to say about it
Visuals are not improved that much but might look better than before for you. Though i guess season one has prettier arts and visuals. But still you're gonna love it. Also facial expressions are insanely improved than before which makes most of the persons look more decent.
The story is entirely about the most beloved and beautiful person, Chloe Price. As you know her from season 1 but you'll know more of her emotions and lovely sides in this story. We'll get to know how much adorable and genuine she is. Like her true love and emotions for Rachel and all her sufferings growing time by time. Her smile and smurk are so beautiful which she inflicts genuinely. Even she gets nervous and awkward infront of Rachel which makes her more adorable. Still no matter what but Chloe is so beloved and precious for me.
I'm getting totally smooth performance on Intel Core i7 7700K, R9 390 STRIX and 6GB Ram with highest presets. But i found some bugs and blurry motions while cutscenes. Thought i haven't found any errors, crashes, glitches nor stuttering yet. So you'll be able to run it even on subordinate configurations.
As always, Life is Strange has the most iconic OST for each episodes. They used different background scores in every situations and episodes till now. Though i loved all of their soundtracks like before. But there are some dedicated songs which are insanely matched with their given moments. So i got nothing to whine out.
So peeps, without any concerns you should try it right now. Also i personally guarantee you that you won't be disappointed with it. So this is definitely recommended to all lovers and new comers.

simply put, this is what id-softs RAGE obviously should have been. or at least what i have wanted from it back then.
a mix of shadow of mordor and RAGE might describe mad max pretty well, i guess.
you get a rather huge open (desert) world that you can freely explore with your car (that you will constantly upgrade and improve) while you can get out of said car at basically any given moment to wander about and search areas that you could either not get to with your car or fight things you don't wanna run over.
the driving is fun, arcady and even works surprisingly well with mouse and keyboard. you will have to fight off other vehicles on the road by either ramming the crap out of them, shooting the drivers or specific car-parts or -even more fun- using your harpoon to rip parts OFF or the driver OUT of the vehicle. i doubt it will ever grow old dragging an opponent behind your car and then catapulting him into the next obstacle.
most of the fighting is focussed on melee (mainly because ammo is rather scarce) and is very arkham city like: press the attack and block button at the correct time to not be screwed over. not the most sophisticated way of doing things, but entertaining and presented in a satisfying way.
the visuals and the sound are above par and both pretty fitting. it's not an easy feat to present a desert that's not boring but actually pretty nice to look at.
in short: it is basically what every open world game is, but put together in a solid and fun way.
mad max offers nothing really new but does it have to? it's simple and plain arcade open world-fun and if that's what you want: you won't be disappointed.
if you want innovation or a thick and intricate plot: wrong game. or rather: wrong franchise :-)
the only thing that bothered me in the first hour or so was the sheer amount of things and info coming at you. but once you finish off the tutorial part of the game and can do whatever the heck you want, that's when mad max really shows off the entertaining value it offers.

The game is great if you're into high octane action. It carries the series quite well and does a great job of playing to its strengths. I feel it best to list the pros and cons of the game.
- Great graphics, beautiful landscapes even though it's such a dry place.
- Interesting characters. Max inherently hasn't much personality but most if not all of his allies make up for that.
- Hard hitting action. On foot each punch feels strong and there is a sense of desperation in Max as he takes on multiple enemies at once.
- The car is the real highlight. Driving feels great, each vehicle handles as it should. Heavy vehicles feel heavy. Great in car action and the explosions look amazing.
- Tons to do.
- Too much OCD scrap collecting. Collecting may be fun to some but I'm not a fan of it.
- Being on foot can get boring if you're having trouble finding the last piece of scrap in a camp.
- Missions can be a little misleading at times. I don't like having my hand held in games, but this one leaves you hanging a few times.
- You'll never find anything special in a camp. It's always the same, either scrap, relics, insignia, or ammo.
In light of its cons, the game is worth a try. It's not for everyone but I really like its style and gameplay. Pick it up at discount if you're not happy with the price. It's a bit of a gem that shouldn't be overlooked.

*Now Spoiler Free!*
Life Is Strange:Before The Storm is a choice-based story game about a teenager who is an "outsider". Someone with not many friends, and a troubled past causing grief and torment in her everyday life.
This is the story of Chloe Price and how she met the one person that changed her life.
*Important notes
-It has Denuvo for DRM
-It is NOT made by Dontnod (makers of Life Is Strange), it is made by DeckNine (Formerly Known As Idolminds)
Everything outside of the demo footage is not as cringy or out-of-character as what had been shown. Granted, there are totally a few things to make me question inconsistencies.. Overall, most of what I had played was alright. I never had any performance issues except for achievements not working.
The story is *alright* I guess. There's a lot of concern with the demystification of a certain character that was key to the first game - but it's still an interesting story nonetheless. There's drama, a bit of action, romance (that I feel is forced), and quite a few mysteries and hidden meanings. Half the fun of games like this is speculation between and after episodes, and there's quite a few loose ends to make you wonder what it is that will happen with your choices.
In terms of choices and action/consequence, there are a lot of things you can choose from but you won't *really* see the effects until the next episode that you play. There's a few cases where it effects you in the same episode, but for the most part it isn't seen right away. The game offers you quite a few ways to play though.
-The demo parts are sometimes hard to get through. There's dialogue that just seems either out-of-character (admittedly, only for brief moments) and Chloe seems super b*tchy compared to the first game. She wasn't perfect in the first game, but it's hard to sit through at times. A perfect example is the demo-footage of her and David. I won't spoil it, but we get it. We know how she feels for him. Does this really need to be said with every line? Does this *really* need to be brought up all the time? At least in the first game it wasn't this annoying - and I'm saying this as someone that has been in Chloe's position and acted like her at times.
-Various other characters seem to both be written differently and the voice acting being completely redone is sometimes not that great. I get that this takes place when everyone is younger, but there are two very specific "vortex club" members that I find very hard to imagine them acting this way.
-On top of odd characters, there are some scenes that are pretty stupid and overdone to try and seem cool. I feel like they're trying to live up to the first game and are constantly overdoing themselves. It isn't a huge problem, but it's certainly noticeable at times.
-Some of the animations are awkward and kinda weird at times. Some of the facial animations are a little odd as well.
-For being this demanding in PC specs, the game looks way worse (in my opinion) than it did in Life Is Strange (the original). They only really put a lot of detail into the main characters. I find it funny how a game this demanding is nowhere near the art style or graphically better. Maybe that's just me not wrapping my head around the requirements jump (probably just the engine switch), but it's still kinda funny to me.
-The ending is very over dramatic, and people are totally not reacting the way people would normally. One of the key characters are actually the most over dramatic and really... "questionable" in this scene. There's  few things that I feel are overdone in the episode, but this is by far the most annoying for me on  personal level.
-Achievements did not work until the 4th re-installation of the game.
I'm mad that they can't get the old voice actors as I feel there was not much emotion behind these characters when it came to speaking sometimes. That's a pretty big deal and a noticable change for anyone that has played the original "Life Is Strange".
This genuinely does feel like a fan-fic that Square Enix said they "needed".  I know that a head at Dontnod had mentioned in an interview that they felt they didn't want to touch Max or Chloe again because they felt the story was perfect where it was.
To add on to that, knowing Rachel Amber and seeing her/what she does with Chloe kind of ruins the mystery of "Rachel Amber" which was one of the major elements to the first game.
I *guess* it's a decent game if you can look past some of this, but I'm hoping the other episodes are better.
This episode wasn't bad, the characters are heavily relatable if you've been in some of their shoes, but I'm nowhere near impacted as I was with the original game. I wish I could treat this game as a solo experience, but it's not possible.
It is moving at times, and it can be emotional... but there's times where it just looks like you're watching a cheesy TV drama. It just feels like a video game adaptation of a fan-fiction story that tries to follow a pre-made world/story. Sometimes, it doesn't work and feels forced on you.
*Released as of 10/19/2017!*
Let me start by saying that "Brave New World" is much better episode in my opinion. It's still pretty slow, and not much *action* happens. Most of what happens here is just character development. In the first episode, we met everyone and got to know the state of "past-arcadia bay". With this new episode, it kind of goes into exploring what we learn in the first episode in order to give us some insight as to why things appear the way they were and are in the first Life Is Strange. For the most part, it is pretty interesting. You actually get a fair bit of answers to everything in Episode 1, but there isn't much that left me questioning anything in this episode. The only things I'm really wondering about are things you learn at the very end of the episode, which isn't much.
Now,
...
There's still some issues with animations seeming very dramatic but the voice not matching the dramatization of the animations. There's also a bit of a problem for me with how a few people talk, and a few minor details that ultimately aren't game-ruining unless you're looking for them.
In the end, I'm pretty pleased with this episode. I feel like it was a step up from the last and I'm extremely happy that the decisions seem more "realistic" so to speak. They seem reasonable and are choices that I actually feel work and make me care about what I'm doing. This is a great improvement, at least in my opinion.
Hell Is Empty is a pretty... interesting episode.
This episode causes some lore problems, at least from my perspective. There's a lot that happens which should be mentioned in LiS 1, but of course that can't happen since that game is already made and we are all here.
Anyways, for what it's worth, the game DOES move in some very interesting directions in terms of what we're used to in the LiS world. Things are more violent, but sometimes a bit cheesy and unrealistic feeling. The ending is a little "meh", but that's most likely just the way I played out certain situations. Overall, it had some pretty great moments.

Let's be clear: Rogue Legacy is not a good game. It is designed from the ground up to waste the player's time in order to create an artificial impression of progress.
In every other roguelike I've played, upgrades and the tasks necessary to unlock them have been an important and even integral part of gameplay. They make the game more fun and provide variety, however I have never considered them *necessary*. To take the most popular game in the genre as an example: a supremely skilled gamer could theoretically beat the considerably challenging Binding of Isaac on their first playthrough. Nobody is going to finish Rogue Legacy on their first playthrough. You start out abysmally weak in every conceivable way from hit points, to damage dealt, to abilities (you can't even double jump), to speed, to mana - absolutely every facet of your existence is defined by its lack of development. And so you must play the game over and over and over and over to earn the requisite coins to purchase persistent upgrades which will facilitate success in playthroughs to come. And there are *a lot* of upgrades, to the point that I questioned whether I was actually getting better at the game or if the game just made itself easier and easier the more I played it, which is the exact opposite of every other roguelike's MO.
Beyond this upgrade system, which demonstrates utter contempt for the player, the game itself is quite clunky. Projectiles which shouldn't penetrate walls will occasionally penetrate walls, room transitions are done in such a way that it is possible to get yourself stuck in a long loop of quick top to bottom movements before awkwardly extricating yourself, and platforming itself consistently demands precise downward slashes simply to make the actual platforms appear which quickly becomes tedious.
I played Rogue Legacy until the point where I unlocked the ability to purchase multiple upgrades which served the exclusive purpose of making it easier to purchase future upgrades. At that point it became apparent that the game was an ouroboros which demanded nothing more than persistence in the absence of skill to see it devour its own tail, rendering the player's input purely incidental.
If you value your time, play something else.

Undertale is and outstanding game! My new favorite game xD

Undertale released September 15th, 2015 to PC. It was funded by a successful Kickstarter and took almost 3 years to develop. The game is written, designed, and composed by Toby Fox. As such, Undertale is an indie game.
Story:
The story follows a child who falls through a crevasse into the underground world of monsters. Monsters and humans fought long ago, the humans emerged as the victors and banished the monsters underground, sealing them beneath with a magic spell. You control the child as you attempt to find your way to the surface.
Along the way to the surface, you meet many monsters, some just for battles and some for the story. However, these aren't just typical video game monsters. All of the monsters you meet have personality and can respond to the player either in or out of battle. Due to this, the player isn't lonely and has plenty of conversations with monsters during the journey to the surface.
Gameplay:
Undertale takes a unique look on battles. It looks like a typical older RPG. Battles are turn-based and you select your options from a menu while you face a pixel monster. If you attack a monster, you time your attacks to maximize damage, such as you would in Super Mario RPG or the Mario and Luigi series. When a monster attacks, the player is put in a brief top-down shooter style mini-game, similar to Raiden or Galaga. Getting hit damages your HP. Killing a monster gets you XP and gold.
However, you never really have to kill monsters in Undertale. Each monster has personality and can speak, as stated earlier. You are often able to speak or perform some sort of action to the monsters that you are in combat with. If you manage to strike up a conversation or placate your opponent, you are given the option to spare the monster instead of killing it. Sparing a monster nets you gold, but no XP.
Why then, would you want to spare monsters? The short answer is that Undertale's story and characters are very reactive to what the player does. In fact, one of the main draws to this game is that the developer seems to have thought of everything. Dialogue will change based on many different factors and multiple endings are possible. It is entirely possible and in fact very likely that even after having played through the game 3 times that you could watch someone else follow the same path as you, yet receive different dialogue.
Undertale takes things a step further, however, by even offering different dialogue after the completion of the game. This game is around 6 hours long, but due to multiple endings and altered dialogue, it should be played at least twice to explore at least half of what Undertale has to offer.
The largest strength this game has is the ability to portray its characters as if they are real. It also truly attempts to dissolve the disconnect between player and character. Meaning, in any other game, you would treat your character as a separate entity. For instance, in any open world RPG, you'd do as you please because no consequence could ever come to the person holding the controller, however, Undertale has a unique way of directing the dialogue directly towards you, rather than your character. Undertale acts like it is a living entity.
In terms of exploration, Undertale is mostly linear. The main path will only very temporarily split for items typically. There are plenty of secrets to be found though, most of which is dialogue, NPCs, or rooms rather than items.
Graphics:
The art style heavily resembles Earthbound when outside of battle. In battle, the character sprites and attacks are mostly black and white. Character sprites are made of pixels and aren't particularly high quality. Monsters can be quite expressionate despite the pixel medium, often having many different facial expressions or even having their models shift around a bit in combat.
The art is very clean and unintrusive. You don't ever really mistake something for something else. There is good use of colors and contrast. Text is always readable, characters are distinct, and it's clear where you can and cannot go. While not being a graphically intensive game, the graphics are perfectly fine.
Sound/FX
Music is also quite fluid and expressionate much like the graphics. A lot of the music seems to reference other songs within the game. Even within the very first encounter in the game, the music does some pitch shifting to represent the tone or mood of the situation at hand. Many character have specific theme songs, which is a great thing that most games seem to lack. In addition to the fantastic theming the music adds, much of it is very memorable and fun. Much of the music seems to be inspired by the chiptune genre, though the music mostly just goes its own way.
Final Thoughts:
As a whole, Undertale isn't very difficult, but it is extremely interactive in the way you fight and dodge attacks as well as being extremely reactive to the decisions you make. The music is very expressionate and memorable. The characters have a lot of personality and are very fun to interact with. And while the game is short, it does have a fair amount of replay value.
If anything, I think Undertale could have been more challenging with its puzzles and battles, but it's not so easy as to detract from the experience. This game plays upon the player's notions of how RPGs work, and as such, I'd recommend this game to anyone who is familiar with RPGs or anyone who likes retro-styled games.

首先，撇开服务器架设不谈，服务器刷新的速度能再慢一点嘛？整个偌大的服务器，能刷新到的物资有多少？你一个小瘪三，上来什么都没有，不被僵尸撸死不讲，光是肚子饿、口渴都可以让你轻易死掉。

I've never written a review before. I feel that this game deserves it.
I can't think of a time where a game has captured a character in such a way that I fall in love with them. That was until Rachel Amber appeared on the scene.
She is complex, intelligent, aggressive, beautiful and most of all she has taken an interest in Chloe Price; the fatherless and depressed girl we know from the original LiS Episodes.
Rachel is portrayed in such a way that you are allowed to build the character for yourself, much like you can with every character in the game. You are never forced to feel or judge a person in a specific way, it is all for you to work out. I like that freedom and it is rare to find a game that allows the player to interact with their characters in such an intimate way.
The story pacing is good and you will not find a moment where you feel bored. The game continually finds new things for you to do and people to interact to. There are certain cliffhanger moments and shocking discoveries that you will find are quite heart-wrenching and sometimes will capture emotions you might have thought impossible in a video game.
The sound design and graphics are as unique and catered to the series as they were in the original LiS. But the move to Unity has allowed the game to be pushed even further in terms of scope and graphical fidelity. The textures are of course muddy at times but it has its gorgeous moments too, especially in scenes where there are alot of Godrays in the shot. This game is not meant to win any graphical awards, but the music choices in the game are as good as the first, if not better. There are alot of acoustic pieces and some rock songs, most of which are curated by Daughter (check them out they are pretty good!). Chloes new voice actor was chosen and specifically trained by Ashley Burch so don't be surprised to hear that she sounds absolutely fine. Chloe sounds exactly as she should and the emotion portrayed is fantastic and definitely on par with Ashleys performance in the first game.
Characters return and they are all as you would expect them to appear; albeit slightly younger in appearance and I look forward to seeing how they are shown in the next episode.
In short, if you enjoyed the first game or have even the slightest bit of interest in a storytelling masterpiece that will keep you entertained and potentially play with your emotions somewhat, buy this game. You will NOT regret your purchase.

I don't normally write many Steam reviews but given the veritably avalanche of rave reviews for a game that I consider very mediocre, I feel obliged to offer a dissenting opinion.
Bluntly put: I have no idea why everybody thinks this is such a great game. Sure, it runs smoothly and it looks nice but those are about the only above average aspects of an otherwise fairly forgettable and annoying experience.
And yes, I know I write this after only a couple of hours of game time. Maybe it somehow gets better after a while but that is still no excuse for such a lame start
Mad Max is first of all enormously unpolished. The key bindings and the menu structure are a mess...in every meny every key does something different (if it works at all), actions are mapped to the most stupid keys imaginable, and for some reason you have to hold rather than press just about every key. Because of ..reasons.
Next, too many of the activites you perform feel like busywork for the sake of it...things like activating balloons, tearing down scarecrows, killing snipers (I dare you to miss, and they don't shoot back 99% of the time), blowing up stuff etc all force you to repeat the same unchallenging, unnecessary and unfun actions time after time again, often accompanied by lengthy unskippable cut-scenes that add absolutely zero. All kinds of stuff that would be automated in better games you either have to do by hand, or can only be unlocked after even more busywork.
This might still be acceptable if the core gameplay (vehicle based combat and on foot exploration/fighting) were any better, but alas. The on foot stuff is at best OK and usually quite tedious (lots of just walking around searching for meaningless stuff to collect) and the fighting is rip-off from Batman, only with a poor camera, zero fluidity and almost no challenge. It can in most cases be cheated by simply mashing the attack button.
I am not too far into the car combat yet, but I am still hoping for somebody to explain to me how it is fun to run endless circles around other vehicles in the hopes of ramming them to pieces at some point (which is once again not much fun given that the car controls like a wet towel and spins wildly out of control after hitting just about anything) or using the ultra-cheap trick of simply harpooing the driver, followed by the boring process of ramming a stationary car to pieces)
For just about everything, I'd say just stick to the Borderlands series. I know that's technically not an open world but at least it provides a much more fun Wasteland experience, has actual characters and story, better car combat and vehicle handling (though the vehicles are one of the poorer parts of Borderlands), and doesn't actively try to waste your time with filler. As for open worlds, even Ubisoft doesn't normally waste your time this badly.

Mad Max The game follows loosely story of the new Mad Max Movie.
Gameplay 8 of 10
You play Max Rockatansky in a dystopian world full of not quite normal people. Collect metal scrap (the new currency) to update your car, a hideout or climb the skill tree that is available for Max. Fight your way through hordes of enemies, either with your shotgun or barehanded. The combat system is a little like the one from the Batman Arkham series. So a little simple, but works quite good for me. And it feels somehow a lot more realistic than in Batman. Infiltrate hangouts, race wild sand races against some quite tough opponents, do little side-missions, collect relicts of the past...and so on.
Graphics     9 of 10
I LOVE it! From the sandy dunes with the beautiful sunsets to the starry bluish nights. Absolutely amazing. My friend is playing it on a 4K tv screen and it's just amazing .The footprints in the sand, the incredible storms, the water. BIG thumbs up. And I might say it’s graphical wise quite a competitor for Fallout 4.
Music          8.5 of 10
The music is generally quite soothing and somber. Very fitting for this post-apocalyptic world.
The part where it really shines is the sound of the car engines. You really feel the V8 engine roaring.
Final Verdict 8.5 of 10
A great game based on a movie. The graphics, the music and the gameplay form an overall nearly perfect game. Why nearly? Sometimes the fighting is a little repetitive and the taking of the hideout as well and the story is not that breathtaking. Still I strongly recommend it. Rarely has any games atmosphere sucked me in that much.

As corny as this sounds, if you loved the original Life is Strange for any reason you'll very likely find enjoyment here for the same. This is a prequel, which comes with the unfortunate "all roads lead to Rome" ending that prequels have to do to respect the originalm story, but this does serve to explore relationships between characters to boost the perception of who they are.
Now, the first question you'll probably ask as a newcomer is "should I play the prequel first or the original game?" Normally I would say the original game, but now the answer isn't so clear-cut since the three episodes for this game have released. It all comes to down to preference, really, but either way you're going to have a great time with this game. A few notes I took were:
- The mechanics are different, forcing you to be more careful with your dialog instead of rewinding in-game, but that adds a sense of importance to the scenes where you need to persuade people.
- The characters lack a lot of likability, however. Chloe, Rachel, Joyce, David, and a few other characters seem to be alright, but for the most part new characters ultimately do not matter. There's a few subplots that go pretty much nowhere, and you don't see 80% of these characters in the main game anyways. They might be likable when you play the game and you might care, but in the grand scheme of things these characters pretty much only exist because the story takes place three years before the original game.
Now, using ALL of the original characters might not be a great idea, and we have to remember that another company is doing development on this game, not Dontnod specifically. So maybe it's for the better. this is coming from someone who's played the original game multiple times through.
- Outfits are actually customizable. Yeah. Before in the first game, you only saw Max in maybe 5 or 6 outfits throughout the game that you couldn't change, because those were all situational. Or maybe she was wearing the same clothes for days straight. Here you can actually choose what Chloe wears, even going for her outfit from the first game if you pre-ordered. Not that these outfits necessarily matter for enjoyment, they don't impact anything, but it's a nice touch.
- The soundtrack is GREAT... but sometimes it isn't so great situationally. Life is Strange at this point picks some really good songs, and i have to admit I was in a bit of doubt when this game would be following more of a punk direction than an indie one, given how Chloe is that much different compared to Max. But I have to say I really liked the soundtrack. There's a "mixtape" option or something that I didn't purchase, that supposedly allows you to change the tracklists and customize which tracks play at which moments. Let me say that some of the default track listing in this game is a bit.. repetitive. The soundtrack is mostly done by a band named Daughter, and while they don't sound bad on their own, some of their songs are really overplayed, like "Burn it Down". The title theme is good and while you hear it often in this game, it's good enough that it doesn't annoy you when it does.
I'm just giving a brief rundown, since I'll be making a video review on this soon in greater detail which I will link here. Bottom line is, buy this game and get set for feels and consequential introspection.

Rogue Legacy is solid conceptually, but ultimately relies too heavily on the player's addiction to the genre to keep them hooked. While the randomized progeny do add some variety to the game, generally it is in the form of either amusement or frustration, rarely strategy. The metroidvania platforming style calls for skilled manuvering, but bizarre hitboxes and sluggish controls will interfere with your mastery more than the difficulty of the enemies themselves. Each area of the game feels the same as the last, sometimes even generating identical rooms with a different coat of paint. Even the enemy challenges presented in more advanced areas are merely faster, more projectile-y versions of their smaller-sprited counterparts. Rogue Legacy will certainly entertain for a short time, but eventually the monotony of raiding the castle and dumping your gold into various stat-sinks will start to feel like more of a chore than a diversion.
Rogue Legacy is perfect if your gaming appetite is sated by spending twenty minutes saving up enough gold to raise a single stat, then dying and playing the same areas over again with a slightly different character. In other words, this game is built for players who have the patience to endure the least pleasant aspects of the procedurally-generated platforming roguelike. For everyone else, I recommend you divert your attention elsewhere.
