I stood there on the thin pole, desperately trying to jump over the railing. After numerous attempt, I accepted the fate that there's no way to jump back where I came from, I glanced over at the lonely dangling platform beside me, almost too far to reach. I've made up my mind, I'll do it, I'll do the leap of faith, it's either I go back base a rich man, or I die in this radiated hollow dome, I held my breath, wanting to take a step back before launching myself forward onto the safe land, almost tripped over, I did a small step and jumped, all my might, I jumped, as far as I could, as hard as my thin legs could launch me. It was far from close, it was almost too far to even grab hold onto the platform, I fell, I fell and fell, the fall feels like an eternity, I close my eyes, bracing myself from what is coming, a cold, lonely death. Everything I did in my life as a naked flashed in front of my very eyes, I prayed to whoever's listening, how I wish god, our holy admin  is here to save me, but luck was sadly not on my side, I reached the bottom, the cracking of my bones crushed my dreams, my very dreams of becoming a rich man in this deserted island. I failed, I lied there, as blood rushed and blurred my vision, I let out an agony cry, no one was there to help, the bare metal feels colder than usual against my hazmat suit. I closed my eyes, as I was greeted by doom, "you've died from falling", I held my breath and looked up, I asked god why? Why me? Why today? I couldn't help it as tears rolled down my rosy cheeks, the salty defeat landed on my waterproof keyboard, "at least my keyboard ain't gonna let me down" I thought, I sighed and hit the respawn button. I was brought back to this cruel world, the familiar sight of the bed room I built, in the castle I built. A place where I call home. Funny how with all these dominations and big base, it feels empty today. Guess it's true, money can't buy you happiness. Cause when you die a lonely death falling off an abandoned dome, you'll realise, that you are just a speck of dust in this vast galaxy.
TLDR: I fell and died.

For a game I thought would be a 'so so' first entry for the Mad Max franchise.....  I'm really loving it. :)
If you are a fan of the universe and have played and enjoyed the recent Batman games (from a gameplay mechanics perspective) definately check this out, you won't be disappointed!

Cons:
- terrible voice acting (I'm Australian... some of those attempts at the Australian action ranged from laughable to borderline offensive)
- predictable A.I.
- repetitive non-storyline gameplay
Pros:
- the Mad Max 'universe'
- optimisation
- fun, easy-to-learn gameplay
- an engaging an immersive storyline
- in-game customisation (Max, and the cars)
'Mad Max' takes the best bits of games like Assassin's Creed, Batman: Arkham Asylum/City/et al, and mish-mashes them into a game that is mostly entertaining and unravels the reality of the world Max exists in. I'm a lover of the Mad Max films first and foremost; I feel that this game does the movies justice... they offer the same things, really:
- the strong, silent type protagonist/anti-hero, Max
- fast cars
- explosions
- brutal "survival of the fittest" combat
- scavenging for materials to push on for a few more hours (days)
- the opportunity to become a legend, just like Mad Max
It's not a perfect game (but then again is there such a thing?) but it's well worth the investment. I'm loving the game and I'm pleased that it was made.

As corny as this sounds, if you loved the original Life is Strange for any reason you'll very likely find enjoyment here for the same. This is a prequel, which comes with the unfortunate "all roads lead to Rome" ending that prequels have to do to respect the originalm story, but this does serve to explore relationships between characters to boost the perception of who they are.
Now, the first question you'll probably ask as a newcomer is "should I play the prequel first or the original game?" Normally I would say the original game, but now the answer isn't so clear-cut since the three episodes for this game have released. It all comes to down to preference, really, but either way you're going to have a great time with this game. A few notes I took were:
- The mechanics are different, forcing you to be more careful with your dialog instead of rewinding in-game, but that adds a sense of importance to the scenes where you need to persuade people.
- The characters lack a lot of likability, however. Chloe, Rachel, Joyce, David, and a few other characters seem to be alright, but for the most part new characters ultimately do not matter. There's a few subplots that go pretty much nowhere, and you don't see 80% of these characters in the main game anyways. They might be likable when you play the game and you might care, but in the grand scheme of things these characters pretty much only exist because the story takes place three years before the original game.
Now, using ALL of the original characters might not be a great idea, and we have to remember that another company is doing development on this game, not Dontnod specifically. So maybe it's for the better. this is coming from someone who's played the original game multiple times through.
- Outfits are actually customizable. Yeah. Before in the first game, you only saw Max in maybe 5 or 6 outfits throughout the game that you couldn't change, because those were all situational. Or maybe she was wearing the same clothes for days straight. Here you can actually choose what Chloe wears, even going for her outfit from the first game if you pre-ordered. Not that these outfits necessarily matter for enjoyment, they don't impact anything, but it's a nice touch.
- The soundtrack is GREAT... but sometimes it isn't so great situationally. Life is Strange at this point picks some really good songs, and i have to admit I was in a bit of doubt when this game would be following more of a punk direction than an indie one, given how Chloe is that much different compared to Max. But I have to say I really liked the soundtrack. There's a "mixtape" option or something that I didn't purchase, that supposedly allows you to change the tracklists and customize which tracks play at which moments. Let me say that some of the default track listing in this game is a bit.. repetitive. The soundtrack is mostly done by a band named Daughter, and while they don't sound bad on their own, some of their songs are really overplayed, like "Burn it Down". The title theme is good and while you hear it often in this game, it's good enough that it doesn't annoy you when it does.
I'm just giving a brief rundown, since I'll be making a video review on this soon in greater detail which I will link here. Bottom line is, buy this game and get set for feels and consequential introspection.

In some ways there are no words. Only punches to the face or a drop kick to the face, or a regular kick to the face. Take my word on one thing. I watched the video, and was like "meh." Not sure what possessed me to buy it but holy crap I almost missed out. Find some way to just give it a try before you skip over. The mechanics are so cool. I had to play to truly experience how cool the combat system was.  Don't be fooled, there will be haters, as is the way of the world. But to be fair here is the situation how I see it.
Price, it is a
high. BUT, only at it's current state. Far as it goes I think mainly what you are buying is a voucher of faith. Faith that this tile by Boneloaf reaches completion. To ME, the experience in this case was almost worth the $20, then again at the time of this review the sale is for $13.39, so even more worth it. Now Devs, brings me a completed game with everything you promise and I can name this a gem an amazing and hilarious jab at fighting games everywhere.
Each button or key is tailored to all work in combination, resulting in an unexpected amount of control. There is a separate button for left and right punch, holding either of these will grab and hold on. Which BTW can be to objects, rails, ledges, walls, clothing or accessories on players (ties etc.), even tails if anybody has one. There is a jump, dive, kick, and lift button. Lifting will raise or attempt to elevate whatever is being held. You Lift players to throw over a cliff or drop them into a grinder. Dangle your buddy off the edge with one hand and repeatedly punch his face with the other. Even then they still may pull you over the rail so hang on! YOu can even use the lift mechanic to climb. Jumping and kicking simultaneously results in a dropkick. Jump and dive is a head-butt. Really cool stuff and supposedly more to come.
There is no online play. Hmm. I know it sucks. Like really bad. Like if there was this one tiny thing it would be a gold mine. Right when you sigh a breathe of relief, that's when your friend grabs your foot at the last second and pulls you in screaming and cursing.
Not saying it comes without problems, the game modes other than the standard gang fights are very incomplete, and mostly novelty until further notice. In any case, this game deserves some attention. I love playing it every time I do. Very little makes me laugh this hard. But I don't play it alone, nor would I recommend anyone do either.

I've had this game for quite a while (Since 0.50). Over all of my time, it's been pretty damn fun, i'm not going to deny that, and it's pretty evident as i've got nearly 900 hours on the bloody game.
When i first got it: I started out, i'd go to Elektro, balota or cherno and have a pretty good time (albeit on my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop at around 10fps) finding loot and players were extremely common, interaction was good, people didn't KOS as much and people talked. I met quite a few people (some were absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing mental).
Mid way through: I had gotten my pc a couple of months after and played dayZ (bearing in mind that most modern games Even now run on my pc). I expected it to run at least at 30fps constant as i did a little research, i did know the optimization was bad, but 30fps was a reasonable estimate. Dayz laughed in my face and said "Ha! ♥♥♥♥ you!" and i ran everywhere, the game looking like a slideshow as 35fps was the limit in countrysides. And in towns, a dreadful 15. Players still roamed the cities and encounters were still fresh and there was lots to do and see, the game still being really buggy and i had died due to some hilarious actions such as walking down the police station stairs, falling through a building and such others. Some time later, they had removed some loot spawns, but loot was still no issue. But they'd removed North east airfield, and restricted the loot in balota,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off a little, but wasn't really much of an issue. Some time later there was a hilarious loot glitch, jail buildings were full of loot (more so than usual) and guard buildings sometimes had full kits, waiting for you to pick up and empty a full clip into the next player you saw.
Since that update, loot has been very scarce and you could only loot up at certain buildings (Now, you pretty much only find a weapon with ammo in Millitary areas). Balota has been dead. Players became few and far between, but you still saw people on the coast.
From that point on, dayz had become dead, and the much needed performance issue that had plagued the game had only been fixed last year-ish, by that point the game was already on it's death bed. At the moment, coastal PVP is a rare occurance, and millitary PVP is still there, but rare. And player interaction is pretty much nonexistant aside from being on the recieving end of a few bullets to the cranium (Not that i mind).
At the moment, all there is to do is 1)Spend ages looting up and go to a millitary area (NWAF or Tisy). 2) Get into a gunfight and get some kills. 3) Die. Repeat steps 1-3 and you basically have the whole current DayZ experience. That's assuming you can actually get into a high pop server as there's usually at maximum and i say MAXIMUM 3 high pop servers and the average is ♥♥♥♥ing atrocious at 1 high-full pop.
It's a damn shame to say this, the feel of the game used to be amazing, there was so much to do and see, but the game is dead and buried at this point and has little hope other than the modding community to save it (If it becomes available within this decade).
I recommend that you save your hard earned money and invest in ARMA 3 (Or 2, if the dayZ mod's still alive) as there's a mod called Exile (Basically dayz with modded guns and other stuff) and it's way more fun. And that's just exile, and for around £10/$15 more, you get a full game, with more than just zombies.

If you think you are going to like this game, you probably will! Prison Architect is pretty much exactly what it sounds like it is going to be. It's a prison simulation game where you manage a prison. But it does that very well!
There are different ways to play but in one way you get a certain number of minimum, normal, and maximum security prisoners dropped off every day. You need to make room in your prison for these guys, you need to keep them happy, and you need to make sure they don't run away or kill each other.
To start off you can either build a large holding cell or smaller individualized cells (the individual cells are much more expensive but it keeps the prisoners happier). Each prisoner has needs like the need to shower, to eat, to sleep, to go out to the yard, to talk to their family, etc. You can see these stats on a per prisoner basis or as an overall stat at the top of your screen. The more unhappy your prisoners are the more likely they are to try to escape, to cause a riot, to kill people, etc.
The other thing you need to keep in mind is money. You are running a for-profit prison after all. You can get money from grants at the start of the game (they are kind of like mini quests where you get half the money up-front and the other half once you complete the objective) and you also get money depending on the number of prisoners you have. You spend money every day on things like food, guards, other staff members, etc. You can hire less staff members or reduce the quality of the food but there are risks to doing those things.(the finance System is better now)

tl;dr: Rated down because of the potential it has vs what you get. The game is repetitive, looks unfinished and rushed, you should hate it, and you should hate yourself for loving it.
(In this review I will talk about the negative thoughts I had during this game, because I need to remind myself to not love it.)
Why repetitive?
The map feels crowded for this kind of post-apocalyptic world, but basically the same thing twenty times. If any game, this would have been a game where they could have made a huge map with minutes of empty space between camps. Oh, right. Camps. Camps are exactly the opposite, they feel empty. Let's admit it, when the only thing you can interact with is 4-12 Scraps to pick up, 3-6 Scrotus Singia, and a War Crier or 2 sometimes, that's not something that should be called "crowded".
Why unfinished and rushed?
When I said unfinished, it is because of the small details you just cannot seem to not pass by. Such as all mini-bosses being exactly the same, but differently colored, and yet you see this exact same type of enemy in 1-2 scrap scavange locations, as if they were somekind of an uncommon common enemy, rather than mini-bosses.  As if they were hastily copy-pasted to the prepared boss fight locations.
Once in a dozen times, you pick up a scrap which activates a script. One example: railroad car hanging off the bridge, pick up scrap, railroad car suddenly drops a little, almost falling down. You see this kind of stuff exactly once. These scripted events are all unique, yet they happen only at 0,1% of all the scavenge locations, or in more meaningful numbers, less than 5 times probably. In the entire game. As if they started doing them, but stopped right away and said "Let's just drop a few more scavange locations." Which in return, caused previously mentioned crowded map.
In addition, I found a Deathrace location off the map, which kind of makes me feel like there was suppose to be something, yet it got cut. Check my public screenshots for location.
Camps. The very last camp is pretty much the only camp that has any significant difference over the previous 36. Why is it just that one camp? I would have loved to play it more than once. Although the atmosphere of the camps, and the locations were very different, and I loved the scenery, it doesn't have too much effect on gameplay.

Enemies? The Hosertanka and the Teeny Hauler look exactly the same. You won't see them that many times. Perhaps less than 10 times combined. Why give 2 different names to the same model? As if the model wasn't ready and they just quickly copied another model in it's place.
Difficulty levels? What difficulty levels? I guess they were busy copy-pasting mini-bosses and adding scavange locations.
As a last word, it would be shame to not mention how pretty the game is and how well it runs. Does it have complex weather/environment effects? No. Billions of lightsources with reflections/bloom/glaze during nighttime? No. Doesn't mean it shouldn't be praised for it's excellent optimization. More than enough happening on the screen to "justify" FPS drops and laggs and freezes as most other current releases do, yet you won't see any.
Overall:
Give it a 6/10 or 7/10, IMPORTANT: try it before you buy it. I love it and I feel dirty because of it.

Mad Max is an open world videogame developed by Avalanche Studios set in the same universe of the Mad Max movies. At the beginning of the game the titular character is roaming the Wasteland when he's ambushed by the warlord Scabrus Scrotus and his pack, has his Interceptor car stolen and is left to die. Max must now reclaim his car from Scrotus thanks to the help of Chumbucket, an odd crippled mechanic, and his new vehicle, the Magnum Opus.
Since the game takes place in the Mad Max universe, your car is an important gameplay element and is not only used to travel around the Wasteland but also to engage in combat with other cars and tear down enemy structures. The Magnum Opus can be completely customized with both cosmetic and RPG-like upgrades. While the former can be unlocked by completing certain side objectives, the latter are bought by using scraps, the main currency of the game, which can be found all over the game's map and can be also gained by completing side missions. Building your car in a way that fits your playstyle is imperative, considering that the different upgrades have certain effects on each other. Car combat is mostly satisfying and can be approached in many different ways depending on the weapons you want to use or the stats of your Manum Opus.
While on feet, Max main focus is to explore the camps he can find around the Wasteland and face his enemies from the various packs in combat. Max can clear in-game challenges with various objectives to gain levels: each level allows you to improve Max abilities and spend special Griffa tokens to gain useful passive abilities. On feet combat can be considered one of the weakest part of Mad Max: while the whole thing is styled after the successful formula of the Arkham series, the game's fist fights feel more clunky and you are given less options to deal with your attackers, making the fights a bit repetitive. While you can unlock more moves by levelling up, borrow shivs and weapons from your enemies to perform more devastating blows and finishers and enter a Fury mode that makes Max hit a lot harder, the main core of combat is about countering attacks at the right time, rinse and repeat. The few boss fights you have to undergo on foot are also very underwhelming, due to each boss having the exact some pattern (as to say, dodge the huge boss attacks till you can unbalance him and hit him for a while until he recovers).
As on open world game, Mad Max puts a lot of emphasis on exploration and literarly conquering the Wasteland for yourself by disrupting enemy activities around the game's map and helping your allies improving their strongholds by doing optional missions for them. While the game does a fine job at making you really want to take on these challenges, some objectives get incredibly repetitive after a while and clearing them feels like a chore more than anything else. Also, while the game apparently puts a lot of emphasis on resource management on your part (especially when it comes to water and food, your only mean to refill your health, and fuel), Mad Max isn't a survival game and therefore the need of said resources tend to become less pressing as the game unfolds.
A final thing that should be noted is that this game has a great presentation. The environments are absolutely gorgeous and reflect very well the main motif of the Mad Max universe, and they also look pretty much alive in-game: there is a day-night cycle, explosions and other effects look stunning to say the least, the Wasteland can experience lighting or sand storms what will force you to seek shelter and there are many NPCs to interact with around the huge desert. The great setting is also helped by a greatly optmized PC port of the game that runs without any issue on most computers and that allows you to set several graphic options to your liking. Mad Max also features a Capture mode that allows you to take a picture of the action by pausing the game at the right moment and adjust the camera positioning and other settings. It's like a Photo mode, but easier to use.
All things considered, while Mad Max could had been really improved on some gameplay elements and made a great masterpiece for the genre, this game still manages to be a pretty solid and gorgeous open world game that should deserve far more praise

I do not recommend Undertale.
It is not an RPG in the classic sense of the word; it is a Bullet-Hell at its core.
I had planned to play the game through twice once I discovered the different playstyles available to players. The first time was slated for experiencing the game as Toby Fox intended: avoiding physical confrontation and being a compassionate character in the face of prejudice. The second playthrough was for the more traditional murder-spree of crushing every foe encountered. Having played through the first time, I'm not sure I want to go through all that again.
I was honestly expecting an RPG experience and that colors everything that follows. It is a weak RPG and more of a Bullet-Hell. I appreciate the earnest attempt at breaking the genre mold, and I am a fan of shaking things up. The character-themed attacks and patterns were inspired and I felt clever for figuring out the unexpected platforming and timing aspects of a "non-action" game, but the cleverness only extends so far. The few puzzles in the game were either childishly simple or bogglingly near-impossible.
The dialogue interwoven with the combat sequences were also a very nice touch. It kept the action alive and kept me paying attention to the whole screen instead of just the small walled-off arena for my little avatar to dodge incoming blows. As the writing goes, I didn't care for the juvenile targeting. The humor, personalities of NPCs, and vocabulary and word-choice was very simple; something a middle-schooler could grasp. Some of this could be explained away as having to fit small words in a little text-box, but plenty of other games with similar limitations have overcome that.
Thematically, the plot was simple too. I don't wish to spoil anything, but it becomes pretty clear very quickly what Toby Fox intended and he does so in a hamfisted manner. There is no subtlety to the message and in the face of this, having warm feelings for the NPCs as you find them feels like your mother telling you you have to be friends with that weird kid in school. Yes, it's the right thing to do, but you don't have any genuine feelings for them (Insert that's what's wrong with society essay). The characters all do mostly fill some kind of weird-kid niche too, all of whom would likely be well at-home on Tumblr, DeviantArt, or any other "we accept everyone." I'm sorry, but you're weird and if you don't conform to what most people consider "normal" you're going to get some odd looks from the general population. This is just a short digression from a game review, so I'll simply leave the topic there.
To move on...
Graphically, the art is crisp and clean, but I don't care for the overworld sequences. The tilesets are strong, and the sprites are big and flat cardboard cutouts. Large swaths of flat color do not make for a pretty character sprite. Some of the incidental NPCs were lovingly designed, and one particular recurring little yellow creature was beautifully animated. It's a shame this kind of love couldn't have been poured into the more frequently used characters and elements.
The music in this game is an absolute gem! I absolutely love and it is better than it deserves to be if it's in this game. Toby Fox knows his way around composition, mood, and rhythm! This is a game soundtrack I could listen to for a very long time and I will seek out getting a copy of it for my own library. The chiptune-instrumented songs get in your head and the loop does not wear out. Bravo!
As much as I don't like this game, I think it could have benefitted from being longer. I've already established this isn't quite an RPG and more of a Bullet-Hell, so that informs this part of the critique, but there is no down-time between major plot points in the game. In other RPGs, something big happens and sets the direction for the next chapter with a lot of dialogue and some scripted sequences. Then there's mostly silence (or lack of exposition or any lengthy reading), and it gives the player time to reflect and absorb what's gone on.
And given the theme of the story and Toby Fox's intent to *not* fight in the game, this is where the grinding would go. One might call it unnecessary fluff or filler, and at some point on the continuum, that can happen. Undertale is at the extreme narrow end of the spectrum in that there is next to zero downtime. The story happens too quickly to be appreciated.
Oh, and the ending. I was prepared to give the game a 3 out of 5 including the combat and music giving a big boost to the score. Lord help the ending. With the ending included in the final score, I will drop it to a weak 2 out of 5 rating. Undertale's ancestor, Earthbound, had a poor US ad campaign by having a tagline of "this game stinks" in reference to the smelly enemies in the game. Undertale: "this game is bad"
...and not in a marketing kind of way trying to sell more copies of games. It's just bad.

Episode 1 review
------------------
The game feels a lot like the original Life is Strange, which is good if you liked the previous installment. The story offers a surprising ammount of freedom to choose yourself, despite the protagonist (Chloe) being pretty.. well defined (♥♥♥♥ everything attitude, etc.). Throughout the first episode there was ample exploring to do, allowing you to use the gained knowledge or items to your advantage.  The story is definitely trying to get going in this episode and perhaps it is trying to hard. It is my only complaint, the story is trying to advance pretty quick which may feel unnatural to the player.
Playtime for this episode was 3.5 hours for me, taking it easy, enjoying the music and exploring around. If you are a slow reader you will take longer, similarly, if you dislike reading then your playtime will be considerably slower (1.5 - 2 hours).
So if you like the previous LiS, enjoy exploring a world or just like interactive stories: this might a game for you. Try LiS Episode 1 (it is free) if you haven't and are considering to buy this game. The way you interact with the world is the same; talking with people, interacting with the environment and having a notebook. No magic powers in this game (yet) though.

Rogue Legacy manages to innovate and bring new elements to the roguelike genre. It is true that permadeath is the name of the game here, but Rogue Legacy sets itself apart.
The first few times through you are going to die, and you are going to die a lot. But with each new attempt through you are going to make it farther, such is the case with every roguelike. The learning curve here is right on track, you learn the enemies' patterns and what to expect when you enter each new room. After about an hour of playtime you start to think "I could use a little more," and you find yourself a movement upgrade, as well as another class with some extra stat padding, and it gets a little better. You start working your way through the castle and eventually you beat your first boss, and it gets a lot better. You upgrade more, earn more classes, and you get hooked.
What this game has is a perfect rate of progression. Your skill and your upgrades combine to create a great experience, where skill is always needed even at higher levels, but the upgrades keep it from feeling stale and monotonous. In this game you are always going through the same basic steps. The rooms don't change much, you'll use all your classes many times, but it never feels the same. Every time through feels fresh, it is diverse where other roguelikes become repetitive. This is what Rogue Legacy offers.
If you are reading this review and have come this far, I would say your interest is great enough to warrant a purchase of this game. If you like character progression but a challenge at the same time, similar to the brand of Demon's Souls and Dark Souls, then you owe it to yourself to try this out.

Small recap. 2013: Tons of people played Arma 2 DayZ Epoch mod, it worked and it went so well that DayZ SA was made. When it became early access it looked promising. The sad truth: Basically this game got abandoned by the developers when we are being honest to ourselves. "But there are still updates and such! You are lying!" The only reason some work still might be done is to make sure they don't have to mass refund eventually.
Steam Early Access just became a thing in 2013. But DayZ SA is the prime example that there needs to be a limit on the Early Access part. We're heading towards the 5th year of Alpha stage, that would be fine if the game wasn't made public. As loads of games need years of development. However, due to the "Early Access" mark it will likey fail.
All in all, save your money. Don't get this. You will 100% regret it.

At about 11 hours in, the game started acting weirder than usual.
The screen flickered. Blood smears would flash on the screen and then disappear. Random colours, or even what looked like enemies... appeared for a fraction of a second, and then disappeared. Like a mirage.

Mad Max is one of the very few games in the modern gaming scene that has lived up to all the hype that surrounded it. It's vast, rich, unique, interactive, alive, and overall a very solid game, plagued only by a few minor issues.
Pros:
+ Acceptably large world (not the biggest, but big enough to be enjoyable and to not feel trapped)
+ Car combat feel, looks, and is awesome
+ Melee combat is reminiscent of  the Arkham and Uncharted series, so it's pretty fluid and, like car combat, awesome
+ Character and car upgrades and customisation are good; not so few as to feel cheap, and not so many as to be overwhelming
+ Graphics are beautiful - sand effects and the lighting are clean and very smooth
+ Performance and optimisation; on my GTX 970 and i5-4690k, it runs at 60fps smooth in all scenarios with everything on the highest setting
+ Very few bugs and not a single crash so far; the few glitches are limited to object clipping and some corpses/objects spazzing when you touch them. Nothing at all game-breaking or seriously affecting
+ Soundtrack is subtle but adds a nice feel to the game
+ The world is, as mentioned before, very vast. In this open world - one that's ever-changing throughout the course of the story - you'll meet many loveable (and sometimes despicable) characters that each have their own unique flair; voice, personality, and honest characters.
+ The camps and strongholds and other wastelanders add a certain level of depth to the game that makes the desolate desert feel that much more alive
NEUTRAL
+- Loads of quests; this can be good because you get more for your money, but it can get overwhelming and a little confusing at times as to what you should or can do next
+- Lots of collectables and unlockables; they're rewarding if you find them all, but doing so can prove quite frustrating
+- Controls. Whilst they're mapped fine for KB&M, it can feel  a little clunky sometimes when trying to jump or something
+- Combat balancing. It keeps it interesting by making it a challenge, so it doesn't get boring to kill things, but there are times when you've got no shotgun shells and there are way too many enemies to comfortably fight off with just your fists
CONS:
- Can be reptitive after a while and when preparing your car for the next stage. Get scrap, install upgrade, get more scrap, upgrade again...
- Sometimes can be a little boring when, as mentioned before, all you're doing is collecting more scrap before going any further
Overall Verdict: 9/10. Mad Max is, at its core, a very solid game, well worth the lower-than-usual A$60 price tag. You get heaps of content and many hours for your money, it's kept alive by a breathing, open world that changes as you play, and it makes you feel like a bada$$ m0therf***er when you're taking on something like a convoy. It plays well, it looks good, and it's exactly what you'd expect from the trailer. It needs some slight balancing improvements and perhaps more clear guidance for quests and interface, but it's only just shy of a perfect 10.
EDIT: I'm leaving my review as recommended, but lowering the score a little. It gets very, very repetitive after a while. New score: 7.5/10.

Original review after 1st Episode
I would never downvote a Life is Strange game, as the original is one of my top five games of all time... Before the Storm's first episode, however, did not at all grab me like the originals first one did. Within a half hour, I was "in it to win it" with that series. This one wasn't quite the same.
Chloe and her backtalk system is not interesting at all. It's easy to guess what you "should pick" to win. It just seems kind of silly. It does fit in with her character, though. I like that we are getting to know Chloe in the time Max was gone, and that it delves more into the friendship with Rachel Amber (I'll always think that is one of the worst names ever lol).
The graphics are the same, which is fine although I feel like the reason they were that style in the first game was due to the "art/photography" theme, which really doesn't have a bearing on this game.
I can't wait for the next episode, ands I'm hoping it will be better/more interesting and not drag like this one did (for me) in a lot of places. I guess my only worry is that with three episodes (besides the extra Max episode) as opposed to five, they really need to step up their game (storywise) in the next episode and move it along. It's tough since in an episodic series, the first episode is used to introduce the characters and set up the story, but with the truncated nature of this series, I feel it dwelt waaaay too long on that.
Now, don't get me wrong. I like the game. I'd probably buy a Life is Strange series even if it written by a monkey and drawn by a five year old, but I really hope the next episode is full of more conflict/story and is more interesting overall.

Mad Max is one of the very few games in the modern gaming scene that has lived up to all the hype that surrounded it. It's vast, rich, unique, interactive, alive, and overall a very solid game, plagued only by a few minor issues.
Pros:
+ Acceptably large world (not the biggest, but big enough to be enjoyable and to not feel trapped)
+ Car combat feel, looks, and is awesome
+ Melee combat is reminiscent of  the Arkham and Uncharted series, so it's pretty fluid and, like car combat, awesome
+ Character and car upgrades and customisation are good; not so few as to feel cheap, and not so many as to be overwhelming
+ Graphics are beautiful - sand effects and the lighting are clean and very smooth
+ Performance and optimisation; on my GTX 970 and i5-4690k, it runs at 60fps smooth in all scenarios with everything on the highest setting
+ Very few bugs and not a single crash so far; the few glitches are limited to object clipping and some corpses/objects spazzing when you touch them. Nothing at all game-breaking or seriously affecting
+ Soundtrack is subtle but adds a nice feel to the game
+ The world is, as mentioned before, very vast. In this open world - one that's ever-changing throughout the course of the story - you'll meet many loveable (and sometimes despicable) characters that each have their own unique flair; voice, personality, and honest characters.
+ The camps and strongholds and other wastelanders add a certain level of depth to the game that makes the desolate desert feel that much more alive
NEUTRAL
+- Loads of quests; this can be good because you get more for your money, but it can get overwhelming and a little confusing at times as to what you should or can do next
+- Lots of collectables and unlockables; they're rewarding if you find them all, but doing so can prove quite frustrating
+- Controls. Whilst they're mapped fine for KB&M, it can feel  a little clunky sometimes when trying to jump or something
+- Combat balancing. It keeps it interesting by making it a challenge, so it doesn't get boring to kill things, but there are times when you've got no shotgun shells and there are way too many enemies to comfortably fight off with just your fists
CONS:
- Can be reptitive after a while and when preparing your car for the next stage. Get scrap, install upgrade, get more scrap, upgrade again...
- Sometimes can be a little boring when, as mentioned before, all you're doing is collecting more scrap before going any further
Overall Verdict: 9/10. Mad Max is, at its core, a very solid game, well worth the lower-than-usual A$60 price tag. You get heaps of content and many hours for your money, it's kept alive by a breathing, open world that changes as you play, and it makes you feel like a bada$$ m0therf***er when you're taking on something like a convoy. It plays well, it looks good, and it's exactly what you'd expect from the trailer. It needs some slight balancing improvements and perhaps more clear guidance for quests and interface, but it's only just shy of a perfect 10.
EDIT: I'm leaving my review as recommended, but lowering the score a little. It gets very, very repetitive after a while. New score: 7.5/10.

This is a darling of the Early Access world, a game that is both set to accomplish it's goals and has a positive relationship with it's community.  While I can't say it will be everyone's cup of tea, it is a game I think most people can enjoy on some level.  Introversion has quite a bit of experience and they've put it to good use giving us a very important feature for an Early Access game: peace of mind.
Prison Architect is a little bit the Sims; except most of your family members are criminals who don't like being at home.  This is what Prison Architect has done very well.  What makes the game compelling is how the prisoners interact with one another, the staff and the prison itself.  Whether they be stealing, starting fist fights, tunneling their way to freedom or receiving an education, the best thing this game has going for it is your inmate population is interesting.  What kind of prison will you run?  A liberal reform school with light security or a inescapable fortress of despair.  Most people will probably settle somewhere in between, and the entertaining part is finding out how your ideas change based on how your prisoners react.
It's clear Introversion understands their gameplay mechanics and how they tie together.  There's no reason to suspect that the end product here will be anything less than a cult classic.  As with any Early Access it is safest to wait, but this one is low risk and I assure you that is a compliment.  The biggest threat of buying early here is that you'll put so much time into it you'll burn yourself out on it before it launches proper.

Episode 1 review
------------------
The game feels a lot like the original Life is Strange, which is good if you liked the previous installment. The story offers a surprising ammount of freedom to choose yourself, despite the protagonist (Chloe) being pretty.. well defined (♥♥♥♥ everything attitude, etc.). Throughout the first episode there was ample exploring to do, allowing you to use the gained knowledge or items to your advantage.  The story is definitely trying to get going in this episode and perhaps it is trying to hard. It is my only complaint, the story is trying to advance pretty quick which may feel unnatural to the player.
Playtime for this episode was 3.5 hours for me, taking it easy, enjoying the music and exploring around. If you are a slow reader you will take longer, similarly, if you dislike reading then your playtime will be considerably slower (1.5 - 2 hours).
So if you like the previous LiS, enjoy exploring a world or just like interactive stories: this might a game for you. Try LiS Episode 1 (it is free) if you haven't and are considering to buy this game. The way you interact with the world is the same; talking with people, interacting with the environment and having a notebook. No magic powers in this game (yet) though.

This innocent little game will always have you hating it, and, coming back for more at the same time. One unique feature is that every time you die, that's it. No respawns, no lives, no second chances. But, fear not! You can select an offspring to continue your journey. Each child will have different characteristics that define them. For example, they might have dwarfism, and be really small, or have vertigo, where you have to play the entire game upside down! Obviously, not all of the traits are good, but they do serve to spice up the game. On top of that, each life, the castle has a new layout, which means you will never have the same map... unless you lock the castle. This is the one feature I didn't like; You can give up a percentage of your gold to lock the castle and keep your progress. It feels like cheating to me. You should have to find all the bosses, not just teleport to them! Despite that, it's a really fun game that will have you hooked. Buy it!

Absolutely love this game. First time in a long time I have been able to sit and play a game for 3-4+ hours in one sitting without getting bored.
The combat is ♥♥♥♥ing awesome. Yes it's a Batman style combat clone... But it's a really good one. Extremely satisfying combat, especially when you've upgraded all of Max's abilities.
The driving is really fun and each car feels different to drive. Making changes to the stats of your car really make a big difference.
The world and the game itself is really well put together, great fun to explore and while the story is a little thin it was more than good enough for me.

Finished it last night. Not sure about the story. Can't say too much about it without spoiling it but it was either pretty good or just an excuse to make you drive to a place, talk to a person and kill some more guys.
That said, I expect it was all intentional, it falls in line with the feeling of the movies and has some fun call-backs here and there. It doesn't really bring anything new to the table and the best way I can describe the whole thing is an enjoyable mix of the Batman games and the Just Cause games.
The vehicle powerups are kind of an odd duck. The ones I thought were going to be useful were actually generally crap compared to the ones that I thought were going to make me a god. It sure doesn't suffer from the same "issue" that Shadow of Mordor did, where by the end of the game you're basically a demi-god traipsing around killing orcs like it's going out of sport. Even towards the end of the game I was finding it difficult to take on even 2 other vehicles at a time if they were sufficiently armoured. One mistake I think they made with the upgrades is either they're really minor and generally inconsequential or a total game-breaker. It's the difference between doing an extra 5% damage per hit with your car or tearing a wheel off for a one hit kill basically.
The ground combat fared much better. It's basically the Batman combat. Block with one button, counter with the punch button. Get funky powerups along the way to unlock better combos and counters. You actually feel more powerful as the game progresses on the ground. I didn't get that with the car. Maybe it's because the car powerups have tradeoffs. Bigger armour and bumpers mean you're slower and have♥♥♥♥♥♥handling. No armour and bumper means you're zippy but have to rely on your powerup weapons rather than the car itself and will get rekt quick in a fight. You have to find a balance lest ye fall victim to crippling overspecialization.
All in all I enjoyed the game, but I'm not sure if i'll keep playing to do all the side crap, it's mostly drive here, clear out a camp, do it again. Enjoyable in doses but tedious and irrelevant in the scheme of things.
Recommended for everyone if you regularly drop 50 bucks or more on games. Recommended when it goes on sale for cheap people like me. 25 bucks or less would be a buy for me if I didn't have it already.

I'm really having a hard time with this game. Playing it is turning into a chore. Chloe (as a protagonist) is just not interesting. Original review after 1st Episode
I would never downvote a Life is Strange game, as the original is one of my top five games of all time... Before the Storm's first episode, however, did not at all grab me like the originals first one did. Within a half hour, I was "in it to win it" with that series. This one wasn't quite the same.
Chloe and her backtalk system is not interesting at all. It's easy to guess what you "should pick" to win. It just seems kind of silly. It does fit in with her character, though. I like that we are getting to know Chloe in the time Max was gone, and that it delves more into the friendship with Rachel Amber (I'll always think that is one of the worst names ever lol).
The graphics are the same, which is fine although I feel like the reason they were that style in the first game was due to the "art/photography" theme, which really doesn't have a bearing on this game.
I can't wait for the next episode, ands I'm hoping it will be better/more interesting and not drag like this one did (for me) in a lot of places. I guess my only worry is that with three episodes (besides the extra Max episode) as opposed to five, they really need to step up their game (storywise) in the next episode and move it along. It's tough since in an episodic series, the first episode is used to introduce the characters and set up the story, but with the truncated nature of this series, I feel it dwelt waaaay too long on that.
Now, don't get me wrong. I like the game. I'd probably buy a Life is Strange series even if it written by a monkey and drawn by a five year old, but I really hope the next episode is full of more conflict/story and is more interesting overall.

The game is seriously fun for the first and second region. Car combat is incredible. If you have a lot of money, buy it just to have a cinematic car combat experience in a game. It's awesome. I also thought chumbucket was a great NPC.
The problem is that the world starts to feel very empty very quickly. I suppose I'm not the right kind of gamer for this kind of game. I want choices and consequences, but the game is devoid of both. A lot of people complain that the mechanics are boring. I think the reason the mechanics become boring (such as looting, tearing down towers, clearing minefields (ok, that mechanic is just REALLY boring), and clearing out bases) is not because they lack awesomeness, but because they do not lead to very exciting outcomes. Once the opus is powerful enough, there is zero incentive to do anything in the game except the story.
For me, when I realise that the only reason I'm doing something in a game is for some mechanical advantage, it's just not interesting anymore. I think mechanics, even mechanics as awesome as the ones in Mad Max, are unsatisfying when they are not embedded in a rich narrative that the player can influence in some way. For example, imagine if Max could make bad choices and descend further and further into madness and violence, or good choices and slowly start to remember who he was before the apocalypse. Imagine also if those choices made during the game had an impact on how the story ended and on the opportunities and events that occur in the game. That would be amazing!
If you don't feel the same way about mechanics and narrative, and just love to blow things up in optimized game world and upgrade a car until it's the most badass thing in the wastes, get this game. You'll have a blast.
If you can relate to what I said, after the first ten hours or so the game will probably start to feel like work. Since $85 (yes, that's how much Australians have to pay) is waaaay to much for 10 hours of enjoyable gameplay, I'd recommend getting this game when it's on sale for $30 Australian at the most.

He made no reply but I could here him pacing in front of the door to my tiny shack. This in rust is very common. Its called a "Door Camper" and will certainly happen to you if you make the mistake of buying this game. So I waited, and waited and waited and waited some more. I watched 2 eppisodes of its always sunny and came back to my comp, opened the door and bam, instantly killed me. There was no delay, and I was right in front of the door before I opened it, he had no warning, he was waiting the whole time I was afk. He wasn't also off watching something or doing anything else, he was sitting there, eyes fixated on my door, with no other distractions whatsoever. He was waiting there for over 1 hour. 60 minutes of his life on Earth gone. An hour staring straight at the door, finger on the trigger, waiting for the moment I would open it. This is the type of person who plays rust. This is the level of sociopathic obsesive autism you will deal with. You cannot win. When you tell other players about the guy who waited on your roof for 3 straight hours, even after you logged off, went to work out and came back, and he was still there and killed you instantly then locked you out of your own base making it his, they will say, "Welcome to Rust"

The are not socially skilled, they are not weel adjusted, they are not independantly succesful, they are not kind or genorous, they are not happy. That said, you are essentially playing the same game over and over again with the rooms slightly shuffled round so I wouldn't recommend it at full price; £4.99 or below would be reasonable.
Two things to note:
1. Despite the core concept supposedly being about your characters developing genealogically, this doesn't actually happen. The traits etc. are random, you can't somehow "breed them out", so ignore that; it's just marketing spin.
2. The controls are occasionally frustrating; characters turn slowly so if you're being attacked from both sides defending yourself can be difficult.
Other than those minor niggles I would heartily recommend this game. Pick it up on sale and you won't regret it!

TL;DR more filler than killer.
This title can, offhandedly, come highly recommended to those who enjoy Arkham-style combat with a fantastic vehicle upgrade system combined with some open-world driving that just feels good and runs like a dream. The game is damned fun, and while some would call the melee fighting "clunky," I found the animations to be satisfying and the sound effects especially so.
Mad Max, however, comes with a rather elaborate "But..."
Even though I will continue playing the game because I enjoy it and find its gameplay satisfying, the game simply doesn't merit its asking price.  $39.99 would have been a bit more reasonable and as such, if you buy it for the asking price, its likely you'll feel gipped.
Mad Max would be a far better value picked up in a Steam sale at less than half of the asking price.  You can get a lot of dollar-per-hour content if you're okay with running around in a rather brown and vapid post-apocalyptic world that, although teeming with life, really only gives agency to the player.  WBGames' other recent non-Arkham-Arkham-style fighting game, Shadow of Mordor, succeeded not just by fluidic combat and easy travel but through dynamic events such as fights between captains and feasts to crash.
Max lacks this dynamism, and the game world feels like it was created for such a system only to lack it at release.  Perhaps a post-release series of DLCs adding mechanics is coming, although I really don't look forward to them.  IF any such mechanic were to arrive, it doesn't seem unreasonable to ask why it couldn't have been included in the original purchase.  Perhaps because it was more important to sell movie tickets than quality gameplay?  It's not my job to speculate.

After almost 250 hours in this game I have decided to rewrite my review.
Borderlands 2 is by far one of, if not the best game I own. The story and lore in this game are so rich and refined, leaving the player wanting more.
The main game tells the story of the vault hunters fighting to save Pandora from Hyperion a corrupt corporation run by the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Handsome Jack. You and up to 3 other friends and are tasked with ending is reign of villainy over Pandora.
Borderlands 2 is full of many interesting and fully developed characters, such as the gentlemen adventurer sir hammerlock, Tiny Tina the 13 year old explosives expert, the vault hunters from the original game and many more. I’ll leave it up to you to discover them.
The main game without DLC is so vast, from the casuistic caverns to the capitalistic shine of opportunity, every area offers the player so much to explore, do and kill.
The DLC for this game adds 4 new player campaigns filled with new areas and enemies.

Tiny Tina’s attack on Dragons Keep is a game of D&D that takes place after the events of the main game. The DLC leads you on an epic quest to save the princess from the handsome sorcerer. As well as many side quests such as collecting crumpets and telling knights to stop being jerks. This is personally my favourite DLC.
In Torgue's Campaign of Carnage the vault hunters must spill the blood of the ultimate cowered to open the vault in the centre of The Badass Crater of Badassitude. This DLC adds many new interesting characters, mainly Mr Torgue who has an explosive personality. And adds another layer to mad moxxies character.
In the DLC Captain Scarlett and Her Pirate's Booty the vault hunter’s goal is to find Captain Blade's Lost Treasure of the Sands. This DLC is slower than the others however it is quite fun to play early on in the game to help you level.
I have played borderlands 2 multiple times as all of the characters and plan to continue until I have over 1000 hours, still I doubt I will stop there. I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes FPS, games with rich stories, and endless loot.

Before I started this game i did have my doubts. How would they keep the game fun without the time travel we have gotten so used to in the first game? How will they make us like Chloe again with the new voiceactress instead of the iconice Ashley Burch? Many people go into this game with expectations that it will be on par with the first Life is Strange and will try to compare the two.
To be honest, as a review of only one episode, they did a pretty decent job. Of course I still like the first game better but I do like playing as Chloe for a change. The story started slow, as a introduction to Chloe's life and not a real plotline yet, but it slowly got a bit better and more emotional. It did have a few awkward scenes in there that they could have done better. They already got a lot of discussion about how their faces didnt show that much emotion and i still notice in the awkward moments.
Its hard getting used to a new voice actress, especially after the great performances of Ashely Burch, but the new voiceactress is likeable and good to get used to. Some minor characters like Dana and Victoria got new VA's too, but i didnt really pay mind to them.
The new playing style is pretty cool too. You have to win arguments against other people to get things your way, otherwise you get the consequences. Some of the dialogue options are very obvious if you want to win, but either way still very fun. Also great improvement on the graphics and the smoothness of the game.
Overall, still giving me a big nostalgic vibe to the first game and it does keep me hungering for the next episode. I do recommend getting this game if you played the first one and absolutely fell in love with it. Its nice to see things from Chloe's perspective for a change.
Also, Hella high graphics.

This game is exactly what I always wanted from a Mad Max game. Granted, I bought a Steam key from a friend pretty cheap, so I am judging the game based on spending $25 for it, not $60.
Pros:
*Open world filled with things to do and some really cool locations to explore.
*Cool storyline.
*Awesome driving with upgrades that really change the feel of your cars.
*Optimized for PC - my PC is decent but not great and it runs it perfectly on ultra-high settings.
*Combat is very Batman: Arkham City, especially once you unlock the cool maneuvers.
*Length: I have 40 hours in, and I am still only at 50% completion.
*The world conversations react to things you have done, so you see your legend grow.
*Never felt like it was a grind for scrap, unlike some negative reviews. Decent pace for upgrading both Max, the strongholds, and vehicles.
*YOU GET TO BE SHINY AND CHROME! WITNESS ME!
Cons:
*Only being able to climb/jump in specific areas means that you will get stuck sometimes. Like, if you fall off a walkway, you may find yourself stuck and unable to climb the ONE FOOT rocks hemming you in.
*Easy. Like, the game is rather  too easy, especially if you are  like me and ignore storyline to do all the side quests and scavenging. By the time you do the storyline, you're walking through boss fights. I usually only die from stupid mistakes, like falling off cliffs or blowing myself up.
*The bosses that rule the strongholds are all the same, just with different amounts of health. I feel like this was a cop-out. "AAAAAAAH.... MEDIOCRE!"
All in all, I am having a BLAST playing this game and recommend it heartily. 9/10 at this price, 7/10 at full price.

Borderlands 2 is a FPSRPG, focused on guns, like, really focused on guns. There is no armor, just guns and some accessories. There is an infinite amount of weapons that can drop, all with typical gun stats like accuracy, damage, reload speed, recoil, etc. But they also have status effects, boosts to stats such as ability cooldowns, and other things that arent typically associated with guns. You only have one active skill, but there are many passive skills, including ones that heavily modify your active ability. Constant shooting and looting can get repetetive, but the fun writing, leveling system, and boss fights keep it interesting, Refreshing game, but can get boring in singleplayer. The environments are way more improved over the previous game, but the drops are a step back in my opinion.

Rogue Legacy has Super Metroid styled Castlevania gameplay with a Dark Souls level of difficulty. The difficulty can disappear as you buy upgrades before you renter the castle, but it will return when you enter new parts of the Castle.  There's isn't much story to it, but then again I stopped reading the journal entries after 7/20 something. Your playable character is on a mission to find the fountain of youth which is hidden inside an enchanted castle. You will need to defeat 4 bosses, 1 from each section of the castle, then a final 2 part boss near the entrance. The final boss door remains locked until the 4 bosses are defeated. When you defeat the final boss you get a credit line you can't skip through, followed by a NEW GAME + mode where the castle's enemies are strengthened, which further ratchets up the difficulty.
Now if none of this didn't sound interesting enough let me highlight some key gameplay features of Rogue Legacy.
- Every time your character dies, he really dies. All of your stats, equipment and gold are transferred to a selectable heir in the next generation. You can choose from 3 possible heirs that will be randomly generated based on what classes you've unlocked. The next generation can have traits that can benefit or hamper gameplay, so from my experience avoid the upside down one at all cost!
- After you choose your heir you can unlock stat bonuses, perks, abilities and classes from this FAMILY TREE menu. If you found gear or runes while in the castle, they are made available to buy outside the castle, but after you unlock the sales people.
- You need to spend as much gold as possible before you renter the castle because there's a demon at the door that takes it all away! This fundamentally will make the game last longer, because you have to perform successful castle runs bringing back enough gold to upgrade or you can't improve the next generation.
- You level up in the game, but it's irrelevant to determine how powerful your character is because your stats don't increase from your LV. All stat increase must be obtained from beating bosses, finding rare chests and slowing buying out the FAMILY TREE. Your level is a marker more for speed runners and hardcore players, like if you can beat the initial playthough of Rouge Legacy before LV 100 you're probably an experienced player. The higher the level the more time and opportunity you've had to buff up your character, which would make the game easy.
- EVERY TIME YOU RENTER THE CASTLE IT RANDOMIZES. The layout of the castle will never be quite the same, or not where you would notice as your grind through heir after heir. This my friend, along with NEW GAME +, is the strength of Rouge Legacy.
The way I see it, this game would be too short if you leveled up too quickly, too boring if the castle stayed the same and too easy if they handed everything to you from the start. They've solved these problems with long grindy gameplay with randomly generated castle rooms, enemies and obstacles. It's an Indie game, so they gave you some room to stretch things out with limited resources. You will find the difficulty to be unbearable at the start, but as long as your bring gold and unlock thing your will gain momentum to do better and better. After you've unlocked everything and have bought everything you will still find value in the many consecutive NEW GAME +s  which seem to have no end.
It makes me wonder what they could do with a better budget without going all Call Of Duty on us. This is my favorite Indie game on Steam. This is supposed to come to PSN in 2014, by then way more people will know about this marvelous never ending game. For sheer fun and coming back for more, wow, it's a great spin on Symphony Of The Night. I can't give it a 5/5 because it lacks a certain gameplay depth I can't explain, it's not complex enough, but it's Indie so what do you expect?

There has been a load of new dungeon based games recently, each with their own take on searching castles and dank caves for loot. Rogue Legacy takes much of its inspiration from the castle based Castlevania games and uses this as a template to build another randomly generating and highly difficult game of exploration, loot and beasties.
Right from the start it’s clear that Rogue Legacy has much more going on than many of the other Rogue-like games of recent times. You start off with your hero entering a castle from a 2D, side on perspective and then proceed to hunt around for treasure and the boss monsters that guard each area. When you die your offspring must then take up the reigns and continue the search.
The continual line of offspring randomly generate into a number of predetermined classes. There are mages, paladins, thieves and others which can then be expanded out into more specialist explorers such as the shinobi and miner. Each class has its own strengths and weaknesses and different weapons and traits that it uses. For instance – the shinobi deals high damage but can’t create a critical hit, while the paladin is a good all-rounder and has the use of a shield.
You get to pick from three randomly created characters at the start of each adventure and these can be in any of the classes you have unlocked so far. Each individual then also has traits which give them their own strengths and weaknesses. There are a massive amount of different traits and these range from things like Gigantism (makes your character bigger), to dyslexia (can’t read signs) and things such as having an affinity with magic or boosting your speed. There’s no real way to know what you’re going to get so you need to adjust your play style accordingly.
Everything in terms of unlocking or levelling is done with the gold you find around the castle. This can be used to up your stats, buy new equipment or unlock the specialist classes. Upon your death any money or equipment you have is passed onto your next character to use and spend. The kicker is that any money left over after upgrading then needs to be given to the gate guard in order to be let back in. This can create a cycle of not getting very far as you don’t quite find enough to upgrade while being out matched by the difficulty.
Rogue Legacy is certainly not here to treat players with kid gloves. It takes a good few hours to get to grips with and to actually feel like you making progress. As gold is the only way to level up you will often find you need to very cautiously go on expeditions just to gather enough of the stuff to get you to the next piece of equipment or upgrade and this can be time consuming.
Though the castle is randomly generated you can use the architect to lock it down. For the price of a percentage of your gold this keeps the room layout the same and allows you to use the teleport squares you may have found to get you right back into the action. The main benefit of this is when you discover a boss. Bosses are fierce and difficult and will require a number of goes to get the better of. If you decide you character is strong enough then getting the castle locked down allows for repeated characters to simply teleport right to them for another go. Once a boss is downed they stay dead for good and once the initial four bosses are defeated this allows access to the final area of the castle.
It’s fair to say this isn’t going to be a game for everyone. It very tough, especially at the beginning and you will need to sink a load of time into it to get you to a point where you feel safe to explore properly. The fact the rooms move around all the time makes it seem a slightly odd decision to base it on the Castelvania template and it can be very frustrating to realise you’ve just wandered into the castle without locking it down, especially if you were heading off to fight one of the bosses. That said, it does carry the same sort of risk reward scenario as games like Dark Souls and every victory feels that much sweeter when you’ve been trying to take the monster down for hours. Once you level up a bit and get used to the game it really does start to get going and you’ll be continually drawn back for more. However, many gamers might not make it that far and that’s a shame as this is probably one of the more inventive indie style games to come out recently.
Approach it patiently and with the knowledge that you are going to die and it offers an experience not really offered elsewhere. It’s a must for fans of the genre but the more casual gamer should probably get their kicks with something a little easier to handle, much like Dark Souls or other Rogue-likes like Spelunky.

TL;DR: Scroll down to the bullet points.
I loved Fury Road and saw that the current user review score for this game was overwhelmingly high at the time of purchase. I'm sure that there are going to be those who look at just the yes/no part of these recommendations and then like or dislike it based solely on whether they agree with that alone. That's fanboyism at work, and it's anti-consumer. The point of the Steam reviews system is to give potential customers an idea of what they're going to get before they buy, and if I had waited until there were more reviews in, I would have been able to make a more informed decision.
Whether or not you like this game will weigh heavily on how much you like open world games as a genre. I spent quite some time clearing all threats from one stronghold's territory to get the final harpoon upgrade so I could pull down any scarecrow I ran into. The whole process felt...dull, really. After searching several areas for scrap, pulling down a few scarecrows, lighting up gas cans in camps, and grinding to find enough scrap for the next upgrade, I decided to focus on the main story instead. Set aside all of the distractions and side activities to leave the story laid bare, and the game just says "generic open world game" all over. There were few moments of the game that I found truly compelling.
If you've played any of the Arkham series games, then the on-foot fighting will feel familiar to you. I found this to be somewhat enjoyable, but when fighting in tight indoor spaces, it can be irritable because you won't see any counter or dodge prompts for enemies that are off-screen. Vehicle based combat was exciting however, especially when fighting a convoy. I bashed my way through enemy vehicles' armor before snatching off their wheels with my harpoon. It was satisfying to take them out one at a time until I reached the war truck leading the convoy. A few thundersticks later and I had earned myself a new hood ornament. The driving mechanics are excellent, and whenever I lost control, it geniuinely felt like it was my fault.
Of course, it would be unfair if I didn't talk about the occasional storm, which occurred once maybe every 4-5 hours I played. Storms can shift you from a leisurely dash across the seabed into a sudden scramble for shelter. Flying debris will murder Max and his car. However, some of the debris can be collected to give you a huge boost in scrap, so it is well worth the risk to brave the winds and snatch a few crates. At one point my car was flaming and about to become a wreck, so I was forced to hug the side of a cliff to block debris from hitting me. Afterward, I drove over to where the loot crates settled and found myself suddenly 1200+ scrap richer. It's a shame that these exciting events are few and far between.
Pros:
- Excellent driving mechanics.
- Thrilling vehicle based combat. Convoys and death races are where this game thrives.
- Good voice acting. Few lines sounded repetitive.
- Great if you love open world games.
- Fits in well with the continuity of the latest film, Fury Road.
- Storms.
Cons:
- Sudden leaps in difficulty in the main story. The game expects you to stay busy with side tasks.
- Camps can be frustrating to navigate. The minimap doesn't zoom in when indoors or out of your car.
- Threat reduction tasks quickly start to feel repetitive, and there isn't enough variety to relieve that.
- Short story with lots of padding. Characters are shallow with little development.
- If you don't like open world games and don't have a burning love for the Mad Max franchise, then this isn't for you.
This game has its moments, but overall, I felt I was just doing busy work for the most part of the game. The open world genre itself isn't enough for me and games need to be filled with more vibrant characters and story. There are many better open world games on Steam right now. Pick this game up when it goes on sale, but not for full price. This sums the game up pretty well:

Prision Architect has a tough task being both a Prision Simulation game and a Fun tycoon game.  It finds most of it's success on the construction aspect of the game.  Designating different rooms, prioritizing security vs expansion, and giving challenges at a pace that is focused yet enjoyable is a strong positive to what this game can offer.
On the other side, the prison managment, there is still very little to accomplish.   During my playtime with PA, they have added the abiltiy to have prisions finish their sentence and leave, I've had prisioners start riots and fires, I've had tunnels that lead to escapes.  Yet, once I'm done building (usually around 200 criminals) I find it hard to not start over.
Typically i stick with a design that has been working for me over the last few alpha builds, so It is a routine.  I get invested and find small ways to improve my design.  Then I get back to 200 and get bored.
In the future, I'm hoping for more interactions with the prisoners, or some end result of what life in my institution has done.  I'm hoping for more end game content.  I get that it's called Prison Architect, but what's left after I'm done building, what is my incentive to build a prison thats more cost effective, or has less riots, or can be run with fewer staff when in the end I'll just give up on it anyway?

Second prison, I was learning - the third prison, I truly feel like I am thinking like an architect, thinking of ways to stop my prisoners from escaping and keeping traffic flows at a reasonable pace.
This is the sort of game that can turn from a peaceful getaway, into absolute chaos within minutes. For example, I went to get a cup of tea and left the game running. Came back to find my Power Station had gone up in flames, thus causing my water supply to dry out. This really did hack my inmates off, as I was literally performing a shakedown (search of all prisoners and possible hiding spots) and had everyone banged up whilst I performed some outer-wall maintenance. The end of it? A riot started - and my prisoners stole the keys off of my guards and tried to make a quick getaway. However, I was quick on the ball and had some Riot Police ready to sort out that little disaster.
There is so much you can do within this game, and you can get lost for hours without even realizing. If you think you're going to like this game, I can assure you, you're going to love it.

To be honest, as a review of only one episode, they did a pretty decent job. Of course I still like the first game better but I do like playing as Chloe for a change. The story started slow, as a introduction to Chloe's life and not a real plotline yet, but it slowly got a bit better and more emotional. It did have a few awkward scenes in there that they could have done better. They already got a lot of discussion about how their faces didnt show that much emotion and i still notice in the awkward moments.
Its hard getting used to a new voice actress, especially after the great performances of Ashely Burch, but the new voiceactress is likeable and good to get used to. Some minor characters like Dana and Victoria got new VA's too, but i didnt really pay mind to them.
The new playing style is pretty cool too. You have to win arguments against other people to get things your way, otherwise you get the consequences. Some of the dialogue options are very obvious if you want to win, but either way still very fun. Also great improvement on the graphics and the smoothness of the game.
Overall, still giving me a big nostalgic vibe to the first game and it does keep me hungering for the next episode. I do recommend getting this game if you played the first one and absolutely fell in love with it. Its nice to see things from Chloe's perspective for a change.
Also, Hella high graphics.

EP 1 REVIEW!
So, I loved the first life is strange. Im a lonely person (typical audiance for this series) and it helped me cope with some stuff.
But at the same time I was very worried going into this game, knowing they were styling the game the same but without the rewind, and a totally new studio.
I've been pleasently suprised! This game is damn good. The mingames, collectable graffiti, and the way Rachel is portrayed all fit together great. The minigames was a pleasent suprise in particular, but it opened up another side of Chloe that is long gone in LiS because of Rachels dissappearence.
I recommend this for anyone who loved the first game, and for anyone looking to get into the series, it could be a starting point, though I would say play the first game.
Pros
-Chloe's different personality, and how she develops from this into LiS
-Chloe and Rachels relationship develops very... naturally. Chloe is that weird outcast and Rachel is that popular girl, and they act like it, edge and cringe included.
-Nice and long first episode, I put a good 4 hours into it. (Nearly)
Cons
-Made me really sad D:
It was worth the preorder and it's worth a buy now.
